items.info: [{"name": "Quick Facts", "text": "The basal lamina is the layer of the basement membrane lying next to the basal surface of the adjoining cell layer; composed of an electron-dense lamina densa and an electron-lucent lamina lucida; sometimes used to denote the lamina densa alone (Dorland, 2011)."}, {"name": "Structure and/or Key Features", "text": "The external lamina (or basal lamina) is made up of several different proteins and carbohydrates, such as collagen, proteoglycans, and glycoproteins. It forms a matrix which surrounds the muscle fiber and plays a central role in its structure and function.\n\nThe term \u201cexternal lamina\u201d replaces \u201cbasal lamina\u201d in nonepithelial cells such as muscle cells, adipocytes, and supporting cells in the peripheral nervous system."}, {"name": "Anatomical Relations", "text": "The external lamina surrounds the muscle fiber and is directly linked to the sarcolemma."}, {"name": "Function", "text": "The external lamina has several important roles in the structure and function of the muscle fiber such as mechanical support to underlying structures. It also acts as a scaffold for many important cells which act on the muscle fiber. The basal lamina matrix is a component of important molecular signaling, i.e., it contains an enzyme, acetylcholinesterase, which breaks down acetylcholine during neuromuscular transmissions. Its role seems to be important in a many functions from development to myogenesis and synaptogenesis."}, {"name": "References", "text": "Dorland, W. (2011) Dorland's Illustrated Medical Dictionary. 32nd edn. Philadelphia, USA: Elsevier Saunders."}]

items.info:
[
  {
    "name" : "Legend",
    "text" : "The urethra has two major divisions: The anterior and posterior urethra, each of which has two parts. The posterior urethra is composed of the prostatic and membranous portions, and the anterior urethra is composed of the bulbous and penile portions. The prostatic urethra begins at the bladder base and extends to the apex of the prostatic gland. The membranous urethra traverses the urogenital diaphragm. It is the shortest portion of the urethra but the area most vulnerable to injury. The bulbous urethra extends from the bottom of the urogenital diaphragm to the suspensory ligament of the penis. The penile urethra is distal to the suspensory ligament and travels through the pendulous portion of the penis. It widens into the fossa navicularis at the distal glans.​
​
The seminal colliculus (verumontanum) is a smooth filling defect along the posterior wall of the prostatic urethra. The seminal colliculus is the location of the opening of the prostatic utricle, and on either side of it, the orifices of the ejaculatory ducts. ​
​
The paired bulbourethral (Cowper) glands lie within the urogenital diaphragm, but their ducts extend approximately 2 cm to enter the bulbous urethra."
  },
  {
    "name" : "Imaging Technique",
    "text" : "A radiograph, or X-ray, is a 2Dimensional image produced by passing high-energy ionizing radiation (X-rays) through the body. As the radiation passes through the body, different tissue types absorb different amounts of radiation. The remaining unabsorbed radiation hits a detector behind the body, thus generating an image. ​​
 ​​
Conventional radiographs are limited to five basic densities. These include (from least to most dense):​​
- air, which appears blackest;​​
- fat, which is a lighter shade of grey than air;​​
- soft tissue or fluid;​​
- calcium (within bone);​​
- metal (present in prosthetic implants), which appears the whitest.​​
 ​​
Bone tends to absorb more radiation than soft tissue or fat, thus bones produce a higher contrast on an x-ray detector and appear white. X-rays travelling though less dense tissues, like fat, or air-filled cavities passes more easily and display different shades of grey on a radiograph.​​
 ​​
Radiographs are a useful tool in recognizing fractures, calcifications, arthritis, osteoporosis, pneumonia, atelectasis, pneumothorax, foreign objects, dental problems, and many more."
  },
  {
    "name" : "Copyright",
    "text" : "Images courtesy Woodward, P. J., Shaaban, A. M. STATdx. Elsevier. Copyright 2025. Images reused with permission.​"
  }

Prostate (Superior; Right)
items.info:
[{"name": "Quick Facts", "text": "Location: Directly inferior to the bladder. 

Arterial Supply: Inferior vesical, internal pudendal, and middle anorectal arteries. 

Venous Drainage: Prostatic venous plexus.

Innervation: Somatic visceral afferent: pudendal nerve; Autonomic: Inferior hypogastric and prostatic plexuses. 

Lymphatic Drainage: External and internal iliac lymph nodes.
"}, {"name": "Structure/Morphology", "text": "The prostate is a walnut-sized, globular fibromuscular gland. It is fixed superiorly to the base of the urinary bladder and sits superior to the pelvic floor.

The prostate is traditionally divided into ill-defined lobes.
—The isthmus of the prostate lies anterior to the urethra and contains little to no glandular tissue.
—The right and left lobes are separated anteriorly by the isthmus. 

Each lobe can be further subdivided into four distinct lobules:
—Inferoposterior lobule lies posterior to the urethra and inferior to the ejaculatory ducts. Readily palpable during a digital rectal examination.
—Inferolateral lobule lies lateral to the urethra, forming the bulk of each lobe.
—Superomedial lobule lies deep to the inferoposterior lobule and directly surround the ejaculatory duct on each side.
—Anteromedial lobule deep to the inferolateral lobular and directly lateral to the urethra.

In addition to the lobe classifications, the prostate can be divided into four different zones: 
—the central zone surrounding the ejaculatory ducts;
—the transitional zone surrounding the proximal urethra;
—the peripheral zone surrounding the distal urethra;
—the stromal zone (also known as the anterior fibromuscular zone) that is comprised of muscles and connective tissue.

The superior aspect of the prostate is termed the base and the inferior aspect is termed the apex. There are two posterolateral surfaces, and an anterior and posterior surface of the prostate.

The prostatic urethra passes directly through the substance of the prostate on its way to the penis. 
"}, {"name": "Anatomical Relations", "text": "The superior aspect of the prostate is termed the base and is continuous with the neck of the bladder. The inferior aspect is termed the apex and marks the junction of the membranous and prostatic urethra. The anterior surface of the prostate lies directly posterior to the pubic arch. It is connected to the pubic bone by the puboprostatic ligament. The inferolateral surfaces of the prostate are related to the anterior muscle fibers of levator ani. They surround the prostate in a sling termed the pubourethral sling or pubourethalis. The posterior surface of the bladder lies anterior to the rectum and the rectourethralis muscle. The superior surface of the prostate is penetrated by two ejaculatory ducts.

The prostate is surrounded by an anatomically variable prostatic capsule which is formed from the surrounding fascia. The prostatic plexus of veins and nerves reside within the capsule. 
"}, {"name": "Function", "text": "The prostate provides passage for urine and sperm to pass out of the body. During ejaculation the prostate secretes a slightly alkaline fluid into the prostatic urethra. Fluid from the prostate, together with seminal fluid from the seminal gland, and sperm from the ductus deferens combine to form semen. "}, {"name": "Arterial Supply", "text": "The prostate revives blood from various sources. Prostatic branches from the inferior vesical artery communicate across the midline of the prostate. The inferior gluteal, internal pudendal, and middle anorectal arteries supply branches to the prostate. "}, {"name": "Venous Drainage", "text": "The prostatic venous plexus surrounds the anterolateral aspect of the prostate. It receives tributaries from the deep dorsal vein of the penis and the vesical venous plexus to drain into the internal iliac veins. "}, {"name": "Innervation", "text": "The prostate receives both autonomic and somatic visceral innervation. The inferior hypogastric plexus supplies the prostate. Nerves traveling to the prostate form a periprostatic nerve plexus within the prostatic capsule. The prostatic plexus supplies the smooth muscle of the prostate and prostatic urethra. The skeletal muscle is supplied by the pudendal nerve. This skeletal muscle contracts and dilates the prostatic urethra."}, {"name": "Lymphatic Drainage", "text": "The lymph of the prostate is drained by the medial group of external iliac nodes, in which the efferent nodes pass to the internal iliac nodes."}, {"name": "List of Clinical Correlates", "text": "—Prostate cancer
—Benign prostatic hyperplasia
"}]

Testis (Lateral Part; Left)
items.info:
[{"name": "Quick Facts", "text": "Location: Within the scrotum.

Arterial Supply: Testicular artery.

Venous Drainage: Pampiniform plexus.

Innervation: Autonomic: Testicular plexus.

Lymphatic Drainage: Lumbar lymph nodes."}, {"name": "Structure/Morphology", "text": "The testes are primary sex organs that play a crucial role in both the male reproductive and endocrine systems. The testes are paired ovoid structures that are in the scrotum. They are composed of up to 900 coiled seminiferous tubules, each averaging more than half a meter long, in which the sperm is produced (Standring, 2016). The testes are enclosed in a tough capsule composed of three tunicae (layers): the tunica vasculosa, albuginea, and vaginalis. "}, {"name": "Anatomical Relations", "text": "The left testis normally lies at a lower level than the right testis within the scrotum. The testes are suspended by the spermatic cord, through which structures entering or exiting the testes travel. The upper pole of the testis is tilted anterolaterally and is attached to the head of the epididymis, whereas the lower pole is tilted anteromedially."}, {"name": "Function", "text": "The placement of the testis in the scrotum and the countercurrent exchange mechanism of the pampiniform plexus ensures that the temperature of the testis is 3–4 °C lower than normal body temperature. This temperature is optimum for sperm production. The two testes produce up to 120 million sperm in the human adult each day (Standring, 2016). Sperm can be stored in the testis and remain fertile for up to a month. During this time, they are kept in an inactive state by multiple inhibitory substances. The testes are also heavily involved in the endocrine system. Leydig cells produce hormones that promote the development of the male reproductive system and secondary male characteristics."}, {"name": "Arterial Supply", "text": "The testes are supplied by the testicular artery, which arises from the abdominal aorta. It travels inferiorly to the pelvis as a retroperitoneal structure. The testicular artery then travels through the inguinal canal by passing through the deep and superficial inguinal rings. Branches enter the mediastinum of the testis and ramify in the tunica vasculosa."}, {"name": "Venous Drainage", "text": "The testes are drained by the pampiniform plexus, a network of vessels that surround the spermatic cord. The pampiniform plexus drains into the left and right testicular veins. The left testicular vein drains into the left renal vein, whereas the right testicular vein drains directly into the inferior vena cava."}, {"name": "Innervation", "text": "The testes are innervated by the testicular plexus. The nerve fibers arise from the tenth and eleventh thoracic spinal segments. They travel to the aortic and renal plexuses and follow the testicular arteries to reach the testis in the pelvis."}, {"name": "Lymphatic Drainage", "text": "Lymphatic drainage of the testis drains into the para-aortic and inter-aortocaval lymph nodes (lumbar nodes)."}, {"name": "List of Clinical Correlates", "text": "—Testicular cancer

—Variocele"}, {"name": "References", "text": "Standring, S. (2016) Gray's Anatomy: The Anatomical Basis of Clinical Practice. Gray's Anatomy Series 41 edn.: Elsevier Limited."}]

[{"name": "Description", "text": "There are normally 31 pairs of spinal nerves: eight cervical, twelve thoracic, five lumbar, five sacral, and one coccygeal. 

Spinal nerves are connected to the spinal cord via two roots. The posterior (dorsal) root contains sensory fibers, in which their cell bodies are located in spinal ganglia. The anterior (ventral) root contains motor fibers and, unlike the posterior roots, their cell bodies are located in anterior regions of the spinal cord. The roots of the spinal nerves split into multiple, smaller rootlets before entering the spinal cord.
"}]

items.name: Axial contrast enhanced CT through the superior abdomen and pelvis, from superior to inferior (4 of 15)
items.info:
[
  {
    "name" : "Legend",
    "text" : "This is the fourth of fifteen arterial phase CT images through the abdomen and pelvis delineating normal arterial anatomy. ​
​
This image demonstrates the gastroduodenal artery extending inferiorly along the anterior aspect of the pancreatic head. Also note the paired lumbar arteries arising along the posterior aspect of the aorta, which are seen from the first to fourth lumbar vertebrae (L1-L4) levels.​
​
The origin of the right inferior phrenic artery can be seen arising from the aorta. It may arise from the celiac truck or the renal artery."
  },
  {
    "name" : "Imaging Technique",
    "text" : "Computed tomography scans (CT or CAT scans) are produced by passing high-energy ionizing radiation (X-rays) through the body. As the radiation passes through the body, different tissue types absorb different amounts of radiation. The remaining unabsorbed radiation hits a detector behind the body, thus generating an image. ​
 ​
While using a similar technique to conventional radiographs in 2D, CTs use mathematical algorithms to scan the body in 3D planes, thus producing a series of consecutive images of an entire field of interest. A CT image is composed of thousands of pixels which is assigned a CT number, or Hounsfield units, from -1000 to +1000. Less dense substances, like air and fat, absorb fewer X-rays, have low CT numbers, and demonstrate decreased attenuation. These tissues appear blacker on the CT images. Denser substances absorb more X-rays, have higher CT numbers, and demonstrate increased attenuation. These tissues display whiter on CT scans. Some examples of CT numbers include:​
- air, which is assigned -1000;​
- fat, which is assigned -40 to -100;​
- water, which is 0;​
- soft tissue, which is 20-100;​
- bone, which 400 to 600.​
 ​
CT scan cans also be used in conjunction with contrast. Intravenous radiofluorescent contrast may be injected into the bloodstream. Contrast can aid in diagnostics in the cardiovascular system (aneurysms, atherosclerosis, etc.) or in identifying if tumors are malignant. Oral contrast may also be administered to investigate digestive issues (Crohn’s disease, diverticulitis, etc.).​
 ​
CT images are commonly taken in a transverse, or axial, orientation, but may also be imaged in coronal or sagittal orientations. When interpreting an axial CT, it is important to orientate the image. The easiest way to do this is to imagine you are standing at the patient’s toes looking up at the body.     "name" : "Imaging Technique",
    "text" : "Computed tomography scans (CT or CAT scans) are produced by passing high-energy ionizing radiation (X-rays) through the body. As the radiation passes through the body, different tissue types absorb different amounts of radiation. The remaining unabsorbed radiation hits a detector behind the body, thus generating an image. ​
 ​
While using a similar technique to conventional radiographs in 2D, CTs use mathematical algorithms to scan the body in 3D planes, thus producing a series of consecutive images of an entire field of interest. A CT image is composed of thousands of pixels which is assigned a CT number, or Hounsfield units, from -1000 to +1000. Less dense substances, like air and fat, absorb fewer X-rays, have low CT numbers, and demonstrate decreased attenuation. These tissues appear blacker on the CT images. Denser substances absorb more X-rays, have higher CT numbers, and demonstrate increased attenuation. These tissues display whiter on CT scans. Some examples of CT numbers include:​
- air, which is assigned -1000;​
- fat, which is assigned -40 to -100;​
- water, which is 0;​
- soft tissue, which is 20-100;​
- bone, which 400 to 600.​

[{"name": "Quick Facts", "text": "A blood vessel includes any of the vessels conveying the blood; an artery, arteriole, capillary, venule, or vein (Dorland, 2011)."}, {"name": "Description", "text": "Arteries supplying blood to the lymph node enter the node at the hilum, while the veins that drain it exit the lymph node here and are accompanied by an efferent lymphatic vessel. 

As the artery enters the medullary region of the node, it divides to supply medullary arterioles which are conveyed in the medullary cords. Each lobule of the lymph node receives an arteriole, however, for descriptive purposes this is not shown in the 3D model. The arterioles continue to branch in the paracortex, or deep cortex, giving rise to capillary beds in the cortex.

Blood from the capillary beds of the cortex drain into the medullary venules within the medullary cords. These venules unify with other venules from other lobules of the lymph node, forming a vein which exists the lymph node at the hilum, along with the efferent lymph vessel and accompanying artery."}, {"name": "References", "text": "Dorland, W. (2011) Dorland's Illustrated Medical Dictionary. 32nd edn. Philadelphia, USA: Elsevier Saunders."}]

items.info:
[{"name": "Quick Facts", "text": "The perineurium is an intermediate layer of connective tissue in a peripheral nerve, surrounding each bundle (fasciculus) of nerve fibers (Dorland, 2011)."}, {"name": "Structure/Morphology", "text": "The perineurium and the extensions of this tissue into the nerve fascicles, known as the perineurial septae, are collectively known as perineurial tissue. 

The perineurium is a continuous connective tissue layer that surrounds each fascicle within the nerve trunk. Perineurial septae extend into the secondary fascicle, subdividing it into several bundles of fibers, or primary fascicles (Carp, 2015).

This tissue is composed of layers of large, flat perineurial cells that are arranged concentrically. The number of layers of the perineurium varies, depending on the location within the nerve. For example, the sciatic nerve may contain 15 layers; however, at the most distal part of the nerve, there may only be one or two layers (Peltonen et al., 2013). Each layer has a prominent basal lamina, up to 500 nm thick, and provides an additional barrier to the nerve fascicle (Standring, 2016).

Perineurial tissue contains a thick extracellular matrix of collagen and fibronectin, which is capable of modulating external stretch forces."}, {"name": "Key Features/Anatomical Relations", "text": "Within the perineurium, primary fascicles are bundled together to form secondary fascicles. At the nerve’s proximal end, the perineurium is continuous with the leptomeningeal coverings (arachnoid and pia) of the spinal cord (Standring, 2016). 

The intrafascicular vessels are located within the perineurial septa (Bilbao and Schmidt, 2014)."}, {"name": "Function", "text": "The perineurium is a metabolically active diffusion barrier. Along with the endoneurium, the perineurium forms a blood—nerve barrier, which plays a role in maintaining osmotic balance and fluid pressure within the endoneurium. It also isolates nerve fibers within the fascicles from pathogens and extraperineual fluids (Standring, 2016). The perineurium also has a role in protection of the nerve fibers contained within. The collagen fiber matrix of the perineurium prevents the fascicle from becoming compressed, or ‘kinked’, during movements, such as flexion of a joint. The perineurium is suspected to play a role in nerve fiber regeneration in the peripheral nervous system. 

The perineurial septa divides the secondary fascicles into the smaller, primary fascicles."}, {"name": "References", "text": "Bilbao, J. M. and Schmidt, R. E. (2014) Biopsy Diagnosis of Peripheral Neuropathy. Springer International Publishing.

Carp, S. (2015) Peripheral Nerve Injury An Anatomical and Physiological Approach for Physical Therapy Intervention. EBL-Schweitzer: F. A. Davis Company.

Dorland, W. (2011) Dorland's Illustrated Medical Dictionary. 32nd edn. Philadelphia, USA: Elsevier Saunders.

Peltonen, S., Alanne, M. and Peltonen, J. (2013) 'Barriers of the peripheral nerve', Tissue Barriers, 1(3), pp. e24956.

Standring, S. (2016) Gray's Anatomy: The Anatomical Basis of Clinical Practice. Gray's Anatomy Series: Elsevier Limited."}]

It is a continuation of the processus vaginalis, which is formed prior to the descent of the fetal testes. When the testes descend from the abdomen to the pelvis, the tunica vaginalis forms two layers: 

—the visceral layer that surrounds the tunica albuginea (except for the posterior portion of the testis);

—the parietal layer that surrounds and extends proximally over a portion of the spermatic cord."}, {"name": "Key Features/ Anatomical Relations", "text": "The tunica vaginalis testis is superficial to the tunica albuginea. There is a cavity containing a small volume of fluid between the visceral and parietal layers of the tunica vaginalis testis."}, {"name": "Function", "text": "The tunica vaginalis testis produces a small volume of fluid to provide lubrication to reduce friction of testes within the scrotum."}, {"name": "List of Clinical Correlates", "text": "— Hydrocele

[
  {
    "name" : "Legend",
    "text" : "This is the fifth of nine axial MRIs through the right ankle, presented from proximal to distal. ​
​
Inferior transverse ligament, also known as intermalleolar ligament, extends from the posterior surface of the medial malleolus to tip of the fibula and courses posterior to the talar body.​
​
The extensor retinaculum has three bands: ​
Lateral, ​
middle, ​
and medial. ​
​
They traverse the tarsal sinus and insert on the dorsal surface of the calcaneus, posterior to the cervical ligament."
  },
  {
    "name" : "Imaging Technique",
    "text" : "Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) is a high-resolution cross-sectional imaging technique. It utilizes hydrogen protons, which are abundantly present in water and water makes up approximately 63% of the average male, and 52% in the average female (Lote, 2012). Hydrogen protons are normally randomly aligned, however, when placed in a magnetic field, the protons align along the same axis as the magnetic field. ​
 ​
A radiofrequency pulse is applied and causes disruption to the magnetization and pushes the protons out of alignment, causing them to spin. This produces two magnetization vectors, longitudinal magnetization (in the direction of the magnetic field) and transverse magnetization (perpendicular to the magnetic field). When the radiofrequency pulse is removed, the magnetization vectors realign with the magnetic field. As a result, longitudinal magnetization starts to increase, known as T1 relaxation or recovery, and transverse magnetization starts to decrease, known as T2 relaxation or decay. Energy is released from the spinning protons as radiofrequency signals (known as the echo). The radiofrequency pulses are repeated and detected to produce an image. ​
 ​
Radiographers can vary the sequence of pulses to create different types of images. The repetition time (TR) between two radiofrequency pulses influences T1 and T2 weighting, meaning that a shorter amount of repetition time between two pulses will generate a T1-weighted image, while pulses with a long echo time (TE) produces T2-weighted images. ​
 ​
Different tissues in the body have different T1 and T2 values, these tissues will appear, not only different from each other, but also different on T1 and T2 MRIs. The bright, or whiter, image implies an increased signal intensity, while darker, or blacker, images have decreased signal intensity. Water or cerebrospinal fluid will appear dark on T1 weighted images and bright on T2-weighted images. ​
 ​
MRI’s are useful to detect cerebral infarction, abnormalities in the brain and spine, diagnosis of knee injuries, and has eliminated the need for myelography. When used in areas such as the abdomen/pelvis and breast it has shown to have high sensitivity in detecting cancer. ​
 ​
Proton-density MRI is another MRI technique, where there is longer TR between two radiofrequency pulses and shorter TE. This technique is useful for detecting joint disease and injury."
  },
  {
    "name" : "Copyright",
    "text" : "Images courtesy Crim, J. R., Rosenberg, Z. S. STATdx. Elsevier. Copyright 2025. Images reused with permission."
  },
  {
    "name" : "References",
    "text" : "Lote, C. J. (2012) Principles of Renal Physiology. Springer Netherlands.​"
  }
]

[
  {
    "name" : "Legend",
    "text" : "This is the fifth of six axial MRIs through the right foot, presented from plantar to dorsal. ​
​
There are four dorsal interosseous muscles, each with two heads ("bipennate") arising from the bases of the adjacent metatarsals. The first dorsal interosseous inserts on the medial aspect of the second proximal phalanx base, and the second to fourth on to the lateral aspect of the base of the second to fourth  metatarsals.​
​
The second to fifth metatarsal bases are joined by dorsal, interosseous, and plantar intermetatarsal ligaments. Stability between the first and second rays is achieved by the three ligaments from the medial (first) cuneiform to the base of the second metatarsal:​
dorsal
interosseous
plantar.
​
The interosseous ligament passing from the medial cuneiform to the second metatarsal ligament is the broadest and strongest and is a true Lisfranc ligament; however, "plantar" and "dorsal Lisfranc ligament" are terms that are commonly and appropriately used."
  },
  {
    "name" : "Imaging Technique",
    "text" : "Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) is a high-resolution cross-sectional imaging technique. It utilizes hydrogen protons, which are abundantly present in water and water makes up approximately 63% of the average male, and 52% in the average female (Lote, 2012). Hydrogen protons are normally randomly aligned, however, when placed in a magnetic field, the protons align along the same axis as the magnetic field. ​
 ​
A radiofrequency pulse is applied and causes disruption to the magnetization and pushes the protons out of alignment, causing them to spin. This produces two magnetization vectors, longitudinal magnetization (in the direction of the magnetic field) and transverse magnetization (perpendicular to the magnetic field). When the radiofrequency pulse is removed, the magnetization vectors realign with the magnetic field. As a result, longitudinal magnetization starts to increase, known as T1 relaxation or recovery, and transverse magnetization starts to decrease, known as T2 relaxation or decay. Energy is released from the spinning protons as radiofrequency signals (known as the echo). The radiofrequency pulses are repeated and detected to produce an image. ​
 ​
Radiographers can vary the sequence of pulses to create different types of images. The repetition time (TR) between two radiofrequency pulses influences T1 and T2 weighting, meaning that a shorter amount of repetition time between two pulses will generate a T1-weighted image, while pulses with a long echo time (TE) produces T2-weighted images. ​
 ​
Different tissues in the body have different T1 and T2 values, these tissues will appear, not only different from each other, but also different on T1 and T2 MRIs. The bright, or whiter, image implies an increased signal intensity, while darker, or blacker, images have decreased signal intensity. Water or cerebrospinal fluid will appear dark on T1 weighted images and bright on T2-weighted images. ​
 ​
MRI’s are useful to detect cerebral infarction, abnormalities in the brain and spine, diagnosis of knee injuries, and has eliminated the need for myelography. When used in areas such as the abdomen/pelvis and breast it has shown to have high sensitivity in detecting cancer. ​
 ​
Proton-density MRI is another MRI technique, where there is longer TR between two radiofrequency pulses and shorter TE. This technique is useful for detecting joint disease and injury."
  },
  {

  },
  {
    "name" : "References",
    "text" : "Lote, C. J. (2012) Principles of Renal Physiology. Springer Netherlands."
  }
]

[
  {
    "name" : "Quick Facts",
    "text" : "The Oropharynx is the middle portion of the pharynx. 

The Pharynx is the musculomembranous part of the alimentary system which extends from the cranial base to the lower margin of the cricoid cartilage; it lies behind the nasal and oral cavities, and extends beyond the larynx. Other parts of the pharynx include the Nasopharynx and the Laryngopharynx which is continuous with the oesophagus.

The oropharynx extends from below the soft plate to the superior margin of the epiglottis. It plays an important role in the first, voluntary phase of swallowing. 

Anatomical Relations:
It emerges from the oropharyngeal isthmus, and is bounded by the soft palate superiorly, and the palatine tonsil, palatoglossal and palatopharyngeal arches laterally. The base of the tongue lies in the oropharynx inferiorly, behind the terminal sulcus and the palatoglossal arches.

Arterial Supply:
The ascending palatine branch of the facial artery. 

Nerve Supply: 
Lesser palatine nerve (a branch of the maxillary nerve) 
Pharyngeal branches of glossopharyngeal nerve 
Greater petrosal nerve (a branch of the facial nerve) 
Lesser petrosal branch of the glossopharyngeal nerve
Carotid Plexus"

items.info:
[{"name": "Quick Facts", "text": "Bone Type: Flat Bone

Articulates with: Clavicle, Costal Cartilages"}, {"name": "Key Features & Anatomical Relationships", "text": "The sternum is located in the midline of the anterior thoracic cage. It runs inferiorly and slightly anterior along the vertical length of the thoracic cage. The anterior surface is convex, while the posterior surface is concave. 

The sternum is composed of three main elements, the manubrium of sternum, body of sternum, and xiphoid process. 

The manubrium of sternum is the most superior part of the bone. It is wedged-shaped and is the widest element of the sternum. It articulates with both clavicles, forming sternoclavicular joints, as well as with the costal cartilages of first and second ribs (or part thereof), forming sternocostal joints. The manubrium of sternum articulates with the body of sternum at the manubriosternal joint. 

The body of sternum is the long rectangular part of the bone. It is thinner than the manubrium of sternum and bears narrowed superior and inferior ends. It articulates with the costal cartilages of the second to seventh ribs, forming sternocostal joints. The body of sternum is attached inferiorly to the xiphoid process at the xiphisternal joint. Up until puberty, the body of sternum is composed of four induvial elements, known as sternebrae. 

The xiphoid process is the most inferior part of the sternum."}, {"name": "Ossification", "text": "Ossification of the sternum commences in the fifth month, in utero, with the appearance of a primary ossification center for the manubrium of sternum. This is quickly followed by another center for the first sternebra, with two more for the second and third sternebrae appearing the seventh and eighth months. Therefore, the sternum usually contains four primary centers of ossification at birth. During the first year of life, a primary center of ossification appears for the fourth sternebra.

During the third to sixth years, the xiphoid process begins to undergo ossification. Fusion of the second and third sternebrae commences usually between the fourth and tenth years, which, in turn fuse with the fourth sternebra during early adolescence. Fusion of the first sternebra finally commences during late adolescence, with complete fusion of the body sternum complete between the twentieth and twenty-fifth years. Fusion of the xiphoid process with the body of sternum usually occurs after the fortieth year of life."}, {"name": "Surface Anatomy", "text": "The sternum is subcutaneous and therefore easily palpated along its anterior surface. The jugular notch may be palpated between the sternal ends of the clavicles. The sternal angle, costal margins, as well as the xiphisternal joint can also be easily located."}, {"name": "Variations", "text": "The xiphoid process may be found to variably point in the same axis as the body or sternum, or more often, anteriorly deviated. The inferior tip of the xiphoid process may variably present a pointed, blunt, bifid, or hooked appearance. Foramina may be occasionally present in both the body of sternum and, more frequently, the xiphoid process."}, {"name": "Vascular Supply", "text": "The sternum primarily receives it arterial supply via sternal branches of internal thoracic artery."}, {"name": "List of Clinical Correlates", "text": "- Fracture of sternum

- Pectus excacatum

- Pectus carinatum"}]

items.info:
[
  {
    "name" : "Quick Facts",
    "text" : "Lymph from the gastrointestinal tract and accessory organs of digestion converge at the intestinal lymph trunk, which empties lymph into the cisterna chyli.

Specifically, lymph from the small intestine is collected by lymph nodes in the mesentery called the juxtaintestinal mesenteric lymph nodes, and flows via the intermediate mesenteric lymph nodes to the superior mesenteric lymph nodes.

The superior mesenteric lymph nodes also collect lymph from the large intestine via the paracolic, epicolic, right colic, ileocolic, middle colic and prececal lymph nodes.

Also draining the large intestine are the inferior mesenteric lymph nodes that collect lymph from the descending and sigmoid parts of the colon via the left colic, superior rectal and sigmoid lymph nodes.

Lymph from the stomach, liver, pancreas, spleen and diaphragm converges on the celiac lymph nodes around the celiac artery, which joins with the lymph from the superior mesenteric lymph nodes to form the intestinal trunk, which empties lymph into the cisterna chyli. Lymph from the superior surface of the diaphragm also occasionally travels to the xiphoid lymph nodes.

From the cisterna chyli, lymph is transported up the thoracic duct, and soon after being joined by the jugular lymph trunk from the head and neck, empties into the venous system at the junction of the left internal jugular vein and the left subclavian vein."
  }
]

items.info:
[
  {
    "name" : "Quick Facts",
    "text" : "The urethra is the tube, approximately 20 cm long in males, that connects the bladder to the genitals for the expulsion of urine during urination, and semen during ejaculation, via the external urethral orifice.

The male urethra can be divided into 4 distinct segments. 
The initial segment is known as the pre-prostatic segment, and it extends approximately 1 cm from the lower portion of the bladder, before traveling through the prostate gland. 

The second segment is known as the prostatic urethra, and it is identified as the portion that travels through the prostate gland.

The third segment is known as the membranous (Intermediate) urethra, and it extends for approximately 1-2 cm anterior to the bulbourethral glands. 

The final segment of the urethra is known as the spongy urethra, and this is the longest portion (approximately 15 cm) that is located in the corpus spongiosum of the penis, extending the length of the entire penis to the glans, where the final bulbous portion is also sometimes referred to as the navicular fossa of the urethra."
  }
]

items.info:
[
  {
    "name" : "Quick Facts",
    "text" : "The proper plantar digital arteries consist of four pairs of arteries that travel in between the toes, one individual artery that lies on the medial side of the great toe, and another individual artery that lies on the lateral side of the 5th toe. 

From their origin, close to the metatarsophalangeal joints, they travel distally, all the way down to the ends of the toes. From medial to lateral, the proper plantar digital arteries are arranged as follows:

- The individual proper plantar digital artery that travels along the medial side of the great toe is the distal continuation of a branch of the 1st plantar metatarsal artery.
- The 1st pair of proper plantar digital arteries are the terminal branches of the 1st plantar metatarsal artery, and they travel along the lateral side of the great toe (1st toe) and the medial side of the 2nd toe.
- The 2nd pair of proper plantar digital arteries are the terminal branches of the 2nd plantar metatarsal artery, and they travel along the lateral side of the 2nd toe and the medial side of the 3rd toe.
- The 3rd pair of proper plantar digital arteries are the terminal branches of the 3rd plantar metatarsal artery, and they travel along the lateral side of the 3rd toe and the medial side of the 4th toe.
- The 4th pair of proper plantar digital arteries are the terminal branches of the 4th plantar metatarsal artery, and they travel along the lateral side of the 4th toe and the medial side of the 5th toe.
- The individual proper plantar digital artery that travels along the lateral side of the 5th toe is the distal continuation of superficial branch of lateral plantar artery. 

Along their course, the proper plantar digital arteries give off dorsal branches as they travel passed the proximal interphalangeal joints of the foot. These branches travel around to the dorsal side of each toe, and then distally, all the way down to the toe nails.

Overall, the proper plantar digital arteries and their branches provide an arterial supply to the plantar aspects of the entire lengths of all toes, as well as the dorsal aspects of the distal halves of the toes."
  }
]

items.info:
[
  {
    "name" : "Quick Facts",
    "text" : "The body of stomach (aka gastric body) is the largest and most central of the four parts of the stomach. 

As such it is the primary location of gastric digestion, involving the churning of food together with proteases and hydrochloric acid to partially break down proteins, kill bacteria, and adjust pH. 

It extends from the cardia of stomach, which is the junction of the stomach with the esophagus, to the pylorus, which is where the stomach empties into the small intestine. 

The body of stomach is continuous with the fundus of stomach when it passes the rostrocaudal level of the cardiac notch. 

The stomach walls are composed of four layers from inside to outside: mucosa, submucosa, muscularis externa, and serosa. These are involved in secretion, innervation, churning and constriction, and connectivity with the peritoneum respectively. Unlike the rest of the gastrointestinal tract, the stomach is made up of three layers of muscle, instead of two, which are unevenly distributed between the different regions of the stomach. 

These three layers of smooth muscle include the inner oblique layer, the middle circular layer, and the outer longitudinal layer."
  }
]

Duodenum
items.info:
[
  {
    "name" : "Quick Facts",
    "text" : "The duodenum is the first portion of the small intestine that is separated from the stomach by the pyloric sphincter. It is the shortest of the three components that make up the small intestine and is continuous with the proceeding jejunal portion of the small intestine. 

Anatomically, the duodenum is divided into four sections; the first part continues from the gastric pylorus for approximately 5 cm after which it curves into the second part, the superior duodenal flexure.

The second part of the duodenum extends inferiorly from the superior duodenal flexure, and is joined by the common bile duct and the pancreatic duct. Together, they are known as the hepatopancreatic duct, which contributes digestive juices from the pancreas and the gallbladder to aid the breakdown of food. 

The third part of the duodenum extends from the inferior duodenal flexure, passing to the left before ascending as the fourth part of the duodenum which itself terminates at the duodenojejunal flexure. 

Unlike the ileum and the jejunum, the duodenum is responsible primarily for the digestion of food, rather than the absorption of essential nutrients from food. 

Like the other components of the small intestine, the duodenum transports its contents through the coordinated peristaltic contraction of its embedded smooth muscle layers. The venous capillaries surrounding the duodenum drain nutrient rich blood from the duodenum directly into the hepatic portal system for cleansing and purification by the liver before systemic circulation."
  }
]

    "text" : "Location: Surround the internal iliac artery and vein.

Drainage: Pelvic viscera (except the testes/ovaries), perineum, gluteal region.

Direction of Flow: Common iliac lymph nodes > Lateral aortic lymph nodes (left) and lateral caval lymph nodes (right) > left and right lumbar lymph trunk > cisterna chyli > thoracic duct."

  {
    "name" : "Description:
Description: (Location & Drainage)
",
    "text" : "The internal iliac lymph nodes are situated along the internal iliac artery. The nodes may be classified into parietal or visceral groups, depending upon the arterial branch they accompany.

The parietal groups include the superior and inferior gluteal lymph nodes and sacral lymph nodes.

The visceral group of nodes lie in close proximity with the visceral branches of the internal iliac artery. The visceral group includes the paravesical, parauterine, paravaginal and pararectal lymph nodes.

Collectively, the internal iliac nodes receive lymph from the viscera of the pelvis, excluding the testes/ovaries. In addition, these nodes drain the perineum and the gluteal region.

The internal iliac lymph nodes send efferent vessels to the common iliac lymph nodes, where drain to the lateral aortic (left side) and caval lymph nodes (right side), the lumbar trunks, and the cisterna chyli.
"

[{"name": "Quick Facts", "text": "Location: At the base of the prostate, between the bladder and rectum.

Arterial Supply: Artery to ductus deferens and inferior vesical artery.

Venous Drainage: Inferior vesical plexus.

Innervation: Sympathetic: Inferior hypogastric nerve; Parasympathetic: Pelvic and inferior hypogastric nerves.

Lymphatic Drainage: Internal iliac lymph nodes."}, {"name": "Structure/Morphology", "text": "The seminal gland is an out pouching of the terminal ductus deferens. It is a coiled tube measuring approximately 3–5 cm in adults, with a volume capacity of approximately 13 ml (Standring, 2016). The right seminal vesical is often larger than the left. However, they both decrease in size with age. 

The seminal gland consists of a highly convoluted duct, which is surrounded by a capsule of connective tissue."}, {"name": "Anatomical Relations", "text": "The seminal glands are posterior to the urinary bladder and prostate, and lateral to the ampulla of the ductus deferens. 

The inferior hypogastric plexus lies posterolaterally on either side on the seminal glands."}, {"name": "Function", "text": "The seminal glands secrete a thick alkaline seminal fluid with fructose, via the ejaculatory duct, into the prostatic urethra. This seminal fluid mixes with sperm from the ductus deferens, to form semen, which is expelled during ejaculation."}, {"name": "Arterial Supply", "text": "The seminal glands are supplied by branches from the Inferior vesical and middle rectal arteries."}, {"name": "Venous Drainage", "text": "The seminal glands are drained by the vesical venous plexus into the internal iliac vein."}, {"name": "Innervation", "text": "The pelvic and inferior hypogastric nerves supply sympathetic and parasympathetic innervation to the seminal gland. Parasympathetic supply is also supplied by the pelvic nerve."}, {"name": "Lymphatic Drainage", "text": "The lymph of the seminal glands is drained into the internal iliac lymph nodes."}, {"name": "References:", "text": "Standring, S. (2016) Gray's Anatomy: The Anatomical Basis of Clinical Practice. Gray's Anatomy Series 41 edn.: Elsevier Limited."}]

items.info:
[{"name": "Quick Facts", "text": "Location: Directly inferior to the bladder. 

Arterial Supply: Inferior vesical, internal pudendal, and middle anorectal arteries. 

Venous Drainage: Prostatic venous plexus.

Innervation: Somatic visceral afferent: pudendal nerve; Autonomic: Inferior hypogastric and prostatic plexuses. 

Lymphatic Drainage: External and internal iliac lymph nodes.
"}, {"name": "Structure/Morphology", "text": "The prostate is a walnut-sized, globular fibromuscular gland. It is fixed superiorly to the base of the urinary bladder and sits superior to the pelvic floor.

The prostate is traditionally divided into ill-defined lobes.
—The isthmus of the prostate lies anterior to the urethra and contains little to no glandular tissue.
—The right and left lobes are separated anteriorly by the isthmus. 

Each lobe can be further subdivided into four distinct lobules:
—Inferoposterior lobule lies posterior to the urethra and inferior to the ejaculatory ducts. Readily palpable during a digital rectal examination.
—Inferolateral lobule lies lateral to the urethra, forming the bulk of each lobe.
—Superomedial lobule lies deep to the inferoposterior lobule and directly surround the ejaculatory duct on each side.
—Anteromedial lobule deep to the inferolateral lobular and directly lateral to the urethra.

In addition to the lobe classifications, the prostate can be divided into four different zones: 
—the central zone surrounding the ejaculatory ducts;
—the transitional zone surrounding the proximal urethra;
—the peripheral zone surrounding the distal urethra;
—the stromal zone (also known as the anterior fibromuscular zone) that is comprised of muscles and connective tissue.

The superior aspect of the prostate is termed the base and the inferior aspect is termed the apex. There are two posterolateral surfaces, and an anterior and posterior surface of the prostate.

The prostatic urethra passes directly through the substance of the prostate on its way to the penis. 
"}, {"name": "Anatomical Relations", "text": "The superior aspect of the prostate is termed the base and is continuous with the neck of the bladder. The inferior aspect is termed the apex and marks the junction of the membranous and prostatic urethra. The anterior surface of the prostate lies directly posterior to the pubic arch. It is connected to the pubic bone by the puboprostatic ligament. The inferolateral surfaces of the prostate are related to the anterior muscle fibers of levator ani. They surround the prostate in a sling termed the pubourethral sling or pubourethalis. The posterior surface of the bladder lies anterior to the rectum and the rectourethralis muscle. The superior surface of the prostate is penetrated by two ejaculatory ducts.

The prostate is surrounded by an anatomically variable prostatic capsule which is formed from the surrounding fascia. The prostatic plexus of veins and nerves reside within the capsule. 
"}, {"name": "Function", "text": "The prostate provides passage for urine and sperm to pass out of the body. During ejaculation the prostate secretes a slightly alkaline fluid into the prostatic urethra. Fluid from the prostate, together with seminal fluid from the seminal gland, and sperm from the ductus deferens combine to form semen. "}, {"name": "Arterial Supply", "text": "The prostate revives blood from various sources. Prostatic branches from the inferior vesical artery communicate across the midline of the prostate. The inferior gluteal, internal pudendal, and middle anorectal arteries supply branches to the prostate. "}, {"name": "Venous Drainage", "text": "The prostatic venous plexus surrounds the anterolateral aspect of the prostate. It receives tributaries from the deep dorsal vein of the penis and the vesical venous plexus to drain into the internal iliac veins. "}, {"name": "Innervation", "text": "The prostate receives both autonomic and somatic visceral innervation. The inferior hypogastric plexus supplies the prostate. Nerves traveling to the prostate form a periprostatic nerve plexus within the prostatic capsule. The prostatic plexus supplies the smooth muscle of the prostate and prostatic urethra. The skeletal muscle is supplied by the pudendal nerve. This skeletal muscle contracts and dilates the prostatic urethra."}, {"name": "Lymphatic Drainage", "text": "The lymph of the prostate is drained by the medial group of external iliac nodes, in which the efferent nodes pass to the internal iliac nodes."}, {"name": "List of Clinical Correlates", "text": "—Prostate cancer
—Benign prostatic hyperplasia
"}]

items.name: Testis
items.info:
[{"name": "Quick Facts", "text": "Location: Within the scrotum.

Arterial Supply: Testicular artery.

Venous Drainage: Pampiniform plexus.

Innervation: Autonomic: Testicular plexus.

Lymphatic Drainage: Lumbar lymph nodes."}, {"name": "Structure/Morphology", "text": "The testes are primary sex organs that play a crucial role in both the male reproductive and endocrine systems. The testes are paired ovoid structures that are in the scrotum. They are composed of up to 900 coiled seminiferous tubules, each averaging more than half a meter long, in which the sperm is produced (Standring, 2016). The testes are enclosed in a tough capsule composed of three tunicae (layers): the tunica vasculosa, albuginea, and vaginalis. "}, {"name": "Anatomical Relations", "text": "The left testis normally lies at a lower level than the right testis within the scrotum. The testes are suspended by the spermatic cord, through which structures entering or exiting the testes travel. The upper pole of the testis is tilted anterolaterally and is attached to the head of the epididymis, whereas the lower pole is tilted anteromedially."}, {"name": "Function", "text": "The placement of the testis in the scrotum and the countercurrent exchange mechanism of the pampiniform plexus ensures that the temperature of the testis is 3–4 °C lower than normal body temperature. This temperature is optimum for sperm production. The two testes produce up to 120 million sperm in the human adult each day (Standring, 2016). Sperm can be stored in the testis and remain fertile for up to a month. During this time, they are kept in an inactive state by multiple inhibitory substances. The testes are also heavily involved in the endocrine system. Leydig cells produce hormones that promote the development of the male reproductive system and secondary male characteristics."}, {"name": "Arterial Supply", "text": "The testes are supplied by the testicular artery, which arises from the abdominal aorta. It travels inferiorly to the pelvis as a retroperitoneal structure. The testicular artery then travels through the inguinal canal by passing through the deep and superficial inguinal rings. Branches enter the mediastinum of the testis and ramify in the tunica vasculosa."}, {"name": "Venous Drainage", "text": "The testes are drained by the pampiniform plexus, a network of vessels that surround the spermatic cord. The pampiniform plexus drains into the left and right testicular veins. The left testicular vein drains into the left renal vein, whereas the right testicular vein drains directly into the inferior vena cava."}, {"name": "Innervation", "text": "The testes are innervated by the testicular plexus. The nerve fibers arise from the tenth and eleventh thoracic spinal segments. They travel to the aortic and renal plexuses and follow the testicular arteries to reach the testis in the pelvis."}, {"name": "Lymphatic Drainage", "text": "Lymphatic drainage of the testis drains into the para-aortic and inter-aortocaval lymph nodes (lumbar nodes)."}, {"name": "List of Clinical Correlates", "text": "—Testicular cancer

—Variocele"}, {"name": "References", "text": "Standring, S. (2016) Gray's Anatomy: The Anatomical Basis of Clinical Practice. Gray's Anatomy Series 41 edn.: Elsevier Limited."}]

items.info:
[{"name": "Quick Facts", "text": "Location: Directly inferior to the bladder. 

Arterial Supply: Inferior vesical, internal pudendal, and middle anorectal arteries. 

Venous Drainage: Prostatic venous plexus.

Innervation: Somatic visceral afferent: pudendal nerve; Autonomic: Inferior hypogastric and prostatic plexuses. 

Lymphatic Drainage: External and internal iliac lymph nodes.
"}, {"name": "Structure/Morphology", "text": "The prostate is a walnut-sized, globular fibromuscular gland. It is fixed superiorly to the base of the urinary bladder and sits superior to the pelvic floor.

The prostate is traditionally divided into ill-defined lobes.
—The isthmus of the prostate lies anterior to the urethra and contains little to no glandular tissue.
—The right and left lobes are separated anteriorly by the isthmus. 

Each lobe can be further subdivided into four distinct lobules:
—Inferoposterior lobule lies posterior to the urethra and inferior to the ejaculatory ducts. Readily palpable during a digital rectal examination.
—Inferolateral lobule lies lateral to the urethra, forming the bulk of each lobe.
—Superomedial lobule lies deep to the inferoposterior lobule and directly surround the ejaculatory duct on each side.
—Anteromedial lobule deep to the inferolateral lobular and directly lateral to the urethra.

In addition to the lobe classifications, the prostate can be divided into four different zones: 
—the central zone surrounding the ejaculatory ducts;
—the transitional zone surrounding the proximal urethra;
—the peripheral zone surrounding the distal urethra;
—the stromal zone (also known as the anterior fibromuscular zone) that is comprised of muscles and connective tissue.

The superior aspect of the prostate is termed the base and the inferior aspect is termed the apex. There are two posterolateral surfaces, and an anterior and posterior surface of the prostate.

The prostatic urethra passes directly through the substance of the prostate on its way to the penis. 
"}, {"name": "Anatomical Relations", "text": "The superior aspect of the prostate is termed the base and is continuous with the neck of the bladder. The inferior aspect is termed the apex and marks the junction of the membranous and prostatic urethra. The anterior surface of the prostate lies directly posterior to the pubic arch. It is connected to the pubic bone by the puboprostatic ligament. The inferolateral surfaces of the prostate are related to the anterior muscle fibers of levator ani. They surround the prostate in a sling termed the pubourethral sling or pubourethalis. The posterior surface of the bladder lies anterior to the rectum and the rectourethralis muscle. The superior surface of the prostate is penetrated by two ejaculatory ducts.

The prostate is surrounded by an anatomically variable prostatic capsule which is formed from the surrounding fascia. The prostatic plexus of veins and nerves reside within the capsule. 
"}, {"name": "Function", "text": "The prostate provides passage for urine and sperm to pass out of the body. During ejaculation the prostate secretes a slightly alkaline fluid into the prostatic urethra. Fluid from the prostate, together with seminal fluid from the seminal gland, and sperm from the ductus deferens combine to form semen. "}, {"name": "Arterial Supply", "text": "The prostate revives blood from various sources. Prostatic branches from the inferior vesical artery communicate across the midline of the prostate. The inferior gluteal, internal pudendal, and middle anorectal arteries supply branches to the prostate. "}, {"name": "Venous Drainage", "text": "The prostatic venous plexus surrounds the anterolateral aspect of the prostate. It receives tributaries from the deep dorsal vein of the penis and the vesical venous plexus to drain into the internal iliac veins. "}, {"name": "Innervation", "text": "The prostate receives both autonomic and somatic visceral innervation. The inferior hypogastric plexus supplies the prostate. Nerves traveling to the prostate form a periprostatic nerve plexus within the prostatic capsule. The prostatic plexus supplies the smooth muscle of the prostate and prostatic urethra. The skeletal muscle is supplied by the pudendal nerve. This skeletal muscle contracts and dilates the prostatic urethra."}, {"name": "Lymphatic Drainage", "text": "The lymph of the prostate is drained by the medial group of external iliac nodes, in which the efferent nodes pass to the internal iliac nodes."}, {"name": "List of Clinical Correlates", "text": "—Prostate cancer
—Benign prostatic hyperplasia
"}]

items.name: Arteries of Pancreas
items.info:
[{"name": "Description", "text": "The pancreas receives its blood supply from both the celiac trunk and the superior mesenteric artery.

The head of the pancreas, and the adjacent duodenum are supplied by four arteries.

- The celiac trunk supplies two arteries, the anterior and posterior superior pancreaticoduodenal arteries, both of which arise from the gastroduodenal artery.

- The superior mesenteric artery supplies the anterior and posterior inferior pancreaticoduodenal arteries.

The anterior arteries supply the anterior aspect of the duodenum, head of the pancreas, uncinate process and anastomose to form the anterior pancreaticoduodenal arcade. Similarly, the posterior arteries supply the posterior aspect of the duodenum and head of the pancreas, as well as the distal end of the bile duct. The posterior arteries may also form a posterior pancreaticoduodenal arcade.

The body and tail of the pancreas are supplied by the several branches from the splenic artery, including the dorsal pancreatic, great pancreatic, and inferior pancreatic arteries and the artery to the tail of the pancreas."}]

It is also known as the inferior terminal trunk of the middle cerebral artery, or the inferior cortical branch of the middle cerebral artery.

From its origin, near the anterior part of the lateral sulcus, it travels posterosuperiorly along the lateral sulcus, inferior to the superior terminal branch. Along its course, the inferior terminal branch of the middle cerebral artery gives off branches; these include the anterior temporal, middle temporal posterior temporal branches, the anterior parietal and posterior parietal arteries, as well as the branch to the angular gyrus.

Overall, the inferior terminal branch of the middle cerebral artery and its branches provide an arterial supply to the temporal and parietal lobes, and the angular gyrus."}]

items.name: Coronal T1-weighted MRI of thighs, posterior to anterior (5 of 9)
items.info:
[
  {
    "name" : "Legend",
    "text" : "This is the fifth of nine coronal MRIs through the thigh, presented from posterior to anterior. ​
​
The deep and superficial femoral vessels are visualized. The obturator internus and externus muscles are visible on either side of the obturator membrane. The adductor longus muscle is difficult to separate from the adductor magnus muscle. ​
​
The vastus lateralis and medialis are seen wrapping around the femur. The most inferior fibers of the vastus medialis are often called the vastus medialis obliquus but are not separable on MR from the remainder of the muscle.​
​
The iliopsoas muscle hugs the medial aspect of the joint as it nears its insertion onto the lesser trochanter. Pectineus will insert on the posterior femur immediately distal to the iliopsoas muscle. "
  },
  {
    "name" : "Imaging Technique",
    "text" : "
Imaging Technique​
Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) is a high-resolution cross-sectional imaging technique. It utilizes hydrogen protons, which are abundantly present in water and water makes up approximately 63% of the average male, and 52% in the average female (Lote, 2012). Hydrogen protons are normally randomly aligned, however, when placed in a magnetic field, the protons align along the same axis as the magnetic field. ​
 ​
A radiofrequency pulse is applied and causes disruption to the magnetization and pushes the protons out of alignment, causing them to spin. This produces two magnetization vectors, longitudinal magnetization (in the direction of the magnetic field) and transverse magnetization (perpendicular to the magnetic field). When the radiofrequency pulse is removed, the magnetization vectors realign with the magnetic field. As a result, longitudinal magnetization starts to increase, known as T1 relaxation or recovery, and transverse magnetization starts to decrease, known as T2 relaxation or decay. Energy is released from the spinning protons as radiofrequency signals (known as the echo). The radiofrequency pulses are repeated and detected to produce an image. ​
 ​
Radiographers can vary the sequence of pulses to create different types of images. The repetition time (TR) between two radiofrequency pulses influences T1 and T2 weighting, meaning that a shorter amount of repetition time between two pulses will generate a T1-weighted image, while pulses with a long echo time (TE) produces T2-weighted images. ​
 ​
Different tissues in the body have different T1 and T2 values, these tissues will appear, not only different from each other, but also different on T1 and T2 MRIs. The bright, or whiter, image implies an increased signal intensity, while darker, or blacker, images have decreased signal intensity. Water or cerebrospinal fluid will appear dark on T1 weighted images and bright on T2-weighted images. ​
 ​
MRI’s are useful to detect cerebral infarction, abnormalities in the brain and spine, diagnosis of knee injuries, and has eliminated the need for myelography. When used in areas such as the abdomen/pelvis and breast it has shown to have high sensitivity in detecting cancer. ​
 ​
Proton-density MRI is another MRI technique, where there is longer TR between two radiofrequency pulses and shorter TE. This technique is useful for detecting joint disease and injury.​
"
  },

  },
  {
    "name" : "References",
    "text" : "Lote, C. J. (2012) Principles of Renal Physiology. Springer Netherlands."

They travel between the superior costotransverse and intertransverse ligaments (or muscle when present), and between the longissimus and iliocostalis muscles, piercing the latissimus dorsi to become superficial."}, {"name": "Branches", "text": "There are no named branches."}, {"name": "Supplied Structures", "text": "Along their course, the lateral dorsal cutaneous branches of the posterior intercostal arteries supply the longissimus thoracis, iliocostalis, and latissimus dorsi muscles, as well as the overlying fascia and skin."}]

items.name: Muscular Branches of Median Nerve (Hand; Left)
items.info:
[{"name": "Description", "text": "The median nerve is formed by the union of lateral and medial cords of brachial plexus. It descends in the arm and crosses the brachial artery from its lateral to its medial side. The median nerve leaves the cubital fossa between the two heads of pronator teres and descends further deep to the flexor digitorum superficialis muscle. The nerve passes deep to the flexor retinaculum (transverse carpal ligament) to enter the palm where it divides into lateral and medial divisions. 

Along its course, the median nerve gives off numerous muscular branches.

—In the axilla and arm: a muscular branch to the pronator teres muscle.

—In the cubital fossa: three muscular branches to flexor carpi radialis, flexor digitorum superficialis and palmaris longus muscles.

—In the forearm: the anterior antebrachial interosseous nerve innervates the deep muscles of the flexor compartment of the forearm, including flexor pollicis longus, the lateral half of the flexor digitorum profundus, and the pronator quadratus.

—In the palm: a lateral division supplies a muscular branch to the thenar muscles and three digital branches. Out of the three digital branches, two supply the thumb and one lateral side of the index finger. The digital branch to the index finger also innervates the first lumbrical. A medial division divides into two common digital branches for the second and third interdigital clefts, supplying the adjoining sides of the index, middle and ring fingers. The common digital branch for the second interdigital cleft also innervates the second lumbrical."}]

Along its course, the superior anorectal veins travel to the left of the superior anorectal artery, within the sigmoid mesocolon."}, {"name": "Tributaries", "text": "The superior anorectal vein is a continuation of the tributaries of the anorectal venous rectal plexus. The vessels establish a connection between the portal venous system and the systemic venous system."}, {"name": "Structures Drained", "text": "The superior anorectal vein drains the upper two-thirds of the rectum, the internal part of the anorectal venous plexus, and the upper anal canal."}, {"name": "List of Clinical Correlates", "text": "- Hemorrhoids (thromboses in the external venous plexus)"}]

Thyrocervical Trunk
items.info:
[{"name": "Quick Facts", "text": "Origin: Subclavian artery.

Course: Ascends medial to the scalenus anterior muscle.

Branches: Suprascapular, transverse cervical, and inferior thyroid arteries.

Supplied Structures: Structures of the neck and scapular region."}, {"name": "Origin", "text": "The thyrocervical trunk arises from the anterior surface of the first part of the subclavian artery."}, {"name": "Course", "text": "The thyrocervical trunk is a short thick vessel that ascends just medial to the scalenus anterior muscle and divides almost immediately from its origin."}, {"name": "Branches", "text": "The suprascapular artery arises from the thyrocervical trunk and passes inferolaterally across the scalenus anterior muscle to reach the superior scapular border.

The transverse cervical artery arises just superior to the suprascapular artery and takes a lateral course across the occipital triangle of the neck.

The inferior thyroid artery is the largest terminal branch of the thyrocervical trunk. It ascends anterior to the scalenus anterior muscle. Sometimes, the ascending cervical artery may arise directly from the thyrocervical trunk, but it usually arises from the inferior thyroid artery."}, {"name": "Supplied Structures", "text": "Branches from the thyrocervical trunk supply various structures of the neck and scapular region.

- The suprascapular artery supplies the supraspinatus and infraspinatus muscles and part of the sternocleidomastoid and the subclavius muscles.

- The transverse cervical artery supplies trapezius and sternocleidomastoid muscles.

- The inferior thyroid artery supplies the inferior poles of the thyroid gland, parathyroid gland, larynx, pharynx, infrahyoid muscles, longus colli, scalenus anterior, and the inferior pharyngeal constrictor muscles."}]

items.name: Lateral Plantar Artery

[{"name": "Quick Facts", "text": "Origin: Terminal branch of posterior tibial artery.

Course: Distally along the lateral aspect of the foot.

Branches: Plantar metatarsal branch.

Supplied Structures: Lateral aspect of plantar surface of the foot."}, {"name": "Origin", "text": "The medial and lateral plantar arteries are the terminal branches of the posterior tibial artery. The posterior tibial artery bifurcates into the medial and lateral plantar arteries in the region of the sustentaculum tali (Tubbs, Shoja and Loukas, 2016). The lateral plantar artery is the larger of these two vessels."}, {"name": "Course", "text": "The lateral plantar artery continues in a lateral direction on the plantar aspect of the quadratus plantae muscle, deep to the flexor digitorum brevis muscle. It then passes over the tendon of the fibularis longus muscle, continues distally along the cuboid, until it reaches the level of the base of the fifth metatarsal. It accompanies the lateral plantar nerve which sits medial to the artery.

At the base of the fifth metatarsal bone, the lateral plantar artery unites with the deep plantar artery from the dorsalis pedis artery to form the plantar arch."}, {"name": "Branches", "text": "The lateral plantar artery gives rise to a plantar metatarsal branch that extends along the lateral surface of the fifth metatarsal bone (Netter, 2011)."}, {"name": "Supplied Structures", "text": "The lateral plantar artery supplies the lateral aspect of the sole of the foot, including muscular, cutaneous, and articular elements. It also contributes to the supply of the plantar aspect of the toes."}, {"name": "References", "text": "Netter, F. H. (2011) Atlas of Human Anatomy. Netter Basic Science Series: Saunders/Elsevier.

items.name: Tooth (Mandibular First Molar)
items.info:
[{"name": "Quick Facts", "text": "The tooth is any of the hard, calcified structures set in the alveolar processes of the mandible and maxilla for mastication of food. In humans, there are two sets of teeth, deciduous and permanent. Each tooth consists of three parts: the crown, the neck, and the root. The solid part includes dentin, forming most of the tooth and resembling true bone; enamel, a very hard inorganic substance, covering the crown; and cementum, covering the root. In the center is the soft pulp (Dorland, 2011)."}, {"name": "Structure and/or Key Feature(s)", "text": "The mandibular first molar shares a simple basic structure with all teeth in the oral cavity. A tooth can be largely divided into the root and the crown, both of which are comprised mostly of dentin; an avascular and acellular connective tissue. The crown projects from the gingiva, and is covered by a hard, semi-translucent layer of enamel. 

The crown meets the root at the neck or cervical margin of the tooth. The root is suspended and anchored by the periodontal ligament in alveolar bone which is covered by a thin layer of bone-like tissue called cement. Collectively, the gingivae, periodontal ligament, alveolar bone, and cement are known as the periodontium (Martini, Nath and Bartholomew, 2017). 

The tooth contains a central pulp cavity of loose connective tissue which houses blood vessels and nerves that supply the surrounding dentin (Kerr, 2000). The pulp cavity narrows in the deeper section of the root to form a pulp or root canal which is continuous with the periodontal ligament via a small apical foramen at the tip of the root. This apical foramen facilitates the entry of vessels and nerves into the pulp cavity (Standring, 2016).

A key feature of the mandibular first molar is the presence of five cusps, specifically two buccal, two lingual and one distal located on the superior aspect of the tooth."}, {"name": "Anatomical Relations", "text": "The mandibular first molar is identified as the molar that is most mesially positioned. Embedded in the mandibular gingiva, it is bordered by the mandibular canine mesially and the second molar distally (Standring, 2016)."}, {"name": "Function", "text": "Molariform teeth, which include both molars and premolars, are responsible for crushing and grinding food. This is facilitated by their large, flattened cusps (Martini, Nath and Bartholomew, 2017).

Incisiform teeth (incisors) are used for clipping and cutting, facilitated by their thin, bladelike crowns. Caniniform teeth (canines) are considered the tearing or piercing teeth, identifiable by their conical shape, sharp ridgeline and pointed tip (Martini, Nath and Bartholomew, 2017)."}, {"name": "References", "text": "Dorland, W. (2011) Dorland's Illustrated Medical Dictionary. 32nd edn. Philadelphia, USA: Elsevier Saunders.

Kerr, J. B. (2007) Atlas of Functional Histology. Elsevier Science Health Science Division.

Martini, F. H., Nath, J. L. and Bartholomew, E. F. (2017) Fundamentals of Anatomy & Physiology. Pearson Education.

Standring, S. (2016) Gray's Anatomy: The Anatomical Basis of Clinical Practice. Gray's Anatomy Series 41 edn.: Elsevier Limited."}]

items.info: [{"name": "Anatomical Relations", "text": "The articular capsules of the metacarpophalangeal joints are the membranous sacs enclosing the articular surface of the distal metacarpal bones and the bases of the proximal phalanges. It is composed of an outer fibrous membrane and an inner synovial membrane. The ligament of the metacarpophalangeal joints, i.e., the palmar, collateral, and accessory collateral ligaments reinforce the articular capsule."}, {"name": "Function", "text": "The articular capsule of the metacarpophalangeal joint ensures that the joint is sealed, thus, keeping the lubricating synovial fluid within the joint. It provides passive stability to the joint by limiting the joint movement. Additionally, it provides active stability by containing numerous proprioceptive nerve endings which relay mechanical information back to the central nervous system (Ralphs and Benjamin, 1994)."}, {"name": "References", "text": "Ralphs, J. items.info: [{"name": "Anatomical Relations", "text": "The nucleus pulposus lies posterior to the center of the vertebral body. It is surrounded by the concentric lamellae of the anulus fibrosus."}, {"name": "Function", "text": "The nucleus pulposus acts as a shock absorber and permits a very limited range of movement between vertebrae. In the elderly, the nucleus pulposus is less jelly-like and it increases its fibrous content. Thus, they lose their flexibility and are more prone to injury (Waxenbaum and Futterman, 2017)."}, {"name": "Structure", "text": "The nucleus pulposus is well developed in both the cervical and the lumbar spine. Postnatally it is a mucoid, gelatinous substance. Over time, collagen fibers from the internal surface of the anulus fibrosus invade and eventually form a gel-like, fibrocartilaginous tissue characteristic of mature intervertebral discs."}, {"name": "References", "text": "Waxenbaum, J. items.info:
[{"name": "Quick Facts", "text": "Origin: Surface of the spinal cord ventral to the ventral horn.

Course: Inferiorly towards the fourth sacral foramen.

Branches: No branches.

Supply: Motor innervation to muscles of the perineum and pelvis. Parasympathetic innervation to the hindgut, kidneys, reproductive organs, and genitals."}, {"name": "Origin", "text": "The anterior root of the fourth sacral nerve originates as a series of rootlets that emerge from the ventrolateral surface of the spinal cord. These quickly merge to form the anterior root."}, {"name": "Course", "text": "The anterior root runs inferiorly. At lumbar and sacral levels, the anterior root descends through the vertebral column until it reaches the fourth sacral foramen. Just before entering this foramen the anterior and posterior roots merge to form the nerve."}, {"name": "Branches", "text": "There are no named branches; however fibers do contribute to the sacral plexus (see supplied structures)."}, {"name": "Supplied Structures", "text": "The anterior root of the fourth sacral nerve contributes to the sacral plexus, particularly the pudendal nerve.

The pudendal nerve arises from the second, third, and fourth sacral nerves. It transmits motor and sensory innervation to the abdomen and pelvic regions. Motor innervation is to the muscles of the perineum (bulbospongiosus, ischiocavernosus, superficial transverse perineal, deep transverse perineal, external anal, and urethral sphincter muscles). In addition, the anterior root of the fourth sacral nerve innervates the levator ani and coccygeus muscles.

The pelvic splanchnic nerve carries parasympathetic innervation to the hindgut organs, kidneys, reproductive organs, and genitals. Parasympathetic fibers exit the spinal cord via the second, third, and fourth sacral nerves, and combine to form the pelvic splanchnic nerve."}]

items.name: Anterior Ethmoidal Artery

Course: Passes within the anterior ethmoidal canal and enters the anterior cranial fossa via the anterior ethmoidal foramen.

Branches: Anterior meningeal, anterior septal, and anterior lateral nasal branches.

Supplied Structures: Anterior ethmoidal cells, frontal sinus, dura mater, and nose."}, {"name": "Origin", "text": "The anterior ethmoidal artery arises from the ophthalmic artery as it passes anteromedially in the orbital cavity."}, {"name": "Course", "text": "The anterior ethmoidal artery passes medially a short distance and enters the anterior ethmoidal canal. It then exits the canal into the anterior cranial fossa via the anterior ethmoidal foramen, just at the anterior end of the lateral edge of the cribriform plate."}, {"name": "Branches", "text": "The anterior ethmoidal artery has ramifications that arise both in the anterior ethmoidal canal (extracranially) and after it emerges from the anterior ethmoidal foramen (intracranially)."}, {"name": "Supplied Structures", "text": "The extracranial ramifications of the anterior ethmoidal artery supply the nasal cavity and septum, as well as the anterior ethmoidal cells and frontal sinus. items.name: Denticulate Ligament (Sacral; Right)
items.info: [{"name": "Structure", "text": "The denticulate ligaments are thin sheets of collagen that extend laterally from the spinal pia mater. They extend out and form triangular shaped attachments to the overlying dura mater."}, {"name": "Key Features/Anatomical Relations", "text": "The denticulate ligaments extend from the foramen magnum rostrally down to the level of the T12 vertebra caudally. On each side, there are typically 18-21 triangular extensions which attach to the spinal dura mater, lateral to the spinal cord. They are thought to help stabilize the spinal cord.
