items.name: Hair Shaft
items.info:
[{"name": "Quick Facts", "text": "The hair shaft is the long cylindrical part that is the major portion of a hair, sometimes referring to only the portion that extends beyond the surface of the skin (Dorland, 2011)."}, {"name": "Structure/Morphology", "text": "The hair shaft is composed of three concentric layers, namely the outer cuticle, middle cortex, and inner medulla. They differ from each other in the types of keratin filaments they possess. Cells in the hair matrix surrounding the dermal papilla are responsible for hair growth. 

The cuticle forms the outer surface of the hair shaft. It is made up of layers of overlapping keratinized squamous cells, which resembles fish scales. The cuticle protects the hair from physical and chemical damage. The cortex is the bulkiest layer of the hair shaft; it is composed of elongated cells containing hard keratin intermediate filaments and may contain melanin contributing to the hair color. The medulla, which is absent in fine hair, is composed of loose aggregates of cells (Standring, 2016)."}, {"name": "References", "text": "Dorland, W. (2011) Dorland's Illustrated Medical Dictionary. 32nd edn. Philadelphia, USA: Elsevier Saunders.

Standring, S. (2016) Gray's Anatomy: The Anatomical Basis of Clinical Practice. Gray's Anatomy Series: Elsevier Limited."}]

items.name: Cilia (of Ependymal Cell)
items.info:
[{"name": "Quick Facts", "text": "Cilia are minute vibratile, hairlike processes that project from the free surface of a cell and are composed of nine pairs of microtubules arrayed around a central pair, anchored to the cellular cortex by the basal bodies. Dynein-powered sliding of the outer microtubules relative to one another causes the cilia to move in rhythmic beats (ciliary beats) that move the cell around in its environment or move fluid or mucous films over the cell surface (Dorland, 2011)."}, {"name": "Structure and/or Key Features", "text": "Cilia are hairlike projections of the apical surface of the plasmalemma of many cells. Each cilium contains a unique (9+2) arrangement of microtubules called an axoneme extending from a basal body and a microtubule-organizing center all located in the apical region of the ciliated cell.

There are three categories of cilia: 

—primary (non-motile) cilia; 

—motile cilia (and flagella);

—nodal cilia which are found only in the embryo.

Motile cilia are about 0.25 μm in diameter and 5–10 μm long and are present in various locations including the apical surface of ependymal cells. In ciliated epithelium, there may be several hundred protecting from the apical cell surface. Their internal structure permits their wave-like motion. Each cilium is firmly anchored to the apical region of the cell cytoplasm by a microtubule organizing center or centriole (Mescher, 2013)."}, {"name": "Anatomical Relations", "text": "The majority of cilia are predominantly found in epithelial cells. Cilia are abundant on the apical surfaces of cuboidal or columnar cells lining the upper respiratory tract and uterine tubes (Mescher, 2013)."}, {"name": "Function", "text": "Motile cilia primarily assist in fluid movement along the surfaces of epithelium, e.g., cerebrospinal fluid along the surfaces of ependymal cells in the ventricles of the brain. As a flagellum, it provides movement of the spermatozoa (Ross and Pawlina, 2006).

Primary cilia can detect physical and biochemical signals (Standring, 2016).

Primary cilia are particularly important for normal tissue morphogenesis (Ross and Pawlina, 2006).

Nodal cilia are important during early development of the embryo (Ross and Pawlina, 2006)."}, {"name": "References", "text": "Dorland, W. (2011) Dorland's Illustrated Medical Dictionary. 32nd edn. Philadelphia, USA: Elsevier Saunders.

Mescher, A. (2013) Junqueira's Basic Histology: Text and Atlas. 13th edn.: McGraw-Hill Education.

Ross, M. H. and Pawlina, W. (2006) Histology: A text and atlas. Lippincott Williams & Wilkins.

Standring, S. (2016) Gray's Anatomy: The Anatomical Basis of Clinical Practice. Gray's Anatomy Series 41 edn.: Elsevier Limited."}]

items.name: Cavernous Nerves of Penis
items.info:
[{"name": "Quick Facts", "text": "Sympathetic Contribution: T11-T12 and L1 spinal cord level.

Parasympathetic Contribution: S1-S4 spinal cord level.

Course: Passes through pelvic plexuses to enter the penis.

Sympathetic Supply: Vasoconstriction of helicine arteries in erectile tissue.

Parasympathetic Supply: Vasodilation of helicine arteries in erectile tissue."}, {"name": "Contributing Nerves", "text": "The cavernous nerves originate in the pelvic plexuses and carry both sympathetic and parasympathetic fibers. The sympathetic contributions originate from the intermediolateral columns at the level of T11-T12 and L1 segments of the spinal cord. Parasympathetic contributions arise from S1-S4 segments of the spinal cord (Standring, 2020)."}, {"name": "Course", "text": "The sympathetic contributions of the cavernous nerves pass through the sympathetic trunk to the pelvic plexus. The parasympathetic fibers pass through the pelvic splanchnic nerves into the pelvic plexuses. 

In males, the fibers run posterolateral to the prostate and exit the pelvis with the urethra through the urogenital diaphragm. They pass into the penis, where fibers distribute to the erectile tissue of the corpus cavernosum and corpus spongiosum."}, {"name": "Branches", "text": "There are no named branches."}, {"name": "Supplied Structures", "text": "The cavernous nerves innervate the helicine arteries in the erectile tissues of the penis. The inhibitory sympathetic fibers cause vasoconstriction, while the excitatory parasympathetic fibers produce vasodilation (Standring, 2020). 

Visceral sensory fibers carrying afferents from the penis pass through cavernous nerve."}, {"name": "References", "text": "Standring, S. (2020) Gray's Anatomy: The Anatomical Basis of Clinical Practice. 42nd edn.: Elsevier Health Sciences."}]

items.name: Cytoplasm
Cranial Bone
items.info:
[{"name": "Quick Facts", "text": "The cranium is the large round superior part of the skull; it encloses the brain, forms the skeleton of the midface, and is made up of the cranial bones held together by sutures, synchondroses, and bony unions (Dorland, 2011)."}, {"name": "Structure", "text": "The bones that make up the neurocranium, the portion of the cranium that houses the brain, are the frontal, parietal, temporal, occipital, ethmoid, and sphenoid bones. The cranial bones are considered flat bones derived from the mesenchyme and develop by intramembranous and endochondral ossification. The bones contain a thin inner and outer layer of compact bone, separated by cancellous bone, known as diploë. The inner layer of compact bone is thinner and more brittle than its external layer (Moore, Dalley and Agur, 2013; Snell, 2011).

The frontal, parietal, temporal, and occipital bones make up the calvaria, which is covered by the scalp. The scalp attaches to the calvaria via the pericranium. The outer surface of the pericranium is loosely fused with the epicranial aponeurosis of the scalp via a loose connective tissue. The inner surface of the pericranium firmly attaches to the calvaria. Due to its elasticity, the pericranium can be easily removed from the calvaria, except at the location of the suture lines where it is firmly attached."}, {"name": "Anatomical Relations", "text": "The cranial bone is located deep to the scalp and superficial to the meninges and brain parenchyma."}, {"name": "Function", "text": "The cranial bones protect the brain within the cranial vault."}, {"name": "List of Clinical Correlates", "text": "—Skull fracture"}, {"name": "References", "text": "Dorland, W. (2011) Dorland's Illustrated Medical Dictionary. 32nd edn. Philadelphia, USA: Elsevier Saunders.

Moore, K. L., Dalley, A. F. and Agur, A. M. R. (2013) Clinically Oriented Anatomy. Clinically Oriented Anatomy 7th edn.: Wolters Kluwer Health/Lippincott Williams & Wilkins.

Snell, R. S. (2011) Clinical Anatomy by Regions. Lippincott Williams & Wilkins."}]

items.name: Geniohyoid Branch of Hypoglossal Nerve
items.info:
[{"name": "Quick Facts", "text": "Origin: Hypoglossal communicating branch of first cervical nerve (C1).

Course: Joins the hypoglossal nerve.

Branches: None.

Supply: Geniohyoid muscle.
"}, {"name": "Origin", "text": "The anterior ramus of the first cervical nerve (C1) provides a communicating branch to the hypoglossal nerve. This communicating branch consists of motor fibers."}, {"name": "Course", "text": "The motor fibers of the communicating branch of the first cervical nerve hitchhike with the hypoglossal nerve as it passes lateral to the external carotid artery. The hypoglossal nerve continues anteriorly, superficial to the external carotid artery but deep to the posterior digastric and stylohyoid muscles on its way to the oral cavity. Near the posterior border of hyoglossus, the fibers originating from the first cervical nerve leave the hypoglossal nerve to reach their target."}, {"name": "Branches", "text": "There are no named branches."}, {"name": "Supplied Structures", "text": "The geniohyoid branch supplies motor innervation to the geniohyoid muscle. "}]

items.name: Superior Vertebral End Plate (T3-T4)
items.info: [{"name": "Anatomical Relations", "text": "The superior vertebral end plate lies on the inferior surface of the vertebral body, which sits superiorly in the intervertebral joint. The end plates are surrounded by smooth bony epiphyseal rims, the annular epiphysis."}, {"name": "Function", "text": "As a part of the intervertebral symphysis, the intervertebral end plates contribute to maintaining the stability of the vertebral column and resisting various forces in movement. They also help to maintain a fluid pressure of the water content of the nucleus pulposus, by preventing the loss of water to the vertebral body."}, {"name": "Structure", "text": "The superior vertebral end plates are bi-layered cartilages; they are flat and lie obliquely. End plates are relatively dense as they contain both hyaline cartilage and fibrocartilage. The fibrocartilage component lies nearer to the disc and is formed by the collagen fibers of the inner two thirds of the annulus fibrosus. The cartilage end plates are typically between 0.1-2.0 mm thick; however, this varies depending on the vertebral region and position (Lotz, Fields and Liebenberg, 2013). In the lumbar region, the end plates are thinner centrally than peripherally."}, {"name": "List of Clinical Correlates", "text": "\u2014Disc Herniation"}, {"name": "References", "text": "Lotz, J. C., Fields, A. J. and Liebenberg, E. C. (2013) 'The role of the vertebral end plate in low back pain', Global Spine J, 3(3), pp. 153-64."}]

items.name: Sensory Nerve Fibers of Taste Buds
items.audio: Sensory Nerve Fibers of Taste Buds.mp3
items.info:
[{"name": "Quick Facts", "text": "General sensory innervation of the anterior two-thirds of the tongue is via the lingual nerve (originating from the mandibular nerve CNV3). Special sensory fibers of the anterior two-thirds of the tongue, excluding the vallate papillae, run within the chorda tympani (a branch of the facial nerve) and its fibers accompanies the lingual nerve. General and special sensory innervation of the posterior one-third of the tongue is conveyed by the glossopharyngeal nerve (CNIX). This includes special sensory innervation of the vallate papillae."}, {"name": "Structure and/or Key Features", "text": "The sensory innervation to the taste buds is elaborate and well distributed. There are various patterns of innervation among the taste buds, with individual sensory nerve fibers splitting and diverging among the taste buds. Other terminal fibers from may be attributed to just one taste bud, but they distribute themselves to the different taste cells comprising that taste bud. In contrast to this, a single taste bud may receive a broad innervation stemming from multiple nerve branch inputs. Overall, these alternating methods of innervation provide a complex neural meshwork coursing throughout the taste buds.

In general, each taste bud receives one of two fiber types. The first type of nerve fiber splits within the periphery of the taste bud, forming a neural web on the outskirts on the bulb-shaped collection of sensory cells. These nerves present as free nerve endings. The other type of nerve fiber forms a central, inner web of innervation. These are arranged in a series of synapses (Standring, 2016).

There is a broad and complex innervation for the tongue’s ordinary and special senses. General sensory innervation of the anterior two-thirds of the tongue is via the lingual nerve (originating from the mandibular nerve CN V3). Special sensory fibers of the anterior two-thirds of the tongue, excluding the vallate papillae, run within the chorda tympani (a branch of the facial nerve) and its fibers accompanies the lingual nerve. General and special sensory innervation of the posterior one third of the tongue are conveyed by the glossopharyngeal nerve (CN IX). This includes special sensory innervation of the vallate papillae."}, {"name": "Function", "text": "The sensation of taste is important for discerning between desirable foods, initiating swallowing, and regulating gastrointestinal secretions. These highly sensitive functions are the primary reasoning behind the broad, dense neural distribution."}, {"name": "References", "text": "Standring, S. (2016) Gray's Anatomy: The Anatomical Basis of Clinical Practice. Gray's Anatomy Series: Elsevier Limited."}]

items.name: Spiral Ligament of Cochlea
items.info:
[{"name": "Quick Facts", "text": "The spiral ligament of cochlea is a band of thickened periosteum in the bony cochlea (Dorland, 2011)."}, {"name": "Structure and/or Key Feature(s)", "text": "The spiral ligament is a large fibrous structure found on the lateral aspect of the cochlear duct, making up a large majority of its outer wall. 

It is composed of groups of interwoven fibers which are attached along the bony wall, the basilar membrane, and the base of the stria vascularis. Within the spiral ligament, there are a large number of fibrocytes with varying morphology, which may be associated with the production and maintenance of these fibers. The different types of fibrocytes are based on their position within the spiral ligament, along with structural features, their size, and orientation (Standring, 2016)."}, {"name": "Anatomical Relations", "text": "The spiral ligament is located within the lateral aspect of the cochlea. It is roughly crescentic in shape and is interfacing between the stria vascularis and the inside of the bony wall. It receives the insertion of the basilar membrane at the basal (or spiral) crest, a triangular projection from the spiral ligament. Its upper and lower regions are closely related to the scala vestibuli and scala tympani, respectively."}, {"name": "Function", "text": "The functions of the spiral ligament are associated with its anatomical neighbors, in particular the basilar membrane and the stria vascularis, and so it is crucial for effective function of the organ of Corti. Given the insertion of the basilar membrane into the spiral ligament, it is directly involved in supporting the orientation of the basilar membrane, and so the overall dynamics involved behind the coordinated processes of the cochlea. It also participates in generating and sustaining a consistent tension throughout the basilar membrane. This tension is suggested to arise by some of the structural fibers which have similar characteristic to the stress fibers produced by the fibroblasts of the spiral ligament.

The spiral ligament is also a crucial for the survival of the stria vascularis since reduced expression of the transport molecules within the ligament can impair potassium ion recycling, causing disruption to the endocochlear potential (Doherty & Linthicum, 2004)."}, {"name": "List of Clinical Correlates", "text": "—Otosclerosis

—Sensory hearing loss"}, {"name": "References", "text": "Doherty, J. K. & Linthicum, F. H., Jr. (2004) Spiral ligament and stria vascularis changes in cochlear otosclerosis: effect on hearing level. Otol Neurotol, 25(4), 457-64.

Dorland, W. (2011) Dorland's Illustrated Medical Dictionary. 32nd edn. Philadelphia, USA: Elsevier Saunders.

Standring, S. (2016) Gray's Anatomy: The Anatomical Basis of Clinical Practice., 41st edition. Elsevier Limited."}]

items.name: Vascular Process of Astrocyte
items.info:
[{"name": "Quick Facts", "text": "The vascular process of astrocytes is a pyramidal expansion of a process of an astrocyte against the wall of a capillary in the central nervous system (Dorland, 2011)."}, {"name": "Structure and/or Key Features", "text": "Astrocytes exhibit multiple radiating processes with bulbous ends which are known as astrocytic end feet. The bulbous ends of the astrocytic end feet extend from the astrocyte cell body and cling to neurons and capillaries, specifically on the basement membrane that surrounds the endothelial cells and pericytes (Marieb, Wilhelm and Mallatt, 2012)."}, {"name": "Function", "text": "Astrocytic end feet extend and attach to the nodes of Ranvier and synapses and so cover these bare areas where a myelin sheath is absent. 

The astrocytic end feet surround endothelial cells and, along with the tight junctions between endothelial cells and the basal lamina, form the blood-brain-barrier (Ross and Pawlina, 2006).

The astrocytic end feet form the glia limitans, a relatively impermeable barrier that surrounds the central nervous system (Ross and Pawlina, 2006)."}, {"name": "References", "text": "Dorland, W. (2011) Dorland's Illustrated Medical Dictionary. 32nd edn. Philadelphia, USA: Elsevier Saunders.

Marieb, E. N., Wilhelm, P. B. and Mallatt, J. (2012) Human Anatomy. fifth edn.: Benjamin Cummings.

Ross, M. H. and Pawlina, W. (2006) Histology: A text and atlas. Lippincott Williams & Wilkins."}]

items.name: Secondary Oocyte
items.info:
[{"name": "Quick Facts", "text": "A secondary oocyte is an oocyte in the period between the first and second maturation division; it is derived from a primary oocyte shortly before ovulation by a division that splits off the first polar body. If fertilized, it divides into an ootid and the second polar body; otherwise, it perishes. In humans, it is a round cell about 0.1 mm in diameter and consists of protoplasm that contains some yolk, enclosed by a thin cell wall, the vitelline membrane. It is surrounded by the zona pellucida and corona radiata (Dorland, 2011)."}, {"name": "Structure and/or Key Feature(s)", "text": "When the first meiotic division is completed in a mature follicle, equal share of chromatin is distributed to each daughter cell but only one receives most of the cytoplasm and becomes the secondary oocyte. It is about 150 μm in diameter. The other (diploid) daughter cell becomes the first polar body and will persist for more than 20 hours after ovulation.

The second meiotic division commences immediately after the first meiotic division is completed. As it leaves the ruptured follicle at ovulation, surrounded by the corona radiata, it is arrested at metaphase in the second meiotic division and this second meiotic division is only completed if it is penetrated by a spermatozoon (Ross and Pawlina, 2006).

For more information, check out our secondary oocyte micromodel."}, {"name": "References", "text": "Dorland, W. (2011) Dorland's Illustrated Medical Dictionary. 32nd edn. Philadelphia, USA: Elsevier Saunders.

Ross, M. H. and Pawlina, W. (2006) Histology: A text and atlas. Lippincott Williams & Wilkins."}]

items.name: Corona Radiata
items.info:
[{"name": "Quick Facts", "text": "The corona radiata is a superficial layer of radially elongated follicular cells surrounding the zona pellucida of a secondary oocyte (Dorland, 2011)."}, {"name": "Structure and/or Key Feature(s)", "text": "The coronal radiata is a layer of granulosa cells (referred to as cumulus cells) surrounding the zona pellucida of a secondary oocyte (Dorland, 2011). Additionally, the corona radiata forms the innermost layer of the cumulus oophorus. The corona radiata and cumulus oophorus span approximately 7-12.5 μm in diameter (Gardner et al., 2008; Harrison, Bonnar and Thompson, 2012). 

The corona radiata forms during folliculogenesis. During the ovarian cycle, cumulus cells make intimate contact with the oocyte and deposit an acellular glycoprotein layer around the surface of the oocyte called the zona pellucida. Cumulus cells remain attached to the zona pellucida and form the corona radiata.

Microvillus projections of the cytoplasm of cumulus cells project through the zona pellucida and form gap junctions with microvilli of the oocyte."}, {"name": "Anatomical Relations", "text": "The corona radiata surrounds the oocyte and is situated immediately external to the zona pellucida."}, {"name": "Function", "text": "Microvillus projections of the cumulus cells project through the zona pellucida and form gap junctions with microvilli of the oocyte. This provides a source of nutritional and regulatory substances, as well as exogenous proteins for the oocyte. 

In order for fertilization to occur, a sperm must penetrate an oocyte by piercing through the corona radiata and zona pellucida that encircle the oocyte. This indirectly reduces the chances of multiple fertilization (Gray and Lewis, 1918)."}, {"name": "References", "text": "Dorland, W. (2011) Dorland's Illustrated Medical Dictionary. 32nd edn. Philadelphia, USA: Elsevier Saunders.

Gardner, D. K., Weissman, A., Howles, C. M. and Shoham, Z. (2008) Textbook of Assisted Reproductive Technologies: Laboratory and Clinical Perspectives. CRC Press.

Gray, H. and Lewis, W. H. (1918) Anatomy of the Human Body. Lea & Febiger.

Harrison, R. F., Bonnar, J. and Thompson, W. (2012) Fertility and Sterility: The Proceedings of the XIth World Congress on Fertility and Sterility, Dublin, June 1983, held under the Auspices of the International Federation of Fertility Societies. Springer Netherlands."}]

items.name: Lobe of Thyroid Gland
items.info:
[{"name": "Quick Facts", "text": "The lobe of thyroid gland is either of the lobes (right or left) of the thyroid gland, located adjacent to either side of the trachea, cricoid cartilage, and thyroid cartilage (Dorland, 2011)."}, {"name": "Structure/Morphology", "text": "The characteristic structure of a compound exocrine gland includes the gland being subdivided into smaller components called lobes. Lobes can be further subdivided into lobules. Intralobular, interlobular, and interlobar ducts will unite all these glandular elements and the secretion product is usually delivered to its destination via a large single excretory duct. 

The thyroid gland is atypical since it is both an exocrine and endocrine gland. Each lobe of the thyroid gland is made up of structures or functional units called thyroid follicles of varying size. Their diameters range from about 0.2 to 1 mm. These measurements probably reflects their real size, and not necessarily the different state of activity of each follicle (Ross and Pawlina, 2016).
"}, {"name": "Anatomical Relations", "text": "Each lobe is separated by the trachea, one lobe is on either side, joined by a very thin isthmus of thyroid secretory units. In about 40% of individuals, a pyramidal-shaped lobe sometimes extends superiorly from the isthmus (Ross and Pawlina, 2016). "}, {"name": "Function", "text": "The thyroid lobes are the more gross anatomical structure of the microscopic thyroid lobules and their functional units called the thyroid follicles."}, {"name": "References", "text": "Dorland, W. (2011) Dorland's Illustrated Medical Dictionary. 32nd edn. Philadelphia, USA: Elsevier Saunders.
Ross, M. H. and Pawlina, W. (2016) Histology: A Text and Atlas. Wolters Kluwer Health.
"}]

items.name: Levator Palpebrae Superioris
items.info:
[{"name": "Quick Facts", "text": "Origin: Lesser wing of sphenoid bone.

Insertion: Superior tarsus and skin of upper eyelid.

Action: Elevates upper eyelid.

Innervation: Superior branch of oculomotor nerve (CNIII).

Arterial Supply: Ophthalmic and supraorbital artery."}, {"name": "Origin", "text": "The levator palpebrae superioris muscle arises from the lower part of the lesser wing of the sphenoid bone, superior to the optic canal."}, {"name": "Insertion", "text": "From its origin, the levator palpebrae superioris extends anteriorly, above the superior rectus muscle. As it extends forward, the muscle broadens and becomes aponeurotic at its anterior end. The deeper aponeurotic fibers attach to the anterior surface of the superior tarsus in the upper eyelid. These fibers are accompanied by smooth muscle fibers, the superior tarsal muscle. The remaining superficial fibers radiate to pass through the orbicularis oculi muscle and attach to the upper eyelid."}, {"name": "Key Features & Anatomical Relations", "text": "The adjoining connective tissue sheaths of levator palpebrae superioris and superior rectus fuse. Where they split to access their distal attachments is where the superior conjunctival fornix is located."}, {"name": "Action", "text": "The levator palpebrae superioris muscle elevates the upper eyelid. It works in opposition to the palpebral part of the orbicularis oculi muscle, which is responsible for closing the eyelids.

Additionally, the levator palpebrae superioris is connected to the superior rectus muscle via a check ligament. Therefore, when the superior rectus muscle contracts and gaze is directed upwards, the upper eyelid is also elevated."}, {"name": "List of Clinical Correlates", "text": "—Ptosis"}]

items.name: Branch of Pulmonary Artery
items.info: [{"name": "Quick Facts", "text": "The pulmonary arteries convey deoxygenated blood toward the lungs (Dorland, 2011)."}, {"name": "Structure/Morphology", "text": "The pulmonary arteries and their branches supply deoxygenated blood from the right ventricle of the heart to the lungs. The more proximal pulmonary arteries and their branches are elastic arteries and extend to the junctions of the bronchi and terminal bronchioles. Muscular type arteries are found more distally and branch into arterioles that extend to the alveolar saccules. The arterioles deliver blood, under low pressure, to the extensive network of capillaries that surround the alveoli (Ovalle et al., 2013)."}, {"name": "Function", "text": "The pulmonary arteries are responsible for supplying deoxygenated blood to the alveoli in order for gas exchange to occur."}, {"name": "References", "text": "Dorland, W. (2011) Dorland's Illustrated Medical Dictionary. 32nd edn. Philadelphia, USA: Elsevier Saunders.\n\nOvalle, W. K., Nahirney, P. C. and Netter, F. H. (2013) Netter's Essential Histology. ClinicalKey 2012: Elsevier Saunders."}]

items.name: Vascular Endothelium (Vein)
Medullary Arteries
items.info: [{"name": "Quick Facts", "text": "The medullary arteries are arteries that arise from the subcapsular arterial plexus. They pass through the cortex to reach the medulla, without providing any branches to the cortex. They join the medullary venous sinus."}, {"name": "Structure and/or Key Features:", "text": "The medullary arteries are one set of arteries that arise from the subcapsular arterial plexus. They are longitudinal vessels that pass through the zones of the cortex, with the trabeculae, or the inward projections of the capsule, to reach the medulla, without providing any branches to the cortex. They join the medullary venous sinus in the medulla of the suprarenal gland. Therefore, the medullary arteries, together with the cortical sinusoids, provide a dual blood supply to the medulla (Inomata & Sasano, 2015)."}, {"name": "Function", "text": "The dual blood supply to the medulla of the suprarenal gland is vital for the rapid transport of both glucocorticoids and enriched blood to the medulla, required in response to stress (Inomata & Sasano, 2015)."}, {"name": "References", "text": "Inomata, A. & Sasano, H. (2015) Practical approaches for evaluating adrenal toxicity in nonclinical safety assessment. J Toxicol Pathol, 28(3), 125-32."}]

items.name: Axoplasm
items.info:
[{"name": "Quick Facts", "text": "The axoplasm is the cytoplasm of an axon (Dorland, 2011)."}, {"name": "Structure", "text": "Most neurons have only one thin axon. The axon arises from the axon hillock. An axon is tubular with a uniform diameter along its entire length although the diameter varies depending on the type of neuron. An axon is bound by plasmalemma known as axolemma. The cytoplasm of an axon is known as the axoplasm. The axoplasm contains mitochondria, cytoskeletal elements, and some cisternae of the smooth endoplasmic reticulum (Mescher, 2013). The axoplasm is devoid of Nissl granules and Golgi complexes (Splittgerber, 2018)."}, {"name": "Function", "text": "Cytoskeletal elements found within the axoplasm provide structural strength to the axon. In addition, they transport substances away from the nerve cell body (anterograde flow). Retrograde flow transports molecules (taken up by endocytosis at the axon terminals) back towards the nerve cell body (Marieb, Wilhelm and Mallatt, 2012; Ross and Pawlina, 2006)."}, {"name": "Clinical Correlates", "text": "—Some viral diseases such as rabies, herpes simplex, herpes zoster, and perhaps poliomyelitis take advantage of axonal transport to spread to different locations in the body.

—Diffuse axonal injury is characterized by disruption of the axon cytoskeleton.

—Stretching of axons during traumatic injury causes physical disruption to, and proteolytic degradation of, the cytoskeleton."}, {"name": "References", "text": "Dorland, W. (2011) Dorland's Illustrated Medical Dictionary. 32nd edn. Philadelphia, USA: Elsevier Saunders.

Marieb, E. N., Wilhelm, P. B. and Mallatt, J. (2012) Human Anatomy. fifth edn.: Benjamin Cummings.

Mescher, A. (2013) Junqueira's Basic Histology: Text and Atlas. 13th edn.: McGraw-Hill Education.

Ross, M. H. and Pawlina, W. (2006) Histology: A text and atlas. Lippincott Williams & Wilkins.

Splittgerber, R. (2018) Snell's Clinical Neuroanatomy. Wolters Kluwer Health."}]

items.name: Mesangium
items.info:
[{"name": "Quick Facts", "text": "The mesangium is the thin membrane that helps support the capillary loops in a renal glomerulus (Dorland, 2011)."}, {"name": "Structure and/or Key Feature(s)", "text": "Within the renal corpuscle, the glomerular basement membrane associated with several capillaries encloses a space containing a population of cells called mesangial cells, which form the mesangium. The mesangium is more prominent at the vascular pole. 

Mesangial cells are also located outside the renal corpuscle but are called extraglomerular mesangial (or lacis) cells and will form part of the juxtaglomerular apparatus (Ross and Pawlina, 2006)."}, {"name": "Anatomical Relations", "text": "Within the renal corpuscle, the glomerular basement membrane associated with several capillaries encloses a space containing a population of cells called mesangial cells."}, {"name": "Function", "text": "The primary function of mesangial cells is to remove trapped residue, etc. from the glomerular basement membrane and filtration slit diaphragm and so maintain these structures free of debris. Whilst they are phagocytic cells they are not derived from precursor cells of the mononuclear phagocytic system (monocytes). Mesangial cells also structurally support podocytes where the basement membrane is absent and synthesize and secrete molecules which have a role in responses to injury to the glomerulus. Mesangial cells also have contractile properties (Ross and Pawlina, 2006)."}, {"name": "Clinical Correlates", "text": "Mesangial cells proliferate in response to certain kidney diseases that are a consequence of abnormal amounts of debris accumulating in the glomerular filtration membrane. 

—Immunoglobulin A (IgA) nephropathy (Berger disease)

—Membranoproliferative glomerulonephritis

—Lupus nephritis

—Diabetic nephropathy"}, {"name": "References", "text": "Dorland, W. (2011) Dorland's Illustrated Medical Dictionary. 32nd edn. Philadelphia, USA: Elsevier Saunders.

Ross, M. H. and Pawlina, W. (2006) Histology: A text and atlas. Lippincott Williams & Wilkins."}]

items.name: Supporting Epithelial Cells
items.info:
[{"name": "Quick Facts", "text": "Supporting cells are cells that serve to provide support and protection and perhaps contribute to the nutrition of principal or other cells of certain organs; included are cells in the membranous labyrinth of the internal ear, olfactory epithelium, taste buds, and seminiferous tubules (Sertoli cells) (Dorland, 2011)."}, {"name": "Structure and/or Key Features", "text": "The olfactory epithelium is made up of various cell types such as basal cells, olfactory sensory neurons, and the supporting epithelial cells (Rao, Vemuri and Carpenter, 2007). 

The supporting cells in the olfactory epithelium can be likened to the glial cells in the nervous system. They are non-neural cells that are located in the apical layer of the olfactory epithelium (Cheok and Karunanayaka, 2018). There are two types of supporting cells, the sustentacular and microvillar cells. 

The microvillar cells take up a superficial location within the olfactory epithelium. They are electron-lucent and shaped like flasks. At the apex of microvillar cells, there are microvilli that extend into the mucus layer that overlies the olfactory epithelium. The thickness of microvillar cells are about one tenth that of olfactory sensory neurons (Standring, 2016). 

The sustentacular cells are columnar cells that divide and partly envelope the olfactory sensory neurons. There are many microvilli situated on the apical surface of the sustentacular cells. These apical microvilli extend into the mucus layer overlying the olfactory epithelium where they are interconnected with the cilia of the olfactory sensory neurons. Desmosomes connect adjacent sustentacular cells near the epithelial surface, while tight junctions connect sustentacular cells and olfactory sensory neurons at the epithelial surface. These bonds aid in the stability of the olfactory epithelium (Standring, 2016)."}, {"name": "Function", "text": "There are two types of supporting cells, the sustentacular cells and microvillar cells. 

The sustentacular cells provide metabolic and physical support for the olfactory epithelium. The physical support is as a result of the bonds formed by desmosomes and tight junctions between adjacent sustentacular cells, as well as between sustentacular cells and olfactory sensory neurons (Cheok and Karunanayaka, 2018; Standring, 2016). 

The function of microvillar cells is not well known. However, their apical microvilli increase the surface area for absorption."}, {"name": "References", "text": "Cheok, A. D. and Karunanayaka, K. (2018) Virtual Taste and Smell Technologies for Multisensory Internet and Virtual Reality. Human–Computer Interaction Series: Springer International Publishing.

Dorland, W. (2011) Dorland's Illustrated Medical Dictionary. 32nd edn. Philadelphia, USA: Elsevier Saunders.

Rao, M. S., Vemuri, M. C. and Carpenter, M. (2007) Neural Development and Stem Cells. Contemporary Neuroscience: Humana Press.

Standring, S. (2016) Gray's Anatomy: The Anatomical Basis of Clinical Practice. Gray's Anatomy Series 41st edition: Elsevier Limited."}]

items.name: Zona Pellucida (of Secondary Ovarian Follicle)
items.info:
[{"name": "Quick Facts", "text": "The zona pellucida is a thick, transparent, noncellular layer or envelope of uniform thickness surrounding an oocyte. Under the light microscope, it appears as a radially striated layer (Dorland, 2011)."}, {"name": "Structure and/or Key Feature(s)", "text": "A zona pellucida forms around the oocyte when it is about 50-80 μm in diameter. This is a tough, eosinophilic or very pink stained, acellular, protective membrane that separates the oocyte and surrounding granulosa cells. Granulosa cells send processes inwards invading the zona pellucida, so that they can form gap junctions with the microvilli of the oocyte."}, {"name": "Anatomical Relations", "text": "A zona pellucida forms around the oocyte."}, {"name": "Function", "text": "In the human female, the zona pellucida contains three classes of glycoproteins (ZP-1, ZP-2 and ZP-3) (Ross and Pawlina, 2006). 

—ZP-1 links ZP-2 and ZP-3.

—ZP-2 is a secondary spermatozoon binding protein.

—ZP-3 is the most significant spermatozoon binding receptor and the inducer of the acrosome reaction (Ross and Pawlina, 2006)."}, {"name": "List of Clinical Correlates", "text": "Failure of ZP-1 to function correctly results in ZP-3 accumulating in the ooplasm and no functional zona pellucida forming around the oocyte (Ross and Pawlina, 2006)."}, {"name": "References", "text": "Dorland, W. (2011) Dorland's Illustrated Medical Dictionary. 32nd edn. Philadelphia, USA: Elsevier Saunders.

Ross, M. H. and Pawlina, W. (2006) Histology: A text and atlas. Lippincott Williams & Wilkins."}]

items.name: Palpebral Branches of Infratrochlear Nerve
items.info:
[{"name": "Quick Facts", "text": "Origin: Infratrochlear nerve.

Course: Exits the orbit along the medial wall, inferior to the trochlea in the superomedial corner of the orbit. It enters the upper and lower eyelids medially.

Branches: None.

Supply: Skin and conjunctiva medial eyelids, lacrimal caruncle, and lacrimal sac."}, {"name": "Origin", "text": "The palpebral branches of the infratrochlear nerve are the terminal branches of the infratrochlear nerve, itself one of two terminal branches of the nasociliary nerve."}, {"name": "Course", "text": "The palpebral branches arise from the infratrochlear nerve as it emerges from the superomedial aspect of the orbit, below the trochlea of the superior oblique muscle. They course superficially within the skin of the eyelids."}, {"name": "Branches", "text": "There are no named branches."}, {"name": "Supplied Structures", "text": "The palpebral branches of the infratrochlear nerve help provide general sensory innervation to the eyelids, lacrimal caruncle, lacrimal sac, and lateral aspect of the nose above the medial canthus (Dorland, 2011)."}, {"name": "References", "text": "Dorland, W. (2011) Dorland's Illustrated Medical Dictionary. 32nd edn. Philadelphia, USA: Elsevier Sauders."}]

items.name: Myelin Sheath (Somatic Motor Efferent)
items.info: [{"name": "Quick Facts", "text": "The myelin sheath is the cylindrical covering on the axons of some neurons; it consists of concentric layers of myelin, formed in the peripheral nervous system by the plasma membrane of Schwann cells, and in the central nervous system by oligodendrocytes. It is interrupted at intervals along its length by gaps known as nodes of Ranvier. Myelin is an electrical insulator that serves to speed the conduction of nerve impulses (Dorland, 2011)."}, {"name": "Structure/Morphology", "text": "The myelin sheath tightly holsters the axon, it is a semi-crystalline lipid-protein-water layer. This layer is discontinuous and interrupted at regular intervals. Schwann cells produce myelin sheaths in the peripheral nervous system. A myelin sheath is formed when the Schwann cell wraps around the nerve axon in a spiral fashion, creating a number of layers, or lamellae. The process is known as myelination. Each myelin-producing cell surrounds only one segment of any given axon. Periodic interruptions where short portions of the axon are left uncovered by myelin are known as the nodes of Ranvier (Patestas and Gartner, 2016)."}, {"name": "Key Features/Anatomical Relations", "text": "Nodes of Ranvier are gaps found in the continuity of the myelin sheath surrounding an axon. At these gaps there is no myelin covering the axon, thus exposing it to the extracellular fluid. The nodes of Ranvier contain a high concentration of voltage-gated sodium channels. These voltage-gated sodium channels enable the nodes to function as generators of action potentials. This is achieved through the exchange of ions into and out of the ion channels."}, {"name": "Function", "text": "The Myelin sheath acts as an insulator for the axons improving their electrical conductance. The myelin sheath also has a protective role in that it acts as a physical barrier separating the axon from the electrically charged atoms and molecules of the extracellular fluid. Myelination has also been shown to reduce the energy required for transmission of action potentials (through the mechanism of saltatory conduction) (Patestas and Gartner, 2016)."}, {"name": "List of Clinical Correlates", "text": "\u2014Demyelinating disease"}, {"name": "References", "text": "Dorland, W. (2011) Dorland's Illustrated Medical Dictionary. 32nd edn. Philadelphia, USA: Elsevier Saunders.\n\nPatestas, M. A. and Gartner, L. P. (2016) A Textbook of Neuroanatomy. Wiley."}]

items.name: Cortex of Suprarenal Gland
items.info:
[{"name": "Quick Facts", "text": "The cortex of suprarenal gland is the outer firm yellowish layer that comprises the larger part of the suprarenal gland, consisting of the zona glomerulosa, the zona fasciculata, and the zona reticularis; it secretes, in response to release of corticotropin by the pulmonary gland, many steroid hormones (Dorland, 2011)."}, {"name": "Structure and/or Key Feature(s)", "text": "The cortex of the suprarenal gland is the outer layer of the suprarenal gland and surrounds all of the medulla, except the hilum. The cortex has a pale-yellow appearance.

The suprarenal cortex is comprised of three morphologically distinct zones. From outermost to innermost, the layers include the zona glomerulosa (10%), zona fasciculata (75%), and the zona reticularis. These layers are functionally separate from each other, producing various steroid hormones among them.

The cortex has a rich blood supply, due to the well supplied capsular plexus. The blood is well distributed throughout the different cortical zones via sinusoids, which end their supply in the medulla. Lymph is drained to the hilum, where a bundle of hilar lymph vessels carries lymph to the lateral aortic lymph nodes.

Adrenocortical secretions are typically controlled hormonally via the hypothalamic-pituitary axis. The zona glomerulosa is primarily regulated via corticotropin (ACTH) and angiotensin II (ANG II), while zona fasciculata and zona reticularis are regulated by ACTH. However, there is also neural control as suprarenal steroid release is also partially regulated via splanchnic nerve innervation (Dijkstra, Binnekade and Tilders, 1996)."}, {"name": "Anatomical Relations", "text": "The cortex of the suprarenal gland is the outer section of the gland and is enveloped by a fibrous capsule and is superjacent to the suprarenal medulla."}, {"name": "Function", "text": "The suprarenal cortex is comprised of three morphologically distinct zones (zona glomerulosa, fasciculata, and reticularis). Each zone is characterized by the expression of specific steroidogenic enzymes, resulting in the production of different hormones e.g., mineralocorticoids, glucocorticoids, and androgens."}, {"name": "Clinical Correlates", "text": "—Suprarenal insufficiency

—Congenital suprarenal hyperplasia"}, {"name": "References", "text": "Dorland, W. (2011) Dorland's Illustrated Medical Dictionary. 32nd edn. Philadelphia, USA: Elsevier Saunders.

Dijkstra, I., Binnekade, R. & Tilders, F. J. (1996) Diurnal variation in resting levels of corticosterone is not mediated by variation in adrenal responsiveness to adrenocorticotropin but involves splanchnic nerve integrity. Endocrinology, 137(2), 540-7."}]

items.name: Paravesical Fossa
items.info: [{"name": "Structure", "text": "The peritoneum is a complex, continuous serous membrane consisting of a layer of mesothelium and varying degrees of connective and adipose tissue. Visually, it\u2019s largely unremarkable, smooth, and has a lubricated surface due to the presence of peritoneal fluid."}, {"name": "Anatomical Relations", "text": "The paravesical fossa is shallow space that lies between the bladder and the anterolateral pelvic wall on each side. These fossae are limited laterally by the peritoneal fold overlaying the round ligament (female) or ductus deferens (male) and continues as the parietal peritoneum of the anterolateral abdominal wall. The fossae are limited medially by the peritoneum reflected over the bladder. Posteriorly, the paravesical fossae are separated from the pararectal fossae on the ipsilateral side by the ureter. In females, it\u2019s also separated by the double peritoneal fold that forms the broad ligament. The obturator canal opens inferior into the paravesical fossae."}, {"name": "Function", "text": "The paravesical fossa is usually shallow although its depth is variable and is affected by the degree of distension of the bladder (Standring, 2016)."}, {"name": "List of Clinical Correlates", "text": "- Ascites\n\n- Adhesions"}, {"name": "References", "text": "Standring, S. (2016) Gray's Anatomy: The Anatomical Basis of Clinical Practice. Gray's Anatomy Series 41 edn.: Elsevier Limited."}]

items.name: Superficial Layers of Epidermis
items.info:
[{"name": "Quick Facts", "text": "The stratum granulosum, or granular layer of epidermis, is the layer of the epidermis between the stratum lucidum and stratum spinosum, which consists of cells containing keratohyalin granules. The stratum lucidum, or clear layer of epidermis, is the translucent layer of the epidermis, just beneath the stratum corneum, particularly noticeable in the thick skin of the palms and soles. The stratum corneum, or horny layer, is the outermost layer of the epidermis, consisting of cells that are dead and desquamating (Dorland, 2011)."}, {"name": "Structure/Morphology", "text": "The superficial layers of the epidermis are composed of the stratum corneum, stratum lucidum, and stratum granulosum. The stratum corneum is composed of about 20 layers of flattened, or squamous, highly keratinized cells. Cells in this layer lack desmosomes; thus, the cells easily dissociate and desquamate from the skin surface (Arda, Goksugur and Tuzun, 2014).

The stratum lucidum is only present in thick skin, i.e., the plantar and palmar skin. It appears as a translucent layer of about five rows of squamous cells. 

The stratum granulosum has 1–5 cellular layers of flattened polygonal granulated cells. It is so called as it contains granules of filaggrin that cross links with keratin. Keratinocytes in the upper layer of the stratum granulosum also contain lamellar bodies, rich in glycolipids. The cells discharge this lipid-rich substance into the intercellular spaces, via exocytosis, thus forming the major epidermal permeability barrier of the skin (Arda, Goksugur and Tuzun, 2014)."}, {"name": "Function", "text": "The epidermis is continuously renewing its epithelial layers. This ensures that the epidermis acts as the body's first line of defense, acting as a barrier against environmental hazards, such as physical, chemical, biochemical and immunological threats (Baroni et al., 2012)."}, {"name": "References", "text": "Arda, O., Goksugur, N. and Tuzun, Y. (2014) 'Basic histological structure and functions of facial skin', Clin Dermatol, 32(1), pp. 3-13.

Baroni, A., Buommino, E., De Gregorio, V., Ruocco, E., Ruocco, V. and Wolf, R. (2012) 'Structure and function of the epidermis related to barrier properties', Clin Dermatol, 30(3), pp. 257-62.

Dorland, W. (2011) Dorland's Illustrated Medical Dictionary. 32nd edn. Philadelphia, USA: Elsevier Saunders."}]

items.name: Redundant Nuclear Envelope
items.info: [{"name": "Quick Facts", "text": "The redundant nuclear envelope is located at the base of the nucleus and contains several nuclear pores."}, {"name": "Structure and/or Key Feature(s)", "text": "Just like every other cell, the nucleus of the sperm has a bilaminar nuclear envelope (inner and outer membranes) that encases the nucleus. Unlike the nuclear envelope in other cells, it is mostly devoid of nuclear pores, which were eliminated during spermatogenesis. However, at the base of the nucleus, an area called the redundant nuclear envelope has an abundance of nuclear pores."}, {"name": "Anatomical Relations", "text": "The redundant nuclear envelope lies in an area at the base of the nucleus, caudal to the posterior ring."}, {"name": "Function", "text": "The function of the redundant nuclear envelope is not well understood. Considering it is situated in the posterior aspect of the nucleus, in an area adjacent to the cytoplasm, it is the only part of the sperm that information exchange between the nucleus and the constituents of the cytoplasm occurs. This theory is also backed up by the presence of nuclear pores in this region of the nuclear envelope, thus, it may have some functional significance (Guraya, 2012)."}, {"name": "References", "text": "Guraya, S. S. (2012) Biology of Spermatogenesis and Spermatozoa in Mammals. Springer Berlin Heidelberg."}]

items.name: Cuticle
items.info:
[{"name": "Quick Facts", "text": "The cuticle is a layer of cells on the external surface of the hair shaft, interlocking with the cuticle of the root sheath (Dorland, 2011)."}, {"name": "Structure/Morphology", "text": "The hair shaft is a rigid cylindrical structure which extends from the dermis or subcutaneous tissue through to the skin surface. The hair is composed of three concentric layers, the medulla, cortex, and cuticle of the hair, originating from the hair bulb at the base of the follicle. 

The cuticle is the outermost layer of the hair shaft, forming the surface of the hair. This is a thin layer composed of heavily keratinized flattened cells arranged as overlapping plates, giving the cuticle a ‘scaly’ appearance. The cuticle encloses the rest of the hair shaft components (Yang et al., 2014, Young, 2006)."}, {"name": "Function", "text": "The cuticle serves as a protective casing for the hair shaft and provides mechanical stability to the cortex."}, {"name": "References", "text": "Dorland, W. (2011) Dorland's Illustrated Medical Dictionary. 32nd edn. Philadelphia, USA: Elsevier Saunders.

Yang, F. C., Zhang, Y. and Rheinstadter, M. C. (2014) 'The structure of people's hair', PeerJ, 2, pp. e619.

Young, B. (2006) Wheater's Functional Histology: A Text and Colour Atlas. Student consult: Churchill Livingstone/Elsevier."}]

items.name: Principal Piece
items.info:
[{"name": "Quick Facts", "text": "The principal piece is the main portion of the tail of a spermatozoon, beginning at the anulus and gradually tapering toward the end piece (Dorland, 2011)."}, {"name": "Structure and/or Key Feature(s)", "text": "The sperm tail can be divided into three main segments: the middle piece, the principal piece, and the end piece. 

The principal piece constitutes the majority of the length of the sperm tail, measuring approximately 40 μm in length and 0.5 μm in width (Standring, 2016). It is composed of a fibrous sheath that envelops the axoneme and outer dense fibers."}, {"name": "Anatomical Relations", "text": "The principal piece is situated between the end ring of the middle piece and the end piece of the tail. It makes up the majority of the length of the sperm tail."}, {"name": "Function", "text": "The principal piece plays a key role in the motility of sperm, especially with the bending of the axoneme during the faster power strokes that facilitates the forward propulsion of the sperm."}, {"name": "References", "text": "Dorland, W. (2011) Dorland's Illustrated Medical Dictionary. 32nd edn. Philadelphia, USA: Elsevier Saunders.
Standring, S. (2016) Gray's Anatomy: The Anatomical Basis of Clinical Practice. Gray's Anatomy Series 41st edition edn.: Elsevier Limited."}]

items.name: Amacrine Granular Cell
items.info:
[{"name": "Quick Facts", "text": "Granular cells are inhibitory interneurons located in the granular layer of the olfactory bulb."}, {"name": "Structure and/or Key Features", "text": "Amacrine granular cells are neurons situated within the internal granular layer of the olfactory bulb. Granular cells are inhibitory interneurons with small cell bodies that are 5–10 μm in diameter, a number of short basal dendrites, long dendritic spines, and no axons. Because they have no axons, their action is totally reliant on dendrite-to-dendrite synapses. The granular cells can be classified into the light and dark subtypes based on how darkly or lightly their nuclei stain (Nieuwenhuys, Voogd and van Huijzen, 2007; Farbman et al., 1992). 

The dendrites of granular cells travel peripherally to the external plexiform layer. Here, the granular cell dendrites synapse with the secondary dendrites of the mitral and tufted cells. Excitation of the mitral and/or tufted cells in turn excites their secondary dendrites, which in turn excites the granular cells. The excited granular cells respond by inhibiting the mitral and tufted cells (Margolis and Getchell, 2013)."}, {"name": "Anatomical Relations", "text": "The olfactory bulb has a layered configuration. From external to internal, the layers include the olfactory nerve layer, glomerular layer, external plexiform layer, mitral cell layer, internal plexiform layer, and the (internal) granular cell layer (Standring, 2016).

The amacrine granular cells mostly lie within the internal granular layer of the olfactory bulb, deep to the mitral cells, although cells are situated in the internal plexiform and mitral cell layers. The granular cell layer is the most discernible layer in the olfactory bulb (Standring, 2016)."}, {"name": "Function", "text": "The inhibitory action of the granular cells plays a vital role in refining the sensory output of the olfactory bulb during olfactory transduction (Balu, Pressler and Strowbridge, 2007). The granular cells may also play a role in forming long-term memories associated with various scents."}, {"name": "Clinical Correlates", "text": "—Anosmia"}, {"name": "References", "text": "Balu, R., Pressler, R. T. and Strowbridge, B. W. (2007) 'Multiple modes of synaptic excitation of olfactory bulb granule cells', J Neurosci, 27(21), pp. 5621-32.

Farbman, A. I., Bard, J. B. L., Barlow, P. W. and Kirk, D. L. (1992) Cell Biology of Olfaction. Developmental and Cell Biology Series: Cambridge University Press.

Margolis, F. L. and Getchell, T. V. (2013) Molecular Neurobiology of the Olfactory System: Molecular, Membranous, and Cytological Studies. Springer US.

Nieuwenhuys, R., Voogd, J. and van Huijzen, C. (2007) The Human Central Nervous System: A Synopsis and Atlas. Steinkopff.

Standring, S. (2016) Gray's Anatomy: The Anatomical Basis of Clinical Practice. Gray's Anatomy Series 41st edition: Elsevier Limited."}]

items.name: Cranial Pia Mater
items.info: [{"name": "Quick Facts", "text": "The pia matter is the innermost of the three membranes (meninges) covering the brain and spinal cord, investing them closely and extending into the depths of the fissures and sulci; it consists of reticular, elastic, and collagenous fibers (Dorland, 2011)."}, {"name": "Structure", "text": "The pia mater is the innermost layer of the meninges and translates as \u201ctender mother,\u201d since it is a delicate vascular membrane. The inner surface of the pia mater is covered by flattened cells which are thin squamous epithelial cells. These flattened cells are derived from the mesenchyme (Pawlina, 2016)."}, {"name": "Key Features/Anatomical Relations", "text": "The cranial pia mater attaches directly to the surface of the brain and is continuous with the perivascular tissue sheath of the blood vessels of the brain. Additionally, the pia mater and the arachnoid fuse around the opening for the cranial nerves as they exit the dura mater (Pawlina, 2016)."}, {"name": "List of Clinical Correlates", "text": "\u2014Leptomeningitis"}, {"name": "References", "text": "Dorland, W. (2011) Dorland's Illustrated Medical Dictionary. 32nd edn. Philadelphia, USA: Elsevier Saunders.\n\nPawlina, W. 2016. Histology: A text and atlas with correlated cell and molecular biology. 7th ed. Philadelphia: Wolters Kluwer."}]

items.name: Vitreous Humor
items.info: [{"name": "Quick Facts", "text": "Vitreous humor is the clear gelatinous substance contained within the interstices of the stroma in the vitreous body of the camera postrema of the eyeball (Dorland, 2011)."}, {"name": "Structure and/or Key Features", "text": "The vitreous humor is a colorless liquid (99% water) contained within the posterior aspect of the eyeball, filling the space between the posterior surface of the lens and iris and the inner surface of the retina. It occupies about four fifths of its overall volume. It is thick and gel-like peripherally and more liquid near its center, which gives it some structure."}, {"name": "Anatomical Relations", "text": "The vitreous humor is loosely attached to the inner surface of the retina, the ciliary body, and the posterior surface of the lens, most especially to the pars plana of the ciliary body and the edge of the optic disc. Because of the lens, the anterior surface of the vitreous humor is hollowed into a deep concavity, the hyaloid fossa, in which the lens sits."}, {"name": "Function", "text": "The vitreous humor helps maintain the shape of the eyeball and its attachment to the outer surface of the retina presses it against the choroid and sclera layers of the eyeball, preventing wrinkling and detachment. Its clarity allows faithful transmission of light from the lens to the retina."}, {"name": "References", "text": "Dorland, W. (2011) Dorland's Illustrated Medical Dictionary. 32nd edn. Philadelphia, USA: Elsevier Saunders."}]

items.name: Vascular Circle of Optic Nerve
items.info: [{"name": "Quick Facts", "text": "The vascular circle of optic nerve is a circle of arteries in the sclera surrounding the site of entrance of the optic nerve (Dorland, 2011)."}, {"name": "Structure and/or Key Feature(s)", "text": "The vascular circle of the optic nerve (circle of Zinn or Haller) is formed by numerous branches of the ophthalmic artery, via the posterior ciliary arteries, that giving rise to about 20 short posterior ciliary arteries. These follow the course of the optic nerve and are apparent around it. Where the nerve pierces the sclera, they form an anastomotic circle that supplies the optic nerve head."}, {"name": "Anatomical Relations", "text": "The short posterior ciliary arteries that form the vascular circle of the optic nerve travel in the subarachnoid space between the intermediate (arachnoidal) and inner (pial) layers of the inner optic nerve sheath."}, {"name": "Function", "text": "The vascular circle of the optic nerve gives off centripetal branches that supply the laminar region of the head of the optic nerve. Additionally, pial vessels arising from the vascular circle pass retrogradely supplying the postlaminar region of the optic nerve head. Other branches arising from the short posterior ciliary arteries pierce the sclera and contribute to the vascularity of the choroid coat of the eye."}, {"name": "References", "text": "Dorland, W. (2011) Dorland's Illustrated Medical Dictionary. 32nd edn. Philadelphia, USA: Elsevier Saunders."}]

items.name: Connecting Stalk of Rod Cell
items.info: [{"name": "Quick Facts", "text": "The connecting stalk joins the outer and inner segments of the photoreceptor cells."}, {"name": "Structure and/or Key Features", "text": "The connecting stalk is the constricted region of the photoreceptor cells that joins the outer and inner segments. It contains a modified connecting cilium that arises from a basal body in the apical region of the inner segment."}, {"name": "Anatomical Relations", "text": "The connecting stalk connects the outer and inner segments of the photoreceptor cells."}, {"name": "Function", "text": "The connecting stalk acts as a conduit between the inner and outer segments of the photoreceptor cells, allowing for the transportation of lipids and proteins from the inner segment to the outer segment."}]

items.name: Interfascicular Veins
items.info: [{"name": "Quick Facts", "text": "The intrafascicular veins are part of the vasa nervorum and help drain the nerve."}, {"name": "Structure/Morphology", "text": "The interfascicular veins are located within the internal epineurium and form part of the vasa nervorum, small vessels that supply blood to peripheral nerves. This network of vessels supplies blood to the interior parts of the nerves and their coverings. The vasa vasorum are located within the connective tissue of the nerve scattered between the fascicles (Boissaud-Cooke, Pidgeon and Tunstall, 2015)."}, {"name": "Anatomical Relations", "text": "The vasa nervorum are the smallest vessels in the epineurial, perineurial, and endoneurial layers."}, {"name": "Function", "text": "The vasa nervorum supply the peripheral nerves with the molecular nutrients needed to carry out their cellular functions and for survival (Carp, 2015)."}, {"name": "References", "text": "Boissaud-Cooke, M., Pidgeon, T. E. and Tunstall, R. (2015) 'Chapter 37 - The Microcirculation of Peripheral Nerves: The Vasa Nervorum A2 - Tubbs, R. Shane', in Rizk, E., Shoja, M.M., Loukas, M., Barbaro, N. & Spinner, R.J. (eds.) Nerves and Nerve Injuries. San Diego: Academic Press, pp. 507-523.\n\nCarp, S. (2015) Peripheral Nerve Injury An Anatomical and Physiological Approach for Physical Therapy Intervention. EBL-Schweitzer: F. A. Davis Company."}]

items.name: Sclera
items.info:
[{"name": "Quick Facts", "text": "The sclera is the tough white outer coat of the eyeball, covering approximately five-sixths of its posterior surface, and continuous anteriorly with the cornea and posteriorly with the external sheath of the optic nerve; it and the cornea constitute the tunica fibrosa bulbi (Dorland, 2011)."}, {"name": "Structure and/or Key Features", "text": "The sclera forms part of the tough white outer fibrous layer for most of the eyeball, covering more than 93% of the surface of the eyeball. Only a small portion of the sclera is visible when the eyeball sits in situ in the orbital cavity. The sclera is replaced by the transparent cornea in the anterior portion of the eyeball (Standring, 2016).

The sclera can vary in thickness, ranging from about 0.3-1 mm. It is composed of collagen fibers that are interlaced, providing the strength and flexibility of the eyeball. The organization of these fibers lends the sclera its opaque appearance."}, {"name": "Anatomical Relations", "text": "The sclera is continuous anteriorly with the cornea at the corneoscleral junction and is attached to the ciliary body. Additionally, it is covered anteriorly by the conjunctiva. 

Posteriorly, the sclera is pierced by the optic nerve medial and slightly inferior to the midline of the eyeball. The outer surface of the sclera is continuous with the dura mater that covers the optic nerve, while the inner surface forms a plate with many perforations, the lamina cribrosa sclerae. Fibers from the optic nerve pass through these small perforations, along with the central retinal artery and vein. 

The internal surface of the sclera is lined by the choroid, thus, separating the sclera from the retina."}, {"name": "Function", "text": "The fibrous layer of the eyeball provides the tensile strength for withstanding intraocular pressure and determines its overall shape. Its toughness helps protect the eye from damage from the external environment. Additionally, the sclera provides the attachment for extraocular (extrinsic) muscles of the eyeball."}, {"name": "Clinical Correlates", "text": "—Scleritis

—Jaundice"}, {"name": "References", "text": "Dorland, W. (2011) Dorland's Illustrated Medical Dictionary. 32nd edn. Philadelphia, USA: Elsevier Saunders.

Standring, S. (2016) Gray's Anatomy: The Anatomical Basis of Clinical Practice. Gray's Anatomy Series 41 edn.: Elsevier Limited."}]

items.name: Nucleus (Inferior)
items.info:
[{"name": "Quick Facts", "text": "The nucleus is a spheroid body within a eukaryotic cell, separated from the cytoplasm by the nuclear envelope, and containing chromatin, a nucleolus, and nucleoplasm. In the nucleus, the cell's genetic information is stored on the chromosomes and RNA transcription and processing occur (Dorland, 2011)."}, {"name": "Structure", "text": "The oocyte nucleus, or germinal vesicle, is a prominent feature of the secondary oocyte and houses the genetic information of the cell. The nucleus is surrounded by a nuclear membrane containing nuclear pores that serve as a functional continuum between the nucleus and the cytoplasm. The nucleus also contains prominent nucleoli (the site of ribosomal RNA transcription, processing, and assembly of ribosomes) and chromatin (either condensed heterochromatin or diffuse euchromatin) (Plant and Zeleznik, 2014).

If fertilization occurs, the secondary oocyte completes meiosis II, creating a mature ovum and a second polar body. The nucleus is now known as the female pronucleus. A third polar body may also be observed if the first polar body undergoes meiosis II.

During fertilization, the plasma membrane of the oocyte fuses with that of the sperm and the nucleus and centriole of the sperm enters the cytoplasm of the oocyte. Nuclei of the oocyte and sperm gravitate towards each other; the male nucleus becomes swollen and forms the male pronucleus. Prior to fusion, each pronucleus duplicates its DNA and split in a normal mitotic division. Half the DNA from the female and male move to opposite poles, with a deep furrow developing and dividing the cytoplasm in two. This establishes a two-cell stage zygote, with a diploid number of chromosomes (Sadler, 2011)."}, {"name": "Key Features/Anatomical Relations", "text": "The nucleus lies within the cytoplasm of the cell, occupying a central position. The nucleus is surrounded by the nuclear membrane, which essentially demarcates the nucleus from the rest of the cell organelles."}, {"name": "Function", "text": "The oocyte nucleus carries the maternal DNA. The primary oocyte nucleus has 46 chromosomes (diploid), while the secondary oocyte has 23 chromosomes (haploid). Like the nucleus in other somatic cells, the nucleus of the oocyte has a variety of functions within a cell, including chromatin organization, DNA replication, and gene expression. These functions are facilitated by the nuclear matrix."}, {"name": "List of Clinical Correlates", "text": "- Infertility 

- Trisomy

- Monosomy

- Nondisjunction"}, {"name": "References", "text": "Dorland, W. (2011) Dorland's Illustrated Medical Dictionary. 32nd edn. Philadelphia, USA: Elsevier Saunders.

Plant, T. M. and Zeleznik, A. J. (2014) Knobil and Neill's Physiology of Reproduction. Elsevier Science.

Sadler, T. W. (2011) Langman's Medical Embryology. Wolters Kluwer Health."}]

items.name: Ovary (Right; Superior)
items.info:
[{"name": "Quick Facts", "text": "Location: Pelvic cavity.

Arterial Supply: Ovarian artery.

Venous Drainage: Ovarian vein.

Innervation: Sympathetic: greater and lesser thoracic and sacral splanchnic nerves; Parasympathetic: pelvic splanchnic nerves (S2 - S4).

Lymphatic Drainage: right, left, and intermediate lumbar lymph nodes."}, {"name": "Structure/Morphology", "text": "The ovaries are approximately 4x2x3cm in size, whitish, and consist of an inner medulla and an outer cortex (Standring, 2016). The cortex surrounds the medulla except at the hilum, where the ovarian vessels and nerves enter the ovary. The cortex itself is covered by a collagenous tunica albuginea and an epithelial layer and contains the ovarian follicles."}, {"name": "Anatomical Relations", "text": "The ovaries sit on the lateral pelvic wall and are retained in place within the pelvic cavity by a portion of the broad ligament called the mesovarium, which encloses the ovary and helps form the ovarian bursa. In addition, the ovary is supported by the suspensory ligament of the ovary and the proper ovarian ligament (round ligament of the ovary).

The fimbriae of the uterine tube, fingerlike mucosal folds of the uterine tube, lie in close proximity to the superior pole of the ovary. On the right-hand side, the ileocecal junction, cecum, and appendix are superolateral to the ovary, while on the left, the sigmoid colon and upper rectum are superolateral to the ovary.

During pregnancy, the ovaries ascend within the pelvic cavity and during the third trimester are situated in the abdominal cavity."}, {"name": "Function", "text": "At birth, females have their full complement of primordial follicles. After puberty, each month, up to 20 primordial follicles begin to develop. However, only one follicle becomes the dominant follicle and undergoes ovulation. The remnant of this follicle becomes the corpus luteum and secretes progesterone and estrogen."}, {"name": "Arterial Supply", "text": "The ovarian arteries arise within the abdominal cavity as branches of the abdominal aorta. They descend into the pelvic cavity where they run within the suspensory ligament and divide into ovarian and tubal branches."}, {"name": "Venous Drainage", "text": "The venous drainage of the ovary forms via pampiniform plexus, which form two ovarian veins that travel with the ovarian artery. These veins usually unite to form a single ovarian vein that drains directly into the inferior vena cava on the right and via the renal vein on the left."}, {"name": "Innervation", "text": "Innervation of the ovary is supplied primarily through fibers that pass through the ovarian plexus. The upper region of the ovary is innervated by nerves derived from renal and aortic plexuses, while the lower portion is innervated by branches of the superior and inferior hypogastric plexuses. Sympathetic innervation of the ovary travels from the thoracic and sacral splanchnic nerves, whereas parasympathetic innervation is supplied through pelvic splanchnic nerves."}, {"name": "Lymphatic Drainage", "text": "Lymph from the reproductive organs such as the ovaries, uterine tube and uterus is received by the right, left, and intermediate lymph node groups (Földi et al., 2012)."}, {"name": "List of Clinical Correlates", "text": "—Ovarian cysts

—Ovarian cancer"}, {"name": "References", "text": "Földi, M., Földi, E., Strößenreuther, R. and Kubik, S. (2012) Földi's Textbook of Lymphology: for Physicians and Lymphedema Therapists. Elsevier Health Sciences.

Standring, S. (2016) Gray's Anatomy: The Anatomical Basis of Clinical Practice. Gray's Anatomy Series 41 edn.: Elsevier Limited."}]

items.name: Epithelial Cell of Spiral Limbus
items.info: [{"name": "Quick Facts", "text": "The upper surface of the spiral limbus contains cells that project outwards and are separated at right angles by furrows, resembling teeth, thus are called the acoustic teeth. The spiral limbus is also covered in epithelium, where the cells overlying the acoustic teeth are squamous, while the cells that sit in between, in the interdental furrows, are flask shaped. These are known as interdental cells. This epithelium is continuous with the vestibular membrane and with the epithelium lining the internal spiral sulcus (Standring, 2016)."}, {"name": "Structure and/or Key Feature(s)", "text": "The upper surface of the spiral limbus contains cells that project outwards and are separated at right angles by furrows, resembling teeth, thus are called the acoustic teeth. The spiral limbus is also covered in epithelium, where the cells overlying the acoustic teeth are squamous, while the cells that sit in between, in the interdental furrows, are flask shaped. These are known as interdental cells. This epithelium is continuous with the vestibular membrane and with the epithelium lining the internal spiral sulcus (Standring, 2016). \n\nThe internal spiral sulcus is the C-shaped concavity on the spiral limbus. A stratified squamous epithelium lines the sulcus and continues up over the vestibular edge and across the auditory teeth."}, {"name": "Function", "text": "The interdental cells of the spiral limbus produce and maintain tectorial membrane components from a developmental stage. The tectorial membrane is a gelatin sheet which is involved in the auditory signal transduction process via disruption of the stereocilia of the specialized hair cells."}, {"name": "References", "text": "Standring, S. (2016) Gray's Anatomy: The Anatomical Basis of Clinical Practice., 41st edition. Elsevier Limited."}]

items.name: Glycogen Granule
items.info:
[{"name": "Quick Facts", "text": "Glycogen is a large polysaccharide similar to amylopectin but more highly branched, consisting of chains of glucose residues in a-(1,4) linkage with branches created by a-(1,6) linkages. It constitutes the major carbohydrate reserve of animals, stored primarily in liver and muscle, and is synthesized and degraded for energy as demanded (Dorland, 2011)."}, {"name": "Structure and/or Key Feature(s)", "text": "Glycogen is the non-membranous storage form of glucose and is common as clusters of granules 25-40 nm in diameter in liver cells, skeletal muscle fibers, and adipocytes. They are a little larger than ribosomes but in the liver cells they can form aggregates about 90-95 nm in diameter."}, {"name": "Anatomical Relations", "text": "Normally glycogen would be located in close proximity to the smooth endoplasmic reticulum (sER), since the enzymes within the sER breakdown glycogen into glucose (Ross and Pawlina, 2006; Ovalle, Nahirney and Netter, 2013; McKinley, O'Loughlin and Pennefather-O'Brien, 2016)."}, {"name": "Function", "text": "Glycogen stored in granules is one of the energy sources for the cell (Ross and Pawlina, 2006; Ovalle, Nahirney and Netter, 2013; McKinley, O'Loughlin and Pennefather-O'Brien, 2016)."}, {"name": "List of Clinical Correlates", "text": "Glycogen storage diseases are inherited disorders that affect the production or breakdown of glycogen. A deficiency in the enzyme glucose-6-phosphate causes abnormal accumulation of glycogen in liver and muscle cells (Ovalle, Nahirney and Netter, 2013)."}, {"name": "References", "text": "Dorland, W. (2011) Dorland's Illustrated Medical Dictionary. 32nd edn. Philadelphia, USA: Elsevier Saunders.

McKinley, M. P., O'Loughlin, V. D. and Pennefather-O'Brien, E. E. (2016) Human Anatomy. 5th edn.: McGraw-Hill Education.
