items.name: Voltage-Gated Sodium Channel
items.info:
[{"name": "Quick Facts", "text": "A sodium channel is a voltage-gated channel selective for the passage of sodium ions; sodium channels are activated by membrane depolarization and are the main causes of depolarization and repolarization of the nerve membrane during the propagation of action potentials (Dorland, 2011)."}, {"name": "Structure", "text": "The voltage-gated sodium channel is created by a single long polypeptide resulting in “pores” in the axolemma that are highly selective to Na+. At a negative resting membrane potential, the pore remains closed. When the membrane is depolarized to threshold, the molecule reconfigures such that Na+ can pass through the pore.

Voltage-gated sodium ion channels can exist in three main conformational states: closed, open, and inactivated. They change from one conformational state to the other on neurotransmitter binding.

Prior to the generation of an action potential, the membrane is at its resting potential and the voltage-gated sodium channels are in their deactivated conformational state. When the membrane potential reaches -55 mV approximately, a conformational change occurs in the sodium ion channel protein and “opens” the channel to allow the influx of sodium ions. This results in the depolarization of the cell and an initiation of the upstroke of the action potential. This step is the “activation” step. At this point, the voltage-gated sodium channel is referred to as being open and active (Ross and Pawlina, 2006; Bear, Connors and Paradiso, 2007).

Following the opening and activation of the voltage-gated sodium channel, influx of sodium ions, and subsequent depolarization, the channel changes its conformational state to “closed” once the action potential generated reaches its threshold (Ross and Pawlina, 2006; Bear, Connors and Paradiso, 2007)."}, {"name": "Anatomical Relations", "text": "Generally, voltage-gated channels in the nervous system are located:

—on the cell body and dendrites of neurons;

—on the nodes of Ranvier and intermodal region in myelinated axons;

—on the axon hillock on unmyelinated axons (Ross and Pawlina, 2006; Bear, Connors and Paradiso, 2007)."}, {"name": "Function", "text": "Voltage-gated sodium channels play a vital role in neurotransmission and neural function. They regulate the passage of sodium between the extracellular and intracellular environments, and so, facilitates the depolarization of neural cells and generation of action potential (Ross and Pawlina, 2006; Bear, Connors and Paradiso, 2007)."}, {"name": "Clinical Correlates", "text": "Traumatic injury to axon may open sodium channels which in turn, causes voltage-gated calcium channels to open and so an influx of calcium ions into the cell. This influx can activate destructive enzymes causing irreparable damage to the cytoskeleton and mitochondria and ultimately neuronal cell death."}, {"name": "References", "text": "Bear, M. F., Connors, B. W. and Paradiso, M. A. (2007) Neuroscience. Lippincott Williams & Wilkins.

Dorland, W. (2011) Dorland's Illustrated Medical Dictionary. 32nd edn. Philadelphia, USA: Elsevier Saunders.

Ross, M. H. and Pawlina, W. (2006) Histology: A text and atlas. Lippincott Williams & Wilkins."}]

items.name: Filiform Papillae
items.info:
[{"name": "Quick Facts", "text": "The filiform papillae are the threadlike elevations that cover most of the tongue surface (Dorland, 2011)."}, {"name": "Structure and/or Key Features", "text": "The filiform papillae are widely distributed along the entire dorsal surface of the tongue. They are threadlike (filum) and usually have peaked or pointed tips, which are more rounded in the anterior regions of the tongue. They are composed of connective tissue cores which are columnar in shape with a central upper depression. These have hair-like protrusions emanating from it, with varying quantity and thickness based on location of papillae (Kobayashi et al., 1994).

The filiform papillae are unique in terms of the lingual papillae as they predominantly have a keratinized stratified squamous epithelium and are the only papillae without taste buds, so they do not participate in gustation. Their role is focused on mastication due to their large population and friction-generating ability."}, {"name": "Function", "text": "The filiform papillae increase the total surface area of the tongue and, thus, the total contact area between the food particles and the tongue."}, {"name": "References", "text": "Dorland, W. (2011) Dorland's Illustrated Medical Dictionary. 32nd edn. Philadelphia, USA: Elsevier Saunders.

Kobayashi, K., Kumakura, M., Shinkai, H. & Ishii, K. (1994) Three-dimensional fine structure of the lingual papillae and their connective tissue cores in the human tongue. Kaibogaku Zasshi, 69(5), 624-35."}]

items.name: Motor Neuron
items.info:
[{"name": "Quick Facts", "text": "A motor neuron is an efferent neuron conveying motor impulses (Dorland, 2011)."}, {"name": "Structure", "text": "Motor neurons are usually made up of large and myelinated alpha-efferent axons. They arise from motor neuron cell bodies in the anterior horns of the gray matter within the spinal cord. Their terminal branches are short unmyelinated twigs which travel through the endomysium to form part of the neuromuscular junction."}, {"name": "Key Features/Anatomical Relations", "text": "The motor neuron axon branches into many terminal branches, which enter the endomysium. The myelin sheath of the axon ends at the neuromuscular junction, however, the terminal branches are covered by a thin layer, the neurilemma, which arises from the outer membrane of the Schwann cell. This external lamina of the Schwann cell, fuses with the sarcolemma, covering the points of contact between axonal branches and the muscle cell (Martini, Nath and Bartholomew, 2017). 

The terminal axonal branches are dilated into a presynaptic structure which sits in shallow depressions on the surface of the muscle fiber. These areas are the receptor regions. The sarcolemma at these points will have deep junctional folds for increased surface area, ready to receive neurotransmitters responsible for muscle contraction."}, {"name": "Function", "text": "The function of the neuromuscular junction is to induce an action potential across the muscle fiber, initiating muscle contraction. 

The nerve action potential travels across the axon of the motor neuron to its terminal branches and to the dilated presynaptic structures which sit within shallow depressions on the muscle fiber. These dilated ends contain both mitochondria and vesicles, the latter of which contain the neurotransmitter, acetylcholine. The nerve action potential triggers the release of acetylcholine which diffuses across the space between the presynaptic dilation and the sarcolemma. This space is called the synaptic cleft. The sarcolemma at these junctions contains a series of folds to increase the surface area as they contain acetylcholine receptors. Once the acetylcholine binds with their respective receptors, it induces an action potential across the muscle. The action potential will move along the surface of the muscle cell, along the t tubules that penetrate the sarcoplasm initiating release of CA2+ which in turn induces the contraction cycle (Standring, 2016)."}, {"name": "List of Clinical Correlates", "text": "—Botulism"}, {"name": "References", "text": "Dorland, W. (2011) Dorland's Illustrated Medical Dictionary. 32nd edn. Philadelphia, USA: Elsevier Saunders.

Martini, F. H., Nath, J. L. and Bartholomew, E. F. (2017) Fundamentals of Anatomy & Physiology. Pearson Education.

Standring, S. (2016) Gray's Anatomy: The Anatomical Basis of Clinical Practice. Gray's Anatomy Series: Elsevier Limited."}]

items.name: Protoplasmic Astrocyte
items.info:
[{"name": "Quick Facts", "text": "Protoplasmic astrocytes are astrocytes found mainly in the gray matter of the brain, having many branching, thick cytoplasmic processes (Dorland, 2011)."}, {"name": "Structure and/or Key Features", "text": "Recognizable by their fibrous, star-shaped appearance and flattened cell body, astrocytes are one of the neuroglial cells of the retina. Other neuroglial cells in the retina include radial glial (Müller) cells and microglia. Astrocytes in the retina may also be described as perivascular cells, as they form an irregular supportive network around retinal fibers and capillaries (Kolb, 1995d; Remington and Goodwin, 2011)."}, {"name": "Anatomical Relations", "text": "In the retina astrocytes are located in the inner layers, typically in the ganglion cell and nerve fiber layers. They are believed to structurally contribute to the inner limiting membrane (Remington and Goodwin, 2011). Astrocytes reach their peak density on the optic nerve head; however, numbers decline in radiating rings traveling away from the nerve head. Astrocytes are absent from the ora serrata and avascular fovea (Kolb, 1995d)."}, {"name": "Function", "text": "Astrocytes are largely responsible for providing structure and support to retinal neurons, while they additionally play a role in the neural tissue reaction to infection or injury (Remington and Goodwin, 2011). They contain glycogen and are believed to provide a source of nutrition, specifically glucose, to the neurons they encircle. Further, it is believed that astrocytes contribute to maintaining ionic homeostasis, specifically regulating potassium levels and metabolizing neurotransmitters (Kolb, 1995d)."}, {"name": "List of Clinical Correlates", "text": "- Gliosis

- Reactive Gliosis"}, {"name": "References", "text": "Dorland, W. (2011) Dorland's Illustrated Medical Dictionary. 32nd edn. Philadelphia, USA: Elsevier Saunders.

Kolb, H. (1995d) 'Simple Anatomy of the Retina', in Kolb, H., Fernandez, E. and Nelson, R. (eds.) Webvision: The Organization of the Retina and Visual System. Salt Lake City (UT): University of Utah Health Sciences Center

Remington, L. A. and Goodwin, D. (2011) Clinical Anatomy of the Visual System E-Book. Elsevier Health Sciences."}]

items.name: Deep Artery of Clitoris
items.info:
[{"name": "Quick Facts", "text": "Origin: Internal pudendal artery.

Course: Anteriorly and traverses the perineal membrane.

Branches: Helicine branches.

Supplied Structures: Corpora cavernosa of the clitoris."}, {"name": "Origin", "text": "The deep artery of clitoris is one of two terminal branches of the internal pudendal artery."}, {"name": "Course", "text": "It travels in an anteromedial direction and must traverse the perineal membrane before it enters the crura of the clitoris. It passes within the corpus cavernosum of the crura and into the body of the clitoris."}, {"name": "Branches", "text": "As it passes through the erectile tissue of the clitoris, the deep artery of clitoris gives off small helicine branches. These helicine branches open into the cavernous spaces, or sinusoids, between the trabeculae of the corpus cavernosum (Toesca, Stolfi and Cocchia, 1996)."}, {"name": "Supplied Structures", "text": "The deep artery of clitoris supplies the corpora cavernosa of the clitoris."}, {"name": "References", "text": "Toesca, A., Stolfi, V. M. and Cocchia, D. (1996) 'Immunohistochemical study of the corpora cavernosa of the human clitoris', Journal of anatomy, 188 (Pt 3), pp. 513-520."}]

items.name: Teniae Coli
items.info:
[{"name": "Quick Facts", "text": "The teniae coli are the three thickened bands, about 0.6 cm wide and one-sixth shorter than the colon, formed by the longitudinal fibers in the tunica muscularis of the large intestine; they extend from the root of the vermiform appendix to the rectum, where the fibers form anterior and posterior layers that they spread out into a continuous layer encircling the tube. The three taeniae are the taenia libera, taenia mesocolica, and taenia omentalis, named according to the attachments to each on the transverse colon (Dorland, 2011)."}, {"name": "Structure/Morphology", "text": "The teniae coli are three strips of longitudinal smooth muscle that run along the colon and reside beneath its outer serosal surface (Moore, Dalley and Agur, 2013)."}, {"name": "Anatomical Relations", "text": "The three teniae are termed the mesocolic tenia, free tenia, and omental tenia. The free tenia is located opposite to the mesentery, the omental tenia is on the posterolateral aspect of the colon, and the mesocolic tenia is on the posteromedial aspect of the colon.

Due to the hepatic flexure at the junction of the transverse colon, the teniae coli have a rotated position. Thus, the anterior free tenia becomes inferior, the posteromedial mesocolic tenia becomes posterior, and the posterolaterally placed omental teniae coli becomes superior. 

Once they reach the sigmoid colon, the teniae expand to take up a greater portion of the circumference of the colon where they form distinct bands located anteriorly and posteriorly. Both of these bands eventually converge and unite to form a complete longitudinal muscle layer, a feature characteristic of the rectum."}, {"name": "Function", "text": "The longitudinal and circular layers of the muscular layer of the colon are responsible for producing peristaltic contractions of the gut, thus propelling the ingested substance through the lumen of the gut. Additionally, contraction of the teniae coli results in bulging of the colonic haustra, giving rise to the sacculation, which give the colon its segmented appearance."}, {"name": "References", "text": "Dorland, W. (2011) Dorland's Illustrated Medical Dictionary. 32nd edn. Philadelphia, USA: Elsevier Saunders.

Moore, K. L., Dalley, A. F. and Agur, A. M. R. (2013) Clinically Oriented Anatomy. Clinically Oriented Anatomy 7th edn.: Wolters Kluwer Health/Lippincott Williams & Wilkins."}]

items.name: External Root Sheath
items.info:
[{"name": "Quick Facts", "text": "The epithelial portion of the hair follicle is divided into the inner root sheath and the outer root sheath. The inner root sheath has three layers: Huxley layer, Henle layer, and the cuticle of the root sheath. The outer root sheath does not have distinct layers and merges with the epidermis near the skin surface (Dorland, 2011)."}, {"name": "Structure/Morphology", "text": "The external root sheath envelops the inner root sheath and the hair shaft. It extends from the hair bulb to the epidermis and opens up to the surface of the skin. This layer and the internal root sheath are produced by the rapidly reproducing matrix cells found in the periphery of the follicular bulb. It shares a cellular composition found in the epidermis along the majority of its length. However, at the level of the hair bulb, the cells are more consistent with that of the stratum basale of the epidermis (Standring, 2016; Joshi, 2011).

Within the external root sheath lies the bulge, this is an enlarged area of the external root sheath just below the level of the sebaceous gland which is a reservoir of stem cells of the hair follicle. The bulge is also the site at which the arrector pili muscle will attach to the hair follicle. The External Root Sheath is separated by the external layer of the hair follicle, the Connective Tissue Sheath, by the Glassy Membrane (a form of basement membrane) (Ohyama, 2007; Young, 2006)."}, {"name": "Function", "text": "Although the external root sheath does not partake in the formation of the hair shaft, it contains functional units of the hair follicle including the bulge of the hair follicle which is a region containing stem cells. It also gives rise to the sebaceous gland of the hair follicle which produces sebum which lubricates and protects the hair shaft and skin surface (Niderla-Bielińska, Jankowska-Steifer and Moskalewski, 2008; Niemann, 2009)."}, {"name": "References", "text": "Dorland, W. (2011) Dorland's Illustrated Medical Dictionary. 32nd edn. Philadelphia, USA: Elsevier Saunders.

Joshi, R. S. (2011) 'The Inner Root Sheath and the Men Associated with it Eponymically', Int J Trichology, 3(1), pp. 57-62.

Niderla-Bielińska, J., Jankowska-Steifer, E. and Moskalewski, S. (2008) Structure and function of outer and inner root sheath of hair follicle. Stem cells of hair follicle.

Niemann, C. (2009) 'Differentiation of the sebaceous gland', Dermato-Endocrinology, 1(2), pp. 64-67.

Ohyama, M. (2007) 'Hair follicle bulge: a fascinating reservoir of epithelial stem cells', J Dermatol Sci, 46(2), pp. 81-9.

Standring, S. (2016) Gray's Anatomy: The Anatomical Basis of Clinical Practice. Gray's Anatomy Series: Elsevier Limited.

Young, B. (2006) Wheater's Functional Histology: A Text and Colour Atlas. Student consult: Churchill Livingstone/Elsevier."}]

items.name: Connecting Stalk of Cone Cell
items.info: [{"name": "Quick Facts", "text": "The connecting stalk joins the outer and inner segments of the photoreceptor cells."}, {"name": "Structure and/or Key Features", "text": "The connecting stalk is the constricted region of the photoreceptor cells that joins the outer and inner segments. It contains a modified connecting cilium that arises from a basal body in the apical region of the inner segment."}, {"name": "Anatomical Relations", "text": "The connecting stalk connects the outer and inner segments of the photoreceptor cells."}, {"name": "Function", "text": "The connecting stalk acts as a conduit between the inner and outer segments of the photoreceptor cells, allowing for the transportation of lipids and proteins from the inner segment to the outer segment."}]

items.name: Articular Plate
items.info: [{"name": "Quick Facts", "text": "The articular plate, basal plate, and the striated columns are referred to as the connecting piece between the sperm head and tail."}, {"name": "Structure and/or Key Feature(s)", "text": "The articular plate is a dense fibrous structure found in the neck of the sperm. It conforms to the concave shape of the basal plate at the base of the nucleus, thus acting like a ball and socket joint at the interface between the head and the neck of the sperm."}, {"name": "Anatomical Relations", "text": "The articular plate is in contact with the basal plate, proximally, and the striated columns are continuous with the articular plate, distally."}, {"name": "Function", "text": "Collectively, the articular plate, basal plate, and the striated columns are referred to as the \u2018connecting piece\u2019 between the sperm head and tail. Therefore, the articular plate acts as a structural anchorage and an articulation between the head and tail."}]

items.name: Desmosome (Cardiac Muscle Cell)
items.info:
[{"name": "Quick Facts", "text": "Desmosomes are a type of adhesive junction that links intermediate filaments and cell membranes within and between cells by homophilic interactions between cadherins (desmogleins and desmocollins); it is a small, discrete, circular, dense body abundant in epithelial cells but occurring also in other cell types. It consists of local differentiations of the apposing cell membranes, with a dense cytoplasmic plaque underlying each membrane, toward which numerous tonofilaments converge; a dense lamina may occur within the intercellular gap (Dorland, 2011)."}, {"name": "Structure and/or Key Features", "text": "Desmosomes are complex disk-shaped structures at the surface of two interfacing cells. In the region of the junction, the cell membranes are separated further apart (about 30 nm). This intercellular space is occupied by a dense band called the intermediate line and represents the site for transmembrane glycoproteins, namely desmoplakins and plakoglobins ,which anchor intermediate filaments.

There is a circular plaque of material on the cytosolic side of the junction called the desmosomal attachment plaque which consists of about 12 different proteins. It is about 400 nm × 250 nm × 10 nm.

In epithelial cells, intermediate cytokeratin filaments of the cytoskeleton are inserted into the attachment plaque and/or loop back into the cytoplasm.

In nonepithelial cells, the intermediate filaments are not cytokeratin but other proteins such as desmin or vimentin (Mescher, 2013; Ross and Pawlina, 2016)."}, {"name": "Function", "text": "The intermediate cytokeratin filaments of the cytoskeleton inserted into the attachment plaque are very strong, so they provide firm adhesion between adjacent cells (Mescher, 2013; Ross and Pawlina, 2016)."}, {"name": "References", "text": "Dorland, W. (2011) Dorland's Illustrated Medical Dictionary. 32nd edn. Philadelphia, USA: Elsevier Saunders.

Mescher, A. (2013) Junqueira's Basic Histology: Text and Atlas. 13th edn.: McGraw-Hill Education.

Ross, M. H. and Pawlina, W. (2016) Histology: A Text and Atlas. Wolters Kluwer Health."}]

items.name: Infraorbital Nerve
items.info:
[{"name": "Quick Facts", "text": "Origin: Maxillary nerve. 

Course: Passes anteriorly from the pterygopalatine fossa into the orbit through the inferior orbital fissure. Travels within the inferior orbital groove along the floor of the orbit. It exits the orbit passing through the infraorbital foramen just below the lower eyelid and onto the cheek.

Branches: Anterior and middle superior alveolar branches, inferior palpebral nerves, external and internal nasal and superior labial branches.

Supply: Conveys general sensory information from the skin of the anterior face overlying the maxilla and the anterior cheek, the upper lip, lateral portions of the nose, and mucosa of the upper lip, anterior-most nasal cavity, and maxillary sinus."}, {"name": "Origin", "text": "The infraorbital nerve originates as one of the major branches of the maxillary nerve within the pterygopalatine fossa. It is often considered the anterior continuation of the maxillary nerve."}, {"name": "Course", "text": "The infraorbital nerve exits the pterygopalatine fossa by passing anteriorly through the inferior orbit fissure. It continues anteriorly along the floor of the orbit in the infraorbital groove. At variable position along its course, the infraorbital groove becomes enclosed superiorly by bone, thus becoming the infraorbital canal. This canal opens distally at the infraorbital foramen of the maxilla where the nerve emerges onto the anterior face, roughly 5-10 mm below the inferior margin of the orbit, lateral to the pyriform aperture of the nasal cavity."}, {"name": "Branches", "text": "The infraorbital nerve gives rise to five branches. 

—The middle and anterior superior alveolar nerves are both given off within the infraorbital groove/canal.

—The inferior palpebral branches form upon emerging from the infraorbital foramen and immediately ascend, passing deep to orbicularis oculi muscle into the lower eyelid

—The nasal branches of the infraorbital nerve also form upon emerging from the infraorbital foramen and immediately pass medially to the lateral surface of the nose.

—The superior labial branches also form upon emerging from the infraorbital foramen and immediately pass inferiorly, deep to levator labii superioris muscle."}, {"name": "Supplied Structures", "text": "The middle and anterior superior alveolar nerves supply the mucosa of the maxillary sinus, as well as the first molar and premolar, and the canine and incisor, upper teeth, respectively. The inferior palpebral nerve supplies the skin of the upper cheek and lower eyelid including the conjunctiva on its inner surface. The nasal branches supply the skin of the medial cheek and lateral nose including the mucosa on its inner surface. The superior labial branches supply the skin of the lower cheek, upper lip (including the philtrum), and vermillion zone, as well as the mucosa of its buccal surface.

The maxillary nerve and its infraorbital branch is properly considered a purely general sensory nerve. However, within the pterygopalatine fossa is housed a major parasympathetic ganglion, the pterygopalatine ganglion, whose postganglionic fibers opportunistically join the branches of the maxillary nerve and follow them to their smooth muscle and glandular targets in the periphery. Those that hitch a ride with the infraorbital nerve innervate the labial oral mucus glands of the upper lip and mucosa."}, {"name": "List of Clinical Correlates", "text": "—Trigeminal neuralgia

—Maxillary sinusitis

—Abscessed upper tooth"}]

items.name: Periglomerular Cell
items.info:
[{"name": "Quick Facts", "text": "The periglomerular cells are nerve cells in the olfactory bulb that have synaptic connections with glomeruli, mitral cells, and tufted cells, and are thought to act as dampers (Dorland, 2011)."}, {"name": "Structure and/or Key Features", "text": "The periglomerular cell is one of the two main types of interneurons in the olfactory bulb. The second type is the granular cell. They are contained almost exclusively within the glomerular layer, which contains the external tufted cells and the axons of other cells. The periglomerular cell synapses with the olfactory sensory neurons, the mitral/tufted cells, and the centrifugal efferent nerve fibers (Standring, 2016; Pignatelli and Belluzzi, 2017; Csillag, 2007). 

The periglomerular cells have axons that project laterally, all of which terminate in the extraglomerular parts of the olfactory bulb (Standring, 2016; Kosaka and Kosaka, 2009). 

The periglomerular cells are the only catecholaminergic neurons located within the olfactory bulb. They are significantly flexible and continuously regenerated throughout a person’s lifetime. Although most of the periglomerular cells are dopaminergic, some are GABAergic (Pignatelli and Belluzzi, 2017).

Some periglomerular cells receive minimal to no inputs from the olfactory sensory neurons and these particular types of periglomerular cells have been known to be located in specific areas within the glomerulus. Thus, the glomerulus essentially has two compartments, the olfactory neuron compartment and the non-olfactory neuron compartment. It is within the olfactory neuron compartment is where periglomerular neurons synapse with mitral/tufted cells and olfactory sensory cells (Kosaka and Kosaka, 2009)."}, {"name": "Anatomical Relations", "text": "The periglomerular cells are located in the periglomerular region, within the glomerular layer of the olfactory bulb."}, {"name": "Function", "text": "The periglomerular cells are tactically located at the entry points of the olfactory bulb where they synapse with olfactory sensory neurons conveying incoming olfactory neural information. This unique positioning at the commencement point of the olfactory bulb circuitry means they play a major role in processing of odors and modification of the olfactory bulb neural interconnections to external stimuli (Pignatelli and Belluzzi, 2017)."}, {"name": "Clinical Correlates", "text": "—Anosmia"}, {"name": "References", "text": "Dorland, W. (2011) Dorland's Illustrated Medical Dictionary. 32nd edn. Philadelphia, USA: Elsevier Saunders.

Kosaka, T. and Kosaka, K. (2009) 'Olfactory Bulb Anatomy', in Squire, L.R. (ed.) Encyclopedia of Neuroscience. Oxford: Academic Press, pp. 59-69.

Pignatelli, A. and Belluzzi, O. (2017) 'Dopaminergic Neurones in the Main Olfactory Bulb: An Overview from an Electrophysiological Perspective', Front Neuroanat, 11, pp. 7.

Standring, S. (2016) Gray's Anatomy: The Anatomical Basis of Clinical Practice. Gray's Anatomy Series 41st edition: Elsevier Limited."}]

items.name: Corona Radiata (Inferior)
items.info:
[{"name": "Quick Facts", "text": "The coronal radiata is a superficial layer of radially elongated follicle cells surrounding the zona pellucida of a secondary oocyte (Dorland, 2011)."}, {"name": "Structure", "text": "The coronal radiata is a layer of granulosa/follicle cells (referred to as cumulus cells) surrounding the zona pellucida of a secondary oocyte (Dorland, 2011). Additionally, the corona radiata forms the innermost layer of the cumulus oophorus. The corona radiata and cumulus oophorus span approximately 7-12.5 μm in diameter (Gardner et al., 2008; Harrison, Bonnar and Thompson, 2012). 

The corona radiata forms during folliculogenesis. During the ovarian cycle, cumulus cells make intimate contact with the oocyte and deposit an acellular glycoprotein layer around the surface of the oocyte called the zona pellucida. Cumulus cells remain attached to the zona pellucida and form the corona radiata.

Microvillus projections of the cytoplasm of cumulus cells project through the zona pellucida and form gap junctions with microvilli of the oocyte."}, {"name": "Key Features/Anatomical Relations", "text": "The corona radiata surrounds the oocyte and is situated immediately external to the zona pellucida."}, {"name": "Function", "text": "Microvillus projections of the cumulus cells project through the zona pellucida and form gap junctions with microvilli of the oocyte. This provides a source of nutritional and regulatory substances, as well as exogenous proteins for the oocyte. 

In order for fertilization to occur, a sperm must penetrate an oocyte by piercing through the corona radiata and zona pellucida that encircle the oocyte. This indirectly reduces the chances of multiple fertilization (Gray and Lewis, 1918)."}, {"name": "List of Clinical Correlates", "text": "- Infertility"}, {"name": "References", "text": "Dorland, W. (2011) Dorland's Illustrated Medical Dictionary. 32nd edn. Philadelphia, USA: Elsevier Saunders.

Gardner, D. K., Weissman, A., Howles, C. M. and Shoham, Z. (2008) Textbook of Assisted Reproductive Technologies: Laboratory and Clinical Perspectives. CRC Press.

Gray, H. and Lewis, W. H. (1918) Anatomy of the Human Body. Lea & Febiger.

Harrison, R. F., Bonnar, J. and Thompson, W. (2012) Fertility and Sterility: The Proceedings of the XIth World Congress on Fertility and Sterility, Dublin, June 1983, held under the Auspices of the International Federation of Fertility Societies. Springer Netherlands.

van Blerkom, J. and Motta, P. (2012) Ultrastructure of Human Gametogenesis and Early Embryogenesis. Springer US."}]

items.name: Dendrite (of Olfactory Sensory Neuron)
items.info:
[{"name": "Quick Facts", "text": "A dendrite is one of the threadlike extensions of the cytoplasm of a neuron, which typically branch into tree-like processes. In unipolar and bipolar neurons, there is a single dendrite, which proximally resembles an axon but branches distally; in multipolar neurons there are many short, branching dendrites. Dendrites form most of the receptive surface of a neuron (Dorland, 2011)."}, {"name": "Structure and/or Key Features", "text": "Dendrites are a component of olfactory sensory neurons. Each dendrite extends from the cell body to the mucus layer overlying the olfactory epithelium. Within the mucus layer, each of these dendritic ends broadens, forming a characteristic knob-like configuration from which up to 20 cilia, or olfactory hairs, diverge from and extend parallel to the epithelial surface. These cilia increase the surface area available for the membrane of the olfactory sensory neurons to identify odor molecules in the mucus layer (Standring, 2016). 

Inhaled airborne odorant molecules are dissolved in the mucus that overlies the olfactory epithelium and bind to odorant-binding proteins. These proteins convey the odor molecules to the cilia of the dendrites where they bind and activate designated receptors on the dendritic cell membranes. Sensory information is subsequently conveyed to the cell body of the olfactory sensory neuron, and on to the olfactory bulb and cerebral cortex (Longstaff, 2005)."}, {"name": "Anatomical Relations", "text": "Olfactory sensory neurons are bipolar neurons that are situated within the olfactory epithelium. Each neuron has two ends. One end has a 2 μm in diameter solitary unbranched dendrite, which extends inferiorly towards the epithelial surface. The other end has a 0.2 μm in diameter unmyelinated axon, which extends superiorly, and traverses the basement membrane on its way to the lamina propria (Standring, 2016). Their cell body lies interposed between the axon and the dendrite in the middle segment of the olfactory epithelium."}, {"name": "Function", "text": "The dendrites are key components of the olfactory sensory neurons that extend towards the epithelial surface. The cilia present on the ends of the dendrites increase the surface area available for the olfactory sensory neuron membrane to identify odor molecules in the mucus layer that overlies the olfactory epithelium (Standring, 2016)."}, {"name": "Clinical Correlates", "text": "—Anosmia"}, {"name": "References", "text": "Dorland, W. (2011) Dorland's Illustrated Medical Dictionary. 32nd edn. Philadelphia, USA: Elsevier Saunders.

Longstaff, A. (2005) Neuroscience. BIOS instant notes 2nd edition: Taylor & Francis.

Standring, S. (2016) Gray's Anatomy: The Anatomical Basis of Clinical Practice. Gray's Anatomy Series 41st edition: Elsevier Limited."}]

items.name: Nerve Plexus of Arrector Muscle of Hair
items.audio: Nerve Plexus of Arrector Muscle of Hair.mp3
items.info:
[{"name": "Quick Facts", "text": "The arrector muscle of the hair, or arrector pili muscle, is innervated by a dense network of noradrenergic sympathetic nerves."}, {"name": "Structure/Morphology", "text": "The arrector pili muscles are innervated by a dense network of noradrenergic nerve fibers of the sympathetic nervous system. These nerve fibers are more commonly seen close to the site of the insertion of the arrector pili muscle to the hair follicle (Standring, 2016, Wang and Gibbons, 2013, Torkamani et al., 2014)."}, {"name": "Function", "text": "These nerves will carry signals to the smooth muscle cells of the arrector pili muscle and initiate a contraction."}, {"name": "References", "text": "Standring, S. (2016) Gray's Anatomy: The Anatomical Basis of Clinical Practice. Gray's Anatomy Series: Elsevier Limited.

Torkamani, N., Rufaut, N. W., Jones, L. and Sinclair, R. D. (2014) 'Beyond goosebumps: does the arrector pili muscle have a role in hair loss?', Int J Trichology, 6(3), pp. 88-94.

Wang, N. and Gibbons, C. H. (2013) Autonomic Nervous System: Chapter 30. Skin biopsies in the assessment of the autonomic nervous system. Handbook of Clinical Neurology: Elsevier Science."}]

items.name: Follicle of Thyroid Gland
items.info:
[{"name": "Quick Facts", "text": "Follicles of thyroid gland are discrete, cystlike units of the thyroid gland that are lined with cuboidal epithelium and are filled with a colloid substance; there are about 30 to each lobule (Dorland, 2011)."}, {"name": "Structure/Morphology", "text": "Each lobule of the thyroid gland is made up of structures or functional units called thyroid follicles. These follicles are of variable size ranging from about 0.2 to 1 mm (Ross and Pawlina, 2016). This probably reflects their real size, and not necessarily the different state of activity of each follicle. Each follicle contains a gel-like mass called colloid. 

The thyroid follicle has two cell types, follicular cells, or T thyrocytes, and parafollicular cells, or C thyrocytes. The wall of the thyroid follicle is formed by the follicular cells, a simple cuboidal or low columnar epithelium. Their apical surfaces contact the lumen of the follicle, which contains colloid, and their basal surfaces rest on a typical basement membrane. The parafollicular cells are found within the thyroid follicle, squeezed with between the basement membrane around the follicular cells. Their apical surfaces do not reach the lumen of the follicle.

Follicular cells are endocrine cells and are the only endocrine cell that synthesizes its hormonal product and stores it extracellularly.
"}, {"name": "Anatomical Relations", "text": "Each lobule of the thyroid gland is made up of structures or functional units called thyroid follicles. Each follicle contains a central gel-like mass called colloid. The outer wall of the thyroid follicle is formed by a simple cuboidal or low columnar epithelium"}, {"name": "Function", "text": "The follicle of the thyroid gland is responsible for synthesizing and secreting the thyroid hormones, T3, and T4, and calcitonin"}, {"name": "References", "text": "Dorland, W. (2011) Dorland's Illustrated Medical Dictionary. 32nd edn. Philadelphia, USA: Elsevier Saunders.
Ross, M. H. and Pawlina, W. (2016) Histology: A Text and Atlas. Wolters Kluwer Health.
"}]

items.name: Basement Membrane (Thyroid Gland)
items.info:
[{"name": "Quick Facts", "text": "The basement membrane is a thin sheet of amorphous extracellular material upon which the basal surfaces of epithelial cells rest; other cells associated with basement membranes are muscle cells, Schwann cells, and fat cells. The membrane is interposed between the cellular elements and the underlying connective tissue. It usually comprises two layers, the basal lamina and the reticular lamina, and is composed of Type IV collagen (which is unique to basement membranes), laminin, fibronectin, and heparan sulfate proteoglycans (Dorland, 2011)."}, {"name": "Structure/Morphology", "text": "Most epithelia are attached to some form of underlying connective tissues by a basal lamina. They are sheets of extracellular proteins and fibrils and are so thin that they can be seen only with an electron microscope. Under many epithelia, additional carbohydrate-rich material is appended to the lower face of the basal lamina. If the accumulation is sufficient to be seen under the light microscope, it is called a basement membrane. 

The basal lamina is synthesized by the epithelial cells and the additional material by the underlying connective tissue cells. Some epithelia do not have a basement membrane but most have a basal lamina (Mescher, 2013; Ross and Pawlina, 2016; McKinley, O'Loughlin and Pennefather-O'Brien, 2016).

"}, {"name": "Anatomical Relations", "text": "The thyroid follicular cells are attached to the underlying connective tissues by a very thin basement membrane."}, {"name": "Function", "text": "The basement membrane can influence the functions of epithelial cells and adheres the epithelium to the underlying connective tissue as a supporting/strengthening component."}, {"name": "References", "text": "Dorland, W. (2011) Dorland's Illustrated Medical Dictionary. 32nd edn. Philadelphia, USA: Elsevier Saunders.
McKinley, M. P., O'Loughlin, V. D. and Pennefather-O'Brien, E. E. (2016) Human Anatomy. 5th edn.: McGraw-Hill Education.
Mescher, A. (2013) Junqueira's Basic Histology: Text and Atlas. 13th edn.: McGraw-Hill Education.
Ross, M. H. and Pawlina, W. (2016) Histology: A Text and Atlas. Wolters Kluwer Health.
"}]

items.name: Motor Nerve Fiber
items.info:
[{"name": "Quick Facts", "text": "A motor nerve is a peripheral efferent nerve that conducts impulses from the spinal cord or brain to motor end plates or other terminals, influencing the activity of muscles and glands (Dorland, 2011)."}, {"name": "Structure", "text": "Myelinated motor nerves travel through the perimysium, which separates the nerve fascicles, to give rise to several unmyelinated terminal branches. The terminal branches are short fibers which travel through the endomysium to synapse with muscle cells, thus forming neuromuscular junctions.

The myelin sheath of the axon of the motor neuron ends at the neuromuscular junction. However the terminal branches are covered by a thin layer, the neurilemma, which arises from the outer membrane of terminal Schwann cells. This external lamina of the terminal Schwann cell fuses with the sarcolemma, covering the points of contact between axonal branches and the muscle cell."}, {"name": "Key Features/Anatomical Relations", "text": "The myelinated motor neuron axon branches into many unmyelinated terminal branches, which enter the endomysium to make up part of the neuromuscular junction. 

Terminal Schwann cells are a specialized type of non-myelinating Schwann cells present at the neuromuscular junction, which envelop the terminal branches and the motor end plate (Armati, 2007). 

The terminal axonal branches are dilated into a presynaptic structure which sits in shallow depressions on the surface of the muscle fiber. These areas are the receptor regions. The sarcolemma at these points will have deep junctional folds for increased surface area, ready to receive neurotransmitters responsible for muscle contraction."}, {"name": "Function", "text": "The motor nerve action potential travels across the motor neuron axon to the terminal branches and to the dilated presynaptic structures which sit within shallow depressions on the muscle fiber. These dilated ends contain both mitochondria and vesicles, the latter of which contain the neurotransmitter, acetylcholine. The nerve action potential triggers the release of acetylcholine which diffuses across the space between the presynaptic dilation and the sarcolemma. This space is called the synaptic cleft. The sarcolemma at these junctions contains a series of folds to increase the surface area as they contain acetylcholine receptors. Once the acetylcholine binds with their respective receptors, it induces an action potential across the muscle. The action potential will move along the surface of the muscle cell, along the t tubules that penetrate the sarcoplasm initiating release of CA2+, which in turn induces the contraction cycle (Standring, 2016)."}, {"name": "List of Clinical Correlates", "text": "—Botulism"}, {"name": "References", "text": "Armati, P. (2007) The Biology of Schwann Cells: Development, Differentiation and Immunomodulation. Cambridge University Press.

Dorland, W. (2011) Dorland's Illustrated Medical Dictionary. 32nd edn. Philadelphia, USA: Elsevier Saunders.

Standring, S. (2016) Gray's Anatomy: The Anatomical Basis of Clinical Practice. Gray's Anatomy Series: Elsevier Limited."}]

items.name: Nucleus (Cardiac Muscle Cell)
items.info: [{"name": "Quick Facts", "text": "The nucleus is a spheroid body within a eukaryotic cell, separated from the cytoplasm by the nuclear envelope, and containing chromatin, a nucleolus, and nucleoplasm. In the nucleus, the cell's genetic information is stored on the chromosomes and RNA transcription and processing occur (Dorland, 2011)."}, {"name": "Structure and/or Key Features", "text": "The nucleus of a cardiac muscle cell (cardiomyocyte) is centrally located and slightly elongated in the direction of the cell/fiber. In routine histological sections, it appears pale stained. Myofibrils of cardiac muscle cells separate and pass around the centrally positioned nucleus. This creates a \u201cbiconical\u201d region of sarcoplasm each end of the nucleus where the cell organelles are concentrated (Ross and Pawlina, 2016)."}, {"name": "Function", "text": "The nucleus is the control center of the cell and houses the genome (genetic information) in eukaryotic cells. It enables DNA replication and synthesizes ribosomal (rRNA), messenger (mRNA), and transfer (tRNA) ribonucleic acid."}, {"name": "References", "text": "Dorland, W. (2011) Dorland's Illustrated Medical Dictionary. 32nd edn. Philadelphia, USA: Elsevier Saunders.\n\nRoss, M. H. and Pawlina, W. (2016) Histology: A Text and Atlas. Wolters Kluwer Health."}]

items.name: Thyroid Plexus
items.info:
[{"name": "Quick Facts", "text": "The thyroid plexus is a nerve plexus that accompanies the superior and inferior thyroid arteries into the region of the larynx, pharynx, and thyroid (Dorland, 2011)."}, {"name": "Structure/Morphology", "text": "The thyroid gland is innervated by the superior, middle, and inferior cervical ganglia of the sympathetic trunk. Postganglionic fibers from the inferior cervical ganglion form a plexus on the inferior thyroid artery and accompany it to the thyroid gland. Some parasympathetic fibers from the vagus nerve, via the recurrent and superior laryngeal nerves, communicate with this plexus (Standring, 2020)."}, {"name": "Anatomical Relations", "text": "The nerve fibers of the thyroid plexus accompany the thyroid arteries, forming a periarterial plexus on their surface."}, {"name": "Function", "text": "These autonomic nerves are likely vasomotor, not secretomotor, and act on the blood perfusion of the thyroid gland rather than regulating glandular secretion activity (Moore, Dalley and Agur, 2013)."}, {"name": "References", "text": "Dorland, W. (2011) Dorland's Illustrated Medical Dictionary. 32nd edn. Philadelphia, USA: Elsevier Saunders.
Moore, K. L., Dalley, A. F. and Agur, A. M. R. (2013) Clinically Oriented Anatomy. Clinically Oriented Anatomy 7th edn.: Wolters Kluwer Health/Lippincott Williams & Wilkins.
Standring, S. (2020) Gray's Anatomy: The Anatomical Basis of Clinical Practice. 42nd edn.: Elsevier Health Sciences.
"}]

items.name: Perifollicular Capillary Network
items.info: [{"name": "Quick Facts", "text": "The perifollicular capillary network is the numerous blood vessels surrounding the thyroid follicles."}, {"name": "Structure/Morphology", "text": "Cells in the thyroid follicles produce hormones and secrete them on their basal surfaces into the interstitium. A network of capillaries lies adjacent to the follicles. They are very fenestrated, which is a typical type of capillary you see in endocrine glands. Fenestrations allow easy movement of fluid from the interstitium, containing the secreted hormones, to pass into the blood, and therefore, be carried to the rest of the body."}, {"name": "Anatomical Relations", "text": "An extensive perifollicular capillary network surrounds the thyroid follicles."}, {"name": "Function", "text": "The extensive perifollicular capillary network enables the hormones produced in the thyroid gland to enter them and be then transported to target tissues throughout the body."}]

items.name: Ciliary Muscle
items.info:
[{"name": "Quick Facts", "text": "Origin: scleral spur.

Insertion: outer layers of choroid and ciliary processes.

Innervation: short ciliary nerves (parasympathetic).

Action: affects shape of the lens in visual accommodation."}, {"name": "Structure and/or Key Feature(s)", "text": "The ciliary muscle is one of the four layers of the ciliary body. It is the second from superficial to deep, located between the supraciliary layer and the stroma. 

It is a smooth muscle composed of cells arranged in varying orientation. The outer muscle fibers are longitudinal, extending into the choroid; the inner muscle fibers are circular, forming a sphincter that parallels the circumference of the lens. Interconnecting muscle fibers run radially forming an interweaving lattice. 

The oculomotor nerve (CN III) provides parasympathetic innervation to the ciliary muscle via the short ciliary nerves, with the superior cervical ganglion providing sympathetic contributions (Giampani & Giampani, 2013)."}, {"name": "Function", "text": "Contraction of the ciliary muscle changes the refractive power of the lens in a process called accommodation."}, {"name": "Clinical Correlates", "text": "—Cycloplegia (paralysis of accommodation)"}, {"name": "References", "text": "Dorland, W. (2011) Dorland's Illustrated Medical Dictionary. 32nd edn. Philadelphia, USA: Elsevier Saunders.

Giampani, A. S. B. and Giampani, J. (2013) Anatomy of Ciliary Body, Ciliary Processes, Anterior Chamber Angle and Collector Vessels. INTECH Open Access Publisher."}]

items.name: End Piece
items.info:
[{"name": "Quick Facts", "text": "The end piece is the terminal portion of the tail of the spermatozoon (Dorland, 2011)."}, {"name": "Structure and/or Key Feature(s)", "text": "The sperm tail can be divided into three main segments: the middle piece, the principal piece, and the end piece. 

The end piece constitutes the terminal 5-10 μm of the sperm tail and is mainly made up of the axoneme covered solely by the plasma membrane.

The axoneme is composed of two centrally located microtubule singlets, which are encased by nine microtubule doublets. Each of the microtubule doublets is made up of a complete α-microtubule, onto which a β-microtubule attaches. 

Towards the terminus of the end piece, the β-microtubules of the axoneme often split from the α-microtubules. The microtubules are of varying lengths and so terminate at different levels (Afzelius et al, 1995)."}, {"name": "Anatomical Relations", "text": "The end piece is situated distal to the principal piece of the sperm tail."}, {"name": "Function", "text": "The end piece plays a role in the motility of sperm, especially with the bending of the axoneme during the faster power strokes that facilitates the forward propulsion of the sperm."}, {"name": "References", "text": "Afzelius, B. A., Dallai, R., Lanzavecchia, S. & Bellon, P. L. (1995) Flagellar structure in normal human spermatozoa and in spermatozoa that lack dynein arms. Tissue Cell, 27(3), 241-7.

Dorland, W. (2011) Dorland's Illustrated Medical Dictionary. 32nd edn. Philadelphia, USA: Elsevier Saunders."}]

items.name: Pinocytotic Vesicle (Uncontracted Smooth Muscle)
items.info: [{"name": "Quick Facts", "text": "A pinocytotic vesicle is any of the small fluid-filled vesicles found in the cytoplasm during pinocytosis, formed by invaginations of the cell membrane (caveolae), which pinch off and become free (Dorland, 2011)."}, {"name": "Structure and/or Key Features", "text": "A pinocytotic vesicle (80\u2013150 nm in diameter) forms when the plasmalemma engulfs fluid or small proteins and any molecules in solution in the extracellular fluid. This process is called pinocytosis and is a common process in almost all human cells."}, {"name": "Anatomical Relations", "text": "Pinocytotic vesicles are located in the apical regions of the cell cytoplasm."}, {"name": "Function", "text": "A pinocytotic vesicle engulfs fluid or small proteins and any molecules in solution in the extracellular fluid."}, {"name": "References", "text": "Dorland, W. (2011) Dorland's Illustrated Medical Dictionary. 32nd edn. Philadelphia, USA: Elsevier Saunders."}]

items.name: Cerebral Arteries
items.info:
[{"name": "Quick Facts", "text": "The cerebral arteries are the arteries supplying the cerebral hemispheres, derived from the internal carotid artery (anterior choroid, anterior cerebral, middle cerebral, and posterior communicating arteries and the circle of Willis) or from the basilar artery (posterior cerebral artery) (Dorland, 2011)."}, {"name": "Structure", "text": "The anterior and middle cerebral arteries are terminal branches of the internal carotid arteries and supply more than 80% of the cerebrum. 

The anterior cerebral arteries anastomose via the anterior communicating artery and supply the superior and medial surfaces of the frontal and parietal lobes. 

The middle cerebral artery is the largest branch of the internal carotid artery. It passes through the lateral sulcus of each hemisphere to supply lateral parts of the parietal and temporal lobes. 

The basilar artery, formed by the union of the right and left vertebral arteries, divides into posterior cerebral arteries. They supply the occipital lobes and the inferomedial temporal lobes. They are connected to the middle cerebral arteries by two short posterior communicating arteries (Marieb, Wilhelm and Mallatt, 2012)."}, {"name": "Function", "text": "The cerebral arteries provide blood to the brain."}, {"name": "List of Clinical Correlates", "text": "—Ischemic or hemorrhagic Stroke"}, {"name": "References", "text": "Dorland, W. (2011) Dorland's Illustrated Medical Dictionary. 32nd edn. Philadelphia, USA: Elsevier Saunders.

Marieb, E. N., Wilhelm, P. B. and Mallatt, J. (2012) Human Anatomy. fifth edn.: Benjamin Cummings."}]

items.name: Visceral Layer of Tunica Vaginalis Testis (Medial Part; Right)
items.audio: Visceral Layer of Tunica Vaginalis Testis (Medial Part).mp3
alt: Visceral Layer of Tunica Vaginalis of Testis (Medial Part; Right)
items.info: [{"name": "Key Features/ Anatomical Relations", "text": "The visceral layer of the tunica vaginalis is a continuation of the processus vaginalis, formed as a part of the descension of the testes. Following the descent, a small sac remains and is referred to as the tunica vaginalis. The parietal and visceral layers of the tunica vaginalis are continuous at the poles of the testes. Between the two layers is the cavity of the tunica vaginalis. The visceral layer is in direct contact with the deeper tunica albuginea."}, {"name": "Function", "text": "The visceral layer of the tunica vaginalis provides lubrication for the testes to decrease the risk of friction caused by movement."}, {"name": "List of Clinical Correlates", "text": "\u2014Indirect inguinal hernia\n\u2014Hydroceles\n"}]

items.name: Myelin Sheath (General Visceral Efferent Parasympathetic)
items.info: [{"name": "Quick Facts", "text": "The myelin sheath is the cylindrical covering on the axons of some neurons; it consists of concentric layers of myelin, formed in the peripheral nervous system by the plasma membrane of Schwann cells, and in the central nervous system by oligodendrocytes. It is interrupted at intervals along its length by gaps known as nodes of Ranvier. Myelin is an electrical insulator that serves to speed the conduction of nerve impulses (Dorland, 2011)."}, {"name": "Structure/Morphology", "text": "The myelin sheath tightly holsters the axon, it is a semi-crystalline lipid-protein-water layer. This layer is discontinuous and interrupted at regular intervals. Schwann cells produce myelin sheaths in the peripheral nervous system. A myelin sheath is formed when the Schwann cell wraps around the nerve axon in a spiral fashion, creating a number of layers, or lamellae. The process is known as myelination. Each myelin-producing cell surrounds only one segment of any given axon. Periodic interruptions where short portions of the axon are left uncovered by myelin are known as the nodes of Ranvier (Patestas and Gartner, 2016)."}, {"name": "Key Features/Anatomical Relations", "text": "Nodes of Ranvier are gaps found in the continuity of the myelin sheath surrounding an axon. At these gaps there is no myelin covering the axon, thus exposing it to the extracellular fluid. The nodes of Ranvier contain a high concentration of voltage-gated sodium channels. These voltage-gated sodium channels enable the nodes to function as generators of action potentials. This is achieved through the exchange of ions into and out of the ion channels."}, {"name": "Function", "text": "The Myelin sheath acts as an insulator for the axons improving their electrical conductance. The myelin sheath also has a protective role in that it acts as a physical barrier separating the axon from the electrically charged atoms and molecules of the extracellular fluid. Myelination has also been shown to reduce the energy required for transmission of action potentials (through the mechanism of saltatory conduction) (Patestas and Gartner, 2016)."}, {"name": "List of Clinical Correlates", "text": "\u2014Demyelinating disease"}, {"name": "References", "text": "Dorland, W. (2011) Dorland's Illustrated Medical Dictionary. 32nd edn. Philadelphia, USA: Elsevier Saunders.\n\nPatestas, M. A. and Gartner, L. P. (2016) A Textbook of Neuroanatomy. Wiley."}]

items.name: Lipofuscin Granule (Cardiac Muscle Cell)
items.info:
[{"name": "Quick Facts", "text": "Lipofuscin is a yellow to brown, granular, iron-negative lipid pigment found particularly in muscle, heart, liver, and nerve cells undergoing slow, regressive change and accumulating in lysosomes with age, being the product of oxidation and polymerization of the membrane lipids of autophagocytosed organelles (Dorland, 2011)."}, {"name": "Structure and/or Key Features", "text": "In cells with a long lifetime i.e., nerve cells (neurons) and cardiac muscle cells (cardiomyocytes), indigestible compounds derived from secondary lysosomes, and retained in the cell cytoplasm as residual bodies, are referred to as lipofuscin, or age pigment. They appear as a yellowish-brown component of the cell cytoplasm (Mescher, 2013; Ross and Pawlina, 2016)."}, {"name": "Anatomical Relations", "text": "Lipofuscin granules are concentrated in the juxtanuclear region in a cardiac muscle cell (Mescher, 2013; Ross and Pawlina, 2016)."}, {"name": "Function", "text": "Lipofuscin granules are indigestible compounds derived from secondary lysosomes (Mescher, 2013; Ross and Pawlina, 2016)."}, {"name": "References", "text": "Dorland, W. (2011) Dorland's Illustrated Medical Dictionary. 32nd edn. Philadelphia, USA: Elsevier Saunders.

Mescher, A. (2013) Junqueira's Basic Histology: Text and Atlas. 13th edn.: McGraw-Hill Education.

Ross, M. H. and Pawlina, W. (2016) Histology: A Text and Atlas. Wolters Kluwer Health."}]

items.name: Internal Root Sheath
items.info:
[{"name": "Quick Facts", "text": "The epithelial portion of the hair follicle is divided into the inner root sheath and the outer root sheath. The inner root sheath has three layers: Huxley layer, Henle layer, and the cuticle of the root sheath. The outer root sheath does not have distinct layers and merges with the epidermis near the skin surface (Dorland, 2011)."}, {"name": "Structure/Morphology", "text": "The internal root sheath is a layer composed of lightly keratinized cells which envelops the lower portion of the hair shaft, it does not extend past the isthmus (the middle segment) of the hair follicle. This layer and the external root sheath are produced by the rapidly reproducing matrix cells found in the periphery of the follicular bulb. The inner root sheath is composed of three concentric layers (from inside to outside), including the cuticle, Huxley’s layer, and Henle’s layer (Standring, 2016; Martini, Nath and Bartholomew, 2017; Joshi, 2011)."}, {"name": "Function", "text": "The inner root sheath forms a tough outer sleeve for the hair, its rigid form protects the hair shaft as it grows."}, {"name": "References", "text": "Dorland, W. (2011) Dorland's Illustrated Medical Dictionary. 32nd edn. Philadelphia, USA: Elsevier Saunders.

Joshi, R. S. (2011) 'The Inner Root Sheath and the Men Associated with it Eponymically', Int J Trichology, 3(1), pp. 57-62.

Martini, F. H., Nath, J. L. and Bartholomew, E. F. (2017) Fundamentals of Anatomy & Physiology. Pearson Education.

Standring, S. (2016) Gray's Anatomy: The Anatomical Basis of Clinical Practice. Gray's Anatomy Series: Elsevier Limited."}]

items.name: Basement Membrane of Parietal Epithelial Cell
items.audio: Basement Membrane of Parietal Epithelial Cell.mp3
items.info:
[{"name": "Quick Facts", "text": "A basement membrane is a thin sheet of amorphous extracellular material upon which the basal surfaces of epithelial cells rest; other cells associated with basement membranes are muscle cells, Schwann cells, and fat cells. The membrane is interposed between the cellular elements and the underlying connective tissue. It usually comprises two layers, the basal lamina and the reticular lamina, and is composed of Type IV collagen (which is unique to basement membranes), laminin, fibronectin, and heparan sulfate proteoglycans (Dorland, 2011)."}, {"name": "Structure and/or Key Feature(s)", "text": "Most epithelia attach to some form of underlying connective tissues by a basal lamina. The basal lamina is a thin sheet of extracellular proteins and fibrils. Additionally, carbohydrate-rich material is attached its lower face. If the accumulation is sufficient, the basal lamina is referred to as a basement membrane.

The basement membrane is synthesized by overlying epithelium and the underlying cells in connective tissue. Some epithelia do not have a basement membrane but most have a basal lamina (Ross and Pawlina, 2016; Ovalle, Nahirney and Netter, 2013)."}, {"name": "Anatomical Relations", "text": "The parietal epithelial cells are attached to the underlying connective tissues by a very thin basement membrane."}, {"name": "Function", "text": "The basal lamina has a profound influence over the physiology of epithelium and a basement membrane adheres the epithelium to the underlying connective tissue being a supporting/strengthening component."}, {"name": "References", "text": "Dorland, W. (2011) Dorland's Illustrated Medical Dictionary. 32nd edn. Philadelphia, USA: Elsevier Saunders.

Ovalle, W. K., Nahirney, P. C. and Netter, F. H. (2013) Netter's Essential Histology. ClinicalKey 2012: Elsevier Saunders.

Ross, M. H. and Pawlina, W. (2006) Histology: A text and atlas. Lippincott Williams & Wilkins."}]

items.name: Detrusor Vesicae (Posterior)
items.info:
[{"name": "Quick Facts", "text": "Origin: Wall of the bladder.

Insertion: Posterior wall of the pubic bone and prostate (if present). 

Action: Assist in micturition by increasing the pressure in the bladder and forcing urine into the urethra.

Nerve Supply: Inferior hypogastric plexus, with parasympathetic fibers originating from S2-S4, and sympathetic fibers originating in the lateral horn of gray matter of T10-L2. 

Arterial Supply: Superior vesical, inferior vesical (if present), vaginal (if present), obturator, and inferior gluteal arteries.
"}, {"name": "Structure/Morphology", "text": "The detrusor vesicae is composed of smooth muscle fibers organized into three layers in the bladder, inner longitudinal, middle circular, and outer longitudinal."}, {"name": "Key Features/ Anatomical Relations", "text": "The detrusor vesicae forms the internal urethral sphincter at the neck of the bladder. It forms a circular loop around the opening of the ureters into the posterior surface of the bladder, preventing reflux of urine from the bladder into the ureters. It is continuous as the detrusor apron over the prostate (Standring, 2020)."}, {"name": "Function", "text": "This smooth muscle layer of the bladder is responsible relaxing the bladder while it fills with urine and contracting during micturition to aid in forcing urine into the urethra. "}, {"name": "List of Clinical Correlates", "text": "—Catheter placement 
—Bladder cancer
"}, {"name": "References", "text": "Standring, S. (2020) Gray's Anatomy: The Anatomical Basis of Clinical Practice. 42nd edn.: Elsevier Health Sciences."}]

items.name: Muscle Fascicle
items.info:
[{"name": "Quick Facts", "text": "A muscle fascicle is a small bundle of muscle fibers (Dorland, 2011)."}, {"name": "Structure", "text": "A muscle fascicle is a bundle of skeletal muscle fibers running parallel to each other, enveloped by a collagenous sheath called the perimysium."}, {"name": "Key Features/Anatomical Relations", "text": "Multiple muscle fascicles collectively make up the skeletal muscle proper and they generally run along the length of the muscle."}, {"name": "Function", "text": "The muscle fascicle is made up of groups of muscle fibers bundled together, resulting in greater cumulative strength of the muscle fibers. This facilitates in allowing the fascicle to produce more force during contraction."}, {"name": "List of Clinical Correlates", "text": "—Myopathy

—Muscular dystrophy

—Neuromuscular disease

—Muscle atrophy

—Myositis"}, {"name": "References", "text": "Dorland, W. (2011) Dorland's Illustrated Medical Dictionary. 32nd edn. Philadelphia, USA: Elsevier Saunders."}]

items.name: Cytosol (Anterosuperior Cut)
items.info: [{"name": "Quick Facts", "text": "The cytosol is the liquid medium of the cytoplasm, i.e., cytoplasm minus organelles and nonmembranous insoluble components (Dorland, 2011)."}, {"name": "Structure and/or Key Feature(s)", "text": "The cytosol (which can occupy about 50% of the cell volume) is an aqueous gel containing solutes, inorganic ions, and organic molecules especially carbohydrates, proteins and lipids. This content is carefully regulated by the cell (McKinley, O'Loughlin and Pennefather-O'Brien, 2016)."}, {"name": "Function", "text": "The cytosol is the aqueous medium for many of the cell\u2019s metabolic activities and movements of materials, organelles, etc."}, {"name": "References", "text": "Dorland, W. (2011) Dorland's Illustrated Medical Dictionary. 32nd edn. Philadelphia, USA: Elsevier Saunders.\n\nMcKinley, M. P., O'Loughlin, V. D. and Pennefather-O'Brien, E. E. (2016) Human Anatomy. 5th edn.: McGraw-Hill Education."}]

items.name: Basal Complex
items.info:
[{"name": "Quick Facts", "text": "The basal complex is the transparent inner layer of the choroid, which is in contact with the pigmented layer of the retina (Dorland, 2011)."}, {"name": "Structure and/or Key Features", "text": "The basal complex, otherwise known as the lamina vitreal or Bruch’s membrane, is a barrier lying between the choroidocapillary and the retinal pigment epithelium. It is 2–4 µm thick and is composed of a central elastic layer flanked by inner and outer fibrous layers of collagen and basement membrane (basal lamina)."}, {"name": "Anatomical Relations", "text": "The basal complex is a thin layer that, at its outer surface abuts the overlying choroidocapillary lamina of the choroid. At its inner surface, it separates this lamina from the retinal pigment epithelium. A potential space, the remnant of the lumen of the embryonic optic vesicle, is present between these two and is a potential site of retinal detachment."}, {"name": "Function", "text": "The basal complex allows for the passage of nutrients, gases, and metabolites between the dense capillary bed of the choroidocapillary and the avascular outer layers of the retina. With age, it can be the site where deposits become embedded. This can impair the passage of substances between the choroid and retina and contribute to retinal photoreceptor degeneration."}, {"name": "List of Clinical Correlates", "text": "- Retinal detachment

- Drusen

- Age-related macular degeneration"}, {"name": "References", "text": "Dorland, W. (2011) Dorland's Illustrated Medical Dictionary. 32nd edn. Philadelphia, USA: Elsevier Saunders."}]

items.name: Atretic Follicle
items.info:
[{"name": "Quick Facts", "text": "An atretic follicle is an ovarian follicle that began to mature but did not become the dominant follicle and has involuted (Dorland, 2011)."}, {"name": "Structure and/or Key Feature(s)", "text": "Most ovarian follicles never complete their maturation and degenerate by a process called atresia during fetal development, early postnatal life, and prior to the onset of puberty. Atresia is mediated by apoptosis of the follicular/granulosa cells.

The oocyte undergoes autolysis and degeneration, and remnants are phagocytosed by macrophages. The zona pellucida is more resistant to autolytic processes that are occurring in the cellular components of the follicle undergoing atresia. It becomes distorted which is a useful diagnostic feature of atresia and is often all that remains of the original follicle until it is slowly broken down.

After puberty, many primary follicles begin to grow at each ovarian cycle. Usually only one will complete maturation in preparation for ovulation. The others fail and become atretic follicles. 

Follicles that developed further before failing will give larger, more complex atretic follicles. Often the glassy membrane, which is formed from a much-thickened basement membrane that is between the membrana granulosa and the theca interna, also remains.

In follicles that were near maturity before undergoing atresia, the theca interna cells often enlarge and remain as clusters of radial strands separated by connective tissue. These cords of cells are called interstitial glands and continue to secrete steroid hormones but in humans are probably not active in follicles undergoing atresia after puberty (Mescher, 2013; Ross and Pawlina, 2006)."}, {"name": "References", "text": "Dorland, W. (2011) Dorland's Illustrated Medical Dictionary. 32nd edn. Philadelphia, USA: Elsevier Saunders.

Mescher, A. (2013) Junqueira's Basic Histology: Text and Atlas. 13th edn.: McGraw-Hill Education.

Ross, M. H. and Pawlina, W. (2006) Histology: A text and atlas. Lippincott Williams & Wilkins."}]

items.name: Third Lumbar Nerve
items.info:
[{"name": "Quick Facts", "text": "Origin: The intervertebral foramen inferior to the third lumbar vertebra.

Course: Laterally to the lumbar plexus.

Branches: Lateral cutaneous nerve of the thigh, femoral, and obturator nerves.

Supply:

Motor innervation of the psoas, iliacus, pectineus, sartorius, quadriceps, and adductor muscles.

Sensory innervation of the back, medial thigh, and knee joint."}, {"name": "Origin", "text": "The third lumbar nerve originates in, or just lateral, to the intervertebral foramen inferior to the third lumbar vertebra. Here, the anterior and posterior roots combine to form the first lumbar nerve proper."}, {"name": "Course", "text": "The third lumbar nerve gives off a posterior ramus, that runs to the epaxial musculature and skin of the lower back, and an anterior ramus, that runs inferior and laterally to the lumbar plexus."}, {"name": "Branches", "text": "The third lumbar nerve gives off a posterior ramus and contributes to three branches from the anterior ramus. These are part of the lumbar plexus and also receive contributing fibers from other lumbar levels. These include the lateral femoral cutaneous (or lateral cutaneous nerve of thigh), femoral, and obturator nerves."}, {"name": "Supplied Structures", "text": "The posterior ramus of the third lumbar nerve supplies the epaxial muscles of the lumbar region, including erector spinae and transversospinal muscles. In addition to cutaneous innervation of the skin over the lower back.

The anterior ramus of the third lumbar nerve contributes to the lumbar plexus and the following nerves and their targets.

—Small branches innervate the iliopsoas muscle.

—The lateral femoral cutaneous nerve contributes to both the second and third lumbar nerves and is only sensory. It innervates the anterior and lateral thigh from the inguinal ligament down to the knee.

—The femoral nerve arises from the second, third, and fourth lumbar nerves. It innervates psoas, iliacus, pectineus, sartorius, and quadriceps muscles (rectus femoris, vastus lateralis, vastus intermedius, and vastus medialis). Sensory innervation of the femoral region is to the anterior and medial thigh.

—The obturator nerve arises from the second, third, and fourth lumbar nerves. It innervates the adductor muscles (gracilis, obturator externus, adductor longus, adductor brevis, and adductor magnus muscles). Sensory innervation of the obturator nerve is received from the skin of the medial thigh."}]

items.info: [{"name": "Structure", "text": "The subcutaneous tissue (superficial fascia) of the breast thickens at the margins to form the circummammary ligament. This divides into a thin anterior lamina and thick posterior lamina. The anterior lamina travels from the posterior surface of the breast and encases the subcutaneous fat and the glandular tissue of the breast. The posterior lamina lies along the posterior surface of the subcutaneous fat and glandular tissue of the breast. "}, {"name": "Anatomical Relations", "text": "The anterior and posterior laminae lie within the subcutaneous tissue layer of the breast. The posterior layer lies anterior to the deep pectoral fascia over the pectoralis major muscle. There is a small space between the posterior lamina and the pectoral fascia called the submammary space that allows for independent movement of the breast from the pectoralis muscle (Standring, 2020)."}, {"name": "Function", "text": "The anterior and posterior laminae provide support to the breast tissue."}, {"name": "List of Clinical Correlates", "text": "\u2014Breast cancer\n\u2014Breast augmentation\n"}, {"name": "References", "text": "Standring, S. (2020) Gray's Anatomy: The Anatomical Basis of Clinical Practice. 42nd edn.: Elsevier Health Sciences."}]

items.name: Cortex of Lymph Node
items.info: [{"name": "Quick Facts", "text": "The cortex is the outer portion of the node, consisting mainly of dense lymphoid tissue and follicles (Dorland, 2011)."}, {"name": "Structure/Morphology", "text": "The cortex is distinguishable by the presence of spherical lymphoid follicles, which are surrounded and separated by interfollicular (or diffuse) cortex."}, {"name": "Anatomical Relations", "text": "The cortex is located in the apical portion of the lymph node, between the subcapsular sinus and the paracortex. The lymphoid follicles present in the cortex are mainly populated with B cells and follicular dendritic cells (Standring, 2016). The number and the staining characteristics (during histological processing) of lymphoid follicles in the cortex greatly rely on the state of the antigen stimulation of the cells in the follicles."}, {"name": "Function", "text": "The cortex functions mainly to house quiescent lymphocytes, antigen-stimulated B-cells, and follicular dendritic cells."}, {"name": "References", "text": "Dorland, W. (2011) Dorland's Illustrated Medical Dictionary. 32nd edn. Philadelphia, USA: Elsevier Saunders.\n\nStandring, S. (2016) Gray's Anatomy: The Anatomical Basis of Clinical Practice.
