items.name: Macule Densa
items.info:
[{"name": "Quick Facts", "text": "The macula densa is a zone of compact, heavily nucleated cells located in the convoluted tubule of the kidney, where it makes contact with the vascular end of the glomerulus; it is closely associated anatomically with the juxtaglomerular cells of the afferent arteriole (Dorland, 2011)."}, {"name": "Structure and/or Key Feature(s)", "text": "The juxtaglomerular complex includes the macula densa, and the juxtaglomerular and mesangial cells.

The distal straight tubule traverses the medulla into the cortex within a medullary ray and aligns itself adjacent to the vascular pole of the renal corpuscle with which it is a component. A clustering of nuclei of epithelial cells lining the distal straight tubule directly adjacent to the afferent arteriole close to the vascular pole of the renal corpuscle form the “macula densa.” 

Smooth muscle cells of adjacent afferent, and sometimes efferent, arterioles exhibit spherical nuclei and their cytoplasm contain secretory granules."}, {"name": "Function", "text": "The juxtaglomerular apparatus regulates blood pressure by activating the renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system. It also sensors blood volume and tubular fluid composition. The macula densa monitors Na+ concentration within the tubular fluid and regulate glomerular filtration rate and the release of renin from the juxtaglomerular cells (Ross and Pawlina, 2006)."}, {"name": "References", "text": "Dorland, W. (2011) Dorland's Illustrated Medical Dictionary. 32nd edn. Philadelphia, USA: Elsevier Saunders.

Ross, M. H. and Pawlina, W. (2006) Histology: A text and atlas. Lippincott Williams & Wilkins."}]

items.name: Nervi Vasorum (Medium Vein)
Soma of Cone Cell
items.info:
[{"name": "Quick Facts", "text": "The soma, or cell body, is the portion of a cell that contains the nucleus, independent of projections such as an axon or dendrites (Dorland, 2011)."}, {"name": "Structure and/or Key Features", "text": "The soma, or cell body, is the region within the photoreceptor cell that houses the nucleus and most of the protein synthesis and metabolic cellular organelles. The soma of the cone cells is large in diameter, measuring around 5 µm (Besharse and Bok, 2011)."}, {"name": "Anatomical Relations", "text": "The soma of the cone cells tends to form a single layer in the inner aspect of the outer nuclear layer and often penetrate the outer limiting membrane. The soma is positioned in between the inner segment and the axonal process of the photoreceptor cells. Besides the somata of other cones and rods, the space between photoreceptor cell bodies contains the outer process of Müller glial cells that at their distal end compose the outer limiting membrane."}, {"name": "Function", "text": "The soma houses the nucleus, which contains the cell’s DNA. It is necessary for gene expression, transcription and translation that forms the cell developmentally and maintains its biochemical structural and metabolic functions."}, {"name": "References", "text": "Besharse, J. and Bok, D. (2011) The Retina and Its Disorders. Elsevier Science, p. 156-162.

Chen, J. and Sampath, A. (2012) 'Structure and Function of Rod and Cone Photoreceptors', Retina Fifth Edition, 1, pp. 342-359.

Dorland, W. (2011) Dorland's Illustrated Medical Dictionary. 32nd edn. Philadelphia, USA: Elsevier Saunders."}]

items.name: Tunica Media of Vessel (Large Vein)
Inferior Rectus Muscle
items.info:
[{"name": "Quick Facts", "text": "Origin: Common tendinous ring.

Insertion: Sclera, on inferior aspect of eyeball, just posterior to the corneosclearal junction.

Action: Depresses, adducts, and laterally rotates eyeball.

Innervation: Inferior branch of oculomotor nerve (CNIII).

Arterial Supply: Infraorbital artery; ophthalmic artery."}, {"name": "Origin", "text": "The inferior rectus muscle originates from a common tendinous ring, just beneath the optic canal."}, {"name": "Insertion", "text": "The inferior rectus muscle inserts on the sclera, obliquely, on the inferior aspect of the eyeball, posterior to the corneoscleral junction. Additional fibers extend from the inferior rectus muscle to the inferior tarsal plate of the lower eyelid. Therefore, when the eyeball is depressed by contraction of the inferior rectus muscle, i.e., gaze is directed downwards, the lower eyelid is also depressed."}, {"name": "Key Features & Anatomical Relations", "text": "From the common tendinous ring, the inferior rectus muscle runs anterolaterally along the floor of the orbit."}, {"name": "Action", "text": "The inferior rectus muscle is primarily involved in depressing the eyeball around the transverse (horizontal) axis, i.e., moves the pupil inferiorly. It is most efficient at doing this when the eyeball is fully abducted. It is also involved in medial rotation (adduction) around the vertical axis and laterally rotation (extorsion) around the anteroposterior axis. These two actions are maximum when the eye is adducted."}]

items.name: Ribosome (Uncontracted Smooth Muscle)
items.info:
[{"name": "Quick Facts", "text": "A ribosome is a large molecular structure, approximately 12 nm wide and 25 nm long, having two dissociable subunits, that is the site of protein synthesis. Ribosomes found in the cytosol of eukaryotes have a sedimentation coefficient of 80S; the subunits have coefficients of 60S and 40S and together contain four different ribosomal RNA (rRNA) chains and about 80 different proteins. Ribosomes found in prokaryotes and mitochondria are smaller (70S, with 50S and 30S subunits containing a total of three rRNAs and 55 proteins) and also differ from eukaryotic ribosomes in their sensitivity to certain antibiotics (Dorland, 2011)."}, {"name": "Structure and/or Key Features", "text": "Ribosomes are protein complexes and consist of rRNA synthesized in the nucleolus. They appear in electron micrographs as small, electron-dense particles 20–30 nm in two different forms (Ross and Pawlina, 2016; McKinley, O'Loughlin and Pennefather-O'Brien, 2016; Ovalle, Nahirney and Netter, 2013)."}, {"name": "Anatomical Relations", "text": "Firstly, ribosomes position loosely within the cytoplasm or as a chain of ribosomes called polyribosomes. 

Secondly, ribosomes (and polyribosomes) can be attached to the membrane of the endoplasmic reticulum."}, {"name": "Function", "text": "Individual ribosomes or polyribosomes in the cytoplasm of the cell freely associated, means they're involved with making proteins that the cell uses for itself.

Proteins synthesized by those ribosomes in collaboration with the endoplasmic reticulum is destined to be exported from the cell or incorporated into the plasmalemma. In some cases, the proteins are stored within the cell e.g., in lysosomes and in the granules of white blood cells (Ross and Pawlina, 2016; McKinley, O'Loughlin and Pennefather-O'Brien, 2016; Ovalle, Nahirney and Netter, 2013)."}, {"name": "References", "text": "McKinley, M. P., O'Loughlin, V. D. and Pennefather-O'Brien, E. E. (2016) Human Anatomy. 5th edn.: McGraw-Hill Education.

Ovalle, W. K., Nahirney, P. C. and Netter, F. H. (2013) Netter's Essential Histology. ClinicalKey 2012: Elsevier Saunders.

Ross, M. H. and Pawlina, W. (2016) Histology: A Text and Atlas. Wolters Kluwer Health."}]

items.name: Dense Body (Uncontracted Smooth Muscle)
items.info: [{"name": "Quick Facts", "text": "A dense body is any of the small regions of increased density in the sarcoplasm of skeletal muscles to which myofilaments seem to attach (Dorland, 2011)."}, {"name": "Structure and/or Key Features", "text": "Dense bodies are functionally similar to Z disks of skeletal and cardiac muscle. They contain attachment proteins, such as alpha-actinin, that bind to thin myofilaments and intermediate filaments."}, {"name": "Anatomical Relations", "text": "Cytoplasmic densities or dense bodies are located at the sarcolemma (cell membrane) of smooth muscle cells and are distributed throughout the sarcoplasm (cytoplasm)."}, {"name": "Function", "text": "Dense bodies are important in transmitting the contractile forces within the cell and at the cell surface, therefore changing the shape of the cell."}, {"name": "References", "text": "Dorland, W. (2011) Dorland's Illustrated Medical Dictionary. 32nd edn. Philadelphia, USA: Elsevier Saunders."}]

items.name: Afferent Glomerular Arterioles
items.info:
[{"name": "Quick Facts", "text": "The afferent glomerular arteriole is a branch of an interlobular artery that goes to a renal glomerulus (Dorland, 2011)."}, {"name": "Structure and/or Key Features", "text": "Afferent glomerular arterioles are small arteries that share a similar structure with small muscle arteries and deliver blood to the nephron. Specifically, afferent arterioles have a muscular layer that is two to three cells thick (Standring, 2016). 

As the afferent arteriole nears the glomerulus, it comes into contact with the distal convoluted tubule. At this point, the wall of the distal convoluted tubule thickens and is known as the macula densa. Further surrounding the macula densa and the afferent arteriole are juxtaglomerular cells and extraglomerular mesangial cells. Collectively, they are known as the juxtaglomerular apparatus. The secretions of the juxtaglomerular apparatus will act upon afferent glomerular arterioles to regulate blood flow and glomerular filtration rate (Pocock et al, 2013)."}, {"name": "Anatomical Relations", "text": "Afferent glomerular arterioles are branches of the interlobular arteries."}, {"name": "Function", "text": "Afferent arterioles are responsible for the delivery of blood to the glomerulus. As afferent arterioles lie adjacent to the juxtaglomerular apparatus, they additionally play an important role in the regulation of blood pressure and glomerular filtration rate. Specifically, small specialized cells called the macula densa in the distal convoluted tubule detect changes in sodium levels of the fluid in the tubule. When sodium levels are high, macula densa trigger afferent arterioles to contract in order to reduce blood flow (Pocock et al, 2013)."}, {"name": "References", "text": "Dorland, W. (2011) Dorland's Illustrated Medical Dictionary. 32nd edn. Philadelphia, USA: Elsevier Saunders.

Pocock, G., Richards, C. D. & Richards, D. A. (2013) Human Physiology, 4 edition. OUP Oxford.

Standring, S. (2016) Gray's Anatomy: The Anatomical Basis of Clinical PracticeElsevier Limited."}]

items.name: Tunica Interna of Vessel (Large Vein)
Neural Microtubule
items.info: [{"name": "Quick Facts", "text": "A microtubule is a tubular cytoplasmic structure, 25 nm in diameter and of variable length, composed of \u03b1- and \u03b2-tubulin dimers, whose orientation imparts polarity; microtubules are involved in maintenance of cell shape and in the movements of organelles and inclusions and form the spindle fibers of mitosis. In cilia and flagella, they are constantly arranged with two single microtubules in the center and nine pairs of doublets arrayed around the central two. A neural microtubule is a microtubule occurring in a neuron (Dorland, 2011)."}, {"name": "Structure", "text": "Processes that radiate from the neuron cell body (soma) are called \u201cneurites.\u201d Typically, there are two types: usually a single axon and then multiple dendrites. Microtubules, which average about 20 nm in diameter, run longitudinally along neurites. Microtubules are \u201cbraided\u201d long strands (polymers) of a small protein called tubulin. Each tubulin molecule is joined by a process called \u201cpolymerization.\u201d The assembly of the microtubule is regulated by microtubule-associated proteins (MAP\u2019s) (Bear, Connors and Paradiso, 2007)."}, {"name": "Function", "text": "Neuronal shape is determined largely by polymerization of the microtubules. Microtubule associated proteins (MAP\u2019s) regulate the assembly and function of the microtubule as well as anchoring microtubules to each other and to other components of the neuron (Bear, Connors and Paradiso, 2007)."}, {"name": "Clinical Correlates", "text": "\u2014Pathological changes in the microtubule-associated proteins (MAP\u2019s) has been implicated in the dementia that accompanies Alzheimer\u2019s disease."}, {"name": "References", "text": "Bear, M. F., Connors, B. W. and Paradiso, M. A. (2007) Neuroscience. Lippincott Williams & Wilkins.\n\nDorland, W. (2011) Dorland's Illustrated Medical Dictionary. 32nd edn. Philadelphia, USA: Elsevier Saunders."}]

items.name: Basement Membrane (Large Vein)
Interfascicular Arteries
items.info: [{"name": "Quick Facts", "text": "The intrafascicular arteries are part of the vasa nervorum and help supply the nerve."}, {"name": "Structure/Morphology", "text": "The interfascicular arteries are located within the internal epineurium and form part of the vasa nervorum, small vessels that supply blood to peripheral nerves. This network of vessels supplies blood to the interior parts of the nerves and their coverings. The vasa vasorum are located within the connective tissue of the nerve scattered between the fascicles (Boissaud-Cooke, Pidgeon and Tunstall, 2015)."}, {"name": "Anatomical Relations", "text": "The vasa nervorum are the smallest vessels in the epineurial, perineurial, and endoneurial layers."}, {"name": "Function", "text": "The vasa nervorum supply the peripheral nerves with the molecular nutrients needed to carry out their cellular functions and for survival (Carp, 2015)."}, {"name": "References", "text": "Boissaud-Cooke, M., Pidgeon, T. E. and Tunstall, R. (2015) 'Chapter 37 - The Microcirculation of Peripheral Nerves: The Vasa Nervorum A2 - Tubbs, R. Shane', in Rizk, E., Shoja, M.M., Loukas, M., Barbaro, N. & Spinner, R.J. (eds.) Nerves and Nerve Injuries. San Diego: Academic Press, pp. 507-523.\n\nCarp, S. (2015) Peripheral Nerve Injury An Anatomical and Physiological Approach for Physical Therapy Intervention. EBL-Schweitzer: F. A. Davis Company."}]

items.name: Endotendon
items.info:
[{"name": "Quick Facts", "text": "The endotendon is the delicate connective tissue separating the secondary bundles (fascicles) of a tendon (Dorland, 2011)."}, {"name": "Structure and/or Key Feature(s)", "text": "The endotendon (or endotenon) is a network of thin loose organized fibrous connective tissue. It is a layer or sheath that envelops collagen bundles, essentially separating the individual fascicles in a tendon unit (Maffulli, Renstrom and Leadbetter, 2005). Endotendon is continuous with the inner surface of the epitendon and at the musculotendinous junction, it continues into the perimysium (Cowin and Doty, 2007). Endotendon is composed of elastin, collagen, and proteoglycans (Nigg and Herzog, 1999)."}, {"name": "Anatomical Relations", "text": "Collagen fibrils aggregate to form collagen fibers, which are bound together by endotendon to form the primary fiber bundles. The primary fiber bundles are held together to form the secondary fiber bundles, and the secondary fiber bundles are bound together to form the tertiary fiber bundles. These units form the tendon. 

The endotendon surrounds and separates individual fascicles in a tendon unit. Epitendon envelopes the fascicles that are surrounded by the endotendon, as well as the functional groups of fascicles surrounded by the peritendon (Cowin and Doty, 2007)."}, {"name": "Function", "text": "Endotendon encompasses and bounds the collagen bundles together as well as enveloping the primary, secondary, and tertiary fiber bundles which make up a tendon unit (Schleip et al., 2013). Endotendon is involved in the hydration of proteoglycan elements located between the endotendon and the fascicles. This involvement enables the collagen bundles to move i.e., glide past each other to facilitate tendon movement (Franchi et al., 2007). 

The endotendon also provides nutrition to the tendon and contributes to wound healing as it carries some small blood vessels, lymphatic verses and nerve fibers to deeper regions of the tendon (Maffulli, Renstrom and Leadbetter, 2005)."}, {"name": "References", "text": "Cowin, S. C. and Doty, S. B. (2007) Tissue Mechanics. Springer New York.

Dorland, W. (2011) Dorland's Illustrated Medical Dictionary. 32nd edn. Philadelphia, USA: Elsevier Saunders.

Franchi, M., Trirè, A., Quaranta, M., Orsini, E. and Ottani, V. (2007) 'Collagen structure of tendon relates to function', ScientificWorldJournal, 7, pp. 404-20.

Maffulli, N., Renstrom, P. and Leadbetter, W. B. (2005) Tendon Injuries: Basic Science and Clinical Medicine. Springer London.

Nigg, B. M. and Herzog, W. (1999) Biomechanics of the Musculo-Skeletal System. Wiley.

Schleip, R., Findley, T. W., Chaitow, L. and Huijing, P. (2013) Fascia: The Tensional Network of the Human Body - E-Book: The science and clinical applications in manual and movement therapy. Elsevier Health Sciences."}]

items.name: Nervi Vasorum (Artery)
Procerus Muscle
items.info:
[{"name": "Quick Facts", "text": "Origin: Fascia covering nasal bone; lateral nasal cartilage.

Insertion: Skin of forehead.

Action: Depresses medial angle of eyebrow; wrinkles skin covering bridge of nose.

Innervation: Temporal and zygomatic branches of facial nerve (CN VII).

Arterial Supply: Facial artery."}, {"name": "Origin", "text": "The procerus muscle arises from the fascia lining the lower part of the nasal bone and from the upper part of the lateral nasal cartilage."}, {"name": "Insertion", "text": "The procerus muscle inserts into the skin of the lower forehead, between the eyebrows."}, {"name": "Key Features & Anatomical Relations", "text": "The procerus muscle is often blended with the medial portion of the formal part of the occipitofrontalis muscle."}, {"name": "Actions", "text": "The procerus muscle depresses the medial angle of the eyebrow and produces transverse wrinkles of the skin covering the bridge of the nose. This action is used when frowning (Standring, 2016)."}, {"name": "List of Clinical Correlates", "text": "- Bell’s palsy"}, {"name": "References", "text": "Standring, S. (2016) Gray's Anatomy: The Anatomical Basis of Clinical Practice. Gray's Anatomy Series 41st edn.: Elsevier Limited."}]

items.name: Subendothelial Layer (Large Vein)
Plasma Membrane (Head; Left)
items.info:
[{"name": "Quick Facts", "text": "The plasma membrane is the structure enveloping a cell, enclosing the cytoplasm and forming a selective permeability barrier; it consists of a lipid bilayer with integral and peripheral proteins and contains channels and pumps to transport substances across the membrane, as well as receptors to receive stimuli from the external environment and transduce them into intracellular signals (Dorland, 2011)."}, {"name": "Structure and/or Key Feature(s)", "text": "The sperm’s plasma membrane is a dynamic structure and is unique when compared with that of somatic cells. It is divided into various domains based on its location, composition, and function. 

In the sperm head, there are two notable regions of the plasma membrane, the acrosomal region and the postacrosomal region. The plasma membrane that surrounds the tail aspect of the sperm is divided into the middle piece, the principal piece, and the distal piece domains (Toshimori, 2000)."}, {"name": "Anatomical Relations", "text": "The plasma membrane is the outermost part of the sperm and it encases the entirety of the sperm cell."}, {"name": "Function", "text": "The plasma membrane plays a number of roles, which are vital for fertilization to occur. Modification of the plasma membrane is paramount for the initiation of processes, such as capacitation, acrosome reaction, and binding of the sperm head with the plasma membrane of the ovum, to occur. Most of these modifications occur as the sperm passes through the epididymis and in the uterine tube, oviduct (or fallopian tube) of the female reproductive tract (Toshimori, 2000)."}, {"name": "References", "text": "Dorland, W. (2011) Dorland's Illustrated Medical Dictionary. 32nd edn. Philadelphia, USA: Elsevier Saunders.

Toshimori, K. (2000) Sperm Plasma Membrane Modifications Associated with Fertilization in Mammals. Journal of Reproduction and Development, 46, 65-78."}]

items.name: Cytoplasm (Middle Piece; Left)
items.info:
[{"name": "Quick Facts", "text": "The cytoplasm is the protoplasm of a cell exclusive of that of the nucleus; it consists of a continuous aqueous solution (cytosol) and the organelles and inclusions suspended in it and is the site of most of the chemical activities of the cell (Dorland, 2011)."}, {"name": "Structure and/or Key Feature(s)", "text": "The cytoplasm of a cell includes an aqueous solution, the cytosol, and the organelles of the cell suspended in it. It is tightly enclosed by the plasma membrane. The sperm contains a limited amount of cytoplasm. During normal spermatogenesis (or maturation), spermatids lose most of their cytoplasm. Remnants may remain as a cytoplasmic droplet at the neck region of the sperm and is shed during ejaculation. However, retention of the droplets may indicate failure of normal maturation and cause infertility (Rengan et al, 2012).

The mature sperm retains a thin layer of cytoplasm underneath the plasma membrane. In the head, the space occupied by cytoplasm between the acrosome and the nucleus is known as the subacrosomal (or perinuclear) space. The cytoplasm between the outer membrane of the acrosome and the plasma membrane is the periacrosomal space."}, {"name": "Function", "text": "The cytoplasm is the site where most chemical activities of the cell occur."}, {"name": "References", "text": "Dorland, W. (2011) Dorland's Illustrated Medical Dictionary. 32nd edn. Philadelphia, USA: Elsevier Saunders.

Rengan, A. K., Agarwal, A., van der Linde, M. & du Plessis, S. S. (2012) An investigation of excess residual cytoplasm in human spermatozoa and its distinction from the cytoplasmic droplet. Reproductive biology and endocrinology : RB&E, 10, 92-92."}]

items.name: Vascular Endothelium (Large Vein)
Paneth Cell (Ileum)
items.info: [{"name": "Quick Facts", "text": "Paneth cells are narrow, pyramidal, or columnar epithelial cells with a round or oval nucleus close to the base, occurring in the fundus of the crypts of Lieberk\u00fchn; they contain large granules that secrete antimicrobial substances such as defensins (Dorland, 2011)."}, {"name": "Structure/Morphology", "text": "Paneth cells are very prominent at the base of the intestinal glands as, when using traditional H&E histological staining, they have acidophilic, apical secretory vesicles."}, {"name": "Function", "text": "Granules in Paneth cells contain lysozyme, an enzyme which digests the cell wall of some bacteria, so Paneth cells have a role in regulating the natural bacterial flora of the small intestine."}, {"name": "References", "text": "Dorland, W. (2011) Dorland's Illustrated Medical Dictionary. 32nd edn. Philadelphia, USA: Elsevier Saunders."}]

items.name: Basement Membrane (Muscular Artery)
Lateral Palpebral Ligament
items.info: [{"name": "Quick Facts", "text": "The lateral palpebral ligament is a ligament that anchors the lateral end of the superior and inferior tarsal plates to the margin of the orbit (Dorland, 2011)."}, {"name": "Structure and/or Key Feature(s)", "text": "The lateral palpebral (canthic) ligament is formed from a dense and fibrous tissue. It passes from the lateral edges of the superior and inferior tarsal plates to the marginal (or Whitnall\u2019s) tubercle on the zygomatic bone (forming part of the orbital margin)."}, {"name": "Anatomical Relations", "text": "The lateral palpebral ligament is found deep to the orbital septum."}, {"name": "Function", "text": "The lateral palpebral ligament, along with the orbital septum, supports the tarsal plates by tethering them to the lateral margin of the orbit. The lateral palpebral ligament is the structure responsible for the surface feature, the lateral canthus or lateral corner of the eye (Parent et al., 1993)."}, {"name": "References", "text": "Dorland, W. (2011) Dorland's Illustrated Medical Dictionary. 32nd edn. Philadelphia, USA: Elsevier Saunders.\n\nParent, A. D., Das, S. K., Mallette, R. A. and Haines, D. E. (1993) 'Significance of the lateral canthal tendon in craniofacial surgery', Pediatr Neurosurg, 19(2), pp. 73-7."}]

items.name: External Elastic Membrane (Muscular Artery)
Connecting Cilium of Cone Cell
items.info: [{"name": "Quick Facts", "text": "The connecting cilium acts as a communicating channel between the inner and outer segments of the photoreceptor cells."}, {"name": "Structure and/or Key Features", "text": "The connecting cilium is a long, slender, nonmotile, microscopic cellular organelle within the photoreceptor connecting stalk. It measures approximately 0.3 \u00b5m in diameter and is composed of microtubules in a 9x2+0 array near the cilium\u2019s base. Here the microtubules are connected to the plasma membrane. This microtubule \u201cdoublet\u201d formation transitions to 9x1+0 singlet array more distally and it continues in that configuration through to the outer segment (Chen and Sampath, 2012)."}, {"name": "Anatomical Relations", "text": "The connecting cilium is fittingly positioned between the inner and outer segments in both rod and cone cells."}, {"name": "Function", "text": "The connecting cilium acts a microscopic channel for the flow of proteins and lipids, from the site of production in the inner segment to the outer segment, with approximately 2,000 opsin molecules transported every minute (Chen and Sampath, 2012)."}, {"name": "References", "text": "Chen, J. and Sampath, A. (2012) 'Structure and Function of Rod and Cone Photoreceptors', Retina Fifth Edition, 1, pp. 342-359."}]

items.name: Internal Elastic Membrane (Muscular Artery)
Lacrimal Apparatus
items.info:
[{"name": "Quick Facts", "text": "The lacrimal apparatus is the system concerned with the secretion and circulation of the tears and the normal fluid of the conjunctival sac; it consists of the lacrimal gland and ducts, and associated structures (Dorland, 2011)."}, {"name": "Structure and/or Key Feature(s)", "text": "The lacrimal apparatus is a system of structures that produces tears (i.e., the lacrimal glands and accessory lacrimal glands) and provides for their collection and eventual drainage into the nasal cavity.

Each tear drop consists of about 7 μl of fluid made primarily by the lacrimal and accessory lacrimal glands with contributions from tarsal sebaceous glands and palpebral sweat glands. Tears are distributed over the cornea (1–2 μl) and along the upper and lower margins of the eyelids (Standring, 2016). This forms a thin film that is spread across the surface of the cornea, from superior and lateral to inferior and medial, by blinking. Some tear fluid is lost through evaporation or absorption into the conjunctiva. However, the majority is collected by two puncta are located along the margin of the superior and inferior eyelids, close to the medial canthus of the eye. The puncta are openings of short ducts, superior and inferior lacrimal canaliculi. The canaliculi transport the tears to the lacrimal sac, and then onto the nasolacrimal duct which directs the tears to the inferior meatus of the nasal cavity."}, {"name": "References", "text": "Dorland, W. (2011) Dorland's Illustrated Medical Dictionary. 32nd edn. Philadelphia, USA: Elsevier Saunders.
Standring, S. (2016) Gray's Anatomy: The Anatomical Basis of Clinical Practice. Gray's Anatomy Series 41 edn.: Elsevier Limited."}]

items.name: General Visceral Efferent Nerve Fiber (Sympathetic)
items.info:
[{"name": "Quick Facts", "text": "Efferent nerve fibers are nerve fibers that convey motor impulses away from the central nervous system toward the periphery; classified according to function as somatic efferent and visceral efferent fibers (Dorland, 2011)."}, {"name": "Structure/Morphology", "text": "The sympathetic general visceral efferent nerve fibers are composed of an unmyelinated axon."}, {"name": "Key Features/Anatomical Relations", "text": "The autonomic nervous system can be broken up into two distinct parts, the sympathetic and parasympathetic divisions. Both divisions have motor neurons that for the most part innervate the same visceral organs; however, they typically cause opposite effects on the body.

The general visceral efferent sympathetic division originates from the thoracolumbar outflow; lateral horn of gray matter of spinal cord segments T1—L2. Each general visceral efferent sympathetic nerve fiber has a preganglionic neuron and a postganglionic neuron which synapse with each other inside the peripheral autonomic ganglion. The ganglia of the general visceral efferent sympathetic division are located close to the central nervous system, and therefore, the preganglionic axon is shorter in length as compared to the postganglionic neuron/axon (with exception of splanchnic nerves). The ganglia are found:

—along the vertebral column and called the sympathetic trunk ganglia;

—anterior to the vertebral column and called the collateral ganglia. 

The sympathetic trunk is connected with the anterior ramus of the spinal nerve with the help of rami communicantes (nerves which interconnect two nerves). There are two types of communicantes; gray and white rami communicantes. These communicantes allow the sympathetic general visceral efferent nerve fibers/neurons to travel from the spinal nerve into the sympathetic chain and vice versa. White ramus communicantes contain myelinated preganglionic axons while gray rami communicantes contain unmyelinated postganglionic axons. There is extensive branching of preganglionic axons in the general visceral efferent sympathetic division."}, {"name": "Function", "text": "General visceral efferent fibers in the sympathetic division transmit information from the central nervous system to an effector organ, such as blood vessels, glands, and visceral smooth muscles. Functionally the general visceral efferent fibers in the sympathetic division prepare the body to cope with emergencies and intense muscular activity; for example, the “fight or flight” response (Patestas and Gartner, 2016)."}, {"name": "References", "text": "Dorland, W. (2011) Dorland's Illustrated Medical Dictionary. 32nd edn. Philadelphia, USA: Elsevier Saunders.

Patton, K. and Thibodeau, G. (2016). Anatomy & physiology. 9th ed. St. Louis, Missouri: Elsevier, p.394.

Patestas, M. and Gartner, L. (2016). A Textbook of Neuroanatomy. 2nd ed. New Jersey: Wiley, Blackwell, pp.64-65."}]

items.name: Smooth Muscle (Muscular Artery)
Membranous Disc of Cone Cell
items.info:
[{"name": "Quick Facts", "text": "The outer segments of rods and cones have flattened membranous discs which bear visual opsin."}, {"name": "Structure and/or Key Features", "text": "The membranous discs of cone cells are present in the outer segment; however, they are less numerous than those in the rod cells and remain attached to the plasma membrane as infoldings at the base of the cell (Standring, 2016). There are additional reports that most, if not all, of the membranous discs in cone outer segments are continuous and remain attached to the plasma membrane, however, many of the connections appear to be very small. Therefore, it is assumed that intradiscal spaces are open to the interphotoreceptor matrix (Heckenlively, Arden and Bach, 2006).

A feature known as cone notches has also been described. These notches distinguish a site of transition between discs that are open to the interphotoreceptor matrix and those that are isolated (Heckenlively, Arden and Bach, 2006). 

While rhodopsin is located on the outer segments of rod cells, a distinct feature of cone cells is the presence of proteins known as cone opsins or photopsins. There are three distinct photopsins, depending on the opsin protein that is present and bound to retinal (Standring, 2016). Each photopsin has a unique spectral sensitivity maximum and distribution.

Similar to rods, the membranous discs of cones are phagocytosed as new ones are manufactured. It should be noted that the incorporation of newly produced proteins in cone cells is more diffuse than that of rod cells."}, {"name": "Anatomical Relations", "text": "The membranous discs of rod cells are located in and extend the length of the outer segment of the rod photoreceptor cell."}, {"name": "Function", "text": "Despite their production in the inner segment of the cone cell, the spectrally distinct visual pigments are transported to the outer segments. The membranous discs are largely responsible for housing and anchoring the visual pigments. Following the absorption of light, a conformational change occurs in the opsin and retinal molecules resulting in the induction of a biochemical cascade which culminates in the production of an electrical signal representing visual information."}, {"name": "List of Clinical Correlates", "text": "- Rod-cone degeneration

- Rod-cone dystrophy"}, {"name": "References", "text": "Heckenlively, J. R., Arden, G. B. and Bach, M. (2006) Principles and Practice of Clinical Electrophysiology of Vision. MIT Press.

Standring, S. (2016) Gray's Anatomy: The Anatomical Basis of Clinical Practice. Gray's Anatomy Series 41 edn.: Elsevier Limited."}]

items.name: Tertiary Ovarian Follicle
items.info:
[{"name": "Quick Facts", "text": "A tertiary (mature) ovarian follicle is an ovarian follicle containing a secondary oocyte and a follicular antrum; its short life ends with ovulation (Dorland, 2011)."}, {"name": "Structure and/or Key Feature(s)", "text": "A secondary follicle grows and matures so that it will ovulate in response to a surge of the luteinizing hormone (LH) from the anterior pituitary gland. It bulges at the periphery of the ovary as a mature (Graafian) follicle. It may have a diameter of 10 mm or more. Its large antrum pushes the granulosa cells to the periphery of the follicle and so it becomes a thin, stratified epithelium. The oocyte will be located at one side and buried in the accumulation of granulosa cells called the cumulus oophorus. But, as the spaces between the granulosa cells continue to enlarge, the oocyte and associated cumulus cells loosen from the rest of the granulosa cell population in preparation for ovulation. The cumulus cells then form a single layer or a “crown” of granulosa cells immediately adjacent to the oocyte called the corona radiata and will accompany the oocyte at ovulation. 

In the mature follicle, the theca interna and externa are well developed. Cells directly outside of the layer of granulosa cells are cuboidal with round nuclei. They form the theca interna. Outside of them, the cells of the theca externa are spindle shaped and run parallel to one another."}, {"name": "Anatomical Relations", "text": "The mature (tertiary) ovarian follicle is located in the outer cortex of the ovary, where it causes the surface of the ovary to bulge (Standring, 2016)."}, {"name": "References", "text": "Dorland, W. (2011) Dorland's Illustrated Medical Dictionary. 32nd edn. Philadelphia, USA: Elsevier Saunders.

Standring, S. (2016) Gray's Anatomy: The Anatomical Basis of Clinical Practice. Gray's Anatomy Series 41 edn.: Elsevier Limited."}]

items.name: Vasa Vasorum (Muscular Artery)
Glomerular Capillary Vessel
items.info:
[{"name": "Quick Facts", "text": "A glomerular capillary is any of the capillaries of a renal glomerulus (Dorland, 2011)."}, {"name": "Structure and/or Key Feature(s)", "text": "Endothelium of glomerular capillaries contains numerous fenestrations about 70–90 nm in diameter and lacks a diaphragm present in fenestrations of capillaries in other body organs (Ross and Pawlina, 2006). The endothelial cells possess water channels permitting rapid movement of water through the epithelium.

Endothelial cells lining the glomerular capillaries exhibit a glycocalyx consisting of a 200–400 nm meshwork of carbohydrate-rich molecules and peripheral membrane proteins (Ross and Pawlina, 2006). Plasma proteins, such as albumin, taken up from the blood coat the luminal surface of the glycocalyx."}, {"name": "Anatomical Relations", "text": "Glomerular capillary vessels are enclosed within the glomerular (Bowman’s) space."}, {"name": "Function", "text": "Glomerular capillaries of the renal corpuscle facilitate the blood-filtering function of the nephron."}, {"name": "List of Clinical Correlates", "text": "Secretory products of the endothelial cells e.g., nitric oxide or prostaglandins (PGE2) play a role in the pathogenesis of several thrombotic glomerular diseases."}, {"name": "References", "text": "Dorland, W. (2011) Dorland's Illustrated Medical Dictionary. 32nd edn. Philadelphia, USA: Elsevier Saunders.

Ross, M. H. and Pawlina, W. (2006) Histology: A text and atlas. Lippincott Williams & Wilkins."}]

items.name: Adipose Tissue
items.info: [{"name": "Quick Facts", "text": "Adipose tissue is a connective tissue made up of fat cells in a meshwork of areolar tissue (Dorland, 2011)."}, {"name": "Structure/Morphology", "text": "Adipose tissue is formed of adipocytes and found inside the dense connective tissue surrounding the fascicles in a nerve."}, {"name": "Key Features/Anatomical Relations", "text": "Interfascicular adipose tissue is directly enclosed by the epineurium."}, {"name": "Function", "text": "Adipose tissue acts as an insulator and facilitates mobility between nerves. This interfascicular fat also serves as a cushion by preventing damage to the nerve fibers during compression. There is also strong evidence to suggest that intrafascicular fat plays a role in regeneration of nerves (Walocko et al., 2016)."}, {"name": "List of Clinical Correlates", "text": "\u2014Lipomatosis of nerve"}, {"name": "References", "text": "Dorland, W. (2011) Dorland's Illustrated Medical Dictionary. 32nd edn. Philadelphia, USA: Elsevier Saunders.\n\nWalocko, F. M., Khouri, R. K., Urbanchek, M. G., Levi, B. and Cederna, P. S. (2016) 'The potential roles for adipose tissue in peripheral nerve regeneration', Microsurgery, 36(1), pp. 81-8."}]

items.name: Basement Membrane (Arteriole)
Tufted Cell
items.info:
[{"name": "Quick Facts", "text": "A tufted cell is a type of neuron in the olfactory bulb; smaller, more numerous, and more superficially located than a mitral cell but with similar functions and connections (Dorland, 2011)."}, {"name": "Structure and/or Key Features", "text": "Tufted cells, to a lesser extent (in comparison to mitral cells), are principal neurons of the olfactory bulb. They form the minor output of the olfactory bulb to the cerebral cortex via the olfactory tract, while the mitral cells form the major output. Although tufted cells are smaller than mitral cells, their branching configuration and synapses are similar. 

Tufted cells are situated throughout the external plexiform layer of the olfactory bulb and at the border of the glomerular layer. The tufted cells extend to inter- and intrabulbar locations, as well as to the piriform cortex (Davis and Eichenbaum, 1991). 

Tufted cells can be grouped into three subtypes, the external, middle, and internal tufted cells. They are situated in close proximity to the boundary between the glomerular layer and the external plexiform layer. They have small cell bodies with a diameter of 10–15 μm. 

The middle tufted cells have medium-sized cell bodies (15–20 μm in diameter) and are situated within the intermediate and superficial aspects of the external plexiform layer. The internal tufted cells have large cell bodies with diameters greater than 20 μm. They are situated in the deep part of the external plexiform layer (Soiza-Reilly, Saggau and Arenkiel, 2015). 

The dendrites of tufted cells arise from the apical aspect of the cell body. They travel superficially to a glomerulus where they each branch (less abundantly in comparison to the mitral cells) forming a dendritic tree of thin dendritic processes (Farbman et al., 1992)."}, {"name": "Anatomical Relations", "text": "Tufted cells are situated throughout the external plexiform layer of the olfactory bulb, and at the border of the glomerular layer."}, {"name": "Function", "text": "Tufted cells play a role in olfactory transduction and facilitate the sense of smell along with the mitral cells. The tufted cells activate other parts of the olfactory system using a number of inter- and intrabulbar interconnections (Arslan, 2014)."}, {"name": "Clinical Correlates", "text": "—Anosmia"}, {"name": "References", "text": "Arslan, O. E. (2014) Neuroanatomical Basis of Clinical Neurology, Second Edition. Taylor & Francis.

Davis, J. L. and Eichenbaum, H. (1991) Olfaction: A Model System for Computational Neuroscience. Bradford Bks: MIT Press.

Dorland, W. (2011) Dorland's Illustrated Medical Dictionary. 32nd edn. Philadelphia, USA: Elsevier Saunders.

Farbman, A. I., Bard, J. B. L., Barlow, P. W. and Kirk, D. L. (1992) Cell Biology of Olfaction. Developmental and Cell Biology Series: Cambridge University Press.

Soiza-Reilly, M., Saggau, P. and Arenkiel, B. R. (2015) Neural Circuits Revealed. Frontiers Research Topics: Frontiers Media SA."}]

items.name: Endoneurium
items.info:
[{"name": "Quick Facts", "text": "The endoneurium is the connective tissue in a peripheral nerve fascicle; it forms an interstitial layer around the neurilemma that surrounds individual myelinated nerve fibers and Remak bundles of unmyelinated fibers (Dorland, 2011)."}, {"name": "Structure/Morphology", "text": "The endoneurium is the connective tissue layer surrounding a nerve fiber (neuron) including the neurolemma and the myelin sheath. This connective tissue is made up of a fibrous matrix largely composed of collagen type III fibers (reticulin), which are arranged into intricate bundles, parallel to the long axis of the nerve. They tend to become somewhat concentrated around individual Schwann cell-axon units and vessels of the endoneurium. The primary cellular constituents of the endoneurium are fibroblasts, however resident macrophages and mast cells are also present (Standring, 2016)."}, {"name": "Anatomical Relations", "text": "The fibrous and cellular components of the endoneurium are bathed in endoneurial fluid at a slightly higher pressure than that found external to the endoneurial channel. Within the endoneurial channel, tiny capillaries are present which are comprised of a single layer of non-fenestrated endothelial cells. These serve as part of the blood-nerve barrier (Peltonen et al., 2013)"}, {"name": "Function", "text": "The endoneurium plays a role in isolating nerve signals. Each peripheral nerve contains numerous axons that transmit to several muscles in the body. The endoneurium is in control of keeping these signals separate ensuring they are transmitted to the correct location. The endoneurium also protects the delicate axons from potential harm. Another function of the endoneurium, which is shared by the perineurium and epineurium, is the protection of neurons from damage (Carp, 2015)."}, {"name": "List of Clinical Correlates", "text": "—Advanced axonal neuropathy"}, {"name": "References", "text": "Carp, S. (2015) Peripheral Nerve Injury An Anatomical and Physiological Approach for Physical Therapy Intervention. EBL-Schweitzer: F. A. Davis Company.

Dorland, W. (2011) Dorland's Illustrated Medical Dictionary. 32nd edn. Philadelphia, USA: Elsevier Saunders.

Peltonen, S., Alanne, M. and Peltonen, J. (2013) 'Barriers of the peripheral nerve', Tissue Barriers, 1(3), pp. e24956.

Standring, S. (2016) Gray's Anatomy: The Anatomical Basis of Clinical Practice. Gray's Anatomy Series: Elsevier Limited."}]

items.name: Dense-core Vesicle
items.info: [{"name": "Quick Facts", "text": "Dense-core vesicles are membrane-bound structures behind a presynaptic membrane, containing neuropeptides."}, {"name": "Structure", "text": "Besides typical synaptic vesicles, many axons contain larger vesicles (about 100 nm in diameter) called secretory vesicles. When viewed with the electron microscope, these vesicles appear dark as they contain a soluble protein. Hence, they are referred to as \u201cdense-core vesicles\u201d."}, {"name": "Function", "text": "Chemically, neurotransmitters are either amino acids, amines, or peptides. Amine and amino acid neurotransmitters are stored in synaptic vesicles, whereas peptide neurotransmitters are found in dense-core vesicles.\n\nSecretory granules that release peptide neurotransmitters require a much greater influx of Ca2+ ions (and so a high frequency of action potentials) and often the release is away from the active zones (Bear, Connors and Paradiso, 2007)."}, {"name": "References", "text": "Bear, M. F., Connors, B. W. and Paradiso, M. A. (2007) Neuroscience. Lippincott Williams & Wilkins."}]

items.name: Cornea
items.info:
[{"name": "Quick Facts", "text": "The cornea is the transparent structure forming the anterior part of the fibrous layer of the eyeball. It consists of five layers: (1) the anterior corneal epithelium, continuous with that of the conjunctiva; (2) the anterior limiting layer (Bowman membrane); (3) the substantia propria, or stroma; (4) the posterior limiting layer (Descemet membrane); and (5) the endothelium of the anterior chamber (Dorland, 2011)."}, {"name": "Structure and/or Key Feature(s)", "text": "The cornea forms a small, anterior most, part of the tough outer fibrous layer of the eyeball. It constitutes about 7% of the external surface of the eyeball, the remainder being sclera. 

The cornea is convex anteriorly, projecting as a dome from the sclera and varies in thickness, from about 670 μm at the corneoscleral junction (where the cornea and sclera become continuous) to 520 μm at the center. The external surface of the cornea is covered by a tear film, lubricating and hydrating its surface.

The cornea consists of five layers including, from anterior to posterior, corneal epithelium, anterior limiting lamina, stroma, posterior limiting lamina, and endothelium.

The corneal epithelium is composed of 5–6 layers of cells and makes up 10% of the corneal thickness. Its role is to protect the surface of the eye from abrasion, preventing the entry of pathogens into the eyeball, while allowing passage of small molecules, such as water and certain ions. Directly behind the corneal epithelium lies the anterior limiting lamina or Bowman’s layer. It is thin, composed of dense collagen fibrils. The thickest layer of the cornea is the substantia propria (or stroma). It is composed of 200–250 layers of collagen fibrils with interposed fibroblasts. All collagen fibrils within a single layer are parallel with each other, and those between layers are orthogonal. This highly regular geometry allows the stroma to retain clarity.

The posterior limiting lamina, or Descemet’s layer, lines the stroma posteriorly and acts as a basement membrane from the underlying endothelium. The endothelium is a single cell layer of squamous cells lining the posterior aspect of the cornea (Standring, 2016)."}, {"name": "Anatomical Relations", "text": "The cornea is continuous with the sclera at the limbus. Here, the epithelial layer of the cornea merges with the epithelium of the conjunctiva. The anterior limiting lamina terminates, and the corneal stroma loses its collagen density and regular geometry. The posterior limiting lamina becomes continuous with the trabecular meshwork, while the endothelium of the cornea is continuous with the epithelium covering the trabeculae."}, {"name": "Function", "text": "The cornea is the most powerful contributor to the optical power of the eye, accounting for 70% of its refractive power. Therefore, changes to the shape of the cornea have significant implications for vision."}, {"name": "Clinical Correlates", "text": "—Astigmatism

—Corneal cataracts"}, {"name": "References", "text": "Dorland, W. (2011) Dorland's Illustrated Medical Dictionary. 32nd edn. Philadelphia, USA: Elsevier Saunders.

Standring, S. (2016) Gray's Anatomy: The Anatomical Basis of Clinical Practice. Gray's Anatomy Series 41 edn.: Elsevier Limited."}]
