items.name: Muscular Layer of Small Intestine (Ileum)
items.info:
[{"name": "Quick Facts", "text": "The muscular layer is the layer of smooth muscle lying between the submucosa and the serosa or the adventitia in many portions of the digestive, respiratory, urinary, and genital tracts (Dorland, 2011)."}, {"name": "Structure/Morphology", "text": "The muscular layer (or muscularis externa) is well developed and composed of an internal circular layer and an external longitudinal layer. Between the two layers are ganglion cells and nerve fibers forming the myenteric (Auerbach’s) plexus. How the smooth muscle cells appear under the microscope will depend on the plane of the section i.e., transverse or longitudinal."}, {"name": "Key Features/Anatomical Relations", "text": "At a few locations along the alimentary tract, the muscular layer thickens to form sphincters. The gastroduodenal sphincter (or pyloric sphincter) is an example in the small intestine. It is located at the junction of the pylorus of the stomach and the duodenum."}, {"name": "Function", "text": "Contractions of the inner circular layer of the muscular layer constricts the lumen and mixes the luminal contents. Contraction of the outer longitudinal layer of the muscular layer propels the contents along the digestive tract. 

The slow, rhythmic contraction of both these muscle layers, under the control of the enteric nervous system, produces peristalsis.

The gastroduodenal sphincter (or pyloric sphincter) controls the release of chyme into the duodenum."}, {"name": "References", "text": "Dorland, W. (2011) Dorland's Illustrated Medical Dictionary. 32nd edn. Philadelphia, USA: Elsevier Saunders."}]

items.name: Muscularis mucosa (Ileum)
items.info:
[{"name": "Quick Facts", "text": "The muscularis mucosa is the thin layer of smooth muscle fibers usually found as a part of the tunica mucosa deep to the lamina propria mucosae (Dorland, 2011)."}, {"name": "Structure/Morphology", "text": "The muscularis mucosa is similar in the three components of the small intestine. It is the deepest part of the mucosa and consists of a very thin inner circular layer of smooth muscle and an equally thin outer longitudinal layer of smooth muscle.

Some small smooth muscle cells travel vertically from the muscularis mucosa to the tips of villi."}, {"name": "Key Features/Anatomical Relations", "text": "The muscularis mucosa is the deepest part of the mucosa and adjacent to the submucosa."}, {"name": "Function", "text": "Contraction of the muscularis mucosa (independent of the peristaltic movement of the entire gut wall) moves the mucosa and form ridges and depressions that facilitate absorption and secretion.

Rhythmic movement of villi is due to the contractions of the smooth muscle cells that travel vertically from the muscularis mucosa to the tips of villi. These contractions occur several times per minute and serve to pump lymph from lacteals into mesenteric lymphatics (Eroschenko, 2008)."}, {"name": "References", "text": "Dorland, W. (2011) Dorland's Illustrated Medical Dictionary. 32nd edn. Philadelphia, USA: Elsevier Saunders.

Eroschenko, V. P. (2008) DiFiore's Atlas of Histology with Functional Correlations. 11th edn.: Wolters Kluwer Health/Lippincott Williams & Wilkins."}]

items.info: [{"name": "Description", "text": "The middle phalanges of the foot are one of the three rows of bones of the toes, the other two being the proximal and distal phalanges. items.name: Serosa of Small Intestine (Duodenum)
items.info:
[{"name": "Quick Facts", "text": "The serosa is the membrane lining the walls of various body cavities, reflected over the surfaces of protruding organs; it consists of mesothelium lying upon a subserosal connective tissue layer, and it secretes a watery exudate (Dorland, 2011)."}, {"name": "Structure/Morphology", "text": "The first 2.5 cm of the duodenum is intraperitoneal, thus is covered by a serosa (i.e., visceral peritoneum). As it becomes retroperitoneal, only the anterior surface of the duodenum is covered by a serosa, with the remaining covered by adventitia. The jejunum and ileum are covered by a serosa. 

Serosa is a serous membrane made of simple squamous epithelium or mesothelium supported by a basement membrane and a small amount of connective tissue.

Adventitia is only connective tissue that binds the gut to surrounding connective tissue of adjoining structures."}, {"name": "Key Features/Anatomical Relations", "text": "The serosa of the small intestine is the outermost layer of the small intestine. It encloses the jejunum and ileum, except at the mesenteric borders, where the serosa is reflected onto the mesentery.

The deep surface of the serosa adheres to the longitudinal muscular layer of the small intestine. The superficial surface of the serosa is an epithelium or mesothelium, which is in contact with surrounding organs or the parietal peritoneum."}, {"name": "Function", "text": "The serosa of the small intestine secretes a serosal fluid. This fluid allows the small intestine to slide across neighboring tissues without creating friction and damage."}, {"name": "References", "text": "Dorland, W. (2011) Dorland's Illustrated Medical Dictionary. 32nd edn. Philadelphia, USA: Elsevier Saunders."}]

items.name: Simple Columnar Epithelium of Mucosa of Small Intestine (Duodenum)
items.audio: Simple Columnar Epithelium of Mucosa of Small Intestine (Duodenum).mp3
items.info: [{"name": "Quick Facts", "text": "Simple columnar epithelium is the single layer of tall, elongated epithelial cells that sits on the mucosal surface of the small and large intestine, stomach, and gallbladder, responsible for absorption and secretion (Ross and Pawlina, 2006)."}, {"name": "Structure/Morphology", "text": "A simple columnar epithelium lines the intestinal tract. The bulk of these epithelial cells are enterocytes. Their nucleus is positioned in the basal domain of the cell. Microvilli extend from their apical surface. Collectively, the microvilli of enterocytes are called a \u201cstriated border.\u201d"}, {"name": "Key Features/Anatomical Relations", "text": "A simple columnar epithelium lines the intestinal tract. It is the innermost layer of the mucosa adjacent to the intestinal lumen and is supported by underlying lamina propria."}, {"name": "Function", "text": "The primary function of the enterocytes is absorption. The striated border increases the surface area for absorption as much as 600 times. \n\nEnterocytes are also secretory cells, primarily producing glycoprotein enzymes that will be reinserted into the apical membrane. They also secrete water and electrolytes (mainly those enterocytes in the intestinal glands) to balance water absorption across the enterocytes lining the villi. This maintains a constant liquified intestinal chyme."}, {"name": "References", "text": "Ross, M. H. and Pawlina, W. (2016) Histology: A Text and Atlas. Wolters Kluwer Health."}]

items.info: [{"name": "Quick Facts", "text": "Simple columnar epithelium is the single layer of tall, elongated epithelial cells that sits on the mucosal surface of the small and large intestine, stomach, and gallbladder, responsible for absorption and secretion (Ross and Pawlina, 2006)."}, {"name": "Structure/Morphology", "text": "A simple columnar epithelium lines the intestinal tract. The bulk of these epithelial cells are enterocytes. Their nucleus is positioned in the basal domain of the cell. Microvilli extend from their apical surface. Collectively, the microvilli of enterocytes are called a \u201cstriated border.\u201d"}, {"name": "Key Features/Anatomical Relations", "text": "A simple columnar epithelium lines the intestinal tract. It is the innermost layer of the mucosa adjacent to the intestinal lumen and is supported by underlying lamina propria."}, {"name": "Function", "text": "The primary function of the enterocytes is absorption. The striated border increases the surface area for absorption as much as 600 times. \n\nEnterocytes are also secretory cells, primarily producing glycoprotein enzymes that will be reinserted into the apical membrane. They also secrete water and electrolytes (mainly those enterocytes in the intestinal glands) to balance water absorption across the enterocytes lining the villi. This maintains a constant liquified intestinal chyme."}, {"name": "References", "text": "Ross, M. H. and Pawlina, W. (2016) Histology: A Text and Atlas. Wolters Kluwer Health."}]

items.name: Submucosa of Small Intestine (Duodenum)
items.info:
[{"name": "Quick Facts", "text": "The submucosa is the layer of dense connective tissue between the mucosa and the muscularis externa in most parts of the digestive, respiratory, urinary, and genital tracts (Dorland, 2011)."}, {"name": "Structure/Morphology", "text": "The submucosa is essentially a dense, irregular connective tissue layer found deep than the mucosa. It contains blood and lymphatic vessels. Blood vessels form large plexuses in the submucosa. Lacteals originating in the lamina propria of villi form a plexus near the muscularis mucosa (the outermost layer of the mucosa). From there, they flow to lymph nodules in the submucosa and unite to accompany blood vessels out of the intestine.

The submucosal (Meissner’s) nerve plexus is only visible as scattered ganglion cell bodies with satellite cells lying within the submucosal elements.

Glandular tissue is prominent in the duodenum (as “Brunner’s” or submucosal glands) where they dominate the lamina propria and the submucosa. These compound tubular glands have both serous (zymogen) and mucous secreting components.

The submucosa (and the lamina propria) in the ileum contains aggregations of lymphoid nodules known as “Peyer’s patches.” They are an important component of the gut associated lymphatic tissue (GALT). In humans there are about 30 patches. Each patch may contain 10–200 lymph nodules. At the luminal surface, they appear as a dome-shaped region devoid of villi. The epithelial surface consists of low cuboidal “M” (microfold) cells rather than absorptive cells (enterocytes) (Ross and Pawlina, 2016)."}, {"name": "Key Features/Anatomical Relations", "text": "Plicae circulares are circular transverse folds that extend up to two thirds the circumference of the lumen. They contain a core of the submucosa. They begin about 5–6 cm beyond the pylorus and are most numerous towards the end or distal part of the duodenum."}, {"name": "Function", "text": "The blood vessels within the submucosa nourish the layers of the intestinal wall as well as removing absorbed products of digestion.

The submucosal (Meissner’s) plexus is mainly responsible for innervating the smooth muscle layers of the muscularis mucosae.

Brunner’s glands secretions are between a pH of 8.1 and 9.3 and contain alkaline glycoproteins and bicarbonate which neutralizes the acidic containing chyme entering the duodenum from the stomach. Another function of these secretions is to create a pH ideal for the actions of pancreatic enzymes delivered to the duodenum.

M cells are antigen-transporting cells and carry antigens from the intestinal lumen to reach immune cells within the lamina propria of the digestive tract or gut associated lymphatic tissue (GALT).

Lacteals and the lymphatic vessels are important for the absorption of lipids."}, {"name": "References", "text": "Dorland, W. (2011) Dorland's Illustrated Medical Dictionary. 32nd edn. Philadelphia, USA: Elsevier Saunders.

Ross, M. H. and Pawlina, W. (2016) Histology: A Text and Atlas. Wolters Kluwer Health."}]

items.name: Spermatogonium
items.info:
[{"name": "Quick Facts", "text": "A spermatogonium is an undifferentiated germ cell of a male, originating in a seminiferous tubule and dividing into two primary spermatocytes (Dorland, 2011)."}, {"name": "Structure/Morphology", "text": "Spermatogonia are the germ cells of spermatozoa. They arise from primordial germ cells that migrate to the genital cords during development of the testes. 

Spermatogonia are only small cells, about 12 μm in diameter, and are located adjacent to the basement membrane of the seminiferous epithelium. At puberty they undergo mitotic divisions producing a renewing population of stem cells, type A dark (Ad) spermatogonia, or type A pale (Ap) spermatogonia. Type A pale (Ap) spermatogonia continue through many mitotic divisions and establish a population of renewing stem cells that will differentiate into progenitor cells (Type B spermatogonia) which will differentiate into primary spermatocytes (Standring, 2020).

When a type B spermatogonium divides and subsequent populations of cells differentiate, these cells do not completely separate but maintain a connection through small cytoplasmic bridges. This intercellular bridge permits communication between the primary and secondary spermatocytes and the spermatids."}, {"name": "Anatomical Relations", "text": "In the fully differentiated testis, spermatogonia are located adjacent to the basement membrane of the seminiferous epithelium."}, {"name": "Function", "text": "Spermatogonia are the germ cells for all spermatozoa."}, {"name": "References", "text": "Dorland, W. (2011) Dorland's Illustrated Medical Dictionary. 32nd edn. Philadelphia, USA: Elsevier Saunders.

Standring, S. (2020) Gray's Anatomy: The Anatomical Basis of Clinical Practice. 42nd edn.: Elsevier Health Sciences."}]

items.name: Proximal Phalanges of Foot
items.info: [{"name": "Description", "text": "The proximal phalanges of the foot are one of the three rows of bones of the toes, the other two being the middle and distal phalanges. There are five proximal phalanges of the foot, each classified as a long bone, which form the proximal segments of each toe. They\u2019re located distal to the metatarsal bones, and proximal to the distal phalanx of the great toe and the middle phalanges of the second, third, fourth, and little toes.\n\nOverall, the proximal phalanges are the largest and longest of the phalanges in the foot, the distal phalanges are the smallest and shortest, and the middle phalanges are intermediate in size."}]

items.name: Internal Surface of Sixth Rib
Caveola (Contracted Smooth Muscle; Posterior)
items.info: [{"name": "Quick Facts", "text": "A caveola is a small (approximately 50 nm), flask-shaped invagination of the plasma membrane occurring in nearly all animal cells, coated with the membrane protein caveolin and rich in cholesterol and sphingolipids. Caveolae are a special form of lipid raft and are associated with endocytosis, budding from the plasma membrane to form pinosomes; they also concentrate signaling molecules and have been implicated in other processes, including the export of cholesterol to serum lipoproteins (Dorland, 2011)."}, {"name": "Structure and/or Key Features", "text": "Most cells in the body utilize a process called pinocytosis to ingest fluid and small protein molecules via small vesicles about 80\u2013150 nm in diameter. It is a continual process, so small vesicles are continually forming at the cell surface. Most of the vesicles eventually fuse with lysosomes although they are very numerous in endothelial cells as they move materials from their surface of origin to the other side. They are also numerous at the surfaces of smooth muscle cells and their initial invaginations from the sarcolemma (plasma membrane) are referred to as caveolae. Cytoplasmic vesicles are in close proximity to sparse amounts of smooth endoplasmic reticulum (sER)."}, {"name": "Anatomical Relations", "text": "Caveolae are numerous at the surfaces of smooth muscle cells and their initial invaginations from the smooth muscle sarcolemma (plasma membrane)."}, {"name": "Function", "text": "Smooth muscle cells lack T tubules. Caveolae and vesicles function to deliver Ca+ to the cytoplasm as a consequence of depolarization of the sarcolemma and activation of voltage-sensitive Ca+ channels or direct activation of gated Ca+ release channels in the sER by a second messenger molecule. Ca+ can also be released into the cytoplasm via ligated Ca+ channels activated by hormones also by second messenger pathways. \n\nIncreasing the intracellular concentration of Ca+ is responsible for contraction of the smooth muscle cell. Contraction of smooth muscle cells is initiated by mechanical impulses, neural stimulation via neurotransmitters such as acetylcholine and norepinephrine, or chemical stimuli of the cells."}, {"name": "References", "text": "Dorland, W. (2011) Dorland's Illustrated Medical Dictionary. 32nd edn. Philadelphia, USA: Elsevier Saunders."}]

items.name: External Lamina (Uncontracted Smooth Muscle; Posterior)
items.info: [{"name": "Quick Facts", "text": "The basal lamina is the layer of the basement membrane lying next to the basal surface of the adjoining cell layer; composed of an electron-dense lamina densa and an electron-lucent lamina lucida; sometimes used to denote the lamina densa alone (Dorland, 2011)."}, {"name": "Structure and/or Key Features", "text": "The external lamina (or basal lamina) is made up of several different proteins and carbohydrates, such as collagen, proteoglycans, and glycoproteins. It forms a matrix which surrounds the muscle fiber and plays a central role in its structure and function.\n\nThe term \u201cexternal lamina\u201d replaces \u201cbasal lamina\u201d in nonepithelial cells such as muscle cells, adipocytes, and supporting cells in the peripheral nervous system."}, {"name": "Anatomical Relations", "text": "The external lamina surrounds the muscle fiber and is directly linked to the sarcolemma."}, {"name": "Function", "text": "The external lamina has several important roles in the structure and function of the muscle fiber such as mechanical support to underlying structures. It also acts as a scaffold for many important cells which act on the muscle fiber. The external lamina matrix has been found to be a component of important molecular signaling, i.e., it contains an enzyme, acetylcholinesterase, which breaks down acetylcholine during neuromuscular transmissions. Its role seems to be important in a wide range of functions from development to myogenesis and synaptogenesis."}, {"name": "References", "text": "Dorland, W. (2011) Dorland's Illustrated Medical Dictionary. 32nd edn. Philadelphia, USA: Elsevier Saunders."}]

items.name: Gap Junction (Contracted Smooth Muscle)
items.info:
[{"name": "Quick Facts", "text": "Gap junctions are a type of intercellular junction comprising a narrowed portion (about 3 nm) of the intercellular space that contains channels or pores (about 2 nm) composed of hexagonal arrays of membrane-spanning proteins around a central lumen (connexon) through which pass ions and small molecules such as most sugars, amino acids, nucleotides, vitamins, hormones, and cyclic AMP. In electrically excitable tissues, these gap junctions serve to transmit electrical impulses via ionic currents and are known as electrotonic synapses; they are present in such tissues as myocardial tissue and the central nervous system (Dorland, 2011)."}, {"name": "Structure and/or Key Features", "text": "Gap junctions appear as a close (2 nm) apposition of adjacent cell membranes. The individual structural unit of a gap junction is the connexon formed from six gap junction proteins called connexins joining together and creating a pore about 1.5–2 nm in diameter (Ovalle, Nahirney and Netter, 2013). Individual connexons of adjacent cells align to form a hydrophilic channel between the adjacent cells."}, {"name": "Anatomical Relations", "text": "Gap junctions appear as a close (2 nm) apposition of adjacent cell membranes."}, {"name": "Function", "text": "Gap junctions permit the exchange of small molecules e.g., ions, signaling molecules (such as hormones), and small metabolites, between adjacent cells causing the cells to act in a coordinated manner.

Contraction of smooth muscle is slow and prolonged. 

Smooth muscle is innervated by the autonomic nervous system (sympathetic and parasympathetic innervation), and in most cases, an individual nerve ending supplies groups of cells, rather than individual cells. Gap junctions connecting adjacent smooth muscle cells allows excitation from a nerve fiber to spread across the cells, resulting in synchronous contractions (Ovalle, Nahirney and Netter, 2013)."}, {"name": "Clinical Correlates", "text": "About 21 members of the connexin protein family have been identified. Mutations in gene coding connexin-26 (Cx26) is associated with congenital deafness; mutations of Cx46 and Cx50 genes have been associated with people with inherited cataracts (Ovalle, Nahirney and Netter, 2013)."}, {"name": "References", "text": "Dorland, W. (2011) Dorland's Illustrated Medical Dictionary. 32nd edn. Philadelphia, USA: Elsevier Saunders.

Ovalle, W. K., Nahirney, P. C. and Netter, F. H. (2013) Netter's Essential Histology. ClinicalKey 2012: Elsevier Saunders."}]

items.info:
[{"name": "Quick Facts", "text": "An intermediate filament is a class of cytoplasmic filaments, 8–11 nm in diameter, that predominantly act as structural components of the cytoskeleton and also allow various movements in cellular processes. Different types contain different, tissue-specific proteins (Dorland, 2011)."}, {"name": "Structure and/or Key Features", "text": "Intermediate filaments are like ropes forming an intersecting cytoskeletal network. They are around 10 nm in diameter and are composed of desmin or vimentin. They attach to the dense bodies, linking them to the sarcolemma (Ovalle, Nahirney and Netter, 2013)."}, {"name": "Function", "text": "Intermediate filaments have a structural role maintaining the stability of cell-to-cell junctions and adherence of the cell to the extracellular matrix. They also function as part of the cytoskeleton, thus supporting the cell (Ross and Pawlina, 2016)."}, {"name": "Clinical Correlates", "text": "–Several diseases can be attributed to defects in the assembly of intermediate filaments. A characteristic of Alzheimer’s disease is disarray of intermediate filaments in some neurons (Ross & Pawlina, 2016).

–“Mallory bodies” in hepatocytes in alcoholic liver cirrhosis is the accumulation of inclusions containing predominantly keratin intermediate filaments (Ross and Pawlina, 2016).

–Some specific types of intermediate filaments occurring in tumors allow the origins of the cell causing the tumor to be identified (Ovalle, Nahirney and Netter, 2013)."}, {"name": "References", "text": "Dorland, W. (2011) Dorland's Illustrated Medical Dictionary. 32nd edn. Philadelphia, USA: Elsevier Saunders.

Ovalle, W. K., Nahirney, P. C. and Netter, F. H. (2013) Netter's Essential Histology. ClinicalKey 2012: Elsevier Saunders.

Ross, M. H. and Pawlina, W. (2016) Histology: A Text and Atlas. Wolters Kluwer Health."}]

items.name: Tarsal Bones
items.info:
[{"name": "Description", "text": "The tarsal bones are one of the three groups of bones of the foot, the other two being the metatarsal bones and the phalanges. They're located between the leg and the metatarsal bones and collectively from the tarsus, which is the skeletal framework of the ankle and hindfoot. The seven tarsal bones are arranged in separate proximal and distal rows, with a single bone interposed between them.

The proximal row consists of the talus and calcaneus. These bones articulate with each other at the subtalar and talocalcaneonavicular joints. The talus articulates proximally with the tibia and fibula, forming the ankle joint.

The distal row consists of, from lateral to medial, the cuboid, lateral cuneiform, intermediate cuneiform, and medial cuneiform bones. The cuneiform bones articulate with each other at intercuneiform joints, while the lateral cuneiform bone articulates with the cuboid bone at the cuneocuboid joint. The cuboid bone articulates proximally with the calcaneus, forming the calcaneocuboid joint. The distal row of tarsal bones articulates distally with the metatarsals, forming the tarsometatarsal joints, which are collectively known as Lisfranc’s joint.

Interposed between the proximal and distal rows, on the medial aspect of the foot, is the single navicular bone. It articulates proximally with the talus at the talocalcaneonavicular joint and distally with all three cuneiform bones at the cuneonavicular joint. The navicular bone articulates laterally with the cuboid bone at the cuboideonavicular joint.

The tarsal bones are classified as short bones. Each tarsal bone is morphologically unique and named according to its perceived shape. The dorsal aspects of the tarsal bones collectively form a slightly convex surface, while their plantar aspects contribute to the formation of both the medial and lateral longitudinal arches, and the transverse arch of the foot. These arches are essential in shock absorption and weight distribution across the foot."}]

items.name: Intermediate Filament (Uncontracted Smooth Muscle)
items.info:
[{"name": "Quick Facts", "text": "An intermediate filament is a class of cytoplasmic filaments, 8–11 nm in diameter, that predominantly act as structural components of the cytoskeleton and also allow various movements in cellular processes. Different types contain different, tissue-specific proteins (Dorland, 2011)."}, {"name": "Structure and/or Key Features", "text": "Intermediate filaments are like ropes forming an intersecting cytoskeletal network. They are around 10 nm in diameter and are composed of desmin or vimentin. They attach to the dense bodies, linking them to the sarcolemma (Ovalle, Nahirney and Netter, 2013)."}, {"name": "Function", "text": "Intermediate filaments have a structural role maintaining the stability of cell-to-cell junctions and adherence of the cell to the extracellular matrix. They also function as part of the cytoskeleton, thus supporting the cell (Ross and Pawlina, 2016)."}, {"name": "Clinical Correlates", "text": "–Several diseases can be attributed to defects in the assembly of intermediate filaments. A characteristic of Alzheimer’s disease is disarray of intermediate filaments in some neurons (Ross & Pawlina, 2016).

–“Mallory bodies” in hepatocytes in alcoholic liver cirrhosis is the accumulation of inclusions containing predominantly keratin intermediate filaments (Ross and Pawlina, 2016).

–Some specific types of intermediate filaments occurring in tumors allow the origins of the cell causing the tumor to be identified (Ovalle, Nahirney and Netter, 2013)."}, {"name": "References", "text": "Dorland, W. (2011) Dorland's Illustrated Medical Dictionary. 32nd edn. Philadelphia, USA: Elsevier Saunders.

Ovalle, W. K., Nahirney, P. C. and Netter, F. H. (2013) Netter's Essential Histology. ClinicalKey 2012: Elsevier Saunders.

Ross, M. H. and Pawlina, W. (2016) Histology: A Text and Atlas. Wolters Kluwer Health."}]

items.name: Calcaneus
items.info:
[{"name": "Quick Facts", "text": "Location: Foot.

Bone Type: Short bone.

Key Features: Calcaneal tuberosity, sustentaculum tali, calcaneal sulcus, and anterior, medial and lateral processes of calcaneal tuberosity.

Articulates With: Talus, cuboid bone.

Arterial Supply: Calcaneal anastomosis; medial and lateral plantar arteries."}, {"name": "Key Features & Anatomical Relations", "text": "The calcaneus (heel bone) is the largest of the seven tarsal bones of the foot. It’s somewhat cube-shaped and is found in the proximal row of tarsal bones. The calcaneus is classified as a short bone and includes the following bony features:

- parts: calcaneal tuberosity, sustentaculum tali and anterior process;

- surfaces: dorsal, plantar, posterior, medial and lateral surfaces, and cuboid articular surface;

- landmarks: medial and lateral processes, calcaneal sulcus, and anterior, middle and posterior talar articular facets.

More information regarding these bony features can be found in the Parts, Surfaces and Landmarks tabs for this bone.

The calcaneus is located:

- proximal to the cuboid bone;

- inferior to the talus.

It articulates with the:

- cuboid bone at the calcaneocuboid joint;

- talus at the subtalar and talocalcaneonavicular joints.

The calcaneus contributes to the formation of the medial and lateral longitudinal arches of the foot."}, {"name": "Ossification", "text": "Ossification of the calcaneus occurs at two ossification centers:

- a large center, which forms the majority of the bone and appears in utero during the third month;

- a small center, which is found along the posterior surface of the bone and appears within the sixth to eighth years.

These two ossification centers fuse during the 14th to 16th years (Standring, 2016)."}, {"name": "Variations", "text": "In some individuals:

- both the sustentaculum tali and fibular trochlea may be very prominent;

- several accessory ossicles may be associated with the calcaneus, including the os calcaneus secondarius and os sustentaculi (Standring, 2016)."}, {"name": "Surface Anatomy", "text": "The following bony features of the calcaneus are relevant to surface anatomy.

- The sustentaculum tali may be palpated as a small prominence located inferior to the medial malleolus.

- The medial process of calcaneal tuberosity may sometimes be deeply palpated along the posteromedial aspect of the foot.

- The lateral surface of the calcaneus is easily palpated as it’s mostly subcutaneous."}, {"name": "List of Clinical Correlates", "text": "- Fracture of calcaneus

- Talocalcaneal coalition

- Calcaneonavicular coalition

- Calcaneocuboid coalition

- Haglund’s heel/syndrome"}, {"name": "References", "text": "Standring, S. (2016) Gray's Anatomy: The Anatomical Basis of Clinical Practice. Gray's Anatomy Series 41st edn.: Elsevier Limited."}]

items.info:
[{"name": "Quick Facts", "text": "A myofilament is any of the numerous ultramicroscopic threadlike structures occurring in bundles in the myofibrils of striated muscle fibers. The thick myosin filaments and the thin actin filaments are together responsible for the contractile properties of muscle. Also present are intermediate filaments, of uncertain function, composed of desmin and vimentin (Dorland, 2011)."}, {"name": "Structure and/or Key Features", "text": "Myofilaments include:

—thick myofilaments composed of myosin (14 nm diameter);

—thin myofilaments composed of actin, tropomyosin, and caldesmon (6–8 nm diameter) (Ovalle, Nahirney and Netter, 2013)."}, {"name": "Anatomical Relations", "text": "The sarcoplasm of striated muscle fibers house numerous numbers of long cylindrical bundles called myofibrils (1–2 μm in diameter) composed of myofilaments. In smooth muscle, they are distributed within the cell sarcoplasm."}, {"name": "Function", "text": "Myofilaments create the contractile forces in smooth muscle."}, {"name": "References", "text": "Dorland, W. items.name: Nucleus (Uncontracted Smooth Muscle)
items.info: [{"name": "Quick Facts", "text": "The nucleus is a spheroid body within a eukaryotic cell, separated from the cytoplasm by the nuclear envelope, and containing chromatin, a nucleolus, and nucleoplasm. In the nucleus, the cell's genetic information is stored on the chromosomes and RNA transcription and processing occur (Dorland, 2011)."}, {"name": "Structure and/or Key Features", "text": "Smooth muscle cells contain a single nucleus occupying the broadest region of the cell. In an uncontracted cell viewed in longitudinal section, the nucleus is an elongated structure with ends tapered. If the cell is sectioned transversely, the nucleus will appear as a circular/rounded profile.\n\nNuclei have a wrinkled or corkscrew appearance when viewed in a longitudinal section after contraction of the cell during fixation. This is a useful characteristic when trying to distinguish a smooth muscle cell from a fibroblast or fibrocyte in routine histological sections."}, {"name": "Anatomical Relations", "text": "Smooth muscle cells contain a single nucleus occupying the broadest region of the cell."}, {"name": "Function", "text": "The nucleus is the control center of the cell and houses the genome (genetic information) in eukaryotic cells. It enables DNA replication and synthesizes ribosomal (rRNA), messenger (mRNA), and transfer (tRNA) ribonucleic acid."}, {"name": "References", "text": "Dorland, W. (2011) Dorland's Illustrated Medical Dictionary. 32nd edn. Philadelphia, USA: Elsevier Saunders."}]

items.name: Pinocytotic Vesicle (Contracted Smooth Muscle)
items.info: [{"name": "Quick Facts", "text": "A pinocytotic vesicle is any of the small fluid-filled vesicles found in the cytoplasm during pinocytosis, formed by invaginations of the cell membrane (caveolae), which pinch off and become free (Dorland, 2011)."}, {"name": "Structure and/or Key Features", "text": "A pinocytotic vesicle (80\u2013150 nm in diameter) forms when the plasmalemma engulfs fluid or small proteins and any molecules in solution in the extracellular fluid. This process is called pinocytosis and is a common process in almost all human cells."}, {"name": "Anatomical Relations", "text": "Pinocytotic vesicles are located in the apical regions of the cell cytoplasm."}, {"name": "Function", "text": "A pinocytotic vesicle engulfs fluid or small proteins and any molecules in solution in the extracellular fluid."}, {"name": "References", "text": "Dorland, W. (2011) Dorland's Illustrated Medical Dictionary. 32nd edn. Philadelphia, USA: Elsevier Saunders."}]

items.name: Medial Cuneiform Bone
items.info:
[{"name": "Quick Facts", "text": "Location: Foot.

Bone Type: Short bone.

Key Features: Proximal and distal articular surfaces, dorsal and plantar surfaces, second metatarsal articular facet, and intermediate cuneiform articular facet.

Articulates With: Navicular bone, first and second metatarsal bones, intermediate cuneiform bone.

Arterial Supply: Dorsalis pedis artery."}, {"name": "Key Features & Anatomical Relations", "text": "The medial (first) cuneiform bone is one of the seven tarsal bones of the foot. It's wedge-shaped and is found in the distal row of tarsal bones. The lateral cuneiform bone is classified as a short bone and includes the following bony features:

- surfaces: dorsal, plantar, medial and lateral surfaces, and proximal and distal articular surfaces;

- landmarks: second metatarsal articular facet and intermediate cuneiform articular facet.

More information regarding these bony features can be found in the Surfaces and Landmarks tabs for this bone.

The medial cuneiform bone is located:

- proximal to the first metatarsal bone;

- distal to the navicular bone;

- medial to the intermediate cuneiform bone and second metatarsal bone.

It articulates with the:

- first and second metatarsal bones, contributing to the formation of the tarsometatarsal joints;

- navicular bone, contributing to the formation of the cuneonavicular joint;

- intermediate cuneiform bone, contributing to the formation of the intercuneiform joints.

The medial cuneiform bone contributes to the formation of the medial longitudinal arch and transverse arch of the foot."}, {"name": "Ossification", "text": "Ossification of the medial cuneiform bone may occur at two ossification centers, which appear within the second year (Standring, 2016)."}, {"name": "Variations", "text": "In some individuals:

- the medial cuneiform bone may be present in a bipartite condition (i.e. divided into two parts);

- an accessory bone may be associated with the medial cuneiform bone (Standring, 2016)."}, {"name": "Surface Anatomy", "text": "With regard to surface anatomy, the medial surface of medial cuneiform bone can be palpated on the medial aspect of the foot, between the tuberosity of navicular bone and the base of first metatarsal bone."}, {"name": "List of Clinical Correlates", "text": "- Fracture of medial cuneiform bone

- Intercuneiform coalition

- Naviculocuneiform coalition"}, {"name": "References", "text": "Standring, S. (2016) Gray's Anatomy: The Anatomical Basis of Clinical Practice. Gray's Anatomy Series 41st edn.: Elsevier Limited."}]

items.name: External Intercostal Muscles
items.info:
[{"name": "Quick Facts", "text": "Origin: Inferior borders of first to eleventh ribs.

Insertion: Superior borders of ribs immediately below origin sites.

Action: Elevate ribs at their costovertebral joints; provide structural support to intercostal spaces.

Innervation: Adjacent intercostal nerves (anterior rami of thoracic nerves).

Arterial Supply: Posterior intercostal arteries, collateral branches of posterior intercostal arteries, anterior intercostal branches of internal thoracic artery, and musculophrenic artery."}, {"name": "Origin", "text": "The external intercostal muscles originate from the inferior borders of the first to eleventh ribs."}, {"name": "Insertion", "text": "The fibers of the external intercostal muscles travel obliquely, in the opposite direction of the internal and innermost intercostal muscles, where:

- the fibers on the posterior aspect of the thorax travel inferolaterally;

- the fibers on the lateral aspect of the thorax travel anteroinferiorly;

- the fibers on the anterior aspect of the thorax travel inferomedially.

The external intercostal muscles insert onto the superior border of the rib that is immediately below its origin site (i.e., the superior borders of the second to twelfth ribs)."}, {"name": "Key Features & Anatomical Relations", "text": "The external intercostal muscles are the outer of the three intercostal muscles in the thorax, the other two being the internal and innermost intercostals. They consist of eleven pairs of flat skeletal muscles.

The external intercostal muscles are found within the intercostal spaces, where they extend from the tubercles to the sternal ends of the ribs. At their anterior ends, these muscles are replaced by the aponeurotic external intercostal membrane, which extends to the anteromedial ends of the intercostal spaces.

The external intercostal muscles are located:

- superficial to the internal intercostal muscles;

- deep to the pectoralis major, pectoralis minor, serratus anterior, and external abdominal oblique muscles."}, {"name": "Actions ", "text": "The external intercostal muscles are involved in multiple actions:

- elevate the ribs at their costovertebral joints during inspiration;

- provide structural support to the intercostal spaces during both inspiration and expiration (Netter, 2011)."}, {"name": "References", "text": "Netter, F. H. (2011) Atlas of Human Anatomy. Netter Basic Science Series: Saunders/Elsevier."}]

items.name: Sarcolemma (Contracted Smooth Muscle; Anterior)
alt: Muscle Cell Membrane (Contracted Smooth Muscle; Anterior)
items.info:
[{"name": "Quick Facts", "text": "The sarcolemma is the delicate plasma membrane that invests every striated muscle fiber (Dorland, 2011)."}, {"name": "Structure and/or Key Features", "text": "The sarcolemma is the fine, delicate, extensible membrane surrounding each muscle fiber. It is composed of a cell, or plasma, membrane which presents an extracellular matrix of collagen fibrils and polysaccharides that make contact with the basal lamina. The sarcolemma also contains tunnel-like invaginations into the sarcoplasm, which are known as transverse tubules (T tubules) in striated muscle and caveolae in smooth muscle (Standring, 2020)."}, {"name": "Anatomical Relations", "text": "Transmembrane proteins found within the sarcolemma facilitate a physical connection between the actin cytoskeleton of the muscle fiber and the extracellular basal lamina (Martini, Nath and Bartholomew, 2017)."}, {"name": "Function", "text": "Like other types of cell membranes, the sarcolemma forms a defined barrier between extracellular and intracellular environments."}, {"name": "References", "text": "Dorland, W. (2011) Dorland's Illustrated Medical Dictionary. 32nd edn. Philadelphia, USA: Elsevier Saunders.

Martini, F. H., Nath, J. L. and Bartholomew, E. F. (2017) Fundamentals of Anatomy & Physiology. Pearson Education.

Standring, S. (2020) Gray's Anatomy: The Anatomical Basis of Clinical Practice. 42nd edn.: Elsevier Health Sciences."}]

items.name: Navicular Bone
items.info:
[{"name": "Quick Facts", "text": "Location: Foot.

Bone Type: Short bone.

Key Features: Tuberosity, plantar process, proximal and distal articular surfaces, and cuboid articular facet.

Articulates With: Talus, cuboid bone, medial, intermediate, and lateral cuneiform bones.

Arterial Supply: Dorsalis pedis and medial plantar arteries."}, {"name": "Key Features & Anatomical Relations", "text": "The navicular bone is one of the seven tarsal bones of the foot. It’s boat-shaped and is the only bone found between the proximal and distal rows of the tarsal bones. It’s classified as a short bone and includes the following bony features:

- parts: tuberosity and plantar process;

- surfaces: dorsal, plantar, medial and lateral surfaces, and proximal and distal articular surfaces;

- landmarks: cuboid articular facet, and medial, intermediate and lateral cuneiform articular facets.

More information regarding these bony features can be found in the Parts, Surfaces and Landmarks tabs for this bone.

The navicular bone is located:

- proximal to the medial, intermediate and lateral cuneiform bones;

- distal to the talus;

- medial to the cuboid bone.

It articulates with the:

- medial, intermediate and lateral cuneiform bones at the cuneonavicular joint;

- cuboid bone at the cuboideonavicular joint;

- talus at the talocalcaneonavicular joint.

The navicular bone contributes to the formation of the medial longitudinal arch of the foot."}, {"name": "Ossification", "text": "Ossification of the navicular bone occurs at one ossification center, which appears within the third year (Standring, 2016)."}, {"name": "Variations", "text": "In some individuals:

- the navicular bone may be present in a bipartite condition (i.e., divided into two parts);

- an accessory ossicle may be associated with the navicular bone (Standring, 2016)."}, {"name": "Surface Anatomy", "text": "With regard to surface anatomy, the tuberosity of navicular bone is subcutaneous and can be palpated as a large bony prominence that is located anteroinferior to the medial malleolus."}, {"name": "List of Clinical Correlates", "text": "- Fracture of navicular bone

- Köhler’s disease

- Calcaneonavicular coalition

- Talonavicular coalition

- Naviculocuneiform coalition

- Cuboideonavicular coalition"}, {"name": "References", "text": "Standring, S. (2016) Gray's Anatomy: The Anatomical Basis of Clinical Practice. Gray's Anatomy Series 41st edn.: Elsevier Limited."}]

Insertion: Superior borders and internal surfaces of ribs immediately below origin sites.

Action: Elevates ribs at their costovertebral joints.

Innervation: Adjacent intercostal nerves (anterior rami of thoracic nerves).

Arterial Supply: Posterior intercostal arteries, collateral branches of posterior intercostal arteries, anterior intercostal branches of internal thoracic artery, and musculophrenic artery."}, {"name": "Origin", "text": "The innermost intercostal muscles originate from the inferior borders and internal surfaces of the first to eleventh ribs."}, {"name": "Insertion", "text": "The fibers of the innermost intercostal muscles travel obliquely, in the same direction as the internal intercostal muscles and the opposite direction of the external intercostal muscles, where:

- the fibers on the lateral aspect of the thorax travel posteroinferiorly;

- the fibers on the anterior aspect of the thorax travel inferolaterally.

The innermost intercostal muscles insert onto the superior border and internal surface of the rib that is immediately below its origin site (i.e., the superior borders and internal surfaces of the second to twelfth ribs)."}, {"name": "Key Features & Anatomical Relations", "text": "The innermost intercostal muscles are the inner of the three intercostal muscles in the thorax, the other two being the external and internal intercostals. They consist of eleven pairs of flat skeletal muscles; however, they may be absent in the superior thoracic region in some individuals.

The innermost intercostal muscles are found within the middle two quarters of the intercostal spaces. They are located:

- superficial to the endothoracic fascia and parietal pleura;

- deep to the internal intercostal muscles, the anterior rami of thoracic nerves (intercostal nerves), and the intercostal vessels."}, {"name": "Actions ", "text": "The innermost intercostal muscles elevate the ribs at their costovertebral joints (Netter, 2011)."}, {"name": "References", "text": "Netter, F. items.name: Nerve Cell Body
items.info:
[{"name": "Quick Facts", "text": "The cell body is the portion of a cell that contains the nucleus, independent of projections such as an axon or dendrites (Dorland, 2011)."}, {"name": "Structure and/or Key Features", "text": "The nerve cell body (often called perikaryon or soma), houses a large, spherical, euchromatic nucleus with a prominent nucleolus, and cytoplasm. The size of cell bodies varies depending on the type of neuron and can range from 5-140 μm (Marieb, Wilhelm and Mallatt, 2012). 

The cytoplasm contains highly developed rough (granular) endoplasmic reticulum and numerous polyribosomes, indicative of the high levels of protein syntheses occurring for both internal use and transport (Ross and Pawlina, 2006). 

The region of the cytoplasm actively synthesizing proteins stains intensely with basic dyes due to the presence of RNA. Large clumps of rough endoplasmic reticulum in large motor neurons are referred to as Nissl bodies or Nissl substance.

The cytoplasm also contains a Golgi complex consisting of parallel arrays of smooth cisternae located around the periphery of the nucleus. Mitochondria are also abundant particularly in the axon hillock but also scattered within all parts of the cytoplasm. Intermediate filaments and microtubules are abundant cytoskeletal elements in the cell body and, in some neurons, lipofuscin is a cytoplasmic inclusion (Mescher, 2013)."}, {"name": "Anatomical Relations", "text": "Neuronal cell bodies are located within the gray matter of the central nervous system or when clustered as nuclei. Cell bodies in the peripheral nervous system are located in sensory or autonomic ganglia. 

Dendrites and axons are processes that extend from the cell body. Axons extend from the nerve cell body at the axon hillock."}, {"name": "Function", "text": "The cell body of a neuron is responsible for controlling all the trophic and receptive functions of the neuron."}, {"name": "References", "text": "Dorland, W. (2011) Dorland's Illustrated Medical Dictionary. 32nd edn. Philadelphia, USA: Elsevier Saunders.

Marieb, E. N., Wilhelm, P. B. and Mallatt, J. (2012) Human Anatomy. fifth edn.: Benjamin Cummings.

Mescher, A. (2013) Junqueira's Basic Histology: Text and Atlas. 13th edn.: McGraw-Hill Education.

Ross, M. H. and Pawlina, W. (2006) Histology: A text and atlas. Lippincott Williams & Wilkins."}]

items.name: Smooth Muscle Tissue
items.info: [{"name": "Quick Facts", "text": "Smooth muscle is a type of muscle without transverse striations in its constituent fibers; it is found in the walls of the viscera and blood vessels and in the dermis and is not under voluntary control (Dorland, 2011)."}, {"name": "Description", "text": "Smooth muscle is a specialized tissue that is not under conscious control, i.e., it is involuntary muscle. Unlike striated muscle (skeletal and cardiac muscle), the myofilaments in smooth (nonstriated) muscle are less organized and their arrangement does not appear as striations under the microscope. \n\nSmooth muscle is adapted to allow prolonged periods of contraction without fatiguing. Contraction is usually regulated by the autonomic nervous system, by both sympathetic and parasympathetic nerves. Additionally, contractions may be controlled by hormones released from the posterior pituitary gland (e.g., oxytocin controls uterine smooth muscle during childbirth) or from the adrenal gland (e.g., epinephrine and norepinephrine)."}, {"name": "Anatomical Relations", "text": "Smooth muscle cells form sheets or aggregated bundles of muscle found in most tissues of the body. It can be found in the walls of hollow tubes (such as blood vessels and the intestines), sacs (such as the stomach, gallbladder, and bladder), sphincters, skin (arrector pili), and the intrinsic muscles of the eye."}, {"name": "Function", "text": "Since smooth muscle is found almost everywhere in the body, it ultimately controls functions of all organs and systems. Through its contraction and relaxation, smooth muscle regulates physiological functions such as digestion, respiration, reproduction, and blood flow."}, {"name": "Clinical Correlates", "text": "\u2014Leiomyomas"}, {"name": "References", "text": "Dorland, W. (2011) Dorland's Illustrated Medical Dictionary. 32nd edn. Philadelphia, USA: Elsevier Saunders."}]

items.name: Conjunctival Glands
items.info: [{"name": "Quick Facts", "text": "The conjunctival glands are accessory lacrimal glands situated deep in the subconjunctival connective tissue, mainly in the upper fornix (Dorland, 2011)."}, {"name": "Structure and/or Key Feature(s)", "text": "The conjunctival glands (of Krause) are accessory lacrimal glands. They are located at the fornix of the conjunctiva, where approximately 40 glands are located in the superior fornix and a quarter as many in the inferior fornix. The accessory lacrimal glands are histologically similar to the main lacrimal gland; however, they lack parasympathetic innervation."}, {"name": "Anatomical Relations", "text": "The conjunctival glands are embedded within the frontal bone, deep to the frontal sinus. The glandular acini converge on a single duct that passes through the conjunctiva forming and anterior layer of the fornix to open onto the inside of the eyelid."}, {"name": "Function", "text": "The accessory lacrimal glands contribute to the production of the aqueous component of tears. This watery secretion maintains hydration of the epithelial surface of the eye, as well as containing several proteins, such as lysozymes and immunoglobulin A, which protect the surface of the eye from infection. The Glands of Krause produce only a small amount, about 10%, of total lacrimal secretions (Conrady, Joos and Patel, 2016). Based on the absence of parasympathetic innervation, it is thought that the accessory lacrimal glands provide basal levels of tear secretion, while the main gland is responsible for reflex tearing (by irritation of the conjunctiva or cornea) when required (Conrady, Joos and Patel, 2016)."}, {"name": "References", "text": "Conrady, C. D., Joos, Z. P. and Patel, B. C. (2016) 'Review: The Lacrimal Gland and Its Role in Dry Eye', J Ophthalmol, 2016, 7542929.\n\nDorland, W. (2011) Dorland's Illustrated Medical Dictionary. 32nd edn. Philadelphia, USA: Elsevier Saunders."}]

items.name: Talus
Thick Myofilament (Contracted Smooth Muscle)
items.info:
[{"name": "Quick Facts", "text": "The thick myofilament is one of the thick contractile myofilaments in a muscle cell, composed mainly of myosin (Dorland, 2011)."}, {"name": "Structure and/or Key Features", "text": "Myosin is the main component of the thick myofilaments. It is a large complex molecule consisting of two identical heavy chains and two pairs of light chains. Each myosin heavy chain consists of two thin, rodlike molecules (2–3 nm thick and 150 nm long) twisted together (Mescher, 2013). 

Small globular projections form the heads of each myosin heavy chain. The heads contain binding sites for both ATP and actin and demonstrate motor and ATPase activity. Four light chains are associated with the head.

A thick myofilament consists of several hundred myosin molecules (1.6 μm long and 14 nm wide) arranged so their rodlike portions overlap, and their globular heads oriented toward either end (Mescher, 2013; Ovalle, Nahirney and Netter, 2013). 

The head of the myosin molecule, and a small portion of the rodlike portion, forms cross-bridges between thin and thick myofilaments. These bridges convert chemical energy into mechanical energy.

Thick myofilaments differ from those in skeletal muscle in that the polarity of the myosin heads is identical along one side of the filament and the opposite on the other side. This allows overlapping thin myofilaments to be pulled along the whole length of the thick myofilament."}, {"name": "Anatomical Relations", "text": "Thick myofilaments are scattered throughout the sarcoplasm of smooth muscle cells."}, {"name": "Function", "text": "Myosin converts chemical energy (ATP) to mechanical energy, and so generates force and movement.

Muscle contraction results from the binding of myosin to actin myofilaments, allowing myosin to function as a motor that drives myofilament sliding and so movement."}, {"name": "References", "text": "Dorland, W. (2011) Dorland's Illustrated Medical Dictionary. 32nd edn. Philadelphia, USA: Elsevier Saunders.

Mescher, A. (2013) Junqueira's Basic Histology: Text and Atlas. 13th edn.: McGraw-Hill Education.

Ovalle, W. K., Nahirney, P. C. and Netter, F. H. (2013) Netter's Essential Histology. ClinicalKey 2012: Elsevier Saunders."}]

items.name: Fibula
Capillary Vessel (Pancreas; Superior)
items.info:
[{"name": "Quick Facts", "text": "A capillary is any of the minute vessels that connect the arterioles and venules, forming a network in nearly all parts of the body. Their walls act as semipermeable membranes for the interchange of various substances, including fluids, between the blood and tissue fluid. The two principal types are continuous and fenestrated capillaries (Dorland, 2011)."}, {"name": "Structure and/or Key Feature(s)", "text": "Whilst the pancreatic islets comprise only about 2% of the mass of the pancreas, they receive up to 15% of the total blood flow to the pancreas. Blood enters the islet in two ways.

—Blood flows directly to the core of the islet then spreads to the periphery. A and D cells cluster along the paths of these vessels.

—Several arterioles enter the periphery of the islets then branch into fenestrated capillaries to flow to the core of the islet. 

Based on the dynamics of this flow supply to the islets, it is probable that the A and D cells receive the flow of blood before the B cells. Large capillaries leave the islets and then branch into a capillary network (resembling a portal system) to supply the acini of the exocrine pancreas (Ross and Pawlina, 2016)."}, {"name": "Function", "text": "Based on the dynamics of the blood supply to the islets and, the efferent blood capillaries that then supply the acini of the exocrine pancreas, secretions from the islet cells can influence the secretions from the acinar cells of the exocrine pancreas (Ross and Pawlina, 2016)."}, {"name": "References", "text": "Dorland, W. (2011) Dorland's Illustrated Medical Dictionary. 32nd edn. Philadelphia, USA: Elsevier Saunders.

Ross, M. H. and Pawlina, W. (2016) Histology: A Text and Atlas. Wolters Kluwer Health."}]

items.name: Patella
items.info:
[{"name": "Quick Facts", "text": "Location: Knee region.

Bone Type: Sesamoid bone.

Key Features: Apex, base, articular and anterior surfaces, vertical ridge, and medial and lateral articular facets.

Articulates With: Femur.

Arterial Supply: Genicular anastomosis."}, {"name": "Key Features & Anatomical Relations", "text": "The patella (or kneecap) is a bone found in the knee region. It’s somewhat triangular and is classified as the largest sesamoid bone. It contains the following bony features:

- surfaces: articular and anterior surfaces, medial and lateral borders, apex, and base;

- landmarks: vertical ridge and medial and lateral facets.

More information regarding these bony features can be found in the Surfaces and Landmarks tabs for this bone.

The patella is located anterior to the knee joint, within the quadriceps tendon. The patellar tendon extends inferiorly from the apex of the patella to the tibial tuberosity. The patella articulates with the femur at the patellofemoral joint, which contributes to the formation of the knee joint.

The patella’s functions are to strengthen the quadriceps tendon for knee extension and to reduce friction between the quadriceps tendon and adjacent bones at the knee joint."}, {"name": "Ossification", "text": "Ossification of the patella occurs at several ossification centers, which appear within the third to sixth years. Complete ossification occurs during early adolescence (Standring, 2016)."}, {"name": "Variations", "text": "In some individuals, the patella may be present in a bipartite or tripartite condition (i.e., divided into two or three parts, respectively). This usually results from failure of the ossification centers to fuse (Tubbs, Shoja and Loukas, 2016)."}, {"name": "Surface Anatomy", "text": "With regard to surface anatomy, the anterior surface of patella is subcutaneous and therefore easily palpated."}, {"name": "List of Clinical Correlates", "text": "- Patellar fracture

- Patellar tracking and dislocation

- Patellofemoral pain syndrome"}, {"name": "References", "text": "Standring, S. (2016) Gray's Anatomy: The Anatomical Basis of Clinical Practice. Gray's Anatomy Series 41st edn.: Elsevier Limited.

Tubbs, R. S., Shoja, M. M. and Loukas, M. (2016) Bergman's Comprehensive Encyclopedia of Human Anatomic Variation. Wiley."}]

items.name: Exocrine Cell of Pancreas
items.info:
[{"name": "Quick Facts", "text": "The exocrine cells of the pancreas are any of the cells lining an acinus, especially applied to the zymogen-secreting cells of the pancreatic acini (Dorland, 2011)."}, {"name": "Structure and/or Key Feature(s)", "text": "The exocrine cells of the pancreas (pancreatic acinar cells or serous secretory cells) are simple, pyramidal in shape. They form clusters or secretory units called acini, due to their acinar or tubuloacinar shape. Acini are supported by a basal lamina and very fine reticular fibers surround the acini.

The exocrine cells of the pancreas contain numerous zymogen granules in their apical cytoplasm which imparts an eosinophilia to the apical region compared to a more basophilic basal region due to the presence of free ribosomes and rough endoplasmic reticulum.

A unique feature of the pancreatic acinus is that centroacinar cells are located within the acinus and form the initial segment of the intercalated duct system (Ross and Pawlina, 2016)."}, {"name": "Function", "text": "Zymogen granules contain (inactive) precursors of digestive enzymes that can digest most food substances."}, {"name": "References", "text": "Dorland, W. (2011) Dorland's Illustrated Medical Dictionary. 32nd edn. Philadelphia, USA: Elsevier Saunders.

Ross, M. H. and Pawlina, W. (2016) Histology: A Text and Atlas. Wolters Kluwer Health."}]

items.name: Hip Bone
items.info:
[{"name": "Description", "text": "The hip bone (coxal, pelvic, or innominate bone) is a large, irregular bone that consists of three parts; the ilium, ischium, and pubis, which are fused together in adults. It’s considered part of the lower limb and is located lateral to the sacrum and lower lumbar vertebrae.

Because the hip bone articulates directly with the axial skeleton at the sacroiliac joint, it's less mobile than the free part of the lower limb. The hip bone articulates with the free part of the lower limb at the hip joint.

Overall, the hip bone provides the bony platform for movements of the lower limb and supports the weight of the body when upright. The “pelvic girdle” is the collective term for the right and left hip bones, sacrum, and coccyx. Unlike the pectoral girdle, the pelvic girdle forms an incomplete ring around the axial skeleton and is weight bearing, making it more stable than the pectoral girdle and therefore less mobile than the pectoral girdle."}, {"name": "Variations", "text": "The hip bone is one of the most sexually dimorphic bones in the skeletal system. This is due to differing morphology and general locomotor requirements between males and females, and the necessity of the hip bones to facilitate childbirth in females.

In general, female hip bones are lighter, thinner, and less robust than males. The pelvic inlet and outlet are wider in females, as well as the greater sciatic notches. Females also have a longer pubis and wider subpubic angle (females = 80-85°; males = 50-60°). The acetabulum tends to be larger in males (Standring, 2020; White and Folkens, 2005)."}, {"name": "List of Clinical Correlates", "text": "- Dislocation of hip joint

- Fracture of acetabulum

- Hip dysplasia"}, {"name": "References", "text": "Standring, S. (2020) Gray's Anatomy: The Anatomical Basis of Clinical Practice. 42nd edn.: Elsevier Health Sciences.

White, T. D. and Folkens, P. A. (2005) The Human Bone Manual. Elsevier Science."}]

items.name: Ilium
Intercalated Duct (Superior)
items.info: [{"name": "Quick Facts", "text": "An intercalated duct is a slender initial portion of the duct systems of salivary glands and the pancreas, interposed between an acinus of a gland and a secretory duct (Dorland, 2011)."}, {"name": "Structure/Morphology", "text": "Centroacinar cells form the initial segment of the intercalated duct system. Intercalated ducts are short and drain to intralobular ducts."}, {"name": "Function", "text": "The intercalated duct adds water and bicarbonate to the pancreatic secretions which neutralizes the acidity of the chyme as it enters the duodenum from the stomach and ensures an optimal pH for the activities of the pancreatic enzymes that are secreted."}, {"name": "References", "text": "Dorland, W. items.name: Pancreatic Islet
items.info:
[{"name": "Quick Facts", "text": "Pancreatic islets are irregular microscopic structures scattered throughout the pancreas and comprising its endocrine part (the endocrine pancreas). They are composed of at least four types of cells: the alpha cells which secrete glucagon; the beta cells which are the most abundant and secrete insulin; the delta cells, which secrete somatostatin; the PP cells which secrete pancreatic polypeptides. Degeneration of the beta cells, whose secretion (insulin) is important in carbohydrate metabolism, is the major cause of type I diabetes mellitus (Dorland, 2011)."}, {"name": "Structure and/or Key Feature(s)", "text": "The pancreatic islets (Islets of Langerhans) constitute the endocrine component of the pancreas. They are clusters of cells embedded within the exocrine pancreatic tissues.

Pancreatic islets can be isolated, small collections of polygonal or rounded cells or occur in clusters of cells of about 100–200 μm in diameter. There are between 1 and 3 million islets in the pancreas; however, they only make up 1–2% of its total volume. In humans, they are most numerous near the tail of the pancreas. An extensive network of fenestrated blood capillaries penetrates each islet (Ross and Pawlina, 2016). Very fine reticular fibers surround the islets and separate them from other pancreatic tissues (Mescher, 2013).

Using certain staining techniques, three major cell types can be distinguished: A (alpha), B (beta), and D (delta) cells. The remaining approximately 5% population of cells does not stain at all. These cell types can be distinguished based on the size and density of secretory granules within the cell cytoplasm using transmission electron microscopy. The relative numbers of these cell types are not uniform throughout the pancreas."}, {"name": "Function", "text": "The endocrine pancreas secretes hormones that regulate blood glucose levels."}, {"name": "List of Clinical Correlates", "text": "—Diabetes mellitus"}, {"name": "References", "text": "Dorland, W. (2011) Dorland's Illustrated Medical Dictionary. 32nd edn. Philadelphia, USA: Elsevier Saunders.

Mescher, A. (2013) Junqueira's Basic Histology: Text and Atlas. 13th edn.: McGraw-Hill Education.

Ross, M. H. and Pawlina, W. (2016) Histology: A Text and Atlas. Wolters Kluwer Health."}]

However, this disappears at the distal ends of the alveolar ducts and the lining is primarily that of type I pneumocytes (Kierszenbaum and Tres, 2020). "}, {"name": "Anatomical Relations", "text": "The alveolar ducts are found between the distal ends of the respiratory bronchioles and the alveolar sacs. Bone Type: Sesamoid bone.

Key Features: Palmar and dorsal surfaces, triquetrum articular facet.

Articulates With: Triquetrum bone.

Arterial Supply: Ulnar artery."}, {"name": "Key Features & Anatomical Relations", "text": "The pisiform bone is one of the eight carpal bones of the hand. It’s pea-shaped and is found in the proximal row of carpal bones. It’s classified as a sesamoid bone and includes the following bony features:

It articulates with the triquetrum bone at the pisotriquetral joint."}, {"name": "Ossification", "text": "Ossification of the pisiform bone occurs at one ossification center, which appears within the ninth to twelfth years (Standring, 2016). Complete ossification occurs during middle to late adolescence."}, {"name": "Variations", "text": "In some individuals, the pisiform bone may be present in a bipartite condition, i.e., divided into two parts (Tubbs, Shoja and Loukas, 2016)."}, {"name": "Surface Anatomy", "text": "With regard to surface anatomy, the pisiform bone can be palpated proximal to the hypothenar eminence."}, {"name": "List of Clinical Correlates", "text": "- Fracture of pisiform bone"}, {"name": "References", "text": "Standring, S. items.name: Basophilic Granule
items.info:
[{"name": "Cell Morphology", "text": "Basophils are the rarest type of leukocytes, accounting for only 0.5% of all leukocytes. The concentration of basophils is around 20-50 per microliter of blood. 

The diameter of a basophil is 10-14 μm, making them larger the erythrocytes. Their nuclei have two lobes that are either U- or S-shaped. The cytoplasm of basophils contains large granules that contain histamine and various molecules which mediate inflammation during an allergic response (Marieb, Wilhelm and Mallatt, 2012).

Basophils have Fc receptors on their cell surface which are antibody receptors that bind to Immunoglobin E (IgE) causing an allergic reaction. Basophils also possess the CD40L protein on their cell surface. CD40L interacts with the CD40 protein that is found on the cell surface of lymphocytes. This interaction results in an additional production of type IgE, therefore, mediating an immune response against parasites (Pawlina, 2016). Basophils have a short lifespan of around 8 hours in the blood (Pawlina, 2016)."}, {"name": "Production", "text": "In the red bone marrow, a hematopoietic stem cell differentiates into a myeloid stem cell which gives rise to basophils. Development usually takes 3-7 days and mature cells are stored in marrow before release into the bloodstream (Pawlina, 2016)."}, {"name": "Function", "text": "Basophils are mediators of allergic and inflammatory responses. Histamine released by basophils is a vasodilator meaning that is increases blood flow and decreases blood pressure. Heparin released by basophils is an anticoagulant which prevents blood from clotting too quickly (Silverthorn et al., 2013). Additionally, like all granulocytes, basophils are phagocytic (Marieb, Wilhelm and Mallatt, 2012)."}, {"name": "List of Clinical Correlates", "text": "- Basophilia

- Basopenia"}, {"name": "References", "text": "Marieb, E. N., Wilhelm, P. B. and Mallatt, J. (2012) Human Anatomy. 14th edn.: Benjamin Cummings.

Pawlina, W. 2016. Histology: A text and atlas with correlated cell and molecular biology. 7th ed. Philadelphia: Wolters Kluwer.

Silverthorn, D. U., Johnson, B. R., Ober, W. C., Garrison, C. W. and Silverthorn, A. C. (2013) Human Physiology: An Integrated Approach. Pearson Education."}]

items.name: Second Metacarpal Bone
Third Metacarpal Bone
Neutrophilic Granule
items.info:
[{"name": "Cell Morphology", "text": "Neutrophils are the most abundant leukocytes, accounting for around 60% of all leukocytes (Eroschenko, 2008). There are around 3000-7000 neutrophils per microliter of blood. They are motile cells and have a diameter of 10-14 μm, making them larger than erythrocytes. 

Neutrophils have a multilobed nucleus that may have a horseshoe shape. The lobes of the nucleus range from 2 to 6 lobes that are interconnected by thin threads of chromatin. Immature neutrophils contain fewer lobes (Pawlina, 2016). 

Neutrophils contain three kinds of cytoplasmic granules and therefore, are classified as granulocytes. These granules contain enzymes and molecules that are involved in immune responses. They also possess various surface receptors which allow them to recognize infectious agents. Neutrophils have a small Golgi apparatus and small number of mitochondria. 

The lifespan of neutrophils ranges from 6 hours to a few days. When a neutrophil reaches its maximum lifespan, it is destroyed via apoptosis and is engulfed by a macrophage (Marieb, Wilhelm and Mallatt, 2012)."}, {"name": "Production", "text": "In the red bone marrow, a hematopoietic stem cell differentiates into a myeloid stem cell which gives rise to neutrophils. Development of neutrophils takes 7-11 days (Marieb, Wilhelm and Mallatt, 2012). Neutrophils leave the blood and enter peripheral connective tissues. They are usually located at sites of infection."}, {"name": "Function", "text": "Neutrophils provide the first line of defense during an inflammatory response. As granulocytes, neutrophils phagocytose bacteria and destroy them by releasing digestive enzymes from their cytoplasmic granules that target the cells walls of bacteria. Other types of granules released by neutrophils mediate and enhance immune responses(Pawlina, 2016). The phagocytic function of neutrophils is driven by chemotactic factors (Eroschenko, 2008)."}, {"name": "List of Clinical Correlates", "text": "- Neutropenia

- Neutrophilia"}, {"name": "References", "text": "Eroschenko, V. P. (2008) DiFiore's Atlas of Histology with Functional Correlations. Wolters Kluwer Health/Lippincott Williams & Wilkins.

Marieb, E. N., Wilhelm, P. B. and Mallatt, J. (2012) Human Anatomy. 14th edn.: Benjamin Cummings.

Pawlina, W. 2016. Histology: A text and atlas with correlated cell and molecular biology. 7th ed. Philadelphia: Wolters Kluwer."}]

items.name: Tunica Media of Vessel
items.info:
[{"name": "Quick Facts", "text": "The tunica media a blood vessel is made up of transverse elastic fibers and smooth muscle cells (Dorland, 2011)."}, {"name": "Structure", "text": "The tunica media is the middle layer of the artery wall and comprises mainly of smooth muscle. This layer is generally the largest layer within arteries.

The composition of the tunica media contributes directly to the mechanical properties of the vessel. The tunica media is formed by layers of smooth muscle cells, which play a role in vasoconstriction and vasodilation. Furthermore, a scarce elastic lamella is present throughout the tunica media enabling it to return to its original shape after being stretched. Small collagen bundles also provide structural support, and proteoglycans embedded throughout the tunica media allow the vessel to withstand compressional forces."}, {"name": "Anatomical Relations", "text": "The tunica media is found between the tunica intima and the tunica externa within the artery wall. The external elastic lamina separates the tunica media from the tunica externa. The internal elastic lamina divides the tunica media from the tunica intima.

The smooth muscle in this layer is predominantly arranged in a helical manner, this means that the smooth muscle is coiled in a spiral fashion. Located towards the outer portion of the tunica media are layers of longitudinal vascular smooth muscle cells that synthesize and secrete elastin, collagen, and other extracellular components to supplement the structural integrity of the tunica media (Pawlina, 2016)."}, {"name": "Function", "text": "The mechanical strength of the tunica media comes from structural collagen and smooth muscle. The smooth muscle coiled around the vessel can contract or relax, altering the diameter of the vessel's lumen, which causes the lumen to decrease or increase. This is known as vasoconstriction and vasodilation, respectively."}, {"name": "List of Clinical Correlates", "text": "—Hypertension"}, {"name": "References", "text": "Dorland, W. (2011) Dorland's Illustrated Medical Dictionary. 32nd edn. Philadelphia, USA: Elsevier Saunders.

Pawlina, W. 2016. Histology: A text and atlas with correlated cell and molecular biology. 7th ed. Philadelphia: Wolters Kluwer."}]

items.info:
[{"name": "Quick Facts", "text": "An alveolar macrophage is a rounded granular type of macrophage, found within the alveoli of the lungs and serving to ingest inhaled particulate matter (Dorland, 2011)."}, {"name": "Structure", "text": "Alveolar macrophages are sometimes called dust cells. They’re located on the interior of the interalveolar septum and on the surface of the alveolus where they scavenge. They contain phagocytosed debris. Those that move over the alveolar surface end up being carried to the pharynx (by mucus) and mostly swallowed. Other macrophages filled with phagocytosed debris reside in the connective tissue elements of the interalveolar septum for the remainder of the person’s life."}, {"name": "Function", "text": "Alveolar macrophages scavenge foreign materials and debris from the alveolar surface as well as the connective tissue spaces within the interalveolar septum."}, {"name": "List of Clinical Correlates", "text": "Macrophages may phagocytose red blood cells that may enter the alveoli in heart failure.

They phagocytose infectious organisms e.g., Mycobacterium tuberculosis but don’t digest these bacteria so any damage to the macrophages can re-release the bacteria and cause recurrent tuberculosis.

Apoptosis of the macrophages in the interalveolar septum can contribute to the development of emphysema (Ross and Pawlina, 2016)."}, {"name": "References", "text": "Dorland, W. (2011) Dorland's Illustrated Medical Dictionary. 32nd edn. Philadelphia, USA: Elsevier Saunders.

Ross, M. H. and Pawlina, W. (2016) Histology: A Text and Atlas. Wolters Kluwer Health."}]

items.name: Pulmonary Alveoli
items.info:
[{"name": "Quick Facts", "text": "The pulmonary alveoli are the small polyhedral outpouchings along the walls of the alveolar sacs and alveolar ducts; through these walls gas exchange takes place between alveolar gas and pulmonary capillary blood (Dorland, 2011)."}, {"name": "Structure", "text": "Pulmonary alveoli are the minute terminal ends of the airway passages and the site for gas exchange between the air and the blood. There are between about 150 and 200 million alveoli in each adult lung creating a combined surface are of about 75 m2 (Ross and Pawlina, 2016).

Thin interalveolar septa sit between adjacent alveoli. These contain the delicate pulmonary interstitium rich in elastic and reticular fibers. Elastic fibers allow the alveoli to expand and passively contract during inspiration and expiration, while reticular fibers prevent the collapse and excessive distension of the alveoli (Mescher, 2013). Additionally, openings in the interalveolar septum allow the circulation of air between adjacent alveoli. These are called the alveolar pores (of Kohn).

An extensive blood capillary network sits within the interalveolar septa to ensure a close approximation between inhaled air and erythrocytes within the blood."}, {"name": "Function", "text": "The pulmonary alveoli allow gas exchange between alveolar gas and pulmonary capillary blood."}, {"name": "List of Clinical Correlates", "text": "In obstructive lung disease where there is a blockage in the passage of air to the alveoli, alveoli distal to the blockage can still be aerated via the pores from adjacent pulmonary acini and lobules (Ross and Pawlina, 2016)."}, {"name": "References", "text": "Dorland, W. (2011) Dorland's Illustrated Medical Dictionary. 32nd edn. Philadelphia, USA: Elsevier Saunders.

Mescher, A. (2013) Junqueira's Basic Histology: Text and Atlas. 13th edn.: McGraw-Hill Education.

Ross, M. H. and Pawlina, W. (2016) Histology: A Text and Atlas. Wolters Kluwer Health."}]

items.name: Pulmonary Capillary
items.info: [{"name": "Quick Facts", "text": "A capillary is any of the minute vessels that connect the arterioles and venules, forming a network in nearly all parts of the body. Their walls act as semipermeable membranes for the interchange of various substances, including fluids, between the blood and tissue fluid. The two principal types are continuous and fenestrated capillaries (Dorland, 2011)."}, {"name": "Structure", "text": "Capillaries of the alveolar septum are derived from branches of the pulmonary artery that carries blood from the right ventricle of the heart. These branches will travel closely with arteries supplying the bronchi and bronchioles. When the blood is oxygenated, it\u2019s collected by pulmonary venous capillaries to form small venules. These venules eventually link with four pulmonary veins that return the blood to the left atrium of the heart.\n\nAll lung tissue other than the alveoli are supplied by bronchial arteries arising directly from the aorta."}, {"name": "Function", "text": "Pulmonary capillaries receive deoxygenated blood from the right ventricle of the heart and then drain into venous capillaries to return oxygenated blood to the left atrium of the heart."}, {"name": "References", "text": "Dorland, W. (2011) Dorland's Illustrated Medical Dictionary. 32nd edn. Philadelphia, USA: Elsevier Saunders."}]

items.name: Surfactant
items.info:
[{"name": "Quick Facts", "text": "Surfactant is a mixture of phospholipids (chiefly lecithin and sphingomyelin) secreted by the alveolar type II cells into the alveoli and respiratory air passages, which reduces the surface tension of pulmonary fluids and thus contributes to the elastic properties of pulmonary tissue (Dorland, 2011)."}, {"name": "Structure", "text": "Surfactant is produced and secreted by the type II pneumocytes. The critical component of surfactant that reduces surface tension is the phospholipid called dipalmitoylphosphatidylcholine (DPPC).

Hydrophobic proteins Surfactant protein A, B, C and D are also necessary for the structure and function of surfactant."}, {"name": "Anatomical Relations", "text": "Surfactant covers the entire inner alveolar surface."}, {"name": "Function", "text": "Surfactant decreases the alveolar surface tension and is involved with removing foreign materials.

—Surfactant protein A maintains surfactant homeostasis i.e., regulating the synthesis and secretion by the type II alveolar cells and also modulating immune responses to fungi, bacteria and viruses.

—Surfactant protein B assists the transport of the lamellar body onto the thin surface of surfactant and is critical in spreading the surfactant across the surface epithelium.

—Surfactant protein C orientates the DPPC within the thin film of surfactant and maintenance of the thin layer of surfactant.

—Surfactant protein D is involved in defense as it can bind to some microorganisms and to lymphocytes. It’s also a participant in local inflammatory responses to acute lung injury (Ross and Pawlina, 2016)."}, {"name": "List of Clinical Correlates", "text": "Surfactant synthesis occurs after the 35th week of fetal life. If there aren’t adequate secretions of surfactant, as is the case with premature infants, the alveoli collapse on successive exhalations. This is neonatal respiratory distress syndrome (RDS)."}, {"name": "References", "text": "Dorland, W. (2011) Dorland's Illustrated Medical Dictionary. 32nd edn. Philadelphia, USA: Elsevier Saunders.

Ross, M. H. and Pawlina, W. (2016) Histology: A Text and Atlas. Wolters Kluwer Health."}]
