items.name: Type II Pneumocyte
items.info:
[{"name": "Quick Facts", "text": "Type II pneumocytes are pleomorphic cells of the pulmonary alveolar epithelium that secrete surfactant and are distinguished by abundant cytoplasm containing numerous lipid-rich multilamellar bodies (Dorland, 2011)."}, {"name": "Structure", "text": "About 5% of the surface area of the alveolar epithelium is occupied by cuboidal type II pneumocytes (type II alveolar cells) that bulge into the air luminal space (Ross and Pawlina, 2016). They have a dome shaped apical surface with numbers of short microvilli. There is some overlap on their lateral margins by the type I pneumocytes which are joined to the type II pneumocytes by occluding junctions.

The apical cytoplasm of the type II pneumocytes is filled with vesicles caused by parallel stacks of membrane lamellae called lamellar bodies about 100–400 nm in diameter (Mescher, 2013). In routine histological sections, they give the impression of a foamy cytoplasm."}, {"name": "Function", "text": "Type II pneumocytes secrete surfactant. The lamellar bodies contain phospholipids, neutral lipids and proteins that are continually secreted onto the air surface space by exocytosis to form an extracellular coating of surfactant. Surfactant decreases the alveolar surface tension but is also involved with removing foreign materials.

Type II pneumocytes are the progenitor cells for type I pneumocytes."}, {"name": "List of Clinical Correlates", "text": "After lung injury, type II pneumocytes divide to provide populations of both type I and type II pneumocytes."}, {"name": "References", "text": "Dorland, W. (2011) Dorland's Illustrated Medical Dictionary. 32nd edn. Philadelphia, USA: Elsevier Saunders.

Mescher, A. (2013) Junqueira's Basic Histology: Text and Atlas. 13th edn.: McGraw-Hill Education.

Ross, M. H. and Pawlina, W. (2016) Histology: A Text and Atlas. Wolters Kluwer Health."}]

items.name: Arteries of the Medullary Cavity
items.info: [{"name": "Quick Facts", "text": "The nutrient artery supplies the medullary cavity."}, {"name": "Structure/Morphology", "text": "The medullary arteries are derived from several external vessels. The epiphysis, metaphysis and diaphysis contain several openings in the bone to permit the passage of blood vessels into the medullary cavity. Within the cavity these vessels branch and anastomose to provide a continuous vascular supply to the entire bone.\n\nIn the diaphysis of long bones, the shaft is supplied by the nutrient artery. If you examine the outer cortical surface of long bones, there is normally a singular nutrient foramen in its diaphysis. This marks the entry point of the nutrient artery as it courses towards the medullary cavity in a passageway called the nutrient canal. The nutrient artery does not branch within the nutrient canal, but upon entry to the medullary cavity, it bifurcates into ascending and descending branches (Standring, 2016). The branches travel to the outer limits of the shaft and anastomose with the epiphyseal and metaphyseal vascular supply."}, {"name": "Anatomical Relations", "text": "The medullary arteries within the shaft form a rich vascular network that forms the medullary sinusoids associated that drain into a central venous sinus. Other branches of the medullary arteries travel towards the cortex. As the blood flow is traveling from the innermost cavity outward, it is called centrifugal blood flow. In the cortex it courses through the perforating canals to supply the nutrient canals of the osteon."}, {"name": "Function", "text": "The medullary arteries form a rich vascular supply for the inner medullary cavity, the spongy bone and also the inner two thirds of cortical bone."}, {"name": "References", "text": "Standring, S. (2016) Gray's Anatomy: The Anatomical Basis of Clinical Practice. Gray's Anatomy Series: Elsevier Limited."}]

items.name: Compact Bone Tissue
items.info:
[{"name": "Quick Facts", "text": "Compact bone is bone substance that is dense and hard (Dorland, 2011)."}, {"name": "Structure/Morphology", "text": "Compact bone forms the outer dense covering of bone tissue. Approximately 80% of bone in the adult human skeleton is composed of compact bone (Draper and Marshall, 2014). Compact bone is comprised of functional units called osteons. In dense, compact regions of long bones, osteons lie parallel to each other and are orientated with the long axis of the bone itself and appear round in cross-section.

In compact bone, osteons are identified by their central, nutrient canal surrounded by 5–20 concentric rings of lamellar bone (Standring, 2016). The bony matrix of the lamellar compact bone is dense and only small spaces called lacunae are found. Interspersed between the osteons of compact bone are nonuniform spaces comprised of interstitial lamellae. The interstitial lamellae have a haphazard orientation which is in contrast to the circumferential lamellae seen surrounding the nutrient canals within the osteons. Inner and outer circumferential lamellar layers are found lining the internal and external surfaces of compact bone."}, {"name": "Anatomical Relations", "text": "The outer circumferential lamellar layer of cortical bone is surrounded by the osteogenic periosteal layer of the periosteum. The innermost portion of the cortical bone is made up of the inner circumferential lamella. This portion of the inner cortical surface is adjacent to the spongy bone. The spongy bone, with its irregular trabeculae, does not completely cover the internal surface of the cortical bone and is lined by an endosteum."}, {"name": "Function", "text": "The arrangement of compact, lamellar bone confers the strength required for structural support to the body. It assists in movement by giving leverage to muscles and by acting as a rigid support for muscle contraction. Compact bone provides structural support for the body and protects internal structures (e.g., the heart and the spinal cord). It also acts as a reservoir for important ions such as calcium and phosphate. The release of these ions is very tightly balanced to preserve mineral homeostasis (Standring, 2016)."}, {"name": "References", "text": "Dorland, W. (2011) Dorland's Illustrated Medical Dictionary. 32nd edn. Philadelphia, USA: Elsevier Saunders.

Draper, N. and Marshall, H. (2014) Exercise Physiology: For Health and Sports Performance. Taylor & Francis.

Standring, S. (2016) Gray's Anatomy: The Anatomical Basis of Clinical Practice. Gray's Anatomy Series: Elsevier Limited."}]

[{"name": "Quick Facts", "text": "Location: Hand.

Bone Type: Long bone.

Articulates With: Fourth metacarpal bone and middle phalanx of ring finger.

Arterial Supply: Proper palmar digital arteries."}, {"name": "Key Features & Anatomical Relations", "text": "The proximal phalanx of the ring finger is one of the fourteen phalangeal bones of the hand. It’s classified as a long bone and includes the following bony features:

- parts: head, body, and base;

- landmarks: proximal and distal articular facets.

More information regarding these bony features can be found in the Parts and Landmarks tabs for this bone.

The proximal phalanx is located:

- distal to the fourth metacarpal bone;

It articulates with the:

- metacarpal bone at the metacarpophalangeal joint."}, {"name": "Ossification", "text": "Ossification of the proximal phalanx of ring finger occurs at two ossification centers, these are found in the:

- body, which appears in utero during the third month;

- base, which appears during the second year.

These ossification centers fuse with each other during the fifteenth to eighteenth years (Standring, 2016)."}, {"name": "Surface Anatomy", "text": "The head, body, and base of the proximal phalanx can be easily palpated."}, {"name": "List of Clinical Correlates", "text": "- Fracture

items.name: External Circumferential Lamella
items.info: [{"name": "Quick Facts", "text": "The circumferential lamella is one of the layers of bone that underlie the periosteum (external circumferential lamella) and endosteum (internal circumferential lamella) (Dorland, 2011)."}, {"name": "Structure/Morphology", "text": "The external circumferential lamellae form lamellar rings that encompass the entire external circumference of the shaft of long bones, akin to the growth rings of a tree."}, {"name": "Anatomical Relations", "text": "The external circumferential lamellae demarcate the separation of bone tissue from the overlying periosteal layer."}, {"name": "Function", "text": "The external circumferential lamellae contribute to the diameter of the diaphysis in long bones. This helps maintain the strength of the bone as well as help it adapt to mechanical loading and stresses (Standring, 2016)."}, {"name": "References", "text": "Dorland, W. (2011) Dorland's Illustrated Medical Dictionary. 32nd edn. Philadelphia, USA: Elsevier Saunders.\n\nStandring, S. (2016) Gray's Anatomy: The Anatomical Basis of Clinical Practice. Gray's Anatomy Series: Elsevier Limited."}]

items.name: Axial Skeleton
Longitudinal Orientation of Collagen Fibrils (of Osteon)
items.audio: Longitudinal Orientation of Collagen Fibrils (of Osteon).mp3
items.info:
[{"name": "Quick Facts", "text": "Within a single osteon concentric lamella, collagen fibers are arranged longitudinally. Fibers in adjacent lamellae alternate in orientation giving the lamellae a helical appearance (Standring, 2016)."}, {"name": "Structure/Morphology", "text": "Longitudinally oriented collagen fibrils are arranged parallel to one another within a single lamella. Between adjacent lamellae, fibrils alternate in orientation. This gives the lamellae a helical pattern, akin to plywood when cut in cross-section. These fibrils are mainly collagen type I, but they have stronger internal cross-linkage between fibrils compared to other connective tissues (Standring, 2016).

There are a variety of orientations that the collagen fibers can take within the bone, including transverse, alternating and longitudinal (Spiesz, Kaminsky and Zysset, 2011). Collagen fibers oriented longitudinally are most common in the long bones, where there is high tensile stress. Transverse collagen fibrils are generally found in compact bone that is exposed to high compression stress."}, {"name": "Anatomical Relations", "text": "Collagen fibrils are a key component of the bone matrix and account for approximately one third of all extracellular matrices in bone tissue. The space between collagen fibrils is larger than those in other connective tissues to facilitate mineral deposition during bone formation."}, {"name": "Function", "text": "The stability of the collagen fibrils and the space between the fibrils aid in the strength and deposition of new bone formation and help confer structural support. In addition, the alternating collagen fibril orientations between different lamellae also help facilitate a greater strength (Standring, 2016)."}, {"name": "References", "text": "Spiesz, E. M., Kaminsky, W. and Zysset, P. K. (2011) 'A quantitative collagen fibers orientation assessment using birefringence measurements: Calibration and application to human osteons', Journal of Structural Biology, 176(3), pp. 302-306.

Standring, S. (2016) Gray's Anatomy: The Anatomical Basis of Clinical Practice. Gray's Anatomy Series: Elsevier Limited."}]

items.name: Medullary Cavity
items.info: [{"name": "Quick Facts", "text": "The medullary cavity is the space in a bone containing the marrow (Dorland, 2011)."}, {"name": "Structure/Morphology", "text": "The medullary cavity is the central space inside bones and is a reservoir for bone marrow. Bone marrow is a highly vascular, gelatinous tissue. It contains hematopoietic stem cells that undergo differentiation into mature blood cells. Marrow that is actively producing blood cells is called red bone marrow. This is infiltrated with adipose tissue as we age and becomes yellow bone marrow (Standring, 2016)."}, {"name": "Anatomical Relations", "text": "The outer walls of the medullary cavity are formed from the trabeculae that protrude into the cavity. The medullary cavity is separated from the bone by a thin endosteal layer."}, {"name": "Function", "text": "The medullary cavity acts as a store for bone marrow, which is capable of blood cell renewal."}, {"name": "References", "text": "Dorland, W. (2011) Dorland's Illustrated Medical Dictionary. 32nd edn. Philadelphia, USA: Elsevier Saunders.\n\nStandring, S. (2016) Gray's Anatomy: The Anatomical Basis of Clinical Practice. Gray's Anatomy Series: Elsevier Limited."}]

items.name: Incus
items.info:
[{"name": "Quick Facts", "text": "Location: Tympanic cavity of the middle ear.

Bone Type: Irregular bone.

Key Features: Body, long limb, short limb, and lenticular process.

Articulates With: Malleus and stapes.

Arterial Supply: Anterior tympanic and stylomastoid arteries."}, {"name": "Key Features & Anatomical Relations", "text": "The incus is one of the three auditory ossicles, the other two being the malleus and stapes. It is a small, anvil-like bone that’s found in the tympanic cavity of the middle ear in the temporal bone. It is classified as an irregular bone and includes the following bony features:

- parts: body, long limb, and short limb;

- landmarks: lenticular process and articular facet for malleus.

More information regarding these bony features can be found in the Parts and Landmarks tabs for this bone.

The incus is located:

- anterolateral to the stapes;

- posteromedial to the malleus.

It articulates with the:

- stapes at the incudostapedial joint;

- malleus at the incudomallear joint."}, {"name": "Ossification", "text": "Ossification of the incus occurs at one ossification center, which is found in its long process and appears in utero during the fourth month. The incus is fully developed by the time of birth (Standring, 2016)."}, {"name": "List of Clinical Correlates", "text": "- Dislocation

- Incus ankylosis

- Cholesteatoma"}, {"name": "References", "text": "Standring, S. (2016) Gray's Anatomy: The Anatomical Basis of Clinical Practice. Gray's Anatomy Series 41st edn.: Elsevier Limited."}]

items.name: Neurovasculature of Central Canal
items.info:
[{"name": "Quick Facts", "text": "The Haversian canal is the central canal of an osteon; it contains blood and lymph vessels, and nerves. Volkmann canals are transverse canals of bone tissue that connect haversian canals with each other and with periosteal and endosteal surfaces, for the passage of blood and lymph vessels and nerves through bone (Dorland, 2011)."}, {"name": "Structure/Morphology", "text": "The central canal is approximately 50 µm in diameter and serves as a conduit for arterial, neuronal, venous, and lymphatic supply to the osteon (Standring, 2016).

The central artery enters the shaft of long bones obliquely through the nutrient foramen and divides into the ascending and descending longitudinal arteries. The longitudinal arteries give off smaller branches into the bone marrow and the surrounding cortex, then they branch off into smaller vessels known as arteries of the central canal.

The lymph vessels enter the medullary cavity accompanying the nutrient vessels of the marrow. Their distribution in the marrow follows the course of the vessels towards the epiphyses where they branch off into smaller lymph vessels. Similarly, the nerves enter the medullary cavity accompanying the nutrient vessels. Their distribution in the marrow follows the course of the vessels towards the epiphyses where they ramify and anastomose. 

The veins that drain the medullary cavity follow the same course as the nutrient arteries and travel within the nutrient canal to exit the bone through the nutrient foramen."}, {"name": "Anatomical Relations", "text": "The central canals are centrally placed in the osteons. They are longitudinal in arrangement and are interconnected by perpendicular perforating channels (Volkmann’s canals). The perforating channels give vascular supply to the osteons via the periosteal and medullary blood vessels. This provides communication between the central canals of the Haversian systems and the surrounding layers of tissue."}, {"name": "Function", "text": "The central canals provide vascular and nerve supply to osteons as well as venous and lymphatic drainage."}, {"name": "References", "text": "Dorland, W. (2011) Dorland's Illustrated Medical Dictionary. 32nd edn. Philadelphia, USA: Elsevier Saunders.

Standring, S. (2016) Gray's Anatomy: The Anatomical Basis of Clinical Practice. Gray's Anatomy Series: Elsevier Limited."}]

items.name: Malleus
items.info:
[{"name": "Quick Facts", "text": "Location: Tympanic cavity of the middle ear.

Bone Type: Irregular bone.

Key Features: Head, neck, handle, and anterior and lateral processes.

Articulates With: Incus.

Arterial Supply: Anterior tympanic and stylomastoid arteries."}, {"name": "Key Features & Anatomical Relations", "text": "The malleus is the largest of the three auditory ossicles, the other two being the incus and stapes. It is a small, hammer-like bone that is found in the tympanic cavity of the middle ear in the temporal bone. It is classified as an irregular bone and includes the following bony features:

- parts: head, neck, and handle;

- landmarks: articular facet for incus and anterior and lateral processes.

More information regarding these bony features can be found in the Parts and Landmarks tabs for this bone.

The malleus is located anterolateral to the incus, articulates with the incus at the incudomallear joint and attaches to the tympanic membrane."}, {"name": "Ossification", "text": "Ossification of the malleus occurs at two ossification centers, these are found in the:

- near the neck of the malleus, which appears in utero during the fourth month;

- anterior process of the malleus, which appears in utero during the sixth month.

The malleus is fully developed by the time of birth (Standring, 2016)."}, {"name": "List of Clinical Correlates", "text": "- Dislocation

- Malleus ankylosis

- Cholesteatoma"}, {"name": "References", "text": "Standring, S. (2016) Gray's Anatomy: The Anatomical Basis of Clinical Practice. Gray's Anatomy Series 41st edn.: Elsevier Limited."}]

items.name: Osteon
items.info:
[{"name": "Quick Facts", "text": "The osteon is the basic unit of structure of compact bone, comprising a central (haversian) canal and its concentrically arranged lamellae, of which there may be 4 to 20, each 3 to 7 μm thick, in a single (haversian) system; such units are directed mainly in the long axis of the bone (Dorland, 2011)."}, {"name": "Structure/Morphology", "text": "Osteons are the cylindrical, functional units of bone. In adults, osteons mainly form in existing compact bone through the continuous process of bone remodeling. In long bones, osteons form parallel to each other and parallel to the long axis of the bone and, thus, appear round in cross-sectional anatomy. Osteons can be identified by their central nutrient (or Haversian) canal, which provides a channel for vasculature, nerves, and lymphatics to travel. A population of cells, the osteoblasts, produce 5–20 rings of lamellar bone that radiate outward from nutrient canal (Standring, 2016). Haversian canals can communicate with each other via Volkmann’s canals, which run obliquely to the axes of the osteons. 

Osteocytes are formed when actively secreting osteoblasts become surrounded by osteoid and become trapped in spaces called lacunae. The osteocytes, in their lacunae, are parallel to the lamellar rings. These lacunae are connected via small channels called canaliculi. The canaliculi radiate from lacunae in a perpendicular orientation. Osteocytes extend their slender cellular process through these spaces to communicate with each other. This facilitates cell-cell communication via gap junctions (Ross and Pawlina, 2006)."}, {"name": "Anatomical Relations", "text": "In cortical bone interstitial lamellae are found in irregular orientations between osteons. They are separated from osteons by a thin layer called the cement line. The internal and external circumferential lamellae are the inner and external limits for osteons in cortical bone."}, {"name": "Function", "text": "Osteons serve as the functional unit of bone. Their thick lamellar rings provide mechanical support and strength to bone. They protect the vascular supply via the nutrient canal. Osteons are constantly remodeling and respond to the biomechanical stresses that they undergo (Standring, 2016)."}, {"name": "References", "text": "Dorland, W. (2011) Dorland's Illustrated Medical Dictionary. 32nd edn. Philadelphia, USA: Elsevier Saunders.

Ross, M. H. and Pawlina, W. (2006) Histology: A text and atlas. Lippincott Williams & Wilkins.

Standring, S. (2016) Gray's Anatomy: The Anatomical Basis of Clinical Practice. Gray's Anatomy Series: Elsevier Limited."}]

items.name: Stapes
items.info:
[{"name": "Quick Facts", "text": "Location: Tympanic cavity of the middle ear.

Bone Type: Irregular bone.

Key Features: Head, neck, base, and anterior and posterior limbs.

Articulates With: Incus.

Arterial Supply: Anterior tympanic and stylomastoid arteries."}, {"name": "Key Features & Anatomical Relations", "text": "The stapes is the smallest of the three auditory ossicles, the other two being the malleus and incus. It is a small, stirrup-like bone that is found in the tympanic cavity of the middle ear in the temporal bone. It is classified as an irregular bone and includes the following bony features:

- parts: head, neck, base, and anterior and posterior limbs;

- landmarks: articular facet of head of stapes.

More information regarding these bony features can be found in the Parts and Landmarks tabs for this bone.

The stapes is located posteromedial to the incus, articulates with the incus at the incudostapedial joint and attaches to the vestibular window of the labyrinthine wall."}, {"name": "Ossification", "text": "Ossification of the stapes occurs at one ossification center, which is found in its base and appears in utero during the fourth month. The stapes is fully developed by the time of birth (Standring, 2016)."}, {"name": "List of Clinical Correlates", "text": "- Dislocation

- Incus ankylosis

- Cholesteatoma"}, {"name": "References", "text": "Standring, S. (2016) Gray's Anatomy: The Anatomical Basis of Clinical Practice. Gray's Anatomy Series 41st edn.: Elsevier Limited."}]

items.name: Periosteal Artery
items.info: [{"name": "Quick Facts", "text": "There is an extensive network of periosteal vessels along the entire length of a bone shaft. They are capable of supplying up to one third of the outer compact bone."}, {"name": "Structure/Morphology", "text": "Osseous blood flow is described as centrifugal (radiating from the central medullary cavity towards the external cortical bone via the nutritional artery) or centripetal (radiating inward from the external periosteum via periosteal arterioles). The centripetal flow accounts for the flow of blood from the periosteum into the outer one third of cortical bone. These vessels enter the outer one third of the cortex and anastomose with the medullary system within the perforating canals. They lie in their respective perforating canals and anastomose with their medullary counterparts to form a rich microvascular network inside cortical bone (Buck and Dumanian, 2012)."}, {"name": "Anatomical Relations", "text": "The periosteum has an intrinsic network of vessels that are derived from adjacent soft tissues such as the musculoperiosteal and fascicoperiosteal plexus from nearby muscles and fascial planes. These vessels form an arteriole network and provide intrinsic blood supply to the periosteum. This network lies between the two periosteal layers. The terminal branches of the intrinsic periosteal arteriole network extend directly into the underlying cortical bone."}, {"name": "Function", "text": "The periosteal artery supplies blood to the periosteum and outer one third of the cortex. In the central canals of the external osteons, the periosteal arteries anastomose with the medullary arteries, forming a periosteocortical anastomosis. This anastomosis represents a direct connection between periosteal blood and blood from the nutrient foramina. This is pertinent for the survival of the outer cortex when medullary blood supply is diminished or blocked."}, {"name": "References", "text": "Buck, D. W., 2nd and Dumanian, G. A. (2012) 'Bone biology and physiology: Part I. The fundamentals', Plast Reconstr Surg., 129(6), pp. 1529-4242."}]

items.name: Bones of Cranium
Periosteum
items.info:
[{"name": "Quick Facts", "text": "Periosteum is a specialized connective tissue covering all bones of the body; in adults, it consists of two layers that are not sharply defined, the external fibrous layer being a network of dense connective tissue containing blood vessels, and the internal osteogenic layer composed of more loosely arranged collagenous bundles with spindle-shaped connective tissue cells, osteogenic precursor cells, and a network of thin elastic fibers (Dorland, 2011)."}, {"name": "Structure/Morphology", "text": "The periosteum is a fibroelastic membrane that lines the external surface of bone tissue and it is divided into two layers. The outer fibrous layer closely resembles dense connective tissue and is highly vascularized. Articular surfaces are devoid of fibrous periosteum and are instead covered by articular cartilage. The inner osteogenic layer contains osteoprogenitor cells which can differentiate into bone-forming osteoblast cells (Dwek, 2010)."}, {"name": "Anatomical Relations", "text": "The outer fibrous layer covers the non-articular surfaces of bones and lies adjacent to the fascial layers of the surrounding soft tissue, e.g., muscle. The inner osteogenic layer lines the innermost component of cortical bone, the inner circumferential lamellar layer.

The relative proportions of the two periosteal layers vary according to the functional state of the bone. The inner cellular layer is thickest during fetal development due to high levels of active bone growth. In adults, the osteogenic layer thins, and the fibrous layer becomes the primary component of the periosteum."}, {"name": "Function", "text": "The fibrous layer assists in supporting the structural integrity of the underlying bone. The rich vascular and neuronal networks provide nutrients and are integral to bone nourishment. The osteogenic layer provides the cells and mechanisms required for bone growth, modeling and bone repair and works in conjunction with the endosteal layer to maintain cortical thickness and bone morphology (Kierszenbaum, 2007)."}, {"name": "References", "text": "Dorland, W. (2011) Dorland's Illustrated Medical Dictionary. 32nd edn. Philadelphia, USA: Elsevier Saunders.

Dwek, J. R. (2010) 'The periosteum: what is it, where is it, and what mimics it in its absence?', Skeletal Radiology, 39(4), pp. 319-323.

Kierszenbaum, A. L. (2007) Histology and Cell Biology: An Introduction to Pathology. Mosby Elsevier."}]

items.name: Inferior Nasal Concha Bone
Spongy Bone
items.info:
[{"name": "Quick Facts", "text": "Spongy bone is bone substance made up of thin intersecting lamellae, usually found internal to compact bone (Dorland, 2011)."}, {"name": "Structure/Morphology", "text": "Spongy bone is arranged into trabeculae. These trabeculae form a mesh-like network of bony spicules of various sizes that are aligned along regions of biomechanical stress. The trabeculae are small semilunar plates of bone of varied dimensions (50-400 µm) (Standring, 2016). Trabeculae project into the medullary cavity from the internal circumferential lamellae of the cortical bone. The trabecular bone is laminated bone with occasional osteons present. Osteons are seen in thick portions of trabeculae, primarily in parts closest to the cortical bone.

Spongy bone is similar to cortical bone in the fact that it is laminated, but osteons are most likely to be present only near cortical bone or in the thicker trabeculae. As it is often devoid of osteons, it relies on diffusion of nutrients through the extracellular fluid within the canalicular system."}, {"name": "Anatomical Relations", "text": "Spongy bone sits inside the internal circumferential lamellae of the cortical bone. It is lined with endosteum which separates it from the marrow cavity internally. The endosteal layer is irregular in appearance as it tightly adheres to the irregular surfaces of the trabeculae."}, {"name": "Function", "text": "The large surface area of spongy bone facilities metabolic activities. Due to its trabecular arrangement, it is lighter than cortical bone and helps reduce the overall weight of the bone (Standring, 2016)."}, {"name": "References", "text": "Dorland, W. (2011) Dorland's Illustrated Medical Dictionary. 32nd edn. Philadelphia, USA: Elsevier Saunders.

Standring, S. (2016) Gray's Anatomy: The Anatomical Basis of Clinical Practice. Gray's Anatomy Series: Elsevier Limited."}]

items.name: Lacrimal Bone
Nasal Bone
Systemic Cardiovascular System
items.info:
[{"name": "Quick Facts", "text": "The system cardiovascular system is the general circulation, carrying oxygenated blood from the left ventricle to various tissues of the body, and returning the venous blood to the right atrium of the heart (Dorland, 2011)."}, {"name": "Structure/Morphology", "text": "The cardiovascular system is a network composed of the heart, venous vessels, arterial vessels, and capillary networks. There are two pathways of circulation recognized in the body, the systemic circulation and the pulmonary circulation.

The systemic circulation is responsible for providing oxygen and nutrient rich blood and removing waste, to and from all tissues in the body. Systemic arteries are responsible for carrying the nutrient and oxygenated blood away from our heart to all of the tissues of our body, while the systemic veins return deoxygenated blood to the heart.

Systemic arteries are all distal branches of the aorta and carry oxygenated blood from the left ventricle of the heart to the capillaries of all tissues of the body. Systemic capillaries are located within the tissues of the body; they are the sites where the exchange of nutrients and waste products occurs between the blood and these tissues. 

The systemic veins are generally described as the blood vessels that carry blood to the heart from all the tissues of the body, except the lungs. Deoxygenated blood enters the right atrium of the heart via the superior or inferior vena cava."}, {"name": "Function", "text": "The oxygen-rich blood is transported to the majority of tissues found in the body. The lungs contain small air sacs called alveoli which are responsible for gas exchange. Alveoli take up carbon dioxide from the blood and release it back into the external environment via exhalation. Inhaled oxygen from the air is passed into the alveoli and diffuses into the blood. This oxygen-rich blood is then pumped back to the heart via the pulmonary veins and the transport of oxygen-rich blood to the body begins again."}, {"name": "References", "text": "Dorland, W. (2011) Dorland's Illustrated Medical Dictionary. 32nd edn. Philadelphia, USA: Elsevier Saunders."}]

items.name: Palatine Bone
Radicular Veins (Coccygeal; Left)
items.info:
[{"name": "Quick Facts", "text": "Origin: Along the roots of the spinal cord.

Course: Pass laterally to accompany the spinal nerves.

Tributaries: None.

Drainage: Anterior and posterior roots and spinal ganglia."}, {"name": "Origin", "text": "The radicular veins are small veins that originate along the anterior and posterior roots of the spinal cord."}, {"name": "Course", "text": "The radicular veins pass laterally in the subarachnoid space towards the intervertebral foramen where they drain into the intervertebral veins."}, {"name": "Tributaries", "text": "The radicular veins give rise to anterior and posterior radicular veins."}, {"name": "Structures Drained", "text": "The radicular veins primarily drain the anterior and posterior roots of the spinal cord, including the spinal (dorsal root) ganglia."}]

items.name: Cardiac Myofibril
items.info:
[{"name": "Quick Facts", "text": "A myofibril is one of the slender threads that can be made visible in a muscle fiber by maceration in certain acids. They run parallel with the long axis of the fiber, and are composed of numerous myofilaments (Dorland, 2011)."}, {"name": "Structure and/or Key Features", "text": "Myofibrils of cardiac muscle cells separate and pass around the centrally positioned nucleus. This creates a “biconical” region of sarcoplasm each end of the nucleus where the cell organelles congregate, particularly densely packed mitochondria and the Golgi apparatus as well as glycogen and lipofuscin granules. Atrial granules in atrial cardiomyocytes (between 0.2-0.4 μm in diameter) will also congregate here (Ross and Pawlina, 2016)."}, {"name": "Anatomical Relations", "text": "Myofibrils of cardiac muscle cells separate and pass around the centrally positioned nucleus. They occupy the bulk of the cardiac muscle cell sarcoplasm.

Glycogen granules are also located in small concentrations between myofibrils (Mescher, 2013; Ross and Pawlina, 2016)."}, {"name": "Function", "text": "Myofibrils are composed of bundles of myofilaments which are the contractile elements of muscle cells."}, {"name": "References", "text": "Dorland, W. items.name: Gap Junction (Cardiac Muscle Cell)
items.info:
[{"name": "Quick Facts", "text": "A gap junction is a type of intercellular junction comprising a narrowed portion (about 3 nm) of the intercellular space that contains channels or pores (about 2 nm) composed of hexagonal arrays of membrane-spanning proteins around a central lumen (connexon) through which pass ions and small molecules such as most sugars, amino acids, nucleotides, vitamins, hormones, and cyclic AMP. In electrically excitable tissues, these gap junctions serve to transmit electrical impulses via ionic currents and are known as electrotonic synapses; they are present in such tissues as myocardial tissue and the central nervous system (Dorland, 2011)."}, {"name": "Structure and/or Key Features", "text": "Gap junctions are also referred to as communicating junctions between adjacent cells. They consist of a tightly packed array of transmembrane channels or pores (Mescher, 2013; Ross and Pawlina, 2016)."}, {"name": "Anatomical Relations", "text": "Gap junctions are present in a variety of tissues including epithelia, nerves, and muscle (Mescher, 2013; Ross and Pawlina, 2016)."}, {"name": "Function", "text": "Gap junctions permit the direct passage of molecules e.g., signaling molecules, ions, and small metabolites, from one cell to another. They are important in cardiac muscle cells because they enable contractions of the cardiac muscle fiber to be coordinated (Mescher, 2013; Ross and Pawlina, 2016)."}, {"name": "References", "text": "Dorland, W. (2011) Dorland's Illustrated Medical Dictionary. 32nd edn. Philadelphia, USA: Elsevier Saunders.

Mescher, A. (2013) Junqueira's Basic Histology: Text and Atlas. 13th edn.: McGraw-Hill Education.

Ross, M. H. and Pawlina, W. (2016) Histology: A Text and Atlas. Wolters Kluwer Health."}]

items.name: Intercalated Disc
items.info:
[{"name": "Quick Facts", "text": "Intercalated discs are the dense bands running between myocardial cells both transversely and longitudinally, forming a stepped configuration. They contain intercellular junctions that link adjacent cells both electrically and mechanically; they are composed mainly of fascia adherens, but desmosomes and gap junctions are also present (Dorland, 2011)."}, {"name": "Structure and/or Key Features", "text": "Two regions of an intercalated disc can be identified, a transverse portion which crosses the cardiac muscle fiber at right angles and a lateral component which runs parallel to the myofilaments.

Three junctional specializations comprise the intercalated disc. 

—The most prominent specialization along the transverse portion (and so responsible for the staining seen in routine preparations) are fascia adherens. They serve as anchor sites for actin filaments of terminal sarcomeres thus holding the cardiac muscle cells together at their ends to form a muscle fiber. 

—Desmosomes (or macula adherens) bind cardiomyocytes to each other along the transverse portion of the intercalated disc as well as the lateral portion. This prevents the cells from pulling apart during contractile activities.

—Gap junctions are present along the lateral component of the intercalated disc and provide ionic continuity between adjacent cells. Their lateral position protects them from contractile forces generated (Mescher, 2013; Ross and Pawlina, 2016)."}, {"name": "Anatomical Relations", "text": "An intercalated disc has two regions:

—a transverse portion which crosses the cardiac muscle fiber at right angles;

—a lateral component which runs parallel to the myofilaments (Mescher, 2013; Ross and Pawlina, 2016)."}, {"name": "Function", "text": "The intercalated disc is an attachment site for cardiac muscle cells as well as maintaining ionic continuity between adjacent cells so that the contractile signal can pass from cell to cell (Mescher, 2013; Ross and Pawlina, 2016)."}, {"name": "References", "text": "Dorland, W. (2011) Dorland's Illustrated Medical Dictionary. 32nd edn. Philadelphia, USA: Elsevier Saunders.

Mescher, A. (2013) Junqueira's Basic Histology: Text and Atlas. 13th edn.: McGraw-Hill Education.

Ross, M. H. and Pawlina, W. (2016) Histology: A Text and Atlas. Wolters Kluwer Health."}]

items.name: Ribosome (Cardiac Muscle Cell)
items.info:
[{"name": "Quick Facts", "text": "A ribosome is a large molecular structure, approximately 12 nm wide and 25 nm long, having two dissociable subunits, that is the site of protein synthesis. Ribosomes found in the cytosol of eukaryotes have a sedimentation coefficient of 80S; the subunits have coefficients of 60S and 40S and together contain four different ribosomal RNA (rRNA) chains and about 80 different proteins. Ribosomes found in prokaryotes and mitochondria are smaller (70S, with 50S and 30S subunits containing a total of three rRNAs and 55 proteins) and also differ from eukaryotic ribosomes in their sensitivity to certain antibiotics (Dorland, 2011)."}, {"name": "Structure and/or Key Features", "text": "Ribosomes are protein complexes and consist of rRNA synthesized in the nucleolus. They appear in electron micrographs as small, electron-dense particles 20–30 nm in two different forms (Ross and Pawlina, 2016; McKinley, O'Loughlin and Pennefather-O'Brien, 2016; Ovalle, Nahirney and Netter, 2013)."}, {"name": "Anatomical Relations", "text": "Firstly, ribosomes position loosely within the cytoplasm or as a chain of ribosomes called polyribosomes. 

Secondly, ribosomes (and polyribosomes) can be attached to the membrane of the endoplasmic reticulum."}, {"name": "Function", "text": "Individual ribosomes or polyribosomes in the cytoplasm of the cell freely associated, means they're involved with making proteins that the cell uses for itself.

Proteins synthesized by those ribosomes in collaboration with the endoplasmic reticulum is destined to be exported from the cell or incorporated into the plasmalemma. In some cases, the proteins are stored within the cell e.g., in lysosomes and in the granules of white blood cells (Ross and Pawlina, 2016; McKinley, O'Loughlin and Pennefather-O'Brien, 2016; Ovalle, Nahirney and Netter, 2013)."}, {"name": "References", "text": "Dorland, W. (2011) Dorland's Illustrated Medical Dictionary. 32nd edn. Philadelphia, USA: Elsevier Saunders.

McKinley, M. P., O'Loughlin, V. D. and Pennefather-O'Brien, E. E. (2016) Human Anatomy. 5th edn.: McGraw-Hill Education.

Ovalle, W. K., Nahirney, P. C. and Netter, F. H. (2013) Netter's Essential Histology. ClinicalKey 2012: Elsevier Saunders.

Ross, M. H. and Pawlina, W. (2016) Histology: A Text and Atlas. Wolters Kluwer Health."}]

items.name: T Tubule (Cardiac Muscle Cell)
items.info:
[{"name": "Quick Facts", "text": "T tubules are the transverse intracellular tubules invaginating from the cell membrane and surrounding the myofibrils of the T system of skeletal and cardiac muscle, serving as a pathway for the spread of electrical excitation within a muscle cell, enabling the nearly simultaneous activation of all myofibrils; in skeletal muscle, a T tubule is the intermediate element of a triad of tubular structures, the other elements being a pair of terminal cisterns (Dorland, 2011)."}, {"name": "Structure and/or Key Features", "text": "T tubules are extensions of the sarcolemma, made up of interconnecting rings, each of which surround individual myofibrils. Similar to the sarcolemma, the tubules are composed of two lipid bilayers. 

T tubules in cardiac muscle cells extend to the myofilaments at the level of the Z-line between the small terminal ends of the sarcoplasmic reticulum network. These terminal ends form a diad at the Z-line i.e., one t tubule and one sarcoplasmic reticulum cisterna. Only one t tubule is associated with each sarcomere in cardiac muscle. As the t tubules (invaginated plasma membrane) pass into the sarcoplasm, they are accompanied by the external lamina (Mescher, 2013; Ross and Pawlina, 2016)."}, {"name": "Anatomical Relations", "text": "T tubules are larger in cardiomyocytes in ventricular myocardium than they are in striated skeletal muscle but less numerous in atrial myocardium (Ross and Pawlina, 2016)."}, {"name": "Function", "text": "The entry of calcium ions into the sarcoplasm from the lumens of T tubules is essential to initiate cardiac muscle contraction (Mescher, 2013; Ross and Pawlina, 2016)."}, {"name": "References", "text": "Dorland, W. (2011) Dorland's Illustrated Medical Dictionary. 32nd edn. Philadelphia, USA: Elsevier Saunders.

Mescher, A. (2013) Junqueira's Basic Histology: Text and Atlas. 13th edn.: McGraw-Hill Education.

Ross, M. H. and Pawlina, W. (2016) Histology: A Text and Atlas. Wolters Kluwer Health."}]

items.name: Basilar Membrane
items.info:
[{"name": "Quick Facts", "text": "The basilar membrane is the wall of the cochlear duct, which separates it from the scala tympani; the spiral organ lies against it (Dorland, 2011)."}, {"name": "Structure and/or Key Feature(s)", "text": "The basilar membrane, or lamina, is an acellular membrane that serves as a barrier, separating the scala tympani and the cochlear duct in the cochlea. It extends longitudinally in the cochlea, parallel to the tectorial membrane. It is attached from the osseous spiral lamina and the tectorial lip of the internal spiral sulcus and inserted into the base of the spiral ligament. It is 35 mm in length. The basilar membrane has two distinct zones, the zona arcuata and the zona pectinata. The zona pectinate is relatively thicker than the zona arcuata (Standring, 2016)."}, {"name": "Anatomical Relations", "text": "The basilar membrane is interjacent between the scala tympani and the cochlear duct. The spiral organ (of Corti) lies superiorly within the cochlear duct. The tympanic lamella and perilymphatic cells lie inferiorly across its surface in the scala tympani."}, {"name": "Function", "text": "The basilar membrane is a delicate structure that is crucial for hearing. Vibrations are communicated with the endolymph in the cochlear duct via the oval window. This causes a slight shift in the position of the basilar membrane. This movement is detected by the displacement of fine stereocilia bundles from the hair cells, which activate specific mechanoelectrical transduction ion channels. The end process here is the conversion of the initial vibration to electrochemical signals which are transmitted along the auditory nerve to their respective processing centers.

The cochlea has a tonotopic organization. This means that different regions of the basilar membrane respond to different frequencies of sound vibration. The membrane is attuned to different frequencies along its length, by which the determining factor in detecting the vibration maximally is the width of the membrane. Narrow areas detecting frequencies as low as 0.1 kHz, while the broadest aspect of the scalae detect up to 20 kHz (Yoshioka & Sakakibara, 2013)."}, {"name": "References", "text": "Dorland, W. (2011) Dorland's Illustrated Medical Dictionary. 32nd edn. Philadelphia, USA: Elsevier Saunders.

Standring, S. (2016) Gray's Anatomy: The Anatomical Basis of Clinical Practice., 41st edition. Elsevier Limited.

Yoshioka, T. & Sakakibara, M. (2013) Physical aspects of sensory transduction on seeing, hearing and smelling. Biophysics (Nagoya-shi), 9, 183-91."}]

items.info: [{"name": "Quick Facts", "text": "The cuboid external supporting cells, or Claudius cells, are the cuboidal cells found in the floor of the external spiral sulcus, external to the organ of Corti (Dorland, 2011)."}, {"name": "Structure and/or Key Feature(s)", "text": "The cuboid external supporting cells (or Claudius cells) are the outer most epithelial cells found within the organ of Corti. They are arranged in numerous rows adjacent to the columnar external supporting cells (or Hensen\u2019s cells). They extend out toward the epithelium of the spiral prominence to line the outer spiral sulcus. They are generally cuboidal in shape and smaller than any of the other epithelial structures associated with the organ of Corti. They form tight junctions with each other to prevent seepage of endolymph in the spaces between them."}, {"name": "Anatomical Relations", "text": "The cuboid external supporting cells are found are the outermost cells associated with the organ of Corti. They are situated outside of the columnar external supporting cells, within the outer spiral sulcus. Their apical surfaces are exposed to the endolymph of the cochlear duct."}, {"name": "Function", "text": "The current function of cuboid external supporting cells is unknown; however, they are generally considered to help support the organ of Corti, as well as forming a tight barrier to the endolymph of the cochlear duct."}, {"name": "References", "text": "Dorland, W. (2011) Dorland's Illustrated Medical Dictionary. 32nd edn. Philadelphia, USA: Elsevier Saunders."}]

items.name: Internal Supporting Cell
items.info: [{"name": "Quick Facts", "text": "The internal supporting cells are a row of columnar supporting cells that delimit the inner boundary of the organ of Corti (Dorland, 2011)."}, {"name": "Structure and/or Key Feature(s)", "text": "The internal supporting cells are one of the three types of epithelial cells that support the inner hair cell. The other supporting cells are the inner phalangeal epithelial cells and the inner pillar cells. \n\nThe internal supporting cells are connected to the surrounding cells via cell junctions, notably adherens junctions and tight junctions, which link them to the other inner border cells, as well as the other supporting cells such as the inner phalangeal epithelial cells. The cells can communicate with each other via established gap junctions."}, {"name": "Anatomical Relations", "text": "The inner border cells, along with the other supporting cells, are inferior to the undersurface of the tectorial membrane, and superior to the basilar membrane. They are the most internal epithelial cells of the organ of Corti. They are interjacent to the inner phalangeal epithelial cells and the epithelial cells lining the inner spiral sulcus."}, {"name": "Function", "text": "The inner border cells have a sturdy cytoskeleton that helps preserve the structural organization of the inner hair cells. Their gap junctions allow for effective communication between cells and are useful in recognizing the presence of damage associated molecular patterns emitted from neighboring cells; thus, they can then initiate or contribute to a localized inflammatory response."}, {"name": "References", "text": "Dorland, W. (2011) Dorland's Illustrated Medical Dictionary. 32nd edn. Philadelphia, USA: Elsevier Saunders."}]

items.name: Perilymphatic Cells of Scala Vestibuli
items.info:
[{"name": "Quick Facts", "text": "The perilymphatic cells maintain the balance of ionic contents in the perilymph and endolymph."}, {"name": "Structure and/or Key Feature(s)", "text": "The inner aspect of the bony labyrinth is lined by perilymphatic cells with interspersed extracellular fibers. These perilymphatic cells have varying cell morphology based on their location in the bony labyrinth.

The perilymphatic cells lining the periosteum and the vestibular membrane facing into the scala vestibuli resemble a squamous epithelium. They contain tight junctions, which creates a diffusion barrier between it and the endolymph in the cochlear duct. 

In the narrower areas of the cochlea, such as where the scala vestibuli approaching the helicotrema, the perilymphatic cells have a different form. They have a stellate or reticular (cross-linked in a network fashion) in appearance and may have thin cytoplasmic projections extending across the space (Standring, 2016). 

Perilymphatic cells on the basilar membrane facing into the scala tympani are cuboidal in shape."}, {"name": "Function", "text": "The perilymphatic cells maintain the balance of ionic contents in the perilymph and endolymph."}, {"name": "List of Clinical Correlates", "text": "—Meniere's disease"}, {"name": "References", "text": "Standring, S. (2016) Gray's Anatomy: The Anatomical Basis of Clinical Practice., 41st edition. Elsevier Limited."}]

items.name: Maxillary First Molar Tooth
items.info:
[{"name": "Quick Facts", "text": "Location: Distal to maxillary second premolar tooth; mesial to maxillary second molar tooth.

Eruption: 16 months (deciduous); 6 to 7 years (permanent).

Key Features: Crown, root, cusps and marginal ridges.

Nerve Supply: Superior dental plexus.

Arterial Supply: Posterior superior alveolar arteries."}, {"name": "Key Features & Anatomical Relations", "text": "The maxillary first molar tooth is one of the three molar teeth that are found in a quadrant of the maxillary dental arcade. It includes the following bony features:

- parts: crown, root, and cervical line;

- surfaces: buccal, lingual, mesial, distal, and occlusal surfaces;

- landmarks: mesiobuccal, mesiolingual, distobuccal, and distolingual cusps, and marginal ridges.

The maxillary first molar tooth is located:

- distal to the maxillary second premolar tooth;

- mesial to the maxillary second molar tooth.

The root of the maxillary first molar tooth is lodged in a dental alveolus of the maxilla."}, {"name": "Development", "text": "The deciduous maxillary first molar tooth undergoes calcification during the fifteenth week in utero, with the development of the crown being completed during the sixth month after birth. Eruption of this tooth occurs during the sixteenth month after birth and the development of the root is completed during the third year.

The permanent maxillary canine tooth undergoes calcification around the time of birth, with the development of the crown being completed during the second to third years. Eruption of this tooth occurs during the sixth to seventh years and the development of the root is completed during the ninth to tenth years (Nelson, 2014)."}, {"name": "Function", "text": "As with all molars, the maxillary first molar tooth has cusped surfaces and is specialized for the crushing or grinding (comminution) of food during mastication."}, {"name": "References", "text": "Nelson, S. J. (2014) Wheeler's Dental Anatomy, Physiology and Occlusion. 10th edn.: Elsevier Health Sciences."}]

items.name: Periosteum
items.info:
[{"name": "Quick Facts", "text": "The periosteum is a specialized connective tissue covering all bones of the body; in adults, it consists of two layers that are not sharply defined, the external layer being a network of dense connective tissue containing blood vessels, and the internal layer composed of more loosely arranged collagenous bundles with spindle-shaped connective tissue cells, osteogenic precursor cells, and a network of thin elastic fibers (Dorland, 2011)."}, {"name": "Structure and/or Key Feature(s)", "text": "The periosteum is a thick layer of well vascularized connective tissue and can be found lining the surfaces of bones, including the delicate bony structures of the inner ear. Its outer fibrous layer is fibrous and becomes more fibroelastic internally due to the abundance of collagen and elastic fibers. The innermost osteogenic layer of the periosteum is believed to be associated with bone growth.

In the cochlea, the periosteum lines many of the surfaces. It lines the cavities of the cochlea, with the membranous labyrinth separated from the periosteum via the perilymphatic cells which line the periosteum in the scala tympani and scala vestibuli.

The periosteum is also modified where it makes up the body of some structures within the cochlea. For example, the spiral ligament is found on the outer aspect of the cochlear duct, forming part of the lateral wall. This is comprised of a denser and well vascularized periosteum. In contrast, the spiral limbus is found on the inner aspect of the cochlea duct. It is the upper plate of the osseous spiral lamina and is composed of thickened periosteum."}, {"name": "Anatomical Relations", "text": "The periosteum is found lining the inner surfaces of the cochlear canals. It is interjacent between the bony walls of these canals and the perilymphatic cells which line its surface."}, {"name": "Function", "text": "The fibrous layer of periosteum provides mechanical strength to the periosteum, which in turn provides considerable support to the bone. The osteogenic periosteal layer provides the necessary cells for bone growth, modeling, and remodeling. In the cochlea, it can support the overlying epithelial and perilymphatic cells across its surface."}, {"name": "References", "text": "Dorland, W. (2011) Dorland's Illustrated Medical Dictionary. 32nd edn. Philadelphia, USA: Elsevier Saunders."}]

items.name: Maxillary First Premolar Tooth
items.info:
[{"name": "Quick Facts", "text": "Location: Distal to maxillary canine tooth; mesial to maxillary second premolar tooth.

Eruption: 10 to 11 years (permanent).

Key Features: Crown, root, marginal ridges, central groove, and buccal and lingual cusps.

Nerve Supply: Superior dental plexus.

Arterial Supply: Posterior superior alveolar arteries."}, {"name": "Key Features & Anatomical Relations", "text": "The maxillary first premolar tooth is one of the two premolar teeth that are found in a quadrant of the maxillary dental arcade. It includes the following bony features:

- parts: crown, root, and cervical line;

- surfaces: buccal, lingual, mesial, distal, and occlusal surfaces;

- landmarks: buccal and lingual cusps, marginal ridges, and central groove.

The maxillary first premolar tooth is located:

- distal to the maxillary canine tooth;

- mesial to the maxillary second premolar tooth.

The root of the maxillary first premolar tooth is lodged in a dental alveolus of the maxilla."}, {"name": "Development", "text": "The permanent maxillary first premolar tooth does not have a deciduous precursor.

The permanent maxillary first premolar tooth undergoes calcification during the second year, with the development of the crown being completed during the fifth to sixth years. Eruption of this tooth occurs during the tenth to eleventh years and the development of the root is completed during the twelfth to thirteenth years (Nelson, 2014)."}, {"name": "Function", "text": "As with all premolar teeth, the function of the maxillary first premolar tooth is to assist the maxillary canine tooth in the gripping (prehension) and tearing of food during mastication."}, {"name": "References", "text": "Nelson, S. J. (2014) Wheeler's Dental Anatomy, Physiology and Occlusion. 10th edn.: Elsevier Health Sciences."}]

items.name: Maxillary Lateral Incisor Tooth
items.info:
[{"name": "Quick Facts", "text": "Location: Distal to maxillary central incisor tooth; mesial to maxillary canine tooth.

Eruption: 11 months (deciduous); 8 to 9 years (permanent).

Key Features: Crown, root, incisal margin, cingulum, and lingual fossa.

Nerve Supply: Superior dental plexus.

Arterial Supply: Anterior superior alveolar arteries."}, {"name": "Key Features & Anatomical Relations", "text": "The maxillary lateral incisor tooth is one of the two incisor teeth that are found in a quadrant of the maxillary dental arcade. It includes the following bony features:

- parts: crown, root, and cervical line;

- surfaces: incisal margin, and labial, lingual, mesial, and distal surfaces;

- landmarks: cingulum, marginal ridges, and lingual fossa.

The maxillary lateral incisor tooth is located:

- distal to the maxillary central incisor tooth;

- mesial to the maxillary canine tooth.

The root of the maxillary lateral incisor tooth is lodged in a dental alveolus of the maxilla."}, {"name": "Development", "text": "The deciduous maxillary lateral incisor tooth undergoes calcification during the sixteenth week in utero, with the development of the crown being completed during the third month after birth. Eruption of this tooth occurs during the eleventh month after birth and the development of the root is completed during the second year.

The permanent maxillary lateral incisor tooth undergoes calcification during the tenth to twelfth months after birth, with the development of the crown being completed during the fourth to fifth years. Eruption of this tooth occurs during the eighth to ninth years and the development of the root is completed during the eleventh year (Nelson, 2014)."}, {"name": "Function", "text": "As with all incisors, the maxillary lateral incisor tooth is bladelike and specializes in the cutting (incision) of food during mastication."}, {"name": "References", "text": "Nelson, S. J. (2014) Wheeler's Dental Anatomy, Physiology and Occlusion. 10th edn.: Elsevier Health Sciences."}]

items.name: Spiral Limbus
items.info: [{"name": "Quick Facts", "text": "The spiral limbus is the thickened periosteum of the osseous spiral lamina at the attachment of the vestibular membrane (Dorland, 2011)."}, {"name": "Structure and/or Key Feature(s)", "text": "The spiral limbus is a thickened layer of periosteum that is found on the uppermost layer of the osseous spiral lamina. The spiral limbus contains a C-shaped concavity known as the internal spiral sulcus. The upper extremity of the \u201cC\u201d is known as the vestibular lip and hangs over the concavity. The lower lip of the concavity is called the tympanic lip. From this endpoint, the tectorial membrane extends across the cochlear duct. The tympanic lip also allows for passage of cochlear nerve filaments via small canals known as the habenula perforata."}, {"name": "Function", "text": "In the lower aspect of the spiral limbus, the tympanic labia, cochlear nerve fibers are given passage to communicate with the specialized hair cells in the spiral organ (of Corti). This passage is called the habenula perforata. Additionally, the spiral limbus also receives the insertion of the basilar membrane, and so, it\u2019s involved in supporting the orientation of the basilar membrane."}, {"name": "References", "text": "Dorland, W. (2011) Dorland's Illustrated Medical Dictionary. 32nd edn. Philadelphia, USA: Elsevier Saunders."}]

items.name: Stria Vascularis
items.info:
[{"name": "Quick Facts", "text": "The stria vascularis is a layer of vascular tissue consisting of epithelial cells, mesothelial cells, and probably some neuroectoderm; it covers the outer wall of the cochlear duct and is thought to secrete the endolymph (Dorland, 2011)."}, {"name": "Structure and/or Key Feature(s)", "text": "The stria vascularis is a complex epithelial structure that is one of the components of the cochlear duct. It overlies the wall of the cochlear duct, adjacent to the spiral ligament. It is a specialized stratified epithelium and, as its name implies, is extensively vascularized. This vascular supply is due to a condensed mesh of capillaries between the epithelial cells.

The stria vascularis is comprised of three main cell types, the marginal cells, intermediate cells, and basal cells. The marginal and basal cells are true epithelial cells, while the intermediate cells are more similar to melanocytes. The marginal cells line the stria vascularis facing directly into the cochlear duct and are involved in ion exchange with the endolymph. The intermediate cells lie below this and are dense in melanin. The basal cells are the deepest cells of the stria vascularis. The marginal cells have descending cytoplasmic extensions, while the intermediate and basal cells have cytoplasmic extensions which project up toward the marginal cells (Standring, 2016)."}, {"name": "Function", "text": "The stria vascularis aids in the production of endolymph. It plays a role in ion transportation, which facilitates the production of the unique ionic concentration of endolymph resulting in the electrical potential of the endolymph. The reason for its dense vasculature is due to the required maintenance of this potential, which is based on sufficient oxygenation of the epithelial cells. This oxygenation is provided and maintained by the dense vasculature of the stria vascularis."}, {"name": "List of Clinical Correlates", "text": "—Sensorineural hearing loss"}, {"name": "References", "text": "Dorland, W. (2011) Dorland's Illustrated Medical Dictionary. 32nd edn. Philadelphia, USA: Elsevier Saunders.

Standring, S. (2016) Gray's Anatomy: The Anatomical Basis of Clinical Practice., 41st edition. Elsevier Limited."}]

items.name: Bones of Thorax
Pulmonary Cardiovascular System
items.info: [{"name": "Quick Facts", "text": "The pulmonary cardiovascular system is the circulation that carries the venous blood from the right ventricle to the lungs, and returning oxygenated blood to the left atrium of the heart (Dorland, 2011)."}, {"name": "Structure/Morphology", "text": "The cardiovascular system is a network composed of the heart, venous vessels, arterial vessels, and capillary networks. There are two pathways of circulation recognized in the body, the systemic circulation and the pulmonary circulation.\n\nThe pulmonary circulation brings deoxygenated blood, via the pulmonary arteries, from the right side of the heart to the lungs. It delivers blood a network of capillaries organized around the alveolar saccules, where gas exchange occurs. This oxygenated blood is then returned to the heart, via the pulmonary vein, to enter the systemic circulation through the left side of the heart. The pulmonary vessels are different from the systemic vessels in that the pulmonary arteries transport deoxygenated blood toward the lungs, while the pulmonary veins return oxygenated blood to the heart."}, {"name": "Function", "text": "Oxygen-low blood is returned to the right side of the heart via the superior and inferior vena cava. It then enters the pulmonary arteries which delivers the blood to the lungs. The lungs contain small air sacs called alveoli which are responsible for gas exchange. Alveoli take up carbon dioxide from the blood and release it back into the external environment via exhalation. Inhaled oxygen from the air is passed into the alveoli and diffuses into the blood. This oxygen-rich blood is then pumped back to the heart via the pulmonary veins and the transport of oxygen-rich blood to the body begins again."}, {"name": "References", "text": "Dorland, W. (2011) Dorland's Illustrated Medical Dictionary. 32nd edn. Philadelphia, USA: Elsevier Saunders."}]

items.name: Ninth Rib
Terminal Bronchiole
items.info:
[{"name": "Quick Facts", "text": "A terminal bronchiole is a small bronchiole, having a diameter 0.5 mm or less; it is a terminal segment of the conducting portion of the respiratory system and does not contain alveoli. Its branches are called respiratory bronchioles (Dorland, 2011)."}, {"name": "Structure/Morphology", "text": "The terminal bronchioles make up the distal part of the conducting portion of the respiratory tract. They have thin walls with a simple histological structure. 

As segmental bronchi branch into terminal bronchioles, there is a gradual change in the epithelium from a pseudostratified to a simple cuboidal epithelium which may or may not contain cilia. The number of ciliated and goblet cells decline in numbers and goblet cells end up being replaced by the Clara cells. The ciliated cells are responsible for beating synchronously, sending foreign particles, such as dust, back up to the bronchi. Clara cells are described as a bronchiolar-specific stem cell population paramount to protecting the airways from environmental hazards and are involved in maintaining lung homeostasis (Reynolds and Malkinson, 2010). 

Helically arranged smooth muscle is organized along the bronchiolar walls, that are capable of constricting the lumen of the airways. The surrounding connective tissue stroma is continuous with the alveolar ducts and terminal alveolar sacs. It contains abundant amounts of predominantly longitudinally aligned elastic fibers (Ovalle et al., 2013)."}, {"name": "Anatomical Relations", "text": "Terminal bronchioles are found distal the tertiary, or segmental bronchi, and proximal to respiratory bronchioles."}, {"name": "Function", "text": "The terminal bronchioles conduct air to the respiratory bronchioles, which terminate at the alveolar ducts, and the alveolar sacs more distally."}, {"name": "References", "text": "Dorland, W. (2011) Dorland's Illustrated Medical Dictionary. 32nd edn. Philadelphia, USA: Elsevier Saunders.

Ovalle, W. K., Nahirney, P. C. and Netter, F. H. (2013) Netter's Essential Histology. ClinicalKey 2012: Elsevier Saunders.

Reynolds, S. D. and Malkinson, A. M. (2010) 'Clara cell: progenitor for the bronchiolar epithelium', Int J Biochem Cell Biol, 42(1), pp. 1-4."}]

items.name: Tenth Rib
Body of Clitoris
items.info: [{"name": "Quick Facts", "text": "The body of the clitoris is the main part of the clitoris, formed by the two fused corpora cavernosa, which are embedded anteriorly in the floor of the vestibule of the vagina (Dorland, 2011)."}, {"name": "Structure and/or Key Feature(s)", "text": "The body of the clitoris is formed by the unattached parts of the two corpora cavernosa. The proximal ends of the cylindrical corpora cavernosa (one on each side of the urogenital triangle) are attached to the pubic arch via the crura (Latin = \u201clegs\u201d) of the clitoris. Their distal ends do not attach to bone. Instead they unite to form the body of the clitoris. The body is significantly smaller than the crura, measuring about 29 mm long and 9 mm wide (Jackson et al., 2019)."}, {"name": "Anatomical Relations", "text": "The body of the clitoris is formed by the union of the right and left clitoral crura at the root of the clitoris. It\u2019s capped by the glans. The body angles posteriorly and is embedded in the connective tissue of the perineum. It's supported by a suspensory ligament attaching superiorly to the pubic symphysis."}, {"name": "Function", "text": "During arousal, blood fills the erectile tissue within the body of the clitoris causing the clitoris to become erect."}, {"name": "References", "text": "Dorland, W. (2011) Dorland's Illustrated Medical Dictionary. 32nd edn. Philadelphia, USA: Elsevier Saunders.\n\nJackson, L. A., Hare, A. M., Carrick, K. S., Ramirez, D. M. O., Hamner, J. J. and Corton, M. M. (2019) 'Anatomy, histology, and nerve density of clitoris and associated structures: clinical applications to vulvar surgery', American Journal of Obstetrics and Gynecology, 221(5), pp. 519.e1-519.e9."}]

items.name: Eleventh Rib
items.info:
[{"name": "Quick Facts", "text": "Location: Thoracic cage.

Bone Type: Flat bone.

Key Features: Head, body, costal end, angle, and costal groove.

Articulates With: Eleventh thoracic vertebra, eleventh costal cartilage.

Arterial Supply: Posterior intercostal and musculophrenic arteries."}, {"name": "Key Features & Anatomical Relations", "text": "The eleventh rib is one of the two floating ribs of the thoracic cage. It is longer and more curved than the twelfth rib. It is considered an atypical rib because it has no neck or tubercle and has only one articular facet on its head.

The eleventh rib is classified as a flat bone and includes the following bony features:

- parts: head, body, and costal end;

- surfaces: internal and external surfaces, and superior and inferior borders;

- landmarks: angle, costal groove, and articular facet on the head.

More information regarding these and other bony features can be found in the Parts, Surfaces, and Landmarks tabs for this bone.

The eleventh rib is located:

- superior to the twelfth rib;

- inferior to tenth rib;

- lateral to the eleventh costal cartilage and eleventh thoracic vertebra.

It articulates with the:

- eleventh costal cartilage at the eleventh costochondral joint;

- eleventh thoracic vertebra at the joint of head of eleventh rib."}, {"name": "Ossification", "text": "Ossification of the eleventh rib occurs at ossification centers found in the:

- body, which appears in utero during the second month;

- head, which appears during puberty.

The ossification center for the head fuses with the body of the eleventh rib within the fourteenth to twentieth years (Cunningham, Scheuer and Black, 2016)."}, {"name": "Variations", "text": "In some individuals:

- the eleventh rib may be fused with adjacent ribs;

- the costal end of the eleventh rib may be bifid in appearance (Tubbs, Shoja and Loukas, 2016)."}, {"name": "Surface Anatomy", "text": "The costal end of the eleventh rib is easily palpated and is located by palpating one rib down from the tenth rib."}, {"name": "List of Clinical Correlates", "text": "- Fracture of eleventh rib

- Aplasia of eleventh rib"}, {"name": "References", "text": "Cunningham, C., Scheuer, L. and Black, S. (2016) Developmental Juvenile Osteology. Elsevier Science.

Tubbs, R. S., Shoja, M. M. and Loukas, M. (2016) Bergman's Comprehensive Encyclopedia of Human Anatomic Variation. Wiley."}]

items.name: Body of Penis
items.info: [{"name": "Quick Facts", "text": "The body of the penis is the free part of the penis from the root to the glans, consisting chiefly of the paired corpora cavernosa penis and the single corpus spongiosum penis (Dorland, 2011)."}, {"name": "Structure and/or Key Feature(s)", "text": "The body makes up the majority of the length of the penis. It's the pendulous part of the penis and is covered entirely by skin. It has three cylindrical masses of erectile tissue, two dorsal corpora cavernosa and a single ventral corpus spongiosum. The corpus spongiosum contains the urethra. A dense fibrous coat, the tunica albuginea, surrounds each corpus."}, {"name": "Anatomical Relations", "text": "The erect penis is the anatomical position. Therefore, the corpora cavernosa are \u201cdorsal\u201d and the single corpus spongiosum is \u201cventral.\u201d"}, {"name": "Function", "text": "The penis is involved in copulation, which culminates in the ejaculation of semen, containing sperm for fertilization of the female oocyte. The penis also functions in micturition (the act of passing urine out of the body)."}, {"name": "References", "text": "Dorland, W. (2011) Dorland's Illustrated Medical Dictionary. 32nd edn. Philadelphia, USA: Elsevier Saunders."}]

items.name: Cavernous Nerve of Clitoris
items.info:
[{"name": "Quick Facts", "text": "Sympathetic Contribution: Sympathetic nerves via the uterovaginal plexus.

Parasympathetic Contribution: S2-S4 spinal cord level.

Course: Passes inferiorly along the lateral walls of the vagina, passing between it and the medial wall of the pelvic floor. It then runs anteriorly, running parallel to the ischiopubic rami to enter the clitoris. 

Sympathetic Supply: Vasoconstriction of helicine arteries in erectile tissue.

Parasympathetic Supply: Vasodilation of helicine arteries in erectile tissue."}, {"name": "Contributing Nerves", "text": "The cavernous nerves carry both sympathetic and parasympathetic fibers. The sympathetic contributions originate from the level of T11-T12 and L1 segments of the spinal cord. Parasympathetic contributions arise from S2-S4 segments of the spinal cord (Standring, 2020). 

The autonomic supply, and thus, the cavernous nerve of the clitoris, is poorly understood and not well described in the literature."}, {"name": "Course", "text": "The autonomic fibers of the cavernous nerves of the clitoris travel within the uterovaginal plexus and vaginal nerves. They are periarterial plexuses that surrounding the vaginal artery. As such, they pass along the external and lateral surfaces of the vagina. At the pelvic floor, they pass between the lateral margin of the vagina and the medial edge of levator ani muscle, arriving in the deep perineal pouch. Once in the perineum, they turn anteriorly and medially between the ischiopubic ramus and the external urethral sphincter, crossing into the superficial perineal pouch (Moszkowicz et al., 2011)."}, {"name": "Branches", "text": "There may be major and minor branches of the main trunk."}, {"name": "Supplied Structures", "text": "The cavernous nerves of the clitoris supply autonomic innervation to the smooth muscle of the arteries in the corpora cavernosum of clitoris."}, {"name": "List of Clinical Correlates", "text": "—Female sexual arousal"}, {"name": "References", "text": "Moszkowicz, D., Alsaid, B., Bessede, T., Zaitouna, M., Penna, C., Benoit, G. and Peschaud, F. (2011) 'Neural supply to the clitoris: immunohistochemical study with three-dimensional reconstruction of cavernous nerve, spongious nerve, and dorsal clitoris nerve in human fetus', J Sex Med, 8(4), pp. 1112-22.

Standring, S. (2020) Gray's Anatomy: The Anatomical Basis of Clinical Practice. 42nd edn.: Elsevier Health Sciences."}]

items.name: True Ribs
items.info:
[{"name": "Description", "text": "The true ribs are one of the three groups of ribs in the thoracic cage, the other two being the false and floating ribs. The true ribs consist of the first to seventh ribs and are classified as “true” because their corresponding costal cartilages attach directly to the sternum.

The true ribs are also known as vertebrosternal ribs since they articulate both:

- posteriorly, with the vertebrae;

- anteriorly, with numerically corresponding costal cartilages that are attached directly to the sternum."}]

items.name: Fifth Rib
items.info:
[{"name": "Quick Facts", "text": "Location: Thoracic cage.

Bone Type: Flat bone.

Key Features: Head, neck, tubercle, body, angle, and costal groove.

Articulates With: Fourth and fifth thoracic vertebrae, fifth costal cartilage.

Arterial Supply: Anterior intercostal branches of internal thoracic and posterior intercostal arteries."}, {"name": "Key Features & Anatomical Relations", "text": "The fifth rib is one of the seven true ribs of the thoracic cage. items.name: Corpora Cavernosa of Clitoris
items.info: [{"name": "Quick Facts", "text": "The corpus cavernosum is a column of erectile tissue on either side of the clitoris (right and left), the two fusing to form the body of the clitoris (Dorland, 2011)."}, {"name": "Structure and/or Key Feature(s)", "text": "The body of the clitoris is composed of two columns of erectile tissue called the corpora cavernosa. They're surrounded by the tunica albuginea and separated from each other by a septum. As their name suggests, the corpora cavernosa are essentially cavernous spaces with a spongy appearance. They contain fibromuscular trabeculae with interspaced sinusoids. The muscle cells present in the trabeculae are orientated but transversely and longitudinally, thus may play a role in mediating blood flow through the sinusoids during tumescence (Toesca, Stolfi and Cocchia, 1996)."}, {"name": "Anatomical Relations", "text": "The corpora cavernosa unite to form the body of the clitoris. They are separated by a septal extension of the tunica albuginea surrounding the corpora. However the septum is incomplete and a communication remains between the corpora cavernosa (Toesca, Stolfi and Cocchia, 1996)."}, {"name": "Function", "text": "The corpora cavernosa form the erectile tissues of the clitoris."}, {"name": "References", "text": "Dorland, W. (2011) Dorland's Illustrated Medical Dictionary. 32nd edn. Philadelphia, USA: Elsevier Saunders.\n\nToesca, A., Stolfi, V. M. and Cocchia, D. items.name: Corpus Spongiosum Penis
items.info:
[{"name": "Quick Facts", "text": "The corpus spongiosum penis is the column of erectile tissue surrounding the urethra in the penis; its distal expansion forms the glans penis (Dorland, 2011)."}, {"name": "Structure and/or Key Feature(s)", "text": "The corpus spongiosum penis is an erectile tissue that surrounds the spongy part of the male urethra within the penis. The proximal and distal parts of the corpus spongiosum are enlarged to form the bulb and glans of the penis. 

Cavernous spaces in the corpus spongiosum are dilatable spaces that fill with blood during erection. However, the corpus spongiosum never becomes as firmly erect as the corpora cavernosa. While it does become engorged with blood, it does not become rigid, which is essential; since it would pinch shut the urethra and prevent ejaculation.

The tunica albuginea is thinner than that of the corpora cavernosa and the cavernous sinuses are smaller in the corpus spongiosum. For these reasons, it's incapable of complete erection."}, {"name": "Anatomical Relations", "text": "The corpus spongiosum is located on the ventral surface of the penile body, whereas the corpus cavernosum is located on the dorsal surface. The spongy (penile) urethra travels throughout the length of the corpus spongiosum."}, {"name": "Function", "text": "Cavernous spaces in the corpus spongiosum fill with blood during erection but not sufficiently to prevent the urethra from closing to allow for ejaculation."}, {"name": "List of Clinical Correlates", "text": "—Urethral catheterization"}, {"name": "References", "text": "Dorland, W. (2011) Dorland's Illustrated Medical Dictionary. 32nd edn. Philadelphia, USA: Elsevier Saunders."}]
