items.name: Ulnar Collateral Ligament
alt: Medial Collateral Ligament of Elbow Joint
items.info:
[{"name": "Anatomical Relations", "text": "The ulnar collateral ligament is located in the medial aspect of the elbow joint and extends between the humerus and the ulna. The ligament is deep to the triceps brachii and flexor carpi ulnaris muscles, and the ulnar nerve. Additionally, it lies deep to the attachment of the flexor digitorum superficialis muscle."}, {"name": "Structure", "text": "The ulnar collateral ligament is triangular and is composed of three components: the anterior, posterior, and inferior ligamentous bands. 

The anterior band is the strongest, attaching from the anterior aspect of the medial epicondyle of the humerus to the proximal part of the coronoid of the ulna. The posterior band of the ulnar collateral ligament of the elbow joint attaches from the posterior part of the medial epicondyle of the humerus to the medial margin of the olecranon of the ulna. The inferior (or oblique) band connects both the distal attachments of the anterior and posterior bands together.
"}, {"name": "Function", "text": "The ulnar collateral ligament acts as a major stabilizer of the elbow joint."}, {"name": "List of Clinical Correlates", "text": "—Ulnar collateral ligament injury (UCL injury)"}]

items.name: Veins of Transverse Colon
items.info:
[{"name": "Quick Facts", "text": "The proximal two thirds of the transverse colon is drained by tributaries of the superior mesenteric vein, while the distal third is drained by tributaries of the inferior mesenteric vein."}, {"name": "Description", "text": "The transverse colon has a broad and varied blood supply. Developmentally, the proximal two thirds are components of the midgut, while the remaining distal third is part of the hindgut. This developmental distinction is important in understanding the patterns of vascularization, innervation, and lymphatic drainage of the large intestine. 

Venous drainage to the proximal two thirds of the transverse colon is provided by the right colic, middle colic, and ileocolic veins, which in turn, drain into the superior mesenteric vein. The distal third of the transverse colon is drained by the left colic vein, a tributary of the inferior mesenteric vein.

The superior and inferior mesenteric veins unite with the splenic vein to form the common hepatic vein, which drains blood into the portal venous system. The nutrient rich blood travels to the liver where it is processed and filtered in the sinusoids. Blood re-enters the systemic circulation via the inferior vena cava."}]

items.name: Coracohumeral Ligament
items.info: [{"name": "Anatomical Relations", "text": "The coracohumeral ligament attaches to the dorsolateral base of the coracoid process. The ligament extends laterally to the greater and lesser tubercles of the humerus. It blends superiorly with the articular capsule and the tendon of supraspinatus muscle, and inferiorly with the superior glenohumeral ligament. The coracohumeral ligament forms a portion of the tunnel of the biceps brachii tendon, which separates the ligament into two bands and giving it a V-shaped appearance."}, {"name": "Function", "text": "The coracohumeral ligament reinforces the articular capsule of the glenohumeral joint. Additionally, it plays a role in stabilizing the glenohumeral joint, preventing superior or inferior dislocation of the humeral head during lateral rotation (Itoi et al., 1998)."}, {"name": "List of clinical correlates", "text": "\u2014Glenohumeral joint dislocation"}, {"name": "References", "text": "Itoi, E., Berglund, L. J., Grabowski, J. J., Naggar, L., Morrey, B. F. and An, K. N. (1998) 'Superior-inferior stability of the shoulder: role of the coracohumeral ligament and the rotator interval capsule', Mayo Clin Proc, 73(6), pp. 508-15."}]

items.name: Alveolar Nerves
items.info: [{"name": "Quick Facts", "text": "The superior and inferior alveolar nerves supply the maxillary and mandibular teeth, respectively."}, {"name": "Anatomical Relations", "text": "The inferior alveolar nerve, a branch of the mandibular division of the trigeminal nerve, follows the same pattern of branching as the inferior alveolar artery. The branches of the inferior alveolar nerve that travel through the root canal are known as pulp sensory nerves. \n\nThese pulpal sensory nerves subsequently branch into the subodontoblastic plexus in the pulp cavity. Additionally, unmyelinated postganglionic sympathetic fibers (vasoconstrictors) from the superior cervical ganglion enter the pulp and innervate arterioles that have arisen from the inferior alveolar artery (Standring, 2016)."}, {"name": "Function", "text": "Alveolar nerves are responsible for supplying sensation to the teeth."}, {"name": "References", "text": "Standring, S. (2016) Gray's Anatomy: The Anatomical Basis of Clinical Practice. Gray's Anatomy Series 41 edn.: Elsevier Limited."}]

items.name: Endoneurium
items.info:
[{"name": "Quick Facts", "text": "The endoneurium is the connective tissue in a peripheral nerve fascicle; it forms an interstitial layer around the neurilemma that surrounds individual myelinated nerve fibers and Remak bundles of unmyelinated fibers (Dorland, 2011)."}, {"name": "Structure/Morphology", "text": "The endoneurium is the connective tissue layer surrounding a nerve fiber (neuron) including the neurolemma and the myelin sheath. This connective tissue is made up of a fibrous matrix largely composed of collagen type III fibers (reticulin), which are arranged into intricate bundles, parallel to the long axis of the nerve. They tend to become somewhat concentrated around individual Schwann cell-axon units and vessels of the endoneurium. The primary cellular constituents of the endoneurium are fibroblasts, however resident macrophages and mast cells are also present (Standring, 2016)."}, {"name": "Anatomical Relations", "text": "The endoneurium is surrounded by endoneurial fluid at a slightly higher pressure than that found external to the endoneurial channel. Within the endoneurial channel, tiny capillaries are present which are comprised of a single layer of non-fenestrated endothelial cells. These serve as part of the blood-nerve barrier (Peltonen, Alanne and Peltonen, 2013)."}, {"name": "Function", "text": "The endoneurium plays a role in isolating nerve signals. Each peripheral nerve contains numerous axons that transmit to several muscles in the body. The endoneurium is in control of keeping these signals separate ensuring they are transmitted to the correct location. The endoneurium also protects the delicate axons from potential harm. Another function of the endoneurium, which is shared by the perineurium and epineurium, is the protection of neurons from damage (Carp, 2015)."}, {"name": "List of Clinical Correlates", "text": "—Advanced axonal neuropathy"}, {"name": "References", "text": "Carp, S. (2015) Peripheral Nerve Injury An Anatomical and Physiological Approach for Physical Therapy Intervention. EBL-Schweitzer: F. A. Davis Company.

Dorland, W. (2011) Dorland's Illustrated Medical Dictionary. 32nd edn. Philadelphia, USA: Elsevier Saunders.

Peltonen, S., Alanne, M. and Peltonen, J. (2013) 'Barriers of the peripheral nerve', Tissue Barriers, 1(3), pp. e24956.

Standring, S. (2016) Gray's Anatomy: The Anatomical Basis of Clinical Practice. Gray's Anatomy Series: Elsevier Limited."}]

items.name: Interlobular Artery
items.info:
[{"name": "Quick Facts", "text": "The interlobular arteries of liver are the arteries originating from the right or left branch of the hepatic artery proper, forming a plexus outside each hepatic lobule and supplying the walls of the interlobular veins and the accompanying bile ducts (Dorland, 2011)."}, {"name": "Structure/Morphology", "text": "The portal triad is the term given to the branches of the portal vein, hepatic artery, and bile duct that pass through the liver together. The term portal triad, however, is a misnomer, since lymphatic vessels and nerves also travel in this arrangement. The hepatic artery carries 25% of the total circulation to the liver, while the portal vein contributes to 75% of the total blood volume (Boron and Boulpaep, 2003). The blood of the hepatic artery is rich in oxygen as it has come directly from the celiac trunk of the abdominal aorta. The portal vein carries blood, rich not only in nutrients but also contains toxins, absorbed from the gastrointestinal tract.

The hepatic artery enters the liver at the porta hepatis, accompanied by the hepatic portal vein. The common bile duct and lymphatics exits the liver via the porta hepatis. The hepatic artery continues to bifurcate into segmental branches to each of the functional segments of the liver. Its terminal branches are the interlobular arteries, at the portal canals at the periphery of the hepatic lobule and send blood to the sinusoids.

The interlobular arteries are muscular arteries and are much smaller than the interlobular veins. They provide capillary networks to supply the interlobular veins (vas vasorum), interlobular bile duct, and parenchyma of the portal tract. The capillary networks either drain into the venous capillaries or enter the sinusoids directly (Krstic, 2013)."}, {"name": "Anatomical Relations", "text": "The interlobular arteries accompany the interlobular veins and the interlobular bile duct. These vessels run parallel to each other in the portal tracts and form the portal triad and send blood to the sinusoids. They are also associated with lymphatic vessels and nerves."}, {"name": "Function", "text": "The interlobular arteries provide oxygenated blood to the liver parenchyma, including the connective tissue of the portal tracts. They also form multiple dense plexus around the interlobular vein and the interlobular biliary duct."}, {"name": "List of Clinical Correlates", "text": "- Veno-occlusive disease"}, {"name": "References", "text": "Dorland, W. (2011) Dorland's Illustrated Medical Dictionary. 32nd edn. Philadelphia, USA: Elsevier Saunders.

Krstic, R. V. (2013) Human Microscopic Anatomy: An Atlas for Students of Medicine and Biology. Springer Berlin Heidelberg."}]

items.name: Cerebral Veins
items.info:
[{"name": "Quick Facts", "text": "The cerebral veins are veins that drain the surfaces or inner regions of the cerebral hemispheres; they are divided into superficial and deep groups (Dorland, 2011)."}, {"name": "Structure", "text": "The cerebral veins that drain venous blood from the brain are classified into superficial and deep veins. They are valveless, possess thin walls, and lack muscular tissue. Cerebral veins and venules in the cerebral cortex or white matter have a larger lumen and thin walls compared to the cerebral arterioles which are surrounded by smooth muscle (Standring, 2016; Snell, 2010).

Cerebral veins pierce the arachnoid and meningeal layer of dura and terminate in the nearest dural venous sinus.

The superficial cerebral veins have thin walls and their external surface area is covered by a single layer of meningeal cells. They are divided into three groups which are the superior, middle, and inferior cerebral veins.

The superior cerebral veins drain the superolateral and medial surfaces of each hemisphere of the brain and eventually open into the superior sagittal sinus. The lateral portion of each hemisphere is drained by the middle cerebral vein which ends in the cavernous sinus.

The inferior cerebral veins on the orbital surface of the frontal lobe join the superior cerebral veins and drain into the superior sagittal sinus. The inferior cerebral veins on the temporal lobe anastomose with the middle cerebral veins and drain into the transverse, superior petrosal, and cavernous sinuses (Standring, 2016).

Deep structures of the brain, such as the thalamus, are drained by internal cerebral veins. These veins unite, forming the great cerebral vein, which drains into the straight sinus."}, {"name": "Key Features/Anatomical Relations", "text": "Cerebral veins end in the nearest dural venous sinuses."}, {"name": "Function", "text": "The cerebral veins drain the cerebrum."}, {"name": "List of Clinical Correlates", "text": "—Thrombosis of the great cerebral vein"}, {"name": "References", "text": "Dorland, W. (2011) Dorland's Illustrated Medical Dictionary. 32nd edn. Philadelphia, USA: Elsevier Saunders.

Moore, K. L., Dalley, A. F. and Agur, A. M. R. (2013) Clinically Oriented Anatomy. Clinically Oriented Anatomy 7th edn.: Wolters Kluwer Health/Lippincott Williams & Wilkins.

Snell, R. S. (2010) Clinical Neuroanatomy. Clinical Neuroanatomy: Wolters Kluwer Health/Lippincott Williams & Wilkins.

Standring, S. (2016) Gray's Anatomy: The Anatomical Basis of Clinical Practice. Gray's Anatomy Series 41st edn.: Elsevier Limited."}]

items.name: Cytoplasm
items.info:
[{"name": "Quick Facts", "text": "The cytoplasm is the protoplasm of a cell exclusive of that of the nucleus; it consists of a continuous aqueous solution (cytosol) and the organelles and inclusions suspended in it and is the site of most of the chemical activities of the cell (Dorland, 2011)."}, {"name": "Structure", "text": "The cytoplasm of the oocyte, or the ooplasm, is essentially a liquid matter that has a granular appearance. It is made up of a small amount of yolk granules, or deuteroplasm, as well as various cell organelles including Golgi apparatus, mitochondria, endoplasmic reticulum, the nucleus, and cortical granules."}, {"name": "Key Features/Anatomical Relations", "text": "The cytoplasm of the oocyte is contained within the plasma membrane."}, {"name": "Function", "text": "The cytoplasm indirectly plays a role in preventing more than one sperm from fertilizing one oocyte. It does this by releasing large amounts of stored calcium, which in turn initiates a cortical reaction. Cortical granules release their enzymatic contents, which modifies the zona pellucida, making it impossible for subsequent sperm to attach to the oocyte (Chiras, 2005; Standring, 2016).

The yolk granules have nutritional constituents contained within them, including lipids, proteins, and polysaccharides, which nourish the embryo in its early phases of its development (Alberta et al., 2008; Rybska et al., 2018)."}, {"name": "List of Clinical Correlates", "text": "- Infertility 

- Assisted reproductive technology"}, {"name": "References", "text": "Alberta, B., Lewis, J., Roberta, K., Johnson, A., Raff, M. and Walter, P. (2008) Molecular Biology of the Cell. Garland Pub - USA.

Chiras, D. D. (2005) Human Biology. Jones and Bartlett Publishers.

Dorland, W. (2011) Dorland's Illustrated Medical Dictionary. 32nd edn. Philadelphia, USA: Elsevier Saunders.

Rybska, M., Knap, S., Jankowski, M., Jeseta, M., Bukowska, D., Antosik, P., Nowicki, M., Zabel, M., Kempisty, B. and Jaśkowski, J. (2018) 'Cytoplasmic and nuclear maturation of oocytes in mammals – Living in the shadow of cells developmental capability', Medical Journal of Cell Biology, 6.

Standring, S. (2016) Gray's Anatomy: The Anatomical Basis of Clinical Practice. Gray's Anatomy Series 41st edition: Elsevier Limited."}]

items.name: End Ring
items.info:
[{"name": "Quick Facts", "text": "The end ring is a dark ringlike structure at the posterior end of the middle piece of a spermatozoon (Dorland, 2011)."}, {"name": "Structure and/or Key Feature(s)", "text": "The end ring or annulus is a fibrous ring that marks the junction between the middle piece and principal piece of the sperm tail. It is made up of tightly packed subunits of filamentous material that measure between 3-4 nm in diameter (Guraya, 2012)."}, {"name": "Anatomical Relations", "text": "The end ring tightly adheres to the plasma membrane of the sperm and the submitochondrial reticulum is attached to the end ring at the point where the middle piece and the principal piece meet."}, {"name": "Function", "text": "The annulus is fundamental for the structural stability, as well as the functional effectiveness of the tail of the sperm. It ensures that cytoplasmic contents are confined and do not progress beyond its distal aspects. There’s also a possibility that the annulus inhibits the caudal displacement of the mitochondria. The annulus is also involved in the development of the fibrous sheath of the principal piece (Plant & Zeleznik, 2014)."}, {"name": "References", "text": "Dorland, W. (2011) Dorland's Illustrated Medical Dictionary. 32nd edn. Philadelphia, USA: Elsevier Saunders.

Guraya, S. S. (2012) Biology of Spermatogenesis and Spermatozoa in Mammals. Springer Berlin Heidelberg.

Plant, T. M. & Zeleznik, A. J. (2014) Knobil and Neill's Physiology of Reproduction. Elsevier Science."}]

items.name: Myelin Sheath (General Visceral Afferent)
items.info: [{"name": "Quick Facts", "text": "The myelin sheath is the cylindrical covering on the axons of some neurons; it consists of concentric layers of myelin, formed in the peripheral nervous system by the plasma membrane of Schwann cells, and in the central nervous system by oligodendrocytes. It is interrupted at intervals along its length by gaps known as nodes of Ranvier. Myelin is an electrical insulator that serves to speed the conduction of nerve impulses (Dorland, 2011)."}, {"name": "Structure/Morphology", "text": "The myelin sheath tightly holsters the axon, it is a semi-crystalline lipid-protein-water layer. This layer is discontinuous and interrupted at regular intervals. Schwann cells produce myelin sheaths in the peripheral nervous system. A myelin sheath is formed when the Schwann cell wraps around the nerve axon in a spiral fashion, creating a number of layers, or lamellae. The process is known as myelination. Each myelin-producing cell surrounds only one segment of any given axon. Periodic interruptions where short portions of the axon are left uncovered by myelin are known as the nodes of Ranvier (Patestas and Gartner, 2016)."}, {"name": "Key Features/Anatomical Relations", "text": "Nodes of Ranvier are gaps found in the continuity of the myelin sheath surrounding an axon. At these gaps there is no myelin covering the axon, thus exposing it to the extracellular fluid. The nodes of Ranvier contain a high concentration of voltage-gated sodium channels. These voltage-gated sodium channels enable the nodes to function as generators of action potentials. This is achieved through the exchange of ions into and out of the ion channels."}, {"name": "Function", "text": "The Myelin sheath acts as an insulator for the axons improving their electrical conductance. The myelin sheath also has a protective role in that it acts as a physical barrier separating the axon from the electrically charged atoms and molecules of the extracellular fluid. Myelination has also been shown to reduce the energy required for transmission of action potentials (through the mechanism of saltatory conduction) (Patestas and Gartner, 2016)."}, {"name": "List of Clinical Correlates", "text": "\u2014Demyelinating disease"}, {"name": "References", "text": "Dorland, W. (2011) Dorland's Illustrated Medical Dictionary. 32nd edn. Philadelphia, USA: Elsevier Saunders.\n\nPatestas, M. A. and Gartner, L. P. (2016) A Textbook of Neuroanatomy. Wiley."}]

items.name: Dendrites
items.info:
[{"name": "Quick Facts", "text": "A dendrite is one of the threadlike extensions of the cytoplasm of a neuron, which typically branch into tree-like processes. In unipolar and bipolar neurons, there is a single dendrite, which proximally resembles an axon but branches distally; in multipolar neurons there are many short, branching dendrites. Dendrites form most of the receptive surface of a neuron (Dorland, 2011)."}, {"name": "Structure and/or Key Features", "text": "Dendrites are short, tree-like, highly branched processes, generally radiating from the cell body, increasing the receptive area of the cell. Dendrites are unmyelinated, usually tapered, and their diameter is greater than the diameter of the neuronal axon. Dendrites become thinner as they branch. The cytoplasm of the dendrites near the cell body contains Nissl granules, ribosomes, rough endoplasmic reticulum, smooth endoplasmic reticulum, mitochondria, microtubules, neurofilaments, and actin filaments. However, they do not contain Golgi complex (Ross and Pawlina, 2006).

Dendrites are overproduced during embryonic development but become reduced in number and size later on (Splittgerber, 2018).

Small mushroom shaped “dendritic spines,” 1–3 μm long and less than 1 μm wide, are connected to the dendrite process."}, {"name": "Anatomical Relations", "text": "Dendrites generally radiate from the neuron cell body."}, {"name": "Function", "text": "Dendrites function as receptors to enable a single neuron to receive and integrate information arriving on numerous axon terminals from other nerve cells or the external environment. Dendritic spines house the synapses communicating with the neuron from other nerve cell processes."}, {"name": "Clinical Correlates", "text": "General anesthetics block synaptic transmission."}, {"name": "References", "text": "Dorland, W. (2011) Dorland's Illustrated Medical Dictionary. 32nd edn. Philadelphia, USA: Elsevier Saunders.

Ross, M. H. and Pawlina, W. (2006) Histology: A text and atlas. Lippincott Williams & Wilkins.

Splittgerber, R. (2018) Snell's Clinical Neuroanatomy. Wolters Kluwer Health."}]

items.name: Radial Fibers of Ciliary Muscle
items.info:
[{"name": "Quick Facts", "text": "The radial fibers of ciliary muscle are the fibers of the ciliary muscle lying between the meridional (external) fibers and the circular (internal) fibers; they run in a radial or oblique direction from one to another and may form a fibrous network (Dorland, 2011)."}, {"name": "Structure and/or Key Feature(s)", "text": "Radial fibers form the middle part of the ciliary muscle. They pass obliquely between the external, meridional and internal, circular muscle fibers, and in this way forming an interweaving lattice.

The oculomotor nerve (CN III) provides parasympathetic innervation to the ciliary muscle via the short ciliary nerves, with the superior cervical ganglion providing sympathetic contributions (Giampani & Giampani, 2013)."}, {"name": "Anatomical Relations", "text": "This intermediate layer of muscle is “sandwiched” between the external meridional layer of ciliary muscle and the internal circular layer of muscle."}, {"name": "Function", "text": "The ciliary body suspends the lens of the eyeball by fines suspensory ligaments. When the ciliary muscle contracts it varies tension on the lens, and this changes its shape and hence its refractive power. This process is called accommodation."}, {"name": "List of Clinical Correlates", "text": "—Hyperopia-aging"}, {"name": "References", "text": "Dorland, W. (2011) Dorland's Illustrated Medical Dictionary. 32nd edn. Philadelphia, USA: Elsevier Saunders.

Giampani, A. S. B. and Giampani, J. (2013) Anatomy of Ciliary Body, Ciliary Processes, Anterior Chamber Angle and Collector Vessels. INTECH Open Access Publisher."}]

items.name: Granulosa (of Tertiary Ovarian Follicle)
items.info:
[{"name": "Quick Facts", "text": "Granulosa cells are cells surrounding the vesicular ovarian follicle and forming the stratum granulosum and cumulus oophorus; after ovulation they are transformed into lutein cells (Dorland, 2011)."}, {"name": "Structure and/or Key Feature(s)", "text": "When a primordial follicle develops into a primary follicle, the single layer of squamous follicular cells proliferates and becomes cuboidal. As the follicle develops, the oocyte secretes specific proteins to form an extracellular layer called the zona pellucida. It is located between the oocyte and the follicle cells. The single layer of cuboidal follicle cells undergoes rapid mitotic divisions to form a stratified epithelium called the granulosa that surrounds the oocyte. These follicular cells are now called granulosa cells. A basement membrane remains in position between the outermost layer of the granulosa cells (which are columnar) and the connective tissue stroma which is destined to become the thecal layers around the developing follicle. 

Extensive gap junctions form between adjacent granulosa cells but in the basal layer there are no tight junctions (zonulae occludens) most likely because nutrients, chemical messengers, etc. from the blood need to nourish the developing oocyte and granulosa cells (Ross and Pawlina, 2006)."}, {"name": "Anatomical Relations", "text": "The granulosa is situated between the primary oocyte and the follicular basement membrane."}, {"name": "Function", "text": "Under the influence of follicle-stimulating hormone (FSH), the granulosa cells transform androstenedione into estrogen. Estrogen then returns to the vascular theca interna and enters the blood stream to be transported throughout the body.

Estrogen stimulates granulosa cells to proliferate increasing the size of the follicle. A surge in the release of FSH and luteinizing hormone (LH) from the anterior pituitary gland occurs about 24 hours before ovulation, which desensitizes the LH receptors on the granulosa cells and the granulosa cells no longer produce estrogen (Ross and Pawlina, 2006; Mescher, 2013)."}, {"name": "References", "text": "Dorland, W. (2011) Dorland's Illustrated Medical Dictionary. 32nd edn. Philadelphia, USA: Elsevier Saunders.

Mescher, A. (2013) Junqueira's Basic Histology: Text and Atlas. 13th edn.: McGraw-Hill Education.

Ross, M. H. and Pawlina, W. (2006) Histology: A text and atlas. Lippincott Williams & Wilkins."}]

items.name: Corona Radiata
items.info:
[{"name": "Quick Facts", "text": "The coronal radiata is a superficial layer of radially elongated follicle cells surrounding the zona pellucida of a secondary oocyte (Dorland, 2011)."}, {"name": "Structure", "text": "The coronal radiata is a layer of granulosa/follicle cells (referred to as cumulus cells) surrounding the zona pellucida of a secondary oocyte (Dorland, 2011). Additionally, the corona radiata forms the innermost layer of the cumulus oophorus. The corona radiata and cumulus oophorus span approximately 7-12.5 μm in diameter (Gardner et al., 2008; Harrison, Bonnar and Thompson, 2012). 

The corona radiata forms during folliculogenesis. During the ovarian cycle, cumulus cells make intimate contact with the oocyte and deposit an acellular glycoprotein layer around the surface of the oocyte called the zona pellucida. Cumulus cells remain attached to the zona pellucida and form the corona radiata.

Microvillus projections of the cytoplasm of cumulus cells project through the zona pellucida and form gap junctions with microvilli of the oocyte."}, {"name": "Key Features/Anatomical Relations", "text": "The corona radiata surrounds the oocyte and is situated immediately external to the zona pellucida."}, {"name": "Function", "text": "Microvillus projections of the cumulus cells project through the zona pellucida and form gap junctions with microvilli of the oocyte. This provides a source of nutritional and regulatory substances, as well as exogenous proteins for the oocyte. 

In order for fertilization to occur, a sperm must penetrate an oocyte by piercing through the corona radiata and zona pellucida that encircle the oocyte. This indirectly reduces the chances of multiple fertilization (Gray and Lewis, 1918)."}, {"name": "List of Clinical Correlates", "text": "- Infertility"}, {"name": "References", "text": "Dorland, W. (2011) Dorland's Illustrated Medical Dictionary. 32nd edn. Philadelphia, USA: Elsevier Saunders.

Gardner, D. K., Weissman, A., Howles, C. M. and Shoham, Z. (2008) Textbook of Assisted Reproductive Technologies: Laboratory and Clinical Perspectives. CRC Press.

Gray, H. and Lewis, W. H. (1918) Anatomy of the Human Body. Lea & Febiger.

Harrison, R. F., Bonnar, J. and Thompson, W. (2012) Fertility and Sterility: The Proceedings of the XIth World Congress on Fertility and Sterility, Dublin, June 1983, held under the Auspices of the International Federation of Fertility Societies. Springer Netherlands.

van Blerkom, J. and Motta, P. (2012) Ultrastructure of Human Gametogenesis and Early Embryogenesis. Springer US."}]

items.name: Arachnoid Granulations
items.info:
[{"name": "Quick Facts", "text": "The arachnoid granulations are small elevations, visible to the naked eye, which project into the superior sagittal sinus and associated venous lacunae and create slight depressions on the inner surface of the cranium; these granulations are the structures through which cerebrospinal fluid is reabsorbed into the venous system (Dorland, 2011)."}, {"name": "Structure", "text": "Arachnoid villi or granulations are out pockets of the arachnoid that protrude into the dura mater and into the dural venous sinuses. They are commonly found in the superior sagittal sinus and lateral lacunae; however, they are also found in the transverse, straight, and superior petrosal sinuses (Standring, 2016). Large accumulations of granulations may cause an impression on the overlying bone, forming indentations on the internal surface of the calvaria, known as granular foveolae (Moore, Dalley and Agur, 2013)."}, {"name": "Function", "text": "Arachnoid granulations allow transport of cerebrospinal fluid from the subarachnoid space into the venous system."}, {"name": "List of Clinical Correlates", "text": "—Hydrocephalus"}, {"name": "References", "text": "Dorland, W. (2011) Dorland's Illustrated Medical Dictionary. 32nd edn. Philadelphia, USA: Elsevier Saunders.

Moore, K. L., Dalley, A. F. and Agur, A. M. R. (2013) Clinically Oriented Anatomy. Clinically Oriented Anatomy 7th edn.: Wolters Kluwer Health/Lippincott Williams & Wilkins.

items.name: Myelin Sheath
items.info:
[{"name": "Quick Facts", "text": "A myelin sheath is the cylindrical covering on the axons of some neurons; it consists of concentric layers of myelin, formed in the peripheral nervous system by the plasma membrane of Schwann cells, and in the central nervous system by oligodendrocytes. It is interrupted at intervals along its length by gaps known as nodes of Ranvier. Myelin is an electrical insulator that serves to speed the conduction of nerve impulses (Dorland, 2011)."}, {"name": "Structure", "text": "The myelin sheath tightly holsters the axon. It is a semi-crystalline lipid-protein-water layer. This layer is discontinuous and interrupted at regular intervals. Schwann cells produce myelin sheaths in the peripheral nervous system. A myelin sheath is formed when the Schwann cell wraps around the nerve axon in a spiral fashion, creating many layers, or lamellae. This is known as myelination. Each myelin-generating cell furnishes myelin for only one segment of any given axon. The periodic interruptions where short portions of the axon are left uncovered by myelin are known as the nodes of Ranvier (Patestas and Gartner, 2016)."}, {"name": "Key Features/Anatomical Relations", "text": "The nodes of Ranvier, which are found periodically along the myelin sheath of myelinated axons, contain a concentration of voltage-gated sodium channels. These voltage-gated sodium channels enable the nodes to function as generators of action potentials. This is achieved through the exchange of ions into and out of the ion channels."}, {"name": "Function", "text": "The Myelin sheath acts as an insulator for the axons improving their electrical conductance. The myelin sheath also has a protective role in that it acts as a physical barrier separating the axon from the electrically charged atoms and molecules of the extracellular fluid. Myelination has also been shown to reduce the energy required for transmission of action potentials (Wang et al., 2008)."}, {"name": "List of Clinical Correlates", "text": "—Demyelinating disease"}, {"name": "References", "text": "Dorland, W. (2011) Dorland's Illustrated Medical Dictionary. 32nd edn. Philadelphia, USA: Elsevier Saunders.

Patestas, M. A. and Gartner, L. P. (2016) A Textbook of Neuroanatomy. Wiley.

Wang, S. S., Shultz, J. R., Burish, M. J., Harrison, K. H., Hof, P. R., Towns, L. C., Wagers, M. W. and Wyatt, K. D. (2008) 'Functional trade-offs in white matter axonal scaling', J Neurosci, 28(15), pp. 4047-56."}]

items.name: General Visceral Afferent Nerve Fiber
items.info: [{"name": "Quick Facts", "text": "Afferent nerve fibers or axons are nerve fibers that convey sensory impulses from the periphery to the central nervous system; classified according to function as somatic afferent and visceral afferent fibers (Dorland, 2011)."}, {"name": "Structure/Morphology", "text": "General visceral afferent nerve fibers are composed of an axon and its surrounding myelin sheath. Visceral afferent fibers are relatively less myelinated (with less lamellar layers) when compared with the somatic nerve fibers."}, {"name": "Key Features/Anatomical Relations", "text": "General visceral afferent nerve fibers are part of the autonomic nervous system."}, {"name": "Function", "text": "General visceral afferent nerve fibers transmit visceral sensory information from the viscera, glands, and blood vessels through the peripheral nervous system to the dorsal gray horn of the spinal cord. This visceral sensory information could include the sensations due to stretch, pain, temperature, chemical changes, irritation in viscera, nausea and hunger. Unlike the general visceral sensations, the special visceral sensations, such as the sense of taste and smell are conveyed to the brain via the special visceral afferent nerve fibers (Patestas and Gartner, 2016)."}, {"name": "References", "text": "Dorland, W. (2011) Dorland's Illustrated Medical Dictionary. 32nd edn. Philadelphia, USA: Elsevier Saunders.\n\nPatestas, M. A. and Gartner, L. P. (2016) A Textbook of Neuroanatomy. Wiley."}]

items.name: Medial Angle of Eye
items.info: [{"name": "Quick Facts", "text": "The medial angle of eye is the angle formed by the medial junction of the superior and inferior eyelids (Dorland, 2011)."}, {"name": "Structure and/or Key Feature(s)", "text": "The medial angle of the eye, or medial canthus, is the point where the medial edges of the eyelids meet, thus, the point where the inner part of the palpebral fissure ends. The shape of the medial angle of the eye can vary between different geographic and ethnic populations. In Caucasians, the medial angle of the eye is completely exposed, while in Asians, the medial canthus is covered by a semilunar fold of skin called the epicanthus."}, {"name": "Anatomical Relations", "text": "The medial canthus is separated from the eyeball by the lacrimal lake (lacus lacrimalis), a small, usually tear filled, triangular space. Within the space is a small tissue body called the lacrimal caruncle. The lacrimal caruncle is modified skin containing fine hairs. Slightly lateral to the medial canthus, along the margins of the superior and inferior eyelids, is a small elevation, the lacrimal papilla. It contains a small opening, the lacrimal punctum, that is the opening into the lacrimal drainage system allowing for removal of tears from the eye."}, {"name": "Function", "text": "The medial angle of the eye provides a rounded space for the lacrimal lake."}, {"name": "List of Clinical Correlates", "text": "- Canthotomy"}, {"name": "References", "text": "Dorland, W. (2011) Dorland's Illustrated Medical Dictionary. 32nd edn. Philadelphia, USA: Elsevier Saunders."}]

items.name: Basal Epithelial Cells
items.info:
[{"name": "Quick Facts", "text": "Basal cells are essentially stem cells, which have the potential to differentiate into supporting cells or olfactory sensory neurons."}, {"name": "Structure and/or Key Features", "text": "The olfactory epithelium is made up of various cell types such as basal cells, olfactory sensory neurons, and non-neuronal supporting cells (Rao, Vemuri and Carpenter, 2007). 

The basal cells are a heterogenous population of epithelial cells and can be grouped into two categories based on histological and cellular characteristics. The categories are the horizontal and the globose basal cells (Standring, 2016). 

The horizontal basal cells are compressed against the basement membrane of the olfactory epithelium. They contain nuclei that are condensed and a cytoplasm that contains a large number of intermediate cytokeratin filaments. The cytokeratin filaments are wedged into desmosomes that are situated between the basal cells and the neighboring supporting cells (Standring, 2016). 

The globose basal cells are circular with pale euchromatic nuclei and cytoplasm, from which new olfactory sensory neurons originate directly (Standring, 2016)."}, {"name": "Function", "text": "The basal cells are essentially stem cells, which have the potential to differentiate into supporting cells or olfactory sensory neurons (Kierszenbaum, 2007)."}, {"name": "References", "text": "Kierszenbaum, A. L. (2007) Histology and Cell Biology: An Introduction to Pathology. Mosby Elsevier.

Rao, M. S., Vemuri, M. C. and Carpenter, M. (2007) Neural Development and Stem Cells. Contemporary Neuroscience: Humana Press.

Standring, S. (2016) Gray's Anatomy: The Anatomical Basis of Clinical Practice. Gray's Anatomy Series 41st edition: Elsevier Limited."}]

items.name: Perirenal Fat Capsule
items.info:
[{"name": "Quick Facts", "text": "The perirenal fat capsule is the investment of fat surrounding the fibrous capsule of the kidney and continuous at the hilum with the fat in the renal sinus (Dorland, 2011)."}, {"name": "Structure and/or Key Features", "text": "The perirenal fat is composed of adipose tissue that surrounds the kidneys and the suprarenal glands. It envelopes the fibrous capsules and is held tight around the organs via the renal fascia (Toldt’s fascia). This fat is typically more solid than normal fat.

In neonates, the perirenal fat capsule has a brown appearance due to the number of iron-containing mitochondria. However, the brown adipose tissue is thought to diminish gradually over the first ten years of life (Cantisani et al., 2003)."}, {"name": "Anatomical Relations", "text": "The perirenal fat capsule is superjacent to the capsule of the suprarenal gland and kidney and is subjacent to the renal fascia (Toldt’s fascia) which tightly wraps it around the organs."}, {"name": "Function", "text": "The perirenal fat capsule serves numerous functions. It provides both protection and structural support to the kidneys and suprarenal glands, by stabilizing their anatomical position. Its primary function is yet to be fully elucidated but is thought to play a role in thermoregulation; generating heat via non-shivering thermogenesis due to its rich vascular supply."}, {"name": "List of Clinical Correlates", "text": "—Nephroptosis"}, {"name": "References", "text": "Cantisani, V., Mortele, K. J., Glickman, J. N., Ricci, P., Passariello, R., Ros, P. R. & Silverman, S. G. (2003) Large retroperitoneal hibernoma in an adult male: CT imaging findings with pathologic correlation. Abdom Imaging, 28(5), 721-4.

Dorland, W. (2011) Dorland's Illustrated Medical Dictionary. 32nd edn. Philadelphia, USA: Elsevier Saunders."}]

items.name: Basement Membrane (of Tertiary Ovarian Follicle)
items.info:
[{"name": "Quick Facts", "text": "The basement membrane is a thin sheet of amorphous extracellular material upon which the basal surfaces of epithelial cells rest; other cells associated with basement membranes are muscle cells, Schwann cells, and fat cells. The membrane is interposed between the cellular elements and the underlying connective tissue. It usually comprises two layers, the basal lamina and the reticular lamina, and is composed of Type IV collagen (which is unique to basement membranes), laminin, fibronectin, and heparan sulfate proteoglycans (Dorland, 2011)."}, {"name": "Structure and/or Key Feature(s)", "text": "Almost all epithelia are attached to some form of underlying connective tissues by a basement membrane.

In the primordial and primary ovarian follicles, the outer surface of the simple squamous and simple cuboidal follicular cells are bound by a basement membrane. As the ovarian follicles develop into secondary and tertiary follicles, the granulosa is bound by a basement membrane that will separate it from the follicular theca (Ross and Pawlina, 2006).

In mature follicles that undergo atresia, the glassy membrane is formed from a much thickened basement membrane that is between the membrana granulosa and the theca interna (Ross and Pawlina, 2006)."}, {"name": "Anatomical Relations", "text": "The follicular basement membrane separates the membrana granulosa from the theca interna layer in developing follicles."}, {"name": "References", "text": "Dorland, W. (2011) Dorland's Illustrated Medical Dictionary. 32nd edn. Philadelphia, USA: Elsevier Saunders.

Ross, M. H. and Pawlina, W. (2006) Histology: A text and atlas. Lippincott Williams & Wilkins."}]

items.name: Scleral Venous Sinus
items.info:
[{"name": "Quick Facts", "text": "The venous sinus of sclera is a circular channel at the junction of the sclera and cornea, which is the main pathway for elimination of aqueous humor from the eye (Dorland, 2011)."}, {"name": "Structure and/or Key Feature(s)", "text": "The scleral venous sinus, or the canal of Schlemm, is a single-layered endothelial lined canal. These specialized endothelial cells act as a barrier for the drainage of aqueous humor from the anterior chamber of the eye and add resistance to the flow of aqueous humor (Kizhatil et al., 2014). 

The anterior wall of the scleral venous sinus is formed from the tough tissue of the sclera. The posterior wall is composed of a triangular mass of trabecular tissue. Aqueous humor drains through the trabecular tissue into the venous sinus."}, {"name": "Anatomical Relations", "text": "The scleral venous sinus is embedded within the inner surface of the sclera adjacent to the cornea near the limbus. Additionally, it is located in the tissue of the iridocorneal angle, an angle formed between the iris and the cornea. It is continuous with the small interscleral veins, which connect the canal with the episcleral veins. Although the scleral venous sinus is continuous with the interscleral veins, it usually does not contain blood. Thus, the scleral venous sinus may be considered a lymphatic vessel."}, {"name": "Function", "text": "The scleral venous sinus removes aqueous humor from the anterior chamber of the eye. It receives aqueous humor at the iridocorneal angle that filters through the trabecular meshwork. Aqueous humor flows into the bloodstream via the episcleral veins. The scleral venous sinus is responsible for about 70-90% of total aqueous humor drainage from the eye (Truong et al., 2014). Therefore, the scleral venous canal plays an important role in regulating intraocular pressure."}, {"name": "List of Clinical Correlates", "text": "—Glaucoma"}, {"name": "References", "text": "Dorland, W. (2011) Dorland's Illustrated Medical Dictionary. 32nd edn. Philadelphia, USA: Elsevier Saunders.

Kizhatil, K., Ryan, M., Marchant, J. K., Henrich, S. and John, S. W. (2014) 'Schlemm's canal is a unique vessel with a combination of blood vascular and lymphatic phenotypes that forms by a novel developmental process', PLoS Biol, 12(7), pp. e1001912.

Truong, T. N., Li, H., Hong, Y. K. and Chen, L. (2014) 'Novel characterization and live imaging of Schlemm's canal expressing Prox-1', PLoS One, 9(5), pp. e98245."}]

items.name: Axonal Process of Rod Cell
items.info:
[{"name": "Quick Facts", "text": "An axonal process is the process of a neuron by which impulses travel away from the cell body; at the terminal arborization of the axon, the impulses are transmitted to other nerve cells or to effector organs (Dorland, 2011)."}, {"name": "Structure and/or Key Features", "text": "The axonal process is the elongated part of the photoreceptor cell that transmits information about the light level in the environment detected by a single photoreceptor and communicated as a voltage change from the cell soma to its synaptic terminal. Rod axons have a diameter of approximately 0.5 µm. 

The length of the axonal process in rod cells varies greatly depending on the species and location within the retina. In primates, axons may measure 200–400 µm in the para-foveal region (Dartt et al., 2010)."}, {"name": "Anatomical Relations", "text": "The axonal process of the rod cells extends from the cell body in the outer nuclear layer to the spherule synaptic terminal in outer plexiform layer of the retina. They are interspersed between the somata and axons of other rod and cone cells and the external radial processes of Müller glial cells."}, {"name": "Function", "text": "The axonal process carries the electrical signal caused by light stimulation or rod outer segments from the soma (cell body) to the synaptic terminal."}, {"name": "References", "text": "Dartt, D. A., Besharse, J., Dana, R., Battelle, B. A., Beebe, D., Bex, P., Bishop, P., Bok, D., D’Amore, P. and Edelhauser, H. (2010) Encyclopedia of the Eye. Elsevier Science, p. 147-152.

Dorland, W. (2011) Dorland's Illustrated Medical Dictionary. 32nd edn. Philadelphia, USA: Elsevier Saunders."}]

items.name: Sarcolemma (Uncontracted Smooth Muscle; Posterior)
alt: Muscle Cell Membrane (Uncontracted Smooth Muscle; Posterior)
items.info:
[{"name": "Quick Facts", "text": "The sarcolemma is the delicate plasma membrane that invests every striated muscle fiber (Dorland, 2011)."}, {"name": "Structure and/or Key Features", "text": "The sarcolemma is the fine, delicate, extensible membrane surrounding each muscle fiber. It is composed of a cell, or plasma, membrane which presents an extracellular matrix of collagen fibrils and polysaccharides that make contact with the basal lamina. The sarcolemma also contains tunnel-like invaginations into the sarcoplasm, which are known as transverse tubules (T tubules) in striated muscle and caveolae in smooth muscle (Standring, 2020)."}, {"name": "Anatomical Relations", "text": "Transmembrane proteins found within the sarcolemma facilitate a physical connection between the actin cytoskeleton of the muscle fiber and the extracellular basal lamina (Martini, Nath and Bartholomew, 2017)."}, {"name": "Function", "text": "Like other types of cell membranes, the sarcolemma forms a defined barrier between extracellular and intracellular environments."}, {"name": "References", "text": "Dorland, W. (2011) Dorland's Illustrated Medical Dictionary. 32nd edn. Philadelphia, USA: Elsevier Saunders.

Martini, F. H., Nath, J. L. and Bartholomew, E. F. (2017) Fundamentals of Anatomy & Physiology. Pearson Education.

Standring, S. (2020) Gray's Anatomy: The Anatomical Basis of Clinical Practice. 42nd edn.: Elsevier Health Sciences."}]

items.name: Superior Peripheral Venous Arcade
items.info:
[{"name": "Quick Facts", "text": "Origin: Upper eyelid.

Course: Along the superior margin of the superior tarsus.

Tributaries: None.

Drainage: Upper eyelid."}, {"name": "Origin", "text": "The superior peripheral venous arcade arises within the upper eyelid."}, {"name": "Course", "text": "The superior peripheral venous arcade extends the length of the upper eyelid, above the superior margin of the superior tarsus (Yanoff & Duker, 2013)."}, {"name": "Tributaries", "text": "There are no named tributaries."}, {"name": "Structures drained", "text": "Pretarsal tissue is drained medially by the angular vein and laterally by the superficial temporal vein, which both drain into the internal jugular vein (Yanoff & Duker, 2013)."}, {"name": "References", "text": "Yanoff, M. & Duker, J. S. (2013) Ophthalmology E-Book: Expert Consult: Online and Print Elsevier Health Sciences."}]

items.name: Endolymph
items.info:
[{"name": "Quick Facts", "text": "Endolymph is the fluid contained in the membranous labyrinth of the ear; it is entirely separate from the perilymph (Dorland, 2011)."}, {"name": "Structure and/or Key Feature(s)", "text": "The cochlear duct is filled with endolymph, an extracellular fluid that is similar in consistency to that of cerebrospinal fluid and has a crucial function in auditory detection. This fluid is produced from the marginal cells of the stria vasculairis, which is located on the outer wall of the cochlear duct. It is also produced by ion diffusion from the perilymph, occurring across the vestibular membrane.

The endolymph, along with the perilymph, are the two inner ear fluids. Compared to perilymph, endolymph has lower sodium and calcium ion concentrations, but higher chloride and potassium ion concentrations. There are also higher levels of glucose and total protein in perilymph. The differences in ionic composition between the endolymph and perilymph of the internal ear are what enables the transductive process for auditory processing. Essentially, mechanical vibrations result in waves of the endolymph, which ultimately results in the transmission of nerve signals along the cochlear nerve (Yamashita, 1976)."}, {"name": "Anatomical Relations", "text": "The endolymph is contained within the cochlear duct. It bathes the apices of the sensory hair cells, as well as other components of the cochlear duct, including the spiral organ (of Corti), stria vascularis, the tectorial membrane, vestibular membrane, and the basilar membrane."}, {"name": "Function", "text": "Vibrations are transmitted from the middle ear to the basilar membrane (via the oval window) and disrupts the endolymph in the cochlear duct. This disruption causes a shift in the position of the special stereocilia bundles of the sensory hair cells. This positional change activates positive ion channels in the stereocilia bundles. Once activated, an influx of endolymphatic potassium and calcium ions occurs, causing a depolarization of the membrane and result in the generation of potentials which result in synaptic transmission via neurotransmitter release. Perilymph does contribute to this as well, as it can contribute calcium ions which influx into the channels in these areas (Standring, 2016)."}, {"name": "List of Clinical Correlates", "text": "—Refractory Meniere’s disease"}, {"name": "References", "text": "Dorland, W. (2011) Dorland's Illustrated Medical Dictionary. 32nd edn. Philadelphia, USA: Elsevier Saunders.

Standring, S. (2016) Gray's Anatomy: The Anatomical Basis of Clinical Practice., 41st edition. Elsevier Limited."}]

items.name: Cytoskeleton
items.info:
[{"name": "Quick Facts", "text": "The cytoskeleton is a three-dimensional cytoplasmic network of protein polymers (microfilaments, intermediate filaments, and microtubules), occurring in eukaryotes, that supports and maintains the shape of the cell and provides motility (both of the whole cell and of organelles and vesicles within the cell) (Dorland, 2011)."}, {"name": "Structure and/or Key Feature(s)", "text": "The cell cytoskeleton includes networks of protein microfilaments, intermediate filaments, and microtubules. Microtubules radiate out to the cell periphery from a microtubule organizing center (MTOC) which is usually located close to the cell nucleus (Ross and Pawlina, 2006)."}, {"name": "Anatomical Relations", "text": "The cytoskeleton is located throughout the cell cytoplasm."}, {"name": "Function", "text": "Microfilaments help to maintain cell shape and, in some specialized cells (e.g., muscle cells), facilitate muscle contraction and intracellular movement.

Intermediate filaments stabilize cell junctions and provide structural support within the cell. 

Microtubules also maintain cell shape and are involved with moving organelles around the cell and supporting all those organelles within the cell. They affect motility of cilia and also the tail piece (flagellum) of the mature sperm (Ross and Pawlina, 2006; Ovalle, Nahirney and Netter, 2013; McKinley, O'Loughlin and Pennefather-O'Brien, 2016)."}, {"name": "References", "text": "Dorland, W. (2011) Dorland's Illustrated Medical Dictionary. 32nd edn. Philadelphia, USA: Elsevier Saunders.

McKinley, M. P., O'Loughlin, V. D. and Pennefather-O'Brien, E. E. (2016) Human Anatomy. 5th edn.: McGraw-Hill Education.

Ross, M. H. and Pawlina, W. (2006) Histology: A text and atlas. Lippincott Williams & Wilkins."}]

items.name: Submucosal Lymphatic Plexus (Duodenum)
items.info: [{"name": "Quick Facts", "text": "The submucosal lymphatic plexus is an interconnecting network of lymph vessels, i.e., the lymphocapillary vessels, collecting vessels, and trunks, which provides drainage of lymph in a one-way flow (Dorland, 2011)."}, {"name": "Structure/Morphology", "text": "Lacteals originate in the lamina propria of villi and form a plexus near the muscular layer (muscularis mucosa) of the small intestine. From there, they flow to lymph nodules in the submucosa and unite to accompany blood vessels out of the intestine."}, {"name": "Function", "text": "Lacteals and the lymphatic vessels are important for the absorption of lipids."}, {"name": "References", "text": "Dorland, W. (2011) Dorland's Illustrated Medical Dictionary. 32nd edn. Philadelphia, USA: Elsevier Saunders."}]

items.name: Lamina Propria
items.info: [{"name": "Quick Facts", "text": "The lamina propria is the connective tissue coat of a mucous membrane just deep to the epithelium and basement membrane (Dorland, 2011)."}, {"name": "Structure and/or Key Features", "text": "The lamina propria is a loose connective areolar tissue layer forming a deeper part of the mucosal layer of the oral mucosa. It serves as a protective barrier, as well as providing immune cells when needed."}, {"name": "Function", "text": "The lamina propria houses a rich supply of immune cells in response to the desquamation of superficial epithelial apoptotic or necrotic cells. It also serves a mechanical protective function by its service as a barrier, preventing internal tissue access of external pathogens and microorganisms."}, {"name": "References", "text": "Dorland, W. (2011) Dorland's Illustrated Medical Dictionary. 32nd edn. Philadelphia, USA: Elsevier Saunders."}, {"name": "Anatomical Relations", "text": "The lamina propria is situated deep to the basement membrane of the olfactory epithelium, separating it from the cribriform plate of the ethmoid bone."}, {"name": "Clinical Correlates", "text": "\u2014Anosmia"}]

items.name: Central Retinal Vein
items.info:
[{"name": "Quick Facts", "text": "Origin: From the venules inside the retina.

Course: Accompanies central retinal artery in the optic nerve.

Tributaries: Superior and inferior nasal and temporal branches.

Drainage: Retina."}, {"name": "Origin", "text": "The central retinal vein arises from the union of the superior and inferior nasal and temporal venules in the retina."}, {"name": "Course", "text": "Within the eyeball, the intraocular part of the central retina vein does not share a similar distribution with the arteries. Arteries, which lie more superficially, can often cross over the veins. In individuals with severe hypertension, the arteries press on the veins causing dilations of the veins.

The extraocular part of the central retinal vein accompanies the central retinal artery within the optic nerve. It is short and drains either directly into the cavernous sinus, or into the superior ophthalmic vein."}, {"name": "Tributaries", "text": "The central retinal vein receives the superior and inferior nasal and temporal venules, which each drain a quadrant of the retina."}, {"name": "Structures drained", "text": "The central retinal vein is responsible for draining the inner layers of the retina of the eyeball including the outer plexiform layer, the inner nuclear layer, the inner plexiform layer, and the ganglion cell layer."}, {"name": "List of Clinical Correlates", "text": "—“Nicking” of central retinal veins as an indication of hypertension observable upon ophthalmoscopic examination"}]

items.name: Primary Spermatocyte
items.info:
[{"name": "Quick Facts", "text": "A primary spermatocyte is a diploid cell that has derived from a spermatogonium and can subsequently begin meiosis and divide into two haploid secondary spermatocytes (Dorland, 2011)."}, {"name": "Structure/Morphology", "text": "Progenitor cells (type B spermatogonia) differentiate into primary spermatocytes. Primary spermatocytes are diploid cells, i.e., they have 46 chromosomes and 4N of DNA. When a primary spermatocyte is formed, it quickly enters the 1st meiotic division and these cells are viewed in more numbers in the prophase of this 1st meiotic division as this stage of meiosis takes about 22 days (Ross and Pawlina, 2016).

Primary spermatocytes are the largest spermatogenic cell and are easily identified by the presence of coiled chromosomes in their nuclei.

Primary spermatocytes undergo two meiotic cell divisions so that the resultant haploid cells, called spermatids, contain half the original chromosome number and amount of DNA. Small cells, called secondary spermatocytes, arise from the first meiotic division."}, {"name": "Anatomical Relations", "text": "Primary spermatocytes are confined to the basal epithelial compartment of the seminiferous epithelium."}, {"name": "Function", "text": "Primary spermatocytes undergo two meiotic cell divisions so that the resultant haploid cells called spermatids contain half the original chromosome number and amount of DNA. 

Small cells, called secondary spermatocytes, arise from the first meiotic division."}, {"name": "References", "text": "Dorland, W. (2011) Dorland's Illustrated Medical Dictionary. 32nd edn. Philadelphia, USA: Elsevier Saunders.

Ross, M. H. and Pawlina, W. (2016) Histology: A Text and Atlas. Wolters Kluwer Health."}]

items.name: Interplexiform Neuron
items.info:
[{"name": "Quick Facts", "text": "Interplexiform neurons are multipolar neurons that link the inner and outer plexiform layers (Dorland, 2011)."}, {"name": "Structure and/or Key Features", "text": "Interplexiform neurons are multipolar neurons that link the inner and outer plexiform layers. They receive synaptic input from the inner plexiform layer and transmit synaptic outputs to the outer plexiform layer. Therefore, they serve a “feedback” function, conveying signals against the general flow of information in the retina (Kolb, 1995a)."}, {"name": "Anatomical Relations", "text": "The cell bodies of the interplexiform neurons are usually located in the inner nuclear layer of the retina. They are postsynaptic neurons that receive input from bipolar, horizontal, and amacrine cells and feedback to photoreceptor cell terminal spherules and pedicles or rods and cones, respectively, in the outer plexiform layer (Standring, 2016)."}, {"name": "Function", "text": "The function of interplexiform neurons has yet to be elucidated; however, some have been identified as GABAergic and dopaminergic and may play a role in adjusting sensitivity of the retina (Standring, 2016)."}, {"name": "List of Clinical Correlates", "text": "- Gliosis

- Reactive Gliosis"}, {"name": "References", "text": "Dorland, W. (2011) Dorland's Illustrated Medical Dictionary. 32nd edn. Philadelphia, USA: Elsevier Saunders.

Kolb, H. (1995a) 'Feedback Loops in the Retina', in Kolb, H., Fernandez, E. and Nelson, R. (eds.) Webvision: The Organization of the Retina and Visual System. Salt Lake City (UT): University of Utah Health Sciences Center.

Standring, S. (2016) Gray's Anatomy: The Anatomical Basis of Clinical Practice. Gray's Anatomy Series 41 edn.: Elsevier Limited."}]

items.name: Meningeal Cranial Dura Mater
alt: Meningeal Layer of Cranial Dura Mater
items.info:
[{"name": "Quick Facts", "text": "The cranial dura matter has a deep meningeal layer adjacent to the arachnoid and a superficial periosteal layer adjacent to the cranium. The periosteal dura is firmly adhered to the meningeal dura in most places, except when they come apart at the dural venous sinuses."}, {"name": "Structure", "text": "The meningeal cranial dura mater is the deep layer of cranial dura mater. It lies superficial to the arachnoid, to which it has a close anatomical relationship. It is firmly adhered to the periosteal layer of dura mater in most places within the cranium, except surrounding the dural venous sinuses, where they diverge to enclose the vessel. 

The meningeal dura mater is penetrated by arachnoid granulations and cerebral vessels, both of reach into the venous sinuses allowing for the movement of CSF and blood respectively."}, {"name": "Key Features/Anatomical Relations", "text": "The meningeal cranial dura mater is closely applied to the arachnoid. Additionally, it surrounds and fuses with the epineurium of each cranial nerve as they exit their designated cranial foramen. The meningeal cranial dura also fuses with the outer adventitia of major vessels, e.g., the internal carotid artery, when it enters the cranial cavity.

Even though the meningeal cranial dura mater is not in close contact with the brain, it reflects inward at certain points known as dural folds. The first is the falx cerebri in which the meningeal dura runs within the longitudinal fissure separating the two cerebral hemispheres. The second is the tentorium cerebelli, a dural fold that separates the cerebellum below from the cerebrum above. A third fold, the falx cerebelli, runs perpendicular to the tentorium cerebelli and separates the two cerebellar hemispheres. Lastly, the diaphragma sellae surrounds the pituitary stalk."}, {"name": "List of Clinical Correlates", "text": "—Subdural hematoma

—Headache"}]

items.name: Nerve Cell Body
items.info:
[{"name": "Quick Facts", "text": "The cell body is the portion of a cell that contains the nucleus, independent of projections such as an axon or dendrites (Dorland, 2011)."}, {"name": "Structure and/or Key Features", "text": "The nerve cell body (often called perikaryon or soma), houses a large, spherical, euchromatic nucleus with a prominent nucleolus, and cytoplasm. The size of cell bodies varies depending on the type of neuron and can range from 5 to 140 μm (Marieb, Wilhelm and Mallatt, 2012). 

The cytoplasm contains highly developed rough (granular) endoplasmic reticulum and numerous polyribosomes, indicative of the high levels of protein syntheses occurring for both internal use and transport (Ross and Pawlina, 2006). 

The region of the cytoplasm actively synthesizing proteins stains intensely with basic dyes due to the presence of RNA. Large clumps of rough endoplasmic reticulum in large motor neurons are referred to as Nissl bodies or Nissl substance.

The cytoplasm also contains a Golgi complex consisting of parallel arrays of smooth cisternae surrounding the nucleus. Mitochondria are also abundant in all parts of the cytoplasm, particularly in the axon hillock. Intermediate filaments and microtubules are abundant cytoskeletal elements in the cell body and, in some neurons, lipofuscin is a cytoplasmic inclusion (Mescher, 2013)."}, {"name": "Anatomical Relations", "text": "Neuronal cell bodies are located within the gray matter of the central nervous system or when clustered as nuclei. Cell bodies in the peripheral nervous system are located in sensory or autonomic ganglia. 

Dendrites and axons are processes that extend from the cell body. Axons extend from the nerve cell body at the axon hillock."}, {"name": "Function", "text": "The cell body of a neuron is responsible for controlling all the trophic and receptive functions of the neuron."}, {"name": "References", "text": "Dorland, W. (2011) Dorland's Illustrated Medical Dictionary. 32nd edn. Philadelphia, USA: Elsevier Saunders.

Marieb, E. N., Wilhelm, P. B. and Mallatt, J. (2012) Human Anatomy. fifth edn.: Benjamin Cummings.

Mescher, A. (2013) Junqueira's Basic Histology: Text and Atlas. 13th edn.: McGraw-Hill Education.

Ross, M. H. and Pawlina, W. (2006) Histology: A text and atlas. Lippincott Williams & Wilkins."}]

items.name: Muscular Layer of Small Intestine (Duodenum)
items.info:
[{"name": "Quick Facts", "text": "The muscular layer is the layer of smooth muscle lying between the submucosa and the serosa or the adventitia in many portions of the digestive, respiratory, urinary, and genital tracts (Dorland, 2011)."}, {"name": "Structure/Morphology", "text": "The muscular layer (or muscularis externa) is well developed and composed of an internal circular layer and an external longitudinal layer. Between the two layers are ganglion cells and nerve fibers forming the myenteric (Auerbach’s) plexus. How the smooth muscle cells appear under the microscope will depend on the plane of the section i.e., transverse or longitudinal."}, {"name": "Key Features/Anatomical Relations", "text": "At a few locations along the alimentary tract, the muscular layer thickens to form sphincters. The gastroduodenal sphincter (or pyloric sphincter) is an example in the small intestine. It is located at the junction of the pylorus of the stomach and the duodenum."}, {"name": "Function", "text": "Contractions of the inner circular layer of the muscular layer constricts the lumen and mixes the luminal contents. Contraction of the outer longitudinal layer of the muscular layer propels the contents along the digestive tract. 

The slow, rhythmic contraction of both these muscle layers, under the control of the enteric nervous system, produces peristalsis.

The gastroduodenal sphincter (or pyloric sphincter) controls the release of chyme into the duodenum."}, {"name": "References", "text": "Dorland, W. (2011) Dorland's Illustrated Medical Dictionary. 32nd edn. Philadelphia, USA: Elsevier Saunders."}]

items.name: Carrier Protein
items.info:
[{"name": "Quick Facts", "text": "A carrier protein is a transport protein that attaches to and carries a specific substance, particularly one that transports the substance across the cell membrane (Dorland, 2011)."}, {"name": "Structure and/or Key Feature(s)", "text": "To provide a passage across the cell membrane, many molecules require one of two types of membrane transport proteins, carrier proteins and channel proteins.

Carrier proteins are highly selective and only transport one type of molecule that is small and water-soluble. Examples of carrier proteins are the Na+/K+ or H+ pumps. These pumps work via active transport and require energy to transport the molecules against their concentration gradient. Other carrier proteins (e.g., glucose carriers) perform passive transport as they do not require energy (Ross and Pawlina, 2016).

What makes carrier proteins different from channel proteins is that channel proteins only transport substances through membranes passively."}, {"name": "Anatomical Relations", "text": "Membrane transport proteins, such as carrier and channel proteins, are components of the plasma membrane. Thus, they are surrounded primarily by phospholipids but also cholesterol, and other protein molecules (Ross and Pawlina, 2016)."}, {"name": "Function", "text": "Carrier proteins are highly selective and only transport one type of molecule that is small and water-soluble."}, {"name": "References", "text": "Dorland, W. (2011) Dorland's Illustrated Medical Dictionary. 32nd edn. Philadelphia, USA: Elsevier Saunders.

Ross, M. H. and Pawlina, W. (2016) Histology: A Text and Atlas. Wolters Kluwer Health."}]

items.name: Integral Membrane Protein
items.info:
[{"name": "Quick Facts", "text": "A membrane protein is a protein found in association with the cell membrane, either attached to (peripheral or extrinsic) or inserted in (integral or intrinsic) the membrane; possible roles include an enzyme, a receptor for a hormone or other molecule, and a mediator of active or passive transport of lipid-insoluble substances across the membrane (Dorland, 2011)."}, {"name": "Structure and/or Key Feature(s)", "text": "Protein molecules make up about 50% of total membrane mass. They are either integral (intrinsic) or peripheral (extrinsic) membrane proteins but most cell membranes contain both types. Peripheral membrane proteins are not embedded in the lipid bilayer and have a looser association with the membrane surfaces. Integral membrane proteins can be either embedded within the lipid bilayer or pass through this bilayer completely and have domains on both the extracellular surface and cytosolic face of the membrane (Ross and Pawlina, 2016; Lowe, Anderson and Anderson, 2018). 

Integral membrane proteins vary hugely in their composition, i.e., there are a great many types of these proteins (Lowe, Anderson and Anderson, 2018). Most integral proteins have components with hydrophobic sidechains that interact with, and so anchor the protein, with the fatty acid chains of the phospholipids. They also have components that span domains for some considerable length within the membrane as well as into the aqueous environment adjacent to both the extracellular surface and the cytosolic face. Integral proteins containing membrane spanning domains are alpha helices or beta strands (Lowe, Anderson and Anderson, 2018).

In general, these proteins are so permanently bound to the membrane you need denaturing agents like detergents or solvents to separate them (Lowe, Anderson and Anderson, 2018)."}, {"name": "Anatomical Relations", "text": "Integral membrane proteins can be either embedded within the lipid bilayer or pass through this bilayer completely and have domains on both the extracellular surface and cytosolic face of the membrane (Lowe, Anderson and Anderson, 2018)."}, {"name": "Function", "text": "Integral proteins on the extracellular surface of the membrane are involved in cell-cell signaling or interactions. Integral proteins within the membrane form channels or pores so molecules can pass through the membrane. Integral proteins on the cytosolic face have more varied functions such as acting as anchors for attachment to the cytoskeletal proteins or triggering intracellular signaling pathways (Lowe, Anderson and Anderson, 2018)."}, {"name": "References", "text": "Dorland, W. (2011) Dorland's Illustrated Medical Dictionary. 32nd edn. Philadelphia, USA: Elsevier Saunders.

Lowe, J. S., Anderson, P. G. and Anderson, S. I. (2018) Stevens & Lowe's Human Histology- E-Book. 5 edn.: Elsevier Health Sciences.

Ross, M. H. and Pawlina, W. (2016) Histology: A Text and Atlas. Wolters Kluwer Health."}]

items.name: Receptor Protein
items.info:
[{"name": "Quick Facts", "text": "A receptor protein is a molecular structure within a cell or on the cell surface and characterized by (1) selective binding of a specific substance and (2) a specific physiologic effect that accompanies the binding, e.g., membrane receptors for peptide hormones, neurotransmitters, antigens, complement fragments, and immunoglobulins, and nuclear receptors for steroid hormones (Dorland, 2011)."}, {"name": "Structure and/or Key Feature(s)", "text": "Membrane proteins are named according to their function. They can be pumps, carrier or channel proteins, receptors, linkers, enzymes, and structural proteins, or serve as a combination of these functions.

Receptor proteins permit the localized binding of ligands in activities such as hormonal stimulation, coated vesicle endocytosis, and antibody reactions to perform certain roles.

Receptors are generally classified into three groups:

—Certain channel proteins;

—Intracellular receptors;

—Cell surface receptors that interact with peptide hormones or catecholamines that cannot penetrate the cell membrane (Ross and Pawlina, 2016).

Receptors proteins include the G-protein coupled receptor family, the catalytic-linked receptor family, and the integrin family of cell-to-extracellular matrix receptors."}, {"name": "Anatomical Relations", "text": "Receptor proteins are a component of the plasma membrane. They are surrounded primarily by phospholipids, cholesterol, and other protein molecules (Ross and Pawlina, 2016)."}, {"name": "Function", "text": "Receptor proteins permit the localized binding of ligands in activities such as hormonal stimulation, coated vesicle endocytosis, and antibody reactions to perform certain roles."}, {"name": "References", "text": "Dorland, W. (2011) Dorland's Illustrated Medical Dictionary. 32nd edn. Philadelphia, USA: Elsevier Saunders.

Ross, M. H. and Pawlina, W. (2016) Histology: A Text and Atlas. Wolters Kluwer Health."}]

items.name: Scala Tympani
items.info:
[{"name": "Quick Facts", "text": "The scala tympani is the perilymph-filled part of the cochlea that is continuous with the scala vestibuli at the helicotrema, is separated from other cochlear structures by the spiral lamina and the spiral membrane of the cochlear duct, and ends blindly near the fenestra cochleae (Dorland, 2011)."}, {"name": "Structure and/or Key Feature(s)", "text": "The scala tympani is one of the main cochlear canals. It is formed by the division of the bony cochlear canal by the osseous spiral lamina (a fine ridge-like projection of bone from the modiolus).

The scala tympani runs from the round window of the vestibule to the helicotrema, where it communicates with the scala vestibuli. The scala tympani is separated from the cochlear duct by the thin basilar membrane. 

The scala tympani is filled with perilymph, which is an extracellular fluid that is of similar consistency to cerebrospinal fluid. The perilymph suspends the membranous labyrinth and serves as a medium to transmit vibrations from the tympanic membrane (via the ossicles) to the endolymph in the cochlear duct, thus stimulating the spiral organ (of Corti). It also receives effluxing potassium released by the depolarization of the stereocilia."}, {"name": "Anatomical Relations", "text": "The boundaries of the scala tympani are the bony wall of the cochlea, the osseous spiral lamina, and the basilar membrane. The scala tympani is subjacent to the cochlear duct."}, {"name": "Function", "text": "The scala tympani contains perilymph. It serves as a medium to transmit the sound-induced vibration of the tympanic membrane to the endolymph within the cochlear duct. This ultimately results in the displacement of the stereocilia bundles (of the hair cells on the basilar membrane) from the tectorial membrane, which activates mechanoelectrical ion channels. These facilitate the neurotransmission along cochlear afferent nerve fibers."}, {"name": "References", "text": "Dorland, W. (2011) Dorland's Illustrated Medical Dictionary. 32nd edn. Philadelphia, USA: Elsevier Saunders."}]

items.name: Stria Vascularis
items.info:
[{"name": "Quick Facts", "text": "The stria vascularis is a layer of vascular tissue consisting of epithelial cells, mesothelial cells, and probably some neuroectoderm; it covers the outer wall of the cochlear duct and is thought to secrete the endolymph (Dorland, 2011)."}, {"name": "Structure and/or Key Feature(s)", "text": "The stria vascularis is a complex epithelial structure that is one of the components of the cochlear duct. It overlies the wall of the cochlear duct, adjacent to the spiral ligament. It is a specialized stratified epithelium and, as its name implies, is extensively vascularized. This vascular supply is due to a condensed mesh of capillaries between the epithelial cells.

The stria vascularis is comprised of three main cell types, the marginal cells, intermediate cells, and basal cells. The marginal and basal cells are true epithelial cells, while the intermediate cells are more similar to melanocytes. The marginal cells line the stria vascularis facing directly into the cochlear duct and are involved in ion exchange with the endolymph. The intermediate cells lie below this and are dense in melanin. The basal cells are the deepest cells of the stria vascularis. The marginal cells have descending cytoplasmic extensions, while the intermediate and basal cells have cytoplasmic extensions which project up toward the marginal cells (Standring, 2016)."}, {"name": "Function", "text": "The stria vascularis aids in the production of endolymph. It plays a role in ion transportation, which facilitates the production of the unique ionic concentration of endolymph resulting in the electrical potential of the endolymph. The reason for its dense vasculature is due to the required maintenance of this potential, which is based on sufficient oxygenation of the epithelial cells. This oxygenation is provided and maintained by the dense vasculature of the stria vascularis."}, {"name": "List of Clinical Correlates", "text": "—Sensorineural hearing loss"}, {"name": "References", "text": "Dorland, W. (2011) Dorland's Illustrated Medical Dictionary. 32nd edn. Philadelphia, USA: Elsevier Saunders.

Standring, S. (2016) Gray's Anatomy: The Anatomical Basis of Clinical Practice., 41st edition. Elsevier Limited."}]

items.name: Interlobar Arteries of Kidney
Subcutaneous Tissue
items.info:
[{"name": "Quick Facts", "text": "The subcutaneous tissue is the layer of loose connective tissue situated just beneath the skin (Dorland, 2011)."}, {"name": "Structure", "text": "The subcutaneous tissue, or superficial fascia, of the scalp is composed of a dense connective tissue. It contains adipose tissue that is separated by fibrous septae. The thickness of the superficial fascia decreases with age (Brennan, Mahadevan and Evans, 2015). 

The subcutaneous tissue is the most vascularized region of the scalp and contains many anastomosing arteries, veins, and lymphatic vessels. The vessels are attached to the fibrous connective tissue, thus, if a vessel is cut, the ends become retracted between the fibrous septae and may lead to profuse bleeding (Ellis and Mahadevan, 2014)."}, {"name": "Key Features/Anatomical Relations", "text": "The subcutaneous tissue of the scalp lies below the skin to which it is firmly attached. It also attaches to the occipitofrontalis muscle and epicranial aponeurosis internally. Posteriorly, it is continuous with the subcutaneous tissue that covers the back of the neck. Laterally, the subcutaneous tissue of the scalp is continuous with the subcutaneous tissue overlying the temporal region."}, {"name": "Function", "text": "The subcutaneous tissue possesses fibers that join the skin of the scalp with the epicranial aponeurosis."}, {"name": "List of Clinical Correlates", "text": "—Scalp laceration

—Hematomas"}, {"name": "References", "text": "Brennan, P. A., Mahadevan, V. and Evans, B. T. (2015) Clinical Head and Neck Anatomy for Surgeons. CRC Press.

Dorland, W. (2011) Dorland's Illustrated Medical Dictionary. 32nd edn. Philadelphia, USA: Elsevier Saunders.

Ellis, H. and Mahadevan, V. (2014) 'The surgical anatomy of the scalp', Surgery (Oxford), 32, pp. e1-e5."}]

items.name: Plasma Membrane (Neck; Left)
items.info:
[{"name": "Quick Facts", "text": "The plasma membrane is the structure enveloping a cell, enclosing the cytoplasm and forming a selective permeability barrier; it consists of a lipid bilayer with integral and peripheral proteins and contains channels and pumps to transport substances across the membrane, as well as receptors to receive stimuli from the external environment and transduce them into intracellular signals (Dorland, 2011)."}, {"name": "Structure and/or Key Feature(s)", "text": "The sperm’s plasma membrane is a dynamic structure and is unique when compared with that of somatic cells. It is divided into various domains based on its location, composition, and function. 

In the sperm head, there are two notable regions of the plasma membrane, the acrosomal region and the postacrosomal region. The plasma membrane that surrounds the tail aspect of the sperm is divided into the middle piece, the principal piece, and the distal piece domains (Toshimori, 2000)."}, {"name": "Anatomical Relations", "text": "The plasma membrane is the outermost part of the sperm and it encases the entirety of the sperm cell."}, {"name": "Function", "text": "The plasma membrane plays a number of roles, which are vital for fertilization to occur.
