Modification of the plasma membrane is paramount for the initiation of processes, such as capacitation, acrosome reaction, and binding of the sperm head with the plasma membrane of the ovum, to occur. Most of these modifications occur as the sperm passes through the epididymis and in the uterine tube, oviduct (or fallopian tube) of the female reproductive tract (Toshimori, 2000)."}, {"name": "References", "text": "Dorland, W. (2011) Dorland's Illustrated Medical Dictionary. 32nd edn. Philadelphia, USA: Elsevier Saunders.

Toshimori, K. (2000) Sperm Plasma Membrane Modifications Associated with Fertilization in Mammals. Journal of Reproduction and Development, 46, 65-78."}]

items.name: Mesangial Matrix
items.info: [{"name": "Quick Facts", "text": "The mesangial matrix helps support podocytes where the basement membrane is absent (Ross and Pawlina, 2006)."}, {"name": "Structure and/or Key Feature(s)", "text": "Within the renal corpuscle, the glomerular basement membrane associated with several capillaries encloses a space containing a population of cells called mesangial cells, which form the mesangium. The mesangium is more prominent at the vascular pole. \n\nMesangial cells are also located outside the renal corpuscle but are called extraglomerular mesangial (or lacis) cells and will form part of the juxtaglomerular apparatus (Ross and Pawlina, 2006)."}, {"name": "Function", "text": "The primary function of mesangial cells is to remove trapped residue, etc. from the glomerular basement membrane and filtration slit diaphragm and so maintain these structures free of debris. Whilst they are phagocytic cells they are not derived from precursor cells of the mononuclear phagocytic system (monocytes). Mesangial cells also structurally support podocytes where the basement membrane is absent and synthesize and secrete molecules which have a role in responses to injury to the glomerulus. Mesangial cells also have contractile properties (Ross and Pawlina, 2006)."}, {"name": "References", "text": "Ross, M. H. and Pawlina, W. (2006) Histology: A text and atlas. Lippincott Williams & Wilkins."}]

items.name: Zonular Fibers
items.info: [{"name": "Quick Facts", "text": "The zonular fibers are the fibers that anchor the lens capsule to the ciliary body and the ciliary part of the retina (Dorland, 2011)."}, {"name": "Structure and/or Key Feature(s)", "text": "The zonular fibers are a series of fine (1\u20132 \u00b5m diameter) fibers that attach to the margin of the lens. The zonular fibers arise from the orbicularis ciliaris (ciliary ring or pars plana) of the ciliary body and extend to the lens in an anterior, posterior, and equatorial grouping. This arrangement of dense fibers forms the suspensory ligament of the lens (ciliary zonules or zonules of Zinn)."}, {"name": "Anatomical Relations", "text": "Zonular fibers pass across the aqueous humor of the posterior chamber, though the posterior-most fibers are abutted posteriorly to the vitreous body. The anterior-most fibers are separated by a short space from the posterior surface of the iris."}, {"name": "Function", "text": "The zonular fibers suspend the lens from the ciliary body where it sits immediately behind the iris. It transmits forces produced by contraction of the ciliary muscle to the lens, resulting in the lens changing shape, allowing the eye to focus on distant objects (accommodation)."}, {"name": "References", "text": "Dorland, W. (2011) Dorland's Illustrated Medical Dictionary. 32nd edn. Philadelphia, USA: Elsevier Saunders."}]

items.name: Denticulate Ligament (Thoracic; Left)
items.info: [{"name": "Structure", "text": "The denticulate ligaments are thin sheets of collagen that extend laterally from the spinal pia mater. They extend out and form triangular shaped attachments to the overlying dura mater."}, {"name": "Key Features/Anatomical Relations", "text": "The denticulate ligaments extend from the foramen magnum rostrally down to the level of the T12 vertebra caudally. On each side, there are typically 18-21 triangular extensions which attach to the spinal dura mater, lateral to the spinal cord. They are thought to help stabilize the spinal cord. The lateral extensions of the denticulate ligaments can be seen laying between the dorsal and ventral nerve roots."}]

items.name: Convoluted Seminiferous Tubules
items.info:
[{"name": "Quick Facts", "text": "The convoluted seminiferous tubules are the numerous delicate, contorted canals within each lobule of the testis; their epithelial linings contain Sertoli cells and germ cells (Dorland, 2011)."}, {"name": "Structure", "text": "Connective tissue radiating into each testis from the tunica albuginea capsule separates the testis into about 250 lobules. Each lobule contains between one and four very convoluted tubules. A convoluted seminiferous tubule forms a loop with each straightened end of the loop being continuous with the rete testis in the mediastinum of the testis.

Each seminiferous tubule is 30–80 cm long and 150–250 μm in diameter. They occupy approximately 60% of the testis volume and have a total length of about 600 m (Ross and Pawlina, 2016). Seminiferous tubules consists of a seminiferous epithelium surrounded by a tunica propria which is essentially a thin layer of elongated myoid cells. 

The seminiferous epithelium is a complex stratified epithelium consisting of spermatogenic cells and supporting columnar sustentocytes (Sertoli cells). Sertoli cells surround and envelope adjacent spermatogenic cells and extend the full thickness of the seminiferous epithelium.

Spermatogenic cells are a constant dividing cell population and will differentiate into spermatozoa. Immature spermatogenic cells are the spermatogonia located against the basement membrane. The most differentiated cells are spermatids which aggregate along the apical borders of the Sertoli cells and the periphery of the lumen of the seminiferous tubule.

It takes about 64 days from the commencement of the division of spermatogonia to the release of spermatozoa into the lumen of the seminiferous tubule. Spermatogenesis does not occur as a synchronous event along the entire length of the tubule. Spermatogenesis is occurring at different times in neighboring parts of the seminiferous epithelium so any given view of a section of the tubule will reveal different phases of spermatogenesis (Standring, 2020)."}, {"name": "Anatomical Relations", "text": "Seminiferous tubules make up 60% of the volume of the testis."}, {"name": "Function", "text": "Seminiferous tubules house the spermatogenic cells that undergo differentiation to form sperm."}, {"name": "References", "text": "Dorland, W. (2011) Dorland's Illustrated Medical Dictionary. 32nd edn. Philadelphia, USA: Elsevier Saunders.

Ross, M. H. and Pawlina, W. (2016) Histology: A Text and Atlas. Wolters Kluwer Health.

Standring, S. (2020) Gray's Anatomy: The Anatomical Basis of Clinical Practice. 42nd edn.: Elsevier Health Sciences."}]

items.name: Lingual papillae
items.info:
[{"name": "Quick Facts", "text": "The lingual papillae include the filiform, fungiform, vallate, and foliate papillae of the tongue (Dorland, 2011)."}, {"name": "Structure and/or Key Features", "text": "The surface of the oral tongue is covered in mucosal projections known as the lingual papillae. They aid in both mastication and gestation. 

There are four main types of lingual papillae, including the filiform, fungiform, vallate, and foliate papillae. Three of the papillae (fungiform, vallate, and foliate papillae) have gustatory function. 

The filiform papillae are the only papillae without taste buds and the only papillae with a keratinized epithelium. They are extensively spread over most of the oral tongue. They are cylindrical and their tips are usually pointed, but may be rounded nearer to the anterior aspect of the tongue.

The fungiform papillae are typically found at the tip of the tongue and on the surrounding local margins, with some scatterings along the dorsum of the tongue. They are dome-shaped and bigger than the filiform papillae.

The vallate papillae are located anterior to the sulcus terminalis. These papillae have a mushroom-like shape and are encircled by marginally raised mucosal mounds (hence, they are also known as the circumvallate papillae). Salivary glands are found in the grooves between the mucosal mounds, while the taste buds are located in their walls and floors.

The foliate papillae lie in furrows along the lateral borders of the sulcus terminalis bilaterally."}, {"name": "Function", "text": "The lingual papillae participate in mastication by increasing friction of the and the contact area between the tongue and food particles. They also participate in gustation, since the majority of them allow for taste detection via their in-house taste buds.

Different tastes are detected at higher sensitivity at different regions of the tongue. The base of the tongue detects bitterness, the anterior tip detects sweetness, and sour and salty taste is most sensitive at the lateral tongue sides."}, {"name": "List of Clinical Correlates", "text": "—Depapillation

—Papillitis"}, {"name": "References", "text": "Dorland, W. (2011) Dorland's Illustrated Medical Dictionary. 32nd edn. Philadelphia, USA: Elsevier Saunders."}]

items.name: Early Primary Ovarian Follicle
items.info: [{"name": "Quick Facts", "text": "The primary ovarian follicle is a growing ovarian follicle comprising a primary oocyte and a single layer of specialized epithelial cells (follicle cells) that surround it (Dorland, 2011)."}, {"name": "Structure and/or Key Feature(s)", "text": "Primordial follicles are individually triggered to begin growing into primary follicles by an unknown spontaneous mechanism. At some random time, the oocyte resumes its progression through meiosis and grows to about 100-150 \u03bcm in diameter. The follicular cells proliferate and enlarge into cuboidal cells that surround the primary oocyte.\n\nAt this stage to follicle is termed the early, unilaminar, primary ovarian follicle. The oocyte secretes an extracellular coat, called the zona pellucida during this transitional stage. This is a tough, eosinophilic or very pink stained, acellular, protective membrane between the oocyte and the follicular cells."}, {"name": "Anatomical Relations", "text": "Early primary ovarian follicles are located within the cortex of the ovary."}, {"name": "References", "text": "Dorland, W. (2011) Dorland's Illustrated Medical Dictionary. 32nd edn. Philadelphia, USA: Elsevier Saunders."}]

items.name: Nucleus (Rod Cell)
items.info:
[{"name": "Quick Facts", "text": "The nucleus is a spheroid body within a eukaryotic cell, separated from the cytoplasm by the nuclear envelope, and containing chromatin, a nucleolus, and nucleoplasm. In the nucleus, the cell's genetic information is stored on the chromosomes and RNA transcription and processing occur (Dorland, 2011)."}, {"name": "Structure and/or Key Features", "text": "The nuclei of rod cells are described as more spherical and smaller than those belonging to cone cells. As a result, rod cell nuclei tend to stain darker than their cone counterparts. Anatomically, rod nuclei form several layers internal (or vitreal) to the cone nuclei (Standring, 2016).

The nuclei of cone cells are larger and more oval-shaped than their rod counterparts. They form a single layer that often fringes the outer limiting membrane (Standring, 2016)."}, {"name": "Anatomical Relations", "text": "The nucleus is located in the soma (or cell body) of the photoreceptor cells and is located in the outer nuclear layer of the retina."}, {"name": "Function", "text": "The nucleus houses the cell’s genetic information and activation of certain genes initiates the process of transcription and translation that direct protein synthesis in the cell."}, {"name": "References", "text": "Dorland, W. (2011) Dorland's Illustrated Medical Dictionary. 32nd edn. Philadelphia, USA: Elsevier Saunders.

Standring, S. (2016) Gray's Anatomy: The Anatomical Basis of Clinical Practice. Gray's Anatomy Series 41 edn.: Elsevier Limited."}]

items.name: Superior Tarsus
items.info:
[{"name": "Quick Facts", "text": "The tarsus is the firm framework of connective tissue that gives shape to the lower eyelid (Dorland, 2011)."}, {"name": "Structure and/or Key Feature(s)", "text": "The superior eyelid contains a thin, elongated plate of tough collagenous tissue called the superior tarsal plate. It is convex shaped to conform to the anterior surface of the eyeball. It has an inferior, free, straight ciliary border adjacent to the hair follicles of the eyelashes, and a superior, convex orbital border that is attached to the orbital septum (palpebral fascia). The superior tarsus is the larger of the two tarsal plates, measuring approximately 2.5 cm long and 10 mm high (Standring, 2016)."}, {"name": "Anatomical Relations", "text": "The free ciliary margins of the tarsal plates end approximately 2 mm from the margin of the eyelid and runs parallel to it. 

The orbital margins of the tarsal plates are bound to margins of the orbital septum and to the palpebral ligaments on each side. The medial palpebral (canthic) ligament passes from the medial ends of both tarsal plates and insets into the anterior lacrimal crest and the frontal process of the maxilla bone that forms part of the medial wall of the orbit. As it inserts into the tarsal plates, the ligament splits to surround the lacrimal canaliculi. The lateral palpebral ligament, on the other hand, is poorly developed. It extends from the lateral edges of the tarsal plates to the zygomatic bone that forms part of the orbital margin.

Superficial to the superior tarsal plate is a thin layer of muscle, the palpebral portion of the orbicularis oculi and small blood vessels of the marginal arterial arcade. Deep to the plate is a thin layer of connective tissue and a layer of the conjunctiva.

A smooth muscle, the superior tarsal muscle, attaches to the superior margin of the superior plate. Additionally, the deep fibers from the aponeurosis of levator palpebrae superioris extend and attach to the anterior surface of the superior tarsus. Thus, both the superior tarsal and levator palpebrae superioris muscles work to raise the eyelid."}, {"name": "Function", "text": "The superior and inferior tarsal plates provide support to the eyelids and determine the shape of the lid."}, {"name": "References", "text": "Dorland, W. (2011) Dorland's Illustrated Medical Dictionary. 32nd edn. Philadelphia, USA: Elsevier Saunders.

Standring, S. (2016) Gray's Anatomy: The Anatomical Basis of Clinical Practice. Gray's Anatomy Series: Elsevier Limited."}]

items.name: Cellular Cement
items.info:
[{"name": "Quick Facts", "text": "The cellular cement is the cementum covering the apical half to two thirds of the tooth root; it contains cementocytes embedded in the calcified matrix and is usually opposed by a layer of acellular cementum (Dorland, 2011)."}, {"name": "Structure and/or Key Feature(s)", "text": "Cellular cement is generally composed of cementocytes in lacunae, joined by canaliculi, in calcified cement. Cellular cement is generally thicker than its acellular counterpart (Foster, 2017).

Cellular cement can be further classified depending on the presence of intrinsic and extrinsic fibers. Cellular mixed fiber cement describes cement in which both extrinsic Sharpey’s fibers and surrounding intrinsic matrix fibers are present in the calcified cement. Extrinsic fibers are produced by the fibroblasts present in the periodontal ligament. Cellular intrinsic fiber cement describes cement in which only intrinsic fibers exist, without any inserting extrinsic periodontal ligament fibers. Cellular intrinsic fiber cement is primarily a reparative cement (Vishwakarma et al., 2014)."}, {"name": "Anatomical Relations", "text": "Cellular cement is described as the portion of cement located in the apical portion of the tooth."}, {"name": "Function", "text": "While the overall function of cement is for tooth support and anchorage, the primary function of cellular cement lies in adaptation, whereby it reshapes the root surface during tooth movement or else compensates for crown wear (Yamamoto et al., 2016)."}, {"name": "References", "text": "Dorland, W. (2011) Dorland's Illustrated Medical Dictionary. 32nd edn. Philadelphia, USA: Elsevier Saunders.

Foster, B. L. (2017) 'On the discovery of cementum', J Periodontal Res, 52(4), pp. 666-685.

Vishwakarma, A., Sharpe, P., Shi, S. and Ramalingam, M. (2014) Stem Cell Biology and Tissue Engineering in Dental Sciences. Elsevier Science.

Yamamoto, T., Hasegawa, T., Hongo, H. and Amizuka, N. (2016) 'Histology of human cementum: Its structure, function, and development', Jpn Dent Sci Rev, 52(3), pp. 63-74."}]

items.name: Eye & Accessory Visual Structures
items.info: [{"name": "Description", "text": "The eye refers to the organ of vision and is composed of the eyeball and optic nerve. The eyeball itself is contained within a bony cavity, the orbit, which is made up of several bones from the facial skeleton. The orbital region overlies the orbit and contains the upper and lower eyelids and lacrimal apparatus. These structures control the exposure of the anterior eyeball to the external environment and lubricate it, respectively. Additionally, the orbital cavity contains accessory visual structures, including the extraocular muscles, which position the eyeball; nerves and vessels that supply the eyeball and its accessory structures; and the conjunctiva, a mucous membrane lining the anterior aspect of the eyeball and posterior aspects of the eyelids."}]

items.name: Pilosebaceous Unit
items.info:
[{"name": "Quick Facts", "text": "The pilosebaceous unit is the complex consisting of a hair follicle, its sebaceous gland, and the arrector pili muscle (Dorland, 2011)."}, {"name": "Structure/Morphology", "text": "The hair, hair follicle, and associated structures, such as the arrector pili muscle and sebaceous glands, are collectively referred to as the pilosebaceous unit (Standring, 2016). 

The hair is a filamentous appendage of the skin composed primarily of the protein keratin. The hair shaft is composed of three concentric layers, namely the outer cuticle, middle cortex, and the inner medulla. They differ from each other in the types of keratin filaments they possess.

The hair follicle is a down growth of the epidermis with its long axis usually traveling obliquely through the skin layers. The hair follicle can extend as far as the hypodermis, but can also be superficial in the reticular layer of the dermis (Standring, 2016). 

The sebaceous glands are small saccular structures that are found in the dermis. Sebaceous glands are usually associated with the hair follicle and produce sebum, which functions as a lubricant for the hair and the exposed surface of the skin.

The arrector pili muscle is formed by bundles of closely packed smooth muscle cells. The muscle extends obliquely attaching to the hair follicle to the papillary layer of the dermis.

The pilosebaceous unit can also include apocrine sweat glands which develop from the hair follicle, just above the opening of the sebaceous glands (Standring, 2016)."}, {"name": "Function", "text": "The pilosebaceous unit is responsible for the production, growth and maintenance of hair. The sebaceous glands within the unit are responsible for producing sebum, which plays an important role in the epidermal barrier and acts as a component of the skin’s immune system."}, {"name": "References", "text": "Dorland, W. (2011) Dorland's Illustrated Medical Dictionary. 32nd edn. Philadelphia, USA: Elsevier Saunders.

Standring, S. (2016) Gray's Anatomy: The Anatomical Basis of Clinical Practice. Gray's Anatomy Series: Elsevier Limited."}]

items.name: Trabecular Sinus
items.info: [{"name": "Quick Facts", "text": "The trabecular sinuses are those surrounding the trabeculae of the lymph node."}, {"name": "Structure/Morphology", "text": "The trabecular sinus originates from the subcapsular sinus. It is one of three sinuses in the lymph nodes, the others include the subcapsular and medullary sinuses. Unlike vascular sinuses, lymphatic sinuses are not open spaces. They are occupied by reticular fibers surrounded by reticular cell processes and macrophages (Willard-Mack, 2006). This forms a meshwork within the sinus, thus slowing down the flow of lymph through the sinus which enhances filtration."}, {"name": "Anatomical Relations", "text": "The trabecular sinus follows the same trajectory as the trabeculae, extending through the cortex. The trabecular sinuses drain into the medullary sinuses."}, {"name": "Function", "text": "The trabecular sinus receives lymph from the subcapsular sinus. The lymph is further filtered by the reticular meshwork in the trabecular sinus, where the antigenic material becomes trapped and phagocytosed by the macrophages."}, {"name": "References", "text": "Willard-Mack, C. L. (2006) 'Normal structure, function, and histology of lymph nodes', Toxicologic Pathology, 5(34), pp. 409-424."}]

items.name: Pancreatic Acinus
items.info:
[{"name": "Quick Facts", "text": "The pancreatic acinus is one of the secretory units of the exocrine pancreas, where pancreatic juice is produced (Dorland, 2011)."}, {"name": "Structure and/or Key Feature(s)", "text": "The exocrine cells of the pancreas (pancreatic acinar cells or serous secretory cells) are simple, pyramidal in shape. They form clusters or secretory units called acini, due to their acinar or tubuloacinar shape. Acini are supported by a basal lamina and very fine reticular fibers surround the acini.

The exocrine cells of the pancreas contain numerous zymogen granules in their apical cytoplasm which imparts an eosinophilia to the apical region compared to a more basophilic basal region due to the presence of free ribosomes and rough endoplasmic reticulum.

A unique feature of the pancreatic acinus is that centroacinar cells are located within the acinus and form the initial segment of the intercalated duct system (Ross and Pawlina, 2016)."}, {"name": "Function", "text": "Zymogen granules contain (inactive) precursors of digestive enzymes that can digest most food substances."}, {"name": "References", "text": "Dorland, W. (2011) Dorland's Illustrated Medical Dictionary. 32nd edn. Philadelphia, USA: Elsevier Saunders.

Ross, M. H. and Pawlina, W. (2016) Histology: A Text and Atlas. Wolters Kluwer Health."}]

items.name: Fibrous Capsule of Kidney
items.info: [{"name": "Quick Facts", "text": "The fibrous capsule of the kidney is the connective tissue investment of the kidney, which continues through the hilus to line the renal sinus (Dorland, 2011)."}, {"name": "Structure and/or Key Feature(s)", "text": "A thin fibrous capsule composed of collagen rich tissue with some elastic and smooth muscle fibers encloses each kidney. Each fibrous capsule is surrounded by renal fascia and a layer of perirenal fat, known as the adipose capsule of the kidney."}, {"name": "Function", "text": "The tough fibrous capsule of the kidney helps to protect the kidney from injury and supports the kidney mass. Additionally, it plays a role in restricting volume changes of the kidney in response to increases in blood pressure (Pocock et al, 2013)."}, {"name": "References", "text": "Dorland, W. (2011) Dorland's Illustrated Medical Dictionary. 32nd edn. Philadelphia, USA: Elsevier Saunders.\n\nPocock, G., Richards, C. D. & Richards, D. A. (2013) Human Physiology, 4 edition. OUP Oxford."}]

items.name: Sensory Receptors
items.info:
[{"name": "Quick Facts", "text": "A sensory receptor is a sensory nerve terminal that responds to stimuli of various kinds; classified in various ways including by the type of stimulus (e.g. chemoreceptor, mechanoreceptor, photoreceptor, and thermoreceptor) and by the location in the body (e.g. exteroceptor, interoceptor, and proprioceptor) (Dorland, 2011)."}, {"name": "Structure/Morphology", "text": "Sensory receptors are specialized cells that detect and respond to physical and chemical stimuli in the environment. The skin receives many stimuli from the external environment, such as touch, stretch, temperature changes, pain, and pressure. For this reason, it is important that the skin have appropriate sensory receptors responding to these stimuli. 

Receptor are classified into three groups:

—mechanoreceptors respond to pressure, touch, and stretch;

—thermoreceptors, which respond to temperature changes in the environment; 

—nociceptors that respond to pain (Arda, Goksugur and Tuzun, 2014). 

Sensory receptors are either encapsulated or unencapsulated. The unencapsulated, free nerve ending receptors are the tactile menisci (or Merkel discs) and peritrichial nerve endings. The encapsulated receptors are the tactile (Meissner), lamellar (Pacinian), and bulbous (Ruffini and Krause end bulbs) corpuscles."}, {"name": "Function", "text": "The function of sensory receptors is to respond to the stimuli from the external environment."}, {"name": "References", "text": "Arda, O., Goksugur, N. and Tuzun, Y. (2014) 'Basic histological structure and functions of facial skin', Clin Dermatol, 32(1), pp. 3-13.

Dorland, W. (2011) Dorland's Illustrated Medical Dictionary. 32nd edn. Philadelphia, USA: Elsevier Saunders."}]

items.name: Portal Triad
items.info:
[{"name": "Quick Facts", "text": "The portal triad is the grouping of the tributaries of the hepatic artery, vein, and bile duct at the angles of the lobules of the liver (Dorland, 2011)."}, {"name": "Structure/Morphology", "text": "The portal triad is the term given to the branches of the portal vein, hepatic artery, and bile duct that pass through the liver together. The term portal triad, however, is a misnomer, since lymphatic vessels and nerves also travel in this arrangement. The hepatic artery carries 25% of the total circulation to the liver, while the portal vein contributes to 75% of the total blood volume (Boron and Boulpaep, 2003). The blood of the hepatic artery is rich in oxygen as it has come directly from the celiac trunk of the abdominal aorta. The portal vein carries blood, not only rich in nutrients, but also toxins, absorbed from the gastrointestinal tract.

At the liver lobule, the terminal branches of the portal vein (interlobular vein) and hepatic artery (interlobular artery), and the interlobular bile ducts are located at the periphery of the lobule and run parallel to each other in the space often termed the portal area or canal. These interlobular vessels in the portal canals are the smallest portal triads.

As the interlobular arteries and veins pass between the lobules, they give off sinusoids. The sinusoids carrying arterial blood join the neighboring sinusoids carrying portal venous blood and extend into the parenchyma of the lobule towards the central vein.

The cuboidal or columnar epithelial-lined interlobular bile ducts receive the bile from the bile canaliculi via the canals of Hering. The interlobular bile ducts eventually drain into the common hepatic duct. 

There are also lymphatic vessels within the portal triad, but these are not easily visible on histological sections. They carry lymph it to the lymph nodes at the porta hepatis. Fibers from the hepatic plexus also travel with the portal triad to innervate the parenchyma and vessels of the liver."}, {"name": "Anatomical Relations", "text": "The portal triad is covered in a perivascular fibrous capsule of loose connective tissue. It provides structural support to the hepatic vessels and their branches and assists in the structural organization of the portal triad."}, {"name": "Function", "text": "The branches of the portal vein and hepatic artery in the portal triad supplies both oxygen-rich and nutrient-rich blood to the hepatocytes. The interlobular bile duct receives bile from the canaliculi."}, {"name": "List of Clinical Correlates", "text": "- Portal triad hemorrhagic injury"}, {"name": "References", "text": "Boron, W. F. and Boulpaep, E. L. (2003) Medical Physiology: A Cellular and Molecular Approach. W.B. Saunders.

Dorland, W. (2011) Dorland's Illustrated Medical Dictionary. 32nd edn. Philadelphia, USA: Elsevier Saunders."}]

items.name: Arachnoid Trabeculae
items.info:
[{"name": "Quick Facts", "text": "The arachnoid trabeculae are the delicate fibrous threads connecting the inner surface of the arachnoid to the pia mater (Dorland, 2011)."}, {"name": "Structure", "text": "The arachnoid trabeculae are thin web-like fibers of loose connective tissue that contain elongated fibroblasts and collagen (Pawlina, 2016). They trabeculae loosely connect the arachnoid with the pia mater. There are more arachnoid trabeculae in the cranial arachnoid than in the spinal arachnoid (Mescher, 2013)."}, {"name": "Key Features/Anatomical Relations", "text": "The arachnoid trabeculae are found within the subarachnoid space. The cerebral arteries and veins are located between the trabecular sheets."}, {"name": "List of Clinical Correlates", "text": "—Hydrocephalus"}, {"name": "References", "text": "Dorland, W. (2011) Dorland's Illustrated Medical Dictionary. 32nd edn. Philadelphia, USA: Elsevier Saunders.

Mescher, A. (2013) Junqueira's Basic Histology: Text and Atlas. 13th edn.: McGraw-Hill Education.

Pawlina, W. 2016. Histology: A text and atlas with correlated cell and molecular biology. 7th ed. Philadelphia: Wolters Kluwer."}]

items.name: Sclera
items.info:
[{"name": "Quick Facts", "text": "The sclera is the tough white outer coat of the eyeball, covering approximately five-sixths of its posterior surface, and continuous anteriorly with the cornea and posteriorly with the external sheath of the optic nerve; it and the cornea constitute the tunica fibrosa bulbi (Dorland, 2011)."}, {"name": "Structure and/or Key Features", "text": "The sclera forms part of the tough white outer fibrous layer for most of the eyeball, covering more than 93% of the surface of the eyeball. Only a small portion of the sclera is visible when the eyeball sits in situ in the orbital cavity. The sclera is replaced by the transparent cornea in the anterior portion of the eyeball (Standring, 2016).

The sclera can vary in thickness, ranging from about 0.3-1 mm. It is composed of collagen fibers that are interlaced, providing the strength and flexibility of the eyeball. The organization of these fibers lends the sclera its opaque appearance."}, {"name": "Anatomical Relations", "text": "The sclera is continuous anteriorly with the cornea at the corneoscleral junction and is attached to the ciliary body. Additionally, it is covered anteriorly by the conjunctiva. 

Posteriorly, the sclera is pierced by the optic nerve medial and slightly inferior to the midline of the eyeball. The outer surface of the sclera is continuous with the dura mater that covers the optic nerve, while the inner surface forms a plate with many perforations, the lamina cribrosa sclerae. Fibers from the optic nerve pass through these small perforations, along with the central retinal artery and vein. 

The internal surface of the sclera is lined by the choroid, thus, separating the sclera from the retina."}, {"name": "Function", "text": "The fibrous layer of the eyeball provides the tensile strength for withstanding intraocular pressure and determines its overall shape. Its toughness helps protect the eye from damage from the external environment. Additionally, the sclera provides the attachment for extraocular (extrinsic) muscles of the eyeball."}, {"name": "Clinical Correlates", "text": "—Scleritis

—Jaundice"}, {"name": "References", "text": "Dorland, W. (2011) Dorland's Illustrated Medical Dictionary. 32nd edn. Philadelphia, USA: Elsevier Saunders.

Standring, S. (2016) Gray's Anatomy: The Anatomical Basis of Clinical Practice. Gray's Anatomy Series 41 edn.: Elsevier Limited."}]

items.name: Respiratory Mucosa
items.info:
[{"name": "Quick Facts", "text": "The mucosa is the mucous lining of various hollow structures, facing the lumen, comprising, in many locations, the epithelium, basement membrane, lamina propria mucosae, and lamina muscularis mucosae (Dorland, 2011)."}, {"name": "Structure/Morphology", "text": "The mucosa of the bronchioles is composed of epithelium with a variety of cellular populations. As segmental bronchi branch into terminal bronchioles, there is a gradual change in the epithelium from a pseudostratified ciliated epithelium with goblet cells to a simple cuboidal epithelium that may be ciliated. The number of ciliated and goblet cells decline in numbers and goblet cells end up being replaced by the Clara cells (Ovalle et al., 2013). 

As the mucosal layer of the terminal bronchioles extends into the respiratory bronchioles, the cellular composition remains similar, primarily consisting of ciliated cuboidal cells with a reduced number of Clara cells. The respiratory mucosal layer is thrown into folds due to the constriction of the overlying smooth muscle fibers."}, {"name": "Anatomical Relations", "text": "The mucosa of the intrapulmonary bronchial tree forms the inner layer on the bronchiole. From deep to superficial, it is composed of its outer epithelium resting on a basement membrane and a lamina propria. The mucosa is surrounded by a submucosa, containing smooth muscle that surrounds it in a spiraled fashion."}, {"name": "Function", "text": "The mucosa is vital in protecting the lungs from environmental insults and maintaining homeostasis.

The ciliated cells are responsible for beating synchronously, sending foreign particles and mucus back up to the bronchi. 

Clara cells are described as a bronchiolar-specific stem cell population paramount to protecting the airways from environmental hazards and are involved in maintaining lung homeostasis. 

Brush cells (tuft, caveolated, multivesicular or fibrillovesicular) have also been identified in the bronchioles. These brush cells present microvilli on their apical surfaces and are responsible for absorption, chemosensing, and repair after mucosal injury (Reid et al., 2005)."}, {"name": "References", "text": "Dorland, W. (2011) Dorland's Illustrated Medical Dictionary. 32nd edn. Philadelphia, USA: Elsevier Saunders.

Ovalle, W. K., Nahirney, P. C. and Netter, F. H. (2013) Netter's Essential Histology. ClinicalKey 2012: Elsevier Saunders.

Reid, L., Meyrick, B., Antony, V. B., Chang, L. Y., Crapo, J. D. and Reynolds, H. Y. (2005) 'The mysterious pulmonary brush cell: a cell in search of a function', Am J Respir Crit Care Med, 172(1), pp. 136-9."}]

items.name: Channel Proteins
items.info:
[{"name": "Quick Facts", "text": "A channel protein is a cell membrane protein containing a transmembrane pore through which ions and small molecules can diffuse; it is most commonly composed of several subunits surrounding the pore (Dorland, 2011)."}, {"name": "Structure and/or Key Feature(s)", "text": "Membrane proteins can be characterized by their function. Some act as pumps, channels, receptors, enzymes, or structural proteins (e.g., junctional complexes between adjacent epithelial cells). Other proteins link the intracellular cytoskeleton to the extracellular matrix (Ross and Pawlina, 2016).

Channel proteins are transmembrane proteins that extend several domains of the plasma membrane and create hydrophilic channels which are ion-selective (Lowe, Anderson and Anderson, 2018)."}, {"name": "Anatomical Relations", "text": "Channel proteins are transmembrane proteins that extend several domains of the plasma membrane (Lowe, Anderson and Anderson, 2018)."}, {"name": "Function", "text": "Protein channels are ion-selective and thei functions are regulated depending on the cell needs. In neurons, channel protein can be voltage-gated ion channels regulated by membrane potentials. They can be ligand-gated ion channels as in the case of neurotransmitters (e.g., acetylcholine receptors in muscle cells) or be regulated by mechanical events (e.g., mechanically gated channels in the inner ear) (Lowe, Anderson and Anderson, 2018)."}, {"name": "References", "text": "Dorland, W. (2011) Dorland's Illustrated Medical Dictionary. 32nd edn. Philadelphia, USA: Elsevier Saunders.

Lowe, J. S., Anderson, P. G. and Anderson, S. I. (2018) Stevens & Lowe's Human Histology- E-Book. 5 edn.: Elsevier Health Sciences.

Ross, M. H. and Pawlina, W. (2016) Histology: A Text and Atlas. Wolters Kluwer Health."}]

items.name: Mucus
items.info:
[{"name": "Quick Facts", "text": "Mucus is the free slime of the mucous membranes, composed of secretion of the glands, along with various inorganic salts, desquamated cells, and leukocytes (Dorland, 2011)."}, {"name": "Structure and/or Key Features", "text": "Mucus is a thin, transparent fluid produced by the epithelial lining of many body tissues. It is composed mainly of high molecular weight glycoproteins (Parke, 2013).

The nasal mucus is secreted by mucus and serous glands in the lamina propria and epithelial goblet cells. It can be grouped into two categories, neutral glycoprotein (fucomucin) and acidic glycoproteins (sialomucin and sulfomucin) (Liron et al., 1998)."}, {"name": "Anatomical Relations", "text": "There is a mucus layer situated at the base of the olfactory epithelium. The olfactory epithelium is made up of olfactory bipolar olfactory sensory neurons and supporting cells. The dendrites of the olfactory sensory neurons project through the olfactory epithelium to form olfactory cilia, which in turn extends into the layer of mucus secreted by the supporting cells (Longstaff, 2005)."}, {"name": "Function", "text": "Mucus layer overlying olfactory epithelium acts as a medium onto which odor molecules are absorbed. The odor molecules bind the odor-binding proteins in the mucus. Within this mucus medium, the odor-binding proteins concentrate the odor molecules which are subsequently able to reach the olfactory cilia (Longstaff, 2005). 

The mucus also serves as a filter for inhaled air; trapping irritants such as dust, smoke particles, bacteria, etc. Furthermore, the mucus serves as a shield for the epithelial layer, protecting the layer from damage caused by drying, extreme temperatures, infectious organisms, and non-infectious particles (Farbman et al., 1992)."}, {"name": "Clinical Correlates", "text": "—Cystic fibrosis 

—Acute respiratory distress syndrome 

—Asthma 

—Fucosidosis"}, {"name": "References", "text": "Dorland, W. (2011) Dorland's Illustrated Medical Dictionary. 32nd edn. Philadelphia, USA: Elsevier Saunders.

Farbman, A. I., Bard, J. B. L., Barlow, P. W. and Kirk, D. L. (1992) Cell Biology of Olfaction. Developmental and Cell Biology Series: Cambridge University Press.

Liron, N., Ostfeld, E., Priel, Z. and Roth, Y. (1998) Cilia, Mucus, and Mucociliary Interactions. Taylor & Francis.

Longstaff, A. (2005) Neuroscience. BIOS instant notes 2nd edition: Taylor & Francis.

Parke, D. (2013) Mucus in Health and Disease. Advances in Experimental Medicine and Biology: Springer US."}]

items.name: Nucleoplasm
items.info:
[{"name": "Quick Facts", "text": "The nucleoplasm is the contents of the cell nucleus other than the nucleolus and chromatin and consisting of interchromatin and perichromatin granules, ribonucleoproteins, and the nuclear matrix (Dorland, 2011)."}, {"name": "Structure and/or Key Feature(s)", "text": "The nucleoplasm occupies the nucleus (apart from the nucleolus and chromatin) and includes a very fine scaffolding network of protein filaments originating from the nuclear pores (Ross and Pawlina, 2006; Ovalle, Nahirney and Netter, 2013; McKinley, O'Loughlin and Pennefather-O'Brien, 2016)."}, {"name": "Function", "text": "Molecules pass through the nucleoplasm as a consequence of the activity of the chromatin and the nucleolus (Ovalle, Nahirney and Netter, 2013)."}, {"name": "References", "text": "Dorland, W. (2011) Dorland's Illustrated Medical Dictionary. 32nd edn. Philadelphia, USA: Elsevier Saunders.

McKinley, M. P., O'Loughlin, V. D. and Pennefather-O'Brien, E. E. (2016) Human Anatomy. 5th edn.: McGraw-Hill Education.

Ovalle, W. K., Nahirney, P. C. and Netter, F. H. (2013) Netter's Essential Histology. ClinicalKey 2012: Elsevier Saunders.

Ross, M. H. and Pawlina, W. (2006) Histology: A text and atlas. Lippincott Williams & Wilkins."}]

items.name: Synaptic Vesicle
items.info:
[{"name": "Quick Facts", "text": "Synptic vesicles are small membrane-bound structures behind a presynaptic membrane, containing neurotransmitters; when depolarization occurs, they fuse with the presynaptic membrane and release the neurotransmitter into the synaptic cleft (Dorland, 2011)."}, {"name": "Structure", "text": "A synaptic vesicle is a membrane-bound structure that contains neurotransmitter, and measures between 30 and 100 nm in diameter (Ross and Pawlina, 2006).

On the presynaptic aspect, synaptic vesicles are concentrated adjacent to the presynaptic density at the presynaptic membrane. This presynaptic density depicts the active zone of the synapses, where neurotransmission occurs (Standring, 2016)."}, {"name": "Anatomical Relations", "text": "Prior to exocytosis, synaptic vesicles are situated within the presynaptic region, adjacent the presynaptic membrane."}, {"name": "Function", "text": "Synaptic vesicles store and release neurotransmitters into the synaptic cleft in order to facilitate the transmission and propagation of nerve impulses (Ross and Pawlina, 2006)."}, {"name": "References", "text": "Dorland, W. (2011) Dorland's Illustrated Medical Dictionary. 32nd edn. Philadelphia, USA: Elsevier Saunders.

Ross, M. H. and Pawlina, W. (2006) Histology: A text and atlas. Lippincott Williams & Wilkins.

Standring, S. (2016) Gray's Anatomy: The Anatomical Basis of Clinical Practice. Gray's Anatomy Series 41 edn.: Elsevier Limited."}]

items.name: Endomysium
items.info:
[{"name": "Quick Facts", "text": "The endomysium is the sheath of delicate reticular fibrils that surrounds each muscle fiber (Dorland, 2011)."}, {"name": "Structure", "text": "The endomysium is the smallest component of the connective tissue which runs throughout the muscle. Unlike the epimysium and perimysium, the endomysium is made up of loose reticular fibers and some fibroblasts scattered throughout (Mescher, 2013)."}, {"name": "Key Features/Anatomical Relations", "text": "The endomysium surrounds individual muscle fibers and their external lamina forming their external environment. The endomysium is continuous with the larger connective tissue septa which constitute the perimysium. Small blood vessels and the smallest axonal terminal branches are present throughout the endomysium (Standring, 2016)."}, {"name": "Function", "text": "The endomysium plays an important role by transferring tension between the myofibrils it surrounds, contractile force produced in these fibers are transmitted to adjacent fibers. 

Due to the presence of the capillary network, it acts as the site of metabolic exchange between the blood and muscle."}, {"name": "References", "text": "Dorland, W. (2011) Dorland's Illustrated Medical Dictionary. 32nd edn. Philadelphia, USA: Elsevier Saunders.

Mescher, A. (2013) Junqueira's Basic Histology: Text and Atlas. 13th edn.: McGraw-Hill Education.

Standring, S. (2016) Gray's Anatomy: The Anatomical Basis of Clinical Practice. Gray's Anatomy Series: Elsevier Limited."}, {"name": "List of Clinical Correlates", "text": "—Myasthenia gravis

—Mysium damage

—Connective tissue disease"}]

items.name: Soma of Rod Cell
items.info: [{"name": "Quick Facts", "text": "The soma, or cell body, is the portion of a cell that contains the nucleus, independent of projections such as an axon or dendrites (Dorland, 2011)."}, {"name": "Structure and/or Key Features", "text": "The soma, or cell body, is the region within the photoreceptor cell that houses the nucleus. The soma of the rod cells is large in diameter, measuring 3\u20135 \u00b5m (Dartt et al., 2010)."}, {"name": "Anatomical Relations", "text": "The soma of the rod cells is located in the outer nuclear layer of the retina and tend to form several layers vitreal to the soma of the cone cells. It is positioned in between the inner segment and the axonal process of the photoreceptor cells."}, {"name": "Function", "text": "The soma houses the nucleus, which contains the cell\u2019s DNA. It is necessary for the development and maintenance of the cell\u2019s biochemical functions."}, {"name": "References", "text": "Dartt, D. A., Besharse, J., Dana, R., Battelle, B. A., Beebe, D., Bex, P., Bishop, P., Bok, D., D\u2019Amore, P. and Edelhauser, H. (2010) Encyclopedia of the Eye. Elsevier Science, p. 147-152.\n\nDorland, W. (2011) Dorland's Illustrated Medical Dictionary. 32nd edn. Philadelphia, USA: Elsevier Saunders."}]

items.name: Medial Branch of Supraorbital Nerve
items.info:
[{"name": "Quick Facts", "text": "Origin: Supraorbital nerve.

Course: Runs from its origin near the supraorbital foramen deep to the belly of the frontalis muscle. It pierces the muscle extending subcutaneously superiorly and medially on the forehead.

Branches: None.

Supply: Conveys general sensation from the forehead, frontal sinus, skin of the upper eyelid, and conjunctiva."}, {"name": "Origin", "text": "The medial branch of the supraorbital nerve is a branch of the supraorbital nerve that originates just before or after the nerve emerges from the supraorbital foramen."}, {"name": "Course", "text": "Initially the medial branch of the supraorbital nerve ascends the forehead deep to the frontalis muscle, but it soon pierces this muscle to become cutaneous. It continues superiorly and medially in forehead towards the scalp."}, {"name": "Branches", "text": "There are no named branches."}, {"name": "Supplied Structures", "text": "The medial branch of the supraorbital nerve is a sensory nerve that conveys general sensation from the skin of the forehead, upper eyelid, including the conjunctiva, and the mucosa of the frontal sinus."}]

items.name: Middle Piece
items.info: [{"name": "Quick Facts", "text": "The middle piece is the anterior portion of the tail of the spermatozoon, bounded by the neck anteriorly and the principal piece posteriorly (Dorland, 2011)."}, {"name": "Structure and/or Key Feature(s)", "text": "The sperm tail can be divided into three main segments: the middle piece, the principal piece, and the end piece. The middle piece of the sperm tail is considered the powerhouse of the sperm, measuring approximately 7 \u03bcm. It contains the proximal part of the axoneme, surrounded by the dense outer fibers, surrounded again by a mitochondrial sheath."}, {"name": "Anatomical Relations", "text": "The middle piece is the most proximal segment of the sperm tail and is situated between the sperm\u2019s neck and the principal piece."}, {"name": "Function", "text": "The function of the middle piece is to stabilize the proximal aspect of the sperm tail. This aids in the effective coordination of the motility of the tail. It also serves as a connection between the sperm head and the tail."}, {"name": "References", "text": "Dorland, W. (2011) Dorland's Illustrated Medical Dictionary. 32nd edn. Philadelphia, USA: Elsevier Saunders."}]

items.name: Myoid Cell
items.info: [{"name": "Quick Facts", "text": "Myoid cells are the cells found in the seminiferous tubules of common laboratory rodents, which cytologically resemble smooth muscle and are presumed to be contractile and to be responsible for the rhythmic shallow contractions of the seminiferous tubules of these species (Dorland, 2011)."}, {"name": "Structure/Morphology", "text": "The myoid layer of the convoluted seminiferous tubules consists of three to five layers of thin contractile cells, called myoid cells, and collagen fibrils."}, {"name": "Anatomical Relations", "text": "The myoid layer is located between the basal compartment and the interstitial connective tissue of the testis."}, {"name": "Function", "text": "Myoid cells are contractile. Leydig cells in the adjacent interstitial tissue produce and secrete oxytocin which stimulates contraction of the myoid cells, thus moving the spermatozoa along the seminiferous tubules towards the rete testis and excurrent ductal system."}, {"name": "References", "text": "Dorland, W. (2011) Dorland's Illustrated Medical Dictionary. 32nd edn. Philadelphia, USA: Elsevier Saunders."}]

items.name: Synaptic Cleft
items.info:
[{"name": "Quick Facts", "text": "The synaptic cleft is a narrow extracellular cleft between the presynaptic and postsynaptic membranes (Dorland, 2011)."}, {"name": "Structure", "text": "The synaptic cleft is a space of between 20 and 50 nm separating the presynaptic neuron from the postsynaptic neuron, or target cell. This cleft is filled with a matrix of fibrous extracellular protein that acts as a “glue” to hold the pre- and postsynaptic membranes closely together. Neurotransmitter molecules must diffuse over this space.

Following docking, priming, and fusion of the synaptic vesicle membrane with the presynaptic membrane, neurotransmitters are released into the synaptic cleft via a process called exocytosis. These neurotransmitters in the synaptic cleft travel across to the postsynaptic membrane via diffusion and interact with the postsynaptic receptors (Ross and Pawlina, 2006)."}, {"name": "Anatomical Relations", "text": "The synaptic cleft is a space located between the presynaptic and postsynaptic neurons."}, {"name": "Function", "text": "The synaptic cleft plays a vital role in neurotransmission. It is a space traveled by neurotransmitters (released by synaptic vesicles from a presynaptic membrane) to reach the postsynaptic membrane (Ross and Pawlina, 2006)."}, {"name": "Clinical Correlates", "text": "—Drugs are being developed now to modify synaptic transmission by interfering with the processes of transmission within the synaptic cleft (Splittgerber, 2018)."}, {"name": "References", "text": "Dorland, W. (2011) Dorland's Illustrated Medical Dictionary. 32nd edn. Philadelphia, USA: Elsevier Saunders.

Ross, M. H. and Pawlina, W. (2006) Histology: A text and atlas. Lippincott Williams & Wilkins.

Splittgerber, R. (2018) Snell's Clinical Neuroanatomy. Wolters Kluwer Health."}]

items.name: Nuclear Vacuole
items.info:
[{"name": "Quick Facts", "text": "A vacuole is any membrane-bound space or cavity within a cell (Dorland, 2011)."}, {"name": "Structure and/or Key Feature(s)", "text": "The nuclear vacuoles are thought to develop as a consequence of incomplete chromatin condensation during the process of spermatogenesis. They have been observed in 90% of structurally and functionally normal sperm, and differ in number, size, and location. Some can be so large that they contort the shape of the sperm head (Guraya, 2012). 

The nuclear vacuoles can exist in both singular and multiple forms and contain materials such as granular cytoplasmic substances and remnants of nuclear and plasma membranes.

The number and size of nuclear vacuoles are indicative of the maturity or immaturity of the nucleus of the sperm. Large vacuoles are mostly observed in mature sperm (Toshimori, 2009)."}, {"name": "Anatomical Relations", "text": "Nuclear vacuoles are situated within the nucleus of the sperm."}, {"name": "Function", "text": "The function of nuclear vacuoles is not well known. It is still unclear whether or not they have an effect on fertilization. However, since nuclear vacuoles are associated with incomplete chromatin condensation, they may be associated with abnormal sperm morphology (Komiya et al, 2014)."}, {"name": "References", "text": "Dorland, W. (2011) Dorland's Illustrated Medical Dictionary. 32nd edn. Philadelphia, USA: Elsevier Saunders.

Guraya, S. S. (2012) Biology of Spermatogenesis and Spermatozoa in Mammals. Springer Berlin Heidelberg.

Komiya, A., Kawauchi, Y., Kato, T., Watanabe, A., Tanii, I. & Fuse, H. (2014) Sperm nuclear vacuoles in relation to acrosome reactions and sperm motility. ScientificWorldJournal, 2014, 178970.

Toshimori, K. (2009) Dynamics of the Mammalian Sperm Head: Modifications and Maturation Events From Spermatogenesis to Egg Activation. Springer."}]

items.name: Crypts of Small Intestine (Duodenum)
items.info:
[{"name": "Quick Facts", "text": "The crypts of small intestines are the straight tubular invaginations of the surface epithelium of the small intestine (Dorland, 2011)."}, {"name": "Structure/Morphology", "text": "Intestinal glands or crypts of Lieberkühn are simple tubular invaginations of the epithelium deep into the lamina propria that extend as far down as the muscularis mucosae. They open at the bases of villi and are composed of simple columnar epithelium that is continuous with the epithelial surface of the villi. 

Cells of the intestinal epithelium (enterocytes) are found within the crypts as well as on the surface of the villi. Goblet cells are scattered throughout the epithelial surface of the villi and within the intestinal glands. Paneth cells are located at the very base of the crypts and appear with reddish granules within their cytoplasm in routine H&E stained sections. Enteroendocrine cells tend to concentrate more in the crypts, while a population of stem cells is also located here."}, {"name": "Function", "text": "The enterocytes’ primary function is absorption. Goblet cells are unicellular mucin secreting glands. Paneth cells secrete antimicrobial substances. Enteroendocrine cells produce various paracrine and endocrine hormones.

The population of stem cells found in the intestinal crypts are responsible for the constant renewal of the mucosal epithelium. The stem cells are capable or differentiating into enterocytes or the secretory cells mentioned above."}, {"name": "References", "text": "Dorland, W. (2011) Dorland's Illustrated Medical Dictionary. 32nd edn. Philadelphia, USA: Elsevier Saunders."}]

items.name: Muscular Layer
items.info:
[{"name": "Quick Facts", "text": "The muscular layer is the layer of smooth muscle lying between the mucosa and the serosa or the adventitia in many portions of the digestive, respiratory, urinary, and genital tracts (Dorland, 2011)."}, {"name": "Structure/Morphology", "text": "The muscular layer of the colon is composed of smooth muscle organized into outer longitudinal and inner circular layers. These layers run perpendicular to each other. The inner circular layer extends the width of the colon and the outer longitudinal fibers are continuous along the length of the colon. The longitudinal layer is thicker near the three teniae coli, due to the dense aggregations of the muscle fibers, and is much thinner between the teniae coli (up to half the thickness) (Fraser et al., 1981).

Innervation to the muscular layer occurs via the myenteric plexus (Auerbach’s plexus), which is located between the two inner and outer smooth muscle layers."}, {"name": "Anatomical Relations", "text": "The muscular layer is found between the submucosa and is the enveloping serosa. The myenteric nerve plexus is located between the inner circular and the outer longitudinal layers."}, {"name": "Function", "text": "The muscular layer allows for the rolling and passage of ingested components via wavelike peristaltic contractions. The rate of peristalsis is modulated by the autonomic nervous system."}, {"name": "References", "text": "Dorland, W. (2011) Dorland's Illustrated Medical Dictionary. 32nd edn. Philadelphia, USA: Elsevier Saunders.

Fraser, I. D., Condon, R. E., Schulte, W. J., DeCosse, J. J. and Cowles, V. E. (1981) 'Longitudinal muscle of muscularis externa in human and nonhuman primate colon', Arch Surg, 116(1), pp. 61-3."}]

items.name: T Tubule
items.info:
[{"name": "Quick Facts", "text": "T tubules are the transverse intracellular tubules invaginating from the cell membrane and surrounding the myofibrils of the T system of skeletal and cardiac muscle, serving as a pathway for the spread of electrical excitation within a muscle cell, enabling the nearly simultaneous activation of all myofibrils; in skeletal muscle, a T tubule is the intermediate element of a triad of tubular structures, the other elements being a pair of terminal cisterns (Dorland, 2011)."}, {"name": "Structure", "text": "Transverse (T) tubules are extensions of the sarcolemma, made up of interconnecting rings, each of which surround individual myofibrils. Similar to the sarcolemma, the tubules are composed of two lipid bilayers."}, {"name": "Key Features/Anatomical Relations", "text": "Transverse tubules run from the sarcolemma transversely across the fiber at the junction of the A- and I-bands. The sarcolemma is the cell membrane that encloses the muscle fiber (Pocock, Richards and Richards, 2013)."}, {"name": "Function", "text": "The primary function of transverse tubules is to facilitate the conduction of signals from outside the fiber to the myofibrils. Transverse tubules are the site for excitation-contraction coupling. When an electric signal excites the sarcolemma, the signal travels down along the T tubules to the sarcoplasmic reticulum, which releases Ca2+ for contraction (Standring, 2016)."}, {"name": "References", "text": "Dorland, W. (2011) Dorland's Illustrated Medical Dictionary. 32nd edn. Philadelphia, USA: Elsevier Saunders.

Pocock, G., Richards, C. D. and Richards, D. A. (2013) Human Physiology. Oxford Core Texts 4 edn.: OUP Oxford.

Standring, S. (2016) Gray's Anatomy: The Anatomical Basis of Clinical Practice. Gray's Anatomy Series: Elsevier Limited."}]

items.name: Corpus Albicans
items.info:
[{"name": "Quick Facts", "text": "The corpus albicans is the white fibrous tissue that replaces the regressing corpus luteum in the human ovary in the latter half of pregnancy, or soon after ovulation when pregnancy does not supervene (Dorland, 2011)."}, {"name": "Structure and/or Key Feature(s)", "text": "After menstruation or at the end of a pregnancy, the corpus luteum degenerates. Lipid droplets accumulate in the cells and the cells undergo autolysis. A whitish scar, the corpus albicans, is the remnant of the original functional corpus luteum.

Each corpus albicans appears as irregular puffy, light pink, bodies composed of masses of delicate collagen fibers amongst which will be the nuclei of fibrocytes. They will disappear after several months (Mescher, 2013; Ross and Pawlina, 2006)."}, {"name": "Anatomical Relations", "text": "The corpus albicans is deep in the ovarian cortex."}, {"name": "References", "text": "Dorland, W. (2011) Dorland's Illustrated Medical Dictionary. 32nd edn. Philadelphia, USA: Elsevier Saunders.

Mescher, A. (2013) Junqueira's Basic Histology: Text and Atlas. 13th edn.: McGraw-Hill Education.

Ross, M. H. and Pawlina, W. (2006) Histology: A text and atlas. Lippincott Williams & Wilkins."}]

items.name: Cell Body (of Olfactory Sensory Neuron)
items.info:
[{"name": "Quick Facts", "text": "The cell body is the portion of a cell that contains the nucleus, independent of projections such as an axon or dendrites (Dorland, 2011)."}, {"name": "Structure and/or Key Features", "text": "The cell body is a component of olfactory sensory neuron. The diameter of each olfactory cell body spans about 5–8 μm. Situated within the cell body is a large nucleus along with one or two nucleoli. The larger aspect of the cytoplasm is concentrated towards the apex of the cell body. This part of the cytoplasm contains the Golgi apparatus, a few mitochondria, endoplasmic reticulum, as well as microtubules and intermediate filaments (Fujita, Kanno and Kobayashi, 2012). 

The cell body narrows superiorly, towards the basal aspect of the olfactory epithelium, to become the axon."}, {"name": "Anatomical Relations", "text": "Olfactory sensory neurons are bipolar neurons that are situated within the olfactory epithelium. Each neuron has two ends. One end has a 2 μm in diameter solitary unbranched dendrite, which extends inferiorly towards the epithelial surface. The other end has a 0.2 μm in diameter unmyelinated axon, which extends superiorly, and traverses the basement membrane on its way to the lamina propria (Standring, 2016). Their cell body lies interposed between the axon and the dendrite in the middle segment of the olfactory epithelium."}, {"name": "Function", "text": "The cell body is a principal part of the olfactory sensory neuron. It essentially receives sensory neural information from the epithelial surface via the dendrites and conveys the information to the olfactory bulb via the axons during the process of olfactory transduction. This facilitates the sense of smell."}, {"name": "Clinical Correlates", "text": "—Anosmia"}, {"name": "References", "text": "Dorland, W. (2011) Dorland's Illustrated Medical Dictionary. 32nd edn. Philadelphia, USA: Elsevier Saunders.

Fujita, T., Kanno, T. and Kobayashi, S. (2012) The Paraneuron. Springer Japan."}]

items.name: Outer Segment of Cone Cell
items.info:
[{"name": "Quick Facts", "text": "The outer segment of a photoreceptor cell is the part of a retinal rod or cone that is between the inner segment and the pigmented epithelium. This part of the photoreceptor contains numerous visual opsin-bearing membranous discs (Dorland, 2011)."}, {"name": "Structure and/or Key Features", "text": "The outer segments of cone cells have a conical appearance and are typically smaller than their rod counterparts. Membranous discs are also present in the outer segments of cones; however, they are less numerous and remain attached to the plasma membrane as infoldings at the base of the cell (Standring, 2016). There are additional reports that most, if not all, of the membranous discs in cone outer segments are continuous and remain attached to the plasma membrane, however, many of the connections appear to be very small. Therefore, it is assumed that intradiscal spaces are open to the interphotoreceptor space (Heckenlively, Arden and Bach, 2006).

A feature known as cone notches has also been described. These notches distinguish a site of transition between discs that are open to the interphotoreceptor space and those that are isolated (Heckenlively, Arden and Bach, 2006). 

The visual pigments accumulate in the membranous discs in the outer segment of the photoreceptor cells. There are three cone cell populations that contain three spectrally distinct visual pigments:

- blue, or short-wave cones;

- green, or middle-wave cones;

- red, or long-wave cones."}, {"name": "Anatomical Relations", "text": "Cone outer segments are located in a layer composed almost entirely of rod and cone outer and inner segments. The outer segment of cone cells make contact with the apical processes of the pigmented layer that interdigitate with these outer segments (Standring, 2016)."}, {"name": "Function", "text": "While the spectrally distinct visual pigments of the cones are produced in the inner segment, they are transported to the outer segments. Here they are incorporated within the membrane of the outer segment. Following the absorption of light, a conformational change occurs in the opsin and retinal molecules resulting in the induction of a biochemical cascade which culminates in the production of an electrical signal representing visual information."}, {"name": "List of Clinical Correlates", "text": "- Best disease 

- Retinal disease"}, {"name": "References", "text": "Dorland, W. (2011) Dorland's Illustrated Medical Dictionary. 32nd edn. Philadelphia, USA: Elsevier Saunders.

Heckenlively, J. R., Arden, G. B. and Bach, M. (2006) Principles and Practice of Clinical Electrophysiology of Vision. MIT Press.

Standring, S. (2016) Gray's Anatomy: The Anatomical Basis of Clinical Practice. Gray's Anatomy Series 41 edn.: Elsevier Limited."}]

items.name: Proteasome
items.info:
[{"name": "Quick Facts", "text": "A proteasome is a large, cylindrical protease complex occurring in both the nucleoplasm and cytoplasm, consisting of a 20S core that in eukaryotes and Archaea is capped by a regulatory complex at one or both ends; it degrades intracellular proteins that have been marked by the attachment of ubiquitin (Dorland, 2011)."}, {"name": "Structure and/or Key Feature(s)", "text": "Sometimes proteins may form that are abnormal or are short-lived proteins that become inactivated (e.g., regulatory proteins). Cells are able to break down these proteins without using lysosomal pathways in large protein complexes called proteasomes (Ross and Pawlina, 2006; Ovalle, Nahirney and Netter, 2013; McKinley, O'Loughlin and Pennefather-O'Brien, 2016)."}, {"name": "Anatomical Relations", "text": "Proteasomes are located throughout the cell cytoplasm."}, {"name": "Function", "text": "The protein complexes (proteasomes) degrade unwanted proteins into amino acids and small polypeptides (Ross and Pawlina, 2006; Ovalle, Nahirney and Netter, 2013; McKinley, O'Loughlin and Pennefather-O'Brien, 2016)."}, {"name": "Clinical Correlates", "text": "One of the consequences of Parkinson’s disease is that the digestion of proteins by proteasomes fails and so the abnormal proteins can affect the death of nerve cells (McKinley, O'Loughlin and Pennefather-O'Brien, 2016)."}, {"name": "References", "text": "Dorland, W. (2011) Dorland's Illustrated Medical Dictionary. 32nd edn. Philadelphia, USA: Elsevier Saunders.

McKinley, M. P., O'Loughlin, V. D. and Pennefather-O'Brien, E. E. (2016) Human Anatomy. 5th edn.: McGraw-Hill Education.

Ovalle, W. K., Nahirney, P. C. and Netter, F. H. (2013) Netter's Essential Histology. ClinicalKey 2012: Elsevier Saunders.

Ross, M. H. and Pawlina, W. (2006) Histology: A text and atlas. Lippincott Williams & Wilkins."}]

items.name: Right Atrium
items.info:
[{"name": "Morphology/ Structure:", "text": "The right atrium sits anterior, inferior, and to the right of the left atrium. It forms a portion of the upper anterior (sternocostal) surface and a portion of the right pulmonary surface of the heart.

The right atrium has thin muscular walls as it functions under low pressure. The posterior wall is smooth while the anterior wall of the right atrium is ridged due to the presence of pectinate muscles. These are roughly parallel bars of muscle that run in an anterolateral direction from the crista terminalis.

The right auricle sits over the base of the ascending aorta and contains pectinate muscle, and therefore, has a ridged internal appearance.

The right atrium receives deoxygenated blood via the superior vena cava, inferior vena cava, and the coronary sinus. The superior vena cava has no valve; however, the inferior vena cava is covered by the Eustachian valve, which runs into the Eustachian ridge. The coronary sinus is covered by the Thebesian valve. The outflow tract consists of the smooth-walled vestibule and marks the location of the right atrioventricular valve (or tricuspid valve)."}, {"name": "Key Features/ Anatomical Relations:", "text": "The smooth and rough portions of the right atrial wall are separated by a groove called the sulcus terminalis externally and by the crista terminalis internally. The sulcus terminalis sits between the openings of the two venae cavae. Its superior edge is the external mark for the site of the sinuatrial node. The crista terminalis is a ridge of muscle lying perpendicular to the rest of the pectinate muscles. Within the upper portion of the crista terminalis, at the opening of the superior vena cava, is the approximate location of the sinuatrial node.  

Between the opening of the coronary sinus and the fossa ovalis is the tendon the inferior pyramidal space (of Todaro), which inserts into the central fibrous body and forms the superior border of the triangle of the atrioventricular node (Koch’s triangle). The septal leaflet of the right atrioventricular valve and the anteromedial aspect of the opening of the coronary sinus form the two other borders of Koch’s triangle. This is an important surgical landmark as its apex denotes the location of the atrioventricular node.

The atria are separated by the interatrial septum. The fossa ovalis is a shallow depression of the interatrial septum, above the inferior vena cava and is a remnant of fetal development.

Externally, the interatrial sulcus (groove of Waterson) divides the two atria. The coronary sulcus (atrioventricular sulcus) divides the atria above from the ventricles below and contains the main trunks of the coronary vessels. It also contains the coronary sinus which marks the confluence of the cardiac veins.
"}, {"name": "Function", "text": "The right atrium receives deoxygenated (venous) blood upon return to the heart. During right atrial relaxation, known as atrial diastole, deoxygenated blood from the upper body, lower body, and coronary circulation fill the right atrium via the superior vena cava, inferior vena cava, and coronary sinus, respectively. When the right atrium contracts, known as atrial systole, it squeezes blood through the right atrioventricular valve and into the right ventricle."}, {"name": "List of Clinical Correlates", "text": "- Atrial septal defects

- Fibrillation"}]

items.name: Ovarian Artery
items.info:
[{"name": "Quick Facts", "text": "Origin: Abdominal aorta.

Course: Descends into the pelvic cavity. 

Branches: Ovarian and tubal branch.

Supplied Structures: Ovary, uterine tube, uterus, and ureter."}, {"name": "Origin", "text": "The ovarian arteries originate as paired branches from the abdominal aorta at the level of L2 vertebra, just inferior to the emerging renal arteries.

During fetal life, the ovarian arteries are short due to the position of the ovaries within the abdomen. Postnatally, the ovaries descend into the pelvic cavity and, therefore, the vessels are identifiable by their long, slender appearance in adults."}, {"name": "Course", "text": "The ovarian artery is retroperitoneal and descends within the abdominal cavity. At its origin, it lies medial to the ureters. It continues in an inferolateral direction and passes anterior to the ureters. The ovarian artery then extends over the external iliac vessels and crosses the pelvic brim.

The artery continues within the pelvic cavity and descends medially within the suspensory ligament of the ovary. As it approaches the lateral aspect of the ovary, it divides into tubal and ovarian branches."}, {"name": "Branches", "text": "Upon its descent, the artery lies in close proximity with the ureter and gives small ureteric branches to the ureter.

The ovarian branch travels in the mesovarium to supply the ovary and the tubal branch travels in the mesosalpinx to supply the distal portion of the uterine tube. Both branches anastomose with the corresponding tubal and ovarian branches of the ascending uterine artery."}, {"name": "Supplied Structures", "text": "Upon its descent, the ovarian artery supplies a portion of the ipsilateral ureter. The ovarian branch supplies the ovary and anastomoses with the ovarian branch of the ascending uterine artery. The tubal branch supplies the distal portion of the uterine tube and anastomoses with the tubal branch of the ascending uterine artery."}]

items.name: Falx Cerebri
items.info: [{"name": "Quick Facts", "text": "The falx cerebri is the sickle-shaped fold of dura mater that extends downward in the longitudinal cerebral fissure and separates the two cerebral hemispheres (Dorland, 2011)."}, {"name": "Structure", "text": "The falx cerebri is a large fold of the meningeal cranial dura mater that projects down into the longitudinal fissure, separating the left and right cerebral hemispheres."}, {"name": "Key Features/Anatomical Relations", "text": "The falx cerebri is the largest fold of meningeal dura mater in the cranium. It runs from the crista galli of the ethmoid bone anteriorly, back to the straight sinus and tentorium cerebelli posteriorly. Its superior margin forms the superior sagittal sinus while its inferior margin lie just above the corpus callosum and contains the inferior sagittal sinus."}, {"name": "References", "text": "Dorland, W. (2011) Dorland's Illustrated Medical Dictionary. 32nd edn. Philadelphia, USA: Elsevier Saunders."}]

items.name: Sweat Glands
items.info:
[{"name": "Quick Facts", "text": "A sweat gland is one of the glands that secrete sweat, located in the dermis or subcutaneous tissue, and opening by a duct on the surface of the body. There are two types: the ordinary or eccrine sweat glands and the apocrine sweat glands (Dorland, 2011)."}, {"name": "Structure/Morphology", "text": "The skin hosts many types of glands, such as sweat and sebaceous glands. Sweat glands are tubular structures in which sweat is secreted and transported out of the skin through the epidermis or via the hair follicle. Two types of sweat glands exist, namely the eccrine and apocrine sweat glands, and differ from each other in their size, histology, distribution, and function.

The apocrine sweat gland develops from the hair follicle, just above the opening of the sebaceous gland. The glands secretory portion is highly coiled, tubular and widely dilated. From here, short ducts connect the secretory portion to the hair follicle where it can secrete its contents. Apocrine sweat is composed of water, electrolytes, lipids, and steroids and appears as a cloudy, viscous secretion. Apocrine glands are not found in all skin, and occur in regions such as the axilla, or arm pit, the mons pubis, the areola of the nipple, and the perianal region (Freinkel and Woodley, 2001; Lu and Fuchs, 2014). 

The secretory portion of the eccrine sweat glands are highly coiled, tubular glands found in the reticular layer of the dermis and upper part of the hypodermis. Unlike the apocrine glands, eccrine glands open directly on the surface of the skin. A secretory duct connects the highly coiled secretory portion of the gland to the epidermis and secretes the sweat contents through a sweat pore on the surface of the epidermis. It secretes sweat that is composed of water, electrolytes, proteins, and inorganic substances. Eccrine sweat glands are found on skin throughout the body, except for the lips and genitalia (Freinkel and Woodley, 2001; Lu and Fuchs, 2014)."}, {"name": "Function", "text": "Sweating is an important function that regulates body temperature. The viscous watery sweat is secreted to the surface of the epidermis. As it evaporates, it dissipates thermal energy, or heat, from the skin, hence, why humans sweat more after exercise or in hot temperatures."}, {"name": "References", "text": "Dorland, W. (2011) Dorland's Illustrated Medical Dictionary. 32nd edn. Philadelphia, USA: Elsevier Saunders.

Freinkel, R. K. and Woodley, D. T. (2001) The Biology of the Skin. Taylor & Francis.

Lu, C. and Fuchs, E. (2014) 'Sweat gland progenitors in development, homeostasis, and wound repair', Cold Spring Harb Perspect Med, 4(2)."}]

items.name: Tunica Intima of Efferent Glomerular Arteriole
items.audio: Tunica Intima of Efferent Glomerular Arteriole.mp3
alt: Tunica Interna of Efferent Glomerular Arteriole
items.info: [{"name": "Quick Facts", "text": "The tunica intima is the inner coat of a blood or lymph vessel, made up of endothelial cells surrounded by longitudinal elastic fibers and connective tissue (Dorland, 2011)."}, {"name": "Structure and/or Key Feature(s)", "text": "The tunica intima is the innermost layer of the afferent and efferent arteriole of the glomerulus. It consists of a simple squamous epithelium (of endothelial cells or endothelium), the basal lamina of the endothelial cell, and an extremely thin subendothelial connective tissue layer."}, {"name": "Anatomical Relations", "text": "An arteriole has three layers (or tunics). The tunica adventitia of an arteriole is the outermost layer of a blood vessel that merges with surrounding loose connective tissue. The tunica media is adjacent to the outer adventitia layer as the middle layer of a blood vessel. The layer adjacent to the blood vessel lumen (or inner layer) is the tunica intima."}, {"name": "Function", "text": "The tunica intima is the epithelial layer adjacent to the lumen (or inner layer) of the arteriole."}, {"name": "References", "text": "Dorland, W. (2011) Dorland's Illustrated Medical Dictionary. 32nd edn. Philadelphia, USA: Elsevier Saunders."}]

items.name: Mesenteric Plexuses
items.info:
[{"name": "Quick Facts", "text": "The transverse colon receives a vast innervation from the superior mesenteric plexus (proximal two thirds of transverse colon) and the inferior mesenteric plexus (distal one third of transverse colon)."}, {"name": "Description", "text": "Developmentally, the proximal two thirds of the transverse colon are components of the midgut, while the remaining distal third is hindgut. This developmental distinction is important in understanding the patterns of vascularization, innervation, and lymphatic drainage of the large intestine. 

The transverse colon receives a vast innervation from the superior mesenteric plexus (proximal two thirds) and the inferior mesenteric plexus (distal one third). It includes:

—autonomic nervous system (sympathetic and parasympathetic), which controls blood flow and motility of the gut;

—extrinsic sensory innervation (visceral afferents), which conveys sensation of colonic distension.

Sympathetic innervation is derived from the sympathetic chain and the aortic plexus. The proximal two thirds of the transverse colon is supplied by postganglionic neurons from the superior mesenteric plexus. The distal third of the transverse colon is supplied by the inferior mesenteric plexus. The vagus nerve (CN X) provides parasympathetic innervation to the proximal two thirds of the transverse colon, while the distal third receives parasympathetic innervation from pelvic splanchnic nerves (S2-S4). 

Visceral afferent nerves from the midgut ascend in tandem with the vagus nerve. In the hindgut, the cell bodies of the visceral afferents reside in the dorsal root ganglia of L2-L3 or S1-S2 (Standring, 2016)."}, {"name": "References", "text": "Standring, S. (2016) Gray's Anatomy: The Anatomical Basis of Clinical Practice. Gray's Anatomy Series 41st edition edn.: Elsevier Limited."}]

items.name: Vasa Nervorum
items.info:
[{"name": "Quick Facts", "text": "The vasa nervorum are the blood vessels supplying the nerves. A single vessel is a vas nervi (Dorland, 2011)."}, {"name": "Structure/Morphology", "text": "The Vasa nervorum are small arteries that supply blood to peripheral nerves. This blood supplies nourishment to the nerve. This network of vessels supplies blood to the interior parts of the nerves and their coverings. The vasa nervorum are located within the connective tissue of the nerve scattered between the fascicles (Boissaud-Cooke et al., 2015)."}, {"name": "Anatomical Relations", "text": "They are the smallest vessels in the epineurial, perineurial, and endoneurial layers."}, {"name": "Function", "text": "The vasa nervorum supply the peripheral nerves with the molecular nutrients needed to carry out their cellular functions and for survival (Carp, 2015)."}, {"name": "References", "text": "Boissaud-Cooke, M., Pidgeon, T. E. and Tunstall, R. (2015) 'The Microcirculation of Peripheral Nerves: The Vasa Nervorum A2’, in Nerves and Nerve Injuries. San Diego: Academic Press, pp. 507-523.

Carp, S. (2015) Peripheral Nerve Injury An Anatomical and Physiological Approach for Physical Therapy Intervention. EBL-Schweitzer: F. A. Davis Company.

Dorland, W. (2011) Dorland's Illustrated Medical Dictionary. 32nd edn. Philadelphia, USA: Elsevier Saunders."}]

items.name: Scala Vestibuli
items.info:
