[{"name": "Quick Facts", "text": "The scala vestibuli is the perilymph-filled part of the cochlea that begins in the vestibule, is separated from other cochlear structures by the spiral lamina and vestibular membrane of the cochlear duct, and becomes continuous with the scala tympani at the helicotrema (Dorland, 2011)."}, {"name": "Structure and/or Key Feature(s)", "text": "The scala vestibuli is one of the main cochlear canals. It is formed by the division of the bony cochlear canal by the osseous spiral lamina (a fine ridge-like projection of bone from the modiolus).

The scala vestibuli runs from the vestibule all the way to the helicotrema, where it communicates with the scala tympani. It is separated from the cochlear duct by a thin vestibular membrane, also known as Reissner’s membrane.

The scala vestibuli is filled with perilymph, which is an extracellular fluid that is of similar consistency to cerebrospinal fluid. The perilymph suspends the membranous labyrinth and serves as a medium to transmit vibrations from the tympanic membrane (via the ossicles) to the endolymph in the cochlear duct, thus stimulating the spiral organ (of Corti). It also receives effluxing potassium released by the depolarization of the stereocilia."}, {"name": "Anatomical Relations", "text": "The boundaries of the scala vestibuli are the bony wall of the cochlea, the osseous spiral lamina, and the vestibular membrane. The scala vestibuli is superjacent to the cochlear duct."}, {"name": "Function", "text": "The scala vestibuli contains perilymph. It serves as a medium to transmit the sound-induced vibration of the tympanic membrane to the endolymph within the cochlear duct. This ultimately results in the displacement of the stereocilia bundles (of the hair cells on the basilar membrane) from the tectorial membrane, which activates mechanoelectrical ion channels. These facilitate neurotransmission along cochlear afferent nerve fibers."}, {"name": "References", "text": "Dorland, W. (2011) Dorland's Illustrated Medical Dictionary. 32nd edn. Philadelphia, USA: Elsevier Saunders."}]

items.name: Fibrous Layer of Articular Capsule of Glenohumeral Joint
items.audio: Fibrous Layer of Articular Capsule of Glenohumeral Joint.mp3
alt: Fibrous Membrane of Articular Capsule of Glenohumeral Joint
items.info: [{"name": "Anatomical Relations", "text": "The fibrous layer of the glenohumeral joint forms the external layer of the articular capsule of the glenohumeral joint. The synovial membrane forms the internal layer of the capsule. The fibrous layer attaches medially to the neck of the glenoid process, at variable distances from the glenoid labrum. Laterally, the fibrous layer attaches to the anatomical neck of the humerus. The lateral fibers of the fibrous layer intermingle with that of the tendons of the rotator cuff muscles (i.e., supraspinatus superiorly, infraspinatus and teres minor posteriorly, and subscapularis anteriorly) and the tendon of the long head of triceps brachii inferiorly, where it attaches to the infraglenoid tubercle."}, {"name": "Structure", "text": "The fibrous layer of the glenohumeral joint is composed of dense fibrous tissue. The fibers are orientated in a spiral fashion so that when the arm is elevated, the fibers tighten the joint (i.e., brings the bones into tighter apposition)."}, {"name": "Function", "text": "The articular capsule of the glenohumeral joint ensures that the joint is sealed, thus, keeping the lubricating synovial fluid within the joint. It provides passive stability to the joint by limiting the joint movement. Additionally, it provides active stability but containing numerous proprioceptive nerve endings which relay mechanical information back to the central nervous system (Ralphs and Benjamin, 1994)."}, {"name": "References", "text": "Ralphs, J. R. and Benjamin, M. (1994) 'The joint capsule: structure, composition, ageing and disease', Journal of Anatomy, 184(Pt 3), pp. 503-509."}]

items.name: Tertiary Fiber Bundles
items.info: [{"name": "Quick Facts", "text": "The tertiary fiber bundle included several secondary bundles surrounded by endotendon."}, {"name": "Structure and/or Key Feature(s)", "text": "The tertiary fiber bundle is an aggregation of several secondary fiber bundles surrounded by endotendon. Tertiary fiber bundles are bound together to form the whole unit of a tendon. It has a complex structure because the fibrils within each collagen fiber are oriented longitudinally, as well as horizontally and transversely. In addition to this, the longitudinal fibers which are oriented parallel to each other, cross each other as they run along the length of a tendon (Kannus, 2000). The diameter of tertiary fiber bundles is estimated to be between 1 and 3 mm (Franchi et al., 2007)."}, {"name": "Anatomical Relations", "text": "Tertiary fiber bundles are bound together to form the whole tendon unit. These tertiary fiber bundles are made up of a bunch of secondary fiber bundles, and the secondary fiber bundles are made up of a bunch of primary fiber bundles. Primary fiber bundles are made up of an aggregation of collagen fibers. The bundles are surrounded by epitendon."}, {"name": "Function", "text": "The complex structure of the tertiary fiber bundles in combination with the primary and secondary fiber bundles enable the tendon do its job of relaying force generated by the muscles to the bone. This facilitates the movement of joints (Kannus, 2000)."}, {"name": "References", "text": "Franchi, M., Trir\u00e8, A., Quaranta, M., Orsini, E. and Ottani, V. (2007) 'Collagen structure of tendon relates to function', ScientificWorldJournal, 7, pp. 404-20.\n\nKannus, P. (2000) 'Structure of the tendon connective tissue', Scand J Med Sci Sports, 10(6), pp. 312-20."}]

items.name: Cortex of Lens
items.info: [{"name": "Quick Facts", "text": "The cortex of lens is the softer, external part of the lens of the eye (Dorland, 2011)."}, {"name": "Structure and/or Key Feature(s)", "text": "The lens consists of three layers, from external to internal: capsule epithelium, and lens fibers. The lens fibers can be further subdivided into the external cortex and internal nucleus. The cortical cells are immature and less densely packed, which conveys to the cortex a disorganization and soft consistency. The cortex represents 16% of the total diameter of the lens (Taylor et al., 1996)."}, {"name": "Function", "text": "The cortex of the lens serves as the \u201cnursery\u201d for the new lens cells formed by the epithelium. A developmental gradient exists whereby newly formed lens cells are found most peripherally in the cortex. As they mature, they get \u201cpushed\u201d (by the formation of even younger cells) inwards, eventually losing organelles and nuclei while forming and organizing crystallins as they enter the nuclear region of the lens."}, {"name": "Clinical Correlates", "text": "\u2014Cataracts"}, {"name": "References", "text": "Dorland, W. (2011) Dorland's Illustrated Medical Dictionary. 32nd edn. Philadelphia, USA: Elsevier Saunders.\n\nTaylor, V. L., al-Ghoul, K. J., Lane, C. W., Davis, V. A., Kuszak, J. R. and Costello, M. J. (1996) 'Morphology of the normal human lens', Invest Ophthalmol Vis Sci, 37(7), pp. 1396-410."}]

items.name: Origin of Longus Colli Muscle
Epicranial Aponeurosis
items.info:
[{"name": "Quick Facts", "text": "The epicranial aponeurosis is the aponeurotic layer of the scalp; the central tendon of the epicranius muscle, connecting the frontal and occipital bellies of the occipitofrontalis muscle, and the temporoparietalis muscles (Dorland, 2011)."}, {"name": "Structure", "text": "The epicranial aponeurosis is the third layer of the scalp and the strongest. It is a thin (approximately 0.5 mm), broad, and strong tendinous sheet that serves as an intermediate tendon between the occipital and frontal bellies of the occipitofrontalis muscle (Brennan, Mahadevan and Evans, 2015). 

The epicranial aponeurosis is tightly bound to the overlying skin via a fibrous subcutaneous tissue. However, it is loosely connected to the underlying pericranium, thus allowing it to move freely, while carrying the skin with it.

Deep lacerations, or cuts, to the scalp can result in continuous bleeding. This is because the underlying epicranial aponeurosis is abundant in elastic fibers, which prevents the vessels in the overlying superficial fascia from retracting."}, {"name": "Key Features/Anatomical Relations", "text": "The epicranial aponeurosis is internal to the dense superficial fascia of the scalp and external to the loose connective tissue of the scalp. 

Posteriorly, it blends with the occipital belly of the occipitofrontalis to insert into the superior nuchal line of the occipital bone. Anteriorly, it is continuous with the frontal portion of the occipitofrontalis muscle and blends with the eyebrows. Laterally, it blends with the temporalis fascia, as well as the anterior and superior auricular muscles and the temporoparietalis muscle. 

The subaponeurotic space, or “danger space,” is a potential space deep to the epicranial aponeurosis. This space contains the loose connective tissue and the emissary veins that link the intracranial dural sinuses with the extracranial veins. Thus, localized infections within this space have the potential to spread intracranially. The subaponeurotic space is limited anteriorly by the frontal belly and posteriorly by the occipital belly of the occipitofrontalis muscle."}, {"name": "Function", "text": "The epicranial aponeurosis serves as a site of origin for the frontal bellies of the occipitofrontalis muscle and a site of insertion for the occipital muscles of the occipitofrontalis muscle. Additionally, it is loosely connected to the underlying loose connective tissue; thus it can move over it freely, carrying the skin and subcutaneous tissue."}, {"name": "List of Clinical Correlates", "text": "—Scalp lacerations

—Scalp infections

—Subgaleal hemorrhage

—Osteomyelitis

—Brain abscess"}, {"name": "References", "text": "Brennan, P. A., Mahadevan, V. and Evans, B. T. (2015) Clinical Head and Neck Anatomy for Surgeons. CRC Press.

Dorland, W. (2011) Dorland's Illustrated Medical Dictionary. 32nd edn. Philadelphia, USA: Elsevier Saunders."}]

items.name: Gingival Nerves
items.info:
[{"name": "Quick Facts", "text": "The gingival nerves relay sensory information to the central nervous system."}, {"name": "Anatomical Relations", "text": "The palatal gingiva of the maxilla receives innervation from the greater palatine nerve, while the buccal gingiva of the maxilla receives innervation from branches of the posterior superior alveolar nerve and the buccal nerve (Standring, 2016).

The buccal gingiva of the mandible receives innervation from the buccal nerve and perforating branches of the inferior alveolar nerve, while the lingual gingiva is innervated by the lingual nerve and perforating branches of the inferior alveolar nerve (Standring, 2016)."}, {"name": "Function", "text": "These nerves are responsible for relaying sensory information, for example pain, from the gingiva."}, {"name": "References", "text": "Hand, A. R. and Frank, M. E. (2015) Fundamentals of Oral Histology and Physiology. Wiley.

Standring, S. (2016) Gray's Anatomy: The Anatomical Basis of Clinical Practice. Gray's Anatomy Series 41 edn.: Elsevier Limited."}]

items.name: Longitudinal Muscular Layer
items.info:
[{"name": "Quick Facts", "text": "The longitudinal muscular layer is the outer layer of the muscular coat (tunica muscularis) of the colon, consisting of longitudinally coursing fibers; it is thick in the regions of the three taeniae coli and very thin between them (Dorland, 2011)."}, {"name": "Structure/Morphology", "text": "The muscular layer of the colon is composed of smooth muscle organized into outer longitudinal and inner circular layers. These layers run perpendicular to each other. The inner circular layer extends the width of the colon and the outer longitudinal fibers are continuous along the length of the colon. 

The longitudinal layer of smooth muscle is thinner than the circular layer except at the teniae coli where the muscle thickens significantly. The teniae coli are strips of longitudinal muscle, which when contracted, give rise to the sacculations of the haustra. Additionally, small fascicles of muscle pass between the longitudinal and circular layers, especially in the region of the teniae coli. This deviation of muscle fibers may help form the haustra (Standring, 2016).

The muscular layer receives its arterial blood supply from permeating capillaries coming from the submucosal arteriolar network and is innervated by the myenteric plexus."}, {"name": "Anatomical Relations", "text": "The longitudinal layer is located between the inner circular layer and the serosa. The myenteric plexus is located between the circular and longitudinal muscular layers."}, {"name": "Function", "text": "The longitudinal muscular layer works with the inner circular layer to provide peristaltic contractions, which facilitates the passage of the intestinal content to the anus for excretion."}, {"name": "References", "text": "Dorland, W. (2011) Dorland's Illustrated Medical Dictionary. 32nd edn. Philadelphia, USA: Elsevier Saunders.

Standring, S. (2016) Gray's Anatomy: The Anatomical Basis of Clinical Practice. Gray's Anatomy Series 41st edition edn.: Elsevier Limited."}]

items.name: Sarcoplasmic Reticulum (Uncontracted Smooth Muscle)
items.info:
[{"name": "Quick Facts", "text": "The sarcoplasmic reticulum is a special form of smooth endoplasmic reticulum found in association with the T tubules in the sarcoplasm of striated muscle and comprising a system of cisternae and tubules forming a plexus around each myofibril. It contains large numbers of calcium pumps and ryanodine receptors and is a storage compartment for calcium ions, which it releases in response to an action potential in the adjacent T tubule to cause muscular contraction (Dorland, 2011)."}, {"name": "Structure and/or Key Features", "text": "The sarcoplasmic reticulum (SR) is an organelle that consists of a network of loose flattened tubules with various compartments, many of which contain Ca2+. The two ends of the SR are wider, thus form terminal sacs called cisternae. Two cisternae of adjacent sarcoplasmic reticula and one transverse tubule form a functional unit called a triad, which operates to elicit the release of Ca2+ from SR stores (Maclennan and Zvaritch, 2011)."}, {"name": "Anatomical Relations", "text": "Sarcoplasmic reticulum is a specialized type of smooth endoplasmic reticulum found in skeletal muscle. It forms a network of tubules that extend through a muscle fiber. The flattened tubules surround, but do not make direct contact with the myofibrils in a muscle fiber."}, {"name": "Function", "text": "The sarcoplasmic reticulum functions as an intracellular calcium store. Depolarization of the sarcoplasmic reticulum membrane results in the release of calcium ions (Ca2+). This release of calcium ions triggers the cascade required for contraction."}, {"name": "Clinical Correlates", "text": "—Fatigue

—Central core disease"}, {"name": "References", "text": "Dorland, W. (2011) Dorland's Illustrated Medical Dictionary. 32nd edn. Philadelphia, USA: Elsevier Saunders.

Maclennan, D. H. and Zvaritch, E. (2011) 'Mechanistic models for muscle diseases and disorders originating in the sarcoplasmic reticulum', Biochim Biophys Acta, 1813(5), pp. 948-64."}]

items.name: External Lamina (Contracted Smooth Muscle; Posterior)
items.info: [{"name": "Quick Facts", "text": "The basal lamina is the layer of the basement membrane lying next to the basal surface of the adjoining cell layer; composed of an electron-dense lamina densa and an electron-lucent lamina lucida; sometimes used to denote the lamina densa alone (Dorland, 2011)."}, {"name": "Structure and/or Key Features", "text": "The external lamina (or basal lamina) is made up of several different proteins and carbohydrates, such as collagen, proteoglycans, and glycoproteins. It forms a matrix which surrounds the muscle fiber and plays a central role in its structure and function.\n\nThe term \u201cexternal lamina\u201d replaces \u201cbasal lamina\u201d in nonepithelial cells such as muscle cells, adipocytes, and supporting cells in the peripheral nervous system."}, {"name": "Anatomical Relations", "text": "The external lamina surrounds the muscle fiber and is directly linked to the sarcolemma."}, {"name": "Function", "text": "The external lamina has several important roles in the structure and function of the muscle fiber such as mechanical support to underlying structures. It also acts as a scaffold for many important cells which act on the muscle fiber. The external lamina matrix has been found to be a component of important molecular signaling, i.e., it contains an enzyme, acetylcholinesterase, which breaks down acetylcholine during neuromuscular transmissions. Its role seems to be important in a wide range of functions from development to myogenesis and synaptogenesis."}, {"name": "References", "text": "Dorland, W. (2011) Dorland's Illustrated Medical Dictionary. 32nd edn. Philadelphia, USA: Elsevier Saunders."}]

items.name: Caveola (Contracted Smooth Muscle; Anterior)
items.info: [{"name": "Quick Facts", "text": "A caveola is a small (approximately 50 nm), flask-shaped invagination of the plasma membrane occurring in nearly all animal cells, coated with the membrane protein caveolin and rich in cholesterol and sphingolipids. Caveolae are a special form of lipid raft and are associated with endocytosis, budding from the plasma membrane to form pinosomes; they also concentrate signaling molecules and have been implicated in other processes, including the export of cholesterol to serum lipoproteins (Dorland, 2011)."}, {"name": "Structure and/or Key Features", "text": "Most cells in the body utilize a process called pinocytosis to ingest fluid and small protein molecules via small vesicles about 80\u2013150 nm in diameter. It is a continual process, so small vesicles are continually forming at the cell surface. Most of the vesicles eventually fuse with lysosomes although they are very numerous in endothelial cells as they move materials from their surface of origin to the other side. They are also numerous at the surfaces of smooth muscle cells and their initial invaginations from the sarcolemma (plasma membrane) are referred to as caveolae. Cytoplasmic vesicles are in close proximity to sparse amounts of smooth endoplasmic reticulum (sER)."}, {"name": "Anatomical Relations", "text": "Caveolae are numerous at the surfaces of smooth muscle cells and their initial invaginations from the smooth muscle sarcolemma (plasma membrane)."}, {"name": "Function", "text": "Smooth muscle cells lack T tubules. Caveolae and vesicles function to deliver Ca+ to the cytoplasm as a consequence of depolarization of the sarcolemma and activation of voltage-sensitive Ca+ channels or direct activation of gated Ca+ release channels in the sER by a second messenger molecule. Ca+ can also be released into the cytoplasm via ligated Ca+ channels activated by hormones also by second messenger pathways. \n\nIncreasing the intracellular concentration of Ca+ is responsible for contraction of the smooth muscle cell. Contraction of smooth muscle cells is initiated by mechanical impulses, neural stimulation via neurotransmitters such as acetylcholine and norepinephrine, or chemical stimuli of the cells."}, {"name": "References", "text": "Dorland, W. (2011) Dorland's Illustrated Medical Dictionary. 32nd edn. Philadelphia, USA: Elsevier Saunders."}]

items.name: Bony Labyrinth (Cochlear Part)
items.info:
[{"name": "Quick Facts", "text": "The bony labyrinth is the interconnected cavities and canals in the petrous portion of the temporal bone, in which the membranous labyrinth, the vestibular aqueduct, and the cochlear aqueduct are lodged; it consists of three parts: the vestibule, the semicircular canals, and the cochlea (Dorland, 2011)."}, {"name": "Structure and/or Key Feature(s)", "text": "The internal ear is located in the petrous part of the temporal bone, where the bone is of a harder consistency than the remaining petrous bone. It consists of a network of inner cavities which are lined by periosteum. These cavities are the cochlea, vestibule, and semicircular canals, which are collectively known as the bony labyrinth. The membranous labyrinth lies within these bony cavities and is separated from the inner aspect of the bony wall by periosteum and perilymph. 

The bony walls of the cochlea are quite porous and contain small canaliculi/micropores. These are mostly found in the osseous spiral lamina and the base of the scala tympani, with fewer found in the scala vestibuli. These canaliculi would appear to provide an extensive communication channel for the fluid between these structures (Standring, 2016).

The bony wall is primarily supplied via the cochlear branches of the labyrinthine artery, which typically originates from the basilar artery, but may originate from the anterior inferior cerebellar artery in some cases. Venous drainage occurs alongside the arterial supply, forming the labyrinthine vein which drains into the inferior petrosal or transverse venous sinuses."}, {"name": "Anatomical Relations", "text": "The internal aspects of the bony wall are lined with periosteum. The external aspect is consistent with the petrous part of the temporal bone, and the lateral aspect is in contact with the middle ear via the stapes."}, {"name": "Function", "text": "The bony labyrinth is the foundation of the structural architecture of the internal ear and the auditory pathways. It protects the membranous labyrinth and its nerve cells to enable successful auditory transmission. It also serves as a protective barrier of possible foreign bodies/pathogens from the middle ear."}, {"name": "List of Clinical Correlates", "text": "—Otosclerosis"}, {"name": "References", "text": "Dorland, W. (2011) Dorland's Illustrated Medical Dictionary. 32nd edn. Philadelphia, USA: Elsevier Saunders.

Standring, S. (2016) Gray's Anatomy: The Anatomical Basis of Clinical Practice., 41st edition. Elsevier Limited"}]

items.name: Basement Membrane
items.info: [{"name": "Quick Facts", "text": "The basement membrane is a thin sheet of amorphous extracellular material upon which the basal surfaces of epithelial cells rest; other cells associated with basement membranes are muscle cells, Schwann cells, and fat cells. The membrane is interposed between the cellular elements and the underlying connective tissue. It usually comprises two layers, the basal lamina and the reticular lamina, and is composed of Type IV collagen (which is unique to basement membranes), laminin, fibronectin, and heparan sulfate proteoglycans (Dorland, 2011)."}, {"name": "Structure and/or Key Features", "text": "The olfactory mucosa is composed of the olfactory epithelium and the lamina propria. The basement membrane essentially separates the lamina propria from the olfactory epithelium. The basal (stem) cells of the olfactory epithelium, through which olfactory cell regenerate, are situated along the basement membrane."}, {"name": "Anatomical Relations", "text": "The basement membrane essentially separates the lamina propria from the olfactory epithelium."}, {"name": "Function", "text": "The principal function of a basement membrane is to provide structural support for the epithelium. In this case, it is the olfactory epithelium."}, {"name": "References", "text": "Dorland, W. (2011) Dorland's Illustrated Medical Dictionary. 32nd edn. Philadelphia, USA: Elsevier Saunders."}]

items.name: Aggregated Lymphoid Nodules of Ileum
items.info:
[{"name": "Quick Facts", "text": "The aggregated lymphoid nodules of small intestine are the oval elevated areas of lymphoid tissue on the mucosa of the small intestine, composed of many lymphoid follicles closely packed together (Dorland, 2011)."}, {"name": "Structure/Morphology", "text": "Diffuse lymphatic tissue and lymphatic nodules occur as single entities along the alimentary tract; however, in the ileum, the submucosa (and the lamina propria) contains aggregations of lymphoid nodules known as “Peyer’s patches.” They are an important component of the gut associated lymphatic tissue (GALT). In humans, there are about 30 patches, with each patch may contain 10–200 lymph nodules. They contain T cells and B lymphocytes. At the luminal surface, a Peyer’s patch appears as a dome-shaped region devoid of villi and the epithelial surface consists of low cuboidal M (microfold) cells rather than absorptive cells (enterocytes)."}, {"name": "Key Features/Anatomical Relations", "text": "Aggregations of lymphoid nodules known as “Peyer’s patches” dominate the submucosa (and the lamina propria) mostly in the ileum."}, {"name": "Function", "text": "Lymphocytes and associated immune cells, e.g., eosinophils, macrophages, and neutrophils, are in the ideal location to recognize antigens and initiate the immune response.

The germinal center indicates that the lymphatic tissue is responding to an antigen resulting in the proliferation of lymphocytes, the differentiation of plasma cells and the production of antibodies.

M cells are antigen-transporting cells and carry antigens from the intestinal lumen to reach immune cells within the lamina propria of the digestive tract or gut associated lymphatic tissue (GALT)."}, {"name": "References", "text": "Dorland, W. (2011) Dorland's Illustrated Medical Dictionary. 32nd edn. Philadelphia, USA: Elsevier Saunders."}]

items.name: Muscular Layer of Small Intestine (Jejunum)
items.info:
[{"name": "Quick Facts", "text": "The muscular layer is the layer of smooth muscle lying between the submucosa and the serosa or the adventitia in many portions of the digestive, respiratory, urinary, and genital tracts (Dorland, 2011)."}, {"name": "Structure/Morphology", "text": "The muscular layer (or muscularis externa) is well developed and composed of an internal circular layer and an external longitudinal layer. Between the two layers are ganglion cells and nerve fibers forming the myenteric (Auerbach’s) plexus. How the smooth muscle cells appear under the microscope will depend on the plane of the section i.e., transverse or longitudinal."}, {"name": "Key Features/Anatomical Relations", "text": "At a few locations along the alimentary tract, the muscular layer thickens to form sphincters. The gastroduodenal sphincter (or pyloric sphincter) is an example in the small intestine. It is located at the junction of the pylorus of the stomach and the duodenum."}, {"name": "Function", "text": "Contractions of the inner circular layer of the muscular layer constricts the lumen and mixes the luminal contents. Contraction of the outer longitudinal layer of the muscular layer propels the contents along the digestive tract. 

The slow, rhythmic contraction of both these muscle layers, under the control of the enteric nervous system, produces peristalsis.

The gastroduodenal sphincter (or pyloric sphincter) controls the release of chyme into the duodenum."}, {"name": "References", "text": "Dorland, W. (2011) Dorland's Illustrated Medical Dictionary. 32nd edn. Philadelphia, USA: Elsevier Saunders."}]

items.name: Tunica Intima of Vessel
items.info:
[{"name": "Quick Facts", "text": "The tunica intima of a blood vessel is made up of endothelial cells surrounded by longitudinal elastic fibers and connective tissue (Dorland, 2011)."}, {"name": "Structure", "text": "The tunica intima is the innermost and narrowest layer of the artery. It’s formed by an endothelium, basement membrane, lamina propria, and an internal elastic membrane. 

The endothelial layer arises from a single continuous layer of endothelial cells. These cells are in direct contact with blood in the lumen. Overlying this is the basement membrane, which is composed of the basal lamina and the reticular lamina. Epithelial cells and collagen fibers make up the basal lamina, while the reticular lamina is secreted by connective tissue cells and contains reticular fibers. The internal elastic lamina separates the tunica intima from the tunica media."}, {"name": "Anatomical Relations", "text": "In smaller arterioles or venules, the tunica intima is usually a single coating of cells, although thickness can differ in larger vessels such as the aorta. Surrounding the tunica intima is a narrow membrane of elastic fibers running parallel to the vessel."}, {"name": "Function", "text": "The tunica intima acts as a barrier between the blood in the lumen and the vessel walls. This barrier function results in the tunica intima partly assisting in the regulation of capillary exchange. Through release of endothelins from the endothelium, the tunica intima can alter blood pressure (Pawlina, 2016). These local chemicals can cause constriction of the smooth muscle within the walls of the vessel. The tunica intima also impedes thrombosis through hindering attachment of blood cells to the vessel wall."}, {"name": "List of Clinical Correlates", "text": "—Thrombosis"}, {"name": "References", "text": "Dorland, W. (2011) Dorland's Illustrated Medical Dictionary. 32nd edn. Philadelphia, USA: Elsevier Saunders.

Pawlina, W. 2016. Histology: A text and atlas with correlated cell and molecular biology. 7th ed. Philadelphia: Wolters Kluwer."}]

items.name: Enterocyte (Jejunum)
items.info:
[{"name": "Quick Facts", "text": "An enterocyte is an epithelial cell of the intestinal wall (Dorland, 2011)."}, {"name": "Structure/Morphology", "text": "Enterocytes are simple, tall columnar epithelial cells with a nucleus positioned in the basal domain of the cell. Microvilli extend from the apical surface. Collectively, the microvilli of enterocytes are called a “striated border.”

Apical borders of adjacent enterocytes are joined by tight junctions and permit selective absorption of substances from the intestinal lumen. The lateral surfaces of the enterocytes exhibit cytoplasmic processes that interdigitate with those of adjacent cells thus increasing the amount of the plasmalemma housing transport enzymes.

The cytoplasm of enterocytes also exhibits specializations of an absorptive cell. Elongated mitochondria and smooth/agranular endoplasmic reticulum (sER) are concentrated in the apical cytoplasm.

The cytoplasm of enterocytes also exhibits specializations of a secretory cell. Stacks of Golgi cisternae are near the nucleus accompanied by free ribosomes and rough/granular endoplasmic reticulum (rER). Small secretory vesicles congregate at the apical border of the cell."}, {"name": "Function", "text": "The primary function of the enterocytes is absorption. The striated border increases the surface area for absorption as much as 600 times. 

Lateral interdigitations of the plasmalemma of adjacent enterocytes expand and enlarge the intercellular compartment during absorption of solutes, water and lipids.

Mitochondria provide the energy required for transport processes and the sER are involved in the absorption of fatty acids and glycerol.

Enterocytes are also secretory cells, primarily producing glycoprotein enzymes that will be reinserted into the apical membrane. They also secrete water and electrolytes (mainly those enterocytes in the intestinal glands to balance water absorption across the enterocytes lining the villi), which maintains a constant liquified intestinal chyme."}, {"name": "References", "text": "Dorland, W. (2011) Dorland's Illustrated Medical Dictionary. 32nd edn. Philadelphia, USA: Elsevier Saunders."}]

items.name: Greater Omentum
items.info:
[{"name": "Quick Facts", "text": "The greater omentum is a prominent peritoneal fold suspended from the greater curvature of the stomach and passing laterally and inferiorly a variable distance in front of the intestines; it is attached to the anterior surface of the transverse colon; a remnant of the dorsal mesogastrium, it comprises the omental apron and several peritoneal ligaments connecting abdominal organs (Dorland, 2011)."}, {"name": "Description", "text": "The greater omentum is a large double sheet of visceral peritoneum that drapes inferiorly from the greater curvature of the stomach. It hangs over the upper abdominal organs and then folds back on itself to attach to the transverse colon.

The greater omentum contains a significant amount of adipose tissue, and it also plays a role in immune function.

The left and right gastroepiploic arteries, which run along the inferior border of the stomach, supply the greater omentum, and an anastomosis of these vessels, called the epiploic arterial arc, lies along its inferior peritoneal fold."}, {"name": "References", "text": "Dorland, W. (2011) Dorland's Illustrated Medical Dictionary. 32nd edn. Philadelphia, USA: Elsevier Saunders."}]

items.name: Inferior Glenohumeral Ligament
items.info: [{"name": "Anatomical Relations", "text": "The glenohumeral ligaments include the superior, middle, and inferior ligaments.\n\nThe inferior glenohumeral ligament arises from the anterior, middle, and inferior glenoid margin. It extends anteriorly and inferiorly to the inferior and medial aspect of the anatomical neck of the humerus."}, {"name": "Structure", "text": "The glenohumeral ligaments are fibrous bands and are only truly evident from within the joint. The anterosuperior margin of the inferior glenohumeral ligament is thickened, forming an anterior band. Posteriorly, the articular capsule also has a thickening, known as the posterior band. Between the anterior and posterior bands, the articular capsule is thin and loose, and forms the axillary pouch (or recess)."}, {"name": "Function", "text": "The inferior glenohumeral ligament reinforces the articular capsule of the glenohumeral joint, particularly the anterior portion of the capsule. Additionally, it is the most important stabilizer of the glenohumeral joint, preventing anterior or inferior dislocation of the humeral head (Burkart and Debski, 2002)."}, {"name": "List of clinical correlates", "text": "\u2014Glenohumeral joint dislocation"}, {"name": "References", "text": "Burkart, A. C. and Debski, R. E. (2002) 'Anatomy and function of the glenohumeral ligaments in anterior shoulder instability', Clin Orthop Relat Res, (400), pp. 32-9."}]

items.name: Middle Glenohumeral Ligament
items.info: [{"name": "Anatomical Relations", "text": "The glenohumeral ligaments include the superior, middle, and inferior ligaments.\n\nThe middle glenohumeral ligament arises from its wide attachment along the anterior glenoid margin, just below the attachment of the superior glenohumeral ligament. It extends laterally and inferiorly to the lesser tubercle of the humerus, deep to the tendon of the subscapularis muscle, with which its fibers blend."}, {"name": "Structure", "text": "The glenohumeral ligaments are fibrous bands and are only truly evident from within the joint."}, {"name": "Function", "text": "The middle glenohumeral ligament reinforces the articular capsule of the glenohumeral joint, particularly the anterior portion of the capsule. Additionally, it provides anterior stability to the head of the humerus during abduction between 45\u00b0 and 60\u00b0 in the scapular plane."}, {"name": "List of clinical correlates", "text": "\u2014Glenohumeral joint dislocation"}]

items.info: [{"name": "Anatomical Relations", "text": "The synovial membrane of the glenohumeral joint forms the internal layer of the articular capsule of the glenohumeral joint. The fibrous membrane forms the external layer of the capsule.\n\nThe tendon of the long head of biceps brachii muscle passes through the glenohumeral joint within the synovial membrane, and the synovial membrane extends and continues with the tendon as far as the surgical neck of the humerus."}, {"name": "Structure", "text": "The synovial membrane of the glenohumeral joint lines the joint cavity and is composed of loose connective tissue. The synovial membrane is responsible for producing synovial fluid, which lubricates the glenohumeral joint."}, {"name": "Function", "text": "The articular capsule of the glenohumeral joint ensures that the joint is sealed, thus, keeping the lubricating synovial fluid within the joint. It provides passive stability to the joint by limiting the joint movement. Additionally, it provides active stability but containing numerous proprioceptive nerve endings which relay mechanical information back to the central nervous system (Ralphs and Benjamin, 1994)."}, {"name": "References", "text": "Ralphs, J. R. and Benjamin, M. (1994) 'The joint capsule: structure, composition, ageing and disease', Journal of Anatomy, 184(Pt 3), pp. 503-509."}]

items.name: Bipolar Neuron
Carpometacarpal Joints
items.info:
[{"name": "Description", "text": "The carpometacarpal joints are the articulations between the base of the metacarpals with the distal row of carpal bones, i.e., the trapezium, trapezoid, capitate, and hamate. 

The first carpometacarpal joint, or the carpometacarpal joint of the thumb, is a saddle (or sellar) synovial joint that allows opposition of the thumb. It is formed by the articulations between the base of the first metacarpal with the trapezium. The joint is stabilized by the palmar, dorsal, and lateral carpometacarpal ligaments on the ulnar side of the joint.

The second to fifth carpometacarpal joints are synovial ellipsoid joints formed by the articulations between the bases of the second to fifth metacarpals and the distal row of carpals. These joints allow slight gliding produced by the long flexor and extensor muscles of the digits. The carpometacarpal joints are stabilized by dorsal and palmar carpometacarpal ligaments."}]

It is composed of an outer fibrous membrane and an inner synovial membrane. The ligament of the interphalangeal joints, i.e., the palmar, collateral, and accessory collateral ligaments reinforce the articular capsule."}, {"name": "Function", "text": "The articular capsule of the interphalangeal joint ensures that the joint is sealed, thus, keeping the lubricating synovial fluid within the joint. It provides passive stability to the joint by limiting the joint movement. Additionally, it provides active stability by containing numerous proprioceptive nerve endings which relay mechanical information back to the central nervous system (Ralphs and Benjamin, 1994)."}, {"name": "References", "text": "Ralphs, J. items.name: Nervi Vasorum (Vein)
Midcarpal Joint
items.info:
[{"name": "Description", "text": "The intercarpal joints consist of:

—the carpal joints between the proximal row of carpal bones

—the carpal joints between the distal row of carpal bones 

—the articulations between the proximal and distal carpal bones which is termed the midcarpal joint. 

The midcarpal joint is a compound articulation formed between the proximal and distal rows of carpal bones. The proximal row is composed of the scaphoid, lunate, and triquetrum, while the distal row is formed by the trapezium, trapezoid, capitate, and hamate. The articulation may be divided into medial and lateral compartments. The head of the capitate and hamate form a convex articulation for the concave scaphoid, lunate, and triquetrum, except most medially, where the curvatures are reversed to form a compound sellar joint. In the lateral compartment, the trapezium and trapezoid articulate with the scaphoid, thus also forming a compound articulation. The midcarpal joint is also a synovial joint.

Numerous midcarpal ligaments help to stabilize the midcarpal joint and may be referred to as intrinsic ligaments of the wrist. Generally, they are stronger and shorter than the extrinsic ligaments, but often form a complex with one another by interdigitating fibers. The midcarpal ligaments include the dorsal, palmar, and interosseous intercarpal ligaments.

Extension and abduction of the hand occur primarily at the midcarpal joint, while flexion and extension of the hand are imitated at the midcarpal joint."}]

items.name: Large Vein
Dorsal Intercarpal Ligaments
items.info: [{"name": "Anatomical Relations", "text": "The dorsal intercarpal ligaments are formed by several bands that extend transversely across the dorsal surface of the carpal bones. They arise from the distal pole of the scaphoid and the trapezoid and pass across the lunate to attach to the triquetrum."}, {"name": "Function", "text": "The dorsal intercarpal ligaments help to stabilize the proximal row of carpal bones in the midcarpal joint."}]

items.name: Dorsal Ulnocarpal Ligament
items.info: [{"name": "Anatomical Relations", "text": "The dorsal ulnocarpal ligament is an extrinsic ligament on the dorsal aspect of the wrist joint. It attaches proximally to the styloid process of the distal ulna and extends distally to the triquetrum (Sch\u00fcnke et al., 2006)."}, {"name": "Structure", "text": "The dorsal ulnocarpal ligament is a strong, fibrous band. The oblique nature of the ligament ensures that the hand follows the radius during pronation of the forearm (Moore et al., 2013)."}, {"name": "Function", "text": "The dorsal ulnocarpal ligament strengthens the articular capsule of the radiocarpal joint (Sch\u00fcnke et al., 2006)."}, {"name": "References", "text": "Moore, K. L., Dalley, A. F. and Agur, A. M. R. (2013) Clinically Oriented Anatomy. Clinically Oriented Anatomy 7th edn.: Wolters Kluwer Health/Lippincott Williams & Wilkins.\n\nSch\u00fcnke, M., Ross, L. M., Schulte, E., Lamperti, E. D., Schumacher, U., Rude, J., Voll, M., Telger, T. C. and Wesker, K. (2006) Thieme Atlas of Anatomy: General Anatomy and Musculoskeletal System. Thieme Atlas of Anatomy: Thieme."}]

items.name: Superficial Veins of Lower Limb
items.info: [{"name": "Description", "text": "The lower limb is made up of six regions: the gluteal, femoral (thigh), knee, leg, talocrural (ankle) and foot regions.\n\nVenous drainage of the lower limb is composed of deep and superficial veins. Perforating veins shunt blood from the superficial system to the deep venous system. Approximately 15% of venous blood is drained in the superficial system and 85% of blood is drained by the deep system. The main superficial veins are the great and small saphenous veins. The main vein of the deep system is the femoral vein (Moore et al, 2013)."}, {"name": "References", "text": "Moore, K. L., Dalley, A. F. and Agur, A. M. R. (2013) Clinically Oriented Anatomy. Clinically Oriented Anatomy 7th edn.: Wolters Kluwer Health/Lippincott Williams & Wilkins."}]

The ulnolunate ligament extends distally in series with the short radiolunate ligament to insert on the palmar aspect of the lunate (Moritomo, 2013)."}, {"name": "Function", "text": "The palmar ulnocarpal ligaments strengthen the articular capsule of the radiocarpal joint and prevent displacement of the head of ulna."}, {"name": "References", "text": "Moritomo, H. The ulnotriquetral ligament extends distally to insert onto the proximal surface of the triquetrum (Moritomo, 2013)."}, {"name": "Function", "text": "The palmar ulnocarpal ligaments strengthen the articular capsule of the radiocarpal joint and prevent displacement of the head of ulna."}, {"name": "References", "text": "Moritomo, H. items.name: Joints of Pectoral Girdle
items.info:
[{"name": "Description", "text": "The pectoral girdle consists of three synovial joints which connect the upper limb to the torso.

The clavicle is attached to the appendicular skeleton at the sternoclavicular joint. Laterally, the clavicle also connects with the acromion of the scapula via the acromioclavicular joint. Both of these joints are supported by several strong ligaments.

The glenohumeral joint is a highly mobile synovial ball and socket joint that consists of the articulation of the glenoid fossa of the scapula and the proximal humeral head. Due to its high mobility, it is not as stable as other joints of the upper limb and dislocations are common.

Additional ligaments not directly associated with the joints of the pectoral girdle also aid in the stability of the region. These include the superior transverse scapular and coracoacromial ligament."}]

items.name: Lobule of Thyroid Gland
items.info: [{"name": "Quick Facts", "text": "The lobules of thyroid gland are irregular areas on the surface of the thyroid gland produced by entrance into the gland of fibrous trabeculae from the sheath (Dorland, 2011)."}, {"name": "Structure/Morphology", "text": "The characteristic structure of a compound exocrine gland includes the gland being subdivided into smaller components called lobes. Lobes can be further subdivided into lobules. Intralobular, interlobular, and interlobar ducts will unite all these glandular elements and the secretion product is usually delivered to its destination via a large single excretory duct. "}, {"name": "Function", "text": "The thyroid lobules are the smallest visible anatomical structure of the thyroid lobes and contain the functional units called the thyroid follicles."}, {"name": "References", "text": "Dorland, W. (2011) Dorland's Illustrated Medical Dictionary. 32nd edn. Philadelphia, USA: Elsevier Saunders."}]

items.name: Coracoacromial Ligament
items.info: [{"name": "Anatomical Relations", "text": "As its name suggests, the coracoacromial ligament attaches from the lateral border of the coracoid process to the apex of the acromion of the scapula. Together, the inferior aspects of the acromion, coracoid process, and the coracoacromial ligament form the coracoacromial arch. This arch forms a protective roof over the head of the humerus, thus, preventing superior displacement from its glenoid cavity.\n\nThe coracoacromial ligament is bordered superiorly by the clavicle and deltoid, and inferiorly by the tendon of the supraspinatus muscle and the subacromial bursa. It is continuous with the deltoid fascia superiorly and the clavipectoral fascia medially."}, {"name": "Structure", "text": "The coracoacromial ligament is a strong, broad, triangular band. The ligament is most commonly seen as Y- or V-shaped (42\u201375%), but may also be seen as undivided (26\u201358%) or multibanded (1\u201315%) (Rothenberg et al., 2017). The coracoacromial ligament is described as being fibrocartilaginous, including areas which are calcified."}, {"name": "Function", "text": "The coracoacromial ligament is a strengthening ligament and plays a role in stabilizing the glenohumeral (shoulder) joint. By being positioned superiorly, it prevents upward dislocation of the glenohumeral joint. It also acts as a tension band between the acromial and coracoid process of the scapula, transmitting forces exerted on the coracoid process by the short head of biceps brachii, pectoralis minor, and coracobrachialis muscles to the acromion. Additionally, forces exerted on the acromion by the deltoid and trapezius muscles are transmitted to the coracoid process, thus limiting the distortional forces applied by these muscles (Rothenberg et al., 2017)."}, {"name": "List of clinical correlates", "text": "\u2014Rotator cuff disease"}, {"name": "References", "text": "Rothenberg, A., Gasbarro, G., Chlebeck, J. and Lin, A. (2017) 'The Coracoacromial Ligament: Anatomy, Function, and Clinical Significance', Orthopaedic Journal of Sports Medicine, 5(4), pp. 2325967117703398."}]

items.name: Synovial Joints of Pectoral Girdle
alt: Synovial Joints of Upper Limb Girdle
items.info:
[{"name": "Description", "text": "Synovial joints are specialized joints that permit free movement between two bones, called articulations. The bones are united by an articular capsule, composed of an outer fibrous membrane and an inner synovial membrane, that encloses the joint. Within the capsule is a potential space containing synovial fluid, produced by the synovial membrane, which helps lubricate the joint during movement. The synovial joints of the pectoral girdle (or shoulder girdle) include the acromioclavicular and sternoclavicular joints.

The acromioclavicular joint is formed between the acromion of the scapula and the acromial end of the clavicle. It is a synovial plane joint and the articular surfaces of the bones are covered by fibrocartilage and are surrounded by a fibrous joint capsule. The joint strengthened superiorly by the acromioclavicular ligament, posteriorly by fibers of the trapezius muscle, and anteriorly by fibers of the deltoid muscle.

The sternoclavicular joint is a synovial sellar (or saddle) joint and is the only articulation between the axial skeleton and the upper limb. The joint is located between the clavicle and the clavicular notches of the sternum and both the articulating surfaces are covered with fibrocartilage. The joint is reinforced by a number of ligaments, including the anterior and posterior sternoclavicular ligaments, and the costoclavicular ligament."}]

items.name: Septum of Scrotum
items.info: [{"name": "Structure/Morphology", "text": "The septum of the scrotum is formed where the dartos fascia of the scrotum unites in the midline and forms a septum that separates the scrotal cavity into left and right sides. "}, {"name": "Key Features/ Anatomical Relations", "text": "The septum of the scrotum is demarcated externally by the raphe of the scrotum, a midline ridge demarcating a line of fusion during embryonic development."}, {"name": "Function", "text": "The septum of the scrotum divides the scrotum in half, thus separating the testes."}]

items.name: Articular Capsule of Acromioclavicular Joint
items.info: [{"name": "Anatomical Relations", "text": "The articular capsule of the acromioclavicular joint completely surrounds the articular margins of the acromion of the scapula and the clavicle. The capsule is weak, and is strengthened by the acromioclavicular ligament superiorly, and to a lesser extent, inferiorly. Additionally, its fibers are intermingled with that of the aponeuroses of the trapezius and deltoid muscles for added strength."}, {"name": "Structure", "text": "The articular capsule of the acromioclavicular joint is a sac-like structure that enclosed the acromioclavicular joint. It is composed of two layers. The external layer, the fibrous membrane, is composed of dense fibrous tissue. The internal layer, the synovial membrane, lines the joint cavity and is composed of loose connective tissue."}, {"name": "Function", "text": "The articular capsule of the acromioclavicular joint ensures that the joint is sealed, thus, keeping the lubricating synovial fluid within the joint. It provides passive stability to the joint by limiting the joint movement. Additionally, it provides active stability by containing numerous proprioceptive nerve endings which relay mechanical information back to the central nervous system (Ralphs and Benjamin, 1994)."}, {"name": "References", "text": "Ralphs, J. R. and Benjamin, M. (1994) 'The joint capsule: structure, composition, ageing and disease', Journal of Anatomy, 184(Pt 3), pp. 503-509."}]

items.name: Conoid Ligament
items.info: [{"name": "Anatomical Relations", "text": "The conoid ligament is one of two parts (along with the trapezoid ligament) that forms the coracoclavicular ligament."}, {"name": "Structure", "text": "As its name suggests, the conoid ligament is triangular or cone-shaped and forms the medial part of the coracoclavicular ligament. It has a broad base that attaches to the conoid tubercle of the clavicle, and narrower apex, which attaches to the upper surface of the coracoid process of the scapula, lateral to the scapular notch.\n\nIt has a free anterior border, while its posterior border is joined with the coronoid ligament."}, {"name": "Function", "text": "As a rule, triangular or cone-shaped ligaments keep structures in close apposition, and therefore, the conoid ligament keeps the coracoid process of the scapula and the clavicle in close apposition."}]

items.name: Interosseous Membrane of Forearm
items.info:
[{"name": "Anatomical Relations", "text": "The interosseous membrane of the forearm joins the shafts of the radius and ulna, forming a syndesmosis. The membrane attaches to the prominent interosseous borders located on the medial and lateral surface of the radius and ulna, respectively.

Distally, the membrane contains an oval aperture, which conducts the anterior interosseous artery from the anterior forearm to the posterior compartment. The posterior interosseous artery passes through a gap between the proximal border of the membrane and the oblique cord of the interosseous membrane.

Anteriorly, the flexor pollicis longus, flexor digitorum profundus, and pronator quadratus muscles attach to the interosseous membrane, while the supinator, abductor pollicis longus, and extensor pollicis brevis, longus, and indicis muscles attach posteriorly."}, {"name": "Structure", "text": "The interosseous membrane of the forearm is a thin, broad, fibrous membrane that extends between the shafts of the radius and ulna, uniting the two bones in a syndesmosis, or fibrous joint. Its fibers course distomedially."}, {"name": "Function", "text": "The interosseous membrane of the forearm provides attachment sites for the deep muscles of the forearm. Additionally, it acts in stabilizing the forearm, preventing migration of the radius from the ulna."}]

items.name: Common Flexor Tendon Sheath
items.info: [{"name": "Anatomical Relations", "text": "The common flexor tendon sheaths envelop the flexor tendons of the digits. There are two separate sheaths for the flexor digitorum superficialis and the flexor digitorum profundus. On occasion, the two sheaths are in communication with each other deep to the flexor retinaculum (Standring, 2016). \n\nThe proximal origin of the common flexor sheaths is 2.5 cm proximal to the flexor retinaculum and extends as far as the mid metacarpals. They are blind ended sacs; however, the sheath for the fifth digit is prolonged."}, {"name": "Structure", "text": "The common flexor sheath has an outer fibrous component and an inner double layered sheath of synovial membrane that is akin to a longitudinal bursa. The synovial layer is composed of an inner visceral layer and an outer parietal layer. The synovium produces a thin layer of lubricating fluid between the visceral and parietal layers which surround the tendons."}, {"name": "Function", "text": "The common flexor sheath provides a well-lubricated, smooth surface that reduces friction during movements of the tendons."}, {"name": "List of Clinical Correlates", "text": "\u2014Tendovaginitis"}, {"name": "References", "text": "Standring, S. (2016) Gray's Anatomy: The Anatomical Basis of Clinical Practice. Gray's Anatomy Series 41st edn.: Elsevier Limited."}]

items.info:
[{"name": "Structure", "text": "The prevertebral fascia is part of the deep investing cervical fascia. As the name suggests, is closely associated with the anterior aspect of the cervical vertebrae."}, {"name": "Anatomical Relations", "text": "The prevertebral fascia extends from the base of the skull, superiorly, to the mediastinum, inferiorly, where it blends with the anterior longitudinal ligament as far down as T4 vertebra (varies between C6 to T4). It covers the anterior surfaces of the cervical vertebral bodies and the longus capitis and colli muscles and extends laterally and posteriorly to cover the scalene muscles, splenius capitis, and levator scapulae. As the subclavian artery and brachial plexus emerge between the scalenus anterior and medius, it drags a portion of the prevertebral fascia with it as the axillary sheath. Posteriorly, the prevertebral fascia attaches to the spinous processes of the cervical vertebrae (Standring, 2016)."}, {"name": "Function", "text": "The prevertebral fascia ensheathes and protects the muscles and neurovasculature deep in the neck and allows fluid movements of the muscles over each other."}, {"name": "List of Clinical Correlates", "text": "—Compartment syndrome

—Endocarditis 

—Mediastinitis"}, {"name": "References", "text": "Standring, S. (2016) Gray's Anatomy: The Anatomical Basis of Clinical Practice, 41st ed. Elsevier Limited."}]

items.info: [{"name": "Structure", "text": "The superficial investing cervical fascia encircles the entire neck. It exists as one layer, deep to the subcutaneous tissue, however, it does divide to encapsulate the trapezius and sternocleidomastoid muscles."}, {"name": "Anatomical Relations", "text": "Superiorly, the superficial investing cervical fascia is fused to the periosteum over the occipital bone, mastoid process, and along the edge of the mandible. \n\nInferiorly, it is adhered to the periosteum of the acromion, clavicle, and manubrium. It has an attachment to aponeurotic fibers of platysma and the infrahyoid muscles (Standring, 2016)."}, {"name": "Function", "text": "The superficial investing cervical fascia supports the viscera of the neck, protects the neurovasculature, and act as dissection planes during surgery."}, {"name": "References", "text": "Standring, S. (2016) Gray's Anatomy: The Anatomical Basis of Clinical Practice, 41st ed. Elsevier Limited."}]

items.name: Buccopharyngeal Fascia
items.info: [{"name": "Structure", "text": "The buccopharyngeal fascia is part of the visceral division of the deep cervical fascia. It commences laterally as it fuses with the periosteum on the posterior alveolar process of the maxilla and the periosteum of the medial pterygoid plate of the sphenoid bone. The fascia travels posteriorly to cover the buccinator muscle and the lateral parts of the superior pharyngeal constrictor muscle before curving posteromedially to cover the back of the superior pharyngeal constrictor (Stecco & Hammer, 2014). It descends in the midline to cover the posterior aspect of middle and inferior pharyngeal constrictor muscles."}, {"name": "Function", "text": "The buccopharyngeal fascia anchors some of the fibers of buccinator muscle to enable coordination of the mouth and pharynx and playing a role in chewing and swallowing (Stecco & Hammer, 2014)."}, {"name": "References", "text": "Stecco, C. & Hammer, W. I. (2014) Functional Atlas of the Human Fascial System E-BookElsevier Health Sciences."}]

items.name: Antebrachial Fascia
items.info:
[{"name": "Anatomical Relations", "text": "The antebrachial fascia is attached to the olecranon, posterior border of the ulna, and the epicondyles of the humerus. Superiorly, it is continuous with the brachial fascia of the arm. Inferiorly the fascia is thickened and becomes the extensor retinaculum posteriorly and palmar carpal ligament anteriorly. 

Veins and nerves pierce the fascia to travel from the deep compartments of the forearm to reach superficial targets."}, {"name": "Structure", "text": "The antebrachial fascia is a dense fascia that is thickest posteriorly and inferiorly."}, {"name": "Function", "text": "The antebrachial fascia gives attachment to tendinous fibers of triceps brachii and biceps brachii. These attachments strengthen the antebrachial fascia. The antebrachial fascia completes the separation of the anterior and posterior muscular compartments of the forearm, which are separated by the interosseous membrane.

The anterior or posterior neuromuscular compartments of the forearm house muscles of similar function and common innervation. Muscles in the anterior compartment of the forearm are mainly flexors, while muscles in the posterior compartment are mainly extensors. The fascial compartments of the upper limb are important clinically because they contain and direct the flow and spread of infection and hemorrhages in the limb."}]
