Blood Plasma
items.info:
[{"name": "Quick Facts", "text": "Plasma is the fluid portion of the blood in which the particulate components are suspended. Plasma is to be distinguished from serum, which is the cell-free portion of the blood from which the fibrinogen has been separated in the process of clotting (Dorland, 2011)."}, {"name": "Composition", "text": "The blood plasma is the liquid component of the blood. It’s a straw-colored sticky fluid that constitutes 55% of blood’s volume. Ninety percent of the blood plasma is composed of water, while the remaining 10% is made up of molecules, such as nutrients, salts, respiratory gases, hormones and plasma proteins (Reece et al., 2014). The blood plasma contains ions such as sodium, magnesium, chloride, calcium, phosphate, potassium, and bicarbonate; nutrients such as sugars, amino acids, and lipids; waste products such as urea, carbon dioxide, and ammonia; hormones, vitamins, oxygen, and proteins such as albumin, fibrinogen globulins and prothrombin (Reece et al., 2014). Albumins account for 60% of all plasma proteins (Silverthorn et al., 2013)."}, {"name": "Function", "text": "The blood plasma suspends the formed elements (erythrocytes, leukocytes, and platelets) of the blood. It acts as a buffer between cells and the external environment (Silverthorn, 2016). The components of the blood plasma along with the blood cells are responsible for osmoregulation, transportation of molecules, and immune defense.

The water of blood plasma functions as a solvent. Blood electrolytes such as sodium, magnesium, chloride, calcium, phosphate, potassium, and bicarbonate are inorganic salts that are found as dissolved ions in the blood plasma. Blood electrolytes function to buffer the blood and maintain its pH at approximately 7.4. Ions in the blood plasma are involved in maintaining the blood’s osmotic balance, regulation of the cell’s membrane permeability, and muscle and nerve activity (Reece et al., 2014).

The plasma proteins primarily help maintain the osmotic balance between the blood and the interstitial fluid by acting as buffers against pH changes (Reece et al., 2014). They’re also involved in coagulation and defense against foreign invaders. They act as carriers and transport iron, steroid hormones, cholesterol, and drugs (Silverthorn et al., 2013).

—Albumin prevents water from diffusing out of the bloodstream into the extracellular matrix of the surrounding tissues. Albumin functions as a carrier protein. It binds and transports hormones such as thyroxine, metabolites, such as bilirubin, and drugs, such as barbiturates (Pawlina, 2016).

—Fibrinogen is the largest plasma protein that is involved in the process of blood clotting. It’s a clotting factor that helps plug leaks when a blood vessel is injured (Marieb, Wilhelm and Mallatt, 2012). 

—Globulins are blood proteins and antibodies. Blood proteins transport lipids, copper, and iron whereas antibodies bind antigens and mark them for phagocytosis by the T lymphocytes (Marieb, Wilhelm and Mallatt, 2012).

—Apolipoprotein is a blood plasma protein that binds lipids to transport them in the blood as they are insoluble in water (Reece et al., 2014). 

—Prothrombin is a plasma protein and the inactive form of thrombin. Thrombin is a protein that converts fibrinogen into fibrin that will form a blood clot during coagulation. 

—Transferrin is an iron-transporting blood protein that binds iron and carries it throughout the body (Silverthorn et al., 2013)."}, {"name": "References", "text": "Dorland, W. (2011) Dorland's Illustrated Medical Dictionary. 32nd edn. Philadelphia, USA: Elsevier Saunders.

Marieb, E. N., Wilhelm, P. B. and Mallatt, J. (2012) Human Anatomy. 14th edn.: Benjamin Cummings.

Pawlina, W. 2016. Histology: A text and atlas with correlated cell and molecular biology. 7th ed. Philadelphia: Wolters Kluwer.

Reece, J. B., Meyers, N., Urry, L. A., Cain, M. L., Wasserman, S. A., Minorsky, P. V., Jackson, R. B., Cooke, B. and Campbell, N. A. (2014) Campbell Biology. Pearson.

Silverthorn, D. U., Johnson, B. R., Ober, W. C., Garrison, C. W. and Silverthorn, A. C. (2013) Human Physiology: An Integrated Approach. Pearson Education."}]

items.name: Lamina of Fourth Cervical Vertebra
Sodium-potassium Pump
items.info:
[{"name": "Quick Facts", "text": "The sodium-potassium pump is an enzyme that spans the plasma membrane and hydrolyzes ATP to maintain the gradients of sodium (Na+) and potassium (K+) across the cell membrane; for each ATP hydrolyzed, three sodium ions are extruded from the cell and two potassium ions are brought in. The gradients are necessary for protein biosynthesis, maintenance of osmotic equilibrium, propagation of nerve impulses, and secondary transport of some molecules (e.g., glucose) across cell membranes (Dorland, 2011)."}, {"name": "Structure", "text": "The Sodium/Potassium pump is a highly specialized transmembrane ATP-dependent transport protein that is situated on the axolemma. It is one of the most vital pumps in neurons and can also be found in the cardiovascular and renal systems.

The following headings describe the role of the sodium/potassium pump in detail."}, {"name": "Resting Membrane Potential (RMP)", "text": "An electrical potential is the difference in ion (i.e., charged particles) concentration between one point and another. Resting membrane potential (RMP) is the charge difference across the plasma membrane and is typically about -70 millivolts (mV) in a “resting neuron.” It is a negative value since there are more negative ions on the inside of the membrane than on the outside. 

It is potential energy that can produce a current under the right circumstances. An electrical current is a flow of charged particles from one point to another. Gated channels are opened and closed by various stimuli, turning electrical currents on and off."}, {"name": "Neural Stimulation", "text": "When a neuron is stimulated, there is a disturbance in the membrane potential. It usually begins at a dendrite, then spreads across the cell body (or soma), and down the axon to the synapses on the terminal boutons. 

A stimulation (e.g., a chemical or ligand) binds to a ligand regulated sodium gate that opens, and so, there is an influx of Na+ into the cell. This results in the membrane voltage to be less negative, or “depolarized,” and as Na+ diffuses a short distance along the inside of the plasma membrane, a current travels from the point of stimulation to the cell’s trigger zone. This local change in voltage is called a “local potential,” and if it is strong enough, may elicit an action potential.

Sometimes the stimulus may make the membrane more negative or hyperpolarize the cell and less likely to produce an action potential."}, {"name": "Action Potential", "text": "An action potential is produced by voltage-regulated gates in the plasma membrane. The majority of the surface of the soma also has smaller numbers of gates to generate an action potential. The trigger zone is near the axon hillock and has enough gates to generate an action potential. If the excitatory local potential is strong enough to spread as far as the trigger zone and the local potential is about 55 mV, then the voltage regulated Na+ gates open quickly (then voltage regulated K+ gates more slowly) to generate an action potential. 

When the membrane potential reaches 0–50 mV (depending on the neuron), the Na+ gates begin closing. Outflow of K+ repolarizes or shifts the voltage back to be negative (in fact more negative than the usual resting potential so the membrane is hyperpolarized for a short time). Removal of K+ from the extracellular fluid by astrocytes restores the original resting potential (Splittgerber, 2018; Bear, Connors and Paradiso, 2007; Ross and Pawlina, 2006)."}, {"name": "Anatomical Relations", "text": "The Sodium/Potassium pumps are located in the plasma membrane."}, {"name": "Function", "text": "Although the sodium/potassium pump is involved in various physiological processes in the human body, including the contraction of cardiac muscle and reabsorption of water in the renal system, it plays a vital role in the generation of an action potential. 

Neurons in the brain use the Sodium/Potassium pump to reset the sodium and potassium concentrations, which are required to generate an action potential following the postsynaptic sodium flow. This enables the pump to be ready for the next cycle of action potential. 

The Sodium/Potassium pump pumps Na+ out of the cell and K+ into the cell. By doing so, they create a concentration gradient between Na+ and K+, thus, maintaining the variations in the chemical constitution between the intracellular and extracellular fluid. The pump keeps K+ concentration higher and Na+ concentration lower within the cell than in the extracellular fluid. Since these ions continuously leak across the membrane, the Sodium/Potassium pump compensates. 

Signals generated by a neuron upset the balance of Na+ and K+; therefore this pump works to restore equilibrium. 

The sodium/potassium pump accounts for about 70% of the energy (ATP) requirement of the nervous system and is why the nervous system demands so much glucose and oxygen (Ross and Pawlina, 2006; Bear, Connors and Paradiso, 2007; Splittgerber, 2018)."}, {"name": "References", "text": "Bear, M. F., Connors, B. W. and Paradiso, M. A. (2007) Neuroscience. Lippincott Williams & Wilkins.

Dorland, W. (2011) Dorland's Illustrated Medical Dictionary. 32nd edn. Philadelphia, USA: Elsevier Saunders.

Ross, M. H. and Pawlina, W. (2006) Histology: A text and atlas. Lippincott Williams & Wilkins.

Splittgerber, R. (2018) Snell's Clinical Neuroanatomy. Wolters Kluwer Health."}]

items.info:
[{"name": "Quick Facts", "text": "The sarcoplasmic reticulum is a special form of smooth endoplasmic reticulum found in association with the T tubules in the sarcoplasm of striated muscle and comprising a system of cisternae and tubules forming a plexus around each myofibril. It contains large numbers of calcium pumps and ryanodine receptors and is a storage compartment for calcium ions, which it releases in response to an action potential in the adjacent T tubule to cause muscular contraction (Dorland, 2011)."}, {"name": "Structure and/or Key Features", "text": "The sarcoplasmic reticulum (SR) is an organelle that consists of a network of loose flattened tubules with various compartments, many of which contain Ca2+. The two ends of the SR are wider, thus form terminal sacs called cisternae. Two cisternae of adjacent sarcoplasmic reticula and one transverse tubule form a functional unit called a triad, which operates to elicit the release of Ca2+ from SR stores (Maclennan and Zvaritch, 2011). 

The sarcoplasmic reticulum is not as well organized in cardiac muscle cells as it is in skeletal muscle cells. 

T tubules of cardiac muscle extend to the myofilaments at the level of the Z-line, between small terminal ends of the sarcoplasmic reticulum network. These terminal ends form a diad at the Z-line (Mescher, 2013; Ross and Pawlina, 2016)."}, {"name": "Anatomical Relations", "text": "Sarcoplasmic reticulum is a specialized type of smooth endoplasmic reticulum found in skeletal muscle. It forms a network of tubules that extend through a muscle fiber. The flattened tubules surround, but do not make direct contact with the myofibrils in a muscle fiber."}, {"name": "Function", "text": "The sarcoplasmic reticulum functions as an intracellular calcium store. Depolarization of the sarcoplasmic reticulum membrane results in the release of calcium ions (Ca2+). This release of calcium ions triggers the cascade required for contraction."}, {"name": "List of Clinical Correlates", "text": "—Fatigue

—Central core disease"}, {"name": "References", "text": "Dorland, W. (2011) Dorland's Illustrated Medical Dictionary. 32nd edn. Philadelphia, USA: Elsevier Saunders.

Maclennan, D. H. and Zvaritch, E. (2011) 'Mechanistic models for muscle diseases and disorders originating in the sarcoplasmic reticulum', Biochim Biophys Acta, 1813(5), pp. 948-64.

Mescher, A. (2013) Junqueira's Basic Histology: Text and Atlas. 13th edn.: McGraw-Hill Education.

Ross, M. H. and Pawlina, W. (2016) Histology: A Text and Atlas. Wolters Kluwer Health."}]

items.name: Collecting Duct
items.info:
[{"name": "Quick Facts", "text": "The renal collecting duct is the arcuate renal tubule, straight collecting tubule, and papillary duct considered together (Dorland, 2011)."}, {"name": "Structure and/or Key Features", "text": "The distal convoluted tubules of nephrons drain their renal filtrate into larger vessels known as collecting ducts. Collecting ducts are approximately 20 mm in length and pass from the cortex and medulla to the renal pelvis. 

In chronological order, the segments of the collecting duct system include connecting tubules, initial collecting tubules, cortical collecting ducts, medullary collecting ducts, and papillary ducts. The connecting tubules of multiple nephrons merge and drain renal filtrate into cortical collecting ducts.

Cortical collecting ducts are located in the cortex, while medullary collecting ducts travel through the medulla. Cortical collecting ducts have a cuboidal cell lining which gradually becomes taller and forms columnar cells as the ducts descend through the medulla. 

The two primary cells of the collecting ducts are principal cells and intercalated cells. Characterized by their pale cytoplasm, principal cells increase in size from the cortex down to the papilla. Intercalated cells have an electron-dense cytoplasm which gives them a darker appearance. These cells are additionally distinguished by the presence of modified microvilli on their luminal surface. Intercalated cells become sparser in the medullary collecting ducts, eventually leaving only principal cells in the papillary collecting ducts (Johnson, Feehally and Floege, 2014)."}, {"name": "Anatomical Relations", "text": "Collecting ducts extend from the cortex, through the medulla, to the tip of the papilla. The ducts progressively anastomose as they pass from the cortex to the papilla."}, {"name": "Function", "text": "The collecting duct plays a pivotal role in fluid electrolyte balance. Specifically, the principal cells of the collecting ducts reabsorb Na+ and water. The darker staining intercalated cells secrete protons and HCO3-. In response to the hormone vasopressin (antidiuretic hormone), the collecting duct reabsorbs water, while in response to the hormone aldosterone, the collecting duct reabsorbs sodium."}, {"name": "List of Clinical Correlates", "text": "—Nephrogenic diabetes insipidus 

—Liddle’s syndrome

—Pseudohypoaldosteronism type 1"}, {"name": "References", "text": "Dorland, W. (2011) Dorland's Illustrated Medical Dictionary. 32nd edn. Philadelphia, USA: Elsevier Saunders.

Johnson, R. J., Feehally, J. & Floege, J. (2014) Comprehensive Clinical NephrologyElsevier Saunders."}]

items.name: Cochlear Duct
items.info:
[{"name": "Quick Facts", "text": "The cochlear duct is a spirally arranged membranous tube in the bony canal of the cochlea along its outer wall, lying between the scala tympani below and the scala vestibuli above (Dorland, 2011)."}, {"name": "Structure and/or Key Feature(s)", "text": "The cochlear duct is one of the main cochlear canals. It is formed by the division of the bony cochlear canal by the osseous spiral lamina (a fine ridge-like projection of bone from the modiolus).

The cochlear duct is situated between the scala vestibuli and scala tympani and is triangular in cross-section. While the scala vestibuli and scala tympani are components of the bony labyrinth, the cochlear duct is primarily a component of the membranous labyrinth.

The cochlear duct extends the length of the bony cochlea, from the cupula in the apex of the cochlea (the lagena) to the ductus reuniens of the saccule of the vestibule. 

The borders of the cochlear duct are formed from a variety of structures. At the outermost border of the cochlear duct, there is a highly vascularized periosteal thickening known as the spiral ligament. The edges of this spiral ligament loop around to attach to two different membranes, which form the superior and inferior borders of the cochlear duct. These membranes are known as vestibular (or Reissner’s) membrane and the basilar membrane, respectively. These membranes stretch longitudinally across the superior and inferior aspect of the cochlear duct to join the osseous spiral lamina positioned opposite the spiral ligament and completes the borders of the canal. The stria vascularis overlies the spiral ligament, projecting inwards to face the cochlear duct.

The cochlear duct houses numerous essential structures which function in harmony to detect sound vibrations, which is processed into neural signals that are carried to the respective processing center within the cerebrum. These structures include the vestibular and basilar membranes, as well as the stria vascularis, tectorial membrane, and spiral organ (of Corti). The cochlear canal is filled with a fluid known as endolymph which has a unique ionic composition that plays a very important role in the above process to detect sound."}, {"name": "Anatomical Relations", "text": "The cochlear duct is interjacent between the scala vestibuli superiorly, and the scala tympani inferiorly. The spiral ligament (along with the stria vascularis) forms the outer border of the cochlear duct. This communicates with the basilar lamina/membrane inferiorly and the vestibular membrane superiorly to form the inferior and superior borders of the cochlear duct. These membranes join the osseous spiral lamina to enclose the cochlear duct, thus separating the endolymph of the cochlear duct from the perilymph of the scala vestibuli and scala tympani."}, {"name": "Function", "text": "The cochlear duct houses a variety of structures which are crucial to the transduction of sound waves to neural impulses for auditory detection. Vibrations are transferred from the middle ear to the basilar membrane via the oval window, which disrupts the endolymph. The endolymph surrounding specialized components of the hair cells of the spiral organ (of Corti) is disturbed, which activates mechanoelectrical transduction channels, resulting in the generation of neural signals within cochlear nerve fibers. The signal is then carried along the cochlear nerve which is transmitted back to the processing center in the cerebrum."}, {"name": "List of Clinical Correlates", "text": "—Cochlear hypoplasia"}, {"name": "References", "text": "Dorland, W. (2011) Dorland's Illustrated Medical Dictionary. 32nd edn. Philadelphia, USA: Elsevier Saunders."}]

items.name: Pulpal Sensory Nerves
items.info: [{"name": "Quick Facts", "text": "The pulpal nerves of the mandibular teeth are sensory nerves that transmit sensation to the inferior alveolar nerve."}, {"name": "Structure and/or Key Feature(s)", "text": "Dental pulp has an extensive innervation network consisting of unmyelinated postganglionic vasoconstrictor sympathetic nerve fibers, and myelinated and unmyelinated sensory nerve fibers. Sensory nerve fibers that arise from the inferior alveolar nerve (specific to mandibular first molar) and that longitudinally traverse the pulp are known as pulpal sensory nerves. The pulpal sensory nerves subsequently branch into the subodontoblastic plexus in the pulp cavity (Standring, 2016)."}, {"name": "Anatomical Relations", "text": "The pulpal sensory nerves travel longitudinally through the pulp and ramify as the subodontoblastic nerve plexus in the pulp cavity (Standring, 2016)."}, {"name": "Function", "text": "The pulpal sensory nerves transmit pain signals from the subodontoblastic nerve plexus of Raschkow to the trigeminal ganglion via the inferior alveolar nerve (Standring, 2016)."}, {"name": "References", "text": "Standring, S. (2016) Gray's Anatomy: The Anatomical Basis of Clinical Practice. Gray's Anatomy Series 41 edn.: Elsevier Limited."}]

items.name: Enterocyte (Duodenum)
items.info:
[{"name": "Quick Facts", "text": "An enterocyte is an epithelial cell of the intestinal wall (Dorland, 2011)."}, {"name": "Structure/Morphology", "text": "Enterocytes are simple, tall columnar epithelial cells with a nucleus positioned in the basal domain of the cell. Microvilli extend from the apical surface. Collectively, the microvilli of enterocytes are called a “striated border.”

Apical borders of adjacent enterocytes are joined by tight junctions and permit selective absorption of substances from the intestinal lumen. The lateral surfaces of the enterocytes exhibit cytoplasmic processes that interdigitate with those of adjacent cells thus increasing the amount of the plasmalemma housing transport enzymes.

The cytoplasm of enterocytes also exhibits specializations of an absorptive cell. Elongated mitochondria and smooth/agranular endoplasmic reticulum (sER) are concentrated in the apical cytoplasm.

The cytoplasm of enterocytes also exhibits specializations of a secretory cell. Stacks of Golgi cisternae are near the nucleus accompanied by free ribosomes and rough/granular endoplasmic reticulum (rER). Small secretory vesicles congregate at the apical border of the cell."}, {"name": "Function", "text": "The primary function of the enterocytes is absorption. The striated border increases the surface area for absorption as much as 600 times. 

Lateral interdigitations of the plasmalemma of adjacent enterocytes expand and enlarge the intercellular compartment during absorption of solutes, water and lipids.

Mitochondria provide the energy required for transport processes and the sER are involved in the absorption of fatty acids and glycerol.

Enterocytes are also secretory cells, primarily producing glycoprotein enzymes that will be reinserted into the apical membrane. They also secrete water and electrolytes (mainly those enterocytes in the intestinal glands to balance water absorption across the enterocytes lining the villi), which maintains a constant liquified intestinal chyme."}, {"name": "References", "text": "Dorland, W. (2011) Dorland's Illustrated Medical Dictionary. 32nd edn. Philadelphia, USA: Elsevier Saunders."}]

items.name: Minor Renal Calyx
items.info:
[{"name": "Quick Facts", "text": "The minor renal calyx is the smaller renal calices that receive urine from the renal papillae and open into the major calices (Dorland, 2011)."}, {"name": "Structure and/or Key Feature(s)", "text": "The minor renal calyces (minor calyx is singular) are described as small chambers of the kidneys, through which urine passes. Specifically, renal filtrate from the renal papilla drain into minor calyces, and into major calyces thereafter. There are approximately 5–11 minor calyces in the kidney, each of which are considered funnel-shaped expansions of the upper urinary tract.

Identified as cup-shaped structures, the minor calyces are composed of a transitional epithelium, an underlying lamina propria, and smooth muscle (Dudek, 2006). The smooth muscle layer of the calyces undergoes rhythmic peristaltic movement to facilitate the flow of renal filtrate."}, {"name": "Anatomical Relations", "text": "The minor renal calyces are positioned at the apex of the renal pyramids. Together with the major renal calyces, they form the renal pelvis."}, {"name": "Function", "text": "Pacemaker cells in the smooth muscle layer of the minor calyces are responsible for initiating peristalsis and propulsion of urine into the major calyces."}, {"name": "References", "text": "Dorland, W. (2011) Dorland's Illustrated Medical Dictionary. 32nd edn. Philadelphia, USA: Elsevier Saunders.

Dudek, R. W. (2006) High-yield KidneyLippincott Williams & Wilkins."}]

items.name: Parietal Epithelial Cell
items.info: [{"name": "Quick Facts", "text": "The parietal layer of the glomerular capsule is composed of a simple squamous epithelium."}, {"name": "Structure and/or Key Feature(s)", "text": "The parietal layer of the glomerular (Bowman\u2019s) capsule contains a simple squamous epithelium (Ovalle, Nahirney and Netter, 2013)."}, {"name": "Anatomical Relations", "text": "Parietal epithelial cells of the glomerular capsule form the parietal layer of the glomerular capsule. At the urinary pole of the renal corpuscle, the squamous parietal epithelial cells abruptly transition to cuboidal epithelial cells of the proximal convoluted tubule."}, {"name": "References", "text": "Ovalle, W. K., Nahirney, P. C. and Netter, F. H. (2013) Netter's Essential Histology. ClinicalKey 2012: Elsevier Saunders."}]

items.name: Mucosa
items.info:
[{"name": "Quick Facts", "text": "The mucosa is the mucous lining of various hollow structures, facing the lumen, comprising, in many locations, the epithelium, basement membrane, lamina propria mucosae, and lamina muscularis mucosae (Dorland, 2011)."}, {"name": "Structure/Morphology", "text": "The mucosa lines the luminal surface of the large intestine and has a smooth, pale appearance. It consists of luminal surface epithelium, the lamina propria, and the muscularis mucosae (aids in the expulsion of intestinal crypt content/secretions particularly mucus secreted from goblet cells). 

The luminal surface of the transverse colon is covered with simple columnar epithelium and goblet cells. The columnar cells have short microvilli located at the apex of their cell surface and tight cell junctions between the cells. The goblet cells are interspersed between the columnar cells. Intestinal crypts (or glands of Lieberkühn) are tubular pits of the mucosa and lie perpendicular to the lumen. They open directly into the lumen through small circular openings. The columnar epithelium extends into the crypts. Stem cells and neuroendocrine cells are also present in the crypts and are usually located near the base of the crypts (Standring, 2016). Stems cells continually divide to replace mucosal epithelial cells above them as they move towards the luminal surface and are shed several days later.

The mucosal regions adjacent to the lymphoid follicles contain microfold cells (M cells). These cells may be cuboidal or flattened and have widely spaced microfolds, rather than microvilli. They aim to take up foreign particles/antigens in the gut and pass them to the lymphoid tissue (Standring, 2016).

The lamina propria forms the intermediate layer between the epithelium and the muscularis mucosae and is made of loose connective tissue. It houses a diverse abundance of different cell types, such as connective tissue cells and immune cells, such as eosinophils, mast cells, and macrophages. It also contains capillaries, nerve fibers, and lymphatic vessels."}, {"name": "Anatomical Relations", "text": "The mucosa faces the gastrointestinal lumen and is in contact with its contents. It is superjacent to the muscularis mucosae and the submucosal layer."}, {"name": "Function", "text": "The mucosa provides a barrier-style protection against diffusion of unwanted particles or pathogens from the lumen to the internal tissues, as well as generating an immune response if the epithelial barrier is broken.

The columnar cells are involved in transepithelial transport functions and the tight junctions serve as a physical barrier that prevents diffusion of content from the gut lumen across the epithelial wall. The goblet cells secrete mucins, which forms and maintains the protective mucus blanket (Specian and Oliver, 1991). Microfold cells allow particle transport from the lumen to the lamina propria, where the immune cells can become involved.

In the intestinal crypts, the stem cells are capable of regenerating the different types of intestinal cells. They mitotically divide and provide cells which drift towards the intestinal luminal surface and primarily differentiate into columnar or goblet cells. The neuroendocrine cells secrete various chemokines and cytokines.

The lamina propria has two main roles. It provides structural support to the epithelium, forming part of the protective barrier separating pathogenic contact with the internal tissues. Additionally, due to its dense population of macrophages and lymphoid cells, it can generate effective immune responses if needed."}, {"name": "List of Clinical Correlates", "text": "—Crohn's disease

—Ulcerative Colitis

—Mucosa associated lymphoid tissue (MALT) lymphoma"}, {"name": "References", "text": "Dorland, W. (2011) Dorland's Illustrated Medical Dictionary. 32nd edn. Philadelphia, USA: Elsevier Saunders.

Specian, R. D. and Oliver, M. G. (1991) 'Functional biology of intestinal goblet cells', Am J Physiol, 260(2 Pt 1), pp. C183-93.

Standring, S. (2016) Gray's Anatomy: The Anatomical Basis of Clinical Practice. Gray's Anatomy Series 41st edition edn.: Elsevier Limited."}]

Urethral Artery
