items.name: Zona Fasciculata of Cortex
items.info:
[{"name": "Quick Facts", "text": "The zona fasciculata is the thick middle layer of the suprarenal cortex; it is the major source of glucocorticoids (Dorland, 2011)."}, {"name": "Structure and/or Key Feature(s)", "text": "The cortex of the suprarenal gland is comprised of three distinct morphological zones, the zona glomerulosa, zona fasciculata, and the zona reticularis. These lie above the medulla of the suprarenal gland. The zona fasciculata is the large zone of the suprarenal cortex and composes nearly 75% of the cortical mass. 

The zona fasciculata is made of cells which are large and polyhedral. These are aligned together to form linear columns, which run the depth of the zona fasciculata. Long sinusoids from the capsular plexus travel alongside these cellular columns, supplying the cortex throughout. The sinusoidal paths end as they come together in the zona reticularis to form a vascular network.

Inside the cells of the zona fasciculata, prominent organelles include a large amount of smooth endoplasmic reticulum present in the basophilic cytoplasm, as well as a large number of lipid droplets. These store cholesterol, the main precursor of steroid biosynthesis. These are important organelles as they relate to the cell’s primary function (Pocock, Richards and Richards, 2013)."}, {"name": "Anatomical Relations", "text": "The zona fasciculata is the intermediate layer of the suprarenal cortex, surrounding by the zona glomerulosa on the outside and the zona reticularis on the inside."}, {"name": "Function", "text": "The primary function of the cortex is to produce steroid hormones. In particular, the zona fasciculata secretes glucocorticoids, such as cortisol. These glucocorticoids are involved in, anti-inflammatory and immunosuppressive processes. They also have a physiological role in the metabolism of carbohydrates and proteins."}, {"name": "Clinical Correlates", "text": "—Cushing’s syndrome"}, {"name": "References", "text": "Dorland, W. (2011) Dorland's Illustrated Medical Dictionary. 32nd edn. Philadelphia, USA: Elsevier Saunders.

Pocock, G., Richards, C. D. & Richards, D. A. (2013) Human Physiology, 4 edition. OUP Oxford."}]

items.name: Thin Myofilament (Uncontracted Smooth Muscle)
items.info:
[{"name": "Quick Facts", "text": "The thin filament is one of the thin contractile myofilaments in a muscle cell, composed mainly of actin (Dorland, 2011)."}, {"name": "Structure and/or Key Features", "text": "Thin myofilaments are composed of actin, tropomyosin, and caldesmon. 

Actin is the main component of the thin myofilament. It is a long filamentous (F-actin) polymer consisting of two strands of globular (G-actin) monomers twisted around each other to form a double helical formation about 1 μm long and 8 nm wide. Each G-actin monomer has a binding site for myosin (Mescher, 2013).

Tropomyosin is a long (about 40 nm), thin molecule consisting of two polypeptide chains and bound head to tail to form filaments that coil over the two actin strands. Each tropomyosin molecule extends along a length of seven G-actin molecules (Mescher, 2013).

Unlike skeletal muscle, smooth muscle cells do not contain troponin (Ovalle, Nahirney and Netter, 2013). Instead, caldesmon interacts with tropomyosin forming a caldesmon-tropomyosin complex, which regulates the interaction of actin with myosin. 

In relaxed smooth muscle, the caldesmon-tropomyosin complex blocks the myosin binding sites on the actin filaments. This is controlled by regulatory molecules (such as calmodulin) that are dependent on Ca2+. Calmodulin binds to Ca2+ creating a Ca2+-calmodulin complex. This complex binds to caldesmon and releases it from actin, thus exposing the myosin binding sites (Ross and Pawlina, 2016; Vetterkind and Morgan, 2012)."}, {"name": "Anatomical Relations", "text": "The bulk of the smooth muscle sarcoplasm contains thin myofilaments of the contractile apparatus. They are attached to cytoplasmic densities or dense bodies (similar to Z lines of skeletal muscle fibers) located at the cell membrane and distributed throughout the sarcoplasm linked to intermediate filaments."}, {"name": "Function", "text": "Muscle contraction results from the binding of myosin to actin myofilaments, allowing myosin to function as a motor that drives myofilament sliding and creating movement."}, {"name": "References", "text": "Dorland, W. (2011) Dorland's Illustrated Medical Dictionary. 32nd edn. Philadelphia, USA: Elsevier Saunders.

Mescher, A. (2013) Junqueira's Basic Histology: Text and Atlas. 13th edn.: McGraw-Hill Education.

Ovalle, W. K., Nahirney, P. C. and Netter, F. H. (2013) Netter's Essential Histology. ClinicalKey 2012: Elsevier Saunders.

Ross, M. H. and Pawlina, W. (2016) Histology: A Text and Atlas. Wolters Kluwer Health.

Vetterkind, S. and Morgan, K. G. (2012) 'Chapter 87 - Regulation of Smooth Muscle Contraction', in Hill, J.A. and Olson, E.N. (eds.) Muscle. Boston/Waltham: Academic Press, pp. 1173-1180."}]

items.name: Rough Endoplasmic Reticulum (Anterosuperior Cut)
items.info:
[{"name": "Quick Facts", "text": "The rough endoplasmic reticulum is a region of the endoplasmic reticulum that bears large numbers of ribosomes on the outer surface of its membrane and is specialized for protein synthesis and folding (Dorland, 2011)."}, {"name": "Structure and/or Key Feature(s)", "text": "The endoplasmic reticulum is a vast membranous network throughout the cell and is the largest organelle in the cell. It consists of sacs, cisterns (or passageways) interconnecting tubules and comes in two forms that each can extend the full extent of the cell cytoplasm. 

One form is called rough endoplasmic reticulum (rER). It’s a network of flattened membranous sacs termed cisternae. It’s also known as granular endoplasmic reticulum (gER), because it has ribosomes and/or polyribosomes associated with the cytosolic side of the membrane. These ribosomes attached to the external face of the membranes of the rough endoplasmic reticulum are attached only when a protein is being made. They become detached after the protein is completed (Ross and Pawlina, 2006; Ovalle, Nahirney and Netter, 2013; McKinley, O'Loughlin and Pennefather-O'Brien, 2016)."}, {"name": "Anatomical Relations", "text": "The rough endoplasmic reticulum (rER) is continuous with the membrane of the nuclear envelope."}, {"name": "Function", "text": "The rough endoplasmic reticulum possesses enzymes and protein complexes. Its protein complexes function as molecular chaperones which guide the nascent (newly formed) protein folding, inhibit aggregation, and monitor the quality of the proteins within the rough endoplasmic reticulum. 

Proteins that are synthesized within the rough endoplasmic reticulum are either destined to become:

- intracellularly stored, such as in lysosomes and specific granules of leukocytes; 

- intracellularly stored prior to exocytosis, such as in exocrine cells;

- incorporated as integral membrane proteins into the plasmalemma. 

The rough endoplasmic reticulum also exhibits a mechanism that prevents faulty proteins that did not fold or assemble properly from being forwarded to other organelles or for secretion. This mechanism is known as the endoplasmic reticulum associated degradation. With this mechanism, unsalvageable proteins translocate back into the cytosol, become conjugated with a regulatory protein known as ubiquitin and are eventually degraded by proteasomes (Mescher, 2013). 

The region of the cytoplasm actively synthesizing proteins stains intensely with basic dyes due to the presence of RNA. Large clumps of rough endoplasmic reticulum in large motor neurons are called Nissl bodies or Nissl substance (Ross and Pawlina, 2006)."}, {"name": "Clinical Correlates", "text": "If the endoplasmic reticulum is stressed, it may activate the “unfolded protein response” (UPR) due to abnormal proteins accumulating within the cistern of the endoplasmic reticulum. The UPR attempts to restore normal function by the endoplasmic reticulum but dysfunction of the UPR can lead to a number of neurodegenerative diseases (Ovalle, Nahirney and Netter, 2013)."}, {"name": "References", "text": "Dorland, W. (2011) Dorland's Illustrated Medical Dictionary. 32nd edn. Philadelphia, USA: Elsevier Sauders.

McKinley, M. P., O'Loughlin, V. D. and Pennefather-O'Brien, E. E. (2016) Human Anatomy. 5th edn.: McGraw-Hill Education.

Mescher, A. (2013) Junqueira's Basic Histology: Text and Atlas. 13th edn.: McGraw-Hill Education.

Ovalle, W. K., Nahirney, P. C. and Netter, F. H. (2013) Netter's Essential Histology. ClinicalKey 2012: Elsevier Saunders.

Ross, M. H. and Pawlina, W. (2006) Histology: A text and atlas. Lippincott Williams & Wilkins."}]

items.name: Cell Membrane
items.info:
[{"name": "Quick Facts", "text": "The cell membrane is the structure enveloping a cell, enclosing the cytoplasm and forming a selective permeability barrier; it consists of a lipid bilayer with integral and peripheral proteins and contains channels and pumps to transport substances across the membrane, as well as receptors to receive stimuli from the external environment and transduce them into intracellular signals (Dorland, 2011)."}, {"name": "Structure and/or Key Feature(s)", "text": "The cell membrane (or plasmalemma) is a bi-layered membrane, containing primarily phospholipids, cholesterol, and protein molecules. About 7.5-10 nm in width, it can have integral proteins attached to either the internal or the external surface of the bilayer. 

Collections of proteins attached to a membrane varies depending on cell type and subcellular location and they are both a structurally and functionally diverse group of molecules (Lowe, Anderson and Anderson, 2018).

The external surface of the cell membrane contains a carbohydrate-rich region termed the glycocalyx which links to cell membrane proteins and lipids (Ross and Pawlina, 2016; Ovalle, Nahirney and Netter, 2013; McKinley, O'Loughlin and Pennefather-O'Brien, 2016)."}, {"name": "Anatomical Relations", "text": "The cell membrane is the external boundary of the cell."}, {"name": "Function", "text": "The cell membrane is the barrier between the very stable internal environment of the cell and the external environment. It allows the transfer of materials across the cell membrane. Oxygen, nutrients, waste products, and other materials, pass in and out of the cell through the cell membrane using a very detailed set of transport processes. Bulk transfer of material occurs through the cell membrane. The bulk intake of materials is called endocytosis and the release of bulk materials is exocytosis. Both processes involve different proteins and other molecules that associate with the cell membrane.

The integral proteins perform very important functions:

—form intercellular junctions;

—create pumps or channels to allow ions and molecules to go in and out of the cell;

—serve as receptors;

—act as enzymes on the surface of the cell;

—act in cell recognition. 

The glycocalyx plays a role in cell recognition and attachments to other cells and extracellular molecules (Ross and Pawlina, 2016; Ovalle, Nahirney and Netter, 2013; McKinley, O'Loughlin and Pennefather-O'Brien, 2016)."}, {"name": "List of Clinical Correlates", "text": "Cystic fibrosis is an inherited disease and is partly due to a defect in the proteins that affect chloride ion (Cl-) channels within the cell membrane. 

Many glycoproteins and glycolipids in the cell membrane act as receptors that mediate various cell activities, cell adhesions, and responses to chemical messengers. Several diseases are a result of defective receptors e.g., target cells of some hormones do not respond because they lack the relevant, competent receptors (McKinley, O'Loughlin and Pennefather-O'Brien, 2016)."}, {"name": "References", "text": "Dorland, W. (2011) Dorland's Illustrated Medical Dictionary. 32nd edn. Philadelphia, USA: Elsevier Saunders.

Lowe, J. S., Anderson, P. G. and Anderson, S. I. (2018) Stevens & Lowe's Human Histology- E-Book. 5 edn.: Elsevier Health Sciences.

McKinley, M. P., O'Loughlin, V. D. and Pennefather-O'Brien, E. E. (2016) Human Anatomy. 5th edn.: McGraw-Hill Education.

Ovalle, W. K., Nahirney, P. C. and Netter, F. H. (2013) Netter's Essential Histology. ClinicalKey 2012: Elsevier Saunders.

Ross, M. H. and Pawlina, W. (2016) Histology: A Text and Atlas. Wolters Kluwer Health."}]

items.name: Diploic Veins
Transport Vesicle
items.info:
[{"name": "Quick Facts", "text": "A transport vesicle is a vesicle, coated with clathrin or coat protein (COP), that carries substances between intracellular compartments (Dorland, 2011)."}, {"name": "Structure and/or Key Feature(s)", "text": "Proteins synthesized by the endoplasmic reticulum are packaged into a transport vesicle. That transport vesicle then enters the “cis face” of the Golgi complex and the components or the products pass from one cisterna to the next via a chain of transport vesicles through the entire Golgi complex. They are then repackaged into a secretory vesicle at the “trans face” (Ross and Pawlina, 2006)."}, {"name": "Anatomical Relations", "text": "Transport vesicles are located entering the “cis face” of the Golgi complex and between cisternae of the Golgi complex."}, {"name": "Function", "text": "Proteins synthesized by the endoplasmic reticulum are packaged into a transport vesicle. That transport vesicle then enters the “cis face” of the Golgi complex and the components or the products pass from one cisterna to the next via a chain of transport vesicles through the entire Golgi complex. They are then repackaged into a secretory vesicle at the “trans face” (Ross and Pawlina, 2006).

Some transport vesicles leave the “trans face” and distribute proteins to a number of intercellular destinations (Ross and Pawlina, 2006)."}, {"name": "References", "text": "Dorland, W. (2011) Dorland's Illustrated Medical Dictionary. 32nd edn. Philadelphia, USA: Elsevier Saunders.

Ross, M. H. and Pawlina, W. (2006) Histology: A text and atlas. Lippincott Williams & Wilkins."}]

items.name: Myenteric Plexus (Duodenum)
items.info:
[{"name": "Quick Facts", "text": "The myenteric plexus is a nerve plexus that is part of the enteric plexus and is within the tunica muscularis (Dorland, 2011)."}, {"name": "Structure/Morphology", "text": "The myenteric (Auerbach’s) plexus is a network of thin bundles of axons and neurons, which may be grouped as small ganglionic clusters. It lies between the inner circular and outer longitudinal layers of the muscular layer (muscularis externa) of the small intestine. The myenteric plexus arises from the periarterial plexus that follows the superior and inferior mesenteric arteries and their terminal branches. All components of the myenteric plexus are continuous with the inner circular muscle nerve fiber bundles, which go on to synapse with the ganglionated and non-ganglionated plexuses of the submucosa. Both the myenteric and the submucosal plexuses make up the enteric (or intrinsic) nervous system.

The enteric nervous system is unique to the digestive system and is autonomic in nature. It extends the entire length of the gastrointestinal tract and is composed of three types of neurons (Standring, 2016).

—Sensory neurons transmit information from receptors in the mucosa and muscle of the gut wall, which respond to mechanical, chemical, thermal, and osmotic stimuli. They project information to the interneurons.

—Motor neurons control the motility and secretions in the gut and may be inhibitory or excitatory.

—Interneurons go between the sensory and motor neurons, thus integrating the information between the two.

The enteric nervous system may function autonomously; however, it does communicate with the central nervous system via parasympathetic and sympathetic fibers. Cross connections between the two allow information from the gut to be relayed to the CNS, and vice versa. Generally, sympathetic inputs cause inhibition of secretions and motor activity and contraction of sphincters and blood vessels (fight or flight response). Parasympathetic stimulation of the enteric nervous system promotes secretions and motor activity and dilation of the sphincters and blood vessels (rest and digest response) (Standring, 2016; Costa, Brookes and Hennig, 2000).

The interstitial cells of Cajal are flat, thin, branched cells are linked to the smooth muscle cells via gap junctions. They overlap with the myenteric plexus, and they are believed to act as pacemakers for myogenic contraction of the muscular layer, modulating the electrical slow wave activity to alter the rhythm of intestine contractions."}, {"name": "Key Features/Anatomical Relations", "text": "The myenteric plexus is situated between the two muscular layers; superjacent to the inner circular smooth muscle layer and subjacent to the outer longitudinal smooth muscle layer."}, {"name": "Function", "text": "The myenteric plexus houses most of the enteric neurons with motor function. These act on the different effector cells within the intestinal system. In conjunction with the interstitial cells of Cajal, this enables the coordinated muscular movements of the intestines, and contributes to immune and endocrine functions (Standring, 2016)."}, {"name": "References", "text": "Costa, M., Brookes, S. J. and Hennig, G. W. (2000) 'Anatomy and physiology of the enteric nervous system', Gut, 47 Suppl 4(Suppl 4), pp. iv15-iv26.

Dorland, W. (2011) Dorland's Illustrated Medical Dictionary. 32nd edn. Philadelphia, USA: Elsevier Saunders.

Standring, S. (2016) Gray's Anatomy: The Anatomical Basis of Clinical Practice. Gray's Anatomy Series 41st edition edn.: Elsevier Limited."}]

items.name: Golgi Complex (Posterior)
items.info:
[{"name": "Quick Facts", "text": "The Golgi complex is an intracellular compartment of eukaryotes, occupying the perinuclear region and consisting of a number of stacked, flattened sacs with associated tubules and vesicles. Its primary function is to process substances synthesized in the endoplasmic reticulum; in addition it synthesizes some carbohydrates. Transport vesicles from the endoplasmic reticulum fuse with the Golgi complex at the cis face, their cargo is processed while passing through the cisternae, and the processed products are transported from the trans face to the trans-Golgi network for sorting and packaging. The mechanism by which cargo moves through the Golgi complex is not clear; one model proposes transport between cisternae by vesicular budding and fusion, while another proposes dynamic remodeling and recycling so that the cisternae themselves change in composition and move in a cis-to-trans direction (Dorland, 2011)."}, {"name": "Structure and/or Key Feature(s)", "text": "The Golgi complex or Golgi apparatus is a crescent shaped, parallel stack of membrane-limited tubules or cisternae. It is closely associated with small vesicles involved in vesicular transport. The Golgi complex is very well developed in secretory cells. The Golgi complex exhibits structural polarity and has a “cis face” or an entry face (which is the convex part of the complex) and a “trans face” or an exit face (Ross and Pawlina, 2006; Ovalle, Nahirney and Netter, 2013; McKinley, O'Loughlin and Pennefather-O'Brien, 2016)."}, {"name": "Anatomical Relations", "text": "The Golgi complex is closely associated with the nucleus and the “cis face” is adjacent to the rough endoplasmic reticulum."}, {"name": "Function", "text": "The Golgi complex accepts proteins and various other molecules synthesized by the endoplasmic reticulum. Each cistern of the Golgi complex contains different types of enzymes and so perform different enzymatic reactions. 

As some proteins move within the Golgi cisternae, carbohydrates and lipids are added to these proteins to form glycoproteins and glycolipids, respectively. In addition, proteins are added to lipids to form lipoproteins. Some proteins are isolated to be included in new plasmalemma.

As these molecules pass further through the Golgi complex, they are sorted and repackaged into a secretory vesicle. These secretory molecules are either destined to become lysosomes, migrate to the plasmalemma, or exported outside of the cell. 

The Golgi apparatus is involved in making carbohydrates (Ross and Pawlina, 2006; Ovalle, Nahirney and Netter, 2013; McKinley, O'Loughlin and Pennefather-O'Brien, 2016)."}, {"name": "List of Clinical Correlates", "text": "Atrophy of the Golgi complex and subsequent functional errors in specific neurons and loss of these neurons in the brain has been implicated in Alzheimer’s disease (Ovalle, Nahirney and Netter, 2013)."}, {"name": "References", "text": "Dorland, W. (2011) Dorland's Illustrated Medical Dictionary. 32nd edn. Philadelphia, USA: Elsevier Saunders.

McKinley, M. P., O'Loughlin, V. D. and Pennefather-O'Brien, E. E. (2016) Human Anatomy. 5th edn.: McGraw-Hill Education.

Ovalle, W. K., Nahirney, P. C. and Netter, F. H. (2013) Netter's Essential Histology. ClinicalKey 2012: Elsevier Saunders.

Ross, M. H. and Pawlina, W. (2006) Histology: A text and atlas. Lippincott Williams & Wilkins."}]

items.name: Tectorial Membrane
items.info:
[{"name": "Quick Facts", "text": "The tectorial membrane is a delicate gelatinous mass extending from the limbus and resting on the spiral organ of the ear and connected with the hairs of the hair cells (Dorland, 2011)."}, {"name": "Structure and/or Key Feature(s)", "text": "The tectorial membrane is an acellular gelatinous sheet that is found within the cochlear duct of the cochlea. It extends longitudinally in the cochlea, parallel to the basilar membrane. Its overall shape is uneven as the upper surface curves outwards while the lower surface is smooth and flat. It is thought to originate via secretion from the interdental cells of the spiral limbus. Its inner aspect is attached to the vestibular edge of the spiral limbus, while its outer aspect becomes thickened and is suspended in the endolymph of the cochlear duct (Standring, 2016).

The tectorial membrane is comprised of a variety of types of collagen, including fibrillar (II, V, and XI) and non-fibrillar (IX) collagen. It is also composed of three main glycoproteins (known as α-tectorin, β-tectorin, and otogelin) which are scattered among it. The total concentration of tectorins constitutes roughly half the total protein content of the tectorial membrane (Richardson, Lukashkin and Russell, 2008). 

The free edge of the tectorial membrane has a dense thickening called the marginal band. Additionally, on the inferior surface, there is a thickening into which the outer hair cells are embedded known as Kimura’s membrane. There is also a longitudinal ridge adjacent to the inner hair cells called Hensen’s strip."}, {"name": "Anatomical Relations", "text": "The tectorial membrane is found within the cochlear duct of the cochlea. It is superior to the spiral organ (of Corti) and its bundles of inner and outer sensory hair cells, with which it is in direct contact with. It is inferior to the vestibular membrane. The inner edge is attached to the spiral limbus."}, {"name": "Function", "text": "The role of the tectorial membrane is yet to be fully elucidated, but it is thought that sections of the tectorial membrane are able to reinforce the traveling waves of vibration (representing a specific frequency), which results in a correct auditory representation of that sound. It plays a critical role in ensuring the outer hair cell bundles drive the hair bundles of the inner hair cells.

In addition, there is a higher calcium ion concentration in the tectorial membrane than in the endolymph surrounding it. This tectorial calcium ion concentration level is depleted in the presence of loud sounds, and these changes in calcium ion concentration between the membrane and the surrounding fluid have notable effects on the function of the sensory hair cells. Essentially, the tectorial membrane influences its local environment in order to mediate hearing sensitivity (Strimbu et al., 2019)."}, {"name": "References", "text": "Dorland, W. (2011) Dorland's Illustrated Medical Dictionary. 32nd edn. Philadelphia, USA: Elsevier Saunders.

Richardson, G. P., Lukashkin, A. N. & Russell, I. J. (2008) The tectorial membrane: one slice of a complex cochlear sandwich. Curr Opin Otolaryngol Head Neck Surg, 16(5), 458-64.

Strimbu, C. E., Prasad, S., Hakizimana, P. & Fridberger, A. (2019) Control of hearing sensitivity by tectorial membrane calcium. Proc Natl Acad Sci U S A, 116(12), 5756-5764."}]

items.name: Origin of Multifidus Muscle
Axon (Somatic Motor Efferent)
items.info:
[{"name": "Quick Facts", "text": "The axon is the process of a neuron by which impulses travel away from the cell body; at the terminal arborization of the axon, the impulses are transmitted to other nerve cells or to effector organs. The larger axons are surrounded by a myelin sheath (Dorland, 2011)."}, {"name": "Structure/Morphology", "text": "Axons are a part of the nerve cell or neuron. They can be described as an appendage of the nerve cell body giving rise to numerous collateral branches containing presynaptic complexes. Axons are comprised of a gelatinous, relatively firm cord of neuronal cytoplasm. This cord is known as the axoplasm. This axoplasm is surrounded by the axonal part of the neuronal cell membrane, which is referred to as the axolemma. Axons vary in diameter from about 0.1 µm to about 20 µm. Axons also vary in length, they can be anywhere between less than 1 cm to more than a meter long (Carp, 2015).

There are two types of axons, myelinated and unmyelinated. Myelinated axons are surrounded by a myelin sheath while unmyelinated axons are not. Nodes of Ranvier refer to the gaps found in the continuity of the myelin sheath surrounding an axon. At these gaps there is no myelin covering the axon and the axon is exposed to the extracellular fluid."}, {"name": "Key Features/Anatomical Relations", "text": "Myelinated axons are concentrically enveloped by myelin which is produced by myelinating Schwann cells. The territory of an individual Schwann cell along the length of the axon is defined as an internode, while the internodal length is the distance between two successive nodes of Ranvier. The span between these nodes varies dependent on axon diameter. It is at these nodes voltage-gated sodium channels are concentrated. Conduction in myelinated axons is saltatory and extremely quick.

Unmyelinated axons are enclosed by overlapping Schwann cells followed by a surrounding basal lamina. Within each Schwann cell, individual axons are usually isolated from their neighbor by delicate processes of cytoplasm. The absence of myelin sheaths and nodes of Ranvier in unmyelinated axons results in electrotonic conduction, not saltatory, and the passage of impulses is therefore relatively slow."}, {"name": "Function", "text": "Axons are the main conducting unit of the neuron. They transfer electrical signals along a range of distances. The nodes of Ranvier function as a generator of action potentials. This is achieved through the region of the membrane exposed at the node of Ranvier possessing special channel proteins, which allow ions to enter and exit the cell (Waxman, Kocsis and Stys, 1995)."}, {"name": "List of Clinical Correlates", "text": "—Tetrodotoxin poisoning"}, {"name": "References", "text": "Carp, S. (2015) Peripheral Nerve Injury An Anatomical and Physiological Approach for Physical Therapy Intervention. EBL-Schweitzer: F. A. Davis Company.

Dorland, W. (2011) Dorland's Illustrated Medical Dictionary. 32nd edn. Philadelphia, USA: Elsevier Saunders.

Waxman, S. G., Kocsis, J. D. and Stys, P. K. (1995) The Axon: Structure, Function, and Pathophysiology. Oxford University Press."}]

items.name: Testis
items.info:
[{"name": "Quick Facts", "text": "Location: Within the scrotum.

Arterial Supply: Testicular artery.

Venous Drainage: Pampiniform plexus.

Innervation: Autonomic: Testicular plexus.

Lymphatic Drainage: Lumbar lymph nodes."}, {"name": "Structure", "text": "The testes are primary sex organs that play a crucial role in both the male reproductive and endocrine systems. The testes are paired ovoid structures that are in the scrotum. They are composed of around 900 coiled seminiferous tubules, with each tubule averaging a half-meter long (Standring, 2020). The testes are encased in a tough capsule composed of the tunica vasculosa, albuginea, and vaginalis."}, {"name": "Anatomical Relations", "text": "The left testis normally lies at a lower level than the right testis within the scrotum. The testes are suspended by the spermatic cord, through which structures entering or exiting the testes travel. The superior pole of the testis is tilted anterolaterally and is attached to the head of the epididymis, whereas the inferior pole faces anteromedially."}, {"name": "Function", "text": "The external location of the testes to the body cavity (within the scrotum) and the countercurrent exchange mechanism of the pampiniform plexus ensures that the temperature of the testis is 3–4 °C lower than normal body temperature. This temperature is optimum for sperm production. The two testes produce up to 120 million sperm in the human adult each day (Standring, 2020). Sperm can be stored in the testis and remain fertile for up to a month. During their storage, they are suppressed by multiple inhibitory substances. The testes are also heavily involved in the endocrine system. Interstitial endocrine cells, better known as Leydig cells, produce hormones that promote the development of the male reproductive system and secondary male characteristics."}, {"name": "List of Clinical Correlates", "text": "—Testicular cancer

—Variocele"}, {"name": "References", "text": "Standring, S. (2020) Gray's Anatomy: The Anatomical Basis of Clinical Practice. 42nd edn.: Elsevier Health Sciences."}]

items.name: Myelin Lamella (Cross Section)
items.info: [{"name": "Structure and/or Key Features", "text": "In the central nervous system, the myelin sheath consists of extensions of the plasmalemma of the oligodendrocyte forming concentric layers (or lamellae) around neighboring axons. The myelin sheath can thicken from a just few lamellae to about 200 lamellae (Standring, 2016)."}, {"name": "References", "text": "Standring, S. (2016) Gray's Anatomy: The Anatomical Basis of Clinical Practice. Gray's Anatomy Series 41 edn.: Elsevier Limited."}]

items.name: External Elastic Membrane
Iris
items.info:
[{"name": "Quick Facts", "text": "The iris is the circular pigmented membrane, behind the cornea, that surrounds the pupil; the most anterior portion of the vascular tunic of the eye, it is made up of a flat bar of circular muscular fibers surrounding the pupil, a thin layer of smooth muscle fibers by which the pupil is dilated, thus regulating the amount of light entering the eye, and posteriorly two layers of pigmented epithelial cells (Dorland, 2011)."}, {"name": "Structure and/or Key Feature(s)", "text": "The iris is an annular structure that lies in the anterior chamber of the eye, between the cornea anteriorly and the lens posteriorly. It acts as a contractile diaphragm to a centrally located aperture called the pupil. 

From an anterior view, the iris can be divided into zones, the large zone adjacent to the ciliary body (ciliary zone) and a smaller internal zone adjacent to the pupil (pupillary zone). These two zones meet at the collarette. Additionally, the iris may contain large depressions called crypts (crypts of Fuchs) (Standring, 2016).

The iris contains several cellular layers. From anterior to posterior these include the anterior border layer, the stroma, and two pigmented epithelial layers. 

The anterior border layer is modified from the stroma layer and contains an increased number of fibroblasts and underlying melanocytes. It blends with the double epithelial layer covering the posterior surface of the iris at the pupillary rim, and with the trabecular connective tissue of the iridocorneal angle (the angle formed by the iris and cornea allowing for aqueous humor to drain).

The stroma is simply composed of fibroblasts and melanocytes nested in a loose connective tissue. It contains blood vessels and nerves as well as smooth muscle cells that form the sphincter pupillae that encircles the pupil.

The posterior surface of the iris is covered by a double layer of pigmented epithelium, which gives rise to a person’s eye color. This double layer is continuous with the double-layered epithelium of the ciliary body. At the pupillary rim, the epithelium curves onto the anterior surface of the iris, forming a ruffled margin, the pupillary ruff. 

The anterior layer of the double-layered epithelium of the iris (confusingly called the anterior epithelium even though it lines the posterior surface of the stroma of the iris) is a sort of myoepithelium, giving rise to the radial, dilator pupillae muscle. It is continuous with the pigmented epithelial layer of the ciliary body. The posterior layer is more heavily pigmented and is continuous with the non-pigmented layer of ciliary epithelium. It lies in contact with the anterior surface of the lens."}, {"name": "Anatomical Relations", "text": "The iris lies between the lens and the cornea and is bathed in aqueous humor. Anteriorly, the pupillary zone of the iris is in contact with the lens. However, because of the convex shape of the lens, the ciliary zone of the iris moves away from the lens forming a space called the posterior chamber of the eye. The space between the cornea and the iris is referred to as the anterior chamber. The posterior surface of the iris has numerous folds that channels the flow of aqueous humor from the posterior chamber to the anterior chamber."}, {"name": "Function", "text": "Light entering the pupil and passing to the retina is regulated by the iris and is controlled by two involuntary muscles, the sphincter pupillae and the dilator pupillae muscle. Additionally, the double-layered pigmented epithelium of the iris restricts light reaching the retina."}, {"name": "References", "text": "Dorland, W. (2011) Dorland's Illustrated Medical Dictionary. 32nd edn. Philadelphia, USA: Elsevier Saunders.

Standring, S. (2016) Gray's Anatomy: The Anatomical Basis of Clinical Practice. Gray's Anatomy Series 41 edn.: Elsevier Limited."}]

items.name: Dendritic Spines
Secondary Fiber Bundles
items.info: [{"name": "Quick Facts", "text": "The secondary fiber bundle includes several primary bundles surrounded by endotendon."}, {"name": "Structure and/or Key Feature(s)", "text": "The secondary fiber bundle is a collection of several primary fiber bundles surrounded by endotendon. Just like the tertiary fiber bundles, the secondary fiber bundles have a complex structure. The fibrils within each collagen fiber are oriented longitudinally, as well as horizontally and transversely. In addition to this, the longitudinal fibers which are oriented parallel to each other, cross each other as they run along the length of a tendon (Kannus, 2000). The diameter of each secondary fiber is estimated to be between 0.15 mm to 1 mm (Franchi et al., 2007)."}, {"name": "Anatomical Relations", "text": "The secondary fiber bundles are bound together to form the tertiary fiber bundles which make up the whole tendon unit. These secondary fiber bundles are made up of a bunch of primary fiber bundles. Primary fiber bundles are made up of an aggregation of collagen fibers and fibrils. The bundles are surrounded by endotendon."}, {"name": "Function", "text": "The complex structure of the primary, secondary, and tertiary fiber bundles enable the tendon do its job of relaying force generated by the muscles to the bone. This facilitates the movement of joints (Kannus, 2000)."}, {"name": "References", "text": "Franchi, M., Trir\u00e8, A., Quaranta, M., Orsini, E. and Ottani, V. (2007) 'Collagen structure of tendon relates to function', ScientificWorldJournal, 7, pp. 404-20.\n\nKannus, P. (2000) 'Structure of the tendon connective tissue', Scand J Med Sci Sports, 10(6), pp. 312-20."}]

items.name: Secondary Spermatocyte
items.info: [{"name": "Quick Facts", "text": "A secondary spermatocyte is one of the two haploid cells into which a primary spermatocyte divides and which in turn gives origin to spermatids (Dorland, 2011)."}, {"name": "Structure/Morphology", "text": "Primary spermatocytes undergo two meiotic cell divisions so that the resultant haploid cells, called spermatids, contain half the original chromosome number and amount of DNA. \n\nSmall cells, called secondary spermatocytes, arise from the first meiotic division. Each cell contains only 23 chromosomes and either an X or a Y chromosome. There is also a reduction from 4N to 2N of DNA in each secondary spermatocyte. These cells are very sparse in the seminiferous epithelium because they rapidly enter the second meiotic division and give rise to spermatids."}, {"name": "Anatomical Relations", "text": "Secondary spermatocytes occupy the adluminal compartment of the seminiferous epithelium."}, {"name": "Function", "text": "Secondary spermatocytes give rise to spermatids."}, {"name": "References", "text": "Dorland, W. (2011) Dorland's Illustrated Medical Dictionary. 32nd edn. Philadelphia, USA: Elsevier Saunders."}]

items.name: Oligodendrocytes
Marginal Artery
Outer Sheath of Optic Nerve
items.info: [{"name": "Quick Facts", "text": "The outer sheath of optic nerve is the thick external sheath of the optic nerve, continuous with the dura mater and connecting it with the sclera (Dorland, 2011)."}, {"name": "Structure and/or Key Feature(s)", "text": "The eye and optic nerve are outgrowths of the brain and as such carry the three layers of meningeal coverings with them. They are called collectively, the optic sheath. Of these, the outer layer is the direct continuation of the dura mater. Upon emergence from the optic canal, the dura splits into an external sublayer, continuous with the periosteum of the orbit, and an internal sublayer, that continues as the external sheath of the optic nerve (Hayreh, 1984). It surrounds and accompanies the optic nerve to the posterior eyeball. As the optic nerve enters the eyeball, the external sheath becomes continuous with the sclera of the eyeball."}, {"name": "Anatomical Relations", "text": "Within the optic canal, the external sheath of the optic nerve (dural sheath) externally lines the canal attached to the periosteum. Upon emergence it splits into a periosteal, outer sublayer and a meningeal, external sheath of the optic nerve (Hayreh, 1984). Internally is the subdural space and the arachnoid sheath."}, {"name": "Function", "text": "The dural sheath is thick and fibrous and like its counterpart in the brain protects the optic nerve."}, {"name": "References", "text": "Dorland, W. (2011) Dorland's Illustrated Medical Dictionary. 32nd edn. Philadelphia, USA: Elsevier Saunders.\n\nHayreh, S. S. (1984) 'The sheath of the optic nerve', Ophthalmologica, 189(1-2), pp. 54-63."}]

items.name: Mesangial Cell
items.info:
[{"name": "Quick Facts", "text": "Mesangial cells are the phagocytic cells found in the mesangium of the glomerulus of the kidney, thought to aid in cleaning the filtration apparatus (Dorland, 2011)."}, {"name": "Structure and/or Key Feature(s)", "text": "Within the renal corpuscle, the glomerular basement membrane associated with several capillaries encloses a space containing a population of cells called mesangial cells, which form the mesangium. The mesangium is more prominent at the vascular pole. 

Mesangial cells are also located outside the renal corpuscle but are called extraglomerular mesangial (or lacis) cells and will form part of the juxtaglomerular apparatus (Ross and Pawlina, 2006)."}, {"name": "Function", "text": "The primary function of mesangial cells is to remove trapped residue, etc. from the glomerular basement membrane and filtration slit diaphragm and so maintain these structures free of debris. Whilst they are phagocytic cells they are not derived from precursor cells of the mononuclear phagocytic system (monocytes). Mesangial cells also structurally support podocytes where the basement membrane is absent and synthesize and secrete molecules which have a role in responses to injury to the glomerulus. Mesangial cells also have contractile properties (Ross and Pawlina, 2006)."}, {"name": "Clinical Correlates", "text": "Mesangial cells proliferate in response to certain kidney diseases that are a consequence of abnormal amounts of debris accumulating in the glomerular filtration membrane. 

—Immunoglobulin A nephropathy (Berger disease)

—Membranoproliferative glomerulonephritis

—Lupus nephritis

—Diabetic nephropathy"}, {"name": "References", "text": "Dorland, W. (2011) Dorland's Illustrated Medical Dictionary. 32nd edn. Philadelphia, USA: Elsevier Saunders.

Ross, M. H. and Pawlina, W. (2006) Histology: A text and atlas. Lippincott Williams & Wilkins."}]

items.name: Sperm
items.info:
[{"name": "Quick Facts", "text": "Sperm is a mature male germ cell, the specific output of the testes. It is the generative element of the semen that serves to fertilize the oocyte and contains the genetic information to be transmitted to the zygote by the male. It consists of a head (or nucleus), a neck, a middle piece, and a tail with an end piece. Spermatozoa, formed in the seminiferous tubules, are derived from spermatogonia, which first develop into spermatocytes, which, in turn, undergo meiosis to produce spermatids; the spermatids then differentiate into spermatozoa (Dorland, 2011)."}, {"name": "Structure and/or Key Feature(s)", "text": "The mature sperm, or spermatozoon, is a highly differentiated and motile haploid cell. It is composed of a head, neck, and tail (flagellum) and measures about 60 μm in length (Plant and Zeleznik, 2014). The sperm is entirely encapsulated in a plasma membrane, which undergoes regional modifications necessary for fertilization to occur.

The sperm head is flattened and pointed in shape and measures approximately 4.5 μm in length, 3 μm in width, and 1 μm in thickness. It is made up of the nucleus, of which the anterior two-thirds is covered by the acrosomal cap, and a scanty cytoplasm. The nucleus contains tightly packed chromatin that is enveloped anteriorly by the acrosomal cap. The sperm head is connected to the tail via a short neck, or connecting piece, which spans approximately 0.3 μm in length (Standring, 2016). 

The tail makes up most of the sperm’s length, measuring about 55 μm. It is made up of three distinct parts: the middle piece, principal piece, and the end piece. The sperm tail contains a number of structural components including the axoneme, mitochondrial sheath, outer dense fibers, and the fibrous sheath. The function of the tail is to propel the sperm forward in a whiplash-like fashion and to generate the energy required for this movement.

Sperm is an end product of a process called spermatogenesis. Spermatogonia are the germ cells from which sperm develops and are situated in the basal compartment of the seminiferous tubules of the fully mature testis. Spermatogonia can be categorized into different cell types including dark-type A, pale-type A, or type B cells. Dark-type A spermatogonia are believed to be the stem cells of the seminiferous epithelium, and undergo a series of mitotic divisions, thus maintaining their own population. Additionally, dark-type A cells undergo differentiation giving rise to pale-type A spermatogonia. The later cells are the precursors for type B spermatogonia and these cells are committed to the spermatogenesis. 

Type B spermatogonia differentiate into primary (or type I) spermatocytes, which migrate to the adluminal compartment of the seminiferous tubules. Primary spermatocytes replicate their DNA shortly after they form and before meiosis commences so each primary spermatocyte contain the normal chromosomal number (2N) and double the amount of DNA (4C). Each chromosome consists of two sister chromatids; hence 4C amount of DNA. 

Meiosis I reduces both the number of chromosomes (from 2N to 1N) and the amount of DNA to the haploid configuration (from 4C to 2C). So, secondary spermatocytes are characterized by a haploid number of chromosomes (1N) and 2C amount of DNA.

DNA replication does not precede Meiosis II so after this division each spermatid has a haploid (1N) number of chromosomes each containing. a single chromatid (1C).

In order to become mature sperm, spermatids undergo a number of cytoplasmic and nuclear changes and is referred to as spermiogenesis. This involves the development of the acrosome and a tail, as well as chromatin condensation. At this stage, the sperm in the seminiferous tubules are highly differentiated, but are still relatively non-motile. They acquire their motility as they pass through the epididymis. 

Fertilization cannot be completed without a process known as capacitation. Capacitation is essentially the functional maturation of a sperm cell and is completed after the sperm has made its journey to the uterine tube (oviduct or fallopian tube). Various structural and biochemical changes occur during capacitation in which sperm change their behaviour, including the acrosome reaction. Following capacitation, sperm develop the ability to penetrate the cumulus of the egg and bind to the zona pellucida. This stimulates the release of digestive enzymes from the acrosome to aid in the dissolution of the zona pellucida in the vicinity of the sperm head, allowing it to access the perivitelline space (Standring, 2016; Plant and Zeleznik, 2014)."}, {"name": "Function", "text": "The principal function of the sperm is to move through the female genital tract, fuse and penetrate the ovum and deliver the male pronucleus containing the genetic material. It also contributes centrioles that help to organize the cytoskeleton of the zygote."}, {"name": "List of Clinical Correlates", "text": "- Infertility"}, {"name": "References", "text": "Dorland, W. (2011) Dorland's Illustrated Medical Dictionary. 32nd edn. Philadelphia, USA: Elsevier Saunders.

Plant, T. M. & Zeleznik, A. J. (2014) Knobil and Neill's Physiology of Reproduction. Elsevier Science.

Standring, S. (2016) Gray's Anatomy: The Anatomical Basis of Clinical Practice. Gray's Anatomy Series 41st edition edn.: Elsevier Limited."}]

items.name: Docked Synaptic Vesicle
items.info:
[{"name": "Quick Facts", "text": "Docked synaptic vesicles are those that fuse with the presynaptic plasma membrane before releasing their contents (neurotransmitter) into the synaptic cleft."}, {"name": "Structure", "text": "Docked synaptic vesicles are vesicles loaded with neurotransmitters that have migrated adjacent to the presynaptic membrane, ready to fuse with the membrane and subsequently release the neurotransmitters into the synaptic cleft via exocytosis. Synaptic vesicles can only be secreted at the active zones after they have. 

A group of transmembrane proteins called Soluble NSF Attachment Receptors (SNAREs), particularly the vesicle-bound v-SNARE and the target-membrane-bound t-SNARE, facilitate the binding of the synaptic vesicles to the presynaptic plasma membrane. Synaptotagmin 1, a vesicle-bound protein, subsequently supersedes the SNARE complex which is later disintegrated and recycled by NSF/SNAP25 protein complexes. This process yields concentrated collections of proteins on the cytoplasmic aspect of the presynaptic plasma membrane which depict the active zones (Ross and Pawlina, 2006).

The membrane of the synaptic vesicle fused to the presynaptic membrane is salvaged by endocytosis and recycled by the smooth endoplasmic reticulum (Ross and Pawlina, 2006)."}, {"name": "Anatomical Relations", "text": "Docked synaptic vesicles are situated in the presynaptic region. More specifically, they are situated in the active zone, adjacent to the presynaptic membrane."}, {"name": "Function", "text": "Synaptic vesicles store and release neurotransmitters into the synaptic cleft in order to facilitate the transmission and propagation of nerve impulses (Ross and Pawlina, 2006)."}, {"name": "References", "text": "Ross, M. H. and Pawlina, W. (2006) Histology: A text and atlas. Lippincott Williams & Wilkins."}]

items.name: Afferent Glomerular Arteriole
items.info: [{"name": "Quick Facts", "text": "The afferent glomerular arteriole is a branch of an interlobular artery that goes to a renal glomerulus (Dorland, 2011)."}, {"name": "Structure and/or Key Feature(s)", "text": "Interlobular arteries provide tiny afferent arterioles that enter the lobule to supply each renal corpuscle. As each arteriole enters the renal corpuscle, it ramifies into a tuft of capillaries called a glomerulus. The tuft of capillaries then rejoin forming an efferent arteriole. This occurs at the \u201cvascular pole.\u201d The efferent arteriole runs for only a short distance before breaking up into a bed of peritubular capillaries. These capillaries nourish the proximal and distal tubules and absorb fluid."}, {"name": "Function", "text": "An afferent arteriole forms the glomerulus, the region where filtration occurs and a glomerular filtrate is formed."}, {"name": "References", "text": "Dorland, W. (2011) Dorland's Illustrated Medical Dictionary. 32nd edn. Philadelphia, USA: Elsevier Saunders."}]

items.name: Tongue
items.info:
[{"name": "Quick Facts", "text": "The tongue is the movable, muscular organ on the floor of the mouth, subserving the special sense of taste and aiding in mastication, deglutition, and the articulation of sound (Dorland, 2011)."}, {"name": "Structure and/or Key Features", "text": "The tongue is a complex muscular organ with very specific and unique functions. It is involved in tasting/gustation, mastication, swallowing, and verbal communication.

The dorsum of the tongue is covered by a modified stratified squamous epithelium. It is primarily divided into two regions; the anterior area (oral tongue; roughly two thirds) and the posterior area (pharyngeal tongue; one third). These regions have separate functions, innervation, and origins. They are differentiated by a V-shaped indent, with the peak leading posteriorly. At the apex of this indentation is the foramen cecum, a remnant of the thyroglossal duct.

Scattered throughout the dorsum of the tongue are different types of papillae, including the filiform, fungiform, vallate, and foliate papillae. These assist in grasping food particles and, for three out of the four papillae types (fungiform, vallate, and foliate), detection of the different tastes of salty, bitter, sour, sweet, and savory (Ikeda, 2002).

There are two main sets of muscles of the tongue, the intrinsic muscles that modify the tongue’s shape, and the extrinsic muscles that alter the position of the tongue. There is a broad and complex innervation for the tongue’s ordinary and special senses. General sensory innervation of the anterior two-thirds of the tongue is via the lingual nerve (originating from the mandibular nerve CN V3). Special sensory fibers of the anterior two-thirds of the tongue, excluding the vallate papillae, run within the chorda tympani (a branch of the facial nerve) and its fibers accompanies the lingual nerve. General and special sensory innervation of the posterior one third of the tongue are conveyed by the glossopharyngeal nerve (CN IX). This includes special sensory innervation of the vallate papillae.

The lingual artery, originating from the external carotid artery, provides the majority of blood supply to the tongue via its dorsal lingual, deep lingual, and sublingual branches. The musculature is well perfused due to the rich anastomotic networks formed from the lingual branches. The dorsum and lateral sides of the tongue are drained by dorsal lingual veins, whilst the tip of the tongue and deeper mass are drained by the deep lingual vein. 

There is a network of lymphatic vessels, due to the dense capillary formations in the tongue. The anterior tongue is drained by submental, submandibular, and juguloomohyoid nodes. Lateral and central part of oral tongue via the submandibular, jugulodigastric, and thyroid lymph nodes. The root of the tongue is drained by the jugulodigastric nodes."}, {"name": "Anatomical Relations", "text": "The tongue presses against the hard palate of the mouth superiorly and is in contact with the teeth and gingiva in its anterior and lateral aspects. 

Posteriorly, the tongue extends past the palatoglossal and palatopharyngeal arches into the oropharynx, passes the palatine tonsils, onwards to the epiglottis. The uvula of the palate lies on the tongue when the tongue is at rest."}, {"name": "Function", "text": "The tongue has many important functions. It is muscular organ which controls the movement of food in the oral cavity and initiates swallowing. It has tactile functions to analyze the texture of food to see if it is compatible for ingestion. It allows for detection of taste via the taste buds housed within the papillae.

The secondary functions of the tongue occur in combination with the rest of the mouth, it enables articulation and elocution of words for speech and helps with singing by altering the resonance throughout the cavity."}, {"name": "List of Clinical Correlates", "text": "—Macroglossia

—Oral candidiasis

—Leukoplakia

—Oral lichen planus"}, {"name": "References", "text": "Dorland, W. (2011) Dorland's Illustrated Medical Dictionary. 32nd edn. Philadelphia, USA: Elsevier Saunders.

Ikeda, K. (2002) New seasonings. Chem Senses, 27(9), 847-9."}]

items.name: Dentinocemental Junction
items.info:
[{"name": "Quick Facts", "text": "The dentinocemental junction is the plane of meeting between the dentin and cementum on the root of a tooth, containing a large amount of protein, particularly collagen, and less inorganic material than either dentin or cementum; it is believed to reduce the mechanical stress and facilitate movement of nutrients between the dentin and cementum (Dorland, 2011)."}, {"name": "Structure and/or Key Feature(s)", "text": "The dentinocemental junction is a thin layer of mineralized hyaline material that is secreted over newly formed dentin, separating dentin from cement. It lies superjacent to the granular layer of Tomes. 

During tooth development, the inner and outer dental epithelia unite at the cervical loop. This meeting point demarcates where the formation of the root begins and the crown ends. The formation of the root is initiated by the proliferation of the fused epithelial cells, known as the epithelial root sheath. This epithelial root sheath is responsible for the initiation of odontoblast differentiation and thus dentin formation in the root. 

Once the first dentin in the root has formed, the innermost cells of the epithelial root sheath secrete hyaline material over the newly formed dentin. Once mineralized, this hyaline material becomes known as the hyaline layer of Hopewell-Smith (Torabinejad, Walton and Fouad, 2014)."}, {"name": "Function", "text": "The dentinocemental junction facilitates adhesion of cement to dentin."}, {"name": "References", "text": "Dorland, W. (2011) Dorland's Illustrated Medical Dictionary. 32nd edn. Philadelphia, USA: Elsevier Saunders.

Torabinejad, M., Walton, R. E. and Fouad, A. (2014) Endodontics - E-Book: Principles and Practice. Elsevier Health Sciences."}]

items.name: Cranial Dura Mater
items.info:
[{"name": "Quick Facts", "text": "The dura mater is the outermost, toughest, and most fibrous of the three membranes (meninges) covering the brain and spinal cord (Dorland, 2011)."}, {"name": "Structure and/or Key Features", "text": "There are three layers that make up the meninges, the dura, arachnoid, and pia mater. The meningeal layers can also be divided according to the stage of their development, including the leptomeninges (arachnoid and pia mater) and pachymeninx (dura mater).

The dura mater is a dense fibrous layer, composed mostly of tightly packed fascicles of collagen in a laminae configuration. It lies external to the arachnoid and is separated from the arachnoid by the subdural space. 

The cranial dura mater has two layers, the external endosteal layer and the internal meningeal layer. The endosteal layer of the cranial dura mater is adherent with the inner surface of the calvaria, particularly at the sutures, the cranial base, and in the vicinity of the foramen magnum. The endosteal layer is continuous with the periosteum on the outer aspect of the calvaria at the cranial foramina, while the meningeal layer is continuous with the spinal dura at the foramen magnum. The two layers are inseparable, except at points where the dural sinuses and dural reflections arise. The meningeal layer of the dura mater is closely associated with the arachnoid and both layers are fused at points where veins course from the brain into the venous sinuses (Moore, Dalley and Agur, 2013; Standring, 2016).

Dural reflections, or infoldings, are formed by the inner meningeal layer of the dura at points where it separates from the external endosteal layer. The dural reflections include the falx cerebri, falx cerebelli, tentorium cerebelli, and diaphragma sellae. These reflections divide the cranial cavity into various compartments (Moore, Dalley and Agur, 2013). 

The falx cerebri is shaped like a crescent. It narrows anteriorly towards the point where it attaches to the crista galli, and widens posteriorly to merge with the tentorium cerebelli. It is the largest of the four dural reflections and is inhabited in the longitudinal fissure between the left and right cerebral hemispheres. The inferior edge of the falx is free and houses the inferior sagittal sinus. The falx cerebri terminates by continuing as the tentorium cerebelli (Moore, Dalley and Agur, 2013).

The falx cerebelli is a small vertical dural reflection that is situated in the posterior cranial fossa, inferior to the tentorium cerebelli. It slightly separates the two cerebral hemispheres. Posteriorly, it is attached to the internal occipital crest and inhabits the occipital sinus (Standring, 2016)

The diaphragma sellae, the smallest of the four dural reflections, is a spherical horizontal sheet that hangs between the clinoid processes and forms a roof over the sella turcica, encircling the pituitary gland. 

The tentorium cerebelli is the second-largest dural reflection and shaped like a crescent. It is situated between the cerebellum and the occipital lobes. It separates the cranial cavity into supra- and infra-tentorial segments where the forebrain and hindbrain are situated, respectively. The falx cerebri affixes itself to the tentorium cerebelli and props it up, hence the similarity to a tent. It connects to the sphenoid bone (rostrally), the petrous portion of the temporal bone (rostrolaterally), the occipital bone, and the parietal bone (posterolaterally) (Moore, Dalley and Agur, 2013)."}, {"name": "Anatomical Relations", "text": "The dura mater forms the external sheet of the meninges and is separated from the arachnoid by the subdural space."}, {"name": "Function", "text": "The principal function of meningeal layers is to protect and provide support to the brain and spinal cord. The dura mater is thickest and most resilient of the three meningeal layers; hence it shields the brain and spinal cord from mechanical trauma.

The dura mater encircles and supports the dural venous sinuses that convey blood from the brain to the heart. It is also responsible for sealing the central nervous system to ensure cerebrospinal fluid is kept within."}, {"name": "Clinical Correlates", "text": "—Subdural hemorrhage 

—Epidural hemorrhage 

—Epidural injections"}, {"name": "References", "text": "Dorland, W. (2011) Dorland's Illustrated Medical Dictionary. 32nd edn. Philadelphia, USA: Elsevier Saunders.

Moore, K. L., Dalley, A. F. and Agur, A. M. R. (2013) Clinically Oriented Anatomy. Clinically Oriented Anatomy 7th edn.: Wolters Kluwer Health/Lippincott Williams & Wilkins.

Standring, S. (2016) Gray's Anatomy: The Anatomical Basis of Clinical Practice. Gray's Anatomy Series 41st edition: Elsevier Limited."}]

items.name: Brain
items.info:
[{"name": "Quick Facts", "text": "The brain is that part of the central nervous system contained within the cranium, comprising the prosencephalon (forebrain: telencephalon plus diencephalon), mesencephalon (midbrain), and rhombencephalon (hindbrain: metencephalon plus myelencephalon). It is derived from the anterior part of the embryonic neural tube. Functions include muscle control and coordination, sensory reception and integration, speech production, memory storage, and the elaboration of thought and emotion (Dorland, 2011)."}, {"name": "Description", "text": "The brain is the most superior and enlarged part of the central nervous system. In humans, the brain is enclosed within the cranium and is situated at a right angle with the spinal cord. The human brain is responsible for receiving, integrating, and processing sensory information; monitoring and maintaining homeostasis of body functions and states; affecting voluntary control of the body's skeletal muscles; and for carrying out higher order executive processing, such as decision-making and generating consciousness. 

The brain can be divided by region into three anatomically distinct portions: the forebrain (prosencephalon), midbrain (mesencephalon), and hindbrain (rhombencephalon). 

The prosencephalon can be further subdivided into the telencephalon, which encompasses the cerebrum, and diencephalon, which contains the thalamus, hypothalamus, subthalamus, and epithalamus. 

The rhombencephalon can also be further divided into two regions, the metencephalon composed of the pons and cerebellum, and the myelencephalon composed of the medulla oblongata and the eighth to twelfth cranial nerves."}, {"name": "References", "text": "Dorland, W. (2011) Dorland's Illustrated Medical Dictionary. 32nd edn. Philadelphia, USA: Elsevier Saunders."}]

items.name: Renal Papilla
items.info: [{"name": "Quick Facts", "text": "The renal papilla is the blunted apex of a renal pyramid, found in the inner zone of the renal medulla and projecting into a minor calix (Dorland, 2011)."}, {"name": "Structure and/or Key Feature(s)", "text": "The renal papillae are described as the apex or pointed end of each renal pyramid. Each papilla projects into a minor calyx, which lies in the central space of the renal pelvis. \n\nA distinct feature of papillae is their sieve-like appearance, which can be attributed to the presence of many small openings on their surface. Each opening represents a small tubule called the papillary duct, into which the collecting tubules within the renal pyramid converge."}, {"name": "Anatomical Relations", "text": "Renal papillae are located the apex of the renal pyramids at the junction of the renal medulla and renal pelvis."}, {"name": "Function", "text": "Renal papillae carry renal filtrate from the papillary ducts to the minor calyces of the renal pelvis via papillary ducts."}, {"name": "List of Clinical Correlates", "text": "\u2014Renal papillary necrosis"}, {"name": "References", "text": "Dorland, W. (2011) Dorland's Illustrated Medical Dictionary. 32nd edn. Philadelphia, USA: Elsevier Saunders."}]

items.name: Olfactory Glomerulus
items.info:
[{"name": "Quick Facts", "text": "The olfactory glomerulus is one of the small globular masses of dense neuropil in the olfactory bulb; it contains the first synapse in the olfactory pathway, and the axons of olfactory cells synapse here with dendrites primarily of mitral cells and tufted cells (Dorland, 2011)."}, {"name": "Structure and/or Key Features", "text": "The glomeruli are circular non-conspicuous areas, with diameters of about 150 μm, and are situated within the glomerular layer of the olfactory bulb (Barlow and Mollon, 1982). 

Each glomerulus is a composite site of synapses, where incoming olfactory nerve fibers split and synapse with the dendrites of mitral, tufted, and periglomerular cells (Standring, 2016; Longstaff, 2005). 

Glomeruli have odor specificity, since each of them receives nerve fibers from olfactory sensory cells that respond to the same category of odors. There are about 2000 glomeruli within each olfactory bulb, each of which receives the nerve fibers of up to 25,000 olfactory sensory cells (Longstaff, 2005). 

The glomeruli are surrounded by the cell bodies of periglomerular cells. The dendritic branches of these periglomerular cells extend into the glomerulus (Barlow and Mollon, 1982)."}, {"name": "Anatomical Relations", "text": "The glomeruli are situated within the glomerular layer of the olfactory bulb. The glomerular layer lies internal to the olfactory nerve layer and external to the external plexiform layer of the olfactory bulb (Barlow and Mollon, 1982)."}, {"name": "Function", "text": "Glomeruli play a key role in odor specification and identification as each glomerulus responds to specific groups of odors."}, {"name": "Clinical Correlates", "text": "—Anosmia"}, {"name": "References", "text": "Barlow, H. B. and Mollon, J. D. (1982) Senses. Cambridge Studies in Philosophy: Cambridge University Press.

Dorland, W. (2011) Dorland's Illustrated Medical Dictionary. 32nd edn. Philadelphia, USA: Elsevier Saunders.

Longstaff, A. (2005) Neuroscience. BIOS instant notes 2nd edition: Taylor & Francis.

Standring, S. (2016) Gray's Anatomy: The Anatomical Basis of Clinical Practice. Gray's Anatomy Series 41st edition: Elsevier Limited."}]

items.name: Retina
items.info:
[{"name": "Quick Facts", "text": "The retina is the innermost of the three tunics of the eyeball, surrounding the vitreous body and continuous posteriorly with the optic nerve. It is divided into the pars optica, which rests upon the choroid, the pars ciliaris, which rests upon the ciliary body, and the pars iridica, which rests upon the posterior surface of the iris. The pars optica is subdivided into an outer, pigmented layer and an inner, transparent or neural layer. The neural layer contains rods, cones, and neurons, and is divided into nine layers. The layer of rods and cones is the percipient part of the retina, responding to visual stimuli by a photochemical reaction. The inner nuclear layer contains retinal ganglion cells whose axons join to form the optic nerve. In the center of the posterior part of the retina is the macula lutea, the most sensitive portion of the retina, with the fovea centralis at its center. About 0.25 cm medial to the fovea is the point of entrance of the optic nerve and the central artery of the retina; at this point the retina is incomplete and forms the blind spot (Dorland, 2011)."}, {"name": "Structure and/or Key Features", "text": "The retina is the innermost layer of the three coats of the eyeball. It is composed of a one-cell thick outer pigmented layer, the retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) and a multilayered inner neural retina. The neural retina contains photoreceptors, the cells that transduce electromagnetic radiation (light) in the visible range to cellular voltage changes. That information is then conveyed to a variety of cell types in successive layers where initial stages of processing occurs. Finally, the information is carried out of the eye by the optic nerve. The full thickness of the retina ranges from less than 100 µm at its edge to a maximum of approximately 300 µm at the foveal rim (Standring, 2016). When examining the fundus oculi (the posterior aspect of the eyeball that light entering the eyeball focuses on) with an ophthalmoscope, the retina is recognizable by blood vessels that enter and emanate from the optic disc. These blood vessels pass across the innermost surface of the retina sending capillary branches diving into its substance as far as the outer plexiform layer supplying all the cells there with oxygen and nutrients.

Another feature of the retina is the central zone, known as the central retina or macula. Measuring approximately 5–6 mm in diameter, the macula is centered temporal and inferior to the optic disc and is easily identifiable as an avascular area with a yellow tinge when viewed with an ophthalmoscope. The yellow tinge gives the region its full name, macula lutea. The middle of the macula is composed of two distinct areas: the fovea centralis and the foveola. The fovea centralis is defined as a small portion of the macula, measuring approximately 1.5 mm in diameter, and contains mainly cone cells. At the very center of the fovea centralis, with a diameter of approximately 0.4 mm (Millodot, 2014). The foveola is a rod-free zone and contains only cone cells. At the fovea each cone cell is connected via a single bipolar cell to a single ganglion cell, thus giving the foveola the maximum visual acuity possible by the retina’s structure. This 1:1:1 arrangement starts to break down in the fovea. At the foveola, light gets direct access to photoreceptors as the cells and processes and the vasculature is swept radially away from its center. The fovea itself has sloped walls of all these processes so that light has to pass through, from the center to the periphery, successively more cells, their processes, and eventually the vasculature that serves them. The fovea, and especially the foveola represents the point of visual fixation of the normal eye as it provides the best visual sharpness. 

Histologically, the retina is comprised of ten distinct cell layers of a variety of epithelial, neural, and glial cells. The outermost layer is a simple layer of cuboidal pigment cells, known as the pigmented layer, or retinal pigment epithelium. The nine layers of cells below this pigmented layer are collectively known as the neural layer. The neural layers (starting with the outermost layer) include the inner and outer segments (or layer of rods and cones), outer limiting layer, outer nuclear layer, outer plexiform layer, inner nuclear layer, inner plexiform layer, ganglionic layer, layer of nerve fibers, and inner limiting layer.

Embryologically, the retina is derived from the two layers formed by the invagination of the optic vesicle to form the optic cup. The outer layer develops into a layer of cuboidal pigment cells that lies between and separates the neural retina and the choroid. The inner layer of the optic vesicle forms the other nine layers of the retina, collectively known as the neural retina (Standring, 2016). The lumen of the optic vesicle becomes obliterated as the inner and outer cup layers come into apposition but persists as a potential space and is the plane along which most retinal detachments occur."}, {"name": "Anatomical Relations", "text": "The retina lines the inner posterior surface of the eyeball and is positioned between the choroid and vitreous body. The retina terminates anteriorly at the ora serrata."}, {"name": "Function", "text": "The retina transforms light energy into neural signals. Light initially enters the eye through the cornea. The pupil regulates the amount of light that enters the eye, while the lens ensures that the images perceived by the eye are focused on the retina.

When light hits the retina, it must first pass through all its inner layers before impinging on the photoreceptor outer segments. This substance of the retina, and especially its vasculature containing dark, red blood can significantly degrade the light signal. Thus, these layers are “pulled aside” and piled up around the central macula, where the foveola is found and given free access to light here without it having to pass through inner retinal layers. This then is the center of fixation, the area of maximum visual acuity in humans. Upon impinging on the photoreceptor cells, a voltage change is initiated. This signal is then carried across a synapse in the outer plexiform layer and back through the inner nuclear layer via bipolar cells. The horizontal and amacrine cells provide lateral intercommunication and signal modification in the outer retina and in the inner retina, respectively. Bipolar cells make synapses onto retinal ganglion cells the axons of which then pass across the retinal in the layer of nerve fibers toward a central converging point, the optic disc. Here they exit the retina as the optic nerve, sending the retinal signals to the visual areas of the brain (Standring, 2016)."}, {"name": "List of Clinical Correlates", "text": "- Retinal tear

- Retinal detachment 

- Diabetic retinopathy

- Epiretinal membrane

- Macular hole

- Macular degeneration

- Retinitis pigmentosa"}, {"name": "References", "text": "Dorland, W. (2011) Dorland's Illustrated Medical Dictionary. 32nd edn. Philadelphia, USA: Elsevier Saunders.

Millodot, M. (2014) Dictionary of Optometry and Visual Science E-Book. Elsevier Health Sciences.

Standring, S. (2016) Gray's Anatomy: The Anatomical Basis of Clinical Practice. Gray's Anatomy Series 41 edn.: Elsevier Limited."}]

items.name: Subcapsular Arterial Plexus
items.info:
[{"name": "Quick Facts", "text": "The suprarenal arteries give rise to the subcapsular arterial plexus, which supplies the cortical and medullary tissue."}, {"name": "Structure and/or Key Feature(s)", "text": "Despite their small size, the suprarenal glands are one of the most extensively vascularized organs. They have a well-established arterial supply via the superior, middle, and inferior suprarenal arteries, which emerge from the inferior phrenic artery, the abdominal aorta, and the renal artery, respectively. 

The suprarenal arteries give rise to the subcapsular arterial plexus, which supplies the cortical and medullary tissue. In fact, three sets of arteries arise from the subcapsular plexus. 

—One set directly supplies the fibrous capsule surrounding the suprarenal gland. 

—The second set of arteries are the cortical sinusoids, which project into the zona glomerulosa and fasciculata and form a dense capillary network as they reach the zona reticularis before entering the medulla. 

—The third set of arteries are the medullary arteries. These do not supply the zones of the cortex. Instead, they travel with the trabeculae, or the inward projections of the capsule, to supply blood to the medulla only (Inomata and Sasano, 2015)."}, {"name": "Function", "text": "The subcapsular arterial plexus ensures adequate perfusion of blood to the fibrous tissue, cortex, and medulla of the suprarenal glands."}, {"name": "References", "text": "Inomata, A. & Sasano, H. (2015) Practical approaches for evaluating adrenal toxicity in nonclinical safety assessment. J Toxicol Pathol, 28(3), 125-32."}]

items.name: Interstitial Lamella and Osteon Concentric Lamella
items.audio: Interstitial Lamella and Osteon Concentric Lamella.mp3
items.info:
[{"name": "Quick Facts", "text": "The interstitial lamella is one of the bony plates that fill in between the osteons. The osteon concentric lamella is one of the concentric bony plates surrounding a haversian canal (Dorland, 2011)."}, {"name": "Structure/Morphology", "text": "The concentric lamellae refer to the arrangement of bone matrix layers that makes up the osteons. In cortical bone, the interstitial lamellae are found in irregular orientations between the osteons (Ross and Pawlina, 2006).

The interstitial lamellae have a haphazard orientation, which is in contrast to the cylindrical concentric lamellae seen surrounding the nutrient canals."}, {"name": "Anatomical Relations", "text": "The interstitial lamellae are the remnants of circumferential lamellae from older osteons (Standring, 2016). They are separated from osteons by a thin layer called the cement line. The cement lines are primarily composed of glycoproteins and proteoglycans with very little collagen.

The concentric lamellae are cylindrical rings of lamellae which are rich in collagen. They surround the nutrient canals of osteons."}, {"name": "Function", "text": "Interstitial lamellae provide rigid support through the continuous process of bone remodeling by filling the spaces between osteons with dense lamellar bone.

The collagen rich concentric lamellae provide integrity and structural support to the compact bone."}, {"name": "References", "text": "Dorland, W. (2011) Dorland's Illustrated Medical Dictionary. 32nd edn. Philadelphia, USA: Elsevier Saunders.

Ross, M. H. and Pawlina, W. (2006) Histology: A text and atlas. Lippincott Williams & Wilkins.

Standring, S. (2016) Gray's Anatomy: The Anatomical Basis of Clinical Practice. Gray's Anatomy Series: Elsevier Limited."}]

items.name: Tunica Externa of Vessel
items.info:
[{"name": "Quick Facts", "text": "The tunica externa of a blood vessel is the outer, fibroelastic coat of vessels, usually in contact with surrounding tissues (Dorland, 2011)."}, {"name": "Structure", "text": "The tunica externa is the outermost layer of the artery wall. It possesses its own network of smaller blood vessels, known as the vasa vasorum, which provide the blood vessel with the molecules and nutrients necessary for cellular activity (Pawlina, 2016). Along with this small network of supportive blood vessels, the tunica externa is innervated by unmyelinated autonomic nerve fibers, the nervi vasorum (Mescher, 2013). The nervi vasorum are efferent autonomic fibers that play a role in vasodilation and vasoconstriction. 

The tunica externa is composed of fibroblasts, scarce smooth muscle cells, and connective tissue, typically elastin and type I collagenous fibers. Recent studies have suggested that the tissue arrangement of tunica externa isn’t a densely packed wall-like structure, commonly seen in alcohol fixed tissue. In fact, it’s composed of a collagen lattice surrounded by fluid filled interstitial spaces (Benias et al., 2018). This has also been described in other tissues, such as lung, renal, dermis, and fascia."}, {"name": "Anatomical Relations", "text": "The external elastic lamina, a layer of elastic tissue, separates the tunica externa from the tunica media."}, {"name": "Function", "text": "The tunica externa serves to anchor the blood vessel in place in the body tissue. Furthermore, the tunica externa acts as a protective layer restricting sudden expansion of the artery and therefore preventing damage to the artery wall."}, {"name": "References", "text": "Benias, P. C., Wells, R. G., Sackey-Aboagye, B., Klavan, H., Reidy, J., Buonocore, D., Miranda, M., Kornacki, S., Wayne, M., Carr-Locke, D. L. and Theise, N. D. (2018) 'Structure and Distribution of an Unrecognized Interstitium in Human Tissues', Scientific Reports, 8(1), pp. 4947.

Dorland, W. (2011) Dorland's Illustrated Medical Dictionary. 32nd edn. Philadelphia, USA: Elsevier Saunders.

Mescher, A. (2013) Junqueira's Basic Histology: Text and Atlas. 13th edn.: McGraw-Hill Education.

Pawlina, W. 2016. Histology: A text and atlas with correlated cell and molecular biology. 7th ed. Philadelphia: Wolters Kluwer."}]

items.name: Enamel
items.info:
[{"name": "Quick Facts", "text": "The enamel is a hard, thin, translucent layer of calcified substance that envelops and protects the dentin of the crown of the tooth; it is the hardest substance in the body and is almost entirely composed of calcium salts (Dorland, 2011)."}, {"name": "Structure and/or Key Feature(s)", "text": "Enamel is described as a highly mineralized, extremely hard and rigid material that covers the crown of the tooth. Semi-translucent and light yellow to white, the enamel lies superficial to the dentin. The boundary between these layers is known as the dentinoenamel junction. Enamel will typically reach a maximum thickness of 2.5 mm over the cusp of the tooth and become thinner at the cervical margins (Standring, 2016).
