items.name: Membrane-bound Organelles
items.info: [{"name": "Quick Facts", "text": "Membrane-bound organelles are those that are surrounded by a membrane, separating their internal compartment from the cytoplasm of the cell."}, {"name": "Description", "text": "Many organelles (e.g., endoplasmic reticulum, Golgi complex, mitochondria, lysosomes and peroxisomes) are surrounded by a membrane that separates the internal compartment of the organelle from the cytoplasm. Thus, these organelles are called membrane-bound organelles (or membranous organelles). The membrane structure is like that of the plasmalemma, but the specific functions of the organelle require additional and unique proteins and/or lipids, etc. enclosed in the membrane.\n\nIn some organelles e.g., mitochondria and lysosomes, the membrane may extend into the internal compartments of the organelle and have specialized functions (Ross and Pawlina, 2006)."}, {"name": "References", "text": "Ross, M. H. and Pawlina, W. (2006) Histology: A text and atlas. Lippincott Williams & Wilkins."}]

items.name: Nerves of Medullary Cavity
items.info: [{"name": "Structure/Morphology", "text": "The nerves enter the medullary cavity accompanying the nutrient vessels. Their distribution in the marrow follows the course of the vessels towards the epiphyses where they ramify and anastomose. Other finer nerves penetrate the cancellous tissue with numerous blood vessels and also ramify in the medulla."}, {"name": "Anatomical Relations", "text": "The nerves of the medullary cavity follow the same course as the nutrient vessels and travel towards the epiphyses."}, {"name": "Function", "text": "These nerves supply both autonomic and sensory innervation to the bone."}]

items.name: Hepatic Lobule
items.info:
[{"name": "Quick Facts", "text": "Hepatic lobules are the small polygonal units composing the substance of the liver, each with a central vein at its center and portal tracts peripherally at the corners (Dorland, 2011)."}, {"name": "Structure/Morphology", "text": "The liver is the largest visceral organ in the human body and weighs approximately 1.5 kg. It is an abdominal organ located in the right hypochondrium and extends into the epigastrium. In some cases, it may reach as far as the left hypochondrium. 

The liver can be organized either anatomically or functionally. Anatomically, the liver is divided into a large right and smaller left lobe by fossae for the gallbladder and the inferior vena cava. The small quadrate and caudate lobes arise from the right lobe.

Functional organization divides the liver into left and right parts, where each part receives its own primary branch of the hepatic artery and a hepatic portal vein and is drained by its own hepatic duct. The caudate lobe is sometimes considered a third part, since its vasculature is independent of other lobes.

The hepatic lobules form the main building blocks of the liver and are arranged adjacent to each other, with some sparse connective tissue dividing them. Hepatocytes are the main epithelial cells of the liver parenchyma. They make up around 80% of the liver volume and 60% of the liver cell population (Standring, 2016). The hepatocytes are arranged as hepatic plates, usually one cell thick and are separated from each other by the sinusoids. A small perisinusoidal space is present between the hepatocytes and the sinusoids. 

Within the liver tissue, distributing branches of the portal vein and hepatic artery supply the sinusoids. Bile from the bile canaliculi drain into branches of the bile duct system (which eventually form the common hepatic duct) follow these vessels supplying the sinusoids to form portal triads.

Liver lobules can be described in different ways relating to their functional unit. These include the classic lobule, the portal lobule, and the liver acinus. These functional units are discussed below."}, {"name": "Classic Hepatic Lobule", "text": "The classic hepatic lobule (which is depicted in this model) is described as a hexagonal arrangement of hepatocytes, organized as hepatic plates, which distribute outwards as radial cords from a single central vein. 

A portal triad is located in a portal area or portal canal at each angle of the hexagon. The portal canal also contains a perivascular fibrous capsule of loose connective tissue and is continuous with the fibrous hepatic capsule, or Glisson’s capsule, that surrounds the liver. At the edges of the portal canals, between the connective tissue and the outermost hepatocytes is the periportal space (of Mall). This is the space in which lymph from the liver is formed. The hepatic lobules are easily distinguishable in some species (e.g., the pig), where there are relatively thick layers of connective tissue between adjacent lobules. However, in humans, this connective tissue is relatively sparse, making each hepatic lobule difficult to distinguish."}, {"name": "Portal Lobule", "text": "The portal lobule is used to emphasize the exocrine functions of the liver, e.g., bile secretion. It is formed by imaginary lines drawn between three central veins of three classic lobules, thus forming a triangle. The interlobular bile duct of the portal triad interjacent between the three lobules is located centrally. The portal lobule demonstrates the drainage of bile from those portions of the three lobules into the interlobular bile duct."}, {"name": "Liver Acinus", "text": "The liver acinus is used to describe the correlation between blood perfusion and metabolic activity of the liver and its relation to liver pathology. It is formed by drawing an imaginary line (short axis) between the portal triads that lie between two classic lobules. The long axis is drawn to the two central veins closest to the short axis, thus forming a diamond-shaped functional unit. 

The hepatocytes of each liver acinus are described in terms of elliptical zones located around the short axis. These zones are important in describing or interpreting toxic effects in the liver parenchyma relating to vascular perfusion.

-Zone 1 are the cells closest to the short axis. Blood rich in oxygen, nutrients, and toxins reaches these cells first. Therefore, these cells are the first to show morphological changes due to toxins or bile duct obstructions. They are also the last to die as a result of reduced blood perfusion and are the first to regenerate.

- Zone 3 contains the cells furthest away from the short axis and closest to the central vein. These cells are the first to show ischemic necrosis as a result of reduced blood perfusion and the first to show fat accumulations. These cells are the last to respond to toxins or bile duct obstructions.

- Zone 2 is found between Zone 1 and 3 and the hepatocytes here respond similar to the cells in the adjacent zones."}, {"name": "Function", "text": "The liver has an extensive number of functions not limited to one particular area, including vascular (lymph formation), metabolic (regulation of synthesis and utility of macronutrients), secretory, and excretory functions. 

The primary exocrine function of the hepatic lobule is the production and secretion of bile. Bile is paramount to the digestive process as it allows for the emulsification of fats. The liver is also important in carbohydrate metabolism, including the production of glucose and glycogen, ketonic body production, and cholesterol metabolism.

The liver produces plasma proteins, such as albumin, lipoproteins, glycoproteins, and clotting factors (fibrinogen and prothrombin). Several vitamins are stored and/or modified in the liver, such as vitamin A, D, and K. The liver also stores, metabolizes, and maintains homeostasis of iron.

The liver degrades drugs and toxins so that they can be eliminated from the body by the kidneys. This involves the cytochrome P450 proteins in the hepatocytes.

The liver also has endocrine-like functions, where it modifies hormones such as vitamin D, thyroxine, growth hormones, insulin, and glucagon."}, {"name": "List of Clinical Correlates", "text": "- Hemochromatosis

- Hepatitis

- Cirrhosis

- Liver disease"}, {"name": "References", "text": "Dorland, W. (2011) Dorland's Illustrated Medical Dictionary. 32nd edn. Philadelphia, USA: Elsevier Saunders.

Standring, S. (2016) Gray's Anatomy: The Anatomical Basis of Clinical Practice. Gray's Anatomy Series 41st edn.: Elsevier Limited."}]

items.name: Microvilli (Thyroid Follicular Cell)
items.info: [{"name": "Quick Facts", "text": "Microvilli are the minute cylindrical processes on the free surface of a cell, organized around a core of cross-linked actin filaments anchored to the terminal web, which increase the surface size of the cell; found especially in cells of the proximal convolution of the renal tubules and of the intestinal epithelium (Dorland, 2011)."}, {"name": "Structure/Morphology", "text": "Thyroid follicular cells possess microvilli on their apical surfaces. They are short in resting follicular cells; however, they elongate and are often branched upon activation (Standring, 2020). "}, {"name": "Anatomical Relations", "text": "Microvilli are found on the apical surface of thyroid follicular cells."}, {"name": "Function", "text": "The microvilli of thyroid follicular cells wrap around segments of the colloid, and by endocytosis, the colloid is brought inside the cell."}, {"name": "References", "text": "Dorland, W. (2011) Dorland's Illustrated Medical Dictionary. 32nd edn. Philadelphia, USA: Elsevier Saunders.\nStandring, S. (2020) Gray's Anatomy: The Anatomical Basis of Clinical Practice. 42nd edn.: Elsevier Health Sciences.\n"}]

Submucosal Vascular Plexus (Duodenum)
items.info: [{"name": "Quick Facts", "text": "The submucosal vascular plexus is a network of intercommunicating blood vessels found in the submucosa."}, {"name": "Structure/Morphology", "text": "Blood vessels (small arteries and veins) form large plexuses in the submucosa."}, {"name": "Function", "text": "The submucosal vascular plexus nourishes the layers of the intestinal wall as well as removing absorbed products of digestion."}]

items.name: Capillary Network
items.info: [{"name": "Quick Facts", "text": "The capillary network surrounds the alveoli and allow for gas exchange to occur."}, {"name": "Structure/Morphology", "text": "An extensive capillary network surrounds the alveoli and alveolar saccules. The capillaries form a special structure with the alveoli, the blood-air barrier, or alveolar-capillary membrane. The basal lamina of the squamous epithelium of the alveoli and the endothelium of the capillaries are fused, thus forming a membrane that allows gas to diffuse across it. This region is less than 2 \u03bcm wide (Ovalle et al., 2013, Simionescu, 2001)."}, {"name": "References", "text": "Ovalle, W. K., Nahirney, P. C. and Netter, F. H. (2013) Netter's Essential Histology. ClinicalKey 2012: Elsevier Saunders.\n\nSimionescu, M. (2001) 'Cellular components of the air-blood barrier', J Cell Mol Med, 5(3), pp. 320-1."}]

items.info:

items.name: Thyroid Colloid
items.info:
[{"name": "Quick Facts", "text": "The thyroid colloid is the colloid in the thyroid follicles; it contains several proteins, including thyroglobulin and CA2 (Dorland, 2011)."}, {"name": "Structure/Morphology", "text": "Within the lumen of the thyroid follicle is a gel-like component called colloid. It’s the stored product thyroglobulin that was synthesized and secreted by the follicular cells.

The thyroglobulin is reabsorbed by the follicular cells via endocytosis from that colloid, which is then broken down and transformed into the two thyroid hormones, T3 and T4. 

Iodide is absorbed into the cell and highly concentrated. It is then oxidized and passed into the colloid as iodine, which forms a complex with the thyroglobulin. This is a very important complex, as when it’s reabsorbed back into the cell, it contributes to the formation of the thyroid hormones. So, two very important functions of this cell, one, to produce the thyroglobulin, and one to concentrate and oxidize iodide that helps form this iodinated thyroglobulin complex inside the colloid (Ross and Pawlina, 2016).
"}, {"name": "Anatomical Relations", "text": "Colloid is found within the lumen of each thyroid follicle."}, {"name": "Function", "text": "Thyroglobulin is stored in the thyroid colloid in the lumen of the follicle and is the location where iodination of the thyroglobulin occurs (Ross and Pawlina, 2016)."}, {"name": "References", "text": "Dorland, W. (2011) Dorland's Illustrated Medical Dictionary. 32nd edn. Philadelphia, USA: Elsevier Saunders.
Ross, M. H. and Pawlina, W. (2016) Histology: A Text and Atlas. Wolters Kluwer Health.
"}]

items.name: Voltage-Gated Channel
items.info:
[{"name": "Quick Facts", "text": "A voltage-gated channel is an ion channel that opens or closes in response to changes in the electrical potential across the cell membrane (Dorland, 2011)."}, {"name": "Structure", "text": "Channel proteins form transmembrane channels with “pores” that allow water and other materials through the plasmalemma of any cell. Some channels are usually open, while others are “gates” that open and close following specific stimuli. 

—Ligand-gated channels respond to a chemical messenger such as a neurotransmitter.

—Mechanical gated channels respond to a mechanical stimulus or stress such as stretch or pressure.

—Voltage-gated channels respond to changes in electrical potential across the plasma membrane.

One property of voltage-gated channels is “gating.” Channels with this property can be opened and closed i.e. “gated” (Splittgerber, 2018). Gating occurs in response to stimuli such as a voltage change, presence of a ligand (e.g., a neurotransmitter), stretch, or pressure (Ross and Pawlina, 2006; Bear, Connors and Paradiso, 2007)."}, {"name": "Anatomical Relations", "text": "Voltage-gated channels in the nervous system are mostly located on the cell body and dendrites of neurons, as well as on the nodes of Ranvier in myelinated axons, and on the axon hillock on unmyelinated axons (Ross and Pawlina, 2006; Bear, Connors and Paradiso, 2007)."}, {"name": "Function", "text": "Voltage-gated channels exhibit ion selectivity in that they exclusively permit the movement of a particular ion such as sodium, potassium, calcium, and chloride across the synaptic membranes during neurotransmission. These ions play pivotal roles in a diverse range of cell physiology, including neural transmission (Ross and Pawlina, 2006; Bear, Connors and Paradiso, 2007)."}, {"name": "References", "text": "Bear, M. F., Connors, B. W. and Paradiso, M. A. (2007) Neuroscience. Lippincott Williams & Wilkins.

Dorland, W. (2011) Dorland's Illustrated Medical Dictionary. 32nd edn. Philadelphia, USA: Elsevier Saunders.

Ross, M. H. and Pawlina, W. (2006) Histology: A text and atlas. Lippincott Williams & Wilkins.

Splittgerber, R. (2018) Snell's Clinical Neuroanatomy. Wolters Kluwer Health."}]

items.name: Duodenum
items.info:
[{"name": "Quick Facts", "text": "Location: Abdominal cavity forming a C-shaped structure around the head of the pancreas.

Arterial Supply: Branches of the celiac trunk (gastroduodenal and superior pancreaticoduodenal arteries) and superior mesenteric artery (inferior pancreaticoduodenal, jejunal, ileal, ileocecal arteries).

Venous Drainage: Superior and inferior pancreaticoduodenal veins, draining to the portal vein and superior mesenteric vein, respectively.

Innervation: Parasympathetic: Vagus nerve (CN X); Sympathetic: celiac ganglia; Visceral afferents: spinal ganglia of T5-T9; Enteric innervation. 

Lymphatic Drainage: Pyloric and pancreaticoduodenal lymph nodes, to celiac and superior mesenteric lymph nodes."}, {"name": "Structure", "text": "The duodenum is about 25–30 cm long and is the first, shortest, and widest part of the small intestine. It is made up of four primary segments: superior, descending, horizontal, and ascending duodenum. These are also known as the first, second, third, and fourth parts of the duodenum, respectively.

The superior and descending duodenum are related to the foregut while the horizontal and ascending segments of the duodenum are related to the midgut. This developmental distinction is important in understanding the patterns of vascularization, innervation, and lymphatic drainage of the duodenum.

The cross-sectional microarchitecture of the duodenum demonstrates mucosa, submucosa, and muscular layers with a thin outer serosal or adventitial covering (Standring, 2016). 

Plicae circulares are circular transverse folds extending up to two thirds the circumference of the lumen containing a core of the submucosa. They begin about 5–6 cm beyond the pylorus and are most numerous towards the distal part of the duodenum.

Villi are 0.5-1.5 mm fingerlike or leaf-like projections of the mucosa covering the entire surface of the small intestine. Their core is lamina propria. 

Absorptive cells or enterocytes lining the villi have specialized microvilli projecting from their apical surfaces. A glycocalyx consisting of glycoproteins project from their apical plasmalemma. Each enterocyte exhibits several thousand microvilli which gives the apical border a striated appearance often called the “striated border” (called a brush border in epithelial cells lining kidney tubules)."}, {"name": "Key Features/Anatomical Relations", "text": "The duodenum is the shortest part of the small intestine, forming a roughly C-shaped structure around the head of the pancreas.

The superior portion of the duodenum begins on the distal side of the pyloric sphincter roughly ventral to the L1 vertebra. The initial part, called the duodenal cap, is intraperitoneal and covered by a mesentery. Shortly thereafter, the superior duodenum dives posteriorly to become retroperitoneal. The superior duodenum is anterior to the bile duct and neck of the pancreas, and posterior to the gallbladder and quadrate lobe of the liver. It’s the portion to which the heaptoduodenal ligament attaches to form the omental (epiploic) foramen. 

The descending portion of the duodenum runs inferiorly along the right edge of the pancreas, from L1 to L3 vertebral levels. It remains retroperitoneal. It passes posterior to the transverse colon and transverse mesocolon, and anterior to the hilum of the right kidney and the right ureter. Bile and pancreatic secretions enter the descending portion of the duodenum via the major duodenal papilla. A variably present minor duodenal papilla also transmits pancreatic enzymes from the accessory pancreatic duct.

The horizontal portion of the duodenum runs medially at the L3 vertebral level. It crosses posterior to the superior mesenteric artery and vein and anterior to the aorta. It courses inferior to the head of the pancreas and across to the left side of the L3 vertebra.

The ascending duodenum runs superiorly to the left of the aorta a few centimeters until turning ventrally when it reaches the body of the pancreas at the L2 vertebral level. Here it becomes intraperitoneal and ends at the duodenojejunal junction. The distal end of the duodenum is attached to the suspensory muscle of the duodenum (or ligament of Treitz), a muscular band extending from the right crus of the diaphragm (Moore, Dalley and Agur, 2013)."}, {"name": "Function", "text": "The duodenum is primarily a site of digestion. Chyme that enters the duodenum from the stomach is neutralized with alkaline mucus secreted by Brunner’s glands of the duodenal mucosa or bicarbonate secreted by the pancreas. 

Entry of chyme into the duodenum also triggers hormonal feedback to: 

—the stomach to slow gastric emptying; 

—the liver and gallbladder to secrete bile which aids in the emulsification and absorption of lipids; 

—the pancreas which releases pancreatic juices for enzymatic digestion of proteins, carbohydrates, fats, and nucleic acids (Sircar, 2016). 

The duodenum is also a site of absorption. It absorbs nonheme iron, sugars, peptides, fats, calcium, and phosphates. Water can move either in or out of the duodenum depending on whether chyme is hypo- or hypertonic.

The plicae circulares, villi, and microvilli amplify the absorptive surface area within the duodenum."}, {"name": "List of Clinical Correlates", "text": "—Gastroenteritis

—Crohn’s disease

—Peptic ulcers

—Duodenitis

—Celiac disease"}, {"name": "References", "text": "Sircar, S. (2016) Principles of Medical Physiology. 2nd edn.: Thieme.

Moore, K. L., Dalley, A. F. and Agur, A. M. R. (2013) Clinically Oriented Anatomy. Clinically Oriented Anatomy 7th edn.: Wolters Kluwer Health/Lippincott Williams & Wilkins.

Standring, S. (2016) Gray's Anatomy: The Anatomical Basis of Clinical Practice. Gray's Anatomy Series 41 edn.: Elsevier Limited."}]

items.name: Presynaptic Axon
items.info:
[{"name": "Quick Facts", "text": "The presynaptic axon is the part of the axon situated before or proximal to a synapse."}, {"name": "Structure", "text": "The presynaptic axon is the axon located before the synapse. It will initiate impulses/signals on the postsynaptic axon via a series of processes upon the arrival of an action potential (Ross and Pawlina, 2006).

In myelinated axons, the area of the axon between the axon hillock and the first region of myelination (about 50–100 μm) is known as the “initial segment.” It is the most excitable region of the axon and the site where action potentials are generated (Ross and Pawlina, 2006; Splittgerber, 2018). Myelin is formed by Schwann cells in the peripheral nervous system and oligodendrocytes in the central nervous system. The axon hillock, as well as the axon terminals are not covered by myelin. 

Axon terminals widen into presynaptic boutons which form synapses with postsynaptic neurons and other target cells, such as muscle fibers and glands."}, {"name": "Anatomical Relations", "text": "The presynaptic axon is a component of a chemical synapse. It is the axon that sits proximal to a synapse. It stems from a specialized area that is devoid of Nissl granules, the axon hillock. The axon hillock is a component of the nerve cell body that essentially connects it to the axon."}, {"name": "Function", "text": "The presynaptic axon is essentially where neurotransmission begins. It is the site where an action potential is initiated, and neural impulses are subsequently propagated across to the receptors on the postsynaptic membrane to exert an excitatory or inhibitory effect depending on the neurotransmitter and the specific receptor (Ross and Pawlina, 2006)."}, {"name": "References", "text": "Ross, M. H. and Pawlina, W. (2006) Histology: A text and atlas. Lippincott Williams & Wilkins.

Splittgerber, R. (2018) Snell's Clinical Neuroanatomy. Wolters Kluwer Health."}]

items.name: Meridional Fibers of Ciliary Muscle
items.info:
[{"name": "Quick Facts", "text": "The meridional fibers of ciliary muscle are the most external fibers of the ciliary muscle that run meridionally or longitudinally from the reticulum trabeculae toward the ciliary processes (Dorland, 2011)."}, {"name": "Structure and/or Key Feature(s)", "text": "The meridional fibers of the ciliary muscles form the external part of the ciliary muscle. The fibers pass longitudinally from the trabecular meshwork of the posterior wall of the scleral venous sinus towards the ciliary processes.

The oculomotor nerve (CN III) provides parasympathetic innervation to the ciliary muscle via the short ciliary nerves, with the superior cervical ganglion providing sympathetic contributions (Giampani & Giampani, 2013)."}, {"name": "Anatomical Relations", "text": "Found just internal to the ciliary stroma layer, the meridional fibers of the ciliary muscle form the external part of the ciliary muscle. Just internal are radial muscle fibers."}, {"name": "Function", "text": "The ciliary body suspends the lens of the eyeball by fines suspensory ligaments. When the ciliary muscle contracts it varies tension on the lens, and this changes its shape and hence its refractive power. This process is called accommodation.

Additionally, since the meridional fibers insert into the trabecular meshwork of the scleral venous sinus, contraction and relaxation of the meridional fibers alters the pore size within the meshwork, thus, facilitating aqueous humor drainage into the scleral venous sinus (canal of Schlemm)."}, {"name": "Clinical Correlates", "text": "—Cycloplegia (paralysis of accommodation)

—Hyperopia-aging"}, {"name": "References", "text": "Dorland, W. (2011) Dorland's Illustrated Medical Dictionary. 32nd edn. Philadelphia, USA: Elsevier Saunders.

Giampani, A. S. B. and Giampani, J. (2013) Anatomy of Ciliary Body, Ciliary Processes, Anterior Chamber Angle and Collector Vessels. INTECH Open Access Publisher."}]

items.name: Hilum of Ovary
items.info: [{"name": "Quick Facts", "text": "The hilum of ovary is the area on the lateral border of the ovary where the vessels and nerves enter (Dorland, 2011)."}, {"name": "Structure and/or Key Feature(s)", "text": "The stroma forms the tissue of the hilum by which the proper ovarian ligament is attached, and through which the blood vessels, nerves, and lymphatic vessels enter. It does not contain any ovarian follicles which are contained within the cortex of the ovary (Standring, 2016)."}, {"name": "Anatomical Relations", "text": "The stroma forms the tissue of the hilum by which the ovarian ligament is attached. The hilum contains hilar cells, as well as irregular tubules, the rete ovarii, the remnants of the embryonic mesonephric (or Wolffian) duct."}, {"name": "Function", "text": "The hilum is the region of the ovary through which blood vessels, nerves, and lymphatic vessels enter the organ."}, {"name": "References", "text": "Dorland, W. (2011) Dorland's Illustrated Medical Dictionary. 32nd edn. Philadelphia, USA: Elsevier Saunders.\n\nStandring, S. (2016) Gray's Anatomy: The Anatomical Basis of Clinical Practice. Gray's Anatomy Series 41 edn.: Elsevier Limited."}]

items.name: Lacrimal Sac
items.info: [{"name": "Quick Facts", "text": "The lacrimal sac is the dilated superior beginning of the nasolacrimal duct located medially within the orbit; it receives the lacrimal canaliculi (Dorland, 2011)."}, {"name": "Structure and/or Key Feature(s)", "text": "The lacrimal sac is the bulbous, closed superior end of the nasolacrimal duct. The superior and inferior lacrimal canaliculi empty into it. The sac serves as a receptacle to collect tears before draining them down the nasolacrimal duct into the nasal cavity. A small slip of orbicularis oculi (the lacrimal portion) passes over the sac facilitating its emptying (Standring, 2016)."}, {"name": "Anatomical Relations", "text": "The lacrimal collecting and drainage system, including the lacrimal sac is located at the medial angle of the eye. Here there is a bony fossa formed by the lacrimal bone (posteriorly) and the frontal process of the maxilla (anteriorly) in which it lies. The small lacrimal portion of orbicularis oculi passes across the ridges of the lacrimal fossa forming the anteromedial relation of the lacrimal sac. The sac continues inferiorly between the lacrimal and maxillary bones exiting the orbit as the nasolacrimal canal."}, {"name": "Function", "text": "The lacrimal sac is part of the apparatus for draining tears from the medial angle of the eye. The lacrimal canaliculi transport tears to the lacrimal sac, and then onto the nasolacrimal duct which directs the tears to the inferior meatus of the nasal cavity. If tear fluid accumulates faster than it can flow down the nasolacrimal duct, it collects here. Contraction of the lacrimal portion of orbicularis oculi (by blinking) can squeeze the sac, propelling the fluid at higher pressure and volume along the drainage system."}, {"name": "References", "text": "Dorland, W. (2011) Dorland's Illustrated Medical Dictionary. 32nd edn. Philadelphia, USA: Elsevier Saunders.\n\nStandring, S. (2016) Gray's Anatomy: The Anatomical Basis of Clinical Practice. Gray's Anatomy Series 41 edn.: Elsevier Limited."}]

items.name: Golgi Complex (Contracted Smooth Muscle)
items.info:
[{"name": "Quick Facts", "text": "The Golgi complex is an intracellular compartment of eukaryotes, occupying the perinuclear region and consisting of a number of stacked, flattened sacs with associated tubules and vesicles. Its primary function is to process substances synthesized in the endoplasmic reticulum; in addition it synthesizes some carbohydrates. Transport vesicles from the endoplasmic reticulum fuse with the Golgi complex at the cis face, their cargo is processed while passing through the cisternae, and the processed products are transported from the trans face to the trans-Golgi network for sorting and packaging. The mechanism by which cargo moves through the Golgi complex is not clear; one model proposes transport between cisternae by vesicular budding and fusion, while another proposes dynamic remodeling and recycling so that the cisternae themselves change in composition and move in a cis-to-trans direction (Dorland, 2011)."}, {"name": "Structure and/or Key Features", "text": "The Golgi complex or Golgi apparatus is a crescent shaped, parallel stack of membrane-limited tubules or cisternae. It is closely associated with small vesicles involved in vesicular transport. The Golgi complex is very well developed in secretory cells. The Golgi complex exhibits structural polarity. It has a “cis face” (or entry face, which is the convex part of the complex) and a “trans face” (or exit face) (Ovalle, Nahirney and Netter, 2013; McKinley, O'Loughlin and Pennefather-O'Brien, 2016; Ross and Pawlina, 2016)."}, {"name": "Anatomical Relations", "text": "The Golgi complex is closely associated with the nucleus and the “cis face” is adjacent to the rough endoplasmic reticulum."}, {"name": "Function", "text": "The Golgi complex accepts proteins and various other molecules synthesized by the endoplasmic reticulum. Each cistern of the Golgi complex contains different types of enzymes and so perform different enzymatic reactions. 

As some proteins move within the Golgi cisternae, carbohydrates and lipids are added to these proteins to form glycoproteins and glycolipids, respectively. In addition, proteins are added to lipids to form lipoproteins. Some proteins are isolated to be included in new plasmalemma.

As these molecules pass further through the Golgi complex, they are sorted and repackaged into a secretory vesicle. These secretory molecules are either destined to become lysosomes, migrate to the plasmalemma, or exported outside of the cell. 

The Golgi apparatus is involved in making carbohydrates (Ovalle, Nahirney and Netter, 2013; McKinley, O'Loughlin and Pennefather-O'Brien, 2016; Ross and Pawlina, 2016)."}, {"name": "Clinical Correlates", "text": "Atrophy of the Golgi complex and subsequent functional errors in specific neurons and loss of these neurons in the brain has been implicated in Alzheimer’s disease (Ovalle, Nahirney and Netter, 2013)."}, {"name": "References", "text": "Dorland, W. (2011) Dorland's Illustrated Medical Dictionary. 32nd edn. Philadelphia, USA: Elsevier Saunders.

McKinley, M. P., O'Loughlin, V. D. and Pennefather-O'Brien, E. E. (2016) Human Anatomy. 5th edn.: McGraw-Hill Education.

Ovalle, W. K., Nahirney, P. C. and Netter, F. H. (2013) Netter's Essential Histology. ClinicalKey 2012: Elsevier Saunders.

Ross, M. H. and Pawlina, W. (2016) Histology: A Text and Atlas. Wolters Kluwer Health."}]

items.name: Endocytosis (Posterior)
items.info:
[{"name": "Quick Facts", "text": "Endocytosis is the uptake by a cell of material from the environment by invagination of its plasma membrane; it includes both phagocytosis and pinocytosis (Dorland, 2011)."}, {"name": "Structure and/or Key Feature(s)", "text": "Many substances enter and leave the cell, and move between different cytoplasmic regions or organelles, by vesicular transport. Vesicles present in the cytoplasm (although appearing structurally similar) reflect different traffic pathways and functional states. In most cases, there is a continual renewal/replacement of the plasma membrane as new vesicles are formed from the cell membrane and enter the cell (endocytosis) or fuse with the plasma membrane to excrete substances (exocytosis).

The general term for the uptake of materials into the cell is called endocytosis. Many endocytotic processes are receptor mediated. Receptors for many substances aggregate on the cell surface as “coated pits.” They bind the ligand and enter the cell as a coated vesicle then quickly lose their clathrin coat and fuse with endosomes. Endosomes form a system of vesicles (early endosomes). These early endosomes recycle some of the plasmalemma components back to the cell surface, particularly clathrin to form new coated pits, then proceed to go deeper into the cell with other endosomes to become late endosomes. 

Some endosomes are functionally connected to the transport vesicles in the rough endoplasmic reticulum (and most likely the Golgi complex) to deliver hydrolytic enzymes to late endosomes that carry a mannose-6-phosphate (M-6-P) receptor. These are endosomes destined to be lysosomes. Early endosomes transport and sort proteins received by endocytosis and direct them to appropriate cellular compartments. Late endosomes are lysosomes.

Most cells in the body utilize a process called pinocytosis to ingest fluid and small protein molecules via small vesicles about 80–150 nm in diameter. It is a continual process, so small vesicles are continually forming at the cell surface. Most of the vesicles eventually fuse with lysosomes although they are very numerous in endothelial cells as they move materials from their surface of origin to the other side. They are also numerous at the surfaces of smooth muscle cells and their initial invaginations from the smooth muscle plasma membrane are referred to as caveolae.

During phagocytosis large particles which include bacteria and foreign materials are ingested into the cell. Pseudopodia from the plasma membrane engulf these large particles into a large vesicle about 250 nm in diameter called a phagosome. An endolysosome (or phagolysosome) forms when the phagosome enters the cell and fuses with a lysosome. The lysosomal contents include hydrolytic enzymes which digest the content within the phagosome. Some of the digested products may be used by the cell but most will be exported out of the cell by exocytosis."}, {"name": "References", "text": "Dorland, W. (2011) Dorland's Illustrated Medical Dictionary. 32nd edn. Philadelphia, USA: Elsevier Saunders.

McKinley, M. P., O'Loughlin, V. D. and Pennefather-O'Brien, E. E. (2016) Human Anatomy. 5th edn.: McGraw-Hill Education.

Ovalle, W. K., Nahirney, P. C. and Netter, F. H. (2013) Netter's Essential Histology. ClinicalKey 2012: Elsevier Saunders.

Ross, M. H. and Pawlina, W. (2006) Histology: A text and atlas. Lippincott Williams & Wilkins."}]

items.name: Circular Fibers
Postsynaptic Region
items.info:
[{"name": "Quick Facts", "text": "The postsynaptic region is the region situated beyond or distal to the synapse."}, {"name": "Structure", "text": "The postsynaptic region is a component of chemical synapses. A chemical synapse is made up of a presynaptic element, a synaptic cleft, and a postsynaptic component and membrane. 

The postsynaptic membrane is the site at which the neurotransmitter will interact with a receptor. Part of the plasmalemma of the postsynaptic neuron exhibits dense material. This postsynaptic density contains a complex arrangement of proteins that translate the neurotransmitter-receptor interaction into an intracellular signal, traffic and anchor neurotransmitter receptors to the postsynaptic membrane, and some proteins modulate the activity of the receptors.

Neurotransmitters diffuse across the synaptic cleft and act on multiple receptors. They act either on:

—metabotropic receptors to activate a G-protein signaling cascade;

—ionotropic receptors to open the membrane ion channels.

Metabotropic channels bind a specific neurotransmitter and interact with G-protein on the intracellular domain. G-protein signals the synthesis of a second messenger. Metabotropic receptors are assoaciated with modulation of neuronal activity.

Ionotropic receptors contain integral transmembrane ion channels called transmitter or ligand-gated channels. If a neurotransmitter binds to ionotropic receptors, the channel opens to allow selective movement of ions in and out of the cell and an action potential is generated in the effector cell. This type of signaling is very fast and occurs in somatic motor pathways in the peripheral nervous system and in major neuronal pathways in the brain.

Depending on which receptors they interact with, various neurotransmitters are capable of generating a diverse range of excitatory or inhibitory postsynaptic actions. The consequent generation of a nerve impulse in a postsynaptic neuron is highly dependent on the addition of both the excitatory and inhibitory neuronal impulses reaching the postsynaptic neuron. 

With excitatory synapses, the release of acetylcholine, glutamine, or serotonin neurotransmitters open transmitter-gated sodium channels (or other cation channels). This results in the influx of sodium into the cell which initiates a local voltage reversal (depolarization) of the postsynaptic membrane, leading to the generation of an action potential and a nerve impulse. 

With inhibitory synapses, the release of γ-aminobutyric acid (GABA) or glycine neurotransmitters open transmitter-gated chloride channels (or other anion channels). This results in the influx of chloride into the cell, leading to hyperpolarization of the postsynaptic membrane. This process renders the postsynaptic membrane more negative, resulting in a more challenging generation of action potential. 

Whether a nerve impulse is generated in a postsynaptic neuron depends on input of excitatory or inhibitory actions from hundreds of synapses on the postsynaptic neuron.

Neurotransmitters bind to their appropriate receptor for only about one millisecond before dissociating from it. If the presynaptic cell continues releasing neurotransmitter, then one molecule will replace the other on the receptor and the postsynaptic cell will be restimulated (Ross and Pawlina, 2006)."}, {"name": "Anatomical Relations", "text": "The postsynaptic region is a part of the distal neuron in a chemical synapse. The postsynaptic region is separated from the presynaptic region by the synaptic cleft."}, {"name": "Function", "text": "The postsynaptic membrane is vital in the process of neurotransmission. It has a number of receptors that are coupled to ion channels within its structure. These receptors are the sites on which neurotransmitters from the presynaptic element bind and act on, opening the ion channels to allow the influx of specific ion channels, to exert excitatory or inhibitory effects that either depolarize or hyperpolarize the postsynaptic neuron (Ross and Pawlina, 2006)."}, {"name": "Clinical Correlates", "text": "—Drugs are being developed now to modify synaptic transmission by interfering with the processes of transmission at the postsynaptic membrane (Splittgerber, 2018).

—Myasthenia gravis is an autoimmune disorder, where antibodies are produced against nicotinic acetylcholine receptors on the postsynaptic membrane.

—In high concentrations, nicotine acts as a blocking agent by stimulating the postganglionic neuron causing and maintaining depolarization such that the postganglionic neuron will fail to respond to any stimulant."}, {"name": "References", "text": "Ross, M. H. and Pawlina, W. (2006) Histology: A text and atlas. Lippincott Williams & Wilkins.

Splittgerber, R. (2018) Snell's Clinical Neuroanatomy. Wolters Kluwer Health."}]

items.name: Myelin Sheath
items.info:
[{"name": "Quick Facts", "text": "The myelin sheath is the cylindrical covering on the axons of some neurons; it consists of concentric layers of myelin, formed in the peripheral nervous system by the plasma membrane of Schwann cells, and in the central nervous system by oligodendrocytes. It is interrupted at intervals along its length by gaps known as nodes of Ranvier. Myelin is an electrical insulator that serves to speed the conduction of nerve impulses (Dorland, 2011)."}, {"name": "Structure", "text": "The myelin sheath is produced by oligodendrocytes in the central nervous system and by Schwann cells in the peripheral nervous system. Myelin sheath formation is more complex in the central nervous system (CNS) than in the peripheral nervous system (PNS). Oligodendrocytes produce long processes that extend towards an axon and wraps its plasmalemma around the axon in concentric layers. In some regions of the CNS, oligodendrocytes can enclose up to fifty axons in separate myelin sheaths (Mancall and Brock, 2011). The area of the axon covered by the myelin sheath is called the internodal segments. The thickness of the myelin sheath during the process of myelination is determined by the axon diameter (Ross and Pawlina, 2006).

Myelin is a whitish lipoprotein complex that consists predominantly of lipid bilayers and membrane proteins. The high lipid content is partly removed by traditional histological processes leaving a characteristic “halo” around the axon (Mescher, 2013). The myelin sheath in the CNS differs from the myelin sheath in the PNS. This is because oligodendrocytes and Schwann cells express different myelin-specific proteins during myelination."}, {"name": "Anatomical Relations", "text": "The myelin sheath extends from the initial segment of the axon until right before its terminal branches."}, {"name": "Function", "text": "The myelin sheath forms an insulating layer around the axon and prevents leakage of the electrical current from the axon. In addition, the myelin sheath increases the speed by which nerve impulses are conducted along the axon and makes the propagation of nerve impulses more energy efficient (Marieb, Wilhelm and Mallatt, 2012).

The myelin sheath also functions to maintain an ideal ionic environment that is suitable for the conduction and propagation of the action potentials (Mescher, 2013)."}, {"name": "Clinical Correlates", "text": "—Demyelinating diseases preferentially damage the myelin sheath and so result in decreased or loss of transmission of nerve impulses along the nerve fiber. In multiple sclerosis, the myelin sheath is destroyed."}, {"name": "References", "text": "Dorland, W. (2011) Dorland's Illustrated Medical Dictionary. 32nd edn. Philadelphia, USA: Elsevier Saunders.

Mancall, E. L. and Brock, D. G. (2011) Gray's Clinical Neuroanatomy: The Anatomic Basis for Clinical Neuroscience. Elsevier Health Sciences.

Marieb, E. N., Wilhelm, P. B. and Mallatt, J. (2012) Human Anatomy. fifth edn.: Benjamin Cummings.

Mescher, A. (2013) Junqueira's Basic Histology: Text and Atlas. 13th edn.: McGraw-Hill Education.

Ross, M. H. and Pawlina, W. (2006) Histology: A text and atlas. Lippincott Williams & Wilkins."}]

items.name: Sperm
items.info:
[{"name": "Quick Facts", "text": "Sperm is a mature male germ cell, the specific output of the testes. It is the generative element of the semen that serves to fertilize the oocyte and contains the genetic information to be transmitted to the zygote by the male. It consists of a head (or nucleus), a neck, a middle piece, and a tail with an end piece. Spermatozoa, formed in the seminiferous tubules, are derived from spermatogonia, which first develop into spermatocytes, which, in turn, undergo meiosis to produce spermatids; the spermatids then differentiate into spermatozoa (Dorland, 2011)."}, {"name": "Structure/Morphology", "text": "The mature sperm, or spermatozoon, is a highly differentiated and motile haploid cell. It is composed of a head, neck, and tail (flagellum) and measures about 60 μm in length (Plant and Zeleznik, 2014). The sperm is entirely encapsulated in a plasma membrane, which undergoes regional modifications necessary for fertilization to occur.

The sperm head is flattened and pointed in shape and measures approximately 4.5 μm long, 3 μm wide, and 1 μm thick. It is made up of the nucleus, of which the anterior two thirds is covered by the acrosomal cap and a scanty cytoplasm. The nucleus contains tightly packed chromatin that is enveloped anteriorly by the acrosomal cap. The sperm head is connected to the tail via a short neck, or connecting piece, which spans approximately 0.3 μm in length (Standring, 2020).

The tail makes up most of the sperm’s length, measuring about 55 μm. It is made up of three distinct parts: the middle piece, principal piece, and the end piece. The sperm tail contains several structural components including the axoneme, mitochondrial sheath, outer dense fibers, and the fibrous sheath. The function of the tail is to propel the sperm forward in a whiplash-like fashion and to generate the energy required for this movement.

Sperm is an end product of a process called spermatogenesis. Sperm in the seminiferous tubules are highly differentiated, but are still relatively non-motile. They acquire their motility as they pass through the epididymis. 

Fertilization cannot be completed without a process known as capacitation. Capacitation is essentially the functional maturation of a sperm cell and is completed after the sperm has made its journey to the uterine tube (oviduct or fallopian tube). Various structural and biochemical changes occur during capacitation in which sperm change their behavior, including the acrosome reaction. Following capacitation, sperm develop the ability to penetrate the cumulus of the egg and bind to the zona pellucida. This stimulates the release of digestive enzymes from the acrosome to aid in the dissolution of the zona pellucida in the vicinity of the sperm head, allowing it to access the perivitelline space (Plant and Zeleznik, 2014; Standring, 2020)."}, {"name": "Function", "text": "The principal function of the sperm is to move through the female genital tract, fuse and penetrate the ovum and deliver the male pronucleus containing the genetic material. It also contributes centrioles that help to organize the cytoskeleton of the zygote."}, {"name": "List of Clinical Correlates", "text": "—Infertility"}, {"name": "References", "text": "Dorland, W. (2011) Dorland's Illustrated Medical Dictionary. 32nd edn. Philadelphia, USA: Elsevier Saunders.

Plant, T. M. & Zeleznik, A. J. (2014) Knobil and Neill's Physiology of Reproduction. Elsevier Science.

Standring, S. (2020) Gray's Anatomy: The Anatomical Basis of Clinical Practice. 42nd edn.: Elsevier Health Sciences."}]

items.name: Nucleus (Monocyte)
items.info:
[{"name": "Cell Morphology", "text": "Monocytes are the largest of the leukocytes, with a diameter of 14-24 μm, and account for 4-8% of leukocytes (100-700 monocytes per microliter of blood) (Marieb, Wilhelm and Mallatt, 2012). Monocytes are larger than lymphocytes and are recognizable from their indented horseshoe or kidney shaped nucleus. The nuclear chromatin of monocytes is not as condensed as it is in lymphocytes and monocytes possess more cytoplasm than lymphocytes. The cytoplasm of monocytes may contain some small dispersed granules, typically lysosomes. However, since monocytes lack obvious granules they are classified as agranulocytes. Monocytes have a well-developed Golgi-apparatus, smooth endoplasmic reticulum, rough endoplasmic reticulum, and small mitochondria."}, {"name": "Production", "text": "In the red bone marrow, hematopoietic stem cells differentiate into myeloid stem cells which give rise to monocytes. Monocytes travel from the bone marrow and circulate in the blood for around 3 days. They then enter body tissues and differentiate into various types of phagocytic cells. Development of monocytes takes 2-3 days (Marieb, Wilhelm and Mallatt, 2012).

Monocytes can differentiate into macrophages found in the lymph nodes, liver, spleen, alveoli, and connective tissue (Pawlina, 2016)."}, {"name": "Function", "text": "When monocytes transform into macrophages they function as antigen presenting cells. That means that they bind antigens and present it to T lymphocytes for recognition and elimination. Macrophages move via an amoeboid movement and phagocytose bacteria, other cells, molecules, and tissue debris (Pawlina, 2016; Marieb, Wilhelm and Mallatt, 2012)."}, {"name": "List of Clinical Correlates", "text": "- Monocytosis

- Monocytopenia"}, {"name": "References", "text": "Eroschenko, V. P. (2008) DiFiore's Atlas of Histology with Functional Correlations. Wolters Kluwer Health/Lippincott Williams & Wilkins.

Marieb, E. N., Wilhelm, P. B. and Mallatt, J. (2012) Human Anatomy. 14th edn.: Benjamin Cummings.

Pawlina, W. 2016. Histology: A text and atlas with correlated cell and molecular biology. 7th ed. Philadelphia: Wolters Kluwer."}]

items.name: Hypothalamus
Primary Oocyte (of Primordial Ovarian Follicle)
items.info:
[{"name": "Quick Facts", "text": "The primary oocyte is an oocyte that has begun but not completed the first maturation division; it is derived from an oogonium by differentiation near the time of birth (Dorland, 2011)."}, {"name": "Structure and/or Key Feature(s)", "text": "Although primary oocytes begin their first meiotic division in utero, the first meiotic prophase remains incomplete until just prior to ovulation, which means many remain arrested in their first meiotic division for 12 to perhaps 50 years.

The primary oocyte of the primordial ovarian follicle is about 30 μm in diameter and has a large round, eccentric, pale nucleus containing one or two prominent nucleoli.

The ooplasm (cytoplasm of an oocyte) contains Golgi membranes and vesicles, endoplasmic reticulum, centrioles, and many mitochondria and lysosomes. These organelles are condensed into a region in the ooplasm referred to as a Balbiani body. The ooplasm also contains stacks of membranes called annulate lamellae.

Organelles increase their numbers and become scattered throughout the ooplasm as the oocyte matures. Lipid droplets and masses of lipochrome pigment may appear. Beneath the plasma membrane (oolemma) special secretory granules called cortical granules appear which contain proteases.

As the zona pellucida is being deposited, many irregular microvilli project from the oolemma into the perivitelline space between the oocyte and the granulosa cells to intermingle with similar microvilli projecting from adjacent granulosa cells. 

When the first meiotic division is completed in a mature follicle equal share of chromatin is distributed to each daughter cell but only one receives most of the cytoplasm to become a secondary oocyte. The other daughter cell becomes the first polar body.

The second meiotic division commences immediately after the first meiotic division is completed (Ross and Pawlina, 2006; Mescher, 2013; McKinley, O'Loughlin and Pennefather-O'Brien, 2016)."}, {"name": "Anatomical Relations", "text": "Primary oocytes are contained within primordial follicles in the ovarian cortex."}, {"name": "List of Clinical Correlates", "text": "The long period of meiotic arrest may expose the primary oocyte to factors which could contribute to errors in meiotic division such as nondisjunction. Such an error results in anomalies such as trisomy of chromosome 21 (Down’s syndrome)."}, {"name": "References", "text": "Dorland, W. (2011) Dorland's Illustrated Medical Dictionary. 32nd edn. Philadelphia, USA: Elsevier Saunders.

McKinley, M. P., O'Loughlin, V. D. and Pennefather-O'Brien, E. E. (2016) Human Anatomy. 5th edn.: McGraw-Hill Education.

Mescher, A. (2013) Junqueira's Basic Histology: Text and Atlas. 13th edn.: McGraw-Hill Education.

Ross, M. H. and Pawlina, W. (2006) Histology: A text and atlas. Lippincott Williams & Wilkins."}]

items.name: Alveolar Basal Lamina
items.info: [{"name": "Quick Facts", "text": "The basal lamina is the layer of the basement membrane lying next to the basal surface of the adjoining cell layer, composed of an electron-dense lamina densa and an electron-lucent lamina lucida; sometimes used to denote the lamina densa alone (Dorland, 2011)."}, {"name": "Structure", "text": "The basal lamina is made up of several different proteins and carbohydrates, such as collagen, proteoglycans, and glycoproteins."}, {"name": "Anatomical Relations", "text": "The alveolar basal lamina is found adjacent to the pneumocytes (alveolar epithelial cells) and the basal lamina of the pulmonary capillaries, the latter to which it\u2019s fused."}, {"name": "Function", "text": "The alveolar basal lamina supports the type I and II pneumocytes."}, {"name": "References", "text": "Dorland, W. (2011) Dorland's Illustrated Medical Dictionary. 32nd edn. Philadelphia, USA: Elsevier Saunders."}]

items.name: Origin of Zygomaticus Minor Muscle
Sustentocyte
Enamel Tissue
items.info:
[{"name": "Quick Facts", "text": "The enamel is a hard, thin, translucent layer of calcified substance that envelops and protects the dentin of the crown of the tooth; it is the hardest substance in the body and is almost entirely composed of calcium salts (Dorland, 2011)."}, {"name": "Structure and/or Key Feature(s)", "text": "Enamel is described as a highly mineralized, extremely hard and rigid material that covers the crown of the tooth. Semi-translucent and light yellow to white, the enamel lies superficial to the dentin. The boundary between these layers is known as the dentinoenamel junction. Enamel will typically reach a maximum thickness of 2.5 mm over the cusp of the tooth and become thinner at the cervical margins (Standring, 2016).

The composition of mature dental enamel is unique amongst mammal tissues, and contains 96% inorganic material, less than 1% organic material, and the rest water. Specifically, the inorganic portion of enamel is composed of hydroxyapatite; a crystalline calcium phosphate compound (Iijima et al., 2010). The organic matrix, although only making up 1% of the enamel, permeates the entire enamel and primarily consists of proteins such as amelogenin and enamelin (Standring, 2016).

At a nanoscopic level, tooth enamel is composed of needle-like apatite crystallites. These crystallites constitute the enamel prisms (Iijima et al., 2010).

Enamel is formed by the internal enamel epithelium, in a process called amelogenesis. This epithelium is composed of a closely linked sheet of narrow, cylindrical cells called ameloblasts. Ameloblast cells are responsible for the deposition of enamel during tooth development, through the process of amelogenesis. During this process, the ameloblast moves away from the enamel, forming a projection surrounding the developing enamel. These projections are a histologic landmark known as Tomes’ processes (Hillson, 2005). 

Prior to tooth eruption from the gum, ameloblasts are broken down, thus removing the enamel’s ability to repair or regenerate itself (Standring, 2016)."}, {"name": "Anatomical Relations", "text": "Enamel forms the outermost layer of the crown of the tooth, lying superficial to the dentin (Standring, 2016)."}, {"name": "Function", "text": "Enamel is responsible for protecting the underlying tooth dentin. Its wholly mineral composition lends to the protection of the dentin against food substances as the decomposition of organic matter has little effect on it (Hillson, 2005)."}, {"name": "List of Clinical Correlates", "text": "—Amelogenesis imperfecta"}, {"name": "References", "text": "Dorland, W. (2011) Dorland's Illustrated Medical Dictionary. 32nd edn. Philadelphia, USA: Elsevier Saunders.

Hillson, S. (2005) Teeth. Cambridge University Press.

Iijima, M., Fan, D., Bromley, K. M., Sun, Z. and Moradian-Oldak, J. (2010) 'Tooth enamel proteins enamelin and amelogenin cooperate to regulate the growth morphology of octacalcium phosphate crystals', Crystal growth & design, 10(11), pp. 4815-4822.

Standring, S. (2016) Gray's Anatomy: The Anatomical Basis of Clinical Practice. Gray's Anatomy Series 41 edn.: Elsevier Limited."}]

items.name: Pituitary Gland
Trabecular Retinaculum
items.info:
[{"name": "Quick Facts", "text": "The trabecular retinaculum is a trabecula of loose fibers found at the iridocorneal angle between the anterior chamber of the eye and the venous sinus of the sclera; the aqueous humor filters through the spaces between the fibers into the sinus and passes into the bloodstream. The reticulum is divided into a corneoscleral part and a uveal part (Dorland, 2011)."}, {"name": "Structure and/or Key Feature(s)", "text": "The trabecular retinaculum, or meshwork, is a triangular-shaped region of connective tissue found at the intersection of the sclera, cornea and base of the iris. It is formed by multiple layers or lamellae which can be defined into three regions, the uveal meshwork, corneoscleral meshwork, and juxtacanalicular region (or cribriform region). These are the filtering partitions of the trabecular meshwork. A fourth, non-filtering region that makes up the anterior part of the triangle inserts under the cornea and extends to the scleral spur.

The outer retinaculum contains about three layers of connective tissue beams that form irregular intertrabecular fenestrations. These layers act as a primary filter of the aqueous humor, removing cellular debris. Beneath is the much denser corneoscleral meshwork composed of 8-15 layers of beams. The fenestrations between the trabeculae become smaller as they move towards the juxtacanalicular region and scleral venous sinus. The juxtacanalicular region is adjacent to the scleral venous sinus, attaching to its endothelium. It is less porous than the other regions of the trabecular retinaculum, thus, contributing to the resistance of aqueous humor flow (Abu-Hassan, Acott and Kelley, 2014)."}, {"name": "Anatomical Relations", "text": "The trabecular retinaculum is located at iridocorneal angle, an angle formed between the iris and the cornea and where the sclera becomes continuous with the cornea (limbus). Its posterior wall is formed by the scleral venous sinus."}, {"name": "Function", "text": "The trabecular meshwork allows for the drainage of aqueous humor from the anterior chamber of the eye. As the aqueous humor passes through the trabecular meshwork, it is filtered, removing cell debris. The meshwork nature provides resistance to flow and is normally set to allow optimum intraocular pressure (Abu-Hassan, Acott and Kelley, 2014)."}, {"name": "List of Clinical Correlates", "text": "—Glaucoma"}, {"name": "References", "text": "Abu-Hassan, D. W., Acott, T. S. and Kelley, M. J. (2014) 'The Trabecular Meshwork: A Basic Review of Form and Function', Journal of ocular biology, 2(1), pp. 

Dorland, W. (2011) Dorland's Illustrated Medical Dictionary. 32nd edn. Philadelphia, USA: Elsevier Saunders."}]

items.name: Inner Hair Cell
items.info:
[{"name": "Quick Facts", "text": "The inner hair cells are flask-shaped auditory hair cells, arranged in a single row on the medial side of the inner tunnel of the organ of Corti; they receive impulses from the outer hair cells and transform them into electrical signals that are given to the cochlear nerve for transmission to an auditory cortex in the brain. These cells are surrounded by supporting phalangeal cells (Dorland, 2011)."}, {"name": "Structure and/or Key Feature(s)", "text": "The hair cells of the cochlea are mechanosensory cells which are found on the superior aspect of the basilar membrane. There are two types, inner and outer hair cells, which possess common features. They are typically elongated cells that contain stereocilia on their apical pole and are associated with a synaptic complex at their basal pole. The inner and outer hair cells are also arranged in rows and the apices of the hair cells inclining in toward each other, at the same angle as the neighboring inner and outer pillar cells. The structural inclination of the hair cells is supported by the closely related supporting cells. These include the border cells and the phalangeal cells. The apices of the hair cells and the supporting cells are linked by tight junctions, adherens junctions, and desmosomes. This forms an impermeable barrier, called the reticular lamina, for the passage of ions. Endolymph (high potassium and low sodium concentrations) engulfs the apical surfaces of the hair cells and the supporting cells, while perilymph (high sodium and low potassium) bathes their lateral and basal aspects. This separation generates an electrochemical gradient along the lamina, forming an endocochlear potential which is necessary for the depolarization of hair cells (Standring, 2016). 

Some differences in the outer and inner hair cells structure separate the distinctive roles both cell types have is sound transduction. There are around 3,500 inner hair cells in the human cochlea, arranged in a single row. This row of inner hair cells is positioned internal to the inner pillar cells and the tunnel of Corti. Individually, the inner hair cells possess an uneven pear shape; they are typically broadest at the basal pole and become narrower toward the apical pole. 

At the apical surface, fine wispy projections known as the stereocilia emerge. There are anywhere between 50 and 60 stereocilia per inner hair cell. They possess many direct connections with each other via lateral and tip links. These stereocilia also ascend in height, within the tallest stereocilia located on the outer aspect of the cell surface. The base of each inner hair cell makes 10–20 synaptic contacts with afferent nerve ending (Goutman, Elgoyhen and Gómez-Casati, 2015)."}, {"name": "Anatomical Relations", "text": "The inner hair cells are located on the superior aspect of the basilar membrane and are the closer of the two hair cell types to the internal sulcus of the spiral lamina. They are inferior and closely related to the underside of the tectorial membrane. They have a lot of epithelial structures neighboring them, providing support to the inclination of the inner hair cell. External to the inner hair cells are the inner and outer pillar cells. The tunnel of Corti is formed by the angling of these pillar cells against each other. Internal to the inner hair cells are the inner phalangeal and inner border cells."}, {"name": "Function", "text": "The hair cells function to transduce the vibrations of the sound energy coming from the middle ear into the cochlea into nerve impulses. The hair cells are extremely sensitive and can detect the frequency and amplification of these sounds. 

Sound waves result in disruption of the surrounding cochlear fluid, which creates deflections of the stereocilia at their base from their original position, thus resulting in mechanotransduction. This is facilitated by the opening of the mechanotransduction cation channels, resulting in a graded depolarization due to ionic transfer between the surrounding endolymph. This information is carried through the afferent synapses and all the way to the auditory processing centers. The inner hair cell nerve synapses provide information about the acoustic environment, rather than sound amplification, which has a stronger association with outer hair cells.

The structural incline of the inner hair cells occurs at an angle similar to that of the incline of the neighboring inner pillar cells. This delicate arrangement is firmly correlated to the sensory performance of the cochlea (Goutman, Elgoyhen and Gómez-Casati, 2015)."}, {"name": "List of Clinical Correlates", "text": "—Sensorineural hearing loss"}, {"name": "References", "text": "Dorland, W. (2011) Dorland's Illustrated Medical Dictionary. 32nd edn. Philadelphia, USA: Elsevier Saunders.

Goutman, J. D., Elgoyhen, A. B. & Gómez-Casati, M. E. (2015) Cochlear hair cells: The sound-sensing machines. FEBS letters, 589(22), 3354-3361.

Standring, S. (2016) Gray's Anatomy: The Anatomical Basis of Clinical Practice., 41st edition. Elsevier Limited."}]

items.name: Infundibular Stalk
Dental Pulp (Cross Section)
items.info:
[{"name": "Quick Facts", "text": "The dental pulp is the richly vascularized and innervated connective tissue of mesodermal origin contained in the central cavity of a tooth and delimited by the dentin; it has formative, nutritive, sensory, and protective functions. The portion within the tooth chamber proper is the pulpa coronalis, and that within the root is the pulpa radicularis (Dorland, 2011)."}, {"name": "Structure and/or Key Feature(s)", "text": "Dental pulp is the specialized loose connective tissue that resides in the central pulp cavity or chamber of the tooth. Unlike other dental tissues such as enamel, dentin or cement, dental pulp is non-mineralized. The pulp itself is the living entity of the tooth and contains connective tissue, blood vessels, and nerves.

Each pulp cavity opens into the tissue surrounding the tooth through the apical foramen of the root. Some teeth may additionally have an accessory canal or foramen. Dental pulp is continuous with the periodontal ligament via the apical and accessory foramen (Standring, 2016).

Pulp has two distinct zones, namely the central zone and peripheral zone, both of which are observed in the coronal and radicular parts of the tooth. The central zone houses arterioles, veins and nerve trunks that enter the pulp cavity through the apical foramen and travel longitudinally to the coronal pulp chamber. The peripheral zone (also known as the odontogenic zone) is comprised of distinct layers, beginning with the outermost layer which lies on the periphery of the pulp known as the odontoblastic layer. The odontoblastic layer is adjacent to the predentin with the cell bodies of the odontoblasts situated in the pulp and their cell processes extending into the dentinal tubules. 

Subjacent to the odontoblast layer is the cell-free zone (also known as the zone of Weil) which contains several bundles of reticular fibers and numerous capillaries and nerves. Subjacent to the cell-free zone is the cell-rich zone that contains numerous fibroblasts and perivascular cells (also known as mesenchymal cells), the latter of which can give rise to odontoblasts, fibroblasts or macrophages. The deep pulp cavity, located medial to the cell-rich zone, contains the subodontoblastic nerve plexus of Raschkow (Chiego, 2014). 

Through the apical foramen, a number of thin-walled arterioles enter and travel longitudinally until they reach the pulp cavity in the crown. Here, they ramify forming a dense capillary network beneath the odontoblast layer. After draining the capillary bed, small venules travel downward and exit the pulp cavity via the apical foramen. 

Along with the arterioles, sensory and sympathetic nerve fibers enter the pulp cavity via the apical foramen. Specifically, sympathetic nerve fibers extend from the superior cervical ganglion, travel into the pulp cavity and innervate the smooth muscle cells of the arterioles to modulate vasoconstriction. 

Additionally, sensory fibers that have arisen from the trigeminal ganglion pass through the apical foramen, travel longitudinally toward the crown and ramify as the nerve plexus of Raschkow. Fibers can extend in an unmyelinated form from this plexus toward the odontoblasts where they lose their Schwann cell sheath. These free nerve endings can sometimes extend up between the odontoblasts and enter the dentinal tubules where they function by transmitting pain stimuli from heat, cold or pressure (Standring, 2016)."}, {"name": "Anatomical Relations", "text": "Dental pulp is located in the root (radicular part) and crown (coronal part) of the tooth and is entirely surrounded and enclosed by dentin (Standring, 2016)."}, {"name": "Function", "text": "Dental pulp plays an important role in the defense process of the tooth whereby it houses cellular components necessary for the recognition and processing of antigens. Its sensory fibers additionally allow for the recognition of different stimuli including thermal change, mechanical deformation or trauma. The blood vessels and nerves housed by the pulp cavity provide nutritive support to the odontoblast layer, which facilitates the odontoblasts in their production of dentin (Yu and Abbott, 2007)."}, {"name": "List of Clinical Correlates", "text": "—Pulpitis"}, {"name": "References", "text": "Chiego, D. J. (2014) Essentials of Oral Histology and Embryology - E-Book: A Clinical Approach. Elsevier Health Sciences.

Dorland, W. (2011) Dorland's Illustrated Medical Dictionary. 32nd edn. Philadelphia, USA: Elsevier Saunders.

Standring, S. (2016) Gray's Anatomy: The Anatomical Basis of Clinical Practice. Gray's Anatomy Series 41 edn.: Elsevier Limited.

Yu, C. and Abbott, P. V. (2007) 'An overview of the dental pulp: its functions and responses to injury', Aust Dent J, 52(1 Suppl), pp. S4-16."}]

items.name: Sarcolemma (Cardiac Muscle Cell)
items.info:
[{"name": "Quick Facts", "text": "The sarcolemma is the delicate plasma membrane that invests every striated muscle fiber (Dorland, 2011)."}, {"name": "Structure and/or Key Features", "text": "The sarcolemma is the fine, delicate, extensible membrane surrounding each muscle fiber. It is composed of a cell, or plasma, membrane which presents an extracellular matrix of collagen fibrils and polysaccharides that make contact with the basal lamina. The sarcolemma also contains tunnel-like invaginations into the sarcoplasm, which are known as transverse tubules in striated muscle and caveolae in smooth muscle (Standring, 2020)."}, {"name": "Anatomical Relations", "text": "Transmembrane proteins found within the sarcolemma facilitate a physical connection between the actin cytoskeleton of the muscle fiber and the extracellular basal lamina (Martini, Nath and Bartholomew, 2017)."}, {"name": "Function", "text": "Like other types of cell membranes, the sarcolemma forms a defined barrier between extracellular and intracellular environments."}, {"name": "References", "text": "Dorland, W. (2011) Dorland's Illustrated Medical Dictionary. 32nd edn. Philadelphia, USA: Elsevier Saunders.

Martini, F. H., Nath, J. L. and Bartholomew, E. F. (2017) Fundamentals of Anatomy & Physiology. Pearson Education.

Standring, S. (2020) Gray's Anatomy: The Anatomical Basis of Clinical Practice. 42nd edn.: Elsevier Health Sciences."}]

items.name: Lamina Propria (Duodenum)
items.info: [{"name": "Quick Facts", "text": "The lamina propria is the connective tissue coat of a mucous membrane (tunica mucosa) just deep to the epithelium and basement membrane (Dorland, 2011)."}, {"name": "Structure/Morphology", "text": "The lamina propria forms the core of each villus and surrounds each intestinal gland. It is loose connective tissue and contains blood vessels and lymphatic vessels (lacteals). \n\nThe lamina propria contains aggregations of lymphocytes and associated immune cells e.g., eosinophils, macrophages, and neutrophils particularly within each villus. This aggregation is referred to as diffuse lymphatic tissue. It also contains many nodules/follicles of lymphatic tissue that represent the GALT (gut associated lymphatic tissue). They are particularly large and numerous in the ileum and are referred to as \u201cPeyer\u2019s patches.\u201d They can extend from the lamina propria to occupy the submucosa."}, {"name": "Key Features/Anatomical Relations", "text": "The lamina propria is immediately underlying the surface epithelium and forms the core of each villus and surrounds each intestinal gland. Its deepest boundary is the muscularis mucosa."}, {"name": "Function", "text": "The lamina propria is the supporting connective tissue of the surface epithelium and underlying intestinal glands. It also supports blood vessels and lymphatic vessels (lacteals) involved in absorption of digested products as well as accommodating cells of the gut associated lymphatic tissue (GALT) that can identify antigens and initiate the immune response."}, {"name": "References", "text": "Dorland, W. (2011) Dorland's Illustrated Medical Dictionary. 32nd edn. Philadelphia, USA: Elsevier Saunders."}]

items.name: Parafollicular Cell
items.info:
[{"name": "Quick Facts", "text": "Parafollicular cells, or C thyrocytes, are ovoid cells with an irregular nucleus and many brown or black cytoplasmic granules, located in the follicular epithelium and interfollicular spaces along with the principal cells of the thyroid follicles, in the follicular epithelium and interfollicular spaces, and which elaborate calcitonin. They arise during embryonic life from the fifth pharyngeal pouches and are incorporated in the thyroid gland in mammals, but form discrete epithelial cell masses (ultimobranchial bodies) in submammalian vertebrates (Dorland, 2011)."}, {"name": "Structure/Morphology", "text": "The thyroid follicle has two cell types, follicular cells, or T thyrocytes, and parafollicular cells, or C thyrocytes. 

Parafollicular cells are located within the basement membrane that surrounds the thyroid follicle. They are either solitary cells or occur in small clusters and have a rather foamy vesicle dominated cytoplasm. At the electron microscope (ultrastructural) level, the vesicles are between 60 and 550 nm in diameter (Ross and Pawlina, 2016). The apex of the parafollicular cells does not reach the lumen of the thyroid follicle, thus they not in contact with the central colloid.
"}, {"name": "Anatomical Relations", "text": "The parafollicular cells are found within the thyroid follicle, squeezed within the basement membrane around the follicular epithelium."}, {"name": "Function", "text": "The parafollicular cells secrete calcitonin which is responsible for lowering calcium levels in the blood."}, {"name": "List of Clinical Correlates", "text": "—Calcitonin can be secreted by several endocrine tumors e.g., medullary carcinoma of the thyroid."}, {"name": "References", "text": "Dorland, W. (2011) Dorland's Illustrated Medical Dictionary. 32nd edn. Philadelphia, USA: Elsevier Saunders.
Ross, M. H. and Pawlina, W. (2016) Histology: A Text and Atlas. Wolters Kluwer Health.
"}]

items.name: Supraoptic Nucleus
Hemorrhagic Body
items.info: [{"name": "Structure and/or Key Feature(s)", "text": "After ovulation, the granulosa and the theca interna remain in the wall of the ovary. The corpus luteum forms from this structure after the oocyte is expelled. This large structure mostly resembles a collapsed epithelial bag as the original wall of the mature follicle is now thrown into deep folds, with an internal cavity. A hemorrhagic body (corpus hemorrhagicum or rubrum) is first formed as this internal cavity is usually filled with loose connective tissue, red blood cells and fibrin deposits resulting from hemorrhaging during ovulation. This is all gradually removed but will remain as a central region in the corpus luteum (Ross and Pawlina, 2006)."}, {"name": "References", "text": "Ross, M. H. and Pawlina, W. (2006) Histology: A text and atlas. Lippincott Williams & Wilkins."}]

items.name: Rod Cell
items.info:
[{"name": "Quick Facts", "text": "The rod cell is one of the two types of visual cells, along with retinal cones, having synapses internally with bipolar retinal cells. Rods serve night vision and detection of motion. Their synaptic terminals are spherical, and their dendritic inner and outer segments are long and cylindrical. Rods have membranous disks, free saccules that contain rhodopsin and are completely enclosed by the outer cell membrane. There are about 120 million rods in the retina. None are in the foveola; the greatest concentration is about 20 degrees away from the fovea centralis, and the density gradually decreases approaching the periphery of the retina (Dorland, 2011)."}, {"name": "Structure and/or Key Features", "text": "Rod cells are one of the two photoreceptor cell types of the retina. Photoreceptors are defined as highly differentiated neuroepithelial cells that are sensitive to light. Rod cells are radially oriented and long, measuring approximately 20–30 µm from the external tip of the outer segment to the inner synaptic terminal, the spherule. They serve a scotopic function, meaning they are maximally sensitive to low levels of monochromatic light. It is estimated there are approximately 92 million rods in the human eye, however, with significant inter-individual variation (Krstic, 2013; Molday and Moritz, 2015; Standring, 2016). 

The foveola of the retina, the center of high acuity color (photopic) vision, is free of rods. However, traveling outward from the foveola, the number of rods increases reaching peak density at the optic disc, before declining again toward the periphery. 

Rod cells are divided into two distinct segments, known as the outer and inner segments, which are connected by a thin connecting stalk. The outer segments of rods are cylindrical and are recognizable by the presence of approximately 1,000 flattened membranous discs with a lobular appearance. These discs originate as deep infoldings of the plasma membrane at the base of the outer segment, but bud off following formation; thus they are no longer connected to the plasma membrane. A distinct feature of the membranous discs is the presence of a photosensitive protein called rhodopsin (Standring, 2016). The inner segment of the rod cells measures up to 1.5 µm, while for cone cells, it is much thicker (5–6 µm). 

The nucleus of the rod cell is housed in the soma (cell body) that is rounder and smaller than for cones. The greater volume density of nucleic acids of rod nuclei makes them stain darker than cones. The rod nuclei are stacked in several layers internal, or vitreal, to the cone nuclei (Standring, 2016).

Rod photoreceptor synaptic terminals take a rounded, lobular form called a “spherule.” The spherules make synaptic connections with bipolar and horizontal cells."}, {"name": "Anatomical Relations", "text": "Processes and parts of rod cells extend across four layers of the retina. The inner and outer segments are located in layers of the same name. The cell then crosses the outer limiting membrane into the outer nuclear layer, where its nucleus and cell body are located. Finally, the synaptic terminals of the cell are in the outer plexiform layer (Standring, 2016).

Rod cells are supported by the processes of glial (Müller) cells that span through the retina, from the internal limiting membrane to the external limiting membrane. These processes fill the extracellular spaces between rods and cones (Standring, 2016)."}, {"name": "Function", "text": "Photoreceptor cells are responsible for the absorption and processing of light, and the subsequent conversion of this light into electrical signals that can be transmitted through the retina. Rod cells are scotopic and function under dim light conditions. Light is absorbed by visual pigments, which are composed of a protein opsin, bounded by a light-absorbing chromophore, retinal (a form of vitamin A). Human photoreceptor cells can synthesize four different types of opsins, thus generating four spectrally distinct visual pigments. The rods contain only one of these pigments, rhodopsin (visual purple). Cones contain three.

Rhodopsin is synthesized in the rod cell somata and is then incorporated in the membrane of outer segments. Light is absorbed by the rhodopsin in the outer segment membranous discs. 

When exposed to light, the retinal molecule becomes activated and changes the configuration of rhodopsin, triggering an intracellular biochemical cascade culminating in the hyperpolarization of the rod cell. This process, in which light is converted into an electrical signal, is known as phototransduction (Standring, 2016; Pepe, 1999).
