items.name: Sarcolemma
items.info:
[{"name": "Quick Facts", "text": "The sarcolemma is the delicate plasma membrane that invests every striated muscle fiber (Dorland, 2011)."}, {"name": "Structure", "text": "The sarcolemma is the fine, delicate, extensible membrane surrounding each muscle fiber. It is composed of a cell, or plasma, membrane which presents an extracellular matrix of collagen fibrils and polysaccharides that make contact with the basal lamina. The sarcolemma also contains tunnel-like invaginations into the sarcoplasm, which are known as transverse tubules (Standring, 2016)."}, {"name": "Key Features/Anatomical Relations", "text": "Transmembrane proteins found within the sarcolemma facilitate a physical connection between the actin cytoskeleton of the muscle fiber and the extracellular basal lamina (Martini et al., 2017)."}, {"name": "Function", "text": "Like other types of cell membranes, the sarcolemma forms a defined barrier between extracellular and intracellular environments."}, {"name": "References", "text": "Dorland, W. (2011) Dorland's Illustrated Medical Dictionary. 32nd edn. Philadelphia, USA: Elsevier Saunders.

Martini, F. H., Nath, J. L. and Bartholomew, E. F. (2017) Fundamentals of Anatomy & Physiology. Pearson Education.

Standring, S. (2016) Gray's Anatomy: The Anatomical Basis of Clinical Practice. Gray's Anatomy Series: Elsevier Limited."}]

It houses neurovasculature, and interstitial endocrine (Leydig) cells."}, {"name": "References", "text": "Dorland, W. (2011) Dorland's Illustrated Medical Dictionary. 32nd edn. items.name: Postsynaptic Membrane
items.info:
[{"name": "Quick Facts", "text": "The postsynaptic membrane is the area of plasma membrane of a postsynaptic cell, either a muscle fiber or a neuron, that is within the synapse and has areas especially adapted for receiving neurotransmitters (Dorland, 2011)."}, {"name": "Structure", "text": "The postsynaptic membrane is the site at which the neurotransmitter will interact with a receptor. Part of the plasmalemma of the postsynaptic neuron exhibits dense material. This postsynaptic density contains a complex arrangement of proteins that translate the neurotransmitter-receptor interaction into an intracellular signal, traffic and anchor neurotransmitter receptors to the postsynaptic membrane, and some proteins modulate the activity of the receptors.

Neurotransmitters diffuse across the synaptic cleft and act on multiple receptors. They act either on:

—metabotropic receptors to activate a G-protein signaling cascade;

—ionotropic receptors to open the membrane ion channels.

Metabotropic channels bind a specific neurotransmitter and interact with G-protein on the intracellular domain. G-protein signals the synthesis of a second messenger. Metabotropic receptors are assoaciated with modulation of neuronal activity.

Ionotropic receptors contain integral transmembrane ion channels called transmitter or ligand-gated channels. If a neurotransmitter binds to ionotropic receptors, the channel opens to allow selective movement of ions in and out of the cell and an action potential is generated in the effector cell. This type of signaling is very fast and occurs in somatic motor pathways in the peripheral nervous system and in major neuronal pathways in the brain .

Depending on which receptors they interact with, various neurotransmitters are capable of generating a diverse range of excitatory or inhibitory postsynaptic actions. The consequent generation of a nerve impulse in a postsynaptic neuron is highly dependent on the addition of both the excitatory and inhibitory neuronal impulses reaching the postsynaptic neuron. 

With excitatory synapses, the release of acetylcholine, glutamine, or serotonin neurotransmitters open transmitter-gated sodium channels (or other cation channels). This results in the influx of sodium into the cell which initiates a local voltage reversal (depolarization) of the postsynaptic membrane, leading to the generation of an action potential and a nerve impulse. 

With inhibitory synapses, the release of γ-aminobutyric acid (GABA) or glycine neurotransmitters open transmitter-gated chloride channels (or other anion channels). This results in the influx of chloride into the cell, leading to hyperpolarization of the postsynaptic membrane. This process renders the postsynaptic membrane more negative, resulting in a more challenging generation of action potential. 

Whether a nerve impulse is generated in a postsynaptic neuron depends on input of excitatory or inhibitory actions from hundreds of synapses on the postsynaptic neuron.

Neurotransmitters bind to their appropriate receptor for only about one millisecond before dissociating from it. If the presynaptic cell continues releasing neurotransmitter then one molecule will replace the other on the receptor and the postsynaptic cell will be restimulated (Ross and Pawlina, 2006)."}, {"name": "Anatomical Relations", "text": "The postsynaptic region is a part of the distal neuron in a chemical synapse. The postsynaptic region is separated from the presynaptic region by the synaptic cleft."}, {"name": "Function", "text": "The postsynaptic membrane is vital in the process of neurotransmission. It has a number of receptors that are coupled to ion channels within its structure. These receptors are the sites on which neurotransmitters from the presynaptic element bind and act on, opening the ion channels to allow the influx of specific ion channels, to exert excitatory or inhibitory effects that either depolarize or hyperpolarize the postsynaptic neuron (Ross and Pawlina, 2006)."}, {"name": "Clinical Correlates", "text": "—Drugs are being developed now to modify synaptic transmission by interfering with the processes of transmission at the postsynaptic membrane (Splittgerber, 2018).

—Myasthenia gravis is an autoimmune disorder, where antibodies are produced against nicotinic acetylcholine receptors on the postsynaptic membrane.

—In high concentrations, nicotine acts as a blocking agent by stimulating the postganglionic neuron causing and maintaining depolarization such that the postganglionic neuron will fail to respond to any stimulant."}, {"name": "References", "text": "Dorland, W. (2011) Dorland's Illustrated Medical Dictionary. 32nd edn. Philadelphia, USA: Elsevier Saunders.

Ross, M. H. and Pawlina, W. (2006) Histology: A text and atlas. Lippincott Williams & Wilkins.

Splittgerber, R. (2018) Snell's Clinical Neuroanatomy. Wolters Kluwer Health."}]

items.name: Basement Membrane (of Convoluted Seminiferous Tubule)
items.info:
[{"name": "Quick Facts", "text": "A basement membrane is a thin sheet of amorphous extracellular material upon which the basal surfaces of epithelial cells rest; other cells associated with basement membranes are muscle cells, Schwann cells, and fat cells. The membrane is interposed between the cellular elements and the underlying connective tissue. It usually comprises two layers, the basal lamina and the reticular lamina, and is composed of Type IV collagen (which is unique to basement membranes), laminin, fibronectin, and heparan sulfate proteoglycans (Dorland, 2011)."}, {"name": "Structure", "text": "Most epithelia attach to some form of underlying connective tissues by a basal lamina. The basal lamina is a thin sheet of extracellular proteins and fibrils. Additionally, carbohydrate-rich material is appended to the lower face of the basal lamina. If the accumulation is sufficient, the basal lamina is referred to as a basement membrane.

The basement membrane is synthesized by the epithelium and the additional material by the underlying connective tissue cells. Some epithelia do not have a basement membrane but most have a basal lamina (Ross and Pawlina, 2016; Ovalle, Nahirney and Netter, 2013)."}, {"name": "Anatomical Relations", "text": "Most epithelia are attached to some form of underlying connective tissues by a basal lamina."}, {"name": "Function", "text": "The basement membrane separates the seminiferous epithelium from the underlying connective tissue within the interstitial compartment of the testis."}, {"name": "References", "text": "Dorland, W. (2011) Dorland's Illustrated Medical Dictionary. 32nd edn. Philadelphia, USA: Elsevier Saunders.

Ovalle, W. K., Nahirney, P. C. and Netter, F. H. (2013) Netter's Essential Histology. ClinicalKey 2012: Elsevier Saunders.

Ross, M. H. and Pawlina, W. (2016) Histology: A Text and Atlas. Wolters Kluwer Health."}]

items.name: Nucleus (Neutrophil)
items.info:
[{"name": "Cell Morphology", "text": "Neutrophils are the most abundant leukocytes, accounting for around 60% of all leukocytes (Eroschenko, 2008). There are around 3000-7000 neutrophils per microliter of blood. They are motile cells and have a diameter of 10-14 μm, making them larger than erythrocytes. 

Neutrophils have a multilobed nucleus that may have a horseshoe shape. The lobes of the nucleus range from 2 to 6 lobes that are interconnected by thin threads of chromatin. Immature neutrophils contain fewer lobes (Pawlina, 2016). 

Neutrophils contain three kinds of cytoplasmic granules and therefore, are classified as granulocytes. These granules contain enzymes and molecules that are involved in immune responses. They also possess various surface receptors which allow them to recognize infectious agents. Neutrophils have a small Golgi apparatus and small number of mitochondria. 

The lifespan of neutrophils ranges from 6 hours to a few days. When a neutrophil reaches its maximum lifespan, it is destroyed via apoptosis and is engulfed by a macrophage (Marieb, Wilhelm and Mallatt, 2012)."}, {"name": "Production", "text": "In the red bone marrow, a hematopoietic stem cell differentiates into a myeloid stem cell which gives rise to neutrophils. Development of neutrophils takes 7-11 days (Marieb, Wilhelm and Mallatt, 2012). Neutrophils leave the blood and enter peripheral connective tissues. They are usually located at sites of infection."}, {"name": "Function", "text": "Neutrophils provide the first line of defense during an inflammatory response. As granulocytes, neutrophils phagocytose bacteria and destroy them by releasing digestive enzymes from their cytoplasmic granules that target the cells walls of bacteria. Other types of granules released by neutrophils mediate and enhance immune responses(Pawlina, 2016). The phagocytic function of neutrophils is driven by chemotactic factors (Eroschenko, 2008)."}, {"name": "List of Clinical Correlates", "text": "- Neutropenia

- Neutrophilia"}, {"name": "References", "text": "Eroschenko, V. P. (2008) DiFiore's Atlas of Histology with Functional Correlations. Wolters Kluwer Health/Lippincott Williams & Wilkins.

Marieb, E. N., Wilhelm, P. B. and Mallatt, J. (2012) Human Anatomy. 14th edn.: Benjamin Cummings.

Pawlina, W. 2016. Histology: A text and atlas with correlated cell and molecular biology. 7th ed. Philadelphia: Wolters Kluwer."}]

items.name: Spiral Organ
items.info:
[{"name": "Quick Facts", "text": "The spiral organ is the organ, resting on the basilar membrane of the cochlear duct, that contains the auditory hair cells, special sensory receptors for hearing, as well as several types of supporting cells, such as the inner and outer pillar cells, inner and outer phalangeal cells, border cells, and Hensen cells (Dorland, 2011)."}, {"name": "Structure and/or Key Feature(s)", "text": "The spiral organ of Corti is a complex structure that is comprised of a variety of sensorineural and supporting cells. Its unique structure enables it to convert the mechanical vibrations transmitted from the middle ear into electrical signals which then generate a cascade of neural signals back to the central nervous system via the cochlear nerve. 

The organ of Corti rests on the upper surface of the basilar membrane within the cochlear duct. The sensory component of the organ of Corti is composed of the hair cells, their stereocilia, and the nerve fibers that synapse at their bases. The inner and outer hair cells are mechanosensory cells. The inner hair cells are irregularly shaped with rounded bodies and arranged in a single row, while the outer hair cells are rod-shaped and insert into the cup shaped apical regions of the external phalangeal epithelial cells. The stereocilia of the inner hair cells have a linear pattern, while the stereocilia of the outer hair cells are organized into a “W” or “V” shape that are in direct contact with the tectorial membrane.

Other cells of the organ of Corti are arranged across the basilar membrane in a specific fashion. They include the supporting cells, phalangeal cells, and pillar cells, and they are found on both sides of the hair cells, as well as in between. These cells help to stabilize the angling position of the hair cells. The phalangeal cells project processes upwards, which expand outwards at the apex of the hair cells. These fill in the gaps between the apices of the hair cells and forms an impermeable barrier known as the reticular lamina. This lamina separates the endolymph and perilymph surrounding the organ of Corti. The endolymph bathes apices of the hair cells, while the perilymph surrounds the basolateral aspects of the hair cells. These two fluids have different ionic compositions, and so, an electrochemical gradient is generated along the thin reticular lamina. This gradient is what enables the depolarization of hair cells.

The pillar cells separate the inner and outer hair cells. They are organized such that they lean toward each other. This arrangement forms a tunnel (of Corti) that is triangular shaped and filled with perilymph.

The organ of Corti primarily receives its blood supply via branches of the labyrinthine artery, and the terminal modiolar spiral artery. The vas spirale lies underneath the tunnel of Corti and exchanges the metabolites from the organ of Corti. Venous drainage occurs alongside these small arterial vessels to form cochlear veins which empty back to greater venous vessels."}, {"name": "Anatomical Relations", "text": "The organ of Corti is inferior to the tectorial membrane and is in direct contact with it via the stereocilia of the outer hair cells. The organ of Corti is situated superior to the basilar membrane."}, {"name": "Function", "text": "Sound waves are transmitted from the middle ear to the internal ear via the ossicles. In the internal ear, these waves disturb the endolymph of the cochlea. This disturbance translates to deflections of the stereocilia from their original position resulting in mechanotransduction. This is facilitated by the opening of the mechanotransduction cation channels, resulting in a graded depolarization due to ionic transfer between the surrounding endolymph. 

The inner hair cells provide information about the acoustic environment, while the outer hair cells help to selectively isolate and amplify certain frequencies. Sound detection is not uniform throughout the cochlea; different regions of the cochlea respond to different sound frequencies. The organ of Corti and basilar membrane are reduced in size and more rigid at the base of the cochlea than the apex. This variation results in the resonance of sound waves that consistently radiate from the base to the apex, and so the high frequency sounds are better heard in the base of the cochlea, while lower-frequency sounds are heard in the apex."}, {"name": "List of Clinical Correlates", "text": "—Sensorineural hearing loss"}, {"name": "References", "text": "Dorland, W. (2011) Dorland's Illustrated Medical Dictionary. 32nd edn. Philadelphia, USA: Elsevier Saunders.

Standring, S. (2016) Gray's Anatomy: The Anatomical Basis of Clinical Practice., 41st edition. Elsevier Limited."}]

items.name: Glycoprotein
items.info: [{"name": "Quick Facts", "text": "A glycoprotein is a conjugated protein containing one or more covalently linked carbohydrate residues. While technically describing conjugates in which the carbohydrate is less than 4 percent by weight, the term is often used generically to include the mucoproteins and proteoglycans (Dorland, 2011)."}, {"name": "Structure and/or Key Feature(s)", "text": "Carbohydrate molecules can attach to the proteins on the surface of the plasma membrane, thus forming glycoproteins. If they attach to the lipids of the bilayer, they form glycolipids. Collectively, they form a layer on the cell surface called the cell coat or glycocalyx (Ross and Pawlina, 2016)."}, {"name": "Anatomical Relations", "text": "Glycoproteins are found on the extracellular surface of the plasma membrane."}, {"name": "Function", "text": "They help create microenvironments on the extracellular membrane surface that play a role in metabolism, cell recognition as well a serving as receptor sites for hormones (Ross and Pawlina, 2016)."}, {"name": "References", "text": "Dorland, W. (2011) Dorland's Illustrated Medical Dictionary. 32nd edn. Philadelphia, USA: Elsevier Saunders.\n\nRoss, M. H. and Pawlina, W. (2016) Histology: A Text and Atlas. Wolters Kluwer Health."}]

items.name: Stereocilium (Outer Hair Cells)
items.info:
[{"name": "Quick Facts", "text": "Stereocilia are long, nonmotile microvilli found on the free surface of hair cells of the internal ear; they have cores of cross-linked actin filaments but, unlike true cilia, do not have axonemes (Dorland, 2011)."}, {"name": "Structure and/or Key Feature(s)", "text": "At the apices of each hair cell there is an emergence of thin, wispy projections known as the stereocilia. Each stereocilium core is comprised of a tight arrangement of parallel, cross-linked actin filaments. The stereocilia vary in number between the inner and outer hair cells, with anywhere between 50 and 60 stereocilia per inner hair cell and 100 stereocilia per outer hair cell. 

The stereocilia of the inner hair cells are organized in a single linear fashion, while the stereocilia of the outer hair cell are organized into three rows of graded height. These rows form a “V” or “W” pattern, depending on the region the outer hair cells are located in the cochlea.

The positioning of the stereocilia is strengthened by the fixation of their basal aspects into a compact fibrillar layer, located just below the apical surface of the stereocilia. This layer is known as the cuticular lamina. The rows of stereocilia have a greater length at the apex of the cochlea and a shorter length at the base. The stereocilia of each hair cell are not of equal length, with the stereocilia of greatest length positioned in the center, and gradually decreasing as they move outwards. This arrangement is vital for the function of the cochlea. This highly precise geometry is essential to detect the nanoscale movements within the fluid of the cochlea.

The stereocilia also possess numerous interconnections with each other. All stereocilia are connected to their neighbors via lateral links, while the shorter stereocilia are further bridged to the taller contiguous stereocilia via tip links; these run from the apex of the shorter stereocilia to the body of the taller adjacent stereocilia. These links provide an adapting support network that keeps the stereocilia connected but also susceptible to displacement by vibration."}, {"name": "Anatomical Relations", "text": "The stereocilia rise from the apical aspect of the hair cells. Their bases are in contact with the cuticular lamina, and their apices are superior to this. Each stereocilium is surrounded by neighboring stereocilia and these are connected via a variety of lateral and tip links. The stereocilia are inferior to the tectorial membrane, with the inner hair cells separated from them by a space that is occupied by the endolymph. The stereocilia of the outer hair cell are in direct contact with the tectorial membrane. Their close contact results in “V” or “W” shaped impressions on the membrane known as Hensen’s ridge."}, {"name": "Function", "text": "The unique stereocilia possess a variety of special functions, such as mechanoelectrical conduction, cochlear amplification, and frequency selectivity. Essentially, sound vibrations cause minute deflections of stereocilia bundles from the original position. The hair cells react with incredible sensitivity and speed to these mechanical vibrations. The vibrations produce a shearing movement between the tectorial membrane and basilar membrane, resulting in stereociliary deflection and a change in the strain of the stereociliary tip links. This causes the ion channels to open and close, with an increase in the strain corresponding to an increase number of ions flowing into the hair cell, leading to an eventual depolarization of the hair cell."}, {"name": "List of Clinical Correlates", "text": "—Deafness (via ototoxicity)"}, {"name": "References", "text": "Dorland, W. (2011) Dorland's Illustrated Medical Dictionary. 32nd edn. Philadelphia, USA: Elsevier Saunders."}]

items.name: Papillary Duct
items.info: [{"name": "Quick Facts", "text": "The papillary duct is a wide terminal tubule in the renal pyramid, formed by the union of several straight collecting tubules and emptying into the renal pelvis in the area cribrosa (Dorland, 2011)."}, {"name": "Structure and/or Key Features", "text": "Papillary ducts are considered the most distal portion of the collecting ducts. Small muscle fibers that extend from the renal papillae to the minor calyces\u2019 contract to facilitate the flow of renal filtrate through the papillary ducts and their openings."}, {"name": "Anatomical Relations", "text": "Papillary ducts pass through the openings in the renal papillae and drain into minor calyces."}, {"name": "Function", "text": "Papillary ducts facilitate the transport of renal filtrate into minor calyces."}, {"name": "References", "text": "Dorland, W. (2011) Dorland's Illustrated Medical Dictionary. 32nd edn. Philadelphia, USA: Elsevier Saunders."}]

items.name: Eyeball
items.info:
[{"name": "Quick Facts", "text": "The eyeball is a large sphere, with the segment of a smaller sphere, the cornea, in front. It is composed of three coats: the external tough fibrous layer, consisting of the white sclera over most of the eyeball and the cornea on the anterior surface; the middle vascular layer or uvea, consisting of the choroid, the ciliary body, and the iris; and the inner layer, which is neural and sensory and consists primarily of the retina. Within the three layers are the refracting media: the aqueous humor, the crystalline lens, and the vitreous humor. The lens is a double convex transparent body between the vitreous and aqueous humors; its convexity is altered by the ciliary muscle during accommodation. Posteriorly, fibers of the optic nerve enter the ganglionic layer and receive sensations from the visual cells of the retina (the retinal rods and retinal cones) (Dorland, 2011)."}, {"name": "Structure /Morphology", "text": "The eyeball is situated inside the anterior part of the orbit. It consists of two partial spheres of different radii that are fused as one structure. The smaller sphere forms the anterior portion of the globe, the larger posterior sphere. The anterior part consists of an outer, clear, cornea and a deeper ciliary body and iris, separated spatially from the cornea. The posterior part is three layers thick and consists of the outer sclera (continuous with the cornea), the intermediate pigmented and vascular cells, the choroid (continuous with the ciliary body), and an inner nervous layer, the retina."}, {"name": "Key Features/Anatomical Relations", "text": "The cornea forms the anterior one sixth of the eyeball. It is normally transparent to allow for the light to enter the eyeball. Its posterior continuation, the sclera, forms the opaque posterior five sixths. It is pierced by numerous vessels and nerve (including the optic nerve) and serves as the site of attachment of various muscles.

The choroid is a pigmented vascular layer that is adherent to the retina internally and attached to the sclera externally. The ciliary muscle and ciliary processes protrude from the anterior margin of the choroid and the form a complete ring around the inside of the eyeball and the outside of the lens. The muscle contributes to accommodation of the lens for near/far vision, while the ciliary processes produce aqueous humor. 

Completing the vascular layer anteriorly is the iris. It projects outwards from the ciliary body as an anular structure pigmented anteriorly so as to provide the basis for “eye color.” The center of the annulus is the pupil. Smooth muscle fibers within the iris control the size of the pupil.

The retina consists of a neural part along the inside of the globe (concerned with vision) and a pigmented supportive layer, just deep to it called the retinal pigment epithelium (RPE). The RPE extends anteriorly to line the posterior surfaces of the ciliary body and iris. The RPE is firmly attached to the choroid. Histologically, the neural part is formed of several alternating layers. The light-sensitive receptors in the retina include cones (for light vision) and rods (for night vision). However, the area where the optic nerve exits the retina posteriorly, is devoid of photoreceptors and is called the optic disc. Lateral to the disc is the site of maximum visual acuity, called the fovea. It contains a very high density of cones within it."}, {"name": "Function", "text": "The eyeballs contain, protect, and support the sensory organs responsible for vision."}, {"name": "References", "text": "Dorland, W. (2011) Dorland's Illustrated Medical Dictionary. 32nd edn. Philadelphia, USA: Elsevier Saunders."}]

items.name: Nucleoplasm (Anterosuperior Cut)
items.info:
[{"name": "Quick Facts", "text": "The nucleoplasm is the contents of the cell nucleus other than the nucleolus and chromatin and consisting of interchromatin and perichromatin granules, ribonucleoproteins, and the nuclear matrix (Dorland, 2011)."}, {"name": "Structure and/or Key Feature(s)", "text": "The nucleoplasm occupies the nucleus (apart from the nucleolus and chromatin) and includes a very fine scaffolding network of protein filaments originating from the nuclear pores (Ross and Pawlina, 2006; Ovalle, Nahirney and Netter, 2013; McKinley, O'Loughlin and Pennefather-O'Brien, 2016)."}, {"name": "Function", "text": "Molecules pass through the nucleoplasm as a consequence of the activity of the chromatin and the nucleolus (Ovalle, Nahirney and Netter, 2013)."}, {"name": "References", "text": "Dorland, W. (2011) Dorland's Illustrated Medical Dictionary. 32nd edn. Philadelphia, USA: Elsevier Saunders.

McKinley, M. P., O'Loughlin, V. D. and Pennefather-O'Brien, E. E. (2016) Human Anatomy. 5th edn.: McGraw-Hill Education.

Ross, M. H. and Pawlina, W. (2006) Histology: A text and atlas. Lippincott Williams & Wilkins."}]

items.name: Erythrocyte
items.info:
[{"name": "Quick Facts", "text": "An erythrocyte is one of the elements found in peripheral blood; the normal mature form is a nonnucleated, yellowish, biconcave disk, adapted by virtue of its configuration and its haemoglobin content to the transport of oxygen (Dorland, 2011)."}, {"name": "Cell Morphology", "text": "Erythrocytes are small red biconcave discoid cells. Erythrocytes are not true cells in that they lack a nucleus, organelles, and cannot divide. Erythrocytes have a diameter of 7–8 μm and are smaller than leukocytes but larger than platelets. The edge of an erythrocyte has a thickness of 2.6 μm, while the center has a thickness of 0.8 μm, thus making them biconcave. Erythrocytes have a longer lifespan than the majority of blood cells and can survive for 100–120 days. Erythrocytes are the most numerous cells in the blood and have a concentration of 4.3-5.7 x 1012 cells/L and 3.9-5.0 x 1012 cells/L in males and females, respectively (Pawlina, 2016). 

In the cytoplasm of an erythrocyte contains hemoglobin, which is an oxygen and carbon dioxide-binding protein. It’s a tetrameric protein meaning that it has four subunits and each subunit contains an iron-containing molecule called heme. An iron atom is located in the center of each heme group and binds to oxygen (Silverthorn et al., 2013; Marieb, Wilhelm and Mallatt, 2012). Therefore, one hemoglobin binds four molecules of oxygen. Each erythrocyte contains 250 million molecules of hemoglobin, meaning each erythrocyte can transport around 1 billion oxygen molecules (Reece et al., 2014). 

Erythrocytes have proteins in their cell membrane called glycophorins. Additionally, erythrocytes possess antigens which attach to the glycophorins. There are three main antigens A, B and O that make the ABO blood group system. All three antigens share the same molecular structure but their difference is the presence of an additional sugar molecule. The presence of these antigens indicates an individual’s blood type (Reece et al., 2014; Pawlina, 2016).

—Erythrocytes that possess the O antigen make the O blood type. 

—Erythrocytes that possess the O and A antigens make the A blood type.

—Erythrocytes that possess the O and B antigens make the B blood type. 

—Erythrocytes that possess the O, A, and B antigens make the AB blood type."}, {"name": "Production", "text": "Erythrocytes are produced in the red bone marrow by pluripotent hematopoietic stem cells and usually takes 5–9 days. A hematopoietic stem cell gives rise to a myeloid stem cell, which undergoes various stages of differentiation until it becomes an erythrocyte. This differentiation is driven by growth factors such as cytokines and hormones. Erythropoietin is a hormone that regulates the synthesis and differentiation of erythrocytes. It is produced by the kidneys when tissues are deprived of oxygen, resulting in an increase in hemoglobin and oxygen transport in the blood circulation. Colony stimulating factors are involved in regulating the production of erythrocytes (Silverthorn et al., 2013).

When erythrocytes approach their maximum lifespan (around 120 days), they become senescent. Subsequently, some erythrocytes rupture while others are phagocytosed by macrophages in the spleen, liver, or bone marrow (Pawlina, 2016)."}, {"name": "Function", "text": "Erythrocytes function only in the bloodstream. Erythrocytes are elastic and able to fold on themselves, thus allowing them to change their shape and pass through narrow capillaries or adapt during osmotic changes. Their biconcave shape increases their surface area, therefore, enhancing the transportation of oxygen. 

Erythrocytes transport oxygen from the lungs to cells and remove carbon dioxide from cells and transport it to the lungs (Silverthorn et al., 2013)."}, {"name": "List of Clinical Correlates", "text": "—Iron-deficiency anemia 

—Hemolytic Anemia (sickle-cell anemia, thalassemia)

—Polycythemia

—Hereditary spherocytosis

—Hereditary elliptocytosis"}, {"name": "References", "text": "Dorland, W. (2011) Dorland's Illustrated Medical Dictionary. 32nd edn. Philadelphia, USA: Elsevier Saunders.

Eroschenko, V. P. (2008) DiFiore's Atlas of Histology with Functional Correlations. Wolters Kluwer Health/Lippincott Williams & Wilkins.

Marieb, E. N., Wilhelm, P. B. and Mallatt, J. (2012) Human Anatomy. 14th edn.: Benjamin Cummings.

Pawlina, W. 2016. Histology: A text and atlas with correlated cell and molecular biology. 7th ed. Philadelphia: Wolters Kluwer.

Reece, J. B., Meyers, N., Urry, L. A., Cain, M. L., Wasserman, S. A., Minorsky, P. V., Jackson, R. B., Cooke, B. and Campbell, N. A. (2014) Campbell Biology. Pearson.

Silverthorn, D. U., Johnson, B. R., Ober, W. C., Garrison, C. W. and Silverthorn, A. C. (2013) Human Physiology: An Integrated Approach. Pearson Education."}]

items.name: Continuous Capillary
items.info:
[{"name": "Quick Facts", "text": "A continuous capillary is one of the two major types of capillaries, found in muscle, skin, lung, central nervous system, and other tissues, and characterized by an uninterrupted endothelium, a continuous basal lamina, fine filaments, and numerous pinocytotic vesicles (Dorland, 2011)."}, {"name": "Structure and/or Key Features", "text": "Capillaries are the smallest blood vessels, often smaller than the diameter of an erythrocyte (red blood cell). They are very thin-walled and made of endothelial cells that form a tube and their supporting basement membrane. Based on their morphology they are classified as being continuous (non-fenestrated), fenestrated, or discontinuous capillaries.

Continuous capillaries are found in connective tissues, muscle tissue, skin, lungs, and in the central nervous system. Each endothelial cell is joined by tight (occluding) junctions. 

Fenestrated capillaries are common in endocrine glands, the kidney, pancreas and the digestive tract. Endothelial cells exhibit very small openings, called fenestrations, through the capillary wall about 70–80 nm in diameter.

Capillaries in the liver, spleen, and bone marrow are typically discontinuous capillaries. The endothelial cells have wide gaps in their cytoplasm and are supported by a discontinuous basement membrane (Ross and Pawlina, 2006)."}, {"name": "Anatomical Relations", "text": "Capillaries are extensive blood vessel networks within tissues at the end of the arterial tree. They link up with venules so blood returns back to the right side of the heart to be then redirected and re-oxygenated in the lungs."}, {"name": "Function", "text": "Capillaries are closely associated with cells and tissues, and so are suited for the exchange of waste products and metabolites, gases, nutrients, etc. between the blood circulation and the extracellular environment of a tissue. Capillaries also deliver chemical messengers from sites of secretions to target organs.

Tight junctions of continuous capillaries restrict exchange with the extracellular environment occurring between endothelial cells.

Fenestrated capillaries facilitate fluid and metabolite absorption.

Discontinuous capillaries permit passage of large proteins e.g., blood plasma proteins across the capillary wall (Ross and Pawlina, 2006)."}, {"name": "References", "text": "Dorland, W. (2011) Dorland's Illustrated Medical Dictionary. 32nd edn. Philadelphia, USA: Elsevier Saunders.

Ross, M. H. and Pawlina, W. (2006) Histology: A text and atlas. Lippincott Williams & Wilkins."}]

items.name: Goblet Cell (Jejunum)
items.info: [{"name": "Quick Facts", "text": "A goblet cell is a unicellular mucous gland found in the epithelium of various mucous membranes, especially that of the respiratory passages and intestines. Droplets of mucinogen collect in the upper part of the cell and distend it, while the basal end remains slender, and the cell assumes the shape of a goblet (Dorland, 2011)."}, {"name": "Structure/Morphology", "text": "Goblet cells are dispersed between enterocytes. They are more numerous in the ileum than in the jejunum or the duodenum. Their unique shape with the apical aggregations of mucinogen granules distending the apical domain of the cell and the narrow basal domain which houses the nucleus is responsible for the name of the cell i.e., it resembles a wine goblet."}, {"name": "Key Features/Anatomical Relations", "text": "A goblet cell is a unicellular mucous gland dispersed between enterocytes in the epithelium lining the small and large intestine."}, {"name": "Function", "text": "Goblet cells secrete mucus. Their main function is to produce mucus which protects and lubricates the surface of the intestines."}, {"name": "References", "text": "Dorland, W. (2011) Dorland's Illustrated Medical Dictionary. 32nd edn. Philadelphia, USA: Elsevier Saunders."}]

items.name: Axon
items.info:
[{"name": "Quick Facts", "text": "The axon is the process of a neuron by which impulses travel away from the cell body; at the terminal arborization of the axon, the impulses are transmitted to other nerve cells or to effector organs. The larger axons are surrounded by a myelin sheath (Dorland, 2011)."}, {"name": "Structure and/or Key Features", "text": "Most neurons have only one thin axon that arises from the axon hillock. An axon is tubular with a uniform diameter along its entire length, although the diameter varies depending on the type of neuron. Very short axons can be 0.1 mm in length, whereas long axons can be about 1 m long. An axon is bound by plasmalemma known as axolemma. The cytoplasm of an axon is known as the axoplasm. The axoplasm contains mitochondria, cytoskeletal elements, and some cisternae of the smooth endoplasmic reticulum. The axoplasm is devoid of Nissl granules and Golgi complexes (Mescher, 2013; Splittgerber, 2018). 

In myelinated axons, the portion between the axon hillock and the first region of myelination (about 50–100 μm) is known as the initial segment. It is the most excitable part of the axon and is where action potentials are generated (Splittgerber, 2018).

In the central nervous system, oligodendrocytes form the myelin sheath that wraps around the axon, whereas in the peripheral nervous system, myelin sheath is formed by Schwann cells. Myelinated axons conduct electrical impulses much faster than non-myelinated axons of the same size. Axons with a large diameter conduct nerve impulses very fast. In contrast, axons with a small diameter, conduct nerve impulses very slowly. The myelin sheath that wraps around the axon becomes segmented at regular intervals by the nodes of Ranvier (or myelin sheath gaps). 

The terminals of axons are unmyelinated. The majority of terminals of an axon expand into presynaptic boutons to either form connections with dendrites, axons, or cell bodies of other neurons. These presynaptic boutons can also form connections peripherally within muscle fibers, glands, or other effector cells.

Usually, axons do not branch close to the cell body but can have some collateral branches along their length and branch profusely right before their termination."}, {"name": "Function", "text": "The axon is the conducting portion of the cell and conveys information away from the nerve cell body towards an effector cell or another neuron. An action potential is generated at the initial segment of the axon. The axolemma is specialized in impulse conduction as it contains various ion channels that are required for generating an action potential (Mescher, 2013; Ross and Pawlina, 2006). 

Cytoskeletal elements found within the axoplasm provide structural strength to the axon. In addition, they transport substances away from the nerve cell body (anterograde flow). Retrograde flow transports molecules (taken up by endocytosis at the axon terminals) back towards the nerve cell body (Ross and Pawlina, 2006; Marieb, Wilhelm and Mallatt, 2012)."}, {"name": "Clinical Correlates", "text": "Axonal retrograde transport has the potential to transport viruses and toxins, etc., back to the nerve cell bodies.

Local anesthetics inhibit sodium transport and therefore the generation of an action potential or nerve impulse.

The axon is dependent on the nerve cell body for maintenance. If the axon is severed, its peripheral length will degenerate."}, {"name": "References", "text": "Dorland, W. (2011) Dorland's Illustrated Medical Dictionary. 32nd edn. Philadelphia, USA: Elsevier Saunders.

Mescher, A. (2013) Junqueira's Basic Histology: Text and Atlas. 13th edn.: McGraw-Hill Education.

Ross, M. H. and Pawlina, W. (2006) Histology: A text and atlas. Lippincott Williams & Wilkins.

Splittgerber, R. (2018) Snell's Clinical Neuroanatomy. Wolters Kluwer Health."}]

items.name: Medullary Venous Sinus
items.info: [{"name": "Quick Facts", "text": "The medullary venous sinus is formed by the convergence of medullary cortical sinusoids and the medullary artery. They merge with the central veins."}, {"name": "Structure and/or Key Features:", "text": "The medullary venous sinus is formed by the convergence of medullary cortical sinusoids and the medullary artery. The venous sinuses pass among the chromaffin cells in the medullary tissue. They go on to merge with the central veins, carrying the secreted hormones in the blood from the various suprarenal regions. At the hilum, the central veins emerge as the left and right suprarenal veins, which empty into the left renal vein on the left, and the inferior vena cava on the right (Inomata and Sasano, 2015)."}, {"name": "Function", "text": "The medullary venous sinus transports the secreted hormones of the suprarenal gland to the systemic circulation."}, {"name": "References", "text": "Inomata, A. & Sasano, H. (2015) Practical approaches for evaluating adrenal toxicity in nonclinical safety assessment. J Toxicol Pathol, 28(3), 125-32."}]

items.name: Glycogen Granule (Cardiac Muscle Cell)
items.info:
[{"name": "Quick Facts", "text": "Glycogen is a large polysaccharide similar to amylopectin but more highly branched, consisting of chains of glucose residues in α—(1,4) linkage with branches created by α—(1,6) linkages. It constitutes the major carbohydrate reserve of animals, stored primarily in liver and muscle, and is synthesized and degraded for energy as demanded (Dorland, 2011)."}, {"name": "Structure and/or Key Features", "text": "Glycogen appears as abundant coarse granules in the sarcoplasm (Mescher, 2013; Ross and Pawlina, 2016)."}, {"name": "Anatomical Relations", "text": "Glycogen granules are concentrated in the juxtanuclear region in a cardiac muscle cell but are also located in small concentrations between myofibrils (Mescher, 2013; Ross and Pawlina, 2016)."}, {"name": "Function", "text": "Glycogen serves as a storage of energy that is used during muscle contraction."}, {"name": "References", "text": "Dorland, W. (2011) Dorland's Illustrated Medical Dictionary. 32nd edn. Philadelphia, USA: Elsevier Saunders.

Mescher, A. (2013) Junqueira's Basic Histology: Text and Atlas. 13th edn.: McGraw-Hill Education.

Ross, M. H. and Pawlina, W. (2016) Histology: A Text and Atlas. Wolters Kluwer Health."}]

items.name: White Matter
items.info:
[{"name": "Quick Facts", "text": "The white matter is the nervous tissue of the brain and spinal cord composed mostly of myelinated nerve fibers arranged in bundles (fasciculi) (Dorland, 2011)."}, {"name": "Structure", "text": "The outer layer of each cerebral hemisphere is composed of a thin (2–4 mm) gray matter, or cerebral cortex, which overlies a thick mass of white matter, or cerebral medulla. Additionally, confined regions of gray matter are distributed between the white matter. These are known as the basal ganglia or basal nuclei. The white matter is devoid of neuronal cell bodies and consists of myelinated axons, non-myelinated axons and oligodendrocytes. The myelinated nerve fibers of the white matter differ, and can be classified into association, commissural, and projection fibers. 

Association fibers are either short or long nerve fibers that connect different cortical regions within the same hemisphere. 

Commissural fibers cross from one side of the central nervous system to the other, therefore, connecting corresponding gray matter areas of the right and left cerebral hemispheres. The largest commissural fiber is the corpus callosum which connects the right and left cerebral hemispheres. 

Projection fibers are nerve fibers that either ascend from caudal regions of the central nervous system towards the cerebral cortex or descend from the cerebral cortex to lower regions. The projection fibers deep to the cerebral white matter form a compact band which is known as the internal capsule. As these projection fibers emerge superior to the internal capsule, they run towards the cerebral cortex or away from it forming a bundle known as corona radiata."}, {"name": "Function", "text": "The organization of white matter allows several areas of the cerebral cortex to communicate with the brainstem and the spinal cord. Commissural fibers connect corresponding gray matter areas of the right and left hemispheres and allows them to function together as a unit. Association fibers are responsible for connecting different parts of the same. Projection fibers are thought to be responsible for sensory information reaching the cerebral cortex."}, {"name": "List of Clinical Correlates", "text": "—Multiple Sclerosis"}, {"name": "References", "text": "Dorland, W. (2011) Dorland's Illustrated Medical Dictionary. 32nd edn. Philadelphia, USA: Elsevier Saunders."}]

items.name: Intrafascicular Veins
items.info: [{"name": "Quick Facts", "text": "The interfascicular veins are part of the vasa nervorum and help drain the nerve."}, {"name": "Structure/Morphology", "text": "The intrafascicular veins are located within the fascicle and form part of the vasa nervorum, small vessels that supply blood to peripheral nerves. This blood supplies nourishment to the nerve. This network of vessels supplies blood to the interior parts of the nerves and their coverings. The vasa vasorum are located within the connective tissue of the nerve scattered between the fascicles (Boissaud-Cooke, Pidgeon and Tunstall, 2015)."}, {"name": "Anatomical Relations", "text": "The vasa nervorum are the smallest vessels in the epineurial, perineurial, and endoneurial layers."}, {"name": "Function", "text": "The vasa nervorum supply the peripheral nerves with the molecular nutrients needed to carry out their cellular functions and for survival (Carp, 2015)."}, {"name": "References", "text": "Boissaud-Cooke, M., Pidgeon, T. E. and Tunstall, R. (2015) 'Chapter 37 - The Microcirculation of Peripheral Nerves: The Vasa Nervorum A2 - Tubbs, R. Shane', in Rizk, E., Shoja, M.M., Loukas, M., Barbaro, N. & Spinner, R.J. (eds.) Nerves and Nerve Injuries. San Diego: Academic Press, pp. 507-523.\n\nCarp, S. (2015) Peripheral Nerve Injury An Anatomical and Physiological Approach for Physical Therapy Intervention. EBL-Schweitzer: F. A. Davis Company."}]

items.name: Perineurial Septum
items.info: [{"name": "Structure/Morphology", "text": "The perineurial septum is an extension of the perineurium that passes through the (secondary) nerve fascicles."}, {"name": "Anatomical Relations", "text": "The intrafascicular vessels are located within the perineurial septa."}, {"name": "Function", "text": "The perineurial septa divides the secondary fascicles into the smaller, primary fascicles (Barral and Croibier, 2007)."}, {"name": "References", "text": "Barral, J. P. and Croibier, A. (2007) Manual Therapy for the Peripheral Nerves. Churchill Livingstone/Elsevier."}]

items.name: Renal Columns
items.info: [{"name": "Quick Facts", "text": "The renal columns are inward extensions of the cortical tissue of the kidney between the renal pyramids (Dorland, 2011)."}, {"name": "Structure and/or Key Feature(s)", "text": "The renal columns are described as medullary extensions of the renal cortex that extend between renal pyramids towards the renal sinus. The renal columns delineate individual lobes of the kidney, aiding in their distinction. Blood vessels, urinary tubules, and fibrous material are contained in the columns."}, {"name": "Function", "text": "The renal columns facilitate anchoring of the renal cortex. The presence of blood vessels in the columns contribute to the filtering function of the kidney."}, {"name": "List of Clinical Correlates", "text": "\u2014Hypertrophied renal column"}, {"name": "References", "text": "Dorland, W. (2011) Dorland's Illustrated Medical Dictionary. 32nd edn. Philadelphia, USA: Elsevier Saunders."}]

items.name: Cross Section of Clitoris & Penis
items.info:
[{"name": "Description", "text": "The male and female external genitalia contain the penis and clitoris, respectively, and are homologous structures. In this model we have created a cross section view through the body of the clitoris and penis so that they can be directly compared. Some key features are discussed below."}, {"name": "Penis", "text": "The penis is the male sex organ and consists of the root, body, and glans. 

The root is attached to the perineum and is anchored to the pubic symphysis by two suspensory ligaments. It contains the crura, bulb, and the ischiocavernosus and bulbospongiosus muscles. The body of the penis is the free pendulous part that is suspended from the root. The body is capped by the glans penis.

The penis contains three cylindrical bodies of erectile tissue, a pair of dorsally located corpora cavernosa and ventrally placed single corpus spongiosum. The corpora cavernosa begin at the crura, which is attached to the internal surface of the ischial ramus on the right and left sides. The corpora extend along the body of the penis to the corona of the glans. 

The corpus spongiosum is a distal continuation of the bulbospongiosus muscle situated between the two crura. It extends throughout the ventral body of the penis. It expands distally to give the glans penis is bulbous shape. The male spongy urethra is located within the corpus spongiosum (Standring, 2016).

The tunica albuginea is a fibroelastic layer that binds the corpora cavernosa and corpus spongiosum. Superficial to that is the fascia of the penis, which supports the tunica albuginea and binds the three corpora together. The skin overlying the body of the penis is thin, highly elastic, and devoid of skin appendages, such as hair and glands. It’s relatively mobile as it is loosely attached to the underlying subcutaneous tissue and fascia of the penis. The skin overlying the glans penis is immobile due to the fact it is directly attached to the underlying tunica albuginea (Moore, Dalley and Agur, 2013)."}, {"name": "Clitoris", "text": "The clitoris is the female erectile organ that consists of two crura, a root, body, and glans.

The crura of the clitoris are the most extensive part of this organ, measuring approximately 50 mm long and 18 mm wide (Jackson et al., 2019). Each crus contains a column of erectile tissue called the corpus cavernosum. The crura extend along the internal surface of the ischiopubic rami towards the midline, where they join at the root of the clitoris. 

The body of the clitoris is significantly smaller than the crura, measuring about 29 mm long and 9 mm wide (Jackson et al., 2019). The corpora cavernosa from each crus extend into the body of the clitoris and they’re surrounded by a tunica albuginea, yet separated by an intermediate septum. The corpora cavernosa are characterized by fibromuscular trabeculae surrounded by numerous irregularly shaped vascular spaces lined by endothelium.

The glans clitoris is the round-ended cap on the body of the clitoris, measuring approximately 8 mm long and 4 mm wide (Jackson et al., 2019). The glans and body is covered by a fold of skin (prepuce) forming a “hood” homologous to the foreskin of the penis. This skin is similar to that over the labia minora, being lightly keratinized with apocrine sweat glands, sebaceous glands, a few hairs, numerous minor blood vessels, and, in particular, many small nerve bundles.

Although the clitoris is anatomically homologous to the more developed penis, unlike the penis, the clitoris is not functionally related to the urethra."}, {"name": "References", "text": "Jackson, L. A., Hare, A. M., Carrick, K. S., Ramirez, D. M. O., Hamner, J. J. and Corton, M. M. (2019) 'Anatomy, histology, and nerve density of clitoris and associated structures: clinical applications to vulvar surgery', American Journal of Obstetrics and Gynecology, 221(5), pp. 519.e1-519.e9.

Moore, K. L., Dalley, A. F. and Agur, A. M. R. (2013) Clinically Oriented Anatomy. Clinically Oriented Anatomy 7th edn.: Wolters Kluwer Health/Lippincott Williams & Wilkins.

Standring, S. (2016) Gray's Anatomy: The Anatomical Basis of Clinical Practice. Gray's Anatomy Series 41 edn.: Elsevier Limited."}]

items.name: Dermis
items.info:
[{"name": "Quick Facts", "text": "The dermis is the layer of the skin deep to the epidermis, consisting of dense irregular connective tissue containing vessels, nerves, and epidermal derivatives; it is divided into a papillary layer and a reticular layer (Dorland, 2011)."}, {"name": "Structure/Morphology", "text": "The dermis is the layer of skin found deep to the epidermis and superficial to the subcutaneous tissue. It is composed of tough fibroelastic tissue that blends with the underlying subcutaneous tissue (hypodermis) such that there is no definitive border, unlike that of the dermoepidermal junction. The dermis supports and adds strength and pliability to the skin. The thickness of the dermis varies from about 0.6 mm in the eyelid and to 3 mm in palmar and plantar skin (Arda, Goksugur and Tuzun, 2014). 

Lymphatic afferent vessels arise at the dermal papillae and converge forming plexuses adjacent to the blood vessels. 

The dermis is also richly innervated, with a network of sensory afferent nerves extending from the papillary dermis, ending at epidermal and dermal receptors.

Other structures found in the dermis include hair follicles, sebaceous and sweat glands, blood and lymph vessels, sensory receptors, and nerves."}, {"name": "Anatomical Relations", "text": "The dermis can be subdivided into two indistinct layers. The superficial layer is the papillary layer and a deep layer called the reticular layer. The papillary layer is a thin layer of loose connective tissue found beneath the epidermis. This part of the dermis contributes to the dermal papillae that interdigitate with the epidermal ridges. It contains collagen type III and elastic fibers, and loops of capillaries supplying blood to the avascular epidermis and to regulate temperature. 

The reticular layer of the dermis, the deep layer, is much thicker than the papillary layer, yet there is no distinct boundary between them. The reticular layer is composed of a dense irregular connective tissue of mostly collagen type I with interspersing elastic fibers. The reticular layer is also continuous with the underlying subcutaneous tissue (hypodermis). A deep plexus of large blood vessels lies at the border between the reticular layer of the dermis and the hypodermis. It supplies numerous branches of capillaries to the papillary layer. 

Recent studies have suggested that the tissue arrangement of the dermis is not a densely packed wall-like structure, commonly seen in alcohol fixed tissue. In fact, it is composed of a collagen lattice surrounded by fluid filled interstitial spaces, the interstitium (Benias et al., 2018). The fluid has been described as pre-lymph where it is collected by lymph capillaries to form lymph. This has also been described in other tissues, such as lung, renal, blood vessel adventitia, and fascia."}, {"name": "Function", "text": "The dermis has a number of key roles. Firstly, it acts as a support for the epidermis and hypodermis. Its elastic fibers give the skin elasticity and pliability. As the dermis contains a rich blood supply, it provides the avascular epidermis with nourishment. In addition, this vasculature acts as a thermoregulator. In cold conditions, blood flow is decreased in the papillary layer to minimize heat lost from the body, while blood flow is increased in the papillary layer in hot conditions (Arda et al., 2014).

The interstitium present in the dermis may serve as a shock absorber, due to the constant distension and compression of the skin and may also play a role in pathologies such as edema (Benias et al., 2018)."}, {"name": "References", "text": "Arda, O., Goksugur, N. and Tuzun, Y. (2014) 'Basic histological structure and functions of facial skin', Clin Dermatol, 32(1), pp. 3-13.

Benias, P. C., Wells, R. G., Sackey-Aboagye, B., Klavan, H., Reidy, J., Buonocore, D., Miranda, M., Kornacki, S., Wayne, M., Carr-Locke, D. L. and Theise, N. D. (2018) 'Structure and Distribution of an Unrecognized Interstitium in Human Tissues', Scientific Reports, 8(1), pp. 4947.

Dorland, W. (2011) Dorland's Illustrated Medical Dictionary. 32nd edn. Philadelphia, USA: Elsevier Saunders."}]

items.name: Pigment Cell of Retina
items.info:
[{"name": "Quick Facts", "text": "The pigmented layer of retina is a layer of pigmented epithelium that is the outer of the two parts of the optic part of the retina, extending from the entrance of the optic nerve to the pupillary margin of the iris. It is important in the turnover of rods and cones and functions as a blood-retina barrier to maintain the ionic environment of the retina (Dorland, 2011)."}, {"name": "Structure and/or Key Features", "text": "The outermost layer of the retina, the pigmented layer, is a composed of pigment cells arranged as a continuous, single row of cuboidal epithelial cells. There are approximately 4-6 million pigment cells in the retina. These cells tend to have a flat appearance in radial section and a hexagonal or pentagonal appearance in surface view (Standring, 2016). 

Pigment cells contain multiple organelles called melanosomes. Melanosomes are described as pigmented cytoplasmic granules that facilitate the synthesis, storage, and transportation of melanin, the common light-absorbing pigment in animals. In retinal pigment cells, melanosomes are retained intracellularly, thus melanosomes and melanin facilitate the absorption of light in this outer epithelial layer of the retina (Wasmeier et al., 2008).

Pigment cells possess actin-rich apical processes, or microvilli, that measure approximately 5-7 µm in length. These microvilli interdigitate between the outer segments of the photoreceptors beneath them (Wasmeier et al., 2008). The basal surface of the pigment cells contains invaginations, which increases the overall surface area of the pigmented layer for the absorption of nutrients. The lateral membranes of the pigment cells are firmly connected by tight junctions, which collectively form the outer blood-retinal barrier (Boulton and Dayhaw-Barker, 2001). 

The shape, size, and appearance of the pigment cells varies depending on their location within the retina. For example, cells in the macula measure approximately 12 µm in length and 14 µm in diameter. Moving away from the macula, cells become wider and flatter, with some cells near the ora serrata measuring approximately 60 µm in diameter (Boulton and Dayhaw-Barker, 2001)."}, {"name": "Anatomical Relations", "text": "The pigment cells extend from the periphery of the optic disc to the ora serrata, where it is continuous with the outer ciliary epithelium. The pigment cells lie between the choroid’s basal complex (Bruch’s membrane) and the layer of rods and cones. 

Embryologically, the retina is derived from the two layers of the invaginated optic vesicle. The outer layer develops into the layer of pigment cells which lies between and separates the neural retina and the choroid. The inner layer of the optic vesicle forms the other nine layers of the retina collectively known as the neural layer (Standring, 2016). Due to differences in the embryological origins of the pigmented layer and the nine layers beneath it, the border between these two areas is not supported by junctional complexes. Therefore, the neural layers and the pigmented layer of the retina can easily become detached, commonly seen in the instance of trauma and disease; this is known as retinal detachment."}, {"name": "Function", "text": "The overall function of the pigment cells is the maintenance and protection of the adjacent photoreceptor cells. They are thought to additionally play an important role in the integrity of the choroidal capillaries (Boulton and Dayhaw-Barker, 2001).

The pigment cells form and act as the outer blood-retinal barrier. As such, it regulates the transepithelial transport of ions, fluid, and metabolites that reach the photoreceptors via specialized transport proteins and lateral plasma membrane barrier junctions. Further, glucose is passively transported, and amino acids are actively absorbed across this epithelial layer, while waste products are removed (Boulton and Dayhaw-Barker, 2001).

Another essential role carried out by the pigment cells is in the transport and storage of retinoids. Retinoids are described as analogs of vitamin A, which are fundamental in the maintenance of the visual cycle. The pigment cells are additionally responsible for the ingestion and degradation of the spent outer segments of photoreceptors via phagocytosis (Boulton and Dayhaw-Barker, 2001).

The pigmented layer plays a critical role in the protection of photoreceptors against light and free radicals. Specifically, the intensity and wavelength of light that reaches the photoreceptors is regulated by macular pigments and melanin which respectively function to filter out reactive blue light and act as a neutral density filter to reduce light passing the pigmented layer. Enzymatic and non-enzymatic antioxidants are also contained within the pigmented layer which neutralize reactive oxygen species, preventing damage to cellular molecules (Boulton and Dayhaw-Barker, 2001).

Finally, the retinal pigment cells secrete a number of growth factors, which supports the integrity of the choriocapillaris endothelium and the photoreceptors (Standring, 2016)."}, {"name": "List of Clinical Correlates", "text": "- Retinal detachment 

- Drusen (macular degeneration)

- Night blindness"}, {"name": "References", "text": "Boulton, M. and Dayhaw-Barker, P. (2001) 'The role of the retinal pigment epithelium: topographical variation and ageing changes', Eye (Lond), 15(Pt 3), pp. 384-9.

Dorland, W. (2011) Dorland's Illustrated Medical Dictionary. 32nd edn. Philadelphia, USA: Elsevier Saunders.

Standring, S. (2016) Gray's Anatomy: The Anatomical Basis of Clinical Practice. Gray's Anatomy Series 41 edn.: Elsevier Limited.

Wasmeier, C., Hume, A. N., Bolasco, G. and Seabra, M. C. (2008) 'Melanosomes at a glance', J Cell Sci, 121(Pt 24), pp. 3995-9."}]

items.name: Inner Sheath of Optic Nerve (Pial Sheath; Left)
items.audio: Inner Sheath of Optic Nerve (Pial Sheath).mp3
alt: Internal Sheath of Optic Nerve (Pial Sheath; Left)
items.info:
[{"name": "Quick Facts", "text": "The inner sheath of optic nerve is the internal sheath of the optic nerve, continuous with the pia mater and arachnoid mater (Dorland, 2011)."}, {"name": "Structure and/or Key Feature(s)", "text": "The eye and optic nerve are outgrowths of the brain and as such carry the three layers of meningeal coverings with them. They are called collectively, the optic sheath. Of these, the inner two layers, arachnoid and pia, are referred to collectively as the inner or internal sheath of the optic nerve. 

The innermost layer of the inner sheath of the optic nerve is continuous with the pia mater of the brain. It is referred to as the pial sheath of the inner sheath of the optic nerve. As the optic nerve enters the eyeball, the inner sheath becomes continuous with the choroid of the eyeball (Dorland, 2011). The pial sheath is vascular and penetrates the optic nerve, subdividing it into 300–400 fascicles (Hayreh, 1984). This organization gives access to the pial blood vessel to supply the optic nerve (Standring, 2016)."}, {"name": "Anatomical Relations", "text": "The pial sheath intimately invests the external surface of the optic nerve and sends extensions within its substance. Externally is the cerebrospinal fluid of the subarachnoid space that separates the pial sheath from the arachnoid sheath. These sheaths surround and accompany the optic nerve up to the eyeball where they become continuous with the choroid coat of the eyeball."}, {"name": "Function", "text": "Similar to the brain, the pial sheath supports the axons of the optic nerve, providing a route for nutrients and oxygen."}, {"name": "References", "text": "Dorland, W. (2011) Dorland's Illustrated Medical Dictionary. 32nd edn. Philadelphia, USA: Elsevier Saunders.

Hayreh, S. S. (1984) 'The sheath of the optic nerve', Ophthalmologica, 189(1-2), pp. 54-63.

Standring, S. (2016) Gray's Anatomy: The Anatomical Basis of Clinical Practice. Gray's Anatomy Series 41 edn.: Elsevier Limited."}]

items.name: Sarcoplasm
items.info: [{"name": "Quick Facts", "text": "The sarcoplasm is the interfibrillary matter of the striated muscles; the substance in which the fibrillae of the muscle fiber are embedded (Dorland, 2011)."}, {"name": "Structure", "text": "The sarcoplasm is the cytoplasm equivalent within muscle cells. It contains many of the same organelles, cytoskeleton, and matrix which is important in many cell functions. The sarcoplasm is slightly adapted to respond to the high energy demands of muscle cells, such as having a higher concentration of glycosomes and myoglobin."}, {"name": "Key Features/Anatomical Relations", "text": "The sarcoplasm is an aqueous substance found within the sarcolemma, which contains many cellular organelles such as the sarcoplasmic reticulum, mitochondria, ribosomes, and Golgi apparatus."}, {"name": "Function", "text": "Similar to the cytoplasm in other cells, the sarcoplasm acts as a medium for many important metabolic processes."}, {"name": "References", "text": "Dorland, W. (2011) Dorland's Illustrated Medical Dictionary. 32nd edn. Philadelphia, USA: Elsevier Saunders."}]
