items.name: Retinal Ganglion Cells
items.info:
[{"name": "Quick Facts", "text": "Retinal ganglion cells are any of those retinal cells that are the third (last) neurons in the vertical linkage of the retina and are analogous to the relays in the spinal cord and brainstem. At least six types of ganglion cells have been classified according to their dendritic patterns (Dorland, 2011)."}, {"name": "Structure and/or Key Features", "text": "Retinal ganglion cells are described as the third-order output neurons of the retina. There are approximately 0.7-1.5 million in the human retina. Retinal ganglion cells exhibit a topographic distribution across the retinal surface. They reach a peak density in a horizontally orientated elliptical ring surrounding the foveal center, though they are absent over the fovea itself (Standring, 2016; Ross and Pawlina, 2006). They are most numerous around in the perifoveal region of macula where they can be found to be stacked up to 10 cells thick. Their density remains high enough to be multiple cells thick in the macular region. Throughout most of the retina, they form a single layer with the distance between neighboring cells increasing with increasing eccentricity. 

Retinal ganglion cell axons pass vitreal into a nerve fiber layer on the inner surface of the retina. These axons converge on the optic nerve head and proceed to exit the eye as the optic nerve. Axons in the human retina are typically non-myelinated, but are surrounded by the processes of radial glial cells and retinal astrocytes (Standring, 2016). Approximately 90% of the axons of retinal ganglion cells terminate within the lateral geniculate nucleus of the thalamus, while the remaining 10% project to subthalamic areas (Remington and Goodwin, 2011). 

There is great morphological variation within the retinal ganglion cell population. Among the parameters on which ganglion cells vary are soma size, axon diameter (and consequent conduction velocity), polarity of primary dendrites (from bipolar, to multipolar), pattern and density of dendritic branching. Central projection target area of ganglion cells in the brain can also vary, thus making classification difficult (Remington and Goodwin, 2011).

Functional subsets of retinal ganglion cells have been identified, though the precise number of types and their function(s) is still being worked out. A popular method for the classification of retinal ganglion cells is by the layer in the lateral geniculate nucleus (LGN) in which they terminate. Located in the thalamus of the brain, the LGN is a relay center for the visual pathway that receives major sensory input from the retina. For example, a class of ganglion cells referred to as “P,” terminate in the parvocellular layers of the LGN. The most common P cell, known as the P1 or midget ganglion cell, has a small cell body with a single dendrite with two distinct levels of stratification of their terminal dendrites. P1 cells may only make contact with a single midget bipolar cell, which in turn only makes contact with a single cone cell forming a direct cone to bipolar to P1 ganglion cell channel that carries high contrast, fine detail and color information. Other ganglion cell types include P2 ganglion cells and M-type ganglion cells. P2 ganglion cells also terminate in the parvocellular layers of the LGN but have dense dendritic branching. M-cells project to the magnocellular layers of the LGN and possess a coarse and spiny dendritic tree (Remington and Goodwin, 2011). M-cells are also major contributors to the retinal input to the superior colliculus and other midbrain targets."}, {"name": "Anatomical Relations", "text": "Retinal ganglion cell bodies, along with displaced amacrine cells, retinal astrocytes, microglia, along with cells of the intraretinal vasculature are found in the ganglion cell layer of the retina. The dendritic processes of the ganglion cells make contact with bipolar and amacrine cells in the inner plexiform layer (Standring, 2016). The axons of ganglion cells pass into the layer of nerve fibers and converge at the optic disc to exit the eye as the optic nerve. Axonal fibers traveling from the medial retina approach the optic disc in a radial pattern. Those approaching the disc from the lateral, or temporal, side of the retina take an arcuate route. A bundle of fibers, known as the papillomacular fasciculus, is formed as axons from the macula travel directly toward the disc (Standring, 2016)."}, {"name": "Function", "text": "Retinal ganglion cells receive visual signals from bipolar and amacrine cells. It carries these signals, via the optic nerve, to the visual centers of the brain, primarily the thalamic relay, lateral geniculate nucleus, midbrain, superior colliculus, and other subthalamic areas."}, {"name": "List of Clinical Correlates", "text": "- Glaucoma

- Neuroretinitis

- Devic’s disease"}, {"name": "References", "text": "Dorland, W. (2011) Dorland's Illustrated Medical Dictionary. 32nd edn. Philadelphia, USA: Elsevier Saunders.

Ross, M. H. and Pawlina, W. (2006) Histology: A text and atlas. Lippincott Williams & Wilkins.

Standring, S. (2016) Gray's Anatomy: The Anatomical Basis of Clinical Practice. Gray's Anatomy Series 41 edn.: Elsevier Limited."}]

items.name: Periodontal Ligament
items.info:
[{"name": "Quick Facts", "text": "The periodontal ligament is the fibrous connective tissue that surrounds the root of a tooth, separating it from and attaching it to the alveolar bone. It extends from the base of the gingival mucosa to the fundus of the bony socket, and its main function is to hold the tooth in its socket (Dorland, 2011)."}, {"name": "Structure and/or Key Feature(s)", "text": "The periodontal ligament is a dense fibrous band of connective tissue occupying the space between the tooth root and alveolar bone. The periodontal ligament space resembles an hourglass, the narrowest point existing at mid-root level. The ligament attaches itself to both the alveolar bone and cement by embedding projections of its collagen fibers, known as Sharpey’s fibers, into these structures. Type I collagen makes up approximately 80% of the collagen in the periodontal ligament, while the remainder is type III (Standring, 2016).

The periodontal ligament measures approximately 0.2-0.4 mm in width and is predominantly composed of collagen fibers with additional oxytalan fibers, fibroblasts, amorphous ground substance, and interstitial tissue. Most of the collagen is gathered into small 5 µm bundles called fibers of the periodontal ligament. There are different categories of fibers that are distinguished by their trajectory and their attachment points (Standring, 2016).

Cells of the periodontal ligament include osteoblasts, osteoclasts, cementoblasts, and odontoblasts, all of which are associated with the development and maintenance of the alveolar bone and cement. It also contains a network of epithelial cells, known as epithelial cell rests of Malassez, which are residual cells from the embryological development of the epithelial root sheath (Berkovitz, Holland and Moxham, 2017).

The periodontal ligament receives and autonomic and sensory nerve supply. The autonomic fibers are responsible for modulating the vasculature tone of the blood vessels, while the sensory fibers are integral for transmitting pain and proprioception signals via what appears to be Ruffini-like endings (Standring, 2016).

The primary blood supply of the periodontal ligament is derived from the appropriate superior and inferior alveolar arteries. Additionally, arteries from the gingiva, such as the palatine and lingual arteries, may also contribute. Blood vessels that supply the ligament are primarily derived from perforation arteries that through the alveolar bone. 

The periodontal ligament, along with the gingiva, alveolar mucosa, cement, and alveolar bone, comprise the periodontium."}, {"name": "Function", "text": "The periodontal ligament has several responsibilities which contribute to the position and overall structural integrity of the tooth. Firstly, it resists displacing forces and protects the dental tissues from damage caused by excessive occlusal loads. Occlusal load describes the stresses generated by surface contact of the upper and lower teeth. 

The periodontal ligament is also responsible for attaining and maintaining a tooth’s functional position in the oral cavity due to its attachment to both the alveolar bone and tooth cement via Sharpey’s fibers. 

The cells of the periodontal ligament, including cementoblasts, odontoclasts, osteoblasts and osteoclasts contribute to the repair and maintenance of alveolar bone and cement. 

The mechanoreceptors of the periodontal ligament provide sensory information relating to forces associated with mastication to facilitate reflex jaw activity (Berkovitz, Holland and Moxham, 2017)."}, {"name": "References", "text": "Berkovitz, B. K. B., Holland, G. R. and Moxham, B. J. (2017) Oral Anatomy, Histology and Embryology. 5th edn.: Elsevier.

Dorland, W. (2011) Dorland's Illustrated Medical Dictionary. 32nd edn. Philadelphia, USA: Elsevier Saunders.

Standring, S. (2016) Gray's Anatomy: The Anatomical Basis of Clinical Practice. Gray's Anatomy Series 41 edn.: Elsevier Limited."}]

items.name: Rete Ovarii
items.info: [{"name": "Structure and/or Key Feature(s)", "text": "During embryological development, mesodermal epithelium lines the urogenital ridges and gives rise to the primary sex cords. In males, the primary sex cords differentiate into the seminiferous tubules, straight tubules and rete testis. The rete ovarii is a structure formed from the primary sex cords in the female and is the equivalent structure to the rete testis in the male. In the ovary, the hilum is where nerves and blood vessels enter the ovary and the rete ovarii are evident as small blind tubules in the ovarian medulla."}]

items.name: Membranous Disc of Rod Cell
items.info:
[{"name": "Quick Facts", "text": "The outer segments of rods and cones have flattened membranous discs which bear visual opsin."}, {"name": "Structure and/or Key Features", "text": "The outer segments of rod cells are composed of approximately 1,000 stacked, flattened membranous discs, or lamellae. These discs originate as deep infoldings of the plasma membrane at the base of the outer segment. The bi-lipid membranous discs become detached from the surrounding plasma membrane following formation and are therefore free floating in the outer segment. 

Embedded within the double membranes of the discs are light-sensitive visual pigment molecules, rhodopsin (Kolb, 1995; Standring, 2016).

There is constant turnover of membranous discs. From proximally, where they are formed at the base of the outer segments older discs are gradually displaced distally, up through the outer segment. At the very tip of the outer segment discs are pinched off, engulfed, and phagocytosed by the apical processes of the pigmented epithelium (Kolb, 1995)."}, {"name": "Anatomical Relations", "text": "The multiple folded bilaminar membrane forming the discs of rod outer segments extend from the connecting stalk at their bases to the distal tip. The tips are surrounded by multiple microvillus processes of retinal pigment epithelium."}, {"name": "Function", "text": "Despite its production in the inner segment of the rod cell, rhodopsin subsequently migrates to the outer segments. The membranous discs of rod cells are largely responsible for housing and anchoring rhodopsin. Rhodopsin controls the absorption and processing of light under dim lighting conditions (Kolb, 1995). Most of the rhodopsin at the tips of rod outer segments are already photoconverted and so the no longer photosensitive pigment is sloughed off and engulfed, and phagocytized by the retinal pigment epithelium."}, {"name": "List of Clinical Correlates", "text": "- Rod-cone degeneration

- Rod-cone dystrophy"}, {"name": "References", "text": "Kolb, H. (1995) 'Photoreceptors', in Kolb, H., Fernandez, E. and Nelson, R. (eds.) Webvision: The Organization of the Retina and Visual System. Salt Lake City (UT): University of Utah Health Sciences Center. Copyright: (c) 2019 Webvision.

Standring, S. (2016) Gray's Anatomy: The Anatomical Basis of Clinical Practice. Gray's Anatomy Series 41 edn.: Elsevier Limited."}]

items.name: Veins of Skin
items.info: [{"name": "Quick Facts", "text": "The veins of the skin begin in the papillae of the skin, form subpapillary plexuses, and open into the subcutaneous veins (Dorland, 2011)."}, {"name": "Structure/Morphology", "text": "The skin contains a rich network of blood and lymph vessels in the dermis and subcutaneous tissue. There are two major plexuses, one located at the region of the dermis and subcutaneous tissue, and one in the superficial part of the dermis that supplies a large network of capillaries to the papillae at the epidermal-dermal junction."}, {"name": "Function", "text": "These vessels supply nourishment to the three layers of the skin, the epidermis, dermis, and subcutaneous tissue. In addition, this vasculature acts as a thermoregulator. In cold conditions, blood flow is decreased in the papillary layer of the dermis to minimize heat lost from the body, while blood flow is increased in the papillary layer in hot conditions (Young, 2006)."}, {"name": "References", "text": "Dorland, W. (2011) Dorland's Illustrated Medical Dictionary. 32nd edn. Philadelphia, USA: Elsevier Saunders.\n\nYoung, B. (2006) Wheater's Functional Histology: A Text and Colour Atlas. Student consult: Churchill Livingstone/Elsevier."}]

items.name: Inner Zone of Renal Medulla
items.info:
[{"name": "Quick Facts", "text": "The inner zone of the medulla is the part of the renal medulla farthest in from the cortex, containing the innermost part of the loop of Henle and of the medullary collecting tubule (Dorland, 2011)."}, {"name": "Structure and/or Key Features", "text": "The inner zone of the renal medulla primarily consists of the descending and ascending thin limbs of the nephron loop, medullary collecting ducts, straight arterioles, and peritubular capillary bed. Straight arterioles tend to be absent near the tips of the renal papillae. Proximal and distal straight tubules are typically only found in the outer medulla (Dudek, 2006). 

Unlike the striated appearance of the outer medulla, the inner medulla has more of a homogenous appearance, which tapers down to a blunt point before projecting into the pelvis of the ureter (Moffat, 1975)."}, {"name": "Anatomical Relations", "text": "The inner zone of the renal medulla surrounds the renal pelvis and lies subjacent to the outer zone of the renal medulla."}, {"name": "Function", "text": "The hypertonic environment of the inner medulla compared to the glomerular filtrate facilitates the reabsorption of water (Pocock et al, 2013)."}, {"name": "References", "text": "Dorland, W. (2011) Dorland's Illustrated Medical Dictionary. 32nd edn. Philadelphia, USA: Elsevier Saunders.

Dudek, R. W. (2006) High-yield KidneyLippincott Williams & Wilkins.

Moffat, D. B. (1975) The Mammalian KidneyCambridge University Press.

Pocock, G., Richards, C. D. & Richards, D. A. (2013) Human Physiology, 4 edition. OUP Oxford."}]

items.name: Emissary Veins of Penis
items.info:
[{"name": "Quick Facts", "text": "Origin: Corpora cavernosa.

Course: Courses through the tunica albuginea and drain into the circumflex or deep dorsal vein of the penis. 

Tributaries: Subalbugineal plexus.

Drainage: Corpora cavernosa of penis."}, {"name": "Origin", "text": "Sinusoidal veins in the spongy trabeculae of the corpora cavernosa form a subalbugineal plexus beneath the tunica albuginea, which open into emissary veins."}, {"name": "Course", "text": "The emissary veins pass through the tunica albuginea and drain into the circumflex or deep dorsal vein of the penis. Emissary veins on the ventrolateral aspect of the corpora cavernosa join the urethral veins and help form the circumflex veins. In the proximal third of the penis, on the dorsomedial aspect, emissary veins unite to form 2-5 deep veins of the penis (cavernous veins) (Quartey, 2006)."}, {"name": "Tributaries", "text": "The emissary veins receive blood from the subalbugineal plexus."}, {"name": "Structures Drained", "text": "Emissary veins drain the erectile tissue of the corpora cavernosa."}, {"name": "References", "text": "Quartey, J. K. M. (2006) 'Anatomy and Blood Supply of the Urethra and Penis', in Schreiter, F. and Jordan, G.H. (eds.) Urethral Reconstructive Surgery. Berlin, Heidelberg: Springer Berlin Heidelberg, pp. 11-17."}]

items.name: Subcutaneous Tissue
items.info: [{"name": "Quick Facts", "text": "The subcutaneous tissue is the layer of loose connective tissue situated just beneath the skin (Dorland, 2011)."}, {"name": "Structure/Morphology", "text": "The subcutaneous tissue (superficial fascia or hypodermis) is found deep to the reticular layer of the dermis. It is composed of loose areolar connective tissue containing adipose tissue. The amount of adipose tissue depends on various aspects, such as the location in the body, sex of the individual and the nutrition of the individual. No adipose tissue is found in the subcutaneous portions of the eyelids, clitoris, or penis. The subcutaneous tissue contains an extensive network of blood vessels. These are important for the rapid uptake of drugs delivered by hypodermal injections, such as insulin (Ross and Pawlina, 2006)."}, {"name": "Function", "text": "The subcutaneous tissue acts as a thermal insulator, stores energy, and functions as a shock absorber. It loosely attaches to underlying deep fascia, aponeurosis, and periosteum, thus allowing skin to glide over these underlying structures."}, {"name": "References", "text": "Dorland, W. (2011) Dorland's Illustrated Medical Dictionary. 32nd edn. Philadelphia, USA: Elsevier Saunders.\n\nRoss, M. H. and Pawlina, W. (2006) Histology: A text and atlas. Lippincott Williams & Wilkins."}]

items.name: Axolemma
items.info:
[{"name": "Quick Facts", "text": "The axolemma is the plasma membrane of an axon (Dorland, 2011)."}, {"name": "Structure", "text": "An axon is bound by plasmalemma (or plasma membrane) known as the axolemma. The axolemma is composed of a lipid bilayer and a submembrane skeleton, which is formed by the protein spectrin and actin, and are linked by ankyrin and a number of other constituents of the transmembrane proteins. This skeletal framework of spectrin and ankyrin aid in the anchoring of voltage-gated channels to the axolemma.

The propagation of nerve impulses depends on the structure of the axolemma, concentrations of electrolytes in the axolemma and the extracellular space, and selective permeability of the axolemma to the specific ions. The nerve signals are conveyed using action potentials that are generated with alterations to the permeability of the axolemma to sodium and potassium ions (Ross and Pawlina, 2006)."}, {"name": "Anatomical Relations", "text": "The axolemma is the plasma membrane of the axonal process."}, {"name": "Function", "text": "The axolemma possesses various transmembrane channels which aid neurotransmission by enabling the passage of various ions, a process which initiates and propagates action potentials (Ross and Pawlina, 2006)."}, {"name": "Clinical Correlates", "text": "—Diffuse axonal injury is characterized by disruption of the axon cytoskeleton.

—Stretching of axons during traumatic injury causes physical disruption to, and proteolytic degradation of, the cytoskeleton."}, {"name": "References", "text": "Dorland, W. (2011) Dorland's Illustrated Medical Dictionary. 32nd edn. Philadelphia, USA: Elsevier Saunders.

Ross, M. H. and Pawlina, W. (2006) Histology: A text and atlas. Lippincott Williams & Wilkins."}]

items.name: Clathrin-coated Vesicle
items.info:
[{"name": "Quick Facts", "text": "A clathrin-coated vesicle is a transport vesicle having a clathrin coat, involved in the transport of products from the Golgi complex to lysosomes, the transport of molecules taken up by endocytosis, and the retrieval of synaptic vesicle membrane following neurotransmitter release (Dorland, 2011)."}, {"name": "Structure and/or Key Feature(s)", "text": "The formation of a phagosome is usually a receptor-mediated process allowing only specific molecules to enter the cell. The receptors specific for a particular molecule accumulate at locations along the plasmalemma where the protein clathrin also accumulates. This accumulation on the cytoplasmic surface of the plasmalemma appears like a coated pit when viewed with an electron microscope. The type of vesicle then formed is referred to as a clathrin-coated vesicle (Ross and Pawlina, 2006)."}, {"name": "Anatomical Relations", "text": "Coated vesicles are located in the apical regions of the cell cytoplasm (Ross and Pawlina, 2006; Ovalle, Nahirney and Netter, 2013; McKinley, O'Loughlin and Pennefather-O'Brien, 2016)."}, {"name": "Function", "text": "A clathrin-coated vesicle contains products ingested by the cell (Ross and Pawlina, 2006)."}, {"name": "References", "text": "Dorland, W. (2011) Dorland's Illustrated Medical Dictionary. 32nd edn. Philadelphia, USA: Elsevier Saunders.

McKinley, M. P., O'Loughlin, V. D. and Pennefather-O'Brien, E. E. (2016) Human Anatomy. 5th edn.: McGraw-Hill Education.

Ovalle, W. K., Nahirney, P. C. and Netter, F. H. (2013) Netter's Essential Histology. ClinicalKey 2012: Elsevier Saunders.

Ross, M. H. and Pawlina, W. (2006) Histology: A text and atlas. Lippincott Williams & Wilkins."}]

items.name: Cytoplasm (End Piece; Right)
items.info:
[{"name": "Quick Facts", "text": "The cytoplasm is the protoplasm of a cell exclusive of that of the nucleus; it consists of a continuous aqueous solution (cytosol) and the organelles and inclusions suspended in it and is the site of most of the chemical activities of the cell (Dorland, 2011)."}, {"name": "Structure and/or Key Feature(s)", "text": "The cytoplasm of a cell includes an aqueous solution, the cytosol, and the organelles of the cell suspended in it. It is tightly enclosed by the plasma membrane. The sperm contains a limited amount of cytoplasm. During normal spermatogenesis (or maturation), spermatids lose most of their cytoplasm. Remnants may remain as a cytoplasmic droplet at the neck region of the sperm and is shed during ejaculation. However, retention of the droplets may indicate failure of normal maturation and cause infertility (Rengan et al, 2012).

The mature sperm retains a thin layer of cytoplasm underneath the plasma membrane. In the head, the space occupied by cytoplasm between the acrosome and the nucleus is known as the subacrosomal (or perinuclear) space. The cytoplasm between the outer membrane of the acrosome and the plasma membrane is the periacrosomal space."}, {"name": "Function", "text": "The cytoplasm is the site where most chemical activities of the cell occur."}, {"name": "References", "text": "Dorland, W. (2011) Dorland's Illustrated Medical Dictionary. 32nd edn. Philadelphia, USA: Elsevier Saunders.

Rengan, A. K., Agarwal, A., van der Linde, M. & du Plessis, S. S. (2012) An investigation of excess residual cytoplasm in human spermatozoa and its distinction from the cytoplasmic droplet. Reproductive biology and endocrinology : RB&E, 10, 92-92."}]

items.name: Arteries of Transverse Colon
items.info: [{"name": "Quick Facts", "text": "The proximal two thirds of the transverse colon is supplied by branches of the superior mesenteric artery, while the distal third is supplied by branches of the inferior mesenteric artery."}, {"name": "Description", "text": "The transverse colon has a broad and varied blood supply. Developmentally, the proximal two thirds are components of the midgut, while the remaining distal third is part of the hindgut. This developmental distinction is important in understanding the patterns of vascularization, innervation, and lymphatic drainage of the large intestine. \n\nThe proximal two thirds of the transverse colon is supplied from the ileocolic, right colic, and middle colic branches from the superior mesenteric artery. The distal third is supplied by the ascending branch of the left colic artery, which arises from the inferior mesenteric artery. These vessels travel from their aortic origin through the mesentery, splitting into smaller branches, and eventually penetrate the colon and omental appendices to provide arterial blood."}]

items.name: Glomerulus
items.info:
[{"name": "Quick Facts", "text": "The glomerulus is a globular tuft formed by capillaries in the kidney, the site of the filtration barrier between the blood and the kidney; it projects into the expanded end of a renal tubule, and together with its surrounding capsule (glomerular capsule) it constitutes a renal corpuscle (Dorland, 2011)."}, {"name": "Structure and/or Key Feature(s)", "text": "The glomerulus is described as a small tuft of convoluted capillaries structurally supported by an extracellular mesangial matrix. Glomerular capillary walls are made of fenestrated endothelial cells, which forms the first layer of the renal corpuscle filtration barrier (Lote, 1994).

The mesangial matrix is composed of macrophages called mesangial cells, which function to prevent the accumulation of macromolecules that have escaped the capillaries and also have a structural role in holding the glomerulus in position (Lote, 1994)."}, {"name": "Anatomical Relations", "text": "Glomerular capillaries originate from an afferent arteriole that enters the capsule at the vascular pole. Blood from the glomerulus drains into an efferent arteriole, which exits the renal corpuscle again at the vascular pole (Kerr, 2007)."}, {"name": "Function", "text": "The glomerulus, specifically its fenestrated capillary wall endothelium, is actively involved in facilitating the transport of water and unwanted solutes from the blood to the renal tubule of the nephron as part of the filtration process."}, {"name": "List of Clinical Correlates", "text": "—Glomerular Disease

—Glomerulosclerosis"}, {"name": "References", "text": "Dorland, W. (2011) Dorland's Illustrated Medical Dictionary. 32nd edn. Philadelphia, USA: Elsevier Saunders.

Kerr, J. B. (2007) Atlas of Functional HistologyElsevier Science Health Science Division.

Lote, C. J. (1994) Principles of Renal PhysiologyChapman & Hall."}]

items.name: Interlobular Veins of Kidney
items.info: [{"name": "Quick Facts", "text": "The interlobular veins are veins that collect blood from the capillary network of the renal cortex and empty into the arcuate veins (Dorland, 2011)."}, {"name": "Structure and/or Key Features", "text": "Interlobular veins receive blood from both the venous ends of peritubular capillaries and straight arterioles. Stellate veins are responsible for draining the most superficial zones of the renal cortex. Interlobular veins receive some straight arterioles as they travel towards the corticomedullary junction before ending in arcuate veins."}, {"name": "Function", "text": "Interlobular veins are responsible for the collection of blood that has circulated the kidneys."}, {"name": "References", "text": "Dorland, W. (2011) Dorland's Illustrated Medical Dictionary. 32nd edn. Philadelphia, USA: Elsevier Saunders."}]

items.name: Juxtaglomerular Complex
items.info:
[{"name": "Quick Facts", "text": "The juxtaglomerular apparatus is a complex in the kidney comprising the juxtaglomerular cells, macula densa, and lacis cells of the polkissen; it is the site of tubuloglomerular feedback for autoregulation of the glomerular filtration rate (Dorland, 2011)."}, {"name": "Structure and/or Key Feature(s)", "text": "The juxtaglomerular complex includes the macula densa, and the juxtaglomerular and mesangial cells.

The distal straight tubule traverses the medulla into the cortex within a medullary ray and aligns itself adjacent to the vascular pole of the renal corpuscle with which it is a component. A clustering of nuclei of epithelial cells lining the distal straight tubule directly adjacent to the afferent arteriole close to the vascular pole of the renal corpuscle form the “macula densa.” 

Smooth muscle cells of adjacent afferent, and sometimes efferent, arterioles exhibit spherical nuclei and their cytoplasm contain secretory granules."}, {"name": "Anatomical Relations", "text": "The juxtaglomerular apparatus includes the macula densa, juxtaglomerular cells, and extraglomerular mesangial cells."}, {"name": "Function", "text": "The juxtaglomerular apparatus regulates blood pressure by activating the renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system. It also sensors blood volume and tubular fluid composition. The macula densa monitors Na+ concentration within the tubular fluid and regulate glomerular filtration rate and the release of renin from the juxtaglomerular cells (Ross and Pawlina, 2006)."}, {"name": "References", "text": "Dorland, W. (2011) Dorland's Illustrated Medical Dictionary. 32nd edn. Philadelphia, USA: Elsevier Saunders.

Ross, M. H. and Pawlina, W. (2006) Histology: A text and atlas. Lippincott Williams & Wilkins."}]

items.name: Intestinal Villi (Jejunum)
items.info:
[{"name": "Quick Facts", "text": "The intestinal villi are the multitudinous threadlike projections that cover the surface of the mucosa of the small intestine and serve as the sites of absorption (by active transport and diffusion) of fluids and nutrients (Dorland, 2011)."}, {"name": "Structure/Morphology", "text": "Intestinal villi are 0.5-1.5 mm long, fingerlike or leaf-like extensions of the mucosa into the lumen of the small intestine (Ovalle, Nahirney and Netter, 2013). The central core of each villus is the lamina propria.

In the duodenum, they are leaf-shaped but gradually adopt a more finger-like shape as they appear in the ileum. Between each villus is the opening of the mucosal and submucosal glands. These are mainly intestinal glands inappropriately referred to as crypts or glands of Lieberkühn."}, {"name": "Function", "text": "Villi magnify the surface area of the intestinal epithelium to maximize secretion and absorption capacity."}, {"name": "References", "text": "Dorland, W. (2011) Dorland's Illustrated Medical Dictionary. 32nd edn. Philadelphia, USA: Elsevier Saunders.

Ovalle, W. K., Nahirney, P. C. and Netter, F. H. (2013) Netter's Essential Histology. ClinicalKey 2012: Elsevier Saunders."}]

items.name: Secondary Lymphoid Nodule
items.info:
[{"name": "Quick Facts", "text": "A secondary lymphoid nodule is a lymphoid nodule that has been exposed to antigen and contains a germinal center with actively proliferating B lymphocytes, having developed from a primary lymphoid nodule (Dorland, 2011)."}, {"name": "Structure/Morphology", "text": "Once antigenic stimulation occurs, the primary lymphoid nodule develops into a secondary lymphoid nodule. The secondary nodule is distinctive in characteristics from the primary nodule, in that it has a germinal center with a surrounding mantle zone.

Germinal centers are the major site for B lymphocyte (or B cell) proliferation, but also contains large and small lymphocytes, dendritic cells, and lymphoblasts. The mantle zone surrounds the germinal centers and contains small, dormant B lymphocytes (Standring, 2016).

T lymphocytes, or T-cells, are found in the surrounding parenchyma of the cortex, known as the interfollicular cortex, and the paracortex."}, {"name": "List of Clinical Correlates", "text": "—Lymphoma

—Hodgkin’s Lymphoma

—Lymphadenopathy"}, {"name": "References", "text": "Dorland, W. (2011) Dorland's Illustrated Medical Dictionary. 32nd edn. Philadelphia, USA: Elsevier Saunders.

Standring, S. (2016) Gray's Anatomy: The Anatomical Basis of Clinical Practice. Gray's Anatomy Series: Elsevier Limited."}]

items.name: Submucosal Lymphatic Plexus (Jejunum)
items.info: [{"name": "Quick Facts", "text": "The submucosal lymphatic plexus is an interconnecting network of lymph vessels, i.e., the lymphocapillary vessels, collecting vessels, and trunks, which provides drainage of lymph in a one-way flow (Dorland, 2011)."}, {"name": "Structure/Morphology", "text": "Lacteals originate in the lamina propria of villi and form a plexus near the muscular layer (muscularis mucosa) of the small intestine. From there, they flow to lymph nodules in the submucosa and unite to accompany blood vessels out of the intestine."}, {"name": "Function", "text": "Lacteals and the lymphatic vessels are important for the absorption of lipids."}, {"name": "References", "text": "Dorland, W. (2011) Dorland's Illustrated Medical Dictionary. 32nd edn. Philadelphia, USA: Elsevier Saunders."}]
