items.name: Neuroglia
Basement Membrane of Distal Convoluted Tubule
items.audio: Basement Membrane of Distal Convoluted Tubule.mp3
items.info:
[{"name": "Quick Facts", "text": "A basement membrane is a thin sheet of amorphous extracellular material upon which the basal surfaces of epithelial cells rest; other cells associated with basement membranes are muscle cells, Schwann cells, and fat cells. The membrane is interposed between the cellular elements and the underlying connective tissue. It usually comprises two layers, the basal lamina and the reticular lamina, and is composed of Type IV collagen (which is unique to basement membranes), laminin, fibronectin, and heparan sulfate proteoglycans (Dorland, 2011)."}, {"name": "Structure and/or Key Feature(s)", "text": "Most epithelia attach to some form of underlying connective tissues by a basal lamina. The basal lamina is a thin sheet of extracellular proteins and fibrils. Additionally, carbohydrate-rich material is attached its lower face. If the accumulation is sufficient, the basal lamina is referred to as a basement membrane.

The basement membrane is synthesized by overlying epithelium and the underlying cells in connective tissue. Some epithelia do not have a basement membrane but most have a basal lamina (Ross and Pawlina, 2016; Ovalle, Nahirney and Netter, 2013)."}, {"name": "Anatomical Relations", "text": "The cuboidal epithelial cells of the distal convoluted tubule are attached to the underlying connective tissues by a very thin basal lamina."}, {"name": "Function", "text": "The basal lamina has a profound influence over the physiology of epithelium and a basement membrane adheres the epithelium to the underlying connective tissue being a supporting/strengthening component."}, {"name": "References", "text": "Dorland, W. (2011) Dorland's Illustrated Medical Dictionary. 32nd edn. Philadelphia, USA: Elsevier Saunders.

Ovalle, W. K., Nahirney, P. C. and Netter, F. H. (2013) Netter's Essential Histology. ClinicalKey 2012: Elsevier Saunders.

Ross, M. H. and Pawlina, W. (2006) Histology: A text and atlas. Lippincott Williams & Wilkins."}]

items.name: Endomysium
items.info:
[{"name": "Quick Facts", "text": "The endomysium is the sheath of delicate reticular fibrils that surrounds each muscle fiber (Dorland, 2011)."}, {"name": "Structure", "text": "The endomysium is a delicate sheath of connective tissue which envelopes each individual skeletal muscle fiber, consisting primarily of type III and type IV collagen (Standring, 2016)."}, {"name": "Key Features/Anatomical Relations", "text": "Endomysium surrounds the individual skeletal muscle fibers within the fascicles and forms their immediate internal environment. The three collagenous sheaths, the epimysium, perimysium, and endomysium unite and fuse where the muscles connect to adjoining structures such as tendons."}, {"name": "Function", "text": "The endomysium is the site of metabolic exchange between blood and the skeletal muscle fiber, as it contains capillaries which supply the muscle fiber. As this layer is composed of collagen and elastin fibers, it contributes to the resistance of a muscle to tensile forces."}, {"name": "List of Clinical Correlates", "text": "—Myasthenia gravis

—Mysium damage

—Connective tissue disease"}, {"name": "References", "text": "Dorland, W. (2011) Dorland's Illustrated Medical Dictionary. 32nd edn. Philadelphia, USA: Elsevier Saunders.

Standring, S. (2016) Gray's Anatomy: The Anatomical Basis of Clinical Practice. Gray's Anatomy Series 41 edn.: Elsevier Limited."}]

items.name: Arteries of Tendon
items.info:
[{"name": "Quick Facts", "text": "An artery is a vessel through which the blood passes away from the heart to the various parts of the body. The wall of an artery consists typically of an outer coat (tunica externa), a middle coat (tunica media), and an inner coat (tunica intima) (Dorland, 2011)."}, {"name": "Structure and/or Key Feature(s)", "text": "The arterial supply to tendons is relatively scanty, and can be divided into three segments:

—the musculotendinous junction;

—the length of the tendon;

—the tendon-bone junction. The blood vessels stem from the perimysium, the periosteum, as well as through the peritendon and mesotendon. The musculotendinous junction gets its blood supply from the superficial blood vessels in surrounding viscera (Maffulli, Renstrom and Leadbetter, 2005).

Small arterioles from surrounding muscle tissue, in addition to small blood vessels that originate from surrounding loose connective tissue and synovial sheaths, branch and anastomose as they travel longitudinally between fascicles. Venae comitantes, as well as the lymphatics, accompany these arterioles and three branches (Standring, 2016).

The blood supply to the biceps femoris tendon is made possible by the arteries coming from the biceps femoris muscle, and also by the arteries that run in the peritendinous sheaths. They include the anastomoses of the popliteal artery, the perforating branches of the profunda femoris artery, and the inferior gluteal artery (Standring, 2016)."}, {"name": "Anatomical Relations", "text": "The small blood vessels in the peritendon take a transverse course towards the tendon, give off various branches, then change direction to travel parallel to the length of the tendon. The vessels gain access into the tendon at a point along the endotendon. 

Arterioles travel longitudinally, each accompanied by two venules. Capillaries travel from the arterioles and connect with the venules, without piercing through the collagen bundles (Maffulli, Renstrom and Leadbetter, 2005)."}, {"name": "Function", "text": "Although tendons in general are relatively poorly vascularized, and are significantly reliant on synovial fluid for nutrition, the arteries still play some important roles. The arteries provide nutrition for the tendon and play a crucial role in tendon injury healing as they convey the necessary reparative cells to the site of tendon injury (Fenwick, Hazleman and Riley, 2002)."}, {"name": "References", "text": "Dorland, W. (2011) Dorland's Illustrated Medical Dictionary. 32nd edn. Philadelphia, USA: Elsevier Saunders.

Fenwick, S. A., Hazleman, B. L. and Riley, G. P. (2002) 'The vasculature and its role in the damaged and healing tendon', Arthritis Res, 4(4), pp. 252-60.

Maffulli, N., Renstrom, P. and Leadbetter, W. B. (2005) Tendon Injuries: Basic Science and Clinical Medicine. Springer London.

Standring, S. (2016) Gray's Anatomy: The Anatomical Basis of Clinical Practice. Gray's Anatomy Series 41 edn.: Elsevier Limited."}]

items.name: Tunica Intima of Vessel (Artery)
Lateral Rectus Muscle
items.info:
[{"name": "Quick Facts", "text": "Origin: Common tendinous ring.

Insertion: Lateral surface of sclera.

Action: Abducts eyeball.

Innervation: Abducens nerve (CNVI).

Arterial Supply: Ophthalmic and lacrimal artery."}, {"name": "Origin", "text": "The lateral rectus muscle arises from the upper and lower lateral parts of the common tendinous ring. Additionally, some muscle fibers arise from the greater wing of the sphenoid."}, {"name": "Insertion", "text": "The lateral rectus muscle passes anteriorly in a horizontal plane along the lateral wall of the orbit. It inserts onto the sclera just posterior to the corneoscleral junction."}, {"name": "Actions", "text": "The lateral rectus muscle works antagonistically with the medial rectus muscle to rotate the eyeball around the vertical axis. For lateral rectus, this means lateral rotation (abduction) exclusively. Working bilaterally this diverges the eyeballs, when attention is drawn to objects that are distant."}, {"name": "List of Clinical Correlates", "text": "—Abducens nerve palsy

—Oculomotor nerve palsy"}]

items.name: Microvilli (Anterior)
items.info:
[{"name": "Quick Facts", "text": "Microvilli are the minute cylindrical processes on the free surface of a cell, organized around a core of cross-linked actin filaments anchored to the terminal web, which increase the surface size of the cell; found especially in cells of the proximal convolution of the renal tubules and of the intestinal epithelium (Dorland, 2011)."}, {"name": "Structure and/or Key Feature(s)", "text": "A microvillus is an extension of cytoplasm from the apical surface of many epithelial cells. Depending on the epithelial cell, a microvillus may be just a small, irregular-shaped projection, or a very tall projection organized as a numerous, closely packed group, over the entire apical surface of the cell. 

Each microvillus contains a core of actin filaments that extends into the apical part of the cell cytoplasm and attaches to a horizontal network of actin filaments called the terminal web. The molecule myosin binds the actin filaments to the plasmalemma of the microvillus.

On some epithelial surfaces, when microvilli are numerous and closely packed, they are often referred to as a striated or brush border (Ross and Pawlina, 2006)."}, {"name": "Anatomical Relations", "text": "A microvillus is an extension of cytoplasm from the apical surface of many epithelial cells."}, {"name": "Function", "text": "Microvilli increase the surface area of the cell and so increase the absorption capability of the epithelial surface. The contractile ability of the terminal web can cause the intermicrovillus space to widen and further increase absorptive capacity (Ross and Pawlina, 2006; McKinley, O'Loughlin and Pennefather-O'Brien, 2016)."}, {"name": "References", "text": "Dorland, W. (2011) Dorland's Illustrated Medical Dictionary. 32nd edn. Philadelphia, USA: Elsevier Sauders.

McKinley, M. P., O'Loughlin, V. D. and Pennefather-O'Brien, E. E. (2016) Human Anatomy. 5th edn.: McGraw-Hill Education.

Ross, M. H. and Pawlina, W. (2006) Histology: A text and atlas. Lippincott Williams & Wilkins."}]

items.name: Nervi Nervorum
items.info: [{"name": "Quick Facts", "text": "The nervi nervorum are the nerves that innervate another nerve."}, {"name": "Structure/Morphology", "text": "The nervi nervorum can be described as the nerves innervating a nerve. These include sympathetic and sensory nerve fibers which are found within the connective tissue of the nerve trunk."}, {"name": "Anatomical Relations", "text": "The nervi nervorum originates from nerve fibers and the perivascular plexus (nerves innervating the blood vessels of the nerve). They serve as the intrinsic innervation of nerve sheaths and are found within all connective tissue coverings of the nerve trunk, including epineurium, perineurium, and endoneurium."}, {"name": "Function", "text": "The nervi nervorum are typically capable of mechanoreceptor function and some are capable of nociception, which is the detection of noxious chemical, mechanical and thermal stimuli (Bove and Light, 1997)."}, {"name": "List of Clinical Correlates", "text": "\u2014Chronic neuropathic pain"}, {"name": "References", "text": "Bove, G. M. and Light, A. R. (1997) 'The nervi nervorum: Missing link for neuropathic pain?', Pain Forum, 6(3), pp. 181-190."}]

items.name: Lamina Propria (Gingiva)
items.info:
[{"name": "Quick Facts", "text": "The lamina propria is the connective tissue coat of a mucous membrane just deep to the epithelium and basement membrane (Dorland, 2011)"}, {"name": "Structure and/or Key Feature(s)", "text": "Lamina propria is a thin layer of connective tissue that comprises part of the oral mucosa. Lying subjacent to the epithelium, it primarily consists of collagen fibers, fibroblasts, vessels and nerves. Mast cells, macrophages and inflammatory cells are also found in the lamina propria. 

Fibroblasts of the lamina propria produce many connective tissue fibers including collagen, reticulin, oxytalan, and elastic fibers (Fehrenbach and Popowics, 2015).

The lamina propria of the attached gingiva has tall connective tissue papillae and rete pegs which gives the overall gingiva tissue a stippled surface effect. The lamina propria is directly attached to the underlying mandible and maxilla (jaw bones), making the attached gingiva firm and immobile. The epithelium and lamina propria attached to the underlying periosteum of the jaw bone is collectively known as a mucoperiosteum. 

The lamina propria of the marginal gingiva is continuous with the lamina propria of the gingival sulcus. Unlike attached gingiva, marginal gingiva is not directly attached to the underlying mandible and maxilla (jaw bones), making it firm but mobile. The lamina propria of the marginal gingiva is also continuous with the lamina propria of the attached gingiva and the periodontal ligament."}, {"name": "Function", "text": "Lamina propria plays an important role in supporting the superjacent mucosal epithelial layer. It facilitates anchoring of the epithelium to the underlying jaw bones and plays a further role in immune defense due to the presence of immune cells (Rajendran and Sivapathasundharam, 2014)."}, {"name": "References", "text": "Dorland, W. (2011) Dorland's Illustrated Medical Dictionary. 32nd edn. Philadelphia, USA: Elsevier Saunders.

Fehrenbach, M. J. and Popowics, T. (2015) Illustrated Dental Embryology, Histology, and Anatomy - E-Book. Elsevier Health Sciences.

Rajendran, A. and Sivapathasundharam, B. (2014) Shafer's Textbook of Oral Pathology. Elsevier Health Sciences."}]

items.name: Bone
items.info:
[{"name": "Quick Facts", "text": "Bone is the hard form of connective tissue that constitutes the majority of the skeleton of most vertebrates; it consists of an organic component (the cells and matrix) and an inorganic, or mineral, component; the matrix contains a framework of collagenous fibers and is impregnated with the mineral component, chiefly calcium phosphate (85%) and calcium carbonate (10%), which imparts the quality of rigidity to bone (Dorland, 2011)."}, {"name": "Description", "text": "The skeletal system is mostly composed of bone, a type of connective tissue that is living, dynamic and highly specialized. Bones are highly variable in their size and proportion due to a range of developmental and environmental factors, such as sexual dimorphism, ethnicity and natural individual variation. 

The skeletal system has a number of functions, including:

—providing structural support to the body;

—serves as an attachment site for muscles and ligaments;

—protects and supports tissues and organs;

—stores minerals, particularly calcium, in the body;

—contains bone marrow, which is the site of blood cell production.

For descriptive purposes, the 206 bones of the skeletal system are divided into two parts: 

—axial skeleton, which is composed of the bones of the head, neck, vertebral column, and thoracic cage. 

—appendicular skeleton, which is composed of the bones of the upper and lower limbs (appendages). 

At the gross anatomical level, there are two types of bone; compact and spongy bone. Both types share the same molecular and cellular components; however, it is the variation of porosity which separates them from each other (Standring, 2016).

—Compact bone (or cortical bone) is solider and denser in appearance. It is mainly found in the walls of the shafts of long bones and the external surfaces of all bones. 

—Spongy bone (cancellous or trabecular bone) has a spongy or honeycomb-like appearance. This is due to minute bony struts within the tissue, known as trabeculae, which creates its porous appearance. It is mainly found in the vertebral bodies, short bones, and the ends of long bones.

Depending on their shape, the bones of the skeleton are categorized into five separate groups, including long, short, flat, irregular, and sesamoid bones.

—Long bones (tubular bones) are those that have an elongated tubular shaft with two expanded ends (e.g., femur, fibula, humerus, ulna).

—Short bones are those that can be of any shape but usually have similar proportions in length and width. They include all the carpal and tarsal bones. 

—Flat bones (tabular bones) bones are those that have a flat, or slightly cupped appearance (e.g., scapula, ribs, and parietal bones).

—Sesamoid bones are those that are found embedded in tendons and joint capsules. They are small and rounded (e.g., patella). 

—Irregular bones are those that do not belong to the any of the other groups and are completely nonuniform in shape (e.g., vertebrae, mandible, and hyoid).

All bones of the human body have defining features which differentiate them from each other. These bony features can be characterized in terms of parts, surfaces, and landmarks."}, {"name": "Reference", "text": "Dorland, W. (2011) Dorland's Illustrated Medical Dictionary. 32nd edn. Philadelphia, USA: Elsevier Saunders.

Standring, S. (2016) Gray's Anatomy: The Anatomical Basis of Clinical Practice. Gray's Anatomy Series: Elsevier Limited."}]

items.name: Outer Dense Fibers (Middle Piece)
items.info:
[{"name": "Quick Facts", "text": "The outer dense fibers are associated with the axoneme and provide strength to the sperm tail."}, {"name": "Structure and/or Key Feature(s)", "text": "The outer dense fibers are noncontractile cytoskeletal structures found in the middle piece and most of the principal piece of the sperm tail. The outer dense fibers consist of nine fibers that lie alongside the axoneme. Each of the nine fibers lie opposite a microtubule doublet of the axoneme. 

From a cross sectional view, the outer dense fibers are tear-shape and are not uniform throughout the length of the tail (Kumar & Sharma, 2017). The thickest fibers are situated within the proximal aspect of the middle piece and fibers 1, 5, 6, and 9 tend to be the thickest here. The fibers terminate in the principal piece as the fibrous sheath begins to taper inwards. It is usually the larger aforementioned fibers that are the last to terminate. (Plant & Zeleznik, 2014)."}, {"name": "Anatomical Relations", "text": "The outer dense fibers are situated within the tail of the sperm. They lie alongside the axoneme and stretch from the distal end of the neck to the distal aspect of the principal piece. Essentially, the fibers extend up to 60% of the length of the principal piece (Plant & Zeleznik, 2014).

In the middle piece of the tail, the outer dense fibers are surrounded by the mitochondrial sheath, while in the middle piece, the outer dense are surrounded by the fibrous sheath.

The striated columns that form part of the neck are continuous with the outer dense fibers."}, {"name": "Function", "text": "The tensile strength of the outer dense fibers aids in shielding the sperm from the damage incurred by the shearing forces met as the sperm travels through the epididymis during ejaculation. Additionally, the outer dense fibers play a role in stabilizing the axoneme, thereby facilitating the motility of the sperm (Zhao et al, 2018). The outer dense fibers, although noncontractile, may provide elastic recoil necessary for sperm motility."}, {"name": "List of Clinical Correlates", "text": "- Asthenozoospermia"}, {"name": "References", "text": "Kumar, A. & Sharma, M. (2017) Basics of Human Andrology: A Textbook. Springer Singapore.

Plant, T. M. & Zeleznik, A. J. (2014) Knobil and Neill's Physiology of Reproduction. Elsevier Science.

Zhao, W., Li, Z., Ping, P., Wang, G., Yuan, X. & Sun, F. (2018) Outer dense fibers stabilize the axoneme to maintain sperm motility. J Cell Mol Med, 22(3), 1755-1768."}]

items.name: Macula
items.info: [{"name": "Quick Facts", "text": "The macula is an irregular yellowish depression on the retina, about 3 degrees wide, lateral to and slightly below the optic disk; it is the site of absorption of short wavelengths of light, and it is thought that its variation in size, shape, and coloring may be related to variant types of color vision (Dorland, 2011)."}, {"name": "Structure and/or Key Feature(s)", "text": "Superior and lateral to the optic disc is a small oval area called the macula or central retina that is characterized on ophthalmoscopic examination by greenish-yellow pigmentation. This region of the retina contains specialized photoreceptors, the cones, responsible for acuity of vision. The fovea centralis is a depression at the center of the macula, which is the site of most acute vision."}, {"name": "Anatomical Relations", "text": "The macula is located in the superior temporal retina. It is an oval area of about 5.5 mm in diameter along the long axis. The macula contains the fovea at its center."}, {"name": "Function", "text": "The macula is responsible for the central, high-resolution, color vision."}, {"name": "List of Clinical Correlates", "text": "\u2014Macular degeneration"}, {"name": "References", "text": "Dorland, W. (2011) Dorland's Illustrated Medical Dictionary. 32nd edn. Philadelphia, USA: Elsevier Saunders."}]

items.name: Voltage-Gated Calcium Channel (Open)
items.info: [{"name": "Quick Facts", "text": "A calcium channel is a voltage-gated channel, very permeable to calcium ions and slightly permeable to sodium ions, that upon activation by membrane depolarization allows calcium to flow into the cell; channels are classified into six subtypes (L, N, P, Q, R, and T) on the basis of electrophysiologic and pharmacologic characteristics. Calcium channels contribute to membrane depolarization during action potentials and stimulate the contraction of cardiac and skeletal muscle and the secretion of neurotransmitters (Dorland, 2011)."}, {"name": "Structure", "text": "Neurotransmitter release occurs upon arrival of an action potential in the axon terminal. Voltage-gated calcium channels undergo a conformational change from closed to open (active). The opening of calcium channels allows the influx of calcium ions from the extracellular space, the fusion of synaptic vesicles with the surrounding presynaptic membrane, and the release of neurotransmitter into the synaptic cleft by exocytosis (Ross and Pawlina, 2006; Bear, Connors and Paradiso, 2007)."}, {"name": "Anatomical Relations", "text": "Generally, voltage-gated channels in the nervous system are mostly located on the cell body and dendrites of neurons, as well as on the nodes of Ranvier in myelinated axons, and on the axon hillock on unmyelinated axons. Voltage-gated calcium channels are situated on the presynaptic membrane."}, {"name": "Function", "text": "Voltage-gated calcium channels are the principal signal transducers of electrical impulses. They convert the depolarization of the cell membrane into an inflow of calcium ions that kickstarts a number of physiological processes including neurotransmission. They modulate the release of neurotransmitters in a synapse, hence facilitate neurotransmission. They are also involved in a number of physiological processes including regulation of the heartbeat and muscle contraction (Ross and Pawlina, 2006; Bear, Connors and Paradiso, 2007)."}, {"name": "Clinical Correlates", "text": "\u2014Traumatic injury to axon may open sodium channels which in turn, causes voltage-gated calcium channels to open and so an influx of calcium ions into the cell. This influx can activate destructive enzymes causing irreparable damage to the cytoskeleton and mitochondria and ultimately neuronal cell death."}, {"name": "References", "text": "Bear, M. F., Connors, B. W. and Paradiso, M. A. (2007) Neuroscience. Lippincott Williams & Wilkins.\n\nDorland, W. (2011) Dorland's Illustrated Medical Dictionary. 32nd edn. Philadelphia, USA: Elsevier Saunders."}]

items.name: Smooth Endoplasmic Reticulum
items.info:
[{"name": "Quick Facts", "text": "The smooth endoplasmic reticulum is a region of the endoplasmic reticulum composed of tubular elements lacking ribosomes and associated with many metabolic processes, including carbohydrate metabolism, the synthesis of lipids, cholesterol, and carbohydrates, and drug metabolism (Dorland, 2011)."}, {"name": "Structure and/or Key Feature(s)", "text": "Smooth endoplasmic reticulum is a network of interconnected membranous tubules and vesicles. It may be an extension of the rough endoplasmic reticulum or, be located separately. It’s also called agranular endoplasmic reticulum, because it has no ribosomes associated with it. In skeletal muscle cells and cardiomyocytes (cardiac muscle cells), the smooth endoplasmic reticulum is known as sarcoplasmic reticulum (Ross and Pawlina, 2006; Ovalle, Nahirney and Netter, 2013; McKinley, O'Loughlin and Pennefather-O'Brien, 2016)."}, {"name": "Anatomical Relations", "text": "The smooth endoplasmic reticulum is continuous with the rough endoplasmic reticulum."}, {"name": "Function", "text": "Smooth endoplasmic reticulum makes fatty acids, phospholipids, and steroids. It also contains a collection of enzymes that degrade toxic substances, drugs, and alcohol. It metabolizes glycogen and is involved with cell membrane production and recycling.

The sarcoplasmic reticulum (in skeletal muscle fibers and cardiomyocytes) stores and releases Ca2+ (Ross and Pawlina, 2006; Ovalle, Nahirney and Netter, 2013; McKinley, O'Loughlin and Pennefather-O'Brien, 2016)."}, {"name": "References", "text": "Dorland, W. (2011) Dorland's Illustrated Medical Dictionary. 32nd edn. Philadelphia, USA: Elsevier Saunders.

McKinley, M. P., O'Loughlin, V. D. and Pennefather-O'Brien, E. E. (2016) Human Anatomy. 5th edn.: McGraw-Hill Education.

Ovalle, W. K., Nahirney, P. C. and Netter, F. H. (2013) Netter's Essential Histology. ClinicalKey 2012: Elsevier Saunders.

Ross, M. H. and Pawlina, W. (2006) Histology: A text and atlas. Lippincott Williams & Wilkins."}]

items.name: Glomerulus
items.info:
[{"name": "Quick Facts", "text": "The glomerulus is a globular tuft formed by capillaries in the kidney, the site of the filtration barrier between the blood and the kidney; it projects into the expanded end of a renal tubule, and together with its surrounding capsule (glomerular capsule) it constitutes a renal corpuscle (Dorland, 2011)."}, {"name": "Structure and/or Key Feature(s)", "text": "The glomerulus is described as a small tuft of convoluted capillaries structurally supported by an extracellular mesangial matrix. Glomerular capillary walls are made of fenestrated endothelial cells, which forms the first layer of the renal corpuscle filtration barrier (Lote, 1994).

The mesangial matrix is composed of macrophages called mesangial cells, which function to prevent the accumulation of macromolecules that have escaped the capillaries and also have a structural role in holding the glomerulus in position (Lote, 1994)."}, {"name": "Anatomical Relations", "text": "Glomerular capillaries originate from an afferent arteriole that enters the capsule at the vascular pole. Blood from the glomerulus drains into an efferent arteriole, which exits the renal corpuscle again at the vascular pole (Kerr, 2007)."}, {"name": "Function", "text": "The glomerulus, specifically its fenestrated capillary wall endothelium, is actively involved in facilitating the transport of water and unwanted solutes from the blood to the renal tubule of the nephron as part of the filtration process."}, {"name": "List of Clinical Correlates", "text": "—Glomerular Disease

—Glomerulosclerosis"}, {"name": "References", "text": "Dorland, W. (2011) Dorland's Illustrated Medical Dictionary. 32nd edn. Philadelphia, USA: Elsevier Saunders.

Kerr, J. B. (2007) Atlas of Functional HistologyElsevier Science Health Science Division.

Lote, C. J. (1994) Principles of Renal PhysiologyChapman & Hall."}]

items.name: Lower Germinal Matrix
items.info:
[{"name": "Quick Facts", "text": "A germinal matrix is an area of reproducing cells, such as the nail matrix. The hair matrix is in the epidermal root of the hair follicle (Dorland, 2011)."}, {"name": "Structure/Morphology", "text": "The germinal matrix lies just above the dermal papilla at the base of the hair bulb. It is a mitotically active region composed of a mixture of cells including melanocytes and Langerhans cells but is predominantly composed of pluripotent keratinocytes."}, {"name": "Function", "text": "The keratinocytes and melanocytes of the hair matrix are responsible for developing the pigmented hair shaft within the follicle, therefore is referred to as the site of hair growth as it causes the hair to elongate. As the pluripotent cells differentiate and develop, they migrate upwards towards the top of the hair bulb. From this point their direction of migration will determine the portion of the hair shaft or the inner root sheath of which they will form (Winkler, 1999, Mysore, 2016)."}, {"name": "References", "text": "Dorland, W. (2011) Dorland's Illustrated Medical Dictionary. 32nd edn. Philadelphia, USA: Elsevier Saunders.

Mysore, V. (2016) Hair Transplantation. Jaypee Brothers,Medical Publishers Pvt. Limited.

Winkler, J. (1999) Apoptosis and Inflammation. Progress in Inflammation Research: Birkhäuser Basel."}]

items.name: Ribosome
items.info:
[{"name": "Quick Facts", "text": "A ribosome is a large molecular structure, approximately 12 nm wide and 25 nm long, having two dissociable subunits, that is the site of protein synthesis. Ribosomes found in the cytosol of eukaryotes have a sedimentation coefficient of 80S; the subunits have coefficients of 60S and 40S and together contain four different ribosomal RNA (rRNA) chains and about 80 different proteins. Ribosomes found in prokaryotes and mitochondria are smaller (70S, with 50S and 30S subunits containing a total of three rRNAs and 55 proteins) and also differ from eukaryotic ribosomes in their sensitivity to certain antibiotics (Dorland, 2011)."}, {"name": "Structure and/or Key Feature(s)", "text": "Ribosomes are protein complexes and consist of rRNA synthesized in the nucleolus. They appear in electron micrographs as small, electron-dense particles 20-30 nm in two different forms. 

Firstly, they could be loosely lying within the cytoplasm. Sometimes, they're combined with a messenger RNA to produce a chain of ribosomes called polyribosomes. 

Secondly, ribosomes (and polyribosomes) can be attached to the membrane of the endoplasmic reticulum.

Because of the phosphate groups of rRNA act as anions, ribosomes are intensely basophilic and so will stain with basic dyes and hematoxylin (Ross and Pawlina, 2006; Ovalle, Nahirney and Netter, 2013; McKinley, O'Loughlin and Pennefather-O'Brien, 2016)."}, {"name": "Anatomical Relations", "text": "Firstly, ribosomes position loosely within the cytoplasm or as a chain of ribosomes called polyribosomes. Secondly, ribosomes (and polyribosomes) can be attached to the membrane of the endoplasmic reticulum."}, {"name": "Function", "text": "Individual ribosomes or polyribosomes in the cytoplasm of the cell are freely associated, meaning they are involved with making proteins that the cell uses for itself.

Proteins synthesized by those ribosomes in collaboration with the endoplasmic reticulum is destined to be exported from the cell or incorporated into the plasmalemma. In some cases, the proteins are stored within the cell e.g., in lysosomes and in the granules of white blood cells (Ross and Pawlina, 2006; Ovalle, Nahirney and Netter, 2013; McKinley, O'Loughlin and Pennefather-O'Brien, 2016)."}, {"name": "References", "text": "Dorland, W. (2011) Dorland's Illustrated Medical Dictionary. 32nd edn. Philadelphia, USA: Elsevier Saunders.

McKinley, M. P., O'Loughlin, V. D. and Pennefather-O'Brien, E. E. (2016) Human Anatomy. 5th edn.: McGraw-Hill Education.

Ovalle, W. K., Nahirney, P. C. and Netter, F. H. (2013) Netter's Essential Histology. ClinicalKey 2012: Elsevier Saunders.

Ross, M. H. and Pawlina, W. (2006) Histology: A text and atlas. Lippincott Williams & Wilkins."}]

items.name: Cytoplasm (Principal Piece; Left)
items.info:
[{"name": "Quick Facts", "text": "The cytoplasm is the protoplasm of a cell exclusive of that of the nucleus; it consists of a continuous aqueous solution (cytosol) and the organelles and inclusions suspended in it and is the site of most of the chemical activities of the cell (Dorland, 2011)."}, {"name": "Structure and/or Key Feature(s)", "text": "The cytoplasm of a cell includes an aqueous solution, the cytosol, and the organelles of the cell suspended in it. It is tightly enclosed by the plasma membrane. The sperm contains a limited amount of cytoplasm. During normal spermatogenesis (or maturation), spermatids lose most of their cytoplasm. Remnants may remain as a cytoplasmic droplet at the neck region of the sperm and is shed during ejaculation. However, retention of the droplets may indicate failure of normal maturation and cause infertility (Rengan et al, 2012).

The mature sperm retains a thin layer of cytoplasm underneath the plasma membrane. In the head, the space occupied by cytoplasm between the acrosome and the nucleus is known as the subacrosomal (or perinuclear) space. The cytoplasm between the outer membrane of the acrosome and the plasma membrane is the periacrosomal space."}, {"name": "Function", "text": "The cytoplasm is the site where most chemical activities of the cell occur."}, {"name": "References", "text": "Dorland, W. (2011) Dorland's Illustrated Medical Dictionary. 32nd edn. Philadelphia, USA: Elsevier Saunders.

Rengan, A. K., Agarwal, A., van der Linde, M. & du Plessis, S. S. (2012) An investigation of excess residual cytoplasm in human spermatozoa and its distinction from the cytoplasmic droplet. Reproductive biology and endocrinology : RB&E, 10, 92-92."}]

items.name: Capillary (Cardiac Muscle Cell)
items.info: [{"name": "Quick Facts", "text": "A capillary is any of the minute vessels that connect the arterioles and venules, forming a network in nearly all parts of the body. Their walls act as semipermeable membranes for the interchange of various substances, including fluids, between the blood and tissue fluid. The two principal types are continuous and fenestrated capillaries (Dorland, 2011)."}, {"name": "Structure and/or Key Features", "text": "Like capillaries elsewhere in the body, capillaries surrounding muscle fibers have a single cell thick endothelial layer. They constitute part of the microcirculation."}, {"name": "Anatomical Relations", "text": "A capillary is a minute vessel that connects arterioles and venules, forming a vascular network in nearly all parts of the body."}, {"name": "Function", "text": "Capillaries are responsible for delivering oxygenated blood to the muscle fiber."}, {"name": "References", "text": "Dorland, W. (2011) Dorland's Illustrated Medical Dictionary. 32nd edn. Philadelphia, USA: Elsevier Saunders."}]

items.name: Axon (Somatic Sensory Afferent)
items.info:
[{"name": "Quick Facts", "text": "The axon is the process of a neuron by which impulses travel away from the cell body; at the terminal arborization of the axon, the impulses are transmitted to other nerve cells or to effector organs. The larger axons are surrounded by a myelin sheath (Dorland, 2011)."}, {"name": "Structure/Morphology", "text": "Axons are a part of the nerve cell or neuron. They can be described as an appendage of the nerve cell body giving rise to numerous collateral branches containing presynaptic complexes. Axons are comprised of a gelatinous, relatively firm cord of neuronal cytoplasm. This cord is known as the axoplasm. This axoplasm is surrounded by the axonal part of the neuronal cell membrane, which is referred to as the axolemma. Axons vary in diameter from about 0.1 µm to about 20 µm. Axons also vary in length, they can be anywhere between less than 1 cm to more than a meter long (Carp, 2015).

There are two types of axons, myelinated and unmyelinated. Myelinated axons are surrounded by a myelin sheath while unmyelinated axons are not. Nodes of Ranvier refer to the gaps found in the continuity of the myelin sheath surrounding an axon. At these gaps there is no myelin covering the axon and the axon is exposed to the extracellular fluid."}, {"name": "Key Features/Anatomical Relations", "text": "Myelinated axons are concentrically enveloped by myelin which is produced by myelinating Schwann cells. The territory of an individual Schwann cell along the length of the axon is defined as an internode, while the internodal length is the distance between two successive nodes of Ranvier. The span between these nodes varies dependent on axon diameter. It is at these nodes voltage-gated sodium channels are concentrated. Conduction in myelinated axons is saltatory and extremely quick.

Unmyelinated axons are enclosed by overlapping Schwann cells followed by a surrounding basal lamina. Within each Schwann cell, individual axons are usually isolated from their neighbor by delicate processes of cytoplasm. The absence of myelin sheaths and nodes of Ranvier in unmyelinated axons results in electrotonic conduction, not saltatory, and the passage of impulses is therefore relatively slow."}, {"name": "Function", "text": "Axons are the main conducting unit of the neuron. They transfer electrical signals along a range of distances. The nodes of Ranvier function as a generator of action potentials. This is achieved through the region of the membrane exposed at the node of Ranvier possessing special channel proteins, which allow ions to enter and exit the cell (Waxman, Kocsis and Stys, 1995)."}, {"name": "List of Clinical Correlates", "text": "—Tetrodotoxin poisoning"}, {"name": "References", "text": "Carp, S. (2015) Peripheral Nerve Injury An Anatomical and Physiological Approach for Physical Therapy Intervention. EBL-Schweitzer: F. A. Davis Company.

Dorland, W. (2011) Dorland's Illustrated Medical Dictionary. 32nd edn. Philadelphia, USA: Elsevier Saunders.

Waxman, S. G., Kocsis, J. D. and Stys, P. K. (1995) The Axon: Structure, Function, and Pathophysiology. Oxford University Press."}]

items.name: Exocytosis (Anterior)
items.info: [{"name": "Quick Facts", "text": "Exocytosis is the discharge of material from a cell by fusion of a membrane-bound vesicle with the plasma membrane and subsequent release of the vesicle's contents into the extracellular environment (Dorland, 2011)."}, {"name": "Structure and/or Key Feature(s)", "text": "Many substances enter and leave the cell, and move between different cytoplasmic regions or organelles, by vesicular transport. Vesicles present in the cytoplasm (although appearing structurally similar) reflect different traffic pathways and functional states. In most cases, there is a continual renewal/replacement of the plasma membrane as new vesicles are formed from the cell membrane and enter the cell (endocytosis) or fuse with the plasma membrane to excrete substances (exocytosis).\n\nExocytosis is the release of bulk materials from the cell, a process whereby a membrane-bound structure within the cell approaches and fuses with the plasma membrane of the cell and release its content into the extracellular environment. An example of exocytosis is the release of digestive enzymes from salivary glands and the exocrine pancreas."}, {"name": "References", "text": "Dorland, W. (2011) Dorland's Illustrated Medical Dictionary. 32nd edn. Philadelphia, USA: Elsevier Saunders."}]

items.name: Nuclear Envelope (Anterosuperior Cut)
items.info:
[{"name": "Quick Facts", "text": "The nuclear envelope is the structure enclosing the cell nucleus and separating it from the cytoplasm, consisting of two concentric lipid bilayers (the inner and outer membranes) separated by a 30 nm wide perinuclear space. The outer membrane is continuous with the rough endoplasmic reticulum, and nuclear pore complexes bridging both membranes provide communication between the nucleus and the cytoplasm (Dorland, 2011)."}, {"name": "Structure and/or Key Feature(s)", "text": "The nuclear membrane (35-75 nm thick) is a double membranous envelope that surrounds the nucleus. It is not continuous as it fuses to form nuclear pores all the way around the nuclear envelope. 

The outer nuclear membrane is continuous with, and of similar structure to, the rough or granular endoplasmic reticulum and so may house ribosomes or polyribosomes.

The inner nuclear membrane has a network of intermediate protein filaments attached to the inner surface called the nuclear or fibrous lamina. This nuclear lamina is a supportive “skeleton” but is also essential for many activities including DNA replication, transcription, and gene regulation.

Between the two nuclear membranes is a perinuclear cisternal space (Ross and Pawlina, 2006; Ovalle, Nahirney and Netter, 2013; McKinley, O'Loughlin and Pennefather-O'Brien, 2016)."}, {"name": "Anatomical Relations", "text": "The nuclear envelope surrounds the nucleus. The outer nuclear membrane is continuous with the rough endoplasmic reticulum."}, {"name": "Function", "text": "The nuclear envelope is a physical barrier that controls the movement of materials between the nucleus and the cell cytoplasm. The fibrous lamina stabilizes the nuclear envelope."}, {"name": "References", "text": "Dorland, W. (2011) Dorland's Illustrated Medical Dictionary. 32nd edn. Philadelphia, USA: Elsevier Sauders.

McKinley, M. P., O'Loughlin, V. D. and Pennefather-O'Brien, E. E. (2016) Human Anatomy. 5th edn.: McGraw-Hill Education.

Ovalle, W. K., Nahirney, P. C. and Netter, F. H. (2013) Netter's Essential Histology. ClinicalKey 2012: Elsevier Saunders.

Ross, M. H. and Pawlina, W. (2006) Histology: A text and atlas. Lippincott Williams & Wilkins."}]

items.name: Periosteal Cranial Dura Mater
alt: Endosteal Layer of Cranial Dura Mater
items.info:
[{"name": "Quick Facts", "text": "The cranial dura matter has a deep meningeal layer adjacent to the arachnoid and a superficial periosteal layer adjacent to the cranium. The periosteal dura is firmly adhered to the meningeal dura in most places, except when they come apart at the dural venous sinuses."}, {"name": "Structure", "text": "The periosteal cranial dura mater is the superficial layer of cranial dura. It is superficial to the meningeal dura and deep to the inner compact layer of bone making up the cranium. The internal surface of the cranium does not exhibit a periosteum, instead the outer layer of dura acts as this periosteum, hence the name. 

The periosteal dura is firmly adhered to the meningeal dura in most places, except when they come apart at the dural venous sinuses. This thick fibrous material blends with the bone at the foramina on the basal surface of the skull and is firmly adhered to the sutures between bones. 

A number of small vessels exist within the dura, the meningeal vessels. If these vessels rupture due to trauma, blood will accumulate in the space between the periosteal dura and the calvaria, the epidural space. The accumulation of blood during epidural hemorrhage is limited to the spaces between the sutures, as the periosteal dura is firmly adhered to the bone here, thus on CT and MRI it presents as a convex lesion."}, {"name": "Key Features/Anatomical Relations", "text": "The periosteal cranial dura mater is adherent to the inner surface of the cranial bones, especially along the sutures and foramina. It is continuous with the pericranium, covering the outer surfaces of the cranial bones, through the cranial sutures and the foramina. Additionally, it is continuous with the periosteum of the orbit via the superior orbital fissure."}, {"name": "List of Clinical Correlates", "text": "—Epidural hematoma

—Headache"}]

items.name: Straight Arteries
items.info:
[{"name": "Quick Facts", "text": "Origin: Marginal artery.

Course: Short course to the colon wall.

Branches: Long and short branches.

Supplied Structures: Colon."}, {"name": "Origin", "text": "The straight arteries are the terminal branches of the marginal artery. They arise from the marginal artery as it travels adjacent to the colon at the mesenteric border."}, {"name": "Course", "text": "From their origins, the straight arteries travel to the colon."}, {"name": "Branches", "text": "The straight arteries give rise to long and short branches, the vasa longa and vasa brevia. 

The short branches pass from the marginal artery towards the wall of the intestine and supplies the area bordering the attachment of the transverse mesocolon to the intestinal wall and the mesocolic teniae. 

The long branches have a more sinusoid course. They pass along the wall of the intestine, from the mesocolic teniae, and extend towards the omental and free teniae before they enter the intestinal wall.

The terminal short and long branches travel via the loose connective subserosa to supply the appendices epiploicae. This is how the serosa receives its blood supply.

A submucosal plexus arises from the long branches. They penetrate the muscular layer of the colon, perpendicular to the long axis of the gut, and continue along the long axis of the colon. Some contributions from the serous plexus may arise (Kachlik, Baca and Stingl, 2010). The submucosal blood vessels extend towards the lumen of the colon as a mucosal plexus."}, {"name": "Supplied Structures", "text": "The straight arteries supply the colon."}, {"name": "List of Clinical Correlates", "text": "—Colonic vascular occlusion

—Splenic flexure ischemia"}]

items.name: Nucleolus
Epimysium
items.info:
[{"name": "Quick Facts", "text": "The epimysium is the fibrous sheath about an entire muscle (Dorland, 2011)."}, {"name": "Structure", "text": "The epimysium is a well-defined layer of dense irregular connective tissue, which completely envelopes the muscle belly. It consists primarily of type I collagen fibers, which are tightly arranged to form a relatively strong fibrous covering of the muscle (Standring, 2016).

Blood vessels travel through this collagenous sheath around the outside of the whole skeletal muscle, providing the skeletal muscle with blood supply.

Nerves travel through the epimysium around the outside of the whole skeletal muscle, innervating the skeletal muscle."}, {"name": "Key Features/Anatomical Relations", "text": "The epimysium surrounds, or envelops the muscle, separating it from the surrounding organs and tissues. The three collagenous sheaths, the epimysium, perimysium, and endomysium, unite and fuse where the muscles connect to adjoining structures such as tendons (Standring, 2016)."}, {"name": "Function", "text": "The epimysium separates the muscle from adjacent structures and carries blood vessels and nerves which supply the muscle tissue. The contraction of muscle requires a vast amount of energy; therefore, an extensive vascular network is necessary in order to deliver this energy to the muscle tissue, and in addition to carry away the by-products (i.e., metabolic waste) of the muscle contraction. The epimysial nerves will innervate the skeletal muscle fascicles and the muscle fibers within them, carrying the signal required to initiate contraction of the muscle tissue (MacIntosh, Gardiner and McComas, 2006). 

As the epimysium is composed of collagen and elastin fibers, it contributes to the resistance of a muscle to tensile forces."}, {"name": "List of Clinical Correlates", "text": "—Vasculitis

—Mysium damage

—Connective tissue disease"}, {"name": "References", "text": "Dorland, W. (2011) Dorland's Illustrated Medical Dictionary. 32nd edn. Philadelphia, USA: Elsevier Saunders.

MacIntosh, B. R., Gardiner, P. F. and McComas, A. J. (2006) Skeletal Muscle: Form and Function. Human Kinetics.

Standring, S. (2016) Gray's Anatomy: The Anatomical Basis of Clinical Practice. Gray's Anatomy Series 41 edn.: Elsevier Limited."}]

items.name: Submucosal Plexus (Ileum)
items.info:
[{"name": "Quick Facts", "text": "The submucosal plexus is a nerve plexus that is part of the enteric plexus and is situated in the submucosa (Dorland, 2011)."}, {"name": "Structure/Morphology", "text": "The submucosal plexus is formed from branches of the myenteric plexus, which arise from the periarterial plexus that follows the superior and inferior mesenteric arteries and their terminal branches. Both the myenteric and the submucosal plexuses make up the enteric (or intrinsic) nervous system. The submucosal plexus itself may be subdivided into inner (or Meissner’s) and outer (or Schabadasch’s) submucosal plexuses (Brehmer, Rupprecht and Neuhuber, 2010). 

The enteric nervous system is unique to the digestive system and is autonomic in nature. It extends the entire length of the gastrointestinal tract and is composed of three types of neurons (Standring, 2016).

—Sensory neurons transmit information from receptors in the mucosa and muscle of the gut wall, which respond to mechanical, chemical, thermal, and osmotic stimuli. They project information to the interneurons.

—Motor neurons control the motility and secretions in the gut and may be inhibitory or excitatory.

—Interneurons go between the sensory and motor neurons, thus integrating the information between the two.

The enteric nervous system may function autonomously; however, it does communicate with the central nervous system via parasympathetic and sympathetic fibers. Cross connections between the two allow for information from the gut to be relayed to the CNS, and vice versa. Generally, sympathetic inputs cause inhibition of secretions and motor activity and contraction of sphincters and blood vessels (fight or flight response). Parasympathetic stimulation of the enteric nervous system promotes secretions and motor activity and dilation of the sphincters and blood vessels (rest and digest response) (Standring, 2016; Costa, Brookes and Hennig, 2000). 

In histological sections, the submucosal (Meissner’s) plexus is only visible as scattered ganglion cell bodies with satellite cells lying within the submucosal elements."}, {"name": "Key Features/Anatomical Relations", "text": "The submucosal plexus is superficial to the muscularis mucosae of the mucosa, and deep to the inner circular muscular layer."}, {"name": "Function", "text": "The submucosal plexus innervates the mucosal epithelium and the smooth muscle of the muscularis mucosa, which facilitate their respective functions of water and ion absorption and interstitial crypt emptying."}, {"name": "References", "text": "Brehmer, A., Rupprecht, H. and Neuhuber, W. (2010) 'Two submucosal nerve plexus in human intestines', Histochem Cell Biol, 133(2), pp. 149-61.

Costa, M., Brookes, S. J. and Hennig, G. W. (2000) 'Anatomy and physiology of the enteric nervous system', Gut, 47 Suppl 4(Suppl 4), pp. iv15-iv26.

Dorland, W. (2011) Dorland's Illustrated Medical Dictionary. 32nd edn. Philadelphia, USA: Elsevier Saunders.

Standring, S. (2016) Gray's Anatomy: The Anatomical Basis of Clinical Practice. Gray's Anatomy Series 41st edition edn.: Elsevier Limited."}]

In the ovarian follicle, the simple cuboidal epithelium secretes components of the zona pellucida."}]

items.name: Ovarian Cortex
items.info:
[{"name": "Quick Facts", "text": "The ovarian cortex is the dense layer of compact stroma in which the ovarian follicles are embedded, forming the peripheral zone around the medulla of the ovary (Dorland, 2011)."}, {"name": "Structure and/or Key Feature(s)", "text": "The ovarian cortex is located in the peripheral region of the ovary and surrounds the ovarian medulla. Embedded within the richly cellular connective tissue of the cortex are the follicles, which are surrounded by smooth muscle fibers (Ross and Pawlina, 2006). The follicles may be small, medium, and large, with each size represents a stage of development. They produce both the female gametes (a haploid ovum = egg) and female sex hormones (Ross and Pawlina, 2006; Mescher, 2013)."}, {"name": "Anatomical Relations", "text": "The ovarian cortex is located deep to the tunica albuginea and superficial to the ovarian medulla."}, {"name": "Function", "text": "Follicles within the ovarian cortex produce both the female gametes (a haploid ovum = egg) and female sex hormones."}, {"name": "References", "text": "Dorland, W. items.name: Distal Convoluted Tubule
Optic Nerve
items.info:
[{"name": "Quick Facts", "text": "Origin: Axons of retinal ganglion cells collect at the optic disc to form the optic nerve head.

Course: Runs posteriorly from the posterior margin of the eye, through the optic canal, and into the cranium.

Branches: Merges with the contralateral optic nerve at the optic chiasm.

Supply: Conveys visual information to the midbrain and thalamus."}, {"name": "Origin", "text": "The optic nerve forms when the axons of retinal ganglion cells converge at the optic disc at the back of the eyeball."}, {"name": "Course", "text": "From the optic nerve head, the nerve axons traverse fenestrations in the sclera, called the lamina cribrosa, to pass through it. Upon emerging from the eyeball, the axons become myelinated by oligodendroglia, approximately doubling the nerve’s diameter. It continues posteriorly across the orbit and exits through the optic canal. At the other end of the canal, it emerges intracranially in the middle cranial fossa, just anterior to the pituitary and flanked by the internal carotid arteries. The nerve has a short intracranial course before merging with its partner from the opposite side to form the optic chiasm."}, {"name": "Branches", "text": "The optic nerve does not branch. However, it merges with the contralateral optic nerve at the optic chiasm, where fibers, from temporal retina, decussate while those from nasal retina, remain ipsilateral."}, {"name": "Supplied Structures", "text": "The optic nerve is a sensory nerve. It conveys all visual information from the retina towards into the brain, primarily to the midbrain (superior colliculus, pretectum), thalamus (lateral geniculate nucleus) and hypothalamus (suprachiasmatic nucleus). Most of its axons will travel to the lateral geniculate nucleus and then on to primary visual cortex to serve conscious vision."}, {"name": "List of Clinical Correlates", "text": "—Visual deficits

—Pupillary light reflex deficits"}]

items.name: Axon (General Visceral Efferent Sympathetic)
items.info:
[{"name": "Quick Facts", "text": "The axon is the process of a neuron by which impulses travel away from the cell body; at the terminal arborization of the axon, the impulses are transmitted to other nerve cells or to effector organs. The larger axons are surrounded by a myelin sheath (Dorland, 2011)."}, {"name": "Structure/Morphology", "text": "Axons are a part of the nerve cell or neuron. They can be described as an appendage of the nerve cell body giving rise to numerous collateral branches containing presynaptic complexes. Axons are comprised of a gelatinous, relatively firm cord of neuronal cytoplasm. This cord is known as the axoplasm. This axoplasm is surrounded by the axonal part of the neuronal cell membrane, which is referred to as the axolemma. Axons vary in diameter from about 0.1 µm to about 20 µm. Axons also vary in length, they can be anywhere between less than 1 cm to more than a meter long (Carp, 2015).

There are two types of axons, myelinated and unmyelinated. Myelinated axons are surrounded by a myelin sheath while unmyelinated axons are not. Nodes of Ranvier refer to the gaps found in the continuity of the myelin sheath surrounding an axon. At these gaps there is no myelin covering the axon and the axon is exposed to the extracellular fluid."}, {"name": "Key Features/Anatomical Relations", "text": "Myelinated axons are concentrically enveloped by myelin which is produced by myelinating Schwann cells. The territory of an individual Schwann cell along the length of the axon is defined as an internode, while the internodal length is the distance between two successive nodes of Ranvier. The span between these nodes varies dependent on axon diameter. It is at these nodes voltage-gated sodium channels are concentrated. Conduction in myelinated axons is saltatory and extremely quick.

Unmyelinated axons are enclosed by overlapping Schwann cells followed by a surrounding basal lamina. Within each Schwann cell, individual axons are usually isolated from their neighbor by delicate processes of cytoplasm. The absence of myelin sheaths and nodes of Ranvier in unmyelinated axons results in electrotonic conduction, not saltatory, and the passage of impulses is therefore relatively slow."}, {"name": "Function", "text": "Axons are the main conducting unit of the neuron. They transfer electrical signals along a range of distances. The nodes of Ranvier function as a generator of action potentials. This is achieved through the region of the membrane exposed at the node of Ranvier possessing special channel proteins, which allow ions to enter and exit the cell (Waxman, Kocsis and Stys, 1995)."}, {"name": "List of Clinical Correlates", "text": "—Tetrodotoxin poisoning"}, {"name": "References", "text": "Carp, S. (2015) Peripheral Nerve Injury An Anatomical and Physiological Approach for Physical Therapy Intervention. EBL-Schweitzer: F. A. Davis Company.

Dorland, W. (2011) Dorland's Illustrated Medical Dictionary. 32nd edn. Philadelphia, USA: Elsevier Saunders.

Waxman, S. G., Kocsis, J. D. and Stys, P. K. (1995) The Axon: Structure, Function, and Pathophysiology. Oxford University Press."}]

items.name: Tunica Albuginea of Ovary
items.info:
[{"name": "Quick Facts", "text": "The tunica albuginea is the layer of dense, white, connective tissue beneath the surface epithelium of the ovary (Dorland, 2011)."}, {"name": "Structure and/or Key Feature(s)", "text": "The tunica albuginea is a dense connective tissue capsule that sits beneath the germinal epithelium of the ovary. Deeper to this, the ovary can be partitioned into an outer cortex and an inner medulla. The stroma of the ovary consists of a connective tissue which is highly cellular. Its fibroblasts are large fusiform cells (Ross and Pawlina, 2006; Mescher, 2013)."}, {"name": "Anatomical Relations", "text": "The tunica albuginea is deep to the germinal epithelium of the ovary."}, {"name": "References", "text": "Dorland, W. (2011) Dorland's Illustrated Medical Dictionary. 32nd edn. Philadelphia, USA: Elsevier Saunders.
