items.name: Mitochondria (Superior)
items.info:
[{"name": "Quick Facts", "text": "Mitochondria are the small spherical to rod-shaped cytoplasmic organelles, consisting of inner and outer bilayer membranes with a space between them. The inner membrane is infolded to form a series of projections (cristae), and the space between the cristae is filled by the mitochondrial matrix, which contains DNA, RNA, ribosomes, and granules. Mitochondria generate energy (in the form of ATP synthesis) by the oxidation of nutrients, and they contain the enzymes of the tricarboxylic acid (Krebs) cycle and for fatty acid oxidation and oxidative phosphorylation. In response to toxic insults, they release enzymes that cause apoptosis. Mitochondria can replicate independently and code for the synthesis of some of their proteins; inheritance of mitochondrial DNA is maternal, and mitochondrial DNA defects cause a variety of diseases (Dorland, 2011)."}, {"name": "Structure", "text": "Mitochondria are small, membrane-bound, ovoid organelles approximately 0.5-2 μm long. Each mitochondrion is lined by an inner and outer membrane. The inner membrane is deeply folded to form deep invaginations, called cristae. The lumen of the mitochondria is surrounded by the inner membrane and contains the mitochondrial matrix (Gouspillou and Hepple, 2017).

Mitochondria contain their own unique DNA, referred to as mitochondrial DNA (or mtDNA), and is different from the nuclear DNA. During fertilization, mitochondria from sperm do not enter the oocyte, therefore, mitochondria in the developing zygote are inherited from the oocyte."}, {"name": "Key Features/Anatomical Relations", "text": "There are numerous mitochondria present in the cytoplasm of the oocyte."}, {"name": "Function", "text": "Mitochondria are the powerhouse and energy production station of the oocyte. They also play a role in apoptosis, as it stores proapoptotic factors, and calcium homeostasis (Dumollard, Duchen and Carroll, 2007).

The mitochondria play a role in the development process of the oocyte, the fusion of the oocyte and the sperm, as well as the growth of the embryo. They modulate growth and development by regulating calcium signaling, producing ATP, reactive oxygen species, and intermediary metabolites (Dumollard, Duchen and Carroll, 2007)."}, {"name": "List of Clinical Correlates", "text": "- Infertility 

- Assisted reproductive technology 

- Heteroplasmy"}, {"name": "References", "text": "Dorland, W. (2011) Dorland's Illustrated Medical Dictionary. 32nd edn. Philadelphia, USA: Elsevier Saunders.

Dumollard, R., Duchen, M. and Carroll, J. (2007) 'The Role of Mitochondrial Function in the Oocyte and Embryo', Current Topics in Developmental Biology: Academic Press, pp. 21-49.

Gouspillou, G. and Hepple, R. T. (2017) Mitochondria in Skeletal Muscle Health, Aging and Diseases. Frontiers Research Topics."}]

items.name: Acrosome
items.info:
[{"name": "Quick Facts", "text": "The acrosome is the cap-like, membrane-bound structure derived from Golgi elements found at the anterior portion of the head of a spermatozoon; it contains lysosomal enzymes and a proteolytic enzyme, which are believed to facilitate entry of spermatozoa into oocytes (Dorland, 2011)."}, {"name": "Structure and/or Key Feature(s)", "text": "The head of the sperm is composed of a nucleus and the acrosome, both of which are surrounded by cytoskeleton and minimal cytoplasm.

The acrosome is a cap-like structure that drapes over about 50-70% of the proximal aspect of the sperm head. It is enclosed by an inner and outer acrosomal membrane. It is derived from the Golgi vesicles during spermatogenesis. It is essentially a hydrolytic and digestive enzyme-rich vesicle that releases its contents on approaching an oocyte in order for fertilization to occur. The acrosome is essentially a specialized lysosome since it contains acid phosphatase, hyaluronidase, neuraminidase and a trypsin-like protease (called acrosin)."}, {"name": "Anatomical Relations", "text": "The acrosome lies just beneath the periacrosomal space and the plasma membrane of the sperm and above the subacrosomal space. The acrosome terminates on reaching the postacrosomal sheath."}, {"name": "Function", "text": "The acrosome is essentially a specialized lysosome since it contains acid phosphatase, hyaluronidase, neuraminidase and a trypsin-like protease (called acrosin). These enzymes are required for the sperm to penetrate the zona pellucida (Grudzinskas and Yovich, 1995). 

Fertilization cannot be completed without a process known as capacitation, of which the acrosome is a necessary participant. Capacitation is essentially the functional maturation of a sperm cell and is completed after the sperm has made its journey to the uterine tube, oviduct (or fallopian tube). Various structural and biochemical changes occur during capacitation in which sperm change their behaviour, including the acrosome reaction. Following capacitation, sperm develop the ability to penetrate the cumulus of the egg and bind to the zona pellucida. This stimulates the release of digestive enzymes from the acrosome to aid in the dissolution of the zona pellucida in the vicinity of the sperm head, allowing it to access the perivitelline space (Standring, 2016; Plant and Zeleznik, 2014)."}, {"name": "List of Clinical Correlates", "text": "- Globozoospermia

- Teratozoospermia"}, {"name": "References", "text": "Dorland, W. (2011) Dorland's Illustrated Medical Dictionary. 32nd edn. Philadelphia, USA: Elsevier Saunders.

Plant, T. M. & Zeleznik, A. J. (2014) Knobil and Neill's Physiology of Reproduction. Elsevier Science.

Standring, S. (2016) Gray's Anatomy: The Anatomical Basis of Clinical Practice. Gray's Anatomy Series 41st edition edn.: Elsevier Limited."}]

items.name: Smooth Muscle Layer (of Efferent Lymphatic Vessel)
items.audio: Smooth Muscle Layer (of Efferent Lymphatic Vessel).mp3
items.info:
[{"name": "Quick Facts", "text": "Smooth muscle is a type of muscle without transverse striations in its constituent fibers; it is found in the walls of the viscera and vessels and in the dermis and is not under voluntary control (Dorland, 2011)."}, {"name": "Structure/Morphology", "text": "Afferent lymphatic vessels contain one or more layers of smooth muscle cells. Efferent lymphatic vessels contain several layers of smooth muscle (6). It has both sympathetic and parasympathetic innervation, therefore, by innervating the smooth muscle cells in the wall of the vessel, they are capable of producing rhythmic contraction. This rhythmic contraction helps the return of lymph back to the venous system, which is also aided by external movements, such as muscle movements and movements from the arteries and veins. This collectively is known as lymph propulsion (7)."}, {"name": "Function", "text": "The smooth muscle layer of the vessel aids the spontaneous contraction of the lymph vessels, thus, driving the propulsion of lymph through the vessels."}, {"name": "References", "text": "Dorland, W. (2011) Dorland's Illustrated Medical Dictionary. 32nd edn. Philadelphia, USA: Elsevier Saunders.

Margaris, K. N. and Black, R. A. (2012) 'Modelling the lymphatic system: challenges and opportunities', J R Soc Interface, 9(69), pp. 601-12.

Rovenska, E. and Rovensky, J. (2011) 'Lymphatic vessels: structure and function', The Israel Medical Association Journal, 11, pp. 762-768."}]

items.name: Myelin Sheath (Somatic Sensory Afferent)
items.info: [{"name": "Quick Facts", "text": "The myelin sheath is the cylindrical covering on the axons of some neurons; it consists of concentric layers of myelin, formed in the peripheral nervous system by the plasma membrane of Schwann cells, and in the central nervous system by oligodendrocytes. It is interrupted at intervals along its length by gaps known as nodes of Ranvier. Myelin is an electrical insulator that serves to speed the conduction of nerve impulses (Dorland, 2011)."}, {"name": "Structure/Morphology", "text": "The myelin sheath tightly holsters the axon, it is a semi-crystalline lipid-protein-water layer. This layer is discontinuous and interrupted at regular intervals. Schwann cells produce myelin sheaths in the peripheral nervous system. A myelin sheath is formed when the Schwann cell wraps around the nerve axon in a spiral fashion, creating a number of layers, or lamellae. The process is known as myelination. Each myelin-producing cell surrounds only one segment of any given axon. Periodic interruptions where short portions of the axon are left uncovered by myelin are known as the nodes of Ranvier (Patestas and Gartner, 2016)."}, {"name": "Key Features/Anatomical Relations", "text": "Nodes of Ranvier are gaps found in the continuity of the myelin sheath surrounding an axon. At these gaps there is no myelin covering the axon, thus exposing it to the extracellular fluid. The nodes of Ranvier contain a high concentration of voltage-gated sodium channels. These voltage-gated sodium channels enable the nodes to function as generators of action potentials. This is achieved through the exchange of ions into and out of the ion channels."}, {"name": "Function", "text": "The Myelin sheath acts as an insulator for the axons improving their electrical conductance. The myelin sheath also has a protective role in that it acts as a physical barrier separating the axon from the electrically charged atoms and molecules of the extracellular fluid. Myelination has also been shown to reduce the energy required for transmission of action potentials (through the mechanism of saltatory conduction) (Patestas and Gartner, 2016)."}, {"name": "List of Clinical Correlates", "text": "\u2014Demyelinating disease"}, {"name": "References", "text": "Dorland, W. (2011) Dorland's Illustrated Medical Dictionary. 32nd edn. Philadelphia, USA: Elsevier Saunders.\n\nPatestas, M. A. and Gartner, L. P. (2016) A Textbook of Neuroanatomy. Wiley."}]

items.name: Basophil
items.info:
[{"name": "Quick Facts", "text": "A basophil is a granular leukocyte with an irregularly shaped, pale-staining nucleus that is partially constricted into two lobes, and with cytoplasm that contains coarse, bluish-black granules of variable size. Basophils contain vasoactive amines such as histamine and serotonin, which are released on appropriate stimulation (Dorland, 2011)."}, {"name": "Cell Morphology", "text": "Basophils are the rarest type of leukocytes, accounting for only 0.5% of all leukocytes. The concentration of basophils is around 20–50 per microliter of blood. 

The diameter of a basophil is 10–14 μm, making them larger the erythrocytes. Their nuclei have two lobes that are either U- or S-shaped. The cytoplasm of basophils contains large granules that contain histamine and various molecules which mediate inflammation during an allergic response (Marieb, Wilhelm and Mallatt, 2012).

Basophils have Fc receptors on their cell surface which are antibody receptors that bind to Immunoglobin E (IgE) causing an allergic reaction. Basophils also possess the CD40L protein on their cell surface. CD40L interacts with the CD40 protein that is found on the cell surface of lymphocytes. This interaction results in an additional production of type IgE, therefore, mediating an immune response against parasites (Pawlina, 2016). Basophils have a short lifespan of around 8 hours in the blood (Pawlina, 2016)."}, {"name": "Production", "text": "In the red bone marrow, a hematopoietic stem cell differentiates into a myeloid stem cell which gives rise to basophils. Development usually takes 3–7 days and mature cells are stored in marrow before release into the bloodstream (Pawlina, 2016)."}, {"name": "Function", "text": "Basophils are mediators of allergic and inflammatory responses. Histamine released by basophils is a vasodilator meaning that is increases blood flow and decreases blood pressure. Heparin released by basophils is an anticoagulant which prevents blood from clotting too quickly (Silverthorn et al., 2013). Additionally, like all granulocytes, basophils are phagocytic (Marieb, Wilhelm and Mallatt, 2012)."}, {"name": "List of Clinical Correlates", "text": "—Basophilia

—Basopenia"}, {"name": "References", "text": "Dorland, W. (2011) Dorland's Illustrated Medical Dictionary. 32nd edn. Philadelphia, USA: Elsevier Saunders.

Marieb, E. N., Wilhelm, P. B. and Mallatt, J. (2012) Human Anatomy. 14th edn.: Benjamin Cummings.

Pawlina, W. 2016. Histology: A text and atlas with correlated cell and molecular biology. 7th ed. Philadelphia: Wolters Kluwer.

Silverthorn, D. U., Johnson, B. R., Ober, W. C., Garrison, C. W. and Silverthorn, A. C. (2013) Human Physiology: An Integrated Approach. Pearson Education."}]

items.name: Efferent Glomerular Arterioles
Nucleus
items.info:
[{"name": "Quick Facts", "text": "The nucleus is a spheroid body within a eukaryotic cell, separated from the cytoplasm by the nuclear envelope, and containing chromatin, a nucleolus, and nucleoplasm. In the nucleus, the cell's genetic information is stored on the chromosomes and RNA transcription and processing occur (Dorland, 2011)."}, {"name": "Structure", "text": "The oocyte nucleus, or germinal vesicle, is a prominent feature of the secondary oocyte and houses the genetic information of the cell. The nucleus is surrounded by a nuclear membrane containing nuclear pores that serve as a functional continuum between the nucleus and the cytoplasm. The nucleus also contains prominent nucleoli (the site of ribosomal RNA transcription, processing, and assembly of ribosomes) and chromatin (either condensed heterochromatin or diffuse euchromatin) (Plant and Zeleznik, 2014).

If fertilization occurs, the secondary oocyte completes meiosis II, creating a mature ovum and a second polar body. The nucleus is now known as the female pronucleus. A third polar body may also be observed if the first polar body undergoes meiosis II.

During fertilization, the plasma membrane of the oocyte fuses with that of the sperm and the nucleus and centriole of the sperm enters the cytoplasm of the oocyte. Nuclei of the oocyte and sperm gravitate towards each other; the male nucleus becomes swollen and forms the male pronucleus. Prior to fusion, each pronucleus duplicates its DNA and split in a normal mitotic division. Half the DNA from the female and male move to opposite poles, with a deep furrow developing and dividing the cytoplasm in two. This establishes a two-cell stage zygote, with a diploid number of chromosomes (Sadler, 2011)."}, {"name": "Key Features/Anatomical Relations", "text": "The nucleus lies within the cytoplasm of the cell, occupying a central position. The nucleus is surrounded by the nuclear membrane, which essentially demarcates the nucleus from the rest of the cell organelles."}, {"name": "Function", "text": "The oocyte nucleus carries the maternal DNA. The primary oocyte nucleus has 46 chromosomes (diploid), while the secondary oocyte has 23 chromosomes (haploid). Like the nucleus in other somatic cells, the nucleus of the oocyte has a variety of functions within a cell, including chromatin organization, DNA replication, and gene expression. These functions are facilitated by the nuclear matrix."}, {"name": "List of Clinical Correlates", "text": "- Infertility 

- Trisomy

- Monosomy

- Nondisjunction"}, {"name": "References", "text": "Dorland, W. (2011) Dorland's Illustrated Medical Dictionary. 32nd edn. Philadelphia, USA: Elsevier Saunders.

Plant, T. M. and Zeleznik, A. J. (2014) Knobil and Neill's Physiology of Reproduction. Elsevier Science.

Sadler, T. W. (2011) Langman's Medical Embryology. Wolters Kluwer Health."}]

items.name: Sinusoid
items.info:
[{"name": "Quick Facts", "text": "A sinusoid is a form of blood channel usually described as a large, irregular capillary, having a discontinuous lining of endothelium, with little or no adventitia; sinusoids are found in the liver, spleen, and bone marrow (Dorland, 2011)."}, {"name": "Structure/Morphology", "text": "The sinusoids are blood capillaries that receive blood from the interlobular veins and arteries and carry it through the hepatic lobule parenchyma to the central vein. The sinusoids arising from the interlobular arteries join the neighboring sinusoids arising from the interlobular veins (which are terminal branches of the hepatic portal vein), which may take place after the sinusoids have traversed the hepatic lobule by a diameter of only one liver cell. The sinusoids extend from the portal triads in a “wave like” fashion throughout the lobule. 

The sinusoids are lined with a thin and highly fenestrated endothelium with a discontinuous basal lamina. Unlike other blood capillaries, the sinusoids of the liver are also lined with specialized macrophages known as stellate sinusoidal macrophages, or Kupffer cells. The Kupffer cells are isolated in that they do not form junctions with their neighboring endothelium. 

As the blood flows through the sinusoids, a substantial amount of the plasma is filtered, via the endothelial fenestrations, into a space between the sinusoid and the surrounding hepatocytes. This space is known as the perisinusoidal space (of Disse) and is typically 0.2-0.5 μm wide (Standring, 2016). The surfaces of the hepatocytes facing the perisinusoidal space have numerous microvilli, which creates a larger surface area of the hepatocyte exposed to the plasma leaking from the sinusoids. Hepatic stellate cells, or Ito cells, are also found in the perisinusoidal space."}, {"name": "Function", "text": "The sinusoids receive a mix of arterial (oxygen rich) and portal venous (nutrient rich) blood from the interlobular arteries and interlobular veins, respectively. These sinusoids pass through the parenchyma of the liver lobule and empty into the central vein. Along its course, plasma leaking into the perisinusoidal space is exposed to the basal surfaces of the hepatocytes, where exchange of materials between the plasma and hepatocytes can occur. 

The sinusoids have a role in detoxifying the blood and in generating an immune response. This occurs via the Kupffer cells, which remove microbial and cellular fragments from circulation, as well as secreting cytokines into the blood. Kupffer cells are also primarily responsible for the removal of damaged red blood cells.

Ito cells are the primary storage site for vitamin A. They release retinol into the perisinusoidal space so that it is transferred to the retina in the blood. However, in pathological conditions, they differentiate into myofibroblasts and synthesize collagen."}, {"name": "List of Clinical Correlates", "text": "- Hemochromatosis

- Night blindness"}, {"name": "References", "text": "Dorland, W. (2011) Dorland's Illustrated Medical Dictionary. 32nd edn. Philadelphia, USA: Elsevier Saunders.

Standring, S. (2016) Gray's Anatomy: The Anatomical Basis of Clinical Practice. Gray's Anatomy Series 41st edn.: Elsevier Limited."}]

items.name: Tunica Adventitia of Efferent Glomerular Arteriole
items.audio: Tunica Adventitia of Efferent Glomerular Arteriole.mp3
alt: Tunica Externa of Efferent Glomerular Arteriole
items.info: [{"name": "Quick Facts", "text": "The tunica adventitia is the outermost covering of an organ, vessel, or other structure, which is made up of connective tissue and elastic fibers and is in contact with surrounding structures (Dorland, 2011)."}, {"name": "Structure and/or Key Feature(s)", "text": "The tunica adventitia of an arteriole is the outermost layer of connective tissue composed mostly of collagen and small amounts of elastic fibers that merge with surrounding loose connective tissue. In both the afferent and efferent arterioles, the tunica adventitia is extremely thin."}, {"name": "Anatomical Relations", "text": "An arteriole has three layers (or tunics). The tunica adventitia of an arteriole is the outermost layer of a blood vessel that merges with surrounding loose connective tissue. The tunica media is adjacent to the outer adventitia layer as the middle layer of a blood vessel. The layer adjacent to the blood vessel lumen (or inner layer) is the tunica intima."}, {"name": "Function", "text": "The tunica adventitia of an arteriole is the outermost layer of connective tissue that merges and attaches the blood vessels with surrounding loose connective tissue."}, {"name": "References", "text": "Dorland, W. (2011) Dorland's Illustrated Medical Dictionary. 32nd edn. Philadelphia, USA: Elsevier Saunders."}]

items.name: Straight Arterioles of Kidney
items.info:
[{"name": "Quick Facts", "text": "The straight arterioles are branches of the arcuate arteries arising from the efferent glomerular arterioles and passing down to the renal pyramids (Dorland, 2011)."}, {"name": "Structure and/or Key Features", "text": "The straight arterioles arise from the efferent arterioles. These capillaries are responsible for the vascular supply of the medulla. Specifically, efferent arterioles divide into peritubular capillaries that surrounds the renal tubules in the cortex and then further divide and into a series of straight arterioles, known as the vasa recta. The straight arterioles enter the medulla and surrounds the nephron loop (Liao & Madersbacher, 2019).

The straight arterioles are primarily located in the inner medulla and near the papilla. They lie in very close proximity with the nephron loops and the medullary and papillary collecting ducts. These tubules along with the straight arterioles can be arranged into bundles known as the medullary rays."}, {"name": "Function", "text": "Straight arterioles are responsible for the delivery of nutrients to the structures of renal medulla. Furthermore, they are responsible for the reabsorption of water and solutes that have been reabsorbed in the nephron loop and collecting ducts."}, {"name": "References", "text": "Dorland, W. (2011) Dorland's Illustrated Medical Dictionary. 32nd edn. Philadelphia, USA: Elsevier Saunders.

Liao, L. & Madersbacher, H. (2019) Neurourology: Theory and PracticeSpringer Netherlands."}]

items.name: Mitochondrion
items.info:
[{"name": "Quick Facts", "text": "Mitochondria are the small spherical to rod-shaped cytoplasmic organelles, consisting of inner and outer bilayer membranes with a space between them. The inner membrane is infolded to form a series of projections (cristae), and the space between the cristae is filled by the mitochondrial matrix, which contains DNA, RNA, ribosomes, and granules. Mitochondria generate energy (in the form of ATP synthesis) by the oxidation of nutrients, and they contain the enzymes of the tricarboxylic acid (Krebs) cycle and for fatty acid oxidation and oxidative phosphorylation. In response to toxic insults, they release enzymes that cause apoptosis. Mitochondria can replicate independently and code for the synthesis of some of their proteins; inheritance of mitochondrial DNA is maternal, and mitochondrial DNA defects cause a variety of diseases (Dorland, 2011)."}, {"name": "Structure and/or Key Features", "text": "The mitochondrion is a double membrane-bound organelle about 0.5-1 μm wide and up to 10 μm in length. The space between the inner and outer membrane is the intermembrane space. 

Mitochondria occur in a variety of shapes and sizes. The only cells that lack mitochondria are erythrocytes (red blood cells) and terminal keratinocytes. 

The outer membranes of the mitochondria are about 6–7 nm thick and have mitochondrial porins which are voltage-dependent anion channels. Ions, metabolites, and small molecules may enter the intermembrane space; however, they cannot pass through the inner mitochondrial membrane. In addition, the outer membrane possesses various receptors, for molecules that translocate in the intermembrane space, and various enzymes. 

The inner mitochondrial membrane is thinner and rich in cardiolipin which is a phospholipid that makes the inner membrane impermeable to ions and less permeable to all other elements. The inner membrane invaginates to form long parallel stacks of membranous components called cristae that run perpendicular to the long axis of the mitochondrion and increase the surface area of the inner membrane. Cristae contain respiratory chain enzymes. Among these respiratory enzymes is ATP synthetase which is responsible for oxidative phosphorylation, a process of cellular respiration and the production of adenosine triphosphate (ATP), which is an energy-rich molecule.

Cristae that form parallel plates in mitochondria produce proteins, whereas in mitochondria that produce steroids, the cristae adopt a tubular form. 

The numbers of mitochondria, as well as the number and complexity of the cristae, will correlate with the activity of the cell. Therefore, very active cells, such as a skeletal muscle fiber and a cardiomyocyte (cardiac muscle cell), will contain large numbers of mitochondria with extensive cristae.

The inner mitochondrial membrane surrounds the mitochondrial fluid (matrix) which contains mitochondrial DNA and RNA. The mitochondrial DNA encodes thirteen enzymes which are involved in the process of oxidative phosphorylation. It also contains two rRNAs, and twenty-two tRNAs that are involved in the translation of mitochondrial mRNA. In addition, mitochondria exhibit a complete system of proteins for protein and ribosomal synthesis. Mitochondrial proteins are formed both by mitochondrial and nuclear DNA. 

Matrix granules that store Ca2+ are also housed within the matrix of the mitochondrion. 

Mitochondria contribute to the acidophilia of the cytoplasm in cells where they aggregate in large numbers."}, {"name": "Anatomical Relations", "text": "The mitochondria are scattered throughout the cell body, dendrites, and axons. They are greater in number at the axon hillock, nodes of Ranvier, and presynaptic endings."}, {"name": "Function", "text": "The mitochondria are the power houses of the cell and produce chemical energy by producing high energy ATP molecules. The mitochondria are also able to induce apoptosis (Ross and Pawlina, 2006)."}, {"name": "Clinical Correlates", "text": "Mutations in mitochondrial DNA result in a number of inherited disorders. Mitochondrial related diseases (mitochondrial myopathies) become most evident in tissues such as skeletal muscle that require large amounts of energy (ATP) generated by mitochondria.

Chronic progressive external ophthalmoplegia affects the inability to move the eyes due to weakening of extraocular muscles and the eyebrows. Leber hereditary optic neuropathy affects vision due to the degeneration of retinal ganglion cells and their axons as a result of mutations in the mitochondrial genome."}, {"name": "References", "text": "Dorland, W. (2011) Dorland's Illustrated Medical Dictionary. 32nd edn. Philadelphia, USA: Elsevier Saunders.

Ross, M. H. and Pawlina, W. (2006) Histology: A text and atlas. Lippincott Williams & Wilkins."}]

items.name: Levator Aponeurosis
items.info:
[{"name": "Quick Facts", "text": "The levator aponeurosis is the anterior extensions of the levator palpebrae superioris muscle. It aids in elevating the upper eyelid (Dorland, 2011)."}, {"name": "Structure and/or Key Feature(s)", "text": "Anteriorly, the tendon of levator palpebrae superioris broadens and thins to form the levator aponeurosis. This aponeurosis has been described as bilaminar, with superficial and deep laminae. 

The fibers of the superficial lamina diverge and pass through the orbicularis oculi muscle and attach to the upper eyelid. Fibers from the deep lamina attach to the anterior surface of the superior tarsal plate of the upper eyelid. These fibers are accompanied by smooth muscle fibers from the superior tarsal muscle."}, {"name": "Function", "text": "The levator aponeurosis transmits the contractions of the levator palpebrae superioris muscle to elevate the upper eyelid. It works in opposition to the normal pull of gravity and the palpebral part of the orbicularis oculi muscle, which close the eyelids (Anderson and Beard, 1977)."}, {"name": "List of Clinical Correlates", "text": "—Ptosis"}, {"name": "References", "text": "Anderson, R. L. and Beard, C. (1977) 'The levator aponeurosis. Attachments and their clinical significance', Arch Ophthalmol, 95(8), pp. 1437-41.

Dorland, W. (2011) Dorland's Illustrated Medical Dictionary. 32nd edn. Philadelphia, USA: Elsevier Saunders."}]

items.name: Interlobular Arteries of Kidney
items.info: [{"name": "Quick Facts", "text": "The interlobular arteries are arteries originating from the arcuate arteries of the kidney and distributed to the renal glomeruli (Dorland, 2011)."}, {"name": "Structure and/or Key Features", "text": "Interlobular arteries arise from the arcuate arteries and diverge radially into the cortex. Some interlobular arteries arise directly from arcuate arteries. \n\nThese interlobular arteries travel towards the superficial cortex. Some interlobular arteries branch, while others can twist and recurve in the direction of the medulla before rerouting to the renal surface. The branches of the interlobular arteries give rise to the afferent arterioles that supply the renal corpuscle. Other interlobular arteries may also traverse the surface of the kidney and anastomose with a capsular plexus."}, {"name": "Function", "text": "The branches of the interlobular arteries give rise to the afferent arterioles that supply the glomeruli."}, {"name": "References", "text": "Dorland, W. (2011) Dorland's Illustrated Medical Dictionary. 32nd edn. Philadelphia, USA: Elsevier Saunders."}]

items.name: Columnar External Supporting Cell
items.info:
[{"name": "Quick Facts", "text": "The columnar external supporting cells, of Hensen cells, are the tall supporting cells arranged in rows adjacent to the last row of outer phalangeal cells, constituting the outer border of the organ of Corti (Dorland, 2011)."}, {"name": "Structure and/or Key Feature(s)", "text": "The columnar external supporting cells (Hensen’s cells or the outer border cells) are one of the three types of cells that form the supporting cells of the outer hair cells. The other cells include the outer pillar cells and the external phalangeal epithelial cells. They are arranged in numerous rows extending out toward the outer spiral sulcus. These border cells are oblong shaped, with the tallest cells nearest to the external phalangeal epithelial cells and outer hair cells. The columnar external supporting cells decrease in height as the rows move out toward the outer spiral sulcus.

Similar to the internal supporting cells, the apical surfaces of these cells are slanted, forming a gradual slope toward the outer hair cells. The slope of the surfaces of the shorter, outermost supporting cells is the steepest. The slope becomes less severe as it moves inwards and upwards. As the slope flattens, the apices of the taller cells become wider, with the innermost row of these border cells having a slight internal overhang in relation to their body. 

The columnar external supporting cells have adherens and tight junctions which link them to the other columnar external supporting cells, as well as the other adjacent supporting cells. They communicate with each other via established gap junctions."}, {"name": "Anatomical Relations", "text": "The columnar external supporting cells are the most external epithelial cells of the organ of Corti. They are interjacent to the outer phalangeal epithelial cells and cuboid external supporting cells (Claudius’ cells)."}, {"name": "Function", "text": "The columnar external supporting cells have a sturdy cytoskeleton that helps preserve the structural organization of the outer hair cells. They communicate effectively with the surrounding cells via gap junctions, allowing for an effective inflammatory response to be generated in the presence of damage or pathogens."}, {"name": "References", "text": "Dorland, W. (2011) Dorland's Illustrated Medical Dictionary. 32nd edn. Philadelphia, USA: Elsevier Saunders."}]

items.name: Veins of Brain
items.info:
[{"name": "Quick Facts", "text": "The brain is drained by the cerebral veins; they drain the surfaces or inner regions of the cerebral hemispheres; they are divided into superficial and deep groups (Dorland, 2011)."}, {"name": "Description", "text": "The veins that drain the brain are found in the subarachnoid space. They are valveless and have thin walls. The cerebral veins pierce the arachnoid and meningeal layer of the dura mater to enter the nearest dural venous sinus (Moore, Dalley and Agur, 2013).

The superior cerebral veins on the superolateral surface of the brain drain into the superior sagittal sinus, while veins on the posteroinferior aspect drain into the transverse, straight, and superior petrosal sinuses. The great cerebral vein is formed by the union of two internal cerebral veins and terminates by merging with the inferior sagittal sinus to form the straight sinus (Moore, Dalley and Agur, 2013)."}, {"name": "References", "text": "Dorland, W. (2011) Dorland's Illustrated Medical Dictionary. 32nd edn. Philadelphia, USA: Elsevier Saunders.

Moore, K. L., Dalley, A. F. and Agur, A. M. R. (2013) Clinically Oriented Anatomy. Clinically Oriented Anatomy 7th edn.: Wolters Kluwer Health/Lippincott Williams & Wilkins."}]

items.name: Amacrine Cells
items.info:
[{"name": "Quick Facts", "text": "An amacrine cell is a type of multipolar neuron, located in the inner nuclear layer of the retina, that lacks an axon (Dorland, 2011)."}, {"name": "Structure and/or Key Features", "text": "Amacrine cells are local circuit neurons, or interneurons. Interneurons, a specific type of neuron that act as an intermediary, affecting the transfer of information between two projection neurons. Amacrine cells are classified as inhibitory interneurons (Standring, 2016) (Standring, 2016). 

They tend to have large cell bodies and lobulated nuclei. Their cellular morphology and pharmacology are quite variable. Most do not have a typical axon; instead they possess what resembles a field of dendrites that acts as both axons and dendrites, i.e., they can be both pre- and postsynaptic. These cell processes extend into the inner plexiform layer where they are presynaptic to bipolar cells, and postsynaptic to retinal ganglionic and other amacrine cells. Thus, they modify signal transfer between the intermediate bipolar cells and the output neurons of the retina, the ganglionic cells (Standring, 2016; Remington and Goodwin, 2011). Other synaptic connections are also found.

It is currently estimated that there are approximately 30–40 different amacrine cell types. Amacrine cells may be categorized depending on their process morphology and stratification (stratified or diffuse). They may be further classified depending on the spread or reach of their processes (narrow-field, small-field, medium-field, and large-field). Additionally, they may be classified by the type of inhibitory neurotransmitter they release. The diversity of amacrine cell types is reflected in the complexity and scale of their signaling role within the retina (Remington and Goodwin, 2011; Balasubramanian and Gan, 2014)."}, {"name": "Anatomical Relations", "text": "The cell bodies of amacrine cells are generally located in the inner nuclear layer, close to the border of the inner plexiform layer, where they are mostly surrounded by other amacrine cells, bipolar cells and Müller cell bodies. Their processes extend into the inner plexiform layer. Some classes of amacrine cell have their bodies located in the ganglionic layer and these are known as displaced amacrine cells. The processes of displaced amacrine cells also extend into the inner plexiform layer (Standring, 2016)."}, {"name": "Function", "text": "Amacrine cells are largely responsible for the detection of directional motion and for regulating our eyes’ ability to adapt to light. They also play a role in establishing the body’s circadian rhythm (Balasubramanian and Gan, 2014). 

Like horizontal neurons, amacrine cells are known as inhibitory neurons. Amacrine cells receive their excitatory input from bipolar cells. They subsequently integrate and regulate the information that reaches ganglion cells via feedback synapses onto bipolar terminals or via feedforward synapses onto ganglion cell dendrites. Amacrine cells may also communicate, via lateral inhibitory synapses, with other amacrine cells (Diamond, 2017). 

Amacrine cells play an important role in shaping the visual signaling transmitted through the retina. For example, inhibitory feedback signals from amacrine cells to bipolar cells sharpen the timing of bipolar cell responses and additionally sharpen the edges of their center-surround receptive fields. Feedforward signals, on the other hand, ensure there is spatial and temporal detail in the receptive field (Diamond, 2017)."}, {"name": "References", "text": "Balasubramanian, R. and Gan, L. (2014) 'Development of Retinal Amacrine Cells and Their Dendritic Stratification', Curr Ophthalmol Rep, 2(3), pp. 100-106.

Diamond, J. S. (2017) 'Inhibitory Interneurons in the Retina: Types, Circuitry, and Function', Annu Rev Vis Sci, 3, pp. 1-24.

Dorland, W. (2011) Dorland's Illustrated Medical Dictionary. 32nd edn. Philadelphia, USA: Elsevier Saunders.

Remington, L. A. and Goodwin, D. (2011) Clinical Anatomy of the Visual System E-Book. Elsevier Health Sciences.

Standring, S. (2016) Gray's Anatomy: The Anatomical Basis of Clinical Practice. Gray's Anatomy Series 41 edn.: Elsevier Limited."}]

items.name: Medullary Cords
items.info:
[{"name": "Quick Facts", "text": "The medullary cords are strands of dense lymphoid tissue surrounded by the sinuses of the medulla of a lymph node (Dorland, 2011)."}, {"name": "Structure/Morphology", "text": "The medullary cords and sinuses constitute the medulla of the lymph node. Medullary cords are usually clearly delineated because of their dense cellularity compared to the surrounding medullary sinuses. The cords are composed of dense, irregular reticular fibers, which are denser than the fibers in the cortex and paracortex. Arterioles and venules supplying and draining blood from the lymph node are conveyed through the medullary cords. 

The medullary cords contain a large number of mature plasma cells, lymphocytes and macrophages. The plasma cells are capable of secreting antibodies into the medullary sinuses or migrate into the sinus so that they enter the lymph that is transported into the efferent lymphatic vessel, and eventually enters the circulatory system."}, {"name": "Function", "text": "The medullary cords anchor and house macrophages, dendritic cells, plasma cells, and B lymphocytes. In addition, blood vessels traverse through the medullary cords (Willard-Mack, 2006)."}, {"name": "References", "text": "Dorland, W. (2011) Dorland's Illustrated Medical Dictionary. 32nd edn. Philadelphia, USA: Elsevier Saunders.

Willard-Mack, C. L. (2006) 'Normal structure, function, and histology of lymph nodes', Toxicologic Pathology, 5(34), pp. 409-424."}]

items.name: Descending Limb of Nephron Loop
alt: Descending Limb of Loop of Henle
items.info:
[{"name": "Quick Facts", "text": "The descending limb is the proximal part of the loop of Henle (Dorland, 2011)."}, {"name": "Structure and/or Key Features", "text": "The nephron loop, more widely known as the loop of Henle, describes the recognizable loop that characterizes the nephron. Its length may measure up to 30 mm in length in juxtamedullary nephrons (Martini, Nath and Bartholomew, 2017).

The nephron loop is comprised of the proximal straight tubule (or thick descending limb), a thin descending limb, a thin ascending limb, and a distal straight tubule (or thick ascending limb).

The descending limb of the nephron loop has two distinct histological segments, the proximal straight tubule, or thick descending limb, and the thin descending limb. The epithelium of the thick descending limb is low simple cuboidal, while the epithelium of the thin segment is simple squamous. Despite being histologically distinct, the thick and thin segment of the descending limb are not as physiologically distinct as they are anatomically, thus, the two segments are often incorrectly referred to as one structure.

The descending thick limb measures approximately 30 µm in diameter while the descending thin limb measures approximately 15 µm (Kerr, 2007). 

The nephron loop is supplied by a series of straight arterioles that branch from the cortical efferent arterioles; these capillaries are also known as the vasa recta."}, {"name": "Anatomical Relations", "text": "The proximal straight tubule or thick descending limb is located distal to the proximal convoluted tubule and proximal to the thin descending limb. The thick descending limb is proximal to the thin ascending limb of the nephron loop.

The descending limb of the nephron loop of juxtamedullary nephrons extend deep through the inner and outer medulla towards the renal papilla."}, {"name": "Function", "text": "The descending limb of the nephron loop is responsible for the reabsorption of water from tubular fluid via aquaporin channels (Martini et al, 2017). This reabsorption increases the osmolarity of the tubular fluid as it passes through the descending portion of the loop."}, {"name": "List of Clinical Correlates", "text": "—Bartter syndrome"}, {"name": "References", "text": "Dorland, W. (2011) Dorland's Illustrated Medical Dictionary. 32nd edn. Philadelphia, USA: Elsevier Saunders.

Kerr, J. B. (2007) Atlas of Functional HistologyElsevier Science Health Science Division.

Martini, F. H., Nath, J. L. & Bartholomew, E. F. (2017) Fundamentals of Anatomy & PhysiologyPearson Education."}]

Under the light microscope, it appears as a radially striated layer (Dorland, 2011)."}, {"name": "Structure and/or Key Feature(s)", "text": "A zona pellucida forms around the oocyte when it is about 50-80 μm in diameter. This is a tough, eosinophilic or very pink stained, acellular, protective membrane that separates the oocyte and surrounding granulosa cells. Granulosa cells send processes inwards invading the zona pellucida, so that they can form gap junctions with the microvilli of the oocyte."}, {"name": "Anatomical Relations", "text": "A zona pellucida forms around the oocyte."}, {"name": "Function", "text": "In the human female, the zona pellucida contains three classes of glycoproteins (ZP-1, ZP-2 and ZP-3) (Ross and Pawlina, 2006). 

—ZP-1 links ZP-2 and ZP-3.

—ZP-2 is a secondary spermatozoon binding protein.

—ZP-3 is the most significant spermatozoon binding receptor and the inducer of the acrosome reaction (Ross and Pawlina, 2006)."}, {"name": "List of Clinical Correlates", "text": "Failure of ZP-1 to function correctly results in ZP-3 accumulating in the ooplasm and no functional zona pellucida forming around the oocyte (Ross and Pawlina, 2006)."}, {"name": "References", "text": "Dorland, W. (2011) Dorland's Illustrated Medical Dictionary. 32nd edn. Philadelphia, USA: Elsevier Saunders.

Ross, M. H. and Pawlina, W. (2006) Histology: A text and atlas. Lippincott Williams & Wilkins."}]

items.info:
[{"name": "Quick Facts", "text": "An A cell is a type of islet cell that is found in the periphery of the pancreatic islets and secretes either somatostatin (alpha1 cells) or glucagon (alpha2 cells) (Dorland, 2011)."}, {"name": "Structure and/or Key Feature(s)", "text": "A cells are mostly located around the periphery of the pancreatic islet and make up about 15–20% of the cell population of the islet. Each cell contains densely packed secretory granules of uniform size of about 250 nm in diameter (Ross and Pawlina, 2016)."}, {"name": "Function", "text": "A cells secrete glucagon which is stored in the granules. Glucagon acts on several tissues to release energy stored in glycogen and fat by glycogenolysis and lipolysis so blood glucose levels increase (Mescher, 2013)."}, {"name": "References", "text": "Dorland, W. (2011) Dorland's Illustrated Medical Dictionary. 32nd edn. Philadelphia, USA: Elsevier Saunders.

items.name: Tarsal Glands
items.info: [{"name": "Quick Facts", "text": "The tarsal glands are sebaceous follicles between the tarsi and the conjunctiva of the eyelids (Dorland, 2011)."}, {"name": "Structure and/or Key Feature(s)", "text": "The tarsal glands are elongated sebaceous glands embedded within the tarsal plates. The glands are arranged parallel to each other and perpendicular to the margin of the eyelid. The superior eyelid contains 25-35 tarsal sebaceous glands, while the inferior eyelid contains 15-25. \n\nEach gland consists of a straight tube that opens on the free palpebral margin at minute orifices. Muscle fibers arising from the palpebral part of the orbicularis oculi muscle are arranged concentrically around the orifices of the ducts (Riolan muscles). This arrangement of muscle around the opening of the ducts may close them or aid in the release of secretions from the ducts."}, {"name": "Anatomical Relations", "text": "The tarsal glands are embedded within the tarsal plate. Their openings are just posterior to the row of cilia that form the eyelashes."}, {"name": "Function", "text": "The tarsal sebaceous glands produce oily secretions that spread over the palpebral margins. This helps in reducing evaporation contributing to the stability of the tear film that covers the anterior surface of the eyeball. The oily secretion increases the surface tension of the tear fluid and preventing spillage of tears onto the face."}, {"name": "List of Clinical Correlates ", "text": "\u2014Stye (external hordeolum)"}, {"name": "References", "text": "Dorland, W. (2011) Dorland's Illustrated Medical Dictionary. 32nd edn. Philadelphia, USA: Elsevier Saunders."}, {"name": "List of Clinical Correlates", "text": "\u2014Stye (external hordeolum)"}]

items.name: Scalp
items.info:
[{"name": "Quick Facts", "text": "The scalp is that part of the skin of the head, exclusive of the face and ears, that is normally covered with hair (Dorland, 2011)."}, {"name": "Structure", "text": "The scalp is a soft tissue that covers the superior, posterior and lateral regions of the head. The scalp consists of five layers, including the skin, superficial fascia, epicranial aponeurosis, loose connective tissue, and pericranium (Moore, Dalley and Agur, 2013). The first three layers move as a unit and are referred as the scalp proper. Additionally, the scalp consists of blood vessels, lymphatics, and nerve fibers.

The scalp has a particularly rich blood supply, with vessels located in the dense superficial fascia. Branches of the external carotid artery supplying the scalp include the occipital, posterior auricular, and superficial temporal arteries. Branches of the internal carotid artery include the supraorbital and supratrochlear arteries (Moore, Dalley and Agur, 2013). 

Venous drainage of the scalp is divided into superficial and deep. Superficial veins include the supratrochlear, supraorbital, superficial temporal, posterior auricular, and occipital veins, all of which drain into the external jugular vein. The deep parts of the scalp in the temporal region are drained by the deep temporal veins (Moore, Dalley and Agur, 2013). 

The cutaneous innervation of the scalp anterior to the auricles is via the trigeminal nerve, while innervation posterior to the auricles is through spinal cutaneous nerves (Moore, Dalley and Agur, 2013)

The scalp does not have any lymph nodes. Instead lymphatic vessels drain lymph from the scalp to the submental, submandibular, parotid, mastoid, and occipital lymph nodes, all of which are located at the junction between the head and neck (Moore, Dalley and Agur, 2013).

A useful acronym may help you remember the layers of the scalp:

S— Skin

C— Connective tissue (subcutaneous tissue)

A— (epicranial) Aponeurosis

L— Loose connective tissue

P— Pericranium."}, {"name": "Key Features/Anatomical Relations", "text": "The scalp covers the head, specifically the neurocranium, from the supraorbital margins of the frontal bone as far as the superior nuchal lines of the occipital bones. It also extends laterally from the temporal fascia to the zygomatic arches."}, {"name": "Function", "text": "The skin layer of the scalp contains sebaceous glands which are exocrine glands that lubricate the skin with an oily substance known as sebum. The dense superficial fascia of the scalp is highly vascularized and contains cutaneous nerves allowing sensation of heat, cold, touch, pressure, and vibration. The epicranial aponeurosis serves as an intermediate tendon that unites the two bellies of the occipitofrontalis muscle. The occipitofrontalis muscle, which is the only scalp muscle, is responsible for moving the scalp on the skull and for raising the eyebrows. The loose connective tissue of the scalp allows movement of the scalp proper. The pericranium is the dense connective tissue that covers the outer surface of the neurocranium and provides minimal blood supply to the underlying cranial bone (Brennan, Mahadevan and Evans, 2015)."}, {"name": "List of Clinical Correlates", "text": "—Scalp lacerations, injuries, infections 

—Subgaleal hemorrhage"}, {"name": "References", "text": "Brennan, P. A., Mahadevan, V. and Evans, B. T. (2015) Clinical Head and Neck Anatomy for Surgeons. CRC Press.

Dorland, W. (2011) Dorland's Illustrated Medical Dictionary. 32nd edn. Philadelphia, USA: Elsevier Saunders.

Moore, K. L., Dalley, A. F. and Agur, A. M. R. (2013) Clinically Oriented Anatomy. Clinically Oriented Anatomy 7th edn.: Wolters Kluwer Health/Lippincott Williams & Wilkins."}]

They can be pumps, channels, receptors, linkers, enzymes, and structural proteins, or serve as a combination of these functions.\n\nMembrane proteins that act as enzymes have a variety of functions, e.g., ATPases have a specific role in ion pumping."}, {"name": "Anatomical Relations", "text": "Membrane proteins acting as enzymes are a component of the plasma membrane. items.name: Blood Vessels
items.info:
[{"name": "Quick Facts", "text": "A blood vessel includes any of the vessels conveying the blood; an artery, arteriole, capillary, venule, or vein (Dorland, 2011)."}, {"name": "Structure", "text": "Blood vessels are tubular structures in which blood circulates around the body, creating a network which, along with the heart, we refer to as the circulatory or cardiovascular system. 

Arteries are types of blood vessels that carry blood away from the heart. They have relatively thick walls that can withstand the high blood pressure forces created by the heart. Arteries are classified into three types:
•	elastic (large or conducting) arteries
•	muscular (medium or distributing) arteries
•	arterioles (or small arteries).

Arterioles deliver blood capillaries. 

Capillaries are the smallest blood vessels, and create vascular networks known as capillary beds. These capillary beds supply all of the body's organs and tissues in the form of an interlacing web. Capillaries walls are one cell thick, allowing the exchange of gases, nutrients, metabolites, and waste to and from tissues.

Veins are blood vessels that receive blood from capillaries and carry blood, in most cases, under low pressure back to the heart. Exceptions to this rule are the portal venous systems where veins carry blood to the liver in the hepatic portal system, or to the pituitary gland in the hypothalamic-hypophyseal portal system. Veins have relatively thin walls compared to arteries, and consequently, have a larger lumen. Like arteries, veins are also classified into three types:
•	venules or small veins
•	medium veins
•	large veins.
"}, {"name": "Anatomical Relations", "text": "Blood vessels create the two circulatory paths in which blood travels; the pulmonary circuit, which runs from the heart to the lungs and back to the heart; and the systemic circuit, which runs from the heart to peripheral tissues and back to the heart.

Arteries and veins of similar size usually accompany each other and are named accordingly, e.g., the femoral vein runs together with the femoral artery and a arteriole is accompanied by a venule. 
"}, {"name": "Function", "text": "Blood vessels are essential in provide a transport system for blood. The blood is also a vehicle through which the tissues of the body communicate with one another. It carries various substances including hormones, nutrients, the waste products of metabolism, oxygen, and carbon dioxide among others. 

The blood vessels are also involved in the regulation of systemic blood flow. Through vasodilation and vasoconstriction of arteries, the lumen can be increased or decreased in diameter, respectively. This change in the lumen allows greater or lesser blood flow through the vessel. This can redirect the blood to where it’s required or reduce/increase blood pressure in the body.

The distensibility of veins enables them to act as a blood reservoir, allowing storage of large volumes of blood. This can occur when blood returning to the heart is disrupted due to low pressure or compression.
"}, {"name": "List of Clinical Correlates", "text": "•	Hypertension"}, {"name": "References", "text": "Dorland, W. (2011) Dorland's Illustrated Medical Dictionary. 32nd edn. Philadelphia, USA: Elsevier Saunders."}]

items.name: Perilymph of Scala Tympani
items.info:
[{"name": "Quick Facts", "text": "Perilymph is the fluid contained within the space separating the membranous labyrinth from the osseous labyrinth; it is entirely separate from the endolymph (Dorland, 2011)."}, {"name": "Structure and/or Key Feature(s)", "text": "The scala tympani is filled with perilymph, an extracellular fluid that is similar in consistency to that of cerebrospinal fluid, especially regarding the perilymph of the scala tympani. It receives some cerebrospinal through the cochlear canaliculus, which carries it from the subarachnoid spaces. Its dominant ion concentration is that of sodium."}, {"name": "Function", "text": "The perilymph is located between the bony labyrinth and the cochlear duct. It serves as a medium to transmit vibrations from the tympanic membrane (via the ossicles) to the endolymph in the cochlear duct, thus stimulating the spiral organ (of Corti). It also receives effluxing potassium released by the depolarization of the stereocilia.

The perilymph plays an important role in the sensory cell depolarization, as it receives the efflux of potassium from calcium-dependent channels in the stereocilia hair cells. It also contributes to the influx of calcium through specific channels located on the side and basal aspects of the hair cells."}, {"name": "References", "text": "Dorland, W. (2011) Dorland's Illustrated Medical Dictionary. 32nd edn. Philadelphia, USA: Elsevier Saunders.

Standring, S. (2016) Gray's Anatomy: The Anatomical Basis of Clinical Practice., 41st edition. Elsevier Limited."}]

items.name: Interlobular Bile Duct
items.info:
[{"name": "Quick Facts", "text": "The interlobular bile ducts are small ducts between the hepatic lobules, draining from the biliary ductules (Dorland, 2011)."}, {"name": "Structure/Morphology", "text": "The biliary system, or biliary tree, is an extensive system of channels that get larger as they move from the hepatic lobules to the gallbladder. In fact, the biliary tree makes up over 2km of channels of varying degree of width (Pawlina, 2016). These channels allow for the passage of bile produced in the liver by passive and active flow in response to hormonal and neural stimuli.

The biliary tree is lined with specialized epithelium called cholangiocytes. They are similar to hepatocytes in that they have microvilli that project into the lumen of the bile ducts Additionally, cholangiocytes possess a primary cilium that can detect bile flow.

The bile canaliculi are the smallest channels of the biliary tree, measuring approximately 0.5 μm in diameter (Pawlina, 2016). Unlike other parts of the biliary tree, the bile canaliculi are not lined with cholangiocytes. Instead, they are formed by localized intercellular spaces between two adjacent hepatocytes. The apical, or lateral, faces of adjacent hepatocytes are joined together via gap junctions and desmosomes. Bile is secreted from the apical faces of the hepatocytes into the bile canaliculi via membrane bound exocytotic vesicles. The tight junctions surrounding the canaliculi prevents bile from entering the sinusoids, thus creating a blood-bile barrier.

Near the periphery of the hepatic lobule, the bile canaliculi transform into canals of Hering, which are composed of hepatocytes with interspersed cuboidal cholangiocytes. Additionally, hepatic stem cells are located in the canals of Hering, which provides regenerative cells for the liver. 

The canals of Hering deliver bile to the slightly larger (1-1.5 μm diameter) intralobular bile ductules, which are lined entirely by cholangiocytes. These ductules deliver bile into the larger interlobular bile ducts, found within the portal triad.

The interlobular bile ducts are 15-40 μm in diameter and are lined by simple cuboidal cholangiocytes (Pawlina, 2016). As the ducts get larger and move towards the porta hepatis, the cells become more columnar. Additionally, the ducts acquire a dense connective tissue coat that contains elastic fibers and smooth muscle cells. Blood supply to the interlobular bile ducts occurs via the peribiliary plexus, formed by capillaries arising from the interlobular arteries (Krstic, 2013).

The interlobular ducts anastomose into progressively larger ducts to eventually form the common hepatic duct (Krstic, 2013). The cystic duct connects the common hepatic duct to the gallbladder, such that bile can flow into and out of the gallbladder via the cystic duct. Distal to this the duct becomes the common bile duct. This duct transports bile to the duodenum."}, {"name": "Anatomical Relations", "text": "The interlobular bile ducts accompany the interlobular arteries and interlobular veins. These vessels run parallel to each other in the portal tracts and form the portal triad. They are also associated with lymphatic vessels and nerves."}, {"name": "Function", "text": "The interlobular bile ducts receive bile, secreted by the hepatocytes, from the bile canaliculi in the parenchyma of the hepatic lobule. The flow of bile is opposite to the sinusoidal blood flow. The interlobular bile ducts transfer bile to the common hepatic duct and then on to the common bile duct, which secretes bile into the second part of the duodenum, in conjunction with pancreatic secretions, to facilitate the emulsification of fats and absorption of vitamin K. Alternatively, the common hepatic duct may transport bile to the cystic duct, which funnels bile into the gallbladder for bile concentration and storage."}, {"name": "List of Clinical Correlates", "text": "- Primary biliary cholangitis

- Intrahepatic cholestasis"}, {"name": "References", "text": "Dorland, W. (2011) Dorland's Illustrated Medical Dictionary. 32nd edn. Philadelphia, USA: Elsevier Saunders.

Krstic, R. V. (2013) Human Microscopic Anatomy: An Atlas for Students of Medicine and Biology. Springer Berlin Heidelberg.

Pawlina, W. 2016. Histology: A text and atlas with correlated cell and molecular biology. 7th ed. Philadelphia: Wolters Kluwer."}]

items.name: Efferent Lymphatic Vessel
items.info:
[{"name": "Quick Facts", "text": "The efferent lymphatic vessel conveys lymph away from the lymph node."}, {"name": "Structure/Morphology", "text": "The lymphatic vessels form a secondary circulation system in the human body, the lymphatic circulation. The vessels form a drainage system, running parallel with veins. Efferent lymphatic vessels are much larger than their afferent counterparts with a diameter as large as 1–2 mm (usually in the lower extremities) (Margaris and Black, 2012).

Efferent lymphatic vessels are composed of an internal monolayer of endothelium, surrounded by several layers of smooth muscle, supported by a continuous basal lamina. Each efferent vessel contains valves, which prevent the retrograde flow or backflow of lymph within the vessel. These are bi-leaflet valves composed of a thin layer of collagen between two layers of endothelial cells. 

A lymphangion is a section of an efferent lymph vessel contained between two sets of valves. It is the lymphangions that give the beaded appearance to efferent lymphatic vessels due to the increased diameter of the vessel between valves. Lymphangions have both sympathetic and parasympathetic innervation, therefore, by innervating the smooth muscle cells in the wall of the vessel, they are capable of producing rhythmic contractions. This rhythmic contraction helps the return of lymph back to the venous system, and also aided by external movements, such as muscle movements and movements from the arteries and veins. This collectively is known as lymph propulsion (Margaris and Black, 2012)."}, {"name": "Function", "text": "Efferent lymphatic vessels convey lymph from the lymph node to larger lymph vessels and ducts. These large ducts drain lymph directly into the venous system. Lymphatic vessels also play an important role in homeostasis of extracellular fluid as they drain tissue, or interstitial, fluid (Benias et al., 2018). On average, 8–12 liters of afferent lymph is produced daily, of which 4–8 L is reabsorbed into the blood in the lymph node. The remaining 4 L is transported in efferent lymphatic vessels back to the venous system directly. Accumulation of fluid results in edema of the affected area (Rovenska and Rovensky, 2011)."}, {"name": "References", "text": "Benias, P. C., Wells, R. G., Sackey-Aboagye, B., Klavan, H., Reidy, J., Buonocore, D., Miranda, M., Kornacki, S., Wayne, M., Carr-Locke, D. L. and Theise, N. D. (2018) 'Structure and Distribution of an Unrecognized Interstitium in Human Tissues', Scientific Reports, 8(1), pp. 4947.

Margaris, K. N. and Black, R. A. (2012) 'Modelling the lymphatic system: challenges and opportunities', J R Soc Interface, 9(69), pp. 601-12.

Rovenska, E. and Rovensky, J. (2011) 'Lymphatic vessels: structure and function', The Israel Medical Association Journal, 11, pp. 762-768."}]

items.name: Sebum
items.info:
[{"name": "Quick Facts", "text": "Sebum is the secretion of the sebaceous glands, a thick, semifluid substance composed of fat and epithelial debris from the cells of the malpighian layer (Dorland, 2011)."}, {"name": "Structure/Morphology", "text": "Sebum is the oily lipid substance produced by the sebaceous glands of the hair follicle. Sebum is primarily composed of a combination of proteins, cholesterol, and triacylglycerides, among other substances. Sebum is excreted from the sebaceous glands through holocrine secretion, a process in which the glandular cells burst in order to release the secretory products. This results in the sebum containing cellular components among the secretory products. The contraction of the arrector pili muscle will force the sebum through the gland opening into the hair follicle and subsequently onto the skin surface (VanPutte et al., 2015, Picardo et al., 2009)."}, {"name": "Function", "text": "The sebum functions as a lubricant for the hair and the exposed surface of the skin, protecting the keratin of the hair and the skin by preventing drying of the tissues. In addition, sebum contributes to antimicrobial activity and photo protection of the skin (Picardo et al., 2009)."}, {"name": "References", "text": "Dorland, W. (2011) Dorland's Illustrated Medical Dictionary. 32nd edn. Philadelphia, USA: Elsevier Saunders.

Picardo, M., Ottaviani, M., Camera, E. and Mastrofrancesco, A. (2009) 'Sebaceous gland lipids', Dermato-endocrinology, 1(2), pp. 68-71.

VanPutte, C. L., Regan, J. L. and Russo, A. F. (2015) Seeley's Essentials of Anatomy and Physiology. McGraw-Hill Education."}]

items.name: Distal Convoluted Tubule
items.info:
[{"name": "Quick Facts", "text": "The distal convoluted tubule is a distal, convoluted part of the renal tubule, extending from the distal straight tubule to the connecting tubule (Dorland, 2011)."}, {"name": "Structure and/or Key Features", "text": "The distal convoluted tubule is considered the final segment of the renal tubule. Measuring approximately 30–50 µm in diameter, the distal convoluted tubule is characterized by a lower height cuboidal epithelium, no brush border of microvilli, and a generally wider lumen (Kerr, 2007). 

The point where the distal convoluted tubule continues on from the distal straight tubule, or thick ascending limb, is demarcated by a region of narrowed, clustered cells, known as the macula densa."}, {"name": "Anatomical Relations", "text": "Along the renal tubule, the distal convoluted tubule succeeds the thick ascending limb and macula densa."}, {"name": "Function", "text": "The distal convoluted tubule is responsible for the selective reabsorption of ions, such as Na+ and Ca2+, and water from the tubular fluid. Na+ is transported through Na+/K+ ATPase pumps. Na+ reabsorption along the distal convoluted tubule is mediated by the hormone aldosterone, which increases the number of Na+/K+ ATPase pumps. K+, on the other hand, is secreted along the distal convoluted tubule (Pocock et al, 2013). 

The distal convoluted tubule regulates pH by absorbing and secreting both bicarbonate and protons (H+) along its length. It is also responsible for the secretion of acids, ammonia, drugs, and toxins (Martini et al, 2017; Pocock et al, 2013)."}, {"name": "List of Clinical Correlates", "text": "—Gitelman syndrome 

—Gordon syndrome"}, {"name": "References", "text": "Dorland, W. (2011) Dorland's Illustrated Medical Dictionary. 32nd edn. Philadelphia, USA: Elsevier Saunders.

Kerr, J. B. (2007) Atlas of Functional HistologyElsevier Science Health Science Division.

Martini, F. H., Nath, J. L. & Bartholomew, E. F. (2017) Fundamentals of Anatomy & PhysiologyPearson Education.

Pocock, G., Richards, C. D. & Richards, D. A. (2013) Human Physiology, 4 edition. OUP Oxford."}]

items.name: Nerves of Tendon
items.info:
[{"name": "Quick Facts", "text": "A nerve is a cordlike structure made up of a collection of fibers that convey impulses between a part of the central nervous system and some other region of the body (Dorland, 2011)."}, {"name": "Structure and/or Key Feature(s)", "text": "The innervation of tendons is mainly afferent and sensory, and these are provided by sensory nerves overlying the tendon, as well as by deep nerves in close proximity with the tendon. The afferent receptors are situated close to the musculotendinous junction. The nerves gain access to the tendon via the endotendon or the mesotendon. The nerves also give off branches which travel to interior aspect of the tendon from the peritendon, via the endotendon (Standring, 2016).

The innervation of the biceps femoris tendon is made possible by the nerves coming from the biceps femoris muscle and those that run in the peritendinous sheaths."}, {"name": "Anatomical Relations", "text": "The nerve supply to tendons is predominantly afferent in nature, and these afferent receptors are situated close to the musculotendinous junction. They penetrate the tendon via the endotendon or the mesotendon. The nerves also give off branches which travel to interior aspect of the tendon from the peritendon via the endotendon (Standring, 2016)."}, {"name": "Function", "text": "The innervation of tendons plays a key role in the occurrence of tendon reflexes. These reflexes can safeguard the muscles and bones from injury (Strandring, 2016)."}, {"name": "References", "text": "Dorland, W. (2011) Dorland's Illustrated Medical Dictionary. 32nd edn. Philadelphia, USA: Elsevier Saunders.

Standring, S. (2016) Gray's Anatomy: The Anatomical Basis of Clinical Practice. Gray's Anatomy Series 41 edn.: Elsevier Limited."}]

items.name: Intrarenal Blood Vessels
items.info:
[{"name": "Quick Facts", "text": "The intrarenal blood vessels are the vessels within the kidney."}, {"name": "Structure and/or Key Features", "text": "Renal arteries are responsible for the delivery of oxygenated blood to the kidneys. Before entering the kidney at the hilum, the renal artery divides and branches into five segmental arteries. The arterial tree of the kidney in descending order consists of segmental arteries, lobar arteries, interlobar arteries, arcuate arteries, interlobular arteries, afferent glomerular arterioles, and finally, within the structure of the nephron, glomerular capillaries (or the glomerulus).

Blood from the glomerulus drains into efferent glomerular arterioles. Thereafter, the efferent glomerular arterioles give rise to straight arterioles or peritubular capillaries. These are drained by the interlobular veins. 

Arcuate veins drain into interlobar veins, which subsequently drain into a large vein that emerges at the hilum of the kidney, known as the renal vein."}, {"name": "Function", "text": "Intrarenal blood vessels are collectively responsible for the transport of blood around the kidney parenchyma and for the delivery of blood to the functional units of the kidney, known as nephrons, for filtration."}, {"name": "List of Clinical Correlates", "text": "—Atheroembolic renal disease

—Intrarenal aneurysms

—Vasculitis"}]

items.name: Gastrointestinal Stem Cell (Jejunum)
items.info: [{"name": "Quick Facts", "text": "Stem cells are undifferentiated cells with the ability to divide and proliferate to provide precursor cells that can differentiate into specialized cells (Dorland, 2011)."}, {"name": "Structure/Morphology", "text": "Stem cells occupy much of the basal regions of the intestinal glands. This population of cells is referred to as the amplifying compartment as these cells are actively undergoing mitosis and will differentiate into absorptive cells or goblet cells as they migrate up the epithelium to the surfaces of the villi and replace epithelial cells as they are \u201csloughed off\u201d the surface during normal intestinal mobility."}, {"name": "Key Features/Anatomical Relations", "text": "Stem cells occupy much of the basal regions of the intestinal glands."}, {"name": "Function", "text": "This population of cells will differentiate into absorptive cells or goblet cells as they migrate up the epithelium to the surfaces of the villi."}, {"name": "References", "text": "Dorland, W. (2011) Dorland's Illustrated Medical Dictionary. 32nd edn. Philadelphia, USA: Elsevier Saunders."}]

items.name: Astrocytes
items.info:
[{"name": "Quick Facts", "text": "An astrocyte is a neuroglial cell of ectodermal origin, characterized by fibrous, protoplasmic, or plasmatofibrous processes (Dorland, 2011)."}, {"name": "Structure and/or Key Features", "text": "Astrocytes are the largest cells of the neuroglia. There are both fibrous astrocytes or protoplasmic astrocytes.

Protoplasmic astrocytes are more prevalent in the gray matter. They possess numerous, branching, cytoplasmic processes. These processes expand to form foot-like processes that cover large areas of blood vessels as well as the “bare areas” or axolemma of myelinated axons e.g., at the nodes of Ranvier. They also extend their processes to the basal lamina of the pia mater to form the glia limitans, an impermeable barrier surrounding the central nervous system (CNS).

Fibrous astrocytes possess fewer processes, have small cell bodies, and are relatively straight. They are more prevalent in the white matter. 

Both fibrous and protoplasmic astrocytes contain intermediate filaments made of glial fibrillary acidic protein (GFAP) to reinforce the cell structure. These prominent bundles of intermediate filaments are more numerous in fibrous astrocytes. Antibodies to GFAP can be used as the basis for specific staining to identify astrocytes in histological sections and in tissue cultures (Ross and Pawlina, 2006)."}, {"name": "Anatomical Relations", "text": "Fibrous astrocytes are more prevalent in the white matter, while protoplasmic astrocytes are more prevalent in the gray matter. 

Almost all of the basement membrane surface area of the microvasculature of the CNS is covered by astrocyte foot-like processes. Astrocytes directly communicate functionally with each other via gap junctions (Ross and Pawlina, 2006)."}, {"name": "Function", "text": "Astrocytes have multiple functions. 

—Astrocytes provide physical and metabolic support to neurons of the CNS by being involved in the movement of metabolites and wastes away from neurons. Astrocytes buffer the concentration of potassium ions in the extracellular space of the brain and so may have an important function during rapid firing of a neuron (Splittgerber, 2018). 

—Astrocytes confine neurotransmitters at the synapse and so act as electrical insulators that prevent axon terminals from influencing neighboring neurons. They also increase the rate of neurotransmitter uptake in regions where neuronal activity is high (Marieb, Wilhelm and Mallatt, 2012). 

—Astrocytes remove excess neurotransmitters by pinocytosis (Ross and Pawlina, 2006).

—Astrocytes regulate blood flow through capillaries in active regions of the brain (Marieb, Wilhelm and Mallatt, 2012).

—They are able to control the diameter of the vessels they contact by secreting specific molecules which trigger either vasodilation or vasoconstriction (Standring, 2016).

—Astrocytes assist in the formation of synapses in developing neural tissue and produce molecules, including the brain growth derived factor, which are necessary for the growth of neurons (Marieb, Wilhelm and Mallatt, 2012).

—They store glycogen which can be broken down into glucose and lactate and provided to nearby neurons in response to norepinephrine/noradrenaline. 

—They may be phagocytic, engulfing degenerated synaptic terminals and secrete cytokines which may regulate the activity of immune cells entering the CNS (Splittgerber, 2018).

—Astrocytes propagate calcium signals that may be involved with memory (Marieb, Wilhelm and Mallatt, 2012).

—Astrocytes assist to maintain tight junctions that join the capillaries of the blood-brain-barrier. Astrocytes cover the nodes of Ranvier and synapses where myelin sheath is absent. They also extend their processes to the pia mater, thus forming the glia limitans, an impermeable barrier surrounding the central nervous system (Ross and Pawlina, 2006)."}, {"name": "Clinical Correlates", "text": "Up to 40–50% of all intracranial tumors are gliomas. The most common are tumors (fibrous astrocytomas and glioblastomas) that arise from astrocytes. 

Following neuronal death after disease, astrocytes proliferate and fill the space once occupied by the neurons, a process known as “Replacement gliosis” (Splittgerber, 2018)."}, {"name": "References", "text": "Dorland, W. (2011) Dorland's Illustrated Medical Dictionary. 32nd edn. Philadelphia, USA: Elsevier Saunders.

Marieb, E. N., Wilhelm, P. B. and Mallatt, J. (2012) Human Anatomy. fifth edn.: Benjamin Cummings.

Ross, M. H. and Pawlina, W. (2006) Histology: A text and atlas. Lippincott Williams & Wilkins.

Splittgerber, R. (2018) Snell's Clinical Neuroanatomy. Wolters Kluwer Health.

Standring, S. (2016) Gray's Anatomy: The Anatomical Basis of Clinical Practice. Gray's Anatomy Series 41 edn.: Elsevier Limited."}]
