items.name: Pancreatic Acinus (Inferior)
items.info:
[{"name": "Quick Facts", "text": "The pancreatic acinus is one of the secretory units of the exocrine pancreas, where pancreatic juice is produced (Dorland, 2011)."}, {"name": "Structure and/or Key Feature(s)", "text": "The exocrine cells of the pancreas (pancreatic acinar cells or serous secretory cells) are simple, pyramidal in shape. They form clusters or secretory units called acini, due to their acinar or tubuloacinar shape. Acini are supported by a basal lamina and very fine reticular fibers surround the acini.

The exocrine cells of the pancreas contain numerous zymogen granules in their apical cytoplasm which imparts an eosinophilia to the apical region compared to a more basophilic basal region due to the presence of free ribosomes and rough endoplasmic reticulum.

A unique feature of the pancreatic acinus is that centroacinar cells are located within the acinus and form the initial segment of the intercalated duct system (Ross and Pawlina, 2016)."}, {"name": "Function", "text": "Zymogen granules contain (inactive) precursors of digestive enzymes that can digest most food substances."}, {"name": "References", "text": "Dorland, W. (2011) Dorland's Illustrated Medical Dictionary. 32nd edn. Philadelphia, USA: Elsevier Saunders.

Ross, M. H. and Pawlina, W. (2016) Histology: A Text and Atlas. Wolters Kluwer Health."}]

items.name: Cranial Dura Mater
items.info:
[{"name": "Quick Facts", "text": "The cranial dura mater is the dura mater covering the brain, composed of two mostly fused layers: an outer periosteal layer (endocranium) adherent to the inner aspect of the cranial bones, analogous to the periosteum of the bony skeleton, and an inner meningeal layer. Venous sinuses and the trigeminal ganglion are located between the layers (Dorland, 2011)."}, {"name": "Structure", "text": "The cranial dura mater is the most superficial of the three meningeal layers and covers the entire brain down to the foramen magnum, where it’s continuous with spinal dura mater. Cranial dura mater is a tough, fibrous, two-layer structure with the outer or periosteal dura forming the periosteum of the cranial bones and the inner meningeal dura lying against the underlying arachnoid mater. For the most part these two dural layers are adhered, but they can be independently visualized at some dural sinuses where the venous cavity separates the periosteal and meningeal dural layers. The periosteal dura is pierced by emissary veins, which bring blood from the overlying bone. The meningeal dura is pierced by cerebral vessels, carrying blood collected in the brain tissue and arachnoid granulations, which bring cerebrospinal fluid to venous sinuses."}, {"name": "Key Features/Anatomical Relations", "text": "The anterior, middle, and posterior meningeal arteries carry blood to the dura and overlying bone. The trigeminal and vagus nerves provide innervation to the vast bulk of the dura, with first to third cervical nerves innervating the dura mater near the foramen magnum."}, {"name": "List of Clinical Correlates", "text": "—Epidural hematoma

—Subdural hematoma

—Headache"}, {"name": "References", "text": "Dorland, W. (2011) Dorland's Illustrated Medical Dictionary. 32nd edn. Philadelphia, USA: Elsevier Saunders."}]

items.name: Artery
items.info:
[
  {
    "name" : "Quick Facts",
    "text" : "An artery is a vessel through which the blood passes away from the heart to the various parts of the body. The wall of an artery consists typically of an outer coat (tunica externa), a middle coat (tunica media), and an inner coat (tunica intima) (Dorland, 2011)."
  },
  {
    "name" : "Structure",
    "text" : "Arteries are types of blood vessels that carry blood away from the heart. They are characterized by their thick walls that can withstand the high blood pressure forces created by the heart. Arteries are classified into three types:
•	elastic (large or conducting) arteries
•	muscular (medium or distributing) arteries
•	arterioles (or small arteries).

The walls of arteries consist of three main layers:
•	the inner layer, the tunica interna (or intima)
•	the middle layer, the tunica media
•	the outer layer, the tunica externa (or adventitia).

The three layers of the arterial wall vary in composition. 
•	The tunica interna is composed of a single layer of compacted endothelial cells, known as the endothelium. The endothelium is one cell thick and lines the lumen. The tunica interna is enclosed by the basement membrane which is made of loose connective tissue to provide support to the endothelium. The tunica interna also consists of an outer subendothelial layer of connective tissue. A fenestrated layer of elastic tissue, the internal elastic lamina, separates the tunica interna from the tunica media. 
•	The tunica media is the thickest layer of arteries and consists mainly of smooth muscle that controls the diameter of the lumen to regulate blood flow and blood pressure. Separating the tunica media from the tunica externa is a layer of elastic tissue called the external elastic lamina. 
•	The tunica externa encapsulates the vessel in the surrounding tissue. This layer consists of connective tissue with varying amounts of elastic and collagenous fibers.

The lumen of an artery (the central hollow region of a blood vessel through which blood flows) is smaller than that of a vein of comparable size. It is this smaller lumen that enables arteries to ensure the pressure needed to maintain blood flow is constant. The thick walls of arteries and the smaller diameter lumens mean arteries have a round appearance in cross section compared to veins.
"
  },
  {
    "name" : "Function",
    "text" : "Arteries carry blood away from the heart and to all body organs and tissues. Their thick muscular walls facilitate this function, enabling blood to be pumped under high pressure around the body. Blood that is transported through arteries is typically oxygen-rich, with the exception of the pulmonary arteries, which carry deoxygenated blood from the heart to the lungs. 

Another function of arteries is the regulation of systemic blood flow. Through vasodilation and vasoconstriction, an arteries’ lumen can be increased or decreased in diameter, respectively. This change in the lumen allows greater or lesser blood flow through the vessel. 

Arteries play an important role in the transport of vital molecules around the body. These molecules include dissolved gases, metabolic waste, nutrients, cells of the immune system and hormones.

"
  },

items.info: [{"name": "Quick Facts", "text": "The articular plate, basal plate, and the striated columns are referred to as the connecting piece between the sperm head and tail."}, {"name": "Structure and/or Key Feature(s)", "text": "The basal plate is an electron dense structure located at the interface between the head and the neck of the sperm. It is attached to the outer membrane of the nuclear envelope. The basal plate is concave in shape and is adjacent to the convex surface of the articular plate. Together, these two structures act like a ball and socket joint."}, {"name": "Function", "text": "Collectively, the articular plate, basal plate, and the striated columns are referred to as the \u2018connecting piece\u2019 between the sperm head and tail. The basal plate allows for the articulation between the head and the neck of the sperm."}]

items.name: Ascending Limb of Nephron Loop
alt: Ascending Limb of Loop of Henle
items.info:
[{"name": "Quick Facts", "text": "The ascending limb is the distal part of the loop of Henle (Dorland, 2011)."}, {"name": "Structure and/or Key Features", "text": "The nephron loop, more widely known as the loop of Henle, describes the recognizable loop that characterizes the nephron. Its length may measure up to 30 mm in juxtamedullary nephrons (Martini, Nath and Bartholomew, 2017).

The nephron loop is comprised of the proximal straight tubule (or thick descending limb), a thin descending limb, a thin ascending limb, and a distal straight tubule (or thick ascending limb).

The ascending limb of the nephron loop arises as the descending thin limb turns back or “loops” back on itself. Measuring approximately 15 µm in diameter, the epithelium of the ascending thin limb is described as simple squamous, continuous with that of the descending thin limb (Kerr, 2007). 

The distal straight tubule, or thick ascending limb, is a continuation of the ascending thin limb of the nephron loop. Measuring approximately 30 µm in diameter, the thick ascending limb has a simple cuboidal epithelium with a brush border (Martini, Nath and Bartholomew, 2017; Kerr, 2007).

The nephron loop is supplied by a series of straight arterioles that branch from the cortical efferent arterioles; these capillaries are known as the vasa recta."}, {"name": "Anatomical Relations", "text": "The thin ascending limb of the nephron loop is located distal to the thin descending limb and proximal to the thick ascending limb. The thick ascending limb, or distal straight tubule is continuous with the distal convoluted tubule. Their point of union is demarcated by a region of narrowed, clustered cells known as the macula densa.

The ascending limb of the nephron loop of juxtamedullary nephrons travels in an upward trajectory through the inner and outer renal medulla."}, {"name": "Function", "text": "The thin ascending limb of the nephron loop is responsible for sodium chloride reabsorption. Sodium is primarily reabsorbed through passive diffusion, while chloride is reabsorbed across chloride channels (Kondo, 1997). As salt (sodium chloride) moves out of the tubules, the osmolarity of the renal filtrate decreases slightly, however, most equilibration of tubular filtrate with the interstitium occurs in the ascending thick limb (Pocock, Richards and Richards, 2013). 

The thick ascending limb, or distal straight limb, is responsible for the reabsorption of ions, mainly Na+ (25–30% of total Na+ reabsorption), K+, and Cl- via active transport. Mg+ and Ca2+ are also reabsorbed here. The primary pumps involved in this reabsorption are the Na+/K+ ATPase, Na+/K+/Cl- cotransporter and the NKCC2 transporter. The thick ascending limb is completely impermeable to water. 

As a result of the ion reabsorption, the urinary filtrate that reaches the distal convoluted tubule is hypotonic, while the medullary environment becomes more hyperosmotic."}, {"name": "List of Clinical Correlates", "text": "—Bartter syndrome"}, {"name": "References", "text": "Dorland, W. (2011) Dorland's Illustrated Medical Dictionary. 32nd edn. Philadelphia, USA: Elsevier Saunders.

Kerr, J. B. (2007) Atlas of Functional HistologyElsevier Science Health Science Division.

Kondo, Y. (1997) Mechanism of sodium chloride reabsorption in the ascending thin limb of Henle's loop. Clinical and Experimental Nephrology, 1(2), 67-75.

Martini, F. H., Nath, J. L. & Bartholomew, E. F. (2017) Fundamentals of Anatomy & PhysiologyPearson Education.

Pocock, G., Richards, C. D. & Richards, D. A. (2013) Human Physiology, 4 edition. OUP Oxford."}]

items.name: Spiral Network of Smooth Muscle Cells
items.audio: Spiral Network of Smooth Muscle Cells.mp3
items.info:
[{"name": "Quick Facts", "text": "Smooth muscle in the walls of the bronchioles wrap around in opposite directions ensuring it can constrict and shorten the bronchioles."}, {"name": "Structure/Morphology", "text": "The smooth muscle layer of the bronchioles is comprised of two sets of fibers, which geodesically wrap around the bronchioles in opposing directions. This ensures that when the smooth muscle contracts, it can both constrict and shorten the bronchioles. This muscular layer is found along the entire intrapulmonary bronchial tree, terminating at the microscopic alveoli (Ovalle et al., 2013). 

The smooth muscle tone is controlled by parasympathetic innervation and is the primary bronchoconstrictor to the bronchiolar tracts. Sympathetic innervation is responsible for bronchodilation, or relaxation of the smooth muscle (Standring, 2016)."}, {"name": "Function", "text": "The smooth muscle is responsible for airway caliber, which is important in maintaining alveolar ventilation and vascular exchange units of the peripheral lung. Dysfunction in the smooth muscle control may contribute to the pathogenesis of disease."}, {"name": "References", "text": "Ovalle, W. K., Nahirney, P. C. and Netter, F. H. (2013) Netter's Essential Histology. ClinicalKey 2012: Elsevier Saunders.

Standring, S. (2016) Gray's Anatomy: The Anatomical Basis of Clinical Practice. Gray's Anatomy Series: Elsevier Limited."}]

items.name: Superior Sagittal Sinus
items.info:
[{"name": "Quick Facts", "text": "Origin: Formed by union of tiny meningeal veins at the crista galli.

Course: Runs backwards within the attached upper margin of the falx cerebrum, from crista galli (anteriorly) to the confluence of sinuses (posteriorly).

Tributaries: Communications with the veins of the frontal sinus, veins of the nose (via foramen cecum), the superior cerebral veins, parietal emissary veins, and venous lacunae. 

Drainage: Anterior cerebral hemispheres."}, {"name": "Origin", "text": "The superior sagittal sinus begins at the crista galli, formed by the union of small meningeal veins."}, {"name": "Course", "text": "The superior sagittal sinus lies within the upper fixed convex margin of the falx cerebrum. It courses in the midline in a shallow groove on the inner aspect of the cranium and grows in caliber as it continues posteriorly. The sinus extends backwards from the crista galli to the confluence of sinuses where it usually turns to the right side to become continuous with the right transverse sinus (Pamir, Black and Fahlbusch, 2010)."}, {"name": "Tributaries", "text": "The superior sagittal sinus communicates anteriorly at the crista galli with the veins of the frontal sinus and nose (via foramen cecum). The sinus has additional connections with the superior cerebral veins, parietal emissary veins, and venous lacunae."}, {"name": "Structures Drained", "text": "Lying along the sagittal groove, the superior sagittal sinus drains lateral aspects of the anterior cerebrum into the confluence of the sinuses."}, {"name": "List of Clinical Correlates", "text": "—Superior sagittal sinus thrombosis"}, {"name": "References", "text": "Pamir, M. N., Black, P. M. and Fahlbusch, R. (2010) Meningiomas E-Book: Expert Consult - Online and Print. Elsevier Health Sciences."}]

items.name: Lumen (of Convoluted Seminiferous Tubules)
items.info: [{"name": "Quick Facts", "text": "A lumen is the cavity or channel within a tube or tubular organ (Dorland, 2011)."}, {"name": "Structure/Morphology", "text": "The seminiferous epithelium, containing cells undergoing spermatogenesis and supporting sustentocytes (Sertoli cells), form the wall of the seminiferous tubule. The lumen of the seminiferous tubules contains spermatozoa within a fluid medium. These spermatozoa are released from the tubule walls after a rather complex process called spermiation. Spermatozoa become free from the Sertoli cells following the removal of junctional complexes between them and the Sertoli cell."}, {"name": "Function", "text": "The tubule lumen is the space for spermatozoa to move along to the intratesticular ducts and the excurrent duct system."}, {"name": "References", "text": "Dorland, W. (2011) Dorland's Illustrated Medical Dictionary. 32nd edn. Philadelphia, USA: Elsevier Saunders."}]

items.name: Nucleus of Lens
Retinal Layers
items.info:
[{"name": "Quick Facts", "text": "The retina is the innermost of the three tunics of the eyeball, surrounding the vitreous body and continuous posteriorly with the optic nerve. It is divided into the pars optica, which rests upon the choroid, the pars ciliaris, which rests upon the ciliary body, and the pars iridica, which rests upon the posterior surface of the iris. The pars optica is subdivided into an outer, pigmented layer and an inner, transparent or neural layer. The neural layer contains rods, cones, and neurons, and is divided into nine layers. The layer of rods and cones is the percipient part of the retina, responding to visual stimuli by a photochemical reaction. The inner nuclear layer contains retinal ganglion cells whose axons join to form the optic nerve. In the center of the posterior part of the retina is the macula lutea, the most sensitive portion of the retina, with the fovea centralis at its center. About 0.25 cm medial to the fovea is the point of entrance of the optic nerve and the central artery of the retina; at this point the retina is incomplete and forms the blind spot (Dorland, 2011)."}, {"name": "Structure and/or Key Feature(s)", "text": "The retina is the innermost, light-sensitive layer of the human eye. It lines the inner posterior surface of the eyeball and is positioned between the choroid and vitreous body. 

Histologically, the retina contains distinct layers of a variety of cells, epithelial, neural, and glial, and their processes. The outermost layer, known as the pigmented layer, is composed of a simple layer of cuboidal pigment cells, or retinal pigment epithelium (RPE). It is separated for the other, internal layers of cells, collectively known as the neural layer or neural retina, by a potential space. The neural layer (starting with the outermost layer) includes: 

- the layer of inner and outer segments (or layer of rods and cones);

- the outer limiting layer (or membrane);

- the outer nuclear layer (ONL), a layer of rod and cone cell bodies;

- the outer plexiform layer (OPL), a synaptic layer;

- the inner nuclear layer (INL), another layer of cell bodies;

- the inner plexiform layer (IPL), another synaptic layer; 

- the ganglionic layer;

- the layer of nerve fibers;

- and the inner limiting layer (or membrane) (Standring, 2016). 

Note that this classic layered arrangement of the retina is absent at the optic nerve head where the axons of the retinal ganglion cells leave the retina to form the optic nerve and all other cell types of the retina are missing. Additionally, various layers are absent or greatly diminished at the fovea and foveola, and along the ora serrata. At the fovea all layers internal to the photoreceptors, i.e., internal to the outer nuclear layer, are moved aside offering direct access of light to the photoreceptors. Surrounding the fovea, the foveola, the layers are distorted by the outward build-up of cells and processes of the OPL and other more internal layers caused by the formation of the fovea. Finally, at the ora serrata, where the retina borders the ciliary body the retinal pigment epithelium merges with the outer pigmented epithelium of the ciliary body, and the neural retina borders the unpigmented ciliary epithelium (Standring, 2016)."}, {"name": "Layer 1—Pigmented Layer ", "text": "The outermost layer of the retina is known as the retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) and lies between the choroid’s basal complex (Bruch’s membrane) and the layer of rod and cone outer segments. A potential space lies at the interface of the RPE with the photoreceptor outer segments, and this is the plane, when the space goes from potential to real, that retinal detachment commonly occurs. The RPE forms a continuous layer of simple cuboidal epithelial pigment cells. There are approximately 4–6 million pigment cells in the retina (Standring, 2016).

Pigment cells contain multiple organelles called melanosomes. Melanosomes are pigmented cytoplasmic granules that facilitate the synthesis, storage, and transportation of melanin, the common light-absorbing pigment in animals. Melanin facilitates the absorption of light in this outer layer of the retina so that it cannot be reflected back to the photoreceptors, through which it has already passed, and degrade an image (Wasmeier et al., 2008). 

Pigment cells possess actin-rich apical processes, or microvilli, that measure approximately 5–7 µm long. These microvilli interdigitate between the outer segments of the photoreceptors found in the superjacent layer (Wasmeier et al., 2008). These processes provide for the inclusion and phagocytosis of the membranes of photoreceptor outer segments that have been shed as the photopigment within them is used up by the light stimulated reaction that transduces light to a cellular membrane voltage change. The basal surface of the pigment cells contains invaginations that increase the surface area of the pigmented layer for the absorption of nutrients from the underlying choroid. The lateral membranes of the pigment cells are firmly connected by tight junctions, which collectively form the outer blood-retinal barrier (Boulton and Dayhaw-Barker, 2001)."}, {"name": "Layer 2—Layer of Inner and Outer Segments ", "text": "The layer of inner and outer segments (or layer of rods and cones) is just internal to the RPE. It contains radially oriented, densely folded and stacked membrane, the outer segments, connected by a fine cilium to a cellular region dense in mitochondria, the inner segment. The outer segment has one of two shapes, a pyramidal or cone shape and a columnar or rod shape and hence the names for the two distinct photoreceptor cells from which they arise. On average, the human retina contains 4.6 million cones and 92 million rods (Standring, 2016). The photoreceptors extend beyond the layer of rods and cones, whereby their cell bodies are housed in the outer nuclear layer, and their synaptic terminals extend as far as the outer plexiform layer. The portions of photoreceptor cells housed in the layer of rods and cones are the inner and outer segments, connected to each other by a thin cilium. 

Rods and cones are ultimately responsible for the conversion of light energy into a neural signal which can be transmitted through the retina. The layer of rods and cones are located in the deepest portion of the neural layer of the retina. Thus, light entering the eyeball must pass through all the layers of the retina before impinging on the site where light is received and transduced."}, {"name": "Layer 3—Outer Limiting Layer ", "text": "The inner processes of retinal radial glia, Müller glia, extend as far externally as the boundary between the inner segments of photoreceptors and forms an interdigitating network with them called the outer (or external) limiting layer of the retina. It is recognized as one of the ten retinal layers in the retina. In fact, it is not a true membrane as it is absent of any basement membrane or basal lamina. Instead, it is composed of a series of zonula adherens junctions between the photoreceptor inner segments and glial cells. Zonula adherens are described as a belt-like adherens junction, which encircles the cells near their apical surfaces (Standring, 2016; Pollard et al., 2017).

The outer limiting membrane plays an important role in the structural integrity and mechanical maintenance of the retina. It may also form part of the blood-retinal barrier, due to the presence of junction proteins and the fact that these proteins are disrupted under pathological conditions. The junctions that comprise this outer limiting membrane likely serve as an anchor for the photoreceptor cells and prevent leakage of the interphotoreceptor matrix (Standring, 2016; Omri et al., 2010)."}, {"name": "Layer 4—Outer Nuclear Layer ", "text": "The outer nuclear layer (ONL) contains the cell bodies, nuclei, and synaptic processes of the photoreceptors. It occupies the space between the outer limiting membrane and the outer plexiform layer. There is great topographic variation in the thickness of the outer nuclear layer reflecting differences in the density of rods and cones at the center (high density of cells, particularly cones) versus the periphery (low density, primarily rods) of the retina. The ONL is approximately four cells thick at the temporal edge, and 8–9 cells thick on the nasal edge, of the optic disc. It is thickest at the fovea, containing as many as 10 layers of exclusively cone nuclei at the fovea (Remington and Goodwin, 2011).

In a histological section, the outer nuclear layer is recognizable by the presence of darkly stained nuclei. Cone nuclei are oval-shaped and larger than rod nuclei. They contain less heterochromatin and stain lighter. The nuclei of cone cells tend to form a separate sublayer within the outer nuclear layer at its internal margin. It may be several cells thick to discontinuous. The nuclei of rod cells stain darker and are generally smaller and rounder. Rod nuclei form several stacked layers external to the cone nuclei (Standring, 2016)."}, {"name": "Layer 5—Outer Plexiform Layer ", "text": "The outer plexiform layer (OPL) is the external synaptic layer between neuron of the outer and inner nuclear layers. It contains a thick outer band of axonal processes from the photoreceptors and a much thinner inner band formed by processes of the neurons of the inner nuclear layer that receive synapses from the photoreceptors (Remington and Goodwin, 2011).

Postsynaptic processes are a key feature of the outer plexiform layer. They largely belong to bipolar and horizontal cells whose cell bodies resides in the inner nuclear layer. The synaptic terminals of the rods and cones receive three postsynaptic processes collectively known as a synaptic triad. The central process of the triad is a bipolar dendrite, while those flanking the triad are horizontal cell processes. Other synaptic contacts within the outer plexiform layers include those between bipolar dendrites and horizontal cells, between horizontal cells themselves, or between bipolar dendrites with photoreceptor cell endings proximal to their synaptic terminal. Electrical messages are also passed between cone cells, and from cone cells to rod cells, allowing some rod and cone signal mixing (Remington and Goodwin, 2011; Kolb, 1995b)."}, {"name": "Layer 6—Inner Nuclear Layer ", "text": "The inner nuclear layer (INL) is a cell body rich zone found between the outer and inner plexiform layers. The high density of cell bodies and their nuclei make the INL, like the ONL, distinguishable by the presence of many darkly stained nuclei. There are several types of cells in the INL that are loosely stratified into discontinuous sub-zones. Closest to the IPL are a class of neuronal interneuron called horizontal cells. Their cell bodies lie just internal to the OPL and it extends horizontal processes parallel to the plane of the OPL and extending into it. The spaces between horizontal cells and the zone internal to them contain bipolar cell bodies often stacked many times wide. The processes of bipolar cells are radially oriented making synaptic connection in the OPL and the inner plexiform layer. They provide for the transfer of information from the photoreceptor cells to the retinal ganglion cells. Intermixed with the innermost bipolar cells are a major class of retinal glia called Müller glia, the principal glial cells of the retina. These cells extend inner and outer radial processes that span most of the width of the retina. On the external side, these make tight junctions with themselves and intervening photoreceptor inner segments to form the outer limiting membrane, and on the internal side tight junctions between them forms the inner limiting membrane. The final class of cell in the INL tends to be located adjacent to the cell body sparse inner plexiform layer though they can be found throughout the INL. Another class of interneuron called amacrine cells, these have laterally extending processes that participate in synaptic interactions between bipolar cells and retinal ganglion cells."}, {"name": "Layer 7—Inner Plexiform Layer", "text": "The inner plexiform layer is the internal layer of neuronal synapses of the retina located between the inner nuclear and ganglion cell layers. It is the site of synapse between second and third-order neurons within the retina and numerous connections with interneurons. Chemical and electrical synapses are common and processes can typically be pre- and postsynaptic making the assignment of a structure as axonal or dendritic difficult. A key feature is the presence of the distal branches of radially orientated bipolar cells. They form synapses onto the dendrites of ganglion cells (Standring, 2016). Additionally, inner plexiform layer contains synaptic connections between amacrine and bipolar cells, amacrine and ganglion cells, and amacrine cells interconnecting with each other (Standring, 2016; Remington and Goodwin, 2011). Some reciprocal inhibitory synapses also occur in the inner plexiform layer, whereby amacrine processes make second contact with bipolar axons to provide negative feedback."}, {"name": "Layer 8—Ganglionic Layer ", "text": "The retinal ganglion cell layer contains the cell bodies of the retinal ganglion cells, the output cells of the retina and certain, displaced, amacrine cell bodies. Its thickness is dependent on position relative to the fovea and surrounding macula. At the center of the fovea, there are no ganglion cells as they, as well as the cells and processes of the IPL and INL, are swept aside to allow light direct access to the photoreceptors. They are piled up in the surrounding parafovea, up to 8–10 cells thick and gradually thin out so that they are no more than two cells thick on the temporal side of the optic nerve head. Over most of the retina, the ganglionic layer is formed of a discontinuous one cell thickness. Near the peripheral edge of the retina, as it approaches the ora serrata, the density of ganglion cell bodies is quite low.

Within the ganglion cell layer, the processes of the radial Müller glial cells surround, support, and separate ganglion cells from one another. Further, one of the primary retinal vascular plexuses, the superficial vascular plexus, is present in the ganglion cell layer (Campbell et al., 2017)."}, {"name": "Layer 9—Layer of Nerve Fibers ", "text": "The axons of retinal ganglion cells form a layer of nerve fibers just internal to the ganglion cell, between it and the vitreous body. These axons are unmyelinated but surrounded by the internal processes of radial glial cells and retinal astrocytes. The axons run parallel to the retinal surface, converging onto the optic disc. The nerve fiber layer is thinnest at the retinal periphery, the ora serrata. However, moving centrally it thickens from the addition of axons from the more central located retinal ganglion cells and is thickest at the optic disc margin. At the optic disc, the axons make a 90° turn into the optic nerve head. They exit the eyeball by passing through fenestrations in the sclera at a structure called the lamina cribrosa (Standring, 2016). The retinal ganglion cell axons form the optic nerve (Cranial Nerve II) and are responsible for transmitting sensory visual signals from the retina to the brain."}, {"name": "Layer 10—Inner Limiting Layer", "text": "The inner limiting membrane is the most vitreously positioned layer of the retina, lying just internal to the layer of nerve fibers. It is formed by the terminations of the internal processes of Müller glia that successively have passed through the inner part of the inner nuclear layer, the inner plexiform layer, the retinal ganglion cells layer, and the optic nerve fiber layer. It is while transiting the later that these processes contribute to “wrapping” the retinal ganglion cell axons. At the interface between the retina and the vitreous these processes flatten out and terminate in what is known as an “endfoot.” This makes the surface of the inner limiting membrane uneven, while the vitreal surface is smooth.

The inner limiting membrane of the retina is continuous at the periphery with that of the ciliary body. Along the margins of the optic disc it undergoes modification, with the Müller cell processes replaced by those of astrocytes (Remington and Goodwin, 2011). Unlike the outer limiting membrane, the inner limiting membrane is a true basement membrane of approximately 0.5-2 μm thickness in the posterior retina (Standring, 2016).

The inner limiting membrane is responsible for creating a boundary between the retina and the vitreous body. Furthermore, it acts as a diffusion barrier between the two structures (Kolb, 1995d)."}, {"name": "List of Clinical Correlates", "text": "- Retinal tear

- Retinal detachment 

- Diabetic retinopathy

- Epiretinal membrane

- Macular hole

- Macular degeneration

- Retinitis pigmentosa"}, {"name": "References", "text": "Boulton, M. and Dayhaw-Barker, P. (2001) 'The role of the retinal pigment epithelium: topographical variation and ageing changes', Eye (Lond), 15(Pt 3), pp. 384-9.

Campbell, J. P., Zhang, M., Hwang, T. S., Bailey, S. T., Wilson, D. J., Jia, Y. and Huang, D. (2017) 'Detailed Vascular Anatomy of the Human Retina by Projection-Resolved Optical Coherence Tomography Angiography', Sci Rep, 7, pp. 42201.

Dorland, W. (2011) Dorland's Illustrated Medical Dictionary. 32nd edn. Philadelphia, USA: Elsevier Saunders.

Kolb, H. (1995b) 'Outer Plexiform Layer', in Kolb, H., Fernandez, E. and Nelson, R. (eds.) Webvision: The Organization of the Retina and Visual System. Salt Lake City (UT): University of Utah Health Sciences Center.

Kolb, H. (1995d) 'Simple Anatomy of the Retina', in Kolb, H., Fernandez, E. and Nelson, R. (eds.) Webvision: The Organization of the Retina and Visual System. Salt Lake City (UT): University of Utah Health Sciences Center

Omri, S., Omri, B., Savoldelli, M., Jonet, L., Thillaye-Goldenberg, B., Thuret, G., Gain, P., Jeanny, J. C., Crisanti, P. and Behar-Cohen, F. (2010) 'The outer limiting membrane (OLM) revisited: clinical implications', Clin Ophthalmol, 4, pp. 183-95.

Pollard, T. D., Earnshaw, W. C., Lippincott-Schwartz, J. and Johnson, G. T. (2017) Cell Biology. Elsevier.

Remington, L. A. and Goodwin, D. (2011) Clinical Anatomy of the Visual System E-Book. Elsevier Health Sciences.

Standring, S. (2016) Gray's Anatomy: The Anatomical Basis of Clinical Practice. Gray's Anatomy Series 41 edn.: Elsevier Limited.

Wasmeier, C., Hume, A. N., Bolasco, G. and Seabra, M. C. (2008) 'Melanosomes at a glance', J Cell Sci, 121(Pt 24), pp. 3995-9."}]

items.name: Insertion of Splenius Colli Muscle
Extraglomerular Mesangial Cell
items.info: [{"name": "Quick Facts", "text": "Extraglomerular mesangial cells are lacelike cells in the pale-staining polkissen of the juxtaglomerular apparatus of the kidney; they have numerous processes to connect gap junctions and are thought to provide electrical coupling among themselves and to the mesangium and glomerular arterioles (Dorland, 2011)."}, {"name": "Structure and/or Key Feature(s)", "text": "Mesangial cells are located within the renal corpuscle and along the vascular pole as a component of the juxtaglomerular apparatus and are called extraglomerular mesangial (or lacis) cells."}, {"name": "Function", "text": "The primary function of mesangial cells is to remove trapped residue, etc. from the glomerular basement membrane and filtration slit diaphragm and so maintain these structures free of debris. Whilst they are phagocytic cells they are not derived from precursor cells of the mononuclear phagocytic system (monocytes). Mesangial cells also structurally support podocytes where the basement membrane is absent and synthesize and secrete molecules which have a role in responses to injury to the glomerulus. Mesangial cells also have contractile properties."}, {"name": "References", "text": "Dorland, W. (2011) Dorland's Illustrated Medical Dictionary. 32nd edn. Philadelphia, USA: Elsevier Saunders."}]

items.info: [{"name": "Quick Facts", "text": "The tarsal muscles are associated with the tarsal plates. They insert into the upper and lower eyelids and aid in widening the palpebral fissure."}, {"name": "Structure and/or Key Feature(s)", "text": "The superior tarsal muscle is a thin layer of smooth muscle associated with the superior tarsal plate. It arises from the inferior surface of the tendon of levator palpebrae superioris muscle and extends to the superior margin of the superior tarsus. Its function is to aid in maximally widening the palpebral fissure. The tarsal muscles receive sympathetic innervation from the internal carotid plexus via the superior cervical ganglion."}, {"name": "Anatomical Relations", "text": "Superficial to the superior tarsal muscle is the levator palpebrae superioris muscle and tendon. A layer of connective tissue and the conjunctiva lies deep to the superior tarsal muscle."}, {"name": "Function", "text": "Contraction of the superior tarsal muscle aids in elevating the upper eyelid."}, {"name": "List of Clinical Correlates", "text": "\u2014Horner\u2019s Syndrome \n\n\u2014Ptosis"}]

items.name: Blood Vessels of Cochlea
items.info:
[{"name": "Quick Facts", "text": "The main blood vessel supplying the cochlea is the labyrinthine artery. The spiral modiolar vein drains the cochlea, emptying into the cochlear veins at the base of the modiolus."}, {"name": "Structure and/or Key Feature(s)", "text": "The main blood vessel supplying the cochlea is the labyrinthine artery. It is typically formed from the basilar artery, but occasionally comes from the anterior inferior cerebellar artery. It branches to form the anterior vestibular and the common cochlear arteries. The latter artery splits even further into the spiral modiolar and vestibulocochlear arteries. The spiral modiolar arteries provide radiating arterioles that reach the spiral limbus, the scala vestibuli, and the stria vascularis. The vestibulocochlear artery predominantly supplies the basal turn of the cochlea (Axelsson, 1988).

The spiral modiolar vein drains the cochlea, emptying into the cochlear veins at the base of the modiolus. The cochlear veins eventually join to become the labyrinthine vein and terminates in the transverse or superior petrosal venous sinuses. A smaller vein draining the basal cochlear turn passes via the cochlear canaliculus to empty into the jugular vein (Axelsson, 1988).

The three canals of the cochlea do not receive the same f blood supply. The scala vestibuli receives a predominantly arterial blood supply whilst the scala tympani receives a venous supply. The cochlear duct is typically supplied via interposing capillaries (Axelsson, 1988)."}, {"name": "Anatomical Relations", "text": "The labyrinthine artery divides into the common cochlear artery and the anterior vestibular artery at the lateral aspect of the internal acoustic meatus. The spiral modiolar artery travels from the base to the apex of the modiolus, while the vestibulocochlear artery divides further and eventually terminates as a capillary plexus among the basal aspect of the cochlea."}, {"name": "References", "text": "Axelsson, A. (1988) Comparative anatomy of cochlear blood vessels. Am J Otolaryngol, 9(6), 278-90."}]

items.name: Origin of Innermost Intercostal Muscles
Lacrimal Nerve
items.info:
[{"name": "Quick Facts", "text": "Origin: Ophthalmic nerve.

Course: Runs from the superior orbital fissure along the superior lateral wall of the orbit, superior to the lateral rectus muscle and out towards the lacrimal gland.

Branches: Lacrimal and palpebral branches, also receives a communicating branch with zygomatic nerve.

Supply: Conveys general sensation from the lacrimal gland, skin, and conjunctiva of the upper lateral eyelid and lateral eye."}, {"name": "Origin", "text": "The lacrimal nerve is a branch of the ophthalmic nerve that originates just proximal to or within the superior orbital fissure."}, {"name": "Course", "text": "The lacrimal nerve runs within the upper aspect of the superior orbital fissure, passing anterolaterally on the superolateral wall of the orbit, superior to the lateral rectus muscle. It is usually accompanied by the lacrimal artery. The nerve eventually enters the lacrimal gland, before emerging from the superolateral aspect of the orbit into the skin and conjunctiva of the lateral aspect of the upper eyelid, and adjacent skin of the lateral corner of the eye, forehead, and scalp."}, {"name": "Branches", "text": "The lacrimal nerve gives glandular and palpebral branches. The glandular branch carries general sensory information from the lacrimal gland. It is joined by the palpebral branch passing from the upper eyelid to form the lacrimal nerve."}, {"name": "Supplied Structures", "text": "The sensory fibers of the lacrimal nerve convey sensation from the lacrimal gland via its glandular branch, as well as the skin and conjunctiva of the upper lateral eyelid and lateral eye via its palpebral branch. The parasympathetic fibers supply the lacrimal gland.

Shortly before reaching the lacrimal gland, the lacrimal nerve may be joined by postganglionic parasympathetic fibers originating in the pterygopalatine ganglion. They receive their preganglionic fibers from the greater petrosal nerve (CN VII) via the nerve of the pterygopalatine canal. These fibers travel with the lacrimal nerve, but are not technically considered part of the lacrimal nerve."}]

items.name: Epidermis
Theca Externa (of Secondary Ovarian Follicle)
items.info:
[{"name": "Quick Facts", "text": "The theca externa is the outer, fibrous layer of the follicular theca (Dorland, 2011)."}, {"name": "Structure and/or Key Feature(s)", "text": "The theca externa is the outmost layer of connective tissue surrounding the follicle, containing collagen fibers and fibroblasts but also some smooth muscle cells.

There is no clear boundary between the two thecal layers and the stroma of the ovary. However, because the cells of the theca interna and the granulosa are morphologically different, as well as the existence of a thick basement membrane between them, the boundary between these layers is clear (Ross and Pawlina, 2006; Mescher, 2013)."}, {"name": "Anatomical Relations", "text": "The theca externa is the outmost layer of connective tissue surrounding the follicle, containing collagen fibers and fibroblasts but also some smooth muscle cells."}, {"name": "References", "text": "Dorland, W. (2011) Dorland's Illustrated Medical Dictionary. 32nd edn. Philadelphia, USA: Elsevier Saunders.

Mescher, A. (2013) Junqueira's Basic Histology: Text and Atlas. 13th edn.: McGraw-Hill Education.

Ross, M. H. and Pawlina, W. (2006) Histology: A text and atlas. Lippincott Williams & Wilkins."}]

items.name: Acellular Cement
items.info:
[{"name": "Quick Facts", "text": "The acellular cement is the cementum without cellular components that covers one third to a half of the tooth root adjacent to the cementoenamel junction; it is usually opposed by a layer of cellular cementum (Dorland, 2011)."}, {"name": "Structure and/or Key Feature(s)", "text": "Acellular cement is generally comprised of extrinsic fibers embedded in calcified cement, with no cells present (Foster, 2017).

Acellular cement can be further classified depending on the presence of inserting collagen fibers from the periodontal ligament (Sharpey’s fibers). Acellular, afibrillar cement describes an indistinct granular layer devoid of inserting collagen fibers or cementocytes. It is essentially a layer of mineralized matrix exclusively produced by cementoblasts. 

Acellular extrinsic fiber cement, on the other hand, is characterized by well-defined collagen type I fibrils, which are part of the densely packed Sharpey’s fibers. This type of acellular cement extends throughout the coronal portion of the root (Vishwakarma et al., 2014)."}, {"name": "Anatomical Relations", "text": "Acellular cement is described as a thin layer of cement that covers the cervical root of the tooth."}, {"name": "Function", "text": "The primary function of acellular cement is to anchor principal fibers of the periodontal ligament to the cervical root (Yamamoto et al., 2016)."}, {"name": "References", "text": "Dorland, W. (2011) Dorland's Illustrated Medical Dictionary. 32nd edn. Philadelphia, USA: Elsevier Saunders.

Foster, B. L. (2017) 'On the discovery of cementum', J Periodontal Res, 52(4), pp. 666-685.

Hand, A. R. and Frank, M. E. (2015) Fundamentals of Oral Histology and Physiology. Wiley."}]

items.name: Cochlear Nerve
items.info:
[{"name": "Quick Facts", "text": "The cochlear nerve is the part of the vestibulocochlear nerve concerned with hearing, consisting of fibers that arise from the bipolar cells in the spiral ganglion and have their receptors in the spiral organ of the cochlea (Dorland, 2011)."}, {"name": "Structure and/or Key Feature(s)", "text": "The cochlear nerve originates as one of two branches of the vestibulocochlear nerve, or the eighth cranial nerve (CNVIII), in the internal acoustic meatus. The cochlear nerve runs from the internal acoustic meatus laterally a short distance to the cochlea within the inner ear. The cochlear nerve is the sensory nerve responsible for hearing. It conveys special sense afferent fibers from the spiral organ of Corti to the cochlear nuclei within the pons and medulla of the brain.

The cochlear nerve is comprised of 30,000–40,000 afferent and efferent somatic nerve fibers. The diameter of these fibers varies, ranging from 1 to 11 μm. The afferent fibers possess myelinated axons, with bipolar cell bodies found in the spiral ganglion (in the modiolus). There are two distinguishable types of ganglion cells, type 1 (95%) and type 2 (5%). Each cell body emits a central process that protrudes toward the organ of Corti and a central process that projects back toward the cochlear nerve. The processes of type 1 cells are myelinated, while those of type 2 are not. From the modiolus, the peripheral branches of both cell types pass to the osseous spiral lamina and the type 1 branches are demyelinated here. From here, they pass via the habenula perforata of the spiral limbus to reach the organ of Corti and its mechanosensory hair cells (Moller, 2000).

At the base of each inner and outer hair cell, there is a cluster of nerve fibers forming a synaptic complex. This inner hair cell complex is comprised of the terminal afferent fibers of ten type 1 ganglion cells, with non-direct, lateral efferent contacts. The outer hair cell complex receives direct efferent contacts. 

The dendrites of the afferent fibers do not run in parallel from the cell body to the hair cell; rather they are grouped into three different groups, depending on how they travel. These are the inner radial, basilar, and outer spiral fibers. 

—The inner radial fibers make up the bulk of the afferent fibers and travel in a linear direction to reach the base of the inner hair cell. 

—The basilar fibers run in a unique path, typically the length of five pillar cells, before deviating at an angle to form part of the afferent supply of the outer spiral bundle. 

—The outer spiral bundle travels toward the base of the cochlea, with branches made of afferent and efferent fibers to supply the base of the outer hair cells. 

The primary difference between the afferent nerve supply to the inner and outer hair cells is that a single inner hair cell is innervated by numerous afferent nerve fibers, whereas a single afferent nerve fiber innervates many outer hair cells. 

Efferent cochlear fibers originate from the olivocochlear system located in the brainstem. They form the interganglionic spiral bundle in the modiolus. These efferent fibers are separated into the lateral and medial groups. The lateral efferent fibers are associated with the inner hair cells. They travel in the inner spiral bundle and synapse lateral to the afferents supplying the inner hair cell. They do not synapse directly with the base of the inner hair cell. In contrast, the medial efferent fibers are associated with the outer hair cells. These are myelinated and travel across the tunnel of Corti to synapse at the base of the outer hair cells. The overall efferent supply is not uniform throughout the cochlea. The inner row of the outer hair cells at the base of the cochlea has the richest supply. This is gradually reduced toward the apex of the cochlea and with the outer rows of the hair cells (Moller, 2000)."}, {"name": "Function", "text": "The afferent fibers of the cochlear nerve relay signals generated from the hair cell back to the auditory processing centers in the brain. These synapses located at the inner hair cell provide information about the acoustic environment. In contrast, the lateral efferent fibers can alter the transmission of these afferent signals by their lateral input to the postsynaptic regions of these fibers. 

Regarding the efferent cochlear fibers, the outer hair cells provide information about the acoustic environment. They possess a strong frequency discrimination, enabling them to alter the sensitivity of specific frequencies. This alteration of sensitivity and specificity is mediated via the medial efferent supply, which enables a change in the mechanical responses of the outer hair cells. These vestibular efferent fibers allow for higher centers to exert control of the activity of the cochlea, adapting it to the external auditory environment, in order to focus on particular sounds or to protect the auditory system."}, {"name": "List of Clinical Correlates", "text": "—Acoustic neuroma"}, {"name": "References", "text": "Dorland, W. (2011) Dorland's Illustrated Medical Dictionary. 32nd edn. Philadelphia, USA: Elsevier Saunders.

Moller, A. R. (2000) Hearing: Its Physiology and Pathophysiology. Elsevier Science."}]

items.name: Stereocilium (Inner Hair Cell)
items.info:
[{"name": "Quick Facts", "text": "Stereocilia are long, nonmotile microvilli found on the free surface of hair cells of the internal ear; they have cores of cross-linked actin filaments but, unlike true cilia, do not have axonemes (Dorland, 2011)."}, {"name": "Structure and/or Key Feature(s)", "text": "At the apices of each hair cell there is an emergence of thin, wispy projections known as the stereocilia. Each stereocilium core is comprised of a tight arrangement of parallel, cross-linked actin filaments. The stereocilia vary in number between the inner and outer hair cells, with anywhere between 50 and 60 stereocilia per inner hair cell and 100 stereocilia per outer hair cell. 

The stereocilia of the inner hair cells are organized in a single linear fashion, while the stereocilia of the outer hair cell are organized into three rows of graded height. These rows form a “V” or “W” pattern, depending on the region the outer hair cells are located in the cochlea.

The positioning of the stereocilia is strengthened by the fixation of their basal aspects into a compact fibrillar layer, located just below the apical surface of the stereocilia. This layer is known as the cuticular lamina. The rows of stereocilia have a greater length at the apex of the cochlea and a shorter length at the base. The stereocilia of each hair cell are not of equal length, with the stereocilia of greatest length positioned in the center, and gradually decreasing as they move outwards. This arrangement is vital for the function of the cochlea. This highly precise geometry is essential to detect the nanoscale movements within the fluid of the cochlea.

The stereocilia also possess numerous interconnections with each other. All stereocilia are connected to their neighbors via lateral links, while the shorter stereocilia are further bridged to the taller contiguous stereocilia via tip links; these run from the apex of the shorter stereocilia to the body of the taller adjacent stereocilia. These links provide an adapting support network that keeps the stereocilia connected but also susceptible to displacement by vibration."}, {"name": "Anatomical Relations", "text": "The stereocilia rise from the apical aspect of the hair cells. Their bases are in contact with the cuticular lamina, and their apices are superior to this. Each stereocilium is surrounded by neighboring stereocilia and these are connected via a variety of lateral and tip links. The stereocilia are inferior to the tectorial membrane, with the inner hair cells separated from them by a space that is occupied by the endolymph. The stereocilia of the outer hair cell are in direct contact with the tectorial membrane. Their close contact results in “V” or “W” shaped impressions on the membrane known as Hensen’s ridge."}, {"name": "Function", "text": "The unique stereocilia possess a variety of special functions, such as mechanoelectrical conduction, cochlear amplification, and frequency selectivity. Essentially, sound vibrations cause minute deflections of stereocilia bundles from the original position. The hair cells react with incredible sensitivity and speed to these mechanical vibrations. The vibrations produce a shearing movement between the tectorial membrane and basilar membrane, resulting in stereociliary deflection and a change in the strain of the stereociliary tip links. This causes the ion channels to open and close, with an increase in the strain corresponding to an increase number of ions flowing into the hair cell, leading to an eventual depolarization of the hair cell."}, {"name": "List of Clinical Correlates", "text": "—Deafness (via ototoxicity)"}, {"name": "References", "text": "Dorland, W. (2011) Dorland's Illustrated Medical Dictionary. 32nd edn. Philadelphia, USA: Elsevier Saunders."}]

items.name: Basal Lamina
items.info: [{"name": "Quick Facts", "text": "The basal lamina is the layer of the basement membrane lying next to the basal surface of the adjoining cell layer; composed of an electron-dense lamina densa and an electron-lucent lamina lucida; sometimes used to denote the lamina densa alone (Dorland, 2011)."}, {"name": "Structure", "text": "The basal lamina is made up of several different proteins and carbohydrates, such as collagen, proteoglycans, and glycoproteins. It forms a matrix which surrounds the muscle fiber and plays a central role in its structure and function."}, {"name": "Key Features/Anatomical Relations", "text": "The basal lamina surrounds the muscle fiber and is directly linked to the sarcolemma."}, {"name": "Function", "text": "The basal lamina has several important roles in the structure and function of the muscle fiber such as mechanical support to underlying structures. It also acts as a scaffold for many important cells which act on the muscle fiber. The basal lamina matrix is a component of important molecular signaling, i.e., it contains an enzyme, acetylcholinesterase, which breaks down acetylcholine during neuromuscular transmissions. Its role seems to be important in many functions from development to myogenesis and synaptogenesis."}, {"name": "List of Clinical Correlates", "text": "\u2014Muscular dystrophy"}, {"name": "References", "text": "Dorland, W. (2011) Dorland's Illustrated Medical Dictionary. 32nd edn. Philadelphia, USA: Elsevier Saunders."}]

items.name: Caveola (Uncontracted Smooth Muscle; Posterior)
items.info: [{"name": "Quick Facts", "text": "A caveola is a small (approximately 50 nm), flask-shaped invagination of the plasma membrane occurring in nearly all animal cells, coated with the membrane protein caveolin and rich in cholesterol and sphingolipids. Caveolae are a special form of lipid raft and are associated with endocytosis, budding from the plasma membrane to form pinosomes; they also concentrate signaling molecules and have been implicated in other processes, including the export of cholesterol to serum lipoproteins (Dorland, 2011)."}, {"name": "Structure and/or Key Features", "text": "Most cells in the body utilize a process called pinocytosis to ingest fluid and small protein molecules via small vesicles about 80\u2013150 nm in diameter. It is a continual process, so small vesicles are continually forming at the cell surface. Most of the vesicles eventually fuse with lysosomes although they are very numerous in endothelial cells as they move materials from their surface of origin to the other side. They are also numerous at the surfaces of smooth muscle cells and their initial invaginations from the sarcolemma (plasma membrane) are referred to as caveolae. Cytoplasmic vesicles are in close proximity to sparse amounts of smooth endoplasmic reticulum (sER)."}, {"name": "Anatomical Relations", "text": "Caveolae are numerous at the surfaces of smooth muscle cells and their initial invaginations from the smooth muscle sarcolemma (plasma membrane)."}, {"name": "Function", "text": "Smooth muscle cells lack T tubules. Caveolae and vesicles function to deliver Ca+ to the cytoplasm as a consequence of depolarization of the sarcolemma and activation of voltage-sensitive Ca+ channels or direct activation of gated Ca+ release channels in the sER by a second messenger molecule. Ca+ can also be released into the cytoplasm via ligated Ca+ channels activated by hormones also by second messenger pathways. \n\nIncreasing the intracellular concentration of Ca+ is responsible for contraction of the smooth muscle cell. Contraction of smooth muscle cells is initiated by mechanical impulses, neural stimulation via neurotransmitters such as acetylcholine and norepinephrine, or chemical stimuli of the cells."}, {"name": "References", "text": "Dorland, W. (2011) Dorland's Illustrated Medical Dictionary. 32nd edn. Philadelphia, USA: Elsevier Saunders."}]

items.name: Enamel Spindles
items.info:
[{"name": "Quick Facts", "text": "The enamel spindles are the clublike structures in the inner third of the dental enamel, believed to be terminals of protoplasmic processes of the odontoblasts that have passed across the dentinoenamel junction (Dorland, 2011)."}, {"name": "Structure and/or Key Feature(s)", "text": "Enamel spindles are the projections of dentinal tubules that occasionally traverse the dentinoenamel junction and extend into the enamel. Often more prevalent at the cusp tips, these spindles appear as a series of dilated ampulla-shaped extensions anchored to the dentinoenamel junction (Berkovitz et al., 2012).

The spindles are formed during tooth development when odontoblast processes become entrapped between ameloblasts prior to and during amelogenesis (Standring, 2016)."}, {"name": "References", "text": "Berkovitz, B. K. B., Boyde, A., Frank, R. M., Höhling, H. J., Moxham, B. J., Nalbandian, J. and Tonge, C. H. (2012) Teeth. Springer Berlin Heidelberg.

Dorland, W. (2011) Dorland's Illustrated Medical Dictionary. 32nd edn. Philadelphia, USA: Elsevier Saunders.

Standring, S. (2016) Gray's Anatomy: The Anatomical Basis of Clinical Practice. Gray's Anatomy Series 41 edn.: Elsevier Limited."}]

items.name: Serosa
items.info: [{"name": "Quick Facts", "text": "The serosa is the membrane lining the walls of various body cavities, reflected over the surfaces of protruding organs; it consists of mesothelium lying upon a subserosal connective tissue layer, and it secretes a watery exudate (Dorland, 2011)."}, {"name": "Structure/Morphology", "text": "The serosa (or visceral peritoneum) is a membrane that lines the outer wall of the transverse colon. It is continuous with the transverse mesocolon, the mesentery that suspends the transverse colon. \n\nThe serosa is composed of two layers. It is a continuous sheet of squamous epithelial cells (mesothelium), which are supported by an underlying layer of thin loose connective tissue. The loose connective tissue separates the mesothelium from the muscular layer."}, {"name": "Anatomical Relations", "text": "The serosa forms the outermost layer of the transverse colon."}, {"name": "Function", "text": "The serosa acts as a protective layer by forming a barrier against potential inflammatory and malignant spread."}, {"name": "List of Clinical Correlates", "text": "\u2014Iatrogenic serosal tear"}, {"name": "References", "text": "Dorland, W. (2011) Dorland's Illustrated Medical Dictionary. 32nd edn. Philadelphia, USA: Elsevier Saunders."}]

items.name: Nucleus (Lymphocyte)
items.info:
[{"name": "Cell Morphology", "text": "Lymphocytes are a type of white blood cells, or leukocyte, and are the chief cells of the immune system. There are three main classes of lymphocytes, B lymphocytes, T lymphocytes, and Natural Killer cells. Lymphocytes make 20-40% of the total leukocytes and 99% of cells in the lymphatic system (Owen et al., 2018). B lymphocytes make up 5-15% of human blood lymphocytes and T lymphocytes make up 70% of human blood lymphocytes (Todd, 2010). Natural killer cells make 10% of the lymphocyte population (Pawlina, 2016).

The majority of B and T lymphocytes are small in size. They have a round-shaped nucleus that occupies most of the cytoplasm. They also have little cytoplasm and condensed nuclear chromatin when inactive. Natural killer cells have a kidney-shaped nucleus and large cytoplasmic granules. The diameter of lymphocytes ranges from 5-17 μm. Activated lymphocytes are larger in size. Natural killer cells are larger than B and T lymphocytes (Pawlina, 2016).

B lymphocytes possess protein receptors for antigens and other proteins on their plasma membrane. T lymphocytes generally possess the CD4+ and CD8+ surface glycoproteins. Natural Killer cells express the surface marker NK1 and cytotoxic granules (Owen et al., 2018).

T lymphocytes have a long lifespan while the lifespan of B lymphocytes varies. Natural killer cells live for around 2 weeks (Vivier et al., 2008)."}, {"name": "Production", "text": "Lymphocytes originate in the red bone marrow from hematopoietic stem cells that give rise to lymphoid stem cells, which give rise to lymphocytes. However, lymphocytes mature in different sites. Development of lymphocytes takes days to weeks (Marieb, Wilhelm and Mallatt, 2012).

B lymphocytes complete their maturation in the bone marrow and T lymphocytes leave the bone marrow as immature cells and complete their maturation and development in the thymus. After their maturation, they enter the bloodstream and migrate to the lymphoid tissues. 

Natural killer cells do not solely develop and mature in the bone marrow but in other lymphoid tissues, including the tonsils, spleen, and lymph nodes (Pawlina, 2016)."}, {"name": "Function", "text": "Lymphocytes are responsible for fighting infectious agents by recognizing antigens, proteins, or glycoproteins located in the plasma membrane of a foreign cell and eliciting an immune response. B lymphocytes are one type of the antigen presenting cells, meaning that they present the antigens to T lymphocytes for destruction. B lymphocytes differentiate into plasma cells, which secrete antibodies (IgA, IgG, IgE, IgM, IgD) that bind to the antigens and mark them for phagocytosis, and Memory B cells, that remain in the lymphoid tissues until the same antigen is encountered again and elicit an immune response more vigorously. 

T lymphocytes differentiate into Helper T cells, that assist with B lymphocyte differentiation via the secretion of cytokines, and Cytotoxic T cells, which kill the virus-infected host cells by causing them to lyse. 

Natural Killer cells recognize surface proteins of infected, cancerous, or stressed cells. When activated, Natural Killer cells kill such cells via apoptosis. Natural Killer cells are important cells of the innate immunity as they aid to control an infection until an adaptive immunity is developed (Owen et al., 2018)."}, {"name": "List of Clinical Correlates", "text": "- DiGeorge syndrome

- AIDS 

- Mononucleosis (“kissing disease”)

- Hodgkin’s lymphoma

- Non-Hodgkin’s lymphoma

- Lymphocytosis"}, {"name": "References", "text": "Marieb, E. N., Wilhelm, P. B. and Mallatt, J. (2012) Human Anatomy. 14th edn.: Benjamin Cummings.

Owen, J., Punt, J., Stranford, S. and Jones, P. (2018) Kuby Immunology. Macmillan Learning.

Pawlina, W. 2016. Histology: A text and atlas with correlated cell and molecular biology. 7th ed. Philadelphia: Wolters Kluwer.

Todd, I. (2010) 'Cells of the Immune System', eLS.

Vivier, E., Tomasello, E., Baratin, M., Walzer, T. and Ugolini, S. (2008) 'Functions of natural killer cells', Nat Immunol, 9(5), pp. 503-10."}]

items.name: Inner Segment of Cone Cell
items.info:
[{"name": "Quick Facts", "text": "The inner segment of a photoreceptor cell is the portion of a retinal rod or cone that is between the external limiting layer and the outer segment; this part contains the Golgi apparatus, endoplasmic reticulum, and numerous mitochondria (Dorland, 2011)."}, {"name": "Structure and/or Key Features", "text": "Measuring approximately 5–6 µm in length, the inner segments of cone cells are generally much broader than that of rod cells. A general feature of inner segments of both rod and cone cells is that they may be divided into two regions, the myoid and the ellipsoid. 

The myoid forms the proximal part of the inner segment, closest to the cell body, and houses the endoplasmic reticulum and Golgi apparatus. The ellipsoid forms the distal portion and contains densely packed mitochondria. Opsin proteins, such as those found in rhodopsin, are produced in the myoid but travel to the outer segment after production to be incorporated into newly forming membranous discs. Opsin proteins are integral components of the visual cycle. As new discs are added proximally, older discs move distally, toward the pigmented epithelium to be phagocytosed (Standring, 2016)."}, {"name": "Anatomical Relations", "text": "The inner segments of cone cells form a retinal layer sublayer between the cone cell body (outer nuclear layer) and the outer segment layer."}, {"name": "Function", "text": "The inner segment of cone cells is highly specialized to supply the energy demand of these cells, and to support their requirements for protein synthesis. The inner segment of the photoreceptor cell is the primary site for these functions in photoreceptors."}, {"name": "References", "text": "Dorland, W. (2011) Dorland's Illustrated Medical Dictionary. 32nd edn. Philadelphia, USA: Elsevier Saunders.

Standring, S. (2016) Gray's Anatomy: The Anatomical Basis of Clinical Practice. Gray's Anatomy Series 41 edn.: Elsevier Limited."}]

items.name: Nucleolus
items.info:
[{"name": "Quick Facts", "text": "The nucleolus is a rounded, dense body, present in the nucleus of eukaryotic cells during interphase, that is the site of ribosomal RNA (rRNA) synthesis and ribosomal subunit assembly. It consists of (a) a fibrillar center, containing the rRNA genes, surrounded by (b) the pars fibrosa, a dense fibrillar component where transcription occurs, and (c) the pars granulosa, a granular component where the ribosomal subunits are assembled. Multiple nucleoli occur in some cells (Dorland, 2011)."}, {"name": "Structure and/or Key Features", "text": "The most predominant, non-membranous structure in the nucleus is the spherical nucleolus. It surrounds rRNA genes that are transcriptionally active. The nucleolus is the site of synthesis of ribosomal ribonucleic acid (rRNA), ribosomal production and assembly. The diameter of the nucleolus is 1–2 mm, but this varies within different populations of cells. In cells that are most active in synthesizing proteins, the nucleolus is well developed and prominent. It is not uncommon for some cells to contain more than one nucleolus (Mescher, 2013).

Like heterochromatin, the nucleolus stains with basic dyes and hematoxylin."}, {"name": "Anatomical Relations", "text": "The nucleolus is located at the center of the nucleus."}, {"name": "Function", "text": "The nucleolus synthesizes and assembles ribosomal ribonucleic acid (rRNA)."}, {"name": "Clinical Correlates", "text": "Nucleoli house proteins for ribosome synthesis and oncogenes and tumor suppressor genes that control cell proliferation. Structural and functional faults in nucleoli have been the basis of a number of disease processes including some types of cancers (McKinley, O'Loughlin and Pennefather-O'Brien, 2016)."}, {"name": "References", "text": "Dorland, W. (2011) Dorland's Illustrated Medical Dictionary. 32nd edn. Philadelphia, USA: Elsevier Saunders.

McKinley, M. P., O'Loughlin, V. D. and Pennefather-O'Brien, E. E. (2016) Human Anatomy. 5th edn.: McGraw-Hill Education.

Mescher, A. (2013) Junqueira's Basic Histology: Text and Atlas. 13th edn.: McGraw-Hill Education."}]

items.name: Fascia of Clitoris
items.info:
[{"name": "Quick Facts", "text": "The fascia of clitoris is the dense fibrous tissue that encloses the two corpora cavernosa of the clitoris (Dorland, 2011)."}, {"name": "Anatomical Relations", "text": "The fascia of the clitoris surrounds the tunica albuginea and the corpora cavernosa of the clitoris. It’s continuous with the perineal fascia that invests the muscles of the superficial perineal space (i.e., bulbospongiosus, ischiocavernosus, and superficial transverse perineal muscles) (Jackson et al., 2019). The neurovascular bundles are located between these layers (Toesca, Stolfi and Cocchia, 1996). The fascia also blends with subcutaneous tissue (superficial fascia) that binds to the thin dermis of the skin over the clitoris."}, {"name": "References", "text": "Dorland, W. (2011) Dorland's Illustrated Medical Dictionary. 32nd edn. Philadelphia, USA: Elsevier Saunders.

Jackson, L. A., Hare, A. M., Carrick, K. S., Ramirez, D. M. O., Hamner, J. J. and Corton, M. M. (2019) 'Anatomy, histology, and nerve density of clitoris and associated structures: clinical applications to vulvar surgery', American Journal of Obstetrics and Gynecology, 221(5), pp. 519.e1-519.e9.

Toesca, A., Stolfi, V. M. and Cocchia, D. (1996) 'Immunohistochemical study of the corpora cavernosa of the human clitoris', Journal of anatomy, 188 (Pt 3), pp. 513-520."}]

items.name: Intermediate Filament (Posterior)
items.info:
[{"name": "Quick Facts", "text": "An intermediate filament is a class of cytoplasmic filaments, 8–11 nm in diameter, that predominantly act as structural components of the cytoskeleton and also allow various movements in cellular processes. Different types contain different, tissue-specific proteins (Dorland, 2011)."}, {"name": "Structure and/or Key Feature(s)", "text": "Intermediate filaments are filaments structured like ropes and have a size range of 8-12 nm. They may consist of several proteins (Ross and Pawlina, 2006)."}, {"name": "Function", "text": "Intermediate filaments have a structural role maintaining the stability of cell to cell junctions and adherence of the cell to the extracellular matrix. They also function as part of the cytoskeleton, thus supporting the cell (Ross and Pawlina, 2006)."}, {"name": "Clinical Correlates", "text": "Several diseases can be attributed to defects in the assembly of intermediate filaments. A characteristic of Alzheimer’s disease is disarray of intermediate filaments in some neurons (Ross & Pawlina, 2016).

“Mallory bodies” in hepatocytes in alcoholic liver cirrhosis is the accumulation of inclusions containing predominantly keratin intermediate filaments (Ross and Pawlina, 2006).

Some specific types of intermediate filaments occurring in tumors allow the origins of the cell causing the tumor to be identified (Ovalle, Nahirney and Netter, 2013)."}, {"name": "References", "text": "Dorland, W. (2011) Dorland's Illustrated Medical Dictionary. 32nd edn. Philadelphia, USA: Elsevier Sauders.

Ovalle, W. K., Nahirney, P. C. and Netter, F. H. (2013) Netter's Essential Histology. ClinicalKey 2012: Elsevier Saunders.

Ross, M. H. and Pawlina, W. (2006) Histology: A text and atlas. Lippincott Williams & Wilkins."}]

items.name: Golgi Complex (Uncontracted Smooth Muscle)
items.info:
[{"name": "Quick Facts", "text": "The Golgi complex is an intracellular compartment of eukaryotes, occupying the perinuclear region and consisting of a number of stacked, flattened sacs with associated tubules and vesicles. Its primary function is to process substances synthesized in the endoplasmic reticulum; in addition it synthesizes some carbohydrates. Transport vesicles from the endoplasmic reticulum fuse with the Golgi complex at the cis face, their cargo is processed while passing through the cisternae, and the processed products are transported from the trans face to the trans-Golgi network for sorting and packaging. The mechanism by which cargo moves through the Golgi complex is not clear; one model proposes transport between cisternae by vesicular budding and fusion, while another proposes dynamic remodeling and recycling so that the cisternae themselves change in composition and move in a cis-to-trans direction (Dorland, 2011)."}, {"name": "Structure and/or Key Features", "text": "The Golgi complex or Golgi apparatus is a crescent shaped, parallel stack of membrane-limited tubules or cisternae. It is closely associated with small vesicles involved in vesicular transport. The Golgi complex is very well developed in secretory cells. The Golgi complex exhibits structural polarity. It has a “cis face” (or entry face, which is the convex part of the complex) and a “trans face” (or exit face) (Ovalle, Nahirney and Netter, 2013; McKinley, O'Loughlin and Pennefather-O'Brien, 2016; Ross and Pawlina, 2016)."}, {"name": "Anatomical Relations", "text": "The Golgi complex is closely associated with the nucleus and the “cis face” is adjacent to the rough endoplasmic reticulum."}, {"name": "Function", "text": "The Golgi complex accepts proteins and various other molecules synthesized by the endoplasmic reticulum. Each cistern of the Golgi complex contains different types of enzymes and so perform different enzymatic reactions. 

As some proteins move within the Golgi cisternae, carbohydrates and lipids are added to these proteins to form glycoproteins and glycolipids, respectively. In addition, proteins are added to lipids to form lipoproteins. Some proteins are isolated to be included in new plasmalemma.

As these molecules pass further through the Golgi complex, they are sorted and repackaged into a secretory vesicle. These secretory molecules are either destined to become lysosomes, migrate to the plasmalemma, or exported outside of the cell. 

The Golgi apparatus is involved in making carbohydrates (Ovalle, Nahirney and Netter, 2013; McKinley, O'Loughlin and Pennefather-O'Brien, 2016; Ross and Pawlina, 2016)."}, {"name": "Clinical Correlates", "text": "Atrophy of the Golgi complex and subsequent functional errors in specific neurons and loss of these neurons in the brain has been implicated in Alzheimer’s disease (Ovalle, Nahirney and Netter, 2013)."}, {"name": "References", "text": "Dorland, W. (2011) Dorland's Illustrated Medical Dictionary. 32nd edn. Philadelphia, USA: Elsevier Saunders.

McKinley, M. P., O'Loughlin, V. D. and Pennefather-O'Brien, E. E. (2016) Human Anatomy. 5th edn.: McGraw-Hill Education.

Ovalle, W. K., Nahirney, P. C. and Netter, F. H. (2013) Netter's Essential Histology. ClinicalKey 2012: Elsevier Saunders.

Ross, M. H. and Pawlina, W. (2016) Histology: A Text and Atlas. Wolters Kluwer Health."}]

items.name: Capillary Vessel (Pancreas)
items.info:
[{"name": "Quick Facts", "text": "A capillary is any of the minute vessels that connect the arterioles and venules, forming a network in nearly all parts of the body. Their walls act as semipermeable membranes for the interchange of various substances, including fluids, between the blood and tissue fluid. The two principal types are continuous and fenestrated capillaries (Dorland, 2011)."}, {"name": "Structure and/or Key Feature(s)", "text": "Whilst the pancreatic islets comprise only about 2% of the mass of the pancreas, they receive up to 15% of the total blood flow to the pancreas. Blood enters the islet in two ways.

—Blood flows directly to the core of the islet then spreads to the periphery. A and D cells cluster along the paths of these vessels.

—Several arterioles enter the periphery of the islets then branch into fenestrated capillaries to flow to the core of the islet. 

Based on the dynamics of this flow supply to the islets, it is probable that the A and D cells receive the flow of blood before the B cells. Large capillaries leave the islets and then branch into a capillary network (resembling a portal system) to supply the acini of the exocrine pancreas (Ross and Pawlina, 2016)."}, {"name": "Function", "text": "Based on the dynamics of the blood supply to the islets and, the efferent blood capillaries that then supply the acini of the exocrine pancreas, secretions from the islet cells can influence the secretions from the acinar cells of the exocrine pancreas (Ross and Pawlina, 2016)."}, {"name": "References", "text": "Dorland, W. (2011) Dorland's Illustrated Medical Dictionary. 32nd edn. Philadelphia, USA: Elsevier Saunders.

Ross, M. H. and Pawlina, W. (2016) Histology: A Text and Atlas. Wolters Kluwer Health."}]

items.name: Free Nerve Endings
items.info: [{"name": "Quick Facts", "text": "A free nerve ending is the type of neural receptor with the simplest form, in which the peripheral nerve fiber divides into fine branches that terminate freely in connective tissue or epithelium (Dorland, 2011)."}, {"name": "Structure/Morphology", "text": "Free nerve endings are widely distributed throughout the skin and form the majority of sensory receptors. They may be myelinated (a\u03b4-fibers) or unmyelinated (C-fibers), both of which have small diameters and low conduction velocity. They are associated with deep tissue of the dermis, the hair follicle, and the dermoepidermal border (Young, 2006)."}, {"name": "Function", "text": "In the dermis, they are responsive to moderate temperature variation, light mechanical touch and noxious stimuli. Free nerve endings are found at the dermoepidermal border and can extend into the epidermis to be intimately associated with the Merkel cells in the stratum basale (see tactile meniscus)."}, {"name": "References", "text": "Dorland, W. (2011) Dorland's Illustrated Medical Dictionary. 32nd edn. Philadelphia, USA: Elsevier Saunders.\n\nYoung, B. (2006) Wheater's Functional Histology: A Text and Colour Atlas. Student consult: Churchill Livingstone/Elsevier."}]

items.name: Pancreatic Acinus (Superior)
items.info:
[{"name": "Quick Facts", "text": "The pancreatic acinus is one of the secretory units of the exocrine pancreas, where pancreatic juice is produced (Dorland, 2011)."}, {"name": "Structure and/or Key Feature(s)", "text": "The exocrine cells of the pancreas (pancreatic acinar cells or serous secretory cells) are simple, pyramidal in shape. They form clusters or secretory units called acini, due to their acinar or tubuloacinar shape. Acini are supported by a basal lamina and very fine reticular fibers surround the acini.

The exocrine cells of the pancreas contain numerous zymogen granules in their apical cytoplasm which imparts an eosinophilia to the apical region compared to a more basophilic basal region due to the presence of free ribosomes and rough endoplasmic reticulum.

A unique feature of the pancreatic acinus is that centroacinar cells are located within the acinus and form the initial segment of the intercalated duct system (Ross and Pawlina, 2016)."}, {"name": "Function", "text": "Zymogen granules contain (inactive) precursors of digestive enzymes that can digest most food substances."}, {"name": "References", "text": "Dorland, W. (2011) Dorland's Illustrated Medical Dictionary. 32nd edn. Philadelphia, USA: Elsevier Saunders.

Ross, M. H. and Pawlina, W. (2016) Histology: A Text and Atlas. Wolters Kluwer Health."}]

items.name: Gingiva
items.info:
[{"name": "Quick Facts", "text": "The gingiva is that part of the oral mucosa overlying the alveolar ridge and crowns of unerupted teeth, encircling the necks of those that have erupted, and serving as the supporting structure for subjacent tissues.
