It is formed by pale pink tissue immovably attached to the bone and the teeth, which joins the alveolar mucosa at the mucogingival junction (Dorland, 2011)."}, {"name": "Structure and/or Key Feature(s)", "text": "The oral mucosa describes the mucous membrane that lines the inside of the mouth. Gingivae, more commonly known as the gums, is one portion of the oral mucosa. It begins at the mucogingival line, surrounds the alveolar processes and cervical portions of the teeth and fits into the interproximal spaces between the teeth. As gingiva meets the cervix of each tooth, it gives rise to a ring of specialized epithelial tissue, known as junctional epithelium, which forms an attachment with the tooth. 

Recognized as the peripheral component of the periodontium, gingivae are generally salmon or coral pink and can be described as having a stippled appearance (Fehrenbach and Popowics, 2015).

The gingiva, along with the alveolar mucosa, cement, periodontal ligament and alveolar bone, comprises the periodontium."}, {"name": "Anatomical Relations", "text": "The gingiva can be classified as free (marginal) gingiva, attached gingiva or interdental gingiva. Attached gingiva adheres to the bone around the roots of the teeth. This keratinized gingival tissue can be distinguished from marginal gingiva due to the presence of surface stippling. The lamina propria of the attached gingiva is directly attached to the jaw bones beneath it, making the attached gingiva firm and immobile. Extensions of the attached gingiva, known as interdental gingiva, extend and travel between adjacent teeth, giving rise to the interdental papillae. Interdental papillae are typically pyramidal, which is particularly visible when teeth are extracted (Wolf and Rateitschak-Pluss, 2011).

Free or marginal gingiva is continuous with the attached gingiva and is located at the gingival margin, or free gingival crest, of each tooth. The free gingival groove separates attached gingiva from the marginal gingiva. The marginal gingiva can vary in width from 0.5-2 mm from the free gingival crest to the attached gingiva. With a stratified squamous epithelium, marginal gingiva follows the scalloped pattern along each tooth established by the cementoenamel junction. Its lamina propria is not directly attached to the underlying jaw bones, making the tissue firm but mobile."}, {"name": "Function", "text": "In general, the gingiva is responsible for surrounding and protecting the teeth and alveolar bone. Interdental papillae have a specific role in the prevention of food impaction by filling in the area between the teeth, apical to their contact area (Rajendran and Sivapathasundharam, 2014)."}, {"name": "List of Clinical Correlates", "text": "—Periodontitis

—Gingivitis"}, {"name": "References", "text": "Dorland, W. (2011) Dorland's Illustrated Medical Dictionary. 32nd edn. Philadelphia, USA: Elsevier Saunders.

Fehrenbach, M. J. and Popowics, T. (2015) Illustrated Dental Embryology, Histology, and Anatomy - E-Book. Elsevier Health Sciences.

Rajendran, A. and Sivapathasundharam, B. (2014) Shafer's Textbook of Oral Pathology. Elsevier Health Sciences.

Wolf, H. F. and Rateitschak-Pluss, E. M. (2011) Color Atlas of Dental Medicine: Periodontology: Periodontology. Thieme."}]

items.name: Synapse
items.info:
[{"name": "Quick Facts", "text": "A synapse is the site of functional apposition between neurons, at which an impulse is transmitted from one neuron to another, usually by a chemical neurotransmitter (e.g., acetylcholine, norepinephrine) released by the axon terminal of the excited (presynaptic) cell. The neurotransmitter diffuses across the synaptic cleft to bind with receptors on the postsynaptic cell membrane, and thereby effects electrical changes in the postsynaptic cell which result in depolarization (excitation) or hyperpolarization (inhibition). Synapses also occur at sites of apposition between nerve endings and effector organs (e.g., the neuromuscular junction). A few synapses in the central nervous system are electrical synapses (Dorland, 2011)."}, {"name": "Structure", "text": "The synapse is the site at which neurons in the nervous system come into close contact with other neurons to form a conducting pathway. Synapses are also sites at which axons of neurons in the autonomic nervous system innervate smooth muscle cells, the myocardium (of the heart), or secretory cells within glands to form a functional pathway. A neuromuscular junction is a synapse that occurs between axons of motor neurons of the brain or spinal cord and skeletal muscle fibers.

Communication between neurons at the synapse takes place in one direction only, from the presynaptic neuron to the postsynaptic neuron, both of which are separated by the synaptic cleft. 

Most synapses in the adult human nervous system are classified as being chemical synapses which involves a chemical substance called a neurotransmitter being released from the presynaptic neuron and diffusing across to change the resting potential of the postsynaptic neuron. A chemical synapse is made up of a presynaptic element, a synaptic cleft, and a postsynaptic membrane (Ross and Pawlina, 2006).

Electrical synapses are more common in the invertebrates and contain gap junctions permitting ions to move between cells, and so, a direct passage of an electrical current occurs. Similar gap junctions in mammals perform this role in smooth muscle cells and cardiomyocytes (cardiac muscle cells) (Ross and Pawlina, 2006).

Synapses between neurons are often referred to as axodendritic (axons and dendrites), axoaxonic (axons and axons), or axosomatic (axons and the cell body). The number of synapses on any one neuron may be in the tens of thousands (Ross and Pawlina, 2006).

In some specialized neurons, dendrites can form synapses with one another, and these are called dendrodendritic synapses. Synapses may be further classified on the appearances of the pre- and postsynaptic membrane. Asymmetrical synapses, or Gray’s type I synapses, have postsynaptic densities thicker than presynaptic densities. Symmetrical synapses, or Gray’s type II synapses, have densities similar on the pre- and postsynaptic membrane. These differences in densities reflect functional divergences; Type I synapses are usually excitatory, whereas type II synapses are inhibitory (Bear, Connors and Paradiso, 2007)."}, {"name": "Function", "text": "Synapses provide a means by which neurons communicate with each other, and with effector cells. Synapses also play a role in facilitating the processing of the neural input by allowing impulses traveling from the presynaptic neuron to the postsynaptic neuron to be processed by other neurons. These other neurons do not have direct access to the impulses, but they have access to the synapse (Ross and Pawlina, 2006)."}, {"name": "List of Clinical Correlates", "text": "—The synapse is a region in the nervous system where neurotransmission can be easily blocked. General anesthetic agents block synaptic transmission (Splittgerber, 2018).

—Drugs are being developed now to modify synaptic transmission by interfering with the processes of transmission at the presynaptic element, within the synaptic cleft and at the postsynaptic membrane (Splittgerber, 2018)."}, {"name": "References", "text": "Bear, M. F., Connors, B. W. and Paradiso, M. A. (2007) Neuroscience. Lippincott Williams & Wilkins.

Dorland, W. (2011) Dorland's Illustrated Medical Dictionary. 32nd edn. Philadelphia, USA: Elsevier Saunders.

Ross, M. H. and Pawlina, W. (2006) Histology: A text and atlas. Lippincott Williams & Wilkins.

Splittgerber, R. (2018) Snell's Clinical Neuroanatomy. Wolters Kluwer Health."}]

items.name: Taste Buds of Fungiform Papillae
items.info: [{"name": "Quick Facts", "text": "A taste bud is one of the minute, bud-shaped sensory organs of the tongue, situated around the bases of the vallate, fungiform, and foliate papillae. It contains several types of specialized epithelial cells, including taste receptor, supporting, and basal cells, and is innervated by gustatory nerve fibers (Dorland, 2011)."}, {"name": "Structure and/or Key Features", "text": "Taste buds are located all over the tongue, but predominantly within the gustatory lingual papillae. The taste buds are not distributed equally and have different populations among the gustatory lingual papillae. \n\nThe taste buds of the fungiform papillae are the least abundant. They may form in groups of small quantities, with the taste buds being clustered close together. They are located at the apex of the papillae, readily in contact with any food particles that they come into contact with."}, {"name": "Function", "text": "The sensation of taste is mediated by the taste buds. The taste buds of the fungiform papillae are based on the apex of the taste buds, prepared for chemosensory activation upon detection of nutrients and toxins in the oral cavity. The information is transmitted to the nerve fibers via synapses located at the base of the taste bud."}, {"name": "References", "text": "Dorland, W. (2011) Dorland's Illustrated Medical Dictionary. 32nd edn. Philadelphia, USA: Elsevier Saunders."}]

items.name: Diaphragma Sellae
Hilus Cells
items.info: [{"name": "Structure and/or Key Feature(s)", "text": "Ovarian hilus cells are located in the hilum of the ovary. Like the interstitial (Leydig) cells of the male gonads, hilar cells in the ovary contain Reinke crystalloids, lipofuscin pigment associated with protein production. They associated with vascular spaces and nonmyelinated nerve fibers."}, {"name": "Function", "text": "Hilus cells may secrete androgens. They respond to hormonal changes during pregnancy and the onset of menopause."}, {"name": "List of Clinical Correlates", "text": "Tumors associated with hilus cells usually lead to masculinization (Ross and Pawlina, 2006)."}, {"name": "References", "text": "Ross, M. H. and Pawlina, W. (2006) Histology: A text and atlas. Lippincott Williams & Wilkins"}]

items.name: Endocrine Component of Pancreas
items.info:
[{"name": "Quick Facts", "text": "The endocrine component of the pancreas is the part of the pancreas that acts as an endocrine gland, consisting of the islets of Langerhans, which secrete insulin, glucagon, somatostatin, and sometimes pancreatic polypeptide directly into the bloodstream (Dorland, 2011)."}, {"name": "Structure and/or Key Feature(s)", "text": "The pancreatic islets (Islets of Langerhans) constitute the endocrine component of the pancreas. They are clusters of cells embedded within the exocrine pancreatic tissues.

Pancreatic islets can be isolated, small collections of polygonal or rounded cells or occur in clusters of cells of about 100–200 μm in diameter. There are between 1 and 3 million islets in the pancreas; however, they only make up 1–2% of its total volume. In humans, they are most numerous near the tail of the pancreas. An extensive network of fenestrated blood capillaries penetrates each islet (Ross and Pawlina, 2016). Very fine reticular fibers surround the islets and separate them from other pancreatic tissues (Mescher, 2013).

Using certain staining techniques, three major cell types can be distinguished: A (alpha), B (beta), and D (delta) cells. The remaining approximately 5% population of cells does not stain at all. These cell types can be distinguished based on the size and density of secretory granules within the cell cytoplasm using transmission electron microscopy. The relative numbers of these cell types are not uniform throughout the pancreas."}, {"name": "Function", "text": "The endocrine pancreas secretes hormones that regulate blood glucose levels."}, {"name": "References", "text": "Dorland, W. (2011) Dorland's Illustrated Medical Dictionary. 32nd edn. Philadelphia, USA: Elsevier Saunders.

Mescher, A. (2013) Junqueira's Basic Histology: Text and Atlas. 13th edn.: McGraw-Hill Education.

Ross, M. H. and Pawlina, W. (2016) Histology: A Text and Atlas. Wolters Kluwer Health."}]

items.name: Vas Spirale
items.info: [{"name": "Quick Facts", "text": "The vas spirale is a prominent vessel in the basilar membrane near the inner tunnel (Dorland, 2011)."}, {"name": "Structure and/or Key Feature(s)", "text": "A layer of vascular connective tissue is found within the tympanic lamella, just underneath the basilar membrane. One of its vessels is enlarged, the vas spirale, and is positioned just below the pillar cells that form the inner tunnel of Corti (Standring, 2016)."}, {"name": "Function", "text": "The organ of Corti receives arterial blood from the vas spirale and the other smaller accompanying spiral vessels. This provides plenty of metabolites and nutrients for the fluid that surrounds and bathes the sensory cells. The microcirculation associated with the organ of Corti is similar to the terminal capillaries found systemically. However, there are a limited number of vessels, and so, obstruction of blood flow and the ensuing consequences may occur more rapidly and severely."}, {"name": "References", "text": "Dorland, W. (2011) Dorland's Illustrated Medical Dictionary. 32nd edn. Philadelphia, USA: Elsevier Saunders.\n\nStandring, S. (2016) Gray's Anatomy: The Anatomical Basis of Clinical Practice., 41st edition. Elsevier Limited."}]

items.name: Peripheral Nerve Fibers
items.info:
[{"name": "Quick Facts", "text": "A nerve fiber is the slender process of a neuron; the term is often synonymous with axon. Nerve fibers are classified on the basis of the presence or absence of a myelin sheath as myelinated or unmyelinated (Dorland, 2011)."}, {"name": "Structure/Morphology", "text": "Peripheral nerves and ganglia make up the peripheral nervous system (PNS) connecting peripheral structures (such as muscles and viscera) to the central nervous system (CNS) (Sherwood, 2012). A nerve fiber is composed of axons, their neurilemma (or neurolemma) and the surrounding endoneurial connective tissue. The neurilemma is the outermost covering of the neuron and refers to the farthermost spiral enwrapping of the Schwann cells that surround the axon of a neuron (Pocock, Richards and Richards, 2013). Within the peripheral nervous system, the nerve fibers can be classified as myelinated (or medullated) nerve fibers and unmyelinated (or non-medullated) nerve fibers. 

Both myelinated and non-myelinated nerve fibers are enveloped by Schwann cells; however, the difference lies in the presence or absence of the myelin sheath and the arrangement of the Schwann cells. 

—In myelinated nerve fibers, the Schwann cells specific to an individual axon are organized as a continuous series of cells wrapping around the axon. The continuous wrappings of the Schwann cells collectively create a fatty insulating layer around the axon, called the myelin sheath. While the outermost fold of the enwrapped Schwann cell membrane, where most of the cellular cytoplasm and nucleus have been pushed, becomes the neurilemma.

—In unmyelinated nerve fibers, the neurilemma is also composed of the outer fold of the Schwann cell membrane, however, the Schwann cells do not form continuous wrappings around the unmyelinated axons, therefore the myelin sheaths are absent. Moreover, in comparison to myelinated fibers, there may be multiple axons enveloped or embedded within the folds of the Schwann cells. 

A nerve consists of a bundle of nerve fibers, or a fascicle which is a “bundle of bundled fibers” in the case of large nerves. Connective tissue layers surround and bind the nerve fibers and fascicles together. These connective tissue layers include the endoneurium, perineurium, and epineurium, which make the nerves reasonably strong and resilient. Blood vessels, known as the vasa nervorum, nourish the nerve fibers and their coverings."}, {"name": "Key Features/Anatomical Relations", "text": "The afferent and efferent axons within a nerve relay different signals. Efferent axons convey motor impulses from motor neurons in the central nervous system to body muscles, glands, and vessels. On the other hand, afferent nerve fibers transfer sensory information to the central nervous system from a sensor, such as a pain receptor (Pocock et al., 2013)"}, {"name": "Function", "text": "Nerves transmit information to and from the central nervous system. In order to accomplish this task, the signals must be converted to electrochemical impulses and, in turn, to action potentials. An action potential is a depolarization of the cell membrane that results in the transmission of an electrical signal down an axon."}, {"name": "List of Clinical Correlates", "text": "—Multiple sclerosis 

—A pinched nerve"}, {"name": "References", "text": "Dorland, W. (2011) Dorland's Illustrated Medical Dictionary. 32nd edn. Philadelphia, USA: Elsevier Saunders.

Pocock, G., Richards, C. D. and Richards, D. A. (2013) Human Physiology. Oxford Core Texts: OUP Oxford.

Sherwood, L. (2012) Human Physiology: From Cells to Systems. Cengage Learning."}]

items.name: Pulmonary Venule
items.info: [{"name": "Quick Facts", "text": "A venule is any of the small vessels that collect blood from the capillary plexuses and join to form veins (Dorland, 2011)."}, {"name": "Structure/Morphology", "text": "The pulmonary venules are responsible for returning oxygenated blood from the lung tissue to the pulmonary veins, which subsequently will transport it back to the left atrium of the heart. The extensive network of capillaries surrounding the alveoli are drained by the pulmonary venules."}, {"name": "Function", "text": "The pulmonary venules return oxygenated blood back to the heart, where it can enter the systemic circulation."}, {"name": "References", "text": "Dorland, W. (2011) Dorland's Illustrated Medical Dictionary. 32nd edn. Philadelphia, USA: Elsevier Saunders."}]

items.name: Cell Membrane
Goblet Cells
items.info: [{"name": "Structure and/or Key Feature(s)", "text": "Goblet cells are a class of columnar epithelial cells that secrete mucus. Such cells are found in many of the body\u2019s tissues, including the conjunctiva of the eye. The density of this cell type in the conjunctival epithelium varies. For example, they tend to be denser in the regions covered by the eyelids where they secrete mucins that contribute to the tear film."}, {"name": "Anatomical Relations", "text": "Goblet cells are found within the conjunctiva especially of the upper eyelid. The conjunctiva is the innermost layer of the eyelid that rests on the external surface of the cornea."}, {"name": "Function", "text": "The goblet cells of the conjunctiva produce mucin that lubricates the ocular surface as well as play a role in protecting the surface of the eyeball from infection."}]

items.name: Origin of Scalenus Medius Muscle
Veins of Tendon
items.info:
[{"name": "Quick Facts", "text": "A vein is a vessel through which blood passes from various organs or parts back to the heart; all veins except the pulmonary veins carry blood low in oxygen. Like arteries, veins have three coats, an inner, middle, and outer, but the coats are not so thick, and they collapse when the vessel is cut. Many veins have valves formed of reduplications of their lining membrane, which prevent the backward flow of blood away from the heart (Dorland, 2011)."}, {"name": "Structure and/or Key Feature(s)", "text": "The venous drainage of tendons accompanies the arterial supply. Venae comitantes, along with the lymphatic vessels accompany the small arterioles that stem from surrounding muscle tissue, as well as their branches (Standring, 2016)."}, {"name": "Anatomical Relations", "text": "The venules travel along with the arterioles. The small blood vessels in the peritendon take a transverse course towards the tendon, give off various branches, then change direction to travel parallel to the length of the tendon. The vessels gain access into the tendon at a point along the endotendon. Arterioles travel longitudinally, each accompanied by two venules. Capillaries travel from the arterioles and connect with the venules, without piercing through the collagen bundles (Maffulli, Renstrom and Leadbetter, 2005)."}, {"name": "Function", "text": "Generally, the function of veins is to convey deoxygenated blood from the body, back to the right atrium of the heart and then to the lungs via the pulmonary arteries to get oxygenated and repeat the cycle. Venous return from the lower limbs is primarily via the deep veins. The femoral and the profunda femoris veins convey deoxygenated blood from the thighs to the heart."}, {"name": "References", "text": "Dorland, W. (2011) Dorland's Illustrated Medical Dictionary. 32nd edn. Philadelphia, USA: Elsevier Saunders.

Maffulli, N., Renstrom, P. and Leadbetter, W. B. (2005) Tendon Injuries: Basic Science and Clinical Medicine. Springer London.

Standring, S. (2016) Gray's Anatomy: The Anatomical Basis of Clinical Practice. Gray's Anatomy Series 41 edn.: Elsevier Limited."}]

items.name: Vein
items.info:
[{"name": "Quick Facts", "text": "A vein is a vessel through which blood passes from various organs or parts back to the heart; all veins except the pulmonary veins carry blood low in oxygen. Like arteries, veins have three coats, an inner, middle, and outer, but the coats are not so thick, and they collapse when the vessel is cut. Many veins have valves formed of reduplications of their lining membrane, which prevent the backward flow of blood away from the heart (Dorland, 2011)."}, {"name": "Structure/Morphology", "text": "Blood from the capillary beds of the cortex drain into the medullary venules within the medullary cords. These venules unify with other venules from other lobules of the lymph node, forming a vein which exists the lymph node at the hilum, along with the efferent lymph vessel and accompanying artery. Each lobule of the lymph node is drained by a vein, however, for descriptive purposes this is not shown in the 3D model.

Lymphocytes are capable of migrating from the venules into the paracortex, or deep cortex, through high endothelial venules. High endothelial venules are so-called due to the specialized characteristics of the endothelial cells in that part of the venules. Instead of a squamous endothelial cell, as seen in regular arteries and veins, and lymphatic vessels, the endothelial cells are cuboidal. They are capable of binding to intravascular lymphocytes and facilitate the passage of the cells from the blood into the reticular tissue of the paracortex. In fact, most lymphocytes enter the lymph nodes through high endothelial venules (Willard-Mack, 2006; Miyasaka and Tanaka, 2004).

As the venule continues into the medullary region of the lymph node, it loses its high endothelium, which has reverted to the squamous endothelium."}, {"name": "References", "text": "Dorland, W. (2011) Dorland's Illustrated Medical Dictionary. 32nd edn. Philadelphia, USA: Elsevier Saunders.

Miyasaka, M. and Tanaka, T. (2004) 'Lymphocyte trafficking across high endothelial venules: dogmas and enigmas', Nat Rev Immunol, 4(5), pp. 360-70.

Willard-Mack, C. L. (2006) 'Normal structure, function, and histology of lymph nodes', Toxicologic Pathology, 5(34), pp. 409-424."}]

items.name: Lacrimal Gland
items.info:
[{"name": "Quick Facts", "text": "The lacrimal gland is either of a pair of glands, one at the superior lateral angle of each orbit, secreting the tears; they are divided into two portions, the orbital and palpebral, by the levator palpebrae superioris muscle (Dorland, 2011)."}, {"name": "Structure and/or Key Feature(s)", "text": "The lacrimal gland is a lobulated exocrine gland. It is located in the superior lateral corner of the orbit (orbital part) extending out into the upper eyelid (palpebral part), continuous with each other posterolaterally around the levator palpebrae superioris muscle. The gland itself contains the secretory unit, the acini, that discharge their aqueous product into a central lumen. Numerous lumens converge on an intercalated duct that opens into the conjunctival sac and is how tears are expelled from the gland. Myoepithelium surrounds the acini and ducts, and these provide mechanical force to expel tears. There are as many as twelve ducts for each gland.

The lacrimal gland is supplied by the lacrimal branch of the ophthalmic artery, with contributions from the infraorbital artery. Blood is drained by the superior ophthalmic vein.

Sensory innervation of the lacrimal gland is provided by the ophthalmic nerve (CN V1). Secretomotor preganglionic parasympathetic innervation of the lacrimal gland is carried by the greater petrosal nerve, a branch of the facial nerve (CN VII). Preganglionic fibers terminate in the pterygopalatine ganglion. Postganglionic fibers reach the gland by following the zygomatic and lacrimal branches of the maxillary nerve (CN V2) or directly from the ganglion. The superior cervical ganglion provides sympathetic fibers to the lacrimal gland."}, {"name": "Anatomical Relations", "text": "The larger orbital part of the lacrimal gland (about the size and shape of an almond) is contained within a shallow fossa on the lateral aspect of the frontal bone. It lies above the levator palpebrae superioris and the lateral rectus muscles. Its inferior surface is attached to the fascia of levator palpebrae superioris; its posterior border is attached to the dense orbital fat; its anterior border is in contact with the orbital septum (palpebral fascia). The smaller palpebral part of the lacrimal gland extends inferior to the levator palpebrae superioris and to the lateral part of the upper eyelid. It is attached to the superior conjunctival fornix."}, {"name": "Function", "text": "The lacrimal gland is responsible for producing the aqueous component of tears. This watery secretion contains several proteins, such as lysozymes and immunoglobulin A, which protect the surface of the eye from infection, while maintaining the hydration of the epithelial surface of the eye."}, {"name": "References", "text": "Dorland, W. (2011) Dorland's Illustrated Medical Dictionary. 32nd edn. Philadelphia, USA: Elsevier Saunders."}]

items.name: Capillary Vessel (Pancreas; Inferior)
items.info:
[{"name": "Quick Facts", "text": "A capillary is any of the minute vessels that connect the arterioles and venules, forming a network in nearly all parts of the body. Their walls act as semipermeable membranes for the interchange of various substances, including fluids, between the blood and tissue fluid. The two principal types are continuous and fenestrated capillaries (Dorland, 2011)."}, {"name": "Structure and/or Key Feature(s)", "text": "Whilst the pancreatic islets comprise only about 2% of the mass of the pancreas, they receive up to 15% of the total blood flow to the pancreas. Blood enters the islet in two ways.

—Blood flows directly to the core of the islet then spreads to the periphery. A and D cells cluster along the paths of these vessels.

—Several arterioles enter the periphery of the islets then branch into fenestrated capillaries to flow to the core of the islet. 

Based on the dynamics of this flow supply to the islets, it is probable that the A and D cells receive the flow of blood before the B cells. Large capillaries leave the islets and then branch into a capillary network (resembling a portal system) to supply the acini of the exocrine pancreas (Ross and Pawlina, 2016)."}, {"name": "Function", "text": "Based on the dynamics of the blood supply to the islets and, the efferent blood capillaries that then supply the acini of the exocrine pancreas, secretions from the islet cells can influence the secretions from the acinar cells of the exocrine pancreas (Ross and Pawlina, 2016)."}, {"name": "References", "text": "Dorland, W. (2011) Dorland's Illustrated Medical Dictionary. 32nd edn. Philadelphia, USA: Elsevier Saunders.

Ross, M. H. and Pawlina, W. (2016) Histology: A Text and Atlas. Wolters Kluwer Health."}]

items.name: Axon (General Visceral Efferent Parasympathetic)
items.info:
[{"name": "Quick Facts", "text": "The axon is the process of a neuron by which impulses travel away from the cell body; at the terminal arborization of the axon, the impulses are transmitted to other nerve cells or to effector organs. The larger axons are surrounded by a myelin sheath (Dorland, 2011)."}, {"name": "Structure/Morphology", "text": "Axons are a part of the nerve cell or neuron. They can be described as an appendage of the nerve cell body giving rise to numerous collateral branches containing presynaptic complexes. Axons are comprised of a gelatinous, relatively firm cord of neuronal cytoplasm. This cord is known as the axoplasm. This axoplasm is surrounded by the axonal part of the neuronal cell membrane, which is referred to as the axolemma. Axons vary in diameter from about 0.1 µm to about 20 µm. Axons also vary in length, they can be anywhere between less than 1 cm to more than a meter long (Carp, 2015).

There are two types of axons, myelinated and unmyelinated. Myelinated axons are surrounded by a myelin sheath while unmyelinated axons are not. Nodes of Ranvier refer to the gaps found in the continuity of the myelin sheath surrounding an axon. At these gaps there is no myelin covering the axon and the axon is exposed to the extracellular fluid."}, {"name": "Key Features/Anatomical Relations", "text": "Myelinated axons are concentrically enveloped by myelin which is produced by myelinating Schwann cells. The territory of an individual Schwann cell along the length of the axon is defined as an internode, while the internodal length is the distance between two successive nodes of Ranvier. The span between these nodes varies dependent on axon diameter. It is at these nodes voltage-gated sodium channels are concentrated. Conduction in myelinated axons is saltatory and extremely quick.

Unmyelinated axons are enclosed by overlapping Schwann cells followed by a surrounding basal lamina. Within each Schwann cell, individual axons are usually isolated from their neighbor by delicate processes of cytoplasm. The absence of myelin sheaths and nodes of Ranvier in unmyelinated axons results in electrotonic conduction, not saltatory, and the passage of impulses is therefore relatively slow."}, {"name": "Function", "text": "Axons are the main conducting unit of the neuron. They transfer electrical signals along a range of distances. The nodes of Ranvier function as a generator of action potentials. This is achieved through the region of the membrane exposed at the node of Ranvier possessing special channel proteins, which allow ions to enter and exit the cell (Waxman, Kocsis and Stys, 1995)."}, {"name": "List of Clinical Correlates", "text": "—Tetrodotoxin poisoning"}, {"name": "References", "text": "Carp, S. (2015) Peripheral Nerve Injury An Anatomical and Physiological Approach for Physical Therapy Intervention. EBL-Schweitzer: F. A. Davis Company.

Dorland, W. (2011) Dorland's Illustrated Medical Dictionary. 32nd edn. Philadelphia, USA: Elsevier Saunders.

Waxman, S. G., Kocsis, J. D. and Stys, P. K. (1995) The Axon: Structure, Function, and Pathophysiology. Oxford University Press."}]

items.name: Muscularis mucosa (Duodenum)
items.info:
[{"name": "Quick Facts", "text": "The muscularis mucosa is the thin layer of smooth muscle fibers usually found as a part of the tunica mucosa deep to the lamina propria mucosae (Dorland, 2011)."}, {"name": "Structure/Morphology", "text": "The muscularis mucosa is similar in the three components of the small intestine. It is the deepest part of the mucosa and consists of a very thin inner circular layer of smooth muscle and an equally thin outer longitudinal layer of smooth muscle.

Some small smooth muscle cells travel vertically from the muscularis mucosa to the tips of villi."}, {"name": "Key Features/Anatomical Relations", "text": "The muscularis mucosa is the deepest part of the mucosa and adjacent to the submucosa."}, {"name": "Function", "text": "Contraction of the muscularis mucosa (independent of the peristaltic movement of the entire gut wall) moves the mucosa and form ridges and depressions that facilitate absorption and secretion.

Rhythmic movement of villi is due to the contractions of the smooth muscle cells that travel vertically from the muscularis mucosa to the tips of villi. These contractions occur several times per minute and serve to pump lymph from lacteals into mesenteric lymphatics (Eroschenko, 2008)."}, {"name": "References", "text": "Dorland, W. (2011) Dorland's Illustrated Medical Dictionary. 32nd edn. Philadelphia, USA: Elsevier Saunders.

Eroschenko, V. P. (2008) DiFiore's Atlas of Histology with Functional Correlations. 11th edn.: Wolters Kluwer Health/Lippincott Williams & Wilkins."}]

items.name: Spermatogenesis
items.info:
[{"name": "Quick Facts", "text": "Spermatogenesis is the process of formation of spermatozoa, including both spermatocytogenesis and spermiogenesis (Dorland, 2011)."}, {"name": "Description", "text": "Spermatogenesis is the process whereby spermatozoa are formed from primitive germ cells called spermatogonia. 

Spermatogenesis begins early in puberty, at about 13–14 years of age, and continues throughout life. An adult male can produce about 1000 new sperm per second and a single ejaculate contains approximately 150 to 250 million sperm (de Kretser, Loveland and O’Bryan, 2016).

The process of spermatogenesis is described below."}, {"name": "Spermatocytogenesis", "text": "Spermatocytogenesis is the first stage of spermatogenesis, whereby spermatogonia develop into spermatocytes and eventually spermatids. There are distinct phases of spermatocytogenesis. 

—Type A dark (Ad) spermatogonia are thought to be the stem cells. They undergo mitotic division at irregular intervals giving rise to either a pair of cells of the same type, or a pair of type A pale (Ap) spermatogonia. 

—Type Ap spermatogonia continue through many mitotic divisions and establish a population of progenitor cells, the type B spermatogonia. 

—Type B spermatogonia undergo mitotic division to produce primary spermatocytes.

—Primary spermatocytes undergo two meiotic cell divisions so that the resultant haploid cells, called spermatids, contain half the original chromosome number and amount of DNA. 

—Small cells, called secondary spermatocytes, arise from the first meiotic division. These cells are very sparse in the seminiferous epithelium because they rapidly enter the second meiotic division and give rise to spermatids.

Cytoplasmic division of type Ad spermatogonia always completes after cell division; however, all other spermatogenic cells retain a connection through small cytoplasmic bridges. This intercellular bridge permits communication between primary and secondary spermatocytes and the spermatids."}, {"name": "Spermiogenesis", "text": "Spermiogenesis is the transformation of spermatids into spermatozoa. Unlike spermatocytogenesis, no cell division during spermiogenesis. There are three phases including the Golgi, acrosomal, and maturation phase.

—During the Golgi phase, spermatids contain free ribosomes, tubules of smooth endoplasmic reticulum, and very prominent Golgi complexes adjacent to the nucleus. Small pro-acrosomal granules (rich in glycoproteins) accumulate in the Golgi complex and rapidly coalesce into acrosomal granules housed within a membrane-bound acrosomal vesicle. The location of the vesicle defines the anterior pole of the developing sperm. A flagellar axoneme begins forming as the centrioles move to a location opposite the site of the future acrosomal cap.

—During the acrosomal phase, the acrosomal vesicle extends over the anterior portion of the condensed nucleus to become the acrosome. It is a specialized lysosome containing hydrolytic enzymes, in particular hyaluronidase, neuraminidase, acid phosphatase and a protease with trypsin-like activity. These enzymes will disperse the cells of the corona radiata and digest the zona pellucida. Also during this phase, the spermatid becomes oriented so that the condensed nucleus elongates and faces the seminiferous epithelium and the axoneme extends into the lumen of the seminiferous tubule. One centriole forms the flagellum and mitochondria begin to collect around its proximal portion, forming a region called the middle piece.

—The maturation phase is characterized by shedding of the cytoplasm and the cytoplasmic bridges as residual bodies which are phagocytosed by sustentocytes (Sertoli cells). Spermatozoa are then released into the seminiferous tubule lumen.

It takes about 64 days from the commencement of the division of type B spermatogonia to the release of spermatozoa into the lumen of the seminiferous tubule. Spermatogenesis does not occur as a synchronous event along the length of the seminiferous tubule. Therefore, any given view of a section of the tubule will reveal different phases of spermatogenesis (Standring, 2020)."}, {"name": "List of Clinical Correlates", "text": "—Cryptorchidism is the failure of the testis to descend into the scrotum and spermatogenesis is inhibited by abdominal temperature.

—A low sperm count may result from malnutrition, alcohol abuse, and certain drugs.

—Immotile cilia syndrome in males is characterized by immotile spermatozoa and as a result infertility (Mescher, 2013)."}, {"name": "References", "text": "de Kretser, D. M., Loveland, K. and O’Bryan, M. (2016) 'Chapter 136 - Spermatogenesis', in Jameson, J.L., De Groot, L.J., de Kretser, D.M., Giudice, L.C., Grossman, A.B., Melmed, S., Potts, J.T. and Weir, G.C. (eds.) Endocrinology: Adult and Pediatric (Seventh Edition). Philadelphia: W.B. Saunders, pp. 2325-2353.e9.

Dorland, W. (2011) Dorland's Illustrated Medical Dictionary. 32nd edn. Philadelphia, USA: Elsevier Saunders.

Mescher, A. (2013) Junqueira's Basic Histology: Text and Atlas. 13th edn.: McGraw-Hill Education.

Standring, S. (2020) Gray's Anatomy: The Anatomical Basis of Clinical Practice. 42nd edn.: Elsevier Health Sciences."}]

items.name: Mitochondria (Cone Cell)
items.info:
[{"name": "Quick Facts", "text": "Mitochondria are the small spherical to rod-shaped cytoplasmic organelles, consisting of inner and outer bilayer membranes with a space between them. The inner membrane is infolded to form a series of projections (cristae), and the space between the cristae is filled by the mitochondrial matrix, which contains DNA, RNA, ribosomes, and granules. Mitochondria generate energy (in the form of ATP synthesis) by the oxidation of nutrients, and they contain the enzymes of the tricarboxylic acid (Krebs) cycle and for fatty acid oxidation and oxidative phosphorylation. In response to toxic insults, they release enzymes that cause apoptosis. Mitochondria can replicate independently and code for the synthesis of some of their proteins; inheritance of mitochondrial DNA is maternal, and mitochondrial DNA defects cause a variety of diseases (Dorland, 2011)."}, {"name": "Structure and/or Key Features", "text": "Mitochondria are small, membrane-bound, ovoid organelles approximately 0.5-2 µm long. Each mitochondrion is lined by an inner and outer membrane. The outer membrane often attaches to other organelles, while the inner membrane is deeply folded to form invaginations, called cristae. The lumen of the mitochondria is surrounded by the inner membrane and contains the mitochondrial matrix (Gouspillou and Hepple, 2017).

Mitochondria contain their own unique DNA, referred to as mitochondrial DNA (or mtDNA), and is different from the nuclear DNA. During fertilization, mitochondria from sperm do not enter the oocyte; therefore, mitochondria are inherited from the mother’s side."}, {"name": "Anatomical Relations", "text": "The mitochondria in photoreceptor cells are most numerous in the apical portion of the inner segment. This region is known as the ellipsoid."}, {"name": "Function", "text": "Mitochondria are the energy powerhouses of the cell as it forms the majority of adenosine triphosphate (ATP) breakdown of which is the main source of chemical energy. Photoreceptors being amongst the most metabolically active cells in the body it is no surprise that they are found in high density here. Specifically, mitochondria are ideally placed in the inner segment ellipsoid where the cellular work of producing photopigment and photoreceptor membranous discs occurs."}, {"name": "References", "text": "Dorland, W. (2011) Dorland's Illustrated Medical Dictionary. 32nd edn. Philadelphia, USA: Elsevier Saunders.

Gouspillou, G. and Hepple, R. T. (2017) Mitochondria in Skeletal Muscle Health, Aging and Diseases. Frontiers Research Topics."}]

items.name: Skeletal System
items.info:
[{"name": "Quick Facts", "text": "The skeletal system includes the bones, cartilages, and joints that form the framework of the body (Dorland, 2011)."}, {"name": "Description", "text": "The skeletal system is mostly composed of bone, a type of connective tissue that is living, dynamic and highly specialized. Bones are highly variable in their size and proportion due to a range of developmental and environmental factors, such as sexual dimorphism, ethnicity and natural individual variation. 

The skeletal system has a number of functions, including:

—providing structural support to the body;

—serves as an attachment site for muscles and ligaments;

—protects and supports tissues and organs;

—stores minerals, particularly calcium, in the body;

—contains bone marrow, which is the site of blood cell production.

For descriptive purposes, the 206 bones of the skeletal system are divided into two parts: 

—axial skeleton, which is composed of the bones of the head, neck, vertebral column, and thoracic cage. 

—appendicular skeleton, which is composed of the bones of the upper and lower limbs (appendages). 

At the gross anatomical level, there are two types of bone; compact and spongy bone. Both types share the same molecular and cellular components; however, it is the variation of porosity which separates them from each other (Standring, 2016).

—Compact bone (or cortical bone) is solider and denser in appearance. It is mainly found in the walls of the shafts of long bones and the external surfaces of all bones. 

—Spongy bone (cancellous or trabecular bone) has a spongy or honeycomb-like appearance. This is due to minute bony struts within the tissue, known as trabeculae, which creates its porous appearance. It is mainly found in the vertebral bodies, short bones, and the ends of long bones.

Depending on their shape, the bones of the skeleton are categorized into five separate groups, including long, short, flat, irregular, and sesamoid bones.

—Long bones (tubular bones) are those that have an elongated tubular shaft with two expanded ends (e.g., femur, fibula, humerus, ulna).

—Short bones are those that can be of any shape but usually have similar proportions in length and width. They include all the carpal and tarsal bones. 

—Flat bones (tabular bones) bones are those that have a flat, or slightly cupped appearance (e.g., scapula, ribs, and parietal bones).

—Sesamoid bones are those that are found embedded in tendons and joint capsules. They are small and rounded (e.g., patella). 

—Irregular bones are those that do not belong to the any of the other groups and are completely nonuniform in shape (e.g., vertebrae, mandible, and hyoid).

All bones of the human body have defining features which differentiate them from each other. These bony features can be characterized in terms of parts, surfaces, and landmarks."}, {"name": "References", "text": "Dorland, W. (2011) Dorland's Illustrated Medical Dictionary. 32nd edn. Philadelphia, USA: Elsevier Saunders.

Standring, S. (2016) Gray's Anatomy: The Anatomical Basis of Clinical Practice. Gray's Anatomy Series: Elsevier Limited."}]

items.name: Bronchial Arteries
items.info: [{"name": "Quick Facts", "text": "The bronchial arteries supply the bronchi and lower trachea, and passing along the posterior sides of the bronchi to ramify about the respiratory bronchioles; distributed also to adjacent lymph nodes and pulmonary vessels (Dorland, 2011)."}, {"name": "Structure/Morphology", "text": "The bronchial arteries provide an arterial supply to the branches of the bronchial trees of the pulmonary system. These arteries belong to the systemic circulation, as opposed to the pulmonary arteries which belong to the pulmonary circulation. \n\nThe bronchial arteries arise from the thoracic descending aorta and supply the lower trachea, bronchi, and bronchioles. They are drained by the pulmonary veins (Dorland, 2011)."}, {"name": "Function", "text": "These arteries carry oxygenated blood toward the pulmonary system in order to nourish the tissues of the bronchioles. These vessels do not partake in gas exchange."}, {"name": "References", "text": "Dorland, W. (2011) Dorland's Illustrated Medical Dictionary. 32nd edn. Philadelphia, USA: Elsevier Saunders."}]

items.name: Dentogingival Fibers
Heterochromatin (Anterosuperior Cut)
items.info:
[{"name": "Quick Facts", "text": "Heterochromatin is the form of chromatin that is darkly staining and tightly coiled in interphase; it is composed of repetitive DNA, is late to replicate, and is transcriptionally inactive (Dorland, 2011)."}, {"name": "Structure and/or Key Feature(s)", "text": "Compact or very condensed chromatin visible with the light microscope is called heterochromatin. It's more tightly packed DNA. 

A clump of chromatin (heterochromatin) frequently seen in female cells is called sex chromatin and is one of the two X chromosomes and is generally inactive.

Heterochromatin stains with basic dyes and hematoxylin (Ross and Pawlina, 2006; Ovalle, Nahirney and Netter, 2013; McKinley, O'Loughlin and Pennefather-O'Brien, 2016)."}, {"name": "Function", "text": "Heterochromatin is prominent in cells that are metabolically quiescent."}, {"name": "References", "text": "Dorland, W. (2011) Dorland's Illustrated Medical Dictionary. 32nd edn. Philadelphia, USA: Elsevier Saunders.

McKinley, M. P., O'Loughlin, V. D. and Pennefather-O'Brien, E. E. (2016) Human Anatomy. 5th edn.: McGraw-Hill Education.

Ovalle, W. K., Nahirney, P. C. and Netter, F. H. (2013) Netter's Essential Histology. ClinicalKey 2012: Elsevier Saunders.

Ross, M. H. and Pawlina, W. (2006) Histology: A text and atlas. Lippincott Williams & Wilkins."}]

items.name: Nucleus (Basophil)
items.info:
[{"name": "Cell Morphology", "text": "Basophils are the rarest type of leukocytes, accounting for only 0.5% of all leukocytes. The concentration of basophils is around 20-50 per microliter of blood. 

The diameter of a basophil is 10-14 μm, making them larger the erythrocytes. Their nuclei have two lobes that are either U- or S-shaped. The cytoplasm of basophils contains large granules that contain histamine and various molecules which mediate inflammation during an allergic response (Marieb, Wilhelm and Mallatt, 2012).

Basophils have Fc receptors on their cell surface which are antibody receptors that bind to Immunoglobin E (IgE) causing an allergic reaction. Basophils also possess the CD40L protein on their cell surface. CD40L interacts with the CD40 protein that is found on the cell surface of lymphocytes. This interaction results in an additional production of type IgE, therefore, mediating an immune response against parasites (Pawlina, 2016). Basophils have a short lifespan of around 8 hours in the blood (Pawlina, 2016)."}, {"name": "Production", "text": "In the red bone marrow, a hematopoietic stem cell differentiates into a myeloid stem cell which gives rise to basophils. Development usually takes 3-7 days and mature cells are stored in marrow before release into the bloodstream (Pawlina, 2016)."}, {"name": "Function", "text": "Basophils are mediators of allergic and inflammatory responses. Histamine released by basophils is a vasodilator meaning that is increases blood flow and decreases blood pressure. Heparin released by basophils is an anticoagulant which prevents blood from clotting too quickly (Silverthorn et al., 2013). Additionally, like all granulocytes, basophils are phagocytic (Marieb, Wilhelm and Mallatt, 2012)."}, {"name": "List of Clinical Correlates", "text": "- Basophilia

- Basopenia"}, {"name": "References", "text": "Marieb, E. N., Wilhelm, P. B. and Mallatt, J. (2012) Human Anatomy. 14th edn.: Benjamin Cummings.

Pawlina, W. 2016. Histology: A text and atlas with correlated cell and molecular biology. 7th ed. Philadelphia: Wolters Kluwer.

Silverthorn, D. U., Johnson, B. R., Ober, W. C., Garrison, C. W. and Silverthorn, A. C. (2013) Human Physiology: An Integrated Approach. Pearson Education."}]

items.name: Transit Amplifying Cell (Duodenum)
items.info: [{"name": "Quick Facts", "text": "Transit amplifying cells are the daughter cells of the intestinal stem cells found in the lower half of the intestinal glands (Ross and Pawlina, 2006)."}, {"name": "Structure/Morphology", "text": "Intermediate cells occupy much of the basal regions of the intestinal glands. This population of cells is known as the amplifying compartment as these cells are actively undergoing mitosis and will differentiate into absorptive cells or goblet cells as they migrate up the epithelium to the surfaces of the villi."}, {"name": "Key Features/Anatomical Relations", "text": "Intermediate cells occupy much of the basal regions of the intestinal glands."}, {"name": "Function", "text": "This population of cells will differentiate into absorptive cells or goblet cells as they migrate up the epithelium to surfaces of the villi."}, {"name": "References", "text": "Ross, M. H. and Pawlina, W. (2016) Histology: A Text and Atlas. Wolters Kluwer Health."}]

items.name: Paracortical Region
items.info: [{"name": "Quick Facts", "text": "The paracortical region is any of the areas of the peripheral lymphoid organs populated by T lymphocytes, e.g., the periarteriolar lymphatic sheath in the spleen, the paracortex in lymph nodes, and the parafollicular areas of gut-associated lymphoid tissue (Dorland, 2011)."}, {"name": "Structure/Morphology", "text": "The paracortical region (or paracortex) is a homogenous zone that contains T lymphocytes and interdigitating dendritic cells. Dendritic cells present processed antigens to the T-cells. When stimulated, the T-cells proliferate and enlarge, thus expanding the paracortical region greatly, but do not produce follicular structures such as those in the cortex. The matured T-cells are dispersed to peripheral sites (Willard-Mack, 2006)."}, {"name": "Anatomical Relations", "text": "The paracortex is an ill-defined zone located between the cortex and the medulla."}, {"name": "Function", "text": "In the paracortex, T-cells proliferate and enlarge when exposed to antigens."}, {"name": "References", "text": "Dorland, W. (2011) Dorland's Illustrated Medical Dictionary. 32nd edn. Philadelphia, USA: Elsevier Saunders.\n\nWillard-Mack, C. L. (2006) 'Normal structure, function, and histology of lymph nodes', Toxicologic Pathology, 5(34), pp. 409-424."}]

items.name: Primary Fiber Bundles
items.info:
[{"name": "Quick Facts", "text": "The primary fibrous bundle includes collagen fibers wrapped in endotendon."}, {"name": "Structure and/or Key Feature(s)", "text": "The primary fiber bundle is an aggregation of collagen fibers, surrounded by endotendon. The quantity of collagen fibers in each primary fiber bundle varies between individual tendons. When transected, it has a triangular shape with relatively sharp corners (Kannus, 2000).

The diameter of individual primary fiber bundles is estimated to be between 15 µm to 400 µm (Franchi et al., 2007). Similar to the secondary and tertiary fiber bundles, the primary fiber bundles have a complex structure considering the complexity of collagen fibers and fibrils with which it is made up of. The fibrils within each collagen fiber are oriented longitudinally, as well as horizontally and transversely. The longitudinal fibers which are oriented parallel to each other, cross each other as they run along the length of a tendon (Kannus, 2000)."}, {"name": "Anatomical Relations", "text": "Collagen fibers are bound together to form several primary fiber bundles. Multiple primary fiber bundles are bunched together to form secondary fiber bundles, and multiple secondary fiber bundles are bunched together to form tertiary fiber bundles. Tertiary fiber bundles are bound together to form the whole tendon unit. The fiber bundles are surrounded by endotendon."}, {"name": "Function", "text": "The complex structure of the primary fiber bundles in combination with the tertiary and secondary fiber bundles enable the tendon to carry out its function of relaying force generated by the muscles to the bone. This facilitates the movement of joints (Kannus, 2000)."}, {"name": "References", "text": "Franchi, M., Trirè, A., Quaranta, M., Orsini, E. and Ottani, V. (2007) 'Collagen structure of tendon relates to function', ScientificWorldJournal, 7, pp. 404-20.

Kannus, P. (2000) 'Structure of the tendon connective tissue', Scand J Med Sci Sports, 10(6), pp. 312-20."}]

items.name: Submucosa of Small Intestine (Jejunum)
items.info:
[{"name": "Quick Facts", "text": "The submucosa is the layer of dense connective tissue between the mucosa and the muscularis externa in most parts of the digestive, respiratory, urinary, and genital tracts (Dorland, 2011)."}, {"name": "Structure/Morphology", "text": "The submucosa is essentially a dense, irregular connective tissue layer found deep than the mucosa. It contains blood and lymphatic vessels. Blood vessels form large plexuses in the submucosa. Lacteals originating in the lamina propria of villi form a plexus near the muscularis mucosa (the outermost layer of the mucosa). From there, they flow to lymph nodules in the submucosa and unite to accompany blood vessels out of the intestine.

The submucosal (Meissner’s) nerve plexus is only visible as scattered ganglion cell bodies with satellite cells lying within the submucosal elements.

Glandular tissue is prominent in the duodenum (as “Brunner’s” or submucosal glands) where they dominate the lamina propria and the submucosa. These compound tubular glands have both serous (zymogen) and mucous secreting components.

The submucosa (and the lamina propria) in the ileum contains aggregations of lymphoid nodules known as “Peyer’s patches.” They are an important component of the gut associated lymphatic tissue (GALT). In humans there are about 30 patches. Each patch may contain 10–200 lymph nodules. At the luminal surface, they appear as a dome-shaped region devoid of villi. The epithelial surface consists of low cuboidal “M” (microfold) cells rather than absorptive cells (enterocytes) (Ross and Pawlina, 2016)."}, {"name": "Key Features/Anatomical Relations", "text": "Plicae circulares are circular transverse folds that extend up to two thirds the circumference of the lumen. They contain a core of the submucosa. They begin about 5–6 cm beyond the pylorus and are most numerous towards the end or distal part of the duodenum."}, {"name": "Function", "text": "The blood vessels within the submucosa nourish the layers of the intestinal wall as well as removing absorbed products of digestion.

The submucosal (Meissner’s) plexus is mainly responsible for innervating the smooth muscle layers of the muscularis mucosae.

Brunner’s glands secretions are between a pH of 8.1 and 9.3 and contain alkaline glycoproteins and bicarbonate which neutralizes the acidic containing chyme entering the duodenum from the stomach. Another function of these secretions is to create a pH ideal for the actions of pancreatic enzymes delivered to the duodenum.

M cells are antigen-transporting cells and carry antigens from the intestinal lumen to reach immune cells within the lamina propria of the digestive tract or gut associated lymphatic tissue (GALT).

Lacteals and the lymphatic vessels are important for the absorption of lipids."}, {"name": "References", "text": "Dorland, W. (2011) Dorland's Illustrated Medical Dictionary. 32nd edn. Philadelphia, USA: Elsevier Saunders.

Ross, M. H. and Pawlina, W. (2016) Histology: A Text and Atlas. Wolters Kluwer Health."}]

items.name: Epineurial Nerves
items.info: [{"name": "Quick Facts", "text": "The epineurial nerves are part of the nervi nervorum and supply the nerve."}, {"name": "Structure/Morphology", "text": "The epineurial nerves are located in the external epineurium and form part of the nervi nervorum. The nervi nervorum can be described as the nerves innervating a nerve. They are made up of sympathetic and sensory nerve fibers found within the connective tissue of the nerve trunk (Bove and Light, 1997)."}, {"name": "Anatomical Relations", "text": "The nervi nervorum originates from nerve fibers and the perivascular plexus (nerves innervating the blood vessels of the nerve). They serve as the intrinsic innervation of nerve sheaths and are found within all connective tissue coverings of the nerve trunk, including epineurium, perineurium and endoneurium."}, {"name": "Function", "text": "The nervi nervorum are typically capable of mechanoreceptor function and some are capable of nociception, which is the detection of noxious chemical, mechanical and thermal stimuli (Bove and Light, 1997)."}, {"name": "References", "text": "Bove, G. M. and Light, A. R. (1997) 'The nervi nervorum: Missing link for neuropathic pain?', Pain Forum, 6(3), pp. 181-190."}]

items.name: Conjunctiva
items.info: [{"name": "Quick Facts", "text": "The conjunctiva is the delicate membrane that lines the eyelids and covers the exposed surface of the sclera (Dorland, 2011)."}, {"name": "Structure and/or Key Feature(s)", "text": "The conjunctiva is a transparent mucous membrane that extends and covers the posterior surface of the eyelids. It then folds back on itself forming the fornices and extends over the eyeball, covering the sclera up to its junction with the cornea."}, {"name": "Anatomical Relations", "text": "The conjunctiva is continuous with the skin of the eyelids and with the lacrimal canaliculi and lacrimal sac."}, {"name": "Function", "text": "The conjunctiva contains cells that produce mucus and tears that lubricate the eye. It also plays a defensive role in protecting the surface of the eyeball from infection."}, {"name": "References", "text": "Dorland, W. (2011) Dorland's Illustrated Medical Dictionary. 32nd edn. Philadelphia, USA: Elsevier Saunders."}]

items.name: D Cell
items.info:
[{"name": "Quick Facts", "text": "A D cell is a type of islet cell that secretes somatostatin (Dorland, 2011)."}, {"name": "Structure and/or Key Feature(s)", "text": "Only about 5–10% of the pancreatic endocrine cells are D cells and they tend to be around the periphery of the islet. The cytoplasm of the D cells contain large, low to medium electron dense secretory granules (containing somatostatin) ranging from 300 nm to 350 nm in diameter (Ross and Pawlina, 2016)."}, {"name": "Function", "text": "D cells secrete somatostatin. Somatostatin inhibits the release of hormones from other islet cells via a paracrine secretion mechanism (Mescher, 2013)."}, {"name": "References", "text": "Dorland, W. (2011) Dorland's Illustrated Medical Dictionary. 32nd edn. Philadelphia, USA: Elsevier Saunders.

Mescher, A. (2013) Junqueira's Basic Histology: Text and Atlas. 13th edn.: McGraw-Hill Education.

Ross, M. H. and Pawlina, W. (2016) Histology: A Text and Atlas. Wolters Kluwer Health."}]

items.name: Endomembrane System
items.info:
[{"name": "Quick Facts", "text": "The endomembrane system refers to the sarcoplasmic reticulum and the transverse tubules (Wirtz et al., 2012)."}, {"name": "Structure", "text": "The endomembrane system of the skeletal muscle fiber refers to the network composed of the sarcoplasmic reticulum and the transverse tubules (Wirtz et al., 2012). Organelles such as the nucleus, ribosomes, endoplasmic reticulum, and mitochondria are often considered part of this system in other cell types. 

The sarcoplasmic reticulum (SR) is an organelle that consists of a network of loose flattened tubules with various compartments, many of which contain Ca2+. The two ends of the SR are wider, thus form terminal sacs called cisternae. Two cisternae of adjacent sarcoplasmic reticula and one transverse tubule form a functional unit called a triad, which operates to elicit the release of Ca2+ from SR stores (Maclennan and Zvaritch, 2011). 

Transverse tubules are extensions of the sarcolemma, made up of interconnecting rings, each of which surround individual myofibrils. Similar to the sarcolemma, the tubules are composed of two lipid bilayers."}, {"name": "Key Features/Anatomical Relations", "text": "Sarcoplasmic reticulum is a specialized type of smooth endoplasmic reticulum found in skeletal muscle. It forms a network of tubules that extend through a muscle fiber. The flattened tubules surround, but do not make direct contact with the myofibrils in a muscle fiber. 

Transverse tubules run from the sarcolemma transversely across the fiber at the junction of the A- and I-bands. The sarcolemma is the cell membrane that encloses the muscle fiber."}, {"name": "Function", "text": "The sarcoplasmic reticulum functions as an intracellular calcium store. Depolarization of the sarcoplasmic reticulum membrane results in the release of calcium ions (Ca2+). This release of calcium ions triggers the cascade required for contraction. 

The primary function of transverse tubules is to facilitate the conduction of signals from outside the fiber to the myofibrils. Transverse tubules are the site for excitation-contraction coupling. When an electric signal excites the sarcolemma, the signal travels down along the T-tubules to the sarcoplasmic reticulum, which releases Ca2+ for contraction."}, {"name": "List of Clinical Correlates", "text": "—Fatigue

—Central core disease"}, {"name": "References", "text": "Maclennan, D. H. and Zvaritch, E. (2011) 'Mechanistic models for muscle diseases and disorders originating in the sarcoplasmic reticulum', Biochim Biophys Acta, 1813(5), pp. 948-64.

Wirtz, K. W. A., Packer, L., Gustafsson, J. Å., Evangelopoulos, A. E. and Changeux, J. P. (2012) New Developments in Lipid-Protein Interactions and Receptor Function. Nato Science Series A:: Springer US."}]

items.name: Myelin Lamella (Longitudinal Section)
items.info: [{"name": "Structure and/or Key Features", "text": "In the central nervous system, the myelin sheath consists of extensions of the plasmalemma of the oligodendrocyte forming concentric layers (or lamellae) around neighboring axons. The myelin sheath can thicken from a just few lamellae to about 200 lamellae (Standring, 2016)."}, {"name": "References", "text": "Standring, S. (2016) Gray's Anatomy: The Anatomical Basis of Clinical Practice. Gray's Anatomy Series 41 edn.: Elsevier Limited."}]

items.name: Perilymphatic Cells of Scala Tympani
items.info:
[{"name": "Quick Facts", "text": "The perilymphatic cells maintain the balance of ionic contents in the perilymph and endolymph."}, {"name": "Structure and/or Key Feature(s)", "text": "The inner aspect of the bony labyrinth is lined by perilymphatic cells with interspersed extracellular fibers. These perilymphatic cells have varying cell morphology based on their location in the bony labyrinth.

The perilymphatic cells lining the periosteum are generally very flat, resembling a squamous epithelium. They contain tight junctions, which creates a diffusion barrier between it and the endolymph in the cochlear duct. Perilymphatic cells on the basilar membrane facing into the scala tympani are cuboidal in shape.

In the narrower areas of the cochlea, such as where the scala vestibuli approaching the helicotrema, the perilymphatic cells have a different form. They have a stellate or reticular (cross-linked in a network fashion) in appearance and may have thin cytoplasmic projections extending across the space (Standring, 2016)."}, {"name": "Function", "text": "The perilymphatic cells maintain the balance of ionic contents in the perilymph and endolymph."}, {"name": "List of Clinical Correlates", "text": "—Meniere's disease"}, {"name": "References", "text": "Standring, S. (2016) Gray's Anatomy: The Anatomical Basis of Clinical Practice., 41st edition. Elsevier Limited."}]

items.name: Choroid
items.info:
[{"name": "Quick Facts", "text": "The choroid is the thin, pigmented, vascular coat of the eyeball extending from the ora serrata to the optic nerve; it furnishes blood supply to the retina and conducts arteries and nerves to the anterior structures (Dorland, 2011)."}, {"name": "Structure and/or Key Features", "text": "Along with the ciliary body and iris, the choroid forms part of the vascular layer of the eyeball. It is approximately 200 µm thick at birth, but this thickness decreases with age (Nickla and Wallman, 2010).

The choroid contains dense vascular beds supported by collagen and elastic connective tissue. The finest of these vessels are on the innermost aspect of the choroid and is called the capillary lamina of the choroid or choriocapillaris. This layer is so vascularized, it is responsible for the “red-eye” that can be observed when using flash photography. External to the choriocapillaris, the choroid contains much larger blood vessels that supply these vascular beds. These are called Haller’s and Sattler’s layers. 

The anterior choriocapillaris receives its blood supply from the long posterior ciliary arteries and recurrent branches of the anterior ciliary arteries, while the posterior choroid receives blood from the short posterior ciliary arteries.

The outermost layer of the choroid is the suprachoroid, which forms the transition between the choroid and the fibrous capsule surrounding it, the sclera. Here, the choroid contains numerous melanocytes that gives it a dark reddish pigmentation."}, {"name": "Anatomical Relations", "text": "The choroid sits between the outer sclera and the inner retina. It extends from the optic nerve posteriorly, where it’s continuous with the internal sheath of the optic nerve. Here, the choroid is firmly attached to the sclera, however, elsewhere it may only be loosely attached to the sclera."}, {"name": "Function", "text": "The vascular beds of the choriocapillaris are vital for supplying the adjacent avascular retina with oxygen and nutrients. There is a strong oxygen/carbon dioxide diffusion gradient between the choroid and the outermost layers of the retina, where the outer segments and cell bodies of the rod and cone photoreceptors are located. As these cells are highly metabolically active, but the layers avascular to maintain clarity, oxygen diffusion from the choroid is essential for retinal function. Additionally, the choroid is likely involved in thermoregulation and modulates intraocular pressure via vasomotor control of blood flow, and drainage of aqueous humor from the anterior chamber via the ureoscleral pathway (Nickla and Wallman, 2010)."}, {"name": "References", "text": "Dorland, W. (2011) Dorland's Illustrated Medical Dictionary. 32nd edn. Philadelphia, USA: Elsevier Saunders.

Nickla, D. L. and Wallman, J. (2010) 'The multifunctional choroid', Prog Retin Eye Res, 29(2), pp. 144-68."}]

items.name: Primary Oocyte (of Early Primary Ovarian Follicle)
items.audio: Primary Oocyte (of Early Primary Ovarian Follicle).mp3
items.info:
[{"name": "Quick Facts", "text": "The primary oocyte is an oocyte that has begun but not completed the first maturation division; it is derived from an oogonium by differentiation near the time of birth (Dorland, 2011)."}, {"name": "Structure and/or Key Feature(s)", "text": "Although primary oocytes begin their first meiotic division in utero, the first meiotic prophase remains incomplete until just prior to ovulation, which means many remain arrested in their first meiotic division for 12 to perhaps 50 years.

The primary oocyte of the primordial ovarian follicle is about 30 μm in diameter and has a large round, eccentric, pale nucleus containing one or two prominent nucleoli.

The ooplasm (cytoplasm of an oocyte) contains Golgi membranes and vesicles, endoplasmic reticulum, centrioles, and many mitochondria and lysosomes. These organelles are condensed into a region in the ooplasm referred to as a Balbiani body. The ooplasm also contains stacks of membranes called annulate lamellae.

Organelles increase their numbers and become scattered throughout the ooplasm as the oocyte matures. Lipid droplets and masses of lipochrome pigment may appear. Beneath the plasma membrane (oolemma) special secretory granules called cortical granules appear which contain proteases.

As the zona pellucida is being deposited, many irregular microvilli project from the oolemma into the perivitelline space between the oocyte and the granulosa cells to intermingle with similar microvilli projecting from adjacent granulosa cells. 

When the first meiotic division is completed in a mature follicle equal share of chromatin is distributed to each daughter cell but only one receives most of the cytoplasm to become a secondary oocyte. The other daughter cell becomes the first polar body.

The second meiotic division commences immediately after the first meiotic division is completed (Ross and Pawlina, 2006; Mescher, 2013; McKinley, O'Loughlin and Pennefather-O'Brien, 2016)."}, {"name": "List of Clinical Correlates", "text": "The long period of meiotic arrest may expose the primary oocyte to factors which could contribute to errors in meiotic division such as nondisjunction. Such an error results in anomalies such as trisomy of chromosome 21 (Down’s syndrome)."}, {"name": "References", "text": "Dorland, W. (2011) Dorland's Illustrated Medical Dictionary. 32nd edn. Philadelphia, USA: Elsevier Saunders.

McKinley, M. P., O'Loughlin, V. D. and Pennefather-O'Brien, E. E. (2016) Human Anatomy. 5th edn.: McGraw-Hill Education.

Mescher, A. (2013) Junqueira's Basic Histology: Text and Atlas. 13th edn.: McGraw-Hill Education.

Ross, M. H. and Pawlina, W. (2006) Histology: A text and atlas. Lippincott Williams & Wilkins."}]
