items.name: Sodium Ions
items.info: [{"name": "Structure", "text": "Sodium ions are positively charged. They are the most abundant ions in the extracellular fluid. \n\nNeurotransmitters released from the presynaptic component diffuse across the synaptic cleft and subsequently bind to and open voltage-gated sodium channels. The influx of sodium into the cell causes local depolarization (reversal of the negative membrane potential of the resting membrane) in the postsynaptic membrane (Ross and Pawlina, 2006)."}, {"name": "Function", "text": "Sodium ions are responsible for the initiation of action potentials in the presynaptic element and the subsequent depolarization of the postsynaptic neuron. Sodium ions also play a role in water balance."}, {"name": "References", "text": "Ross, M. H. and Pawlina, W. (2006) Histology: A text and atlas. Lippincott Williams & Wilkins."}]

items.name: Granulosa Lutein Cell
items.info:
[{"name": "Quick Facts", "text": "Granulosa lutein cells are lutein cells of the corpus luteum derived from granulosa cells (Dorland, 2011)."}, {"name": "Structure and/or Key Feature(s)", "text": "Granulosa lutein cells do not divide after ovulation but do increase in size (20–35 µm in diameter) and make up about 80% of the parenchyma of the corpus luteum. As granulosa cells in the preovulatory follicle, they were predominantly protein secreting cells. After ovulation they undergo a process called luteinization, where they differentiate into steroid secreting cells. Therefore, granulosa lutein cells contain numerous lipid droplets, large amounts of smooth (agranular) endoplasmic reticulum, and mitochondria with tubular cristae (Mescher, 2013; Ross & Pawlina, 2016)."}, {"name": "Function", "text": "Granulosa lutein cells synthesize estrogens, progesterone, and inhibin. Inhibin regulates the synthesis and secretion of FSH from the anterior pituitary."}, {"name": "References", "text": "Dorland, W. (2011) Dorland's Illustrated Medical Dictionary. 32nd edn. Philadelphia, USA: Elsevier Saunders.

Mescher, A. (2013) Junqueira's Basic Histology: Text and Atlas. 13th edn.: McGraw-Hill Education.

Ross, M. H. and Pawlina, W. (2006) Histology: A text and atlas. Lippincott Williams & Wilkins."}]

items.name: First Polar Body (Inferior)
items.info:
[{"name": "Quick Facts", "text": "Polar bodies are small nonfunctional cells with a haploid chromosome complement, consisting of a small amount of cytoplasm and a nucleus, resulting from unequal division of the primary oocyte(first polar body) and, if fertilization occurs, of the secondary oocyte(second polar body) (Dorland, 2011)."}, {"name": "Structure", "text": "The first polar body forms at the completion of the first meiotic division of the primary oocyte. The diploid (contains 46 chromosomes) primary oocyte completes meiosis I the day before ovulation, which results in the production of two haploid daughter cells (containing 23 chromosomes). These daughter cells are the secondary oocyte and the first polar body, both of which have identical chromosomal content. 

The secondary oocyte and the first polar body differ in size as a result of the uneven manner in which the cytoplasm is shared between the two cells. The secondary oocyte is estimated to be 100 times larger in size that the first polar body. The first polar body, under normal circumstances, does not proceed to meiosis II with the secondary oocyte (Gitlin, Gibbons and Gosden, 2003; Meneely et al., 2017).

The polar body possesses a nucleus, ribosomes, Golgi apparatus, mitochondria, and cortical granules, and a number of additional cytoplasmic material, all with an uncertain level of functionality. The first polar body usually disintegrates by way of apoptosis within 24 hours.

The secondary oocyte commences meiosis II, which is arrested at metaphase until fertilization occurs."}, {"name": "Key Features/Anatomical Relations", "text": "The first polar body is located between the zona pellucida and the cell membrane of the secondary oocyte. The name “polar body” was coined from its polar position in the oocyte (Schmerler and Wessel, 2011)."}, {"name": "Function", "text": "The function of the first polar body is to rid the secondary oocyte of the extra haploid set of chromosomes after meiosis I is completed.

The first polar body is useful in the process of artificial reproductive techniques. For instance, the structural assessment of the first polar body is used to assess fertilization, development, and implantation/pregnancy outcomes following in-vitro fertilization (IVF) and intracytoplasmic sperm injection (ICSI) (Gitlin, Gibbons and Gosden, 2003).

Polar bodies may also play a vital role in the evaluation of human genetic diseases. The genetic material situated within polar bodies can be used to ascertain the quality of an oocyte, as well as identify genetic aberrations in a minimally invasive assay (Schmerler and Wessel, 2011). Genetic analysis of the first polar body can be useful in screening for single gene defects in maternal mutations (Strauss and Barbieri, 2009)."}, {"name": "List of Clinical Correlates", "text": "- Polar body biopsy 

- Preimplantation genetic diagnosis 

- Twinning 

- Prenatal diagnosis 

- Assisted reproductive technology"}, {"name": "References", "text": "Dorland, W. (2011) Dorland's Illustrated Medical Dictionary. 32nd edn. Philadelphia, USA: Elsevier Saunders.

Gitlin, S. A., Gibbons, W. E. and Gosden, R. G. (2003) 'Oocyte biology and genetics revelations from polar bodies', Reprod Biomed Online, 6(4), pp. 403-9.

Meneely, P. M., Hoang, R. D., Okeke, I. N. and Heston, K. (2017) Genetics: Genes, Genomes, and Evolution. Oxford University Press.

Schmerler, S. and Wessel, G. M. (2011) 'Polar bodies--more a lack of understanding than a lack of respect', Molecular reproduction and development, 78(1), pp. 3-8.

Strauss, J. F. and Barbieri, R. L. (2009) Yen and Jaffe's Reproductive Endocrinology: Physiology, Pathophysiology, and Clinical Management. Saunders/Elsevier."}]

items.name: Loose Connective Tissue
items.info:
[{"name": "Quick Facts", "text": "Loose connective tissue is a type of connective tissue in which the interlacing collagen and elastin fibers are not tightly packed; it provides connections between adjacent structures but allows them to move independently; it also has a greater density of cells and vessels than dense connective tissue (Dorland, 2011)."}, {"name": "Structure", "text": "The loose connective tissue is the fourth layer of the scalp. It is composed of a thin layer of loose fibroareolar tissue that contains a network of reticular and elastic fibers and collagen. It is loosely bound to the overlying epicranial aponeurosis, which accounts for the mobility of the scalp over the underlying calvaria.

Emissary veins traverse the loose connective tissue layer of the scalp and, along with the diploic veins, connect the intracranial dural sinuses with the extracranial veins. The loose connective tissue is often called the subaponeurotic space, or “danger space,” since localized infections within this layer have the potential to spread intracranially (Thompson and Yeung, 2016). The subaponeurotic space is limited anteriorly by the frontal belly and posteriorly by the occipital belly of the occipitofrontalis muscle."}, {"name": "Key Features/Anatomical Relations", "text": "The loose connective tissue of the scalp separated the epicranial aponeurosis from the pericranium of the calvaria."}, {"name": "Function", "text": "The loose connective tissue of the scalp allows the scalp proper (the skin, superficial fascia, and epicranial aponeurosis) to glide over the calvaria."}, {"name": "List of Clinical Correlates", "text": "—Scalp lacerations

—Scalp infections

—Subgaleal hemorrhage

—Osteomyelitis

—Brain abscess"}, {"name": "References", "text": "Dorland, W. (2011) Dorland's Illustrated Medical Dictionary. 32nd edn. Philadelphia, USA: Elsevier Saunders.

Thompson, S. H. and Yeung, A. Y. (2016) 'Anatomy Relevant to Head, Neck, and Orofacial Infections', in Hupp, J.R. and Ferneini, E.M. (eds.) Head, Neck, and Orofacial Infections. St. Louis: Elsevier, pp. 60-93."}]

items.name: Peripolar Cell
items.info: [{"name": "Quick Facts", "text": "Peripolar cells are a population of cells found at the vascular poles of the glomerular capsule (Gardiner et al., 1991)."}, {"name": "Structure and/or Key Feature(s)", "text": "The peripolar cells contain numerous cytoplasmic granules, which appear to be secretory. They are usually spare and variable in number (Gardiner, More and Lindop, 1986)."}, {"name": "Anatomical Relations", "text": "The peripolar cells are found at the vascular pole of the renal corpuscle and are associated with the afferent arteriole."}, {"name": "Function", "text": "It is suggested that peripolar cells form part of the juxtaglomerular apparatus. They may be secretory cells that play a role in renal tubular function (Gardiner, More and Lindop, 1986)."}, {"name": "References", "text": "Gardiner, D. S., Downie, I., Gibson, I. W., More, I. A. and Lindop, G. B. (1991) 'The glomerular peripolar cell: a review', Histol Histopathol, 6(4), pp. 567-73.\n\nGardiner, D. S., More, I. A. and Lindop, G. B. (1986) 'The granular peripolar cell of the human glomerulus: an ultrastructural study', Journal of anatomy, 146, pp. 31-43."}]

items.name: Cytoplasm (End Piece; Left)
items.info:
[{"name": "Quick Facts", "text": "The cytoplasm is the protoplasm of a cell exclusive of that of the nucleus; it consists of a continuous aqueous solution (cytosol) and the organelles and inclusions suspended in it and is the site of most of the chemical activities of the cell (Dorland, 2011)."}, {"name": "Structure and/or Key Feature(s)", "text": "The cytoplasm of a cell includes an aqueous solution, the cytosol, and the organelles of the cell suspended in it. It is tightly enclosed by the plasma membrane. The sperm contains a limited amount of cytoplasm. During normal spermatogenesis (or maturation), spermatids lose most of their cytoplasm. Remnants may remain as a cytoplasmic droplet at the neck region of the sperm and is shed during ejaculation. However, retention of the droplets may indicate failure of normal maturation and cause infertility (Rengan et al, 2012).

The mature sperm retains a thin layer of cytoplasm underneath the plasma membrane. In the head, the space occupied by cytoplasm between the acrosome and the nucleus is known as the subacrosomal (or perinuclear) space. The cytoplasm between the outer membrane of the acrosome and the plasma membrane is the periacrosomal space."}, {"name": "Function", "text": "The cytoplasm is the site where most chemical activities of the cell occur."}, {"name": "References", "text": "Dorland, W. (2011) Dorland's Illustrated Medical Dictionary. 32nd edn. Philadelphia, USA: Elsevier Saunders.

Rengan, A. K., Agarwal, A., van der Linde, M. & du Plessis, S. S. (2012) An investigation of excess residual cytoplasm in human spermatozoa and its distinction from the cytoplasmic droplet. Reproductive biology and endocrinology : RB&E, 10, 92-92."}]

However, occasionally they travel separately and exit as an emissary vein (Standring, 2016)."}, {"name": "References", "text": "Standring, S. items.info: [{"name": "Structure and/or Key Feature(s)", "text": "The subcutaneous tissue of the clitoris is the loose external layer of fascia. It's continuous with the membranous layer of subcutaneous tissue of the perineum (Jackson et al., 2019)."}, {"name": "References", "text": "Jackson, L. A., Hare, A. M., Carrick, K. S., Ramirez, D. M. O., Hamner, J. J. and Corton, M. M. (2019) 'Anatomy, histology, and nerve density of clitoris and associated structures: clinical applications to vulvar surgery', American Journal of Obstetrics and Gynecology, 221(5), pp. 519.e1-519.e9."}]

items.name: Orbiculus ciliaris
items.info: [{"name": "Quick Facts", "text": "The orbiculus ciliaris is the thin part of the ciliary body extending between its crown and the ora serrata retinae (Dorland, 2011)."}, {"name": "Structure and/or Key Feature(s)", "text": "The orbiculus ciliaris (ciliary ring or pars plana) is the proximal, or posterior, part of the ciliary body that is directly continuous with the retina by way of the ora serrata. \n\nIt is covered by a double layer of highly organized epithelium. The outer layer is pigmented with melanin, while the inner layer is unpigmented. At the ora serrata, the retina pigment epithelium is continuous with the pigmented layer of the orbiculus ciliaris. The inner, unpigmented, neural retina is continuous with the unpigmented layer of the orbiculus ciliaris. Anteriorly, the epithelium continues over the corona ciliaris to merge with the epithelium on the posterior iris."}, {"name": "Anatomical Relations", "text": "The suspensory ligaments passing radially from the margin of the lens pass through the corona ciliaris portion of the ciliary body at the ciliary folds. They are anchored to the basal lamina of the superficial epithelial layer of the orbiculus ciliaris."}, {"name": "Function", "text": "The orbiculus ciliaris helps suspend the lens by tightly binding the zonular fibers of the lens. Therefore, when the smooth muscle of the ciliary body contracts, it changes the refractive power of the lens in a process called accommodation."}, {"name": "List of Clinical Correlates", "text": "\u2014Access to the interior of the eyeball for injection of intraocular surgical instruments is typically accomplished at the level of the orbiculus ciliaris (ciliary ring) where they are least likely to damage the lens or retina."}, {"name": "References", "text": "Dorland, W. (2011) Dorland's Illustrated Medical Dictionary. 32nd edn. Philadelphia, USA: Elsevier Saunders."}]

items.name: Deep Artery of Penis
items.info:
[{"name": "Quick Facts", "text": "Origin: Internal pudendal artery.

Course: Penetrates the perineal membrane to enter the crus and supply the crus and corpus cavernosum of the body. 

Branches: Helicine branches. 

Supplied Structures: Corpora cavernosa of the penis.
"}, {"name": "Origin", "text": "The deep artery of the penis is one of two terminal branches of the internal pudendal artery, the other being the dorsal artery of the penis. "}, {"name": "Course", "text": "The deep artery of the penis penetrates the perineal membrane to enter the corpora cavernosa in the crus of the penis. It continues towards the glans penis. "}, {"name": "Branches", "text": "Within each corpus cavernosum, the deep artery of the penis gives off several helicine branches. They open directly into the vascular spaces supported and enclosed by the trabeculae (Standring, 2020)."}, {"name": "Supplied Structures", "text": "The deep artery of the penis supplies the corpora cavernosa in the crus, body, and glans of the penis."}, {"name": "Clinical Correlates", "text": "Stimulation from sympathetic neurons maintains the smooth muscle in the tunica media of the helicine arteries in a tonic contractile state. The arteries remain coiled and the little blood that flows through them passes directly to the deep dorsal vein. Stimulation from parasympathetic neurons relaxes the tonic state and blood flows into the corpora cavernosa resulting in penile erection. One unique feature of these arteries is the presence of valves which prevent the flow of blood back through the corpora cavernosa.

The relaxation of the artery wall, due to parasympathetic innervation, is mediated by nitric oxide (NO). NO binds to guanylate cyclase increasing levels of cyclic guanosine monophosphate (cGMP) which then stimulates relaxation of the smooth muscle in the tunica media and so dilation of blood vessels and penile erection. Erection subsides when cGMP is broken down by cGMP specific phosphodiesterase type 5 (PDE5).

Drugs used to treat erectile dysfunction prevent PDE5 from breaking down cGMP and so the effects of NO are increased, and vasodilation occurs resulting in penile erection."}, {"name": "References", "text": "Standring, S. (2020) Gray's Anatomy: The Anatomical Basis of Clinical Practice. 42nd edn.: Elsevier Health Sciences."}]

items.name: Somatic Sensory Afferent Nerve Fiber
items.info: [{"name": "Quick Facts", "text": "Afferent nerve fibers or axons are nerve fibers that convey sensory impulses from the periphery to the central nervous system; classified according to function as somatic afferent and visceral afferent fibers (Dorland, 2011)."}, {"name": "Structure/Morphology", "text": "Somatic sensory afferent nerve fibers are composed of cell bodies and axons and their surrounding myelin sheath."}, {"name": "Key Features/Anatomical Relations", "text": "Somatic sensory afferent nerves have pseudounipolar cell bodies that are located in the dorsal root ganglia of spinal and cranial nerves."}, {"name": "Function", "text": "Somatic sensory afferent nerve fibers transmit sensory information from the sensory organs to the central nervous system. The general sensations, such as the sense of touch, pain, pressure, vibration, temperature, and proprioception from skin, body wall, limbs, and joints are relayed into the dorsal root ganglia of the spinal nerves. While the special sensations, such as the sense of vision, taste, hearing, smell, and balance/equilibrium are relayed into the peripheral ganglia of the cranial nerves. From the ganglia onwards, the sensory information is then conducted to the central nervous system; spinal cord and brain (Patestas and Gartner, 2016)."}, {"name": "References", "text": "Dorland, W. (2011) Dorland's Illustrated Medical Dictionary. 32nd edn. Philadelphia, USA: Elsevier Saunders.\n\nPatestas, M. and Gartner, L. (2016). A Textbook of Neuroanatomy. 2nd ed. New Jersey: Wiley, Blackwell."}]

items.name: Fibrous Layer of Periosteum
items.info:
[{"name": "Quick Facts", "text": "Periosteum is a specialized connective tissue covering all bones of the body; in adults, it consists of two layers that are not sharply defined, the external fibrous layer being a network of dense connective tissue containing blood vessels, and the internal osteogenic layer composed of more loosely arranged collagenous bundles with spindle-shaped connective tissue cells, osteogenic precursor cells, and a network of thin elastic fibers (Dorland, 2011)."}, {"name": "Structure/Morphology", "text": "The fibrous layer of periosteum is the outermost enveloping layer of the bone. It consists of dense regular connective tissue containing fibroblast cells dispersed among an organized framework of collagen fibers. It may contain some elastic fibers, however, not as much as the osteogenic layer. Also found within the fibrous layer of periosteum are several blood and lymphatic vessels, as well as nerves (mainly sensory). These form plexuses before branching into the underlying compact bone below, via perforating canals, also known as Volkmann’s canals (Omelyanenko et al., 2016)."}, {"name": "Anatomical Relations", "text": "The fibrous layer of periosteum covers the entire bone except for its articular surfaces, and areas of muscle attachment. This is in contrast to the osteogenic layer of periosteum which can be discontinuous around the metaphysis of the bone. Fibers of tendons, ligaments, and fascia attach to the fibrous layer of periosteum, before extending further in the compact bone."}, {"name": "Function", "text": "The fibrous layer of periosteum provides mechanical strength to the periosteum, which in turn provides considerable support to the bone. It also assists in transmission of mechanical forces produced by a muscular contraction across a greater area of the bone. The fibrous layer of periosteum has an integral role in the maintenance of bone structure by means of the vasculature and nerves which it transmits to the underlying bone. Due to the presence of sensory receptors, the fibrous layer of periosteum is the most pain-sensitive area of bone, which can be caused by a number of factors including trauma and osteoarthritis (Standring, 2016). In addition, the periosteum is thought to play a major role in the bone-healing process by providing cells to the site of injury."}, {"name": "List of Clinical Correlates", "text": "—Periostitis/periosteal reaction"}, {"name": "References", "text": "Dorland, W. (2011) Dorland's Illustrated Medical Dictionary. 32nd edn. Philadelphia, USA: Elsevier Saunders.

Omelyanenko, N. P., Slutsky, L. I. and Mironov, S. P. (2016) Connective Tissue: Histophysiology, Biochemistry, Molecular Biology. CRC Press.

Standring, S. (2016) Gray's Anatomy: The Anatomical Basis of Clinical Practice. Gray's Anatomy Series: Elsevier Limited."}]

items.name: Endocytosis (Anterior)
items.info:
[{"name": "Quick Facts", "text": "Endocytosis is the uptake by a cell of material from the environment by invagination of its plasma membrane; it includes both phagocytosis and pinocytosis (Dorland, 2011)."}, {"name": "Structure and/or Key Feature(s)", "text": "Many substances enter and leave the cell, and move between different cytoplasmic regions or organelles, by vesicular transport. Vesicles present in the cytoplasm (although appearing structurally similar) reflect different traffic pathways and functional states. In most cases, there is a continual renewal/replacement of the plasma membrane as new vesicles are formed from the cell membrane and enter the cell (endocytosis) or fuse with the plasma membrane to excrete substances (exocytosis).

The general term for the uptake of materials into the cell is called endocytosis. Many endocytotic processes are receptor mediated. Receptors for many substances aggregate on the cell surface as “coated pits.” They bind the ligand and enter the cell as a coated vesicle then quickly lose their clathrin coat and fuse with endosomes. Endosomes form a system of vesicles (early endosomes). These early endosomes recycle some of the plasmalemma components back to the cell surface, particularly clathrin to form new coated pits, then proceed to go deeper into the cell with other endosomes to become late endosomes. 

Some endosomes are functionally connected to the transport vesicles in the rough endoplasmic reticulum (and most likely the Golgi complex) to deliver hydrolytic enzymes to late endosomes that carry a mannose-6-phosphate (M-6-P) receptor. These are endosomes destined to be lysosomes. Early endosomes transport and sort proteins received by endocytosis and direct them to appropriate cellular compartments. Late endosomes are lysosomes.

Most cells in the body utilize a process called pinocytosis to ingest fluid and small protein molecules via small vesicles about 80–150 nm in diameter. It is a continual process, so small vesicles are continually forming at the cell surface. Most of the vesicles eventually fuse with lysosomes although they are very numerous in endothelial cells as they move materials from their surface of origin to the other side. They are also numerous at the surfaces of smooth muscle cells and their initial invaginations from the smooth muscle plasma membrane are referred to as caveolae.

During phagocytosis large particles which include bacteria and foreign materials are ingested into the cell. Pseudopodia from the plasma membrane engulf these large particles into a large vesicle about 250 nm in diameter called a phagosome. An endolysosome (or phagolysosome) forms when the phagosome enters the cell and fuses with a lysosome. The lysosomal contents include hydrolytic enzymes which digest the content within the phagosome. Some of the digested products may be used by the cell but most will be exported out of the cell by exocytosis."}, {"name": "References", "text": "Dorland, W. (2011) Dorland's Illustrated Medical Dictionary. 32nd edn. Philadelphia, USA: Elsevier Saunders.

McKinley, M. P., O'Loughlin, V. D. and Pennefather-O'Brien, E. E. (2016) Human Anatomy. 5th edn.: McGraw-Hill Education.

Ovalle, W. K., Nahirney, P. C. and Netter, F. H. (2013) Netter's Essential Histology. ClinicalKey 2012: Elsevier Saunders.

Ross, M. H. and Pawlina, W. (2006) Histology: A text and atlas. Lippincott Williams & Wilkins."}]

items.name: Lymph Vessels of Ovary
items.info:
[{"name": "Quick Facts", "text": "Location: Arise in the cortex of the ovary.

Drainage: Parenchyma of ovary.

Direction of Flow: 

Right side: Precaval & lateral caval nodes > right lumbar trunk > cisterna chyli > thoracic duct.

Left side: Preaortic and lateral aortic nodes > intestinal trunk and left lumbar trunk > cisterna chyli > thoracic duct."}, {"name": "Description", "text": "The lymphatic vessels of the ovary arise as a dense network around the follicles and corpus luteum in the cortex of the ovary. As the vessels pass through the medulla, and towards the hilum of the ovary, the network transitions into 6-8 collector vessels that exit the ovary accompanied by the blood vessels (Földi et al., 2012).

The collecting vessels ascend with the ovarian artery. The ovarian lymph vessels on the right side drain into the precaval and lateral caval nodes that are located near the renal vein. On the left side, the lymph vessels terminate in the preaortic and lateral aortic nodes near the left renal vein (Földi et al., 2012)."}, {"name": "References", "text": "Földi, M., Földi, E., Strößenreuther, R. and Kubik, S. (2012) Földi's Textbook of Lymphology: for Physicians and Lymphedema Therapists. Elsevier Health Sciences."}]

items.name: Tunica Albuginea of Corpus Spongiosum Penis
items.audio: Tunica Albuginea of Corpus Spongiosum Penis.mp3
items.info: [{"name": "Quick Facts", "text": "The tunica albuginea of corpus spongiosum penis is the dense, white, fibroelastic sheath that encloses the corpus spongiosum of the penis (Dorland, 2011)."}, {"name": "Structure and/or Key Feature(s)", "text": "Due to the smaller density of erectile tissue in the corpus spongiosum, the tunica albuginea is thinner in comparison to the thick tunica albuginea covering the corpus cavernosum."}, {"name": "Function", "text": "The elastic nature of the tunica albuginea allows blood to flow easily through the dorsal arteries of the penis to initiate an erection. The deep fascia of the penis, which is less elastic, puts pressure on the dorsal vein of the penis near the root to prevent blood from leaving the penis."}, {"name": "References", "text": "Dorland, W. (2011) Dorland's Illustrated Medical Dictionary. 32nd edn. Philadelphia, USA: Elsevier Saunders."}]

items.name: Presynaptic Region
items.info:
[{"name": "Quick Facts", "text": "The presynaptic region is the part of the axon situated before or proximal to a synapse."}, {"name": "Structure", "text": "The presynaptic region is the terminal end of the axon of the first (presynaptic) neuron. It contains membrane-bound vesicles ranging from 30 to 100 nm in diameter. Small vesicles up to about 50 nm are called synaptic vesicles and contain neurotransmitters. Larger vesicles (about 100 nm in diameter) are referred to as dense-core vesicles (or secretory granules) and contain neuropeptides. Amine and amino acid neurotransmitters are stored in synaptic vesicles, whereas peptide neurotransmitters are found in dense-core vesicles. Each type of neurotransmitter can be stored within the same axon terminal. However, each neurotransmitter is released under different conditions. Additionally, different neurons release different neurotransmitters and the rate of synaptic transmission is variable (Bear, Connors and Paradiso, 2007).

Each different neurotransmitter may be synthesized in different ways.

Enzymes that facilitate the synthesis of amino acid and amine neurotransmitters are located at the axonal terminal for the rapid facilitation of neurotransmitter synthesis. Special proteins called transporters located on the vesicle membrane then capture and concentrate the neurotransmitter inside the vesicle (Bear, Connors and Paradiso, 2007). The presynaptic region contains many small mitochondria, which provide ATP for the synthesis of new transmitter substance (Splittgerber, 2018).

Peptide neurotransmitter is synthesized by rough endoplasmic reticulum (rER), which is then sorted and packaged by the Golgi complex in the cell body. These neurotransmitters reach the axon terminal by anterograde axoplasmic transport, probably using microtubules as transporting vehicles (Ross and Pawlina, 2006).

Synaptic vesicles are concentrated adjacent to presynaptic densities on the axoplasmic side of the presynaptic axolemma. These densities often appear as a field of pyramids and represent accumulations of proteins and are called active zones where synaptic vesicles attach and release neurotransmitters (Bear, Connors and Paradiso, 2007).

Membrane that has been added by vesicles fusing with the presynaptic membrane is returned into the axoplasm by endocytosis and synaptic vesicles are reformed by smooth endoplasmic reticulum (sER) within the axon terminal (Bear, Connors and Paradiso, 2007).

Release of the neurotransmitter is triggered by the arrival of the action potential. Depolarization of the terminal membrane opens voltage-gated calcium channels in the active zones. Ca2+ ions flooding the axoplasm at the axon terminal from the extracellular space is the signal for synaptic vesicles to dock at the active zones of the presynaptic membrane and release neurotransmitter by exocytosis (Bear, Connors and Paradiso, 2007).

Secretory granules that release peptide neurotransmitters require a much greater influx of Ca2+ ions (and so a high frequency of action potentials) and often the release is away from the active zones (Bear, Connors and Paradiso, 2007)."}, {"name": "Function", "text": "The presynaptic region is the terminal end of the first (presynaptic) neuron in the chemical synapse, which houses neurotransmitter-filled synaptic vesicles that facilitate neurotransmission by fusing with the presynaptic membrane and releasing neurotransmitters into the synaptic cleft (Ross and Pawlina, 2006)."}, {"name": "List of Clinical Correlates", "text": "—Drugs are being developed now to modify synaptic transmission by interfering with the processes of transmission at the presynaptic element (Splittgerber, 2018)."}, {"name": "References", "text": "Bear, M. F., Connors, B. W. and Paradiso, M. A. (2007) Neuroscience. Lippincott Williams & Wilkins.

Ross, M. H. and Pawlina, W. (2006) Histology: A text and atlas. Lippincott Williams & Wilkins.

Splittgerber, R. (2018) Snell's Clinical Neuroanatomy. Wolters Kluwer Health."}]

items.name: Horizontal Neurons
items.info:
[{"name": "Quick Facts", "text": "A horizontal cell is a retinal neuron; there are two types, and their functions are unclear. Each cell has a multipolar soma in the internal nuclear layer and one long neurite and several short ones. All the neurites serve as both axons and dendrites, extending along and ramifying within the internal nuclear layer. The long neurites synapse in the outer plexiform layer with both pedicles and spherules; the short neurites synapse either with pedicles or with spherules (Dorland, 2011)."}, {"name": "Structure and/or Key Features", "text": "Horizontal neurons are described as interconnecting neurons that transfer information in a lateral or horizontal direction. Interconnecting neurons, or interneurons, are specific types that act as an intermediary role in the transfer of information between two projection neurons. Horizontal cells are specifically classified as inhibitory interneurons (Standring, 2016). 

Horizontal cells have a cell body located at the external margin of the inner nuclear layer, a single long axon, and several shorter dendrites with branching terminals. They synapse with bipolar and photoreceptor cells. Additionally they are connected to neighboring horizontal cells by gap junctions forming an extensive, interconnected network (Remington and Goodwin, 2011).

There are three morphologically distinct types of horizontal neurons in the retina, commonly called H1, H2, and H3 horizontal cells. The dendrites of H1 and H3 horizontal neurons form synaptic connections with cone cells, while their axons connect with rod cells. On the other hand, both axons and dendrites of H2 horizontal neurons form synaptic connections with cone cells only (Standring, 2016; Kolb, 1995c)."}, {"name": "Anatomical Relations", "text": "The cell bodies of horizontal neurons are located along the external margin of the inner nuclear layer of the retina. Their long processes extend out along the junction between the outer plexiform and inner nuclear layers, running parallel to the retinal surface. They subsequently enter the outer plexiform layer and terminate there."}, {"name": "Function", "text": "Horizontal neurons are largely responsible for helping the eyes to adjust under both bright and dim light. They additionally have a role in contrast enhancement and distinguishing opposing colors (Twig, Levy and Perlman, 2003).

Horizontal neurons are described as inhibitory interneurons. When photoreceptor cells transduce light energy into a neural signal that is transmitted to bipolar and ganglion cells, horizontal cells provide feedback and feedforward inhibition to photoreceptor and bipolar cells, respectively. In the retina, this is known as lateral inhibition. As such, horizontal neurons help to integrate and regulate signals from photoreceptor cells (Diamond, 2017). It should be noted that considering photoreceptors have an intrinsic response whereby light-evoked “activation” of the cell results in hyperpolarization, the inhibitory feedback provided by horizontal neurons results in the depolarization of photoreceptor cells. 

H1 horizontal neurons have dendrites that synapse with approximately 7–18 cones, while their axons terminate at the rod spherule. In this sense, H1 neurons facilitate communication and integration of signals between rod and cone cells. In this way, they play a role in the shift from scotopic (night) to photopic (day) vision and vice versa. Similar to H1 neurons, H3 neurons have a large dendritic tree that contacts many cones. Interestingly, H3 neurons seem to avoid blue cones; therefore, they are likely selective for red and green cones. The termination of the H3 axon remains unclear but are likely to contact both rod and cone cells. H2 neurons have processes, both dendrites and axons, that simply connect cones and are believed"}, {"name": "References", "text": "Diamond, J. S. (2017) 'Inhibitory Interneurons in the Retina: Types, Circuitry, and Function', Annu Rev Vis Sci, 3, pp. 1-24.

Dorland, W. (2011) Dorland's Illustrated Medical Dictionary. 32nd edn. Philadelphia, USA: Elsevier Saunders.

Kolb, H. (1995c) 'Photoreceptors', in Kolb, H., Fernandez, E. and Nelson, R. (eds.) Webvision: The Organization of the Retina and Visual System. Salt Lake City (UT): University of Utah Health Sciences Center.

Remington, L. A. and Goodwin, D. (2011) Clinical Anatomy of the Visual System E-Book. Elsevier Health Sciences.

Standring, S. (2016) Gray's Anatomy: The Anatomical Basis of Clinical Practice. Gray's Anatomy Series 41 edn.: Elsevier Limited.

Twig, G., Levy, H. and Perlman, I. (2003) 'Color opponency in horizontal cells of the vertebrate retina', Prog Retin Eye Res, 22(1), pp. 31-68."}]

items.name: Alveolar Blood Vessels
items.info:
[{"name": "Quick Facts", "text": "The superior and inferior alveolar vessels supply the maxillary and mandibular teeth, respectively."}, {"name": "Anatomical Relations", "text": "The primary arteries to the teeth are derived from one of the terminal branches of the carotid artery, namely the maxillary artery. The teeth in the maxilla are supplied by branches from the superior alveolar artery, while lower teeth in the mandible are supplied by branches from the inferior alveolar arteries (Standring, 2016).

The maxilla is supplied by the posterior, middle and anterior superior alveolar arteries. The mandible and the mandibular molars and premolars are supplied by the inferior alveolar artery, which passes through the mandibular canal to reach these structures. As the inferior alveolar artery passes through the canal, it branches and enters minute holes at the apex of each root to supply the pulp. Branches of the inferior alveolar artery that travel through the root canal up to the pulp cavity are known as pulpal vessels (Standring, 2016).

Veins from the mandible, and specifically the mandibular first molar, drain into plexuses around the root apices or vessels in the interdental septa, and then into several inferior alveolar veins. The inferior alveolar veins can then drain into either the facial vein or the pterygoid venous plexus (Standring, 2016)."}, {"name": "Function", "text": "Alveolar blood vessels supply and nourish the pulp of the tooth."}, {"name": "References", "text": "Standring, S. (2016) Gray's Anatomy: The Anatomical Basis of Clinical Practice. Gray's Anatomy Series 41 edn.: Elsevier Limited."}]

items.name: Multipolar Neuron
Central Retinal Artery
items.info:
[{"name": "Quick Facts", "text": "Origin: Ophthalmic artery.

Course: Runs inside the optic nerve to reach the eyeball.

Branches: Superior and inferior nasal and temporal branches.

Supplied Structures: Retina."}, {"name": "Origin", "text": "The central retinal artery is the small, first branch of the ophthalmic artery."}, {"name": "Course", "text": "The central retinal artery arises just below the optic nerve. For a short time, it lies inferiorly in the dural sheath surrounding the optic nerve, and then enters the optic nerve to course towards the retina (extraocular part). It enters the eyeball through the lamina cribrosa, where it gives off several branches (intraocular part). The intraocular part course over the innermost surface of the retina, superficial to the ganglion cell layer. It sends small branches into the retina that extend through and supply cells of the ganglion cell layer, the inner plexiform layer, the inner nuclear layer, and the outer plexiform layer. It does not supply the rod and cone photoreceptors of the outer nuclear layer which are served by diffusion from the choriocapillaris."}, {"name": "Branches", "text": "The intraocular part of the central retinal artery divides into superior and inferior temporal, and superior and inferior nasal branches, each of which supply a quadrant of the retina. The superior and inferior temporal branches arc above and below the macula but do not supply structures at the depths of the fovea."}, {"name": "Supplied Structures", "text": "The central retinal artery supplies the inner layers of the retina of the eyeball."}, {"name": "List of Clinical Correlates", "text": "—Papilledema"}]

items.name: Pars Nervosa of Hypophysis
Calcium Ions
items.info:
[{"name": "Structure", "text": "Calcium ions are referred to as second messengers. This is because the cellular response to specific stimuli requires alterations in the concentration of cellular calcium. 

Voltage-gated calcium channels in the presynaptic membrane modulate the release of neurotransmitter from the synaptic vesicles. When a nerve impulse arrives at the synaptic bouton, it initiates the reversal of the voltage (depolarization) across the membrane in the region, causing the voltage-gated calcium channels in the plasma membrane of the synaptic bouton to open. Calcium subsequently flows in from the extracellular space, synaptic vesicles fuse to the surrounding presynaptic membrane, and neurotransmitter is released into the synaptic cleft by exocytosis (Ross and Pawlina, 2006)."}, {"name": "Function", "text": "Calcium ions form part of the teeth and bones. They play a role in blood clotting, muscle contraction, as well as the release of neurotransmitters from the presynaptic neuron."}, {"name": "Clinical Correlates", "text": "The extracellular concentration of calcium ions, just like potassium ions, is maintained within a very narrow range because changes in the concentration have significant effects on the functioning of excitable tissues like the nerves and the muscles. A decrease in the extracellular concentration of calcium, renders axolemma more permeable to sodium ions, making the neurons more electrically excitable, resulting in anomalies such as spontaneous action potentials that lead to hyperexcitability and tetany. On the other hand, an increase in the extracellular concentration of calcium renders the axolemma less permeable to sodium ions, making the neurons involved less electrically excitable. This has an inhibitory effect on action potentials, resulting in paralysis or weakness of the muscles (VanPutte, Regan and Russo, 2015)."}, {"name": "References", "text": "Ross, M. H. and Pawlina, W. (2006) Histology: A text and atlas. Lippincott Williams & Wilkins.

VanPutte, C. L., Regan, J. L. and Russo, A. F. (2015) Seeley's Essentials of Anatomy and Physiology. McGraw-Hill Education."}]

items.name: Paneth Cell (Jejunum)
items.info: [{"name": "Quick Facts", "text": "Paneth cells are narrow, pyramidal, or columnar epithelial cells with a round or oval nucleus close to the base, occurring in the fundus of the crypts of Lieberk\u00fchn; they contain large granules that secrete antimicrobial substances such as defensins (Dorland, 2011)."}, {"name": "Structure/Morphology", "text": "Paneth cells are very prominent at the base of the intestinal glands as, when using traditional H&E histological staining, they have acidophilic, apical secretory vesicles."}, {"name": "Function", "text": "Granules in Paneth cells contain lysozyme, an enzyme which digests the cell wall of some bacteria, so Paneth cells have a role in regulating the natural bacterial flora of the small intestine."}, {"name": "References", "text": "Dorland, W. (2011) Dorland's Illustrated Medical Dictionary. 32nd edn. Philadelphia, USA: Elsevier Saunders."}]

items.name: Sweat
items.info:
[{"name": "Quick Facts", "text": "Sweat is the liquid secreted by the sweat glands, having a salty taste and a pH that varies from 4.5 to 7.5. That produced by the eccrine sweat glands is clear with a faint characteristic odor, and contains water, sodium chloride, and traces of albumin, urea, and other compounds; its composition varies according to factors such as fluid intake, external temperature and humidity, and some hormonal activity. Sweat produced by the larger, deeper, apocrine sweat glands of the axillae contains, in addition, organic material that on bacterial decomposition produces a strong odor (Dorland, 2011)."}, {"name": "Structure/Morphology", "text": "Sweat is produced by both apocrine and eccrine glands of the skin. The type of sweat that is produced in each gland differs as the cellular composition and function of the cells of the glands is different. 

Sweat produced by eccrine glands is primarily composed of water (approximately 99-99.5%) and both inorganic and organic solutes, including electrolytes such as chloride and sodium (Freinkel and Woodley, 2001). Eccrine sweat is odorless and colorless with a similar viscosity to water. 

Sweat produced by apocrine glands is composed of water, electrolytes, lipids, and steroids and appears as a cloudy, viscous secretion. Although the secretion is initially odorless, bacteria found on the skin can produce odoriferous compounds."}, {"name": "Function", "text": "Sweating is an important function that regulates body temperature. The viscous watery sweat is secreted to the surface of the epidermis. As it evaporates, it dissipates thermal energy, or heat, from the skin, hence, why humans sweat more during exercise or in hot temperatures. The sweat glands are also excretory organs, eliminating a variety of organic compounds in addition to heavy metals out of the body."}, {"name": "References", "text": "Dorland, W. (2011) Dorland's Illustrated Medical Dictionary. 32nd edn. Philadelphia, USA: Elsevier Saunders.

Freinkel, R. K. and Woodley, D. T. (2001) The Biology of the Skin. Taylor & Francis."}]

items.name: Fascicular Arrangement
items.info:
[{"name": "Quick Facts", "text": "A muscle fascicle is a small bundle of muscle fibers (Dorland, 2011)."}, {"name": "Structure", "text": "A muscle fascicle is a bundle of skeletal muscle fibers running parallel to each other, enveloped by a collagenous sheath called the perimysium. The arrangement and distribution of these fascicles, and hence, the orientation of the muscle fibers is directly related to the force, range, and direction of the movement of the muscle. 

The fascicular arrangement of muscle can take many forms including the circular arrangement seen in muscles such as the orbicularis oris, the convergent (or triangular) arrangement seen in the pectoralis major, or the strap-like shape muscles seen in the sartorius muscle (Standring, 2016).

In this muscle, the biceps femoris muscle, the fascicles are organized in a parallel arrangement and lie along the long axis of the muscle within the “belly” of the muscle and will converge at either end where a tendon is then found. This arrangement of fibers results in what is called a fusiform muscle."}, {"name": "Function", "text": "The muscle fascicle bundles groups of muscle fibers together, resulting in greater cumulative strength of the muscle fibers. This facilitates in allowing the fascicle to produce more force during contraction. The arrangement of these fibers determines in what direction the muscle will “pull” as it contracts."}, {"name": "References", "text": "Dorland, W. (2011) Dorland's Illustrated Medical Dictionary. 32nd edn. Philadelphia, USA: Elsevier Saunders.

Standring, S. (2016) Gray's Anatomy: The Anatomical Basis of Clinical Practice. Gray's Anatomy Series 41 edn.: Elsevier Limited."}]

items.name: Skeletal Muscle Fiber
items.info:
[{"name": "Quick Facts", "text": "Muscle fibers are elongated cellular structures in striated muscle tissue. A skeletal muscle fiber is a cylindrical multinucleate syncytial cell (Dorland, 2011)."}, {"name": "Structure", "text": "Muscle fibers are long, cylindrical multinucleated cells. The cytoplasm of a muscle fiber, the sarcoplasm, is enclosed by a plasma membrane called the sarcolemma. The sarcoplasm of the cell contains chains of long cylindrical structures called myofibrils that extend the length of the muscle fiber. Numerous nuclei occupy the space between adjacent myofibrils and the sarcolemma (Mescher, 2013)."}, {"name": "Key Features/Anatomical Relations", "text": "Each muscle fiber is embedded in a delicate connective tissue layer, called the endomysium. Muscle fibers are arranged in bundles, surrounded by another connective tissue layer called the perimysium. These bundles of muscle fibers are called fascicles (Pocock et al., 2013)."}, {"name": "Function", "text": "Muscle fibers are composed of myofibrils. Myofibrils contain numerous sarcomeres, which are the functional contractile units of the muscle."}, {"name": "List of Clinical Correlates", "text": "—Muscular atrophy

—Muscular dystrophy 

—Fibrosis

—Fibrositis"}, {"name": "References", "text": "Dorland, W. (2011) Dorland's Illustrated Medical Dictionary. 32nd edn. Philadelphia, USA: Elsevier Saunders.

Mescher, A. (2013) Junqueira's Basic Histology: Text and Atlas. 13th edn.: McGraw-Hill Education.

Pocock, G., Richards, C. D. and Richards, D. A. (2013) Human Physiology. Oxford Core Texts 4 edn.: OUP Oxford."}]

items.name: Ovarian Cycle
items.info:
[{"name": "Quick Facts", "text": "The ovarian cycle is that part of a menstrual cycle or estrous cycle which involves physiologic changes in the ovary, including development and rupture of the follicle, discharge of the oocyte, and corpus luteum formation and regression. It is divided into the follicular phase and the luteal phase (Dorland, 2011)."}, {"name": "Description", "text": "The menstrual cycle is a natural event in the female reproductive system that begins at about 11–13 years of age (menarche) and ends between 45–55 years of age (menopause). During this period, specific morphological and physiological changes occur in the ovary and the uterus to prepare for a possible pregnancy. The menstrual cycle includes the ovarian cycle and the uterine cycle.

The ovarian cycle refers to changes occurring in ovarian follicles, while the uterine cycle describes the changes in the endometrium of the uterus. Both cycles have three phases."}, {"name": "Ovarian Cycle", "text": "The follicular phase is the first part of the ovarian cycle whereby ovarian follicles mature and prepare to release an oocyte. It lasts from the beginning of menstruation (Day 1) to ovulation (Day 14), however, this is the most variable phase of the cycle and predicting ovulation is seldom reliable.

Ovulation is the second phase of the ovarian cycle in which a secondary oocyte is released from a mature follicle into the infundibulum of the uterine tube. 

The luteal phase is the final phase of the ovarian cycle. During the luteal phase, the follicle that has undergone ovulation is transformed into the corpus luteum, which produces progesterone.

The ovarian cycle is explained as a monthly event due to the cyclical release of follicle-stimulating hormone (FSH) and luteinizing hormone (LH) from the anterior pituitary gland. However, in reality, maturation of a follicle may take up to 12 months. A primary follicle takes about 290 days to develop into a late secondary follicle. It may take an additional 60 days of further development until ovulation of a secondary oocyte from a mature follicle (McKinley, O'Loughlin and Pennefather-O'Brien, 2016; Ovalle, Nahirney and Netter, 2013)."}, {"name": "List of Clinical Correlates", "text": "The ovarian cycle can be interrupted by any hormonal disturbances (pathological or manipulated) and so the basis for use of many oral contraceptives."}, {"name": "References", "text": "Dorland, W. (2011) Dorland's Illustrated Medical Dictionary. 32nd edn. Philadelphia, USA: Elsevier Saunders.

McKinley, M. P., O'Loughlin, V. D. and Pennefather-O'Brien, E. E. (2016) Human Anatomy. 5th edn.: McGraw-Hill Education.

Ovalle, W. K., Nahirney, P. C. and Netter, F. H. (2013) Netter's Essential Histology. ClinicalKey 2012: Elsevier Saunders."}]

items.name: Intracellular Membrane Fusion Proteins
items.info: [{"name": "Quick Facts", "text": "Intracellular membrane fusion proteins guide the binding of synaptic vesicles to the presynaptic cell membrane."}, {"name": "Structure", "text": "Before releasing neurotransmitter into the synaptic cleft, the synaptic vesicle must bind to and fuse with the presynaptic plasma membrane. This process is mediated by transmembrane proteins referred to as \u201cSNAREs\u201d (soluble NSF attachment receptors). NSF is an ATPase found in plasma membranes of eukaryotic cells and is involved in the transfer of the membrane making up the vesicle with another membrane compartment e.g., the plasma membrane (Ross and Pawlina, 2006). \n\nv-SNARE (vesicle-bound) and t-SNARE (target-membrane-bound) proteins are just two of the major proteins involved (Ross and Pawlina, 2006)."}, {"name": "Function", "text": "Before releasing neurotransmitter into the synaptic cleft, the synaptic vesicle must bind to and fuse with the presynaptic plasma membrane. This process is mediated by transmembrane proteins referred to as \u201cSNAREs\u201d (soluble NSF attachment receptors) (Ross and Pawlina, 2006)."}, {"name": "References", "text": "Ross, M. H. and Pawlina, W. (2006) Histology: A text and atlas. Lippincott Williams & Wilkins."}]

items.name: Axoneme (End Piece)
items.info:
[{"name": "Quick Facts", "text": "The axoneme is the central core of a cilium or flagellum, consisting of a central pair of microtubules surrounded by nine other microtubule pairs (Dorland, 2011)."}, {"name": "Structure and/or Key Feature(s)", "text": "The axoneme forms the core structure of the sperm tail. It is a cylindrical cytoskeletal structure that extends from the neck to the point where the tail terminates. 

The axoneme is composed of two centrally located microtubule singlets, which are encased by nine microtubule doublets. This is commonly referred to as the “9 + 2” complex. 

The major component proteins of the axoneme are cytoskeletal tubulin and the motor protein dynein. The microtubules are composed of dimers of α-tubulin and β-tubulin. Each of the microtubule doublets is made up of a complete α-microtubule, onto which a β-microtubule attaches. Two dynein arms extend from the α-microtubule to the β-microtubule of the neighboring doublet (Plant & Zeleznik, 2014)."}, {"name": "Anatomical Relations", "text": "The axoneme stretches across the entire length of the tail, from the neck region (just beneath the centriole) to the point where the tail terminates. The axoneme is the only structure present in the final 5–7 μm of the sperm tail (Standring, 2016).

The central pair of microtubules extend beyond the middle piece into the neck of the sperm, as far as the articular plate (capitulum). The outer doublets end just distal to the neck, where there is the remnants of the distal centriole (Plant & Zeleznik, 2014)."}, {"name": "Function", "text": "The axoneme acts as scaffold for the sperm tail, providing it with support and an ability to bend and unbend in various directions.

The motor dyneins associated with the microtubules of the axoneme have ATPase activity. Dyneins hydrolyze ATP and undergo a conformational change. They reach towards the minus end of the β-microtubule, resulting in the α- and β-microtubules in a doublet to slide past one another. The coordinated sliding in the doublets results in the propagation of a bending wave down the tail of the sperm, resulting in motility (Plant & Zeleznik, 2014).

The central pair of microtubules in the axoneme of the spermatozoon is involved in specific aspects of motility. The pair coordinates the sliding movements of the doublet microtubules, as well as taxis and reversal of the tail’s beating motion. These roles are essential for fertilization as evidence has shown that the absence of central pair form the spermatozoon tail results in the paralysis of the axoneme, and thus infertility (Linck et al, 2016)."}, {"name": "List of Clinical Correlates", "text": "- 9+0 syndrome"}, {"name": "References", "text": "Dorland, W. (2011) Dorland's Illustrated Medical Dictionary. 32nd edn. Philadelphia, USA: Elsevier Saunders.

Linck, R. W., Chemes, H. & Albertini, D. F. (2016) The axoneme: the propulsive engine of spermatozoa and cilia and associated ciliopathies leading to infertility. J Assist Reprod Genet, 33(2), 141-56.

Plant, T. M. & Zeleznik, A. J. (2014) Knobil and Neill's Physiology of Reproduction. Elsevier Science.

Standring, S. (2016) Gray's Anatomy: The Anatomical Basis of Clinical Practice. Gray's Anatomy Series 41st edition edn.: Elsevier Limited."}]

items.name: Fungiform Papillae
items.info:
[{"name": "Quick Facts", "text": "The fungiform papillae are the knoblike projections on the tongue, scattered singly among the filiform papillae (Dorland, 2011)."}, {"name": "Structure and/or Key Features", "text": "The majority of the fungiform papillae are located at the anterior margin of the tongue, including the tip of the tongue. There are some located among the filiform papillae along the dorsum of the tongue. 

The fungiform papillae have broad spherical heads; hence their name is derived from the Latin for mushroom. Their taste buds are located at the apex of the papillae, readily in contact with any food particles that they come into contact with. The papillae tend to be larger and slightly flatter than the filiform papillae. They are red due to their densely vascularized core and thin epithelium.

The fungiform papillae are protected by stratified squamous non-keratinized epithelium and participate in gustation."}, {"name": "Function", "text": "The fungiform papillae are one of the three types of lingual papillae involved in gustation, which is the detection of the different tastes of salty, bitter, sour, and sweet, and savory (Ikeda, 2002). It is important that all areas of the tongue are responsive to the different modalities of taste. However, some taste buds respond to a greater amount of chemical activation, while some respond to less. The simultaneous activation of different taste buds is what leads to the recognition of specific tastes."}, {"name": "References", "text": "Dorland, W. (2011) Dorland's Illustrated Medical Dictionary. 32nd edn. Philadelphia, USA: Elsevier Saunders.

Ikeda, K. (2002) New seasonings. Chem Senses, 27(9), 847-9."}]

items.name: Origin of Levator Scapulae Muscle
Internal Circumferential Lamella
items.info: [{"name": "Quick Facts", "text": "The circumferential lamella is one of the layers of bone that underlie the periosteum (external circumferential lamella) and endosteum (internal circumferential lamella) (Dorland, 2011)."}, {"name": "Structure/Morphology", "text": "The internal circumferential lamellae surround the inner circumference of the cortical component of long bones. It follows the contours of trabecular bone."}, {"name": "Anatomical Relations", "text": "The internal circumferential lamellae are the interface between the cortical bone and the inner spongy bone and medullary cavity."}, {"name": "Function", "text": "The inner circumferential lamellae contribute to the diameter of the diaphysis in long bones. This helps maintain the strength of the bone as well as help it adapt to mechanical loading and stresses (Standring, 2016)."}, {"name": "References", "text": "Dorland, W. (2011) Dorland's Illustrated Medical Dictionary. 32nd edn. Philadelphia, USA: Elsevier Saunders.\n\nStandring, S. (2016) Gray's Anatomy: The Anatomical Basis of Clinical Practice. Gray's Anatomy Series: Elsevier Limited."}]

items.name: Arteries of Perimysium
items.info:
[{"name": "Description", "text": "The contraction of muscle requires a vast amount of energy; therefore, an extensive vascular network is necessary in order to deliver this energy to the muscle tissue, in addition to removing the by-products (i.e., metabolic waste) of the muscle contraction. Arteries travel through the collagenous sheath, the perimysium, in between the fascicles, providing the muscle fibers within the fascicles with arterial blood supply. Nerves and blood vessels typically follow a similar branching course through the connective tissue of the perimysium."}, {"name": "List of Clinical Correlates", "text": "—Myopathy

—Necrotizing fasciitis

—Limb infarction"}]

items.name: Elastic Fibers
items.info: [{"name": "Structure/Morphology", "text": "Longitudinal bands of elastic fibers are present in the submucosa of the bronchioles and extend to the alveoli."}, {"name": "Function", "text": "Elastic fibers in the walls of the bronchioles act as a spring preventing the walls from collapsing, as these tracts lack the cartilaginous plates that bronchi have to maintain a patent airway. This also applied for the alveoli, where the elastic fibers also aid the expulsion of air (Starcher, 1986)."}, {"name": "References", "text": "Starcher, B. C. (1986) 'Elastin and the lung', Thorax, 41(8), pp. 577-85."}]

items.name: Blood-Air Barrier
Lens
items.info: [{"name": "Quick Facts", "text": "The lens is the transparent biconvex body of the eye situated between the posterior chamber and the vitreous body, constituting part of the refracting mechanism of the eye (Dorland, 2011)."}, {"name": "Structure and/or Key Feature(s)", "text": "The lens is a partially elastic, biconvex, transparent structure held posterior to the iris and anchored in place by fine, zonular fibers that extend from the ciliary ring (or pars plana) to the lens margin.\n\nStructurally, the lens is made of three layers. Its core is formed of long, thin, transparent cells called lens fibers that have a very regular geometry to form an optically clear structure. The lens fibers are covered anteriorly by a single layer of epithelium and the entire structure is surrounded by the lens capsule. There is a complete absence of blood vessels and nerves within the lens, as they would interfere with light passing through it and degrade the visual image."}, {"name": "Anatomical Relations", "text": "The lens is suspended posterior to the iris and anterior to the vitreous body (hyaloid fossa). It is bathed in aqueous humor that serves to provide nutrients and remove metabolic waste in the absence of internal vasculature. Centrally, the lens is in contact with the pupillary region of the iris, however, because of its convex shape, moving towards the lens periphery, a space is formed, called the posterior chamber of the eye."}, {"name": "Function", "text": "Although the cornea is the major player in refracting light entering the eyeball, the ability of the lens to change its convexity via the zonular fibers allows fine-tuning of the focus of the images passing through it onto the retina."}, {"name": "Clinical Correlates", "text": "\u2014Cataracts"}, {"name": "References", "text": "Dorland, W. (2011) Dorland's Illustrated Medical Dictionary. 32nd edn. Philadelphia, USA: Elsevier Saunders."}]

items.name: Primary Oocyte (of Late Primary Ovarian Follicle)
items.audio: Primary Oocyte (of Late Primary Ovarian Follicle).mp3
items.info:
[{"name": "Quick Facts", "text": "The primary oocyte is an oocyte that has begun but not completed the first maturation division; it is derived from an oogonium by differentiation near the time of birth (Dorland, 2011)."}, {"name": "Structure and/or Key Feature(s)", "text": "Although primary oocytes begin their first meiotic division in utero, the first meiotic prophase remains incomplete until just prior to ovulation, which means many remain arrested in their first meiotic division for 12 to perhaps 50 years.

The primary oocyte of the primordial ovarian follicle is about 30 μm in diameter and has a large round, eccentric, pale nucleus containing one or two prominent nucleoli.

The ooplasm (cytoplasm of an oocyte) contains Golgi membranes and vesicles, endoplasmic reticulum, centrioles, and many mitochondria and lysosomes. These organelles are condensed into a region in the ooplasm referred to as a Balbiani body. The ooplasm also contains stacks of membranes called annulate lamellae.

Organelles increase their numbers and become scattered throughout the ooplasm as the oocyte matures. Lipid droplets and masses of lipochrome pigment may appear. Beneath the plasma membrane (oolemma) special secretory granules called cortical granules appear which contain proteases.

As the zona pellucida is being deposited, many irregular microvilli project from the oolemma into the perivitelline space between the oocyte and the granulosa cells to intermingle with similar microvilli projecting from adjacent granulosa cells. 

When the first meiotic division is completed in a mature follicle equal share of chromatin is distributed to each daughter cell but only one receives most of the cytoplasm to become a secondary oocyte. The other daughter cell becomes the first polar body.

The second meiotic division commences immediately after the first meiotic division is completed (Ross and Pawlina, 2006; Mescher, 2013; McKinley, O'Loughlin and Pennefather-O'Brien, 2016)."}, {"name": "List of Clinical Correlates", "text": "The long period of meiotic arrest may expose the primary oocyte to factors which could contribute to errors in meiotic division such as nondisjunction. Such an error results in anomalies such as trisomy of chromosome 21 (Down’s syndrome)."}, {"name": "References", "text": "Dorland, W. (2011) Dorland's Illustrated Medical Dictionary. 32nd edn. Philadelphia, USA: Elsevier Saunders.

McKinley, M. P., O'Loughlin, V. D. and Pennefather-O'Brien, E. E. (2016) Human Anatomy. 5th edn.: McGraw-Hill Education.

Mescher, A. (2013) Junqueira's Basic Histology: Text and Atlas. 13th edn.: McGraw-Hill Education.

Ross, M. H. and Pawlina, W. (2006) Histology: A text and atlas. Lippincott Williams & Wilkins."}]

items.name: Connecting Cilium of Rod Cell
items.info: [{"name": "Quick Facts", "text": "The connecting cilium acts as a communicating channel between the inner and outer segments of the photoreceptor cells."}, {"name": "Structure and/or Key Features", "text": "The connecting cilium is a long, slender, nonmotile, microscopic cellular organelle within the photoreceptor connecting stalk. It measures approximately 0.3 \u00b5m in diameter and is composed of microtubules in a 9x2+0 array near the cilium\u2019s base. Here the microtubules are connected to the plasma membrane. This microtubule \u201cdoublet\u201d formation transitions to 9x1+0 singlet array more distally and it continues in that configuration through to the outer segment (Chen and Sampath, 2012)."}, {"name": "Anatomical Relations", "text": "The connecting cilium is fittingly positioned between the inner and outer segments in both rod and cone cells."}, {"name": "Function", "text": "The connecting cilium acts a microscopic channel for the flow of proteins and lipids, from the site of production in the inner segment to the outer segment, with approximately 2,000 opsin molecules transported every minute (Chen and Sampath, 2012)."}, {"name": "References", "text": "Chen, J. and Sampath, A. (2012) 'Structure and Function of Rod and Cone Photoreceptors', Retina Fifth Edition, 1, pp. 342-359."}]

items.name: Terminal Bouton
Autonomic Nerve Fiber (Smooth Muscle Tissue)
items.info:
[{"name": "Quick Facts", "text": "Autonomic nerve fibers are peripheral nerve fibers that innervate smooth muscle, cardiac muscle, and glandular epithelium, or synapse in autonomic ganglia. They either stimulate and activate the muscle or tissue (preganglionic and postganglionic visceral efferent fibers) or receive sensory impulses from them (visceral afferent fibers) (Dorland, 2011)."}, {"name": "Structure and/or Key Features", "text": "Smooth muscle contraction is not subject to voluntary control and is regulated, in most cases, by sympathetic and parasympathetic nerves of the autonomic nervous system. 

Nerve fibers have enlargements, or swellings, called varicosities that are in close contact with a smooth muscle cell. Within the varicosities are synaptic vesicles containing neuromuscular transmitters, such as acetylcholine or norepinephrine (noradrenaline). 

Unlike the neuromuscular junctions in skeletal muscle where the nerve terminal is in direct contact with the muscle cells, the nerve terminals are located some distance from the smooth muscle cells. Synaptic vesicles released rely on diffusion to reach the adjacent target smooth muscle cells, which may be at a distance of 10–20 μm (Ross and Pawlina, 2016). Vesicles bind to the sarcolemma of the smooth muscle cells to stimulate a contraction. However, neurotransmitters do not reach all the smooth muscle cells. Instead, gap junctions between adjacent cells allows the signal to pass from one cell to the next and enables communication between cells to regulate the coordinated contraction of the entire sheet of smooth muscle (Ovalle, Nahirney and Netter, 2013)."}, {"name": "Anatomical Relations", "text": "Nerve fibers travel within the connective tissue between the smooth muscle bundles."}, {"name": "Function", "text": "Autonomic nerve fibers release neurotransmitters that bind to the sarcolemma of smooth muscle cells, triggering muscle contraction."}, {"name": "References", "text": "Dorland, W. (2011) Dorland's Illustrated Medical Dictionary. 32nd edn. Philadelphia, USA: Elsevier Saunders.

Ovalle, W. K., Nahirney, P. C. and Netter, F. H. (2013) Netter's Essential Histology. ClinicalKey 2012: Elsevier Saunders.

Ross, M. H. and Pawlina, W. (2016) Histology: A Text and Atlas. Wolters Kluwer Health."}]

items.name: Serosa of Small Intestine (Ileum)
items.info:
[{"name": "Quick Facts", "text": "The serosa is the membrane lining the walls of various body cavities, reflected over the surfaces of protruding organs; it consists of mesothelium lying upon a subserosal connective tissue layer, and it secretes a watery exudate (Dorland, 2011)."}, {"name": "Structure/Morphology", "text": "The first 2.5 cm of the duodenum is intraperitoneal, thus is covered by a serosa (i.e., visceral peritoneum). As it becomes retroperitoneal, only the anterior surface of the duodenum is covered by a serosa, with the remaining covered by adventitia. The jejunum and ileum are covered by a serosa. 

Serosa is a serous membrane made of simple squamous epithelium or mesothelium supported by a basement membrane and a small amount of connective tissue.

Adventitia is only connective tissue that binds the gut to surrounding connective tissue of adjoining structures."}, {"name": "Key Features/Anatomical Relations", "text": "The serosa of the small intestine is the outermost layer of the small intestine. It encloses the jejunum and ileum, except at the mesenteric borders, where the serosa is reflected onto the mesentery.

The deep surface of the serosa adheres to the longitudinal muscular layer of the small intestine. The superficial surface of the serosa is an epithelium or mesothelium, which is in contact with surrounding organs or the parietal peritoneum."}, {"name": "Function", "text": "The serosa of the small intestine secretes a serosal fluid. This fluid allows the small intestine to slide across neighboring tissues without creating friction and damage."}, {"name": "References", "text": "Dorland, W. (2011) Dorland's Illustrated Medical Dictionary. 32nd edn. Philadelphia, USA: Elsevier Saunders."}]

items.name: Lacrimal Canaliculus
items.info: [{"name": "Quick Facts", "text": "The lacrimal canaliculus is the short passage in an eyelid, beginning at the punctum, that leads from the lacrimal lake to the lacrimal sac (Dorland, 2011)."}, {"name": "Structure and/or Key Feature(s)", "text": "Lacrimal canaliculi are small drainage channels from each eyelid that collect tears. They are found just adjacent to the medial angle of the eye. Tears collect here and pass through a punctum to enter either the superior or inferior lacrimal canaliculus. Each canaliculus is initially vertical as it travels medially from its punctum. It then widens forming an ampulla and passes towards the lacrimal sac. The superior and inferior canaliculi unite forming a common lacrimal canaliculus, which drains into the lacrimal sac (Standring, 2016)."}, {"name": "Anatomical Relations", "text": "The orbicularis oculi muscle fibers interweave between the lacrimal canaliculi forming a \u201csphincter-like\u201d arrangement that can facilitate tear drainage."}, {"name": "Function", "text": "The lacrimal canaliculi are responsible for draining tears from the medial angle of the eye. Each tear drop consists of about 7 \u03bcl of fluid. Some of the tear fluid is lost to evaporation or absorption into the conjunctiva; however, the majority is drained via the nasolacrimal drainage system. Tears collect at the medial angle of the eye (medial canthus) and by way of the puncta drain into the superior and inferior lacrimal canaliculi. These transport the tears to the lacrimal sac, and then into the nasolacrimal duct that directs the tears to the nasal cavity."}, {"name": "References", "text": "Dorland, W. (2011) Dorland's Illustrated Medical Dictionary. 32nd edn. Philadelphia, USA: Elsevier Saunders.\n\nStandring, S. (2016) Gray's Anatomy: The Anatomical Basis of Clinical Practice. Gray's Anatomy Series 41 edn.: Elsevier Limited."}]

items.name: Cranial Dura
Cell Membrane (Anterior)
Fibrous Sheath
items.info:
[{"name": "Quick Facts", "text": "The fibrous sheath surrounds the principal piece of the tail of a spermatozoon (Dorland, 2011)."}, {"name": "Structure and/or Key Feature(s)", "text": "The fibrous sheath is a cylindrical cytoskeletal structure that determines the scope of the principal piece of the sperm tail and is adherent to the plasma membrane.

The fibrous sheath takes the shape of a tapering cylinder, which constitutes two longitudinal filamentous columns affixed by circumferential ribs. The longitudinal columns course along the edges of microtubule doublets three and eight of the axoneme and are affixed to the outer dense fibers three and eight in the proximal aspect of the principal piece (Plant & Zeleznik, 2014). 

The circumferential ribs of the fibrous sheath are made up of tightly packed circumferentially arranged filamentous material. Each rib measures approximately 50nm in width and lies 10-20nm away from the adjacent ribs. The ribs widened distally as they fuse with the longitudinal columns and with themselves. 

At the distal aspect of the fibrous sheath, the thickness of the ribs is significantly reduced. The ribs, as well as the outer dense columns terminate at the distal margin of the principal piece (Plant & Zeleznik, 2014)."}, {"name": "Anatomical Relations", "text": "The fibrous sheath is located in the principal piece of the tail of the sperm. It is situated outside of the axoneme and the outer dense fibers. It lies deep to the plasma membrane and is adherent to it."}, {"name": "Function", "text": "The fibrous sheath regulates the directionality of the sperm’s tail beat, thereby restricting the sliding of the microtubule doublets in the axoneme during tail motion, as well as regulating the bending of the tail (Plant & Zeleznik, 2014)."}, {"name": "List of Clinical Correlates", "text": "- Fibrous sheath dysplasia

- Flagella dyskinesia 

- Asthenozoospermia"}, {"name": "References", "text": "Dorland, W. (2011) Dorland's Illustrated Medical Dictionary. 32nd edn. Philadelphia, USA: Elsevier Saunders.

Plant, T. M. & Zeleznik, A. J. (2014) Knobil and Neill's Physiology of Reproduction. Elsevier Science."}]

items.name: Gray Matter
items.info:
[{"name": "Quick Facts", "text": "The gray matter is the nervous tissue of the brain and spinal cord composed of nerve cell bodies, unmyelinated nerve processes, and glia (Dorland, 2011)."}, {"name": "Structure", "text": "The outer layer of each cerebral hemisphere is composed of a thin (2–4 mm) gray matter, or cerebral cortex, which overlies a thick mass of white matter, or cerebral medulla. Additionally, confined regions of gray matter are distributed between the white matter. These are known as the basal ganglia or basal nuclei. The gray matter consists of neuronal cell bodies, neuronal dendrites, axons, and neuroglia (neuronal supporting cells). Synapses between neurons occur in the gray matter (Pawlina, 2016).

The gray matter of the cerebral cortex consists of different cell types and it is therefore divided in six layers. 

—The first and most superficial layer of the gray matter of the cerebral cortex is the molecular layer (or plexiform layer). It contains predominantly of neuroglial cells which maintain homeostasis, protect and support neurons, and form myelin. Additionally, Cajal cells are found in this layer. A great number of synapses between different neurons occur in this layer. 

—The second layer is the external granular layer, which contains various types of neuroglial cells and small pyramidal cells. 

—The third layer is the external pyramidal layer which constitutes mainly of medium-sized pyramidal cells. 

—The fourth layer is the internal granular layer. This layer is thin and consists of small granule cells, pyramidal cells, and neuroglia. 

—The fifth layer is the internal pyramidal layer and consists of neuroglia and large pyramidal cells. 

—The sixth and deepest layer is the multiform layer, or polymorphic layer, and consists of intermixed cells that vary in size and shape. The cells that make up this layer are the fusiform cells, stellate cells, and cells of Martinotti (Eroschenko, 2008)."}, {"name": "Function", "text": "The gray matter possesses most of the cell bodies of the neurons in the brain; therefore, the gray matter is involved in sensory perception and voluntary motor function, as well as integrating diverse information and allowing purposeful action."}, {"name": "List of Clinical Correlates", "text": "—Alcohol abuse

—Alzheimer’s disease

—Dementia

—Parkinson’s disease"}, {"name": "References", "text": "Dorland, W. (2011) Dorland's Illustrated Medical Dictionary. 32nd edn. Philadelphia, USA: Elsevier Saunders.

Eroschenko, V. P. (2008) DiFiore's Atlas of Histology with Functional Correlations. Point (Lippincott Williams and Wilkins) Series: Wolters Kluwer Health/Lippincott Williams & Wilkins.

Pawlina, W. 2016. Histology: A text and atlas with correlated cell and molecular biology. 7th ed. Philadelphia: Wolters Kluwer."}]

items.name: Golgi Complex (Rod Cell)
items.info: [{"name": "Quick Facts", "text": "The Golgi complex is an intracellular compartment of eukaryotes, occupying the perinuclear region and consisting of a number of stacked, flattened sacs with associated tubules and vesicles. Its primary function is to process substances synthesized in the endoplasmic reticulum; in addition it synthesizes some carbohydrates. Transport vesicles from the endoplasmic reticulum fuse with the Golgi complex at the cis face, their cargo is processed while passing through the cisternae, and the processed products are transported from the trans face to the trans-Golgi network for sorting and packaging. The mechanism by which cargo moves through the Golgi complex is not clear; one model proposes transport between cisternae by vesicular budding and fusion, while another proposes dynamic remodeling and recycling so that the cisternae themselves change in composition and move in a cis-to-trans direction (Dorland, 2011)."}, {"name": "Structure and/or Key Features", "text": "The Golgi complex, or Golgi apparatus, is a membranous intracellular organelle. It is composed of several flattened stacks, or cisternae, and measures approximated 5\u201310 \u00b5m in area (Pawlina, 2016)."}, {"name": "Anatomical Relations", "text": "The Golgi complex is often found in the myoid zone of the photoreceptor inner segment. This zone is located between the cell nucleus and the zone of high mitochondria density (ellipsoid zone)."}, {"name": "Function", "text": "The Golgi complex is responsible for the modification, sorting, and packaging of proteins and lipids for intracellular or extracellular transport. Therefore, a large number of vesicles are associated with the Golgi complex."}, {"name": "References", "text": "Dorland, W. (2011) Dorland's Illustrated Medical Dictionary. 32nd edn. Philadelphia, USA: Elsevier Saunders.\n\nPawlina, W. 2016. Histology: A text and atlas with correlated cell and molecular biology. 7th ed. Philadelphia: Wolters Kluwer."}]

items.name: Renal Corpuscle
items.info:
[{"name": "Quick Facts", "text": "The renal corpuscle is a body that forms the beginning of a nephron, consisting of a glomerulus surrounded by the glomerular capsule (an expanded portion of the renal tubule) (Dorland, 2011)."}, {"name": "Structure and/or Key Features", "text": "The renal corpuscle is a small, rounded structure comprised of a central tuft of convoluted capillaries, known as the glomerulus, enveloped by an invaginated sphere, known as the glomerular capsule. The glomerular capsule is described as the dilated proximal part of the renal tubule (Kerr, 2007). 

The glomerulus is described as a small tuft of convoluted capillaries structurally supported by an extracellular mesangial matrix. The glomerular capsule is comprised of an outer parietal layer and inner visceral layer. The inner visceral layer is composed of specialized epithelial cells, called podocytes. Podocytes are distinct cells characterized by their foot processes, known as pedicels. Pedicels of adjacent podocytes interdigitate to form filtration slits. A small cavity between the inner visceral wall and the outer parietal wall of the glomerular capsule exists. This cavity is known as Bowman’s space and is continuous with the proximal convoluted tubule.
