items.info: [{"name": "Quick Facts", "text": "The longitudinal muscular layer of small intestine is the outer layer of the muscular coat (tunica muscularis or muscularis externa) of the small intestine, consisting of longitudinally coursing fibers (Dorland, 2011)."}, {"name": "Structure/Morphology", "text": "The cross-sectional microarchitecture of the small intestine demonstrates mucosa, submucosa, and muscular (inner circular and outer longitudinal) layers with a thin outer serosal covering.\n\nThe longitudinal muscular layer forms the outer muscle fibers of the muscular layer and its fibers are smooth muscle cells which are oriented roughly parallel to the long axis of the digestive canal."}, {"name": "Function", "text": "The outer longitudinal muscular layer, together with the circular muscle layer, act to create rhythmic peristaltic contractions. This mixes chyme and pushes contents distally."}, {"name": "References", "text": "Dorland, W. (2011) Dorland's Illustrated Medical Dictionary. 32nd edn. Philadelphia, USA: Elsevier Saunders."}]

items.name: Dental Pulp Tissue
items.info:
[{"name": "Quick Facts", "text": "The dental pulp is the richly vascularized and innervated connective tissue of mesodermal origin contained in the central cavity of a tooth and delimited by the dentin; it has formative, nutritive, sensory, and protective functions. The portion within the tooth chamber proper is the pulpa coronalis, and that within the root is the pulpa radicularis (Dorland, 2011)."}, {"name": "Structure and/or Key Feature(s)", "text": "Dental pulp is the specialized loose connective tissue that resides in the central pulp cavity or chamber of the tooth. Unlike other dental tissues such as enamel, dentin or cement, dental pulp is non-mineralized. The pulp itself is the living entity of the tooth and contains connective tissue, blood vessels, and nerves.

Each pulp cavity opens into the tissue surrounding the tooth through the apical foramen of the root. Some teeth may additionally have an accessory canal or foramen. Dental pulp is continuous with the periodontal ligament via the apical and accessory foramen (Standring, 2016).

Pulp has two distinct zones, namely the central zone and peripheral zone, both of which are observed in the coronal and radicular parts of the tooth. The central zone houses arterioles, veins and nerve trunks that enter the pulp cavity through the apical foramen and travel longitudinally to the coronal pulp chamber. The peripheral zone (also known as the odontogenic zone) is comprised of distinct layers, beginning with the outermost layer which lies on the periphery of the pulp known as the odontoblastic layer. The odontoblastic layer is adjacent to the predentin with the cell bodies of the odontoblasts situated in the pulp and their cell processes extending into the dentinal tubules. 

Subjacent to the odontoblast layer is the cell-free zone (also known as the zone of Weil) which contains several bundles of reticular fibers and numerous capillaries and nerves. Subjacent to the cell-free zone is the cell-rich zone that contains numerous fibroblasts and perivascular cells (also known as mesenchymal cells), the latter of which can give rise to odontoblasts, fibroblasts or macrophages. The deep pulp cavity, located medial to the cell-rich zone, contains the subodontoblastic nerve plexus of Raschkow (Chiego, 2014). 

Through the apical foramen, a number of thin-walled arterioles enter and travel longitudinally until they reach the pulp cavity in the crown. Here, they ramify forming a dense capillary network beneath the odontoblast layer. After draining the capillary bed, small venules travel downward and exit the pulp cavity via the apical foramen. 

Along with the arterioles, sensory and sympathetic nerve fibers enter the pulp cavity via the apical foramen. Specifically, sympathetic nerve fibers extend from the superior cervical ganglion, travel into the pulp cavity and innervate the smooth muscle cells of the arterioles to modulate vasoconstriction. 

Additionally, sensory fibers that have arisen from the trigeminal ganglion pass through the apical foramen, travel longitudinally toward the crown and ramify as the nerve plexus of Raschkow. Fibers can extend in an unmyelinated form from this plexus toward the odontoblasts where they lose their Schwann cell sheath. These free nerve endings can sometimes extend up between the odontoblasts and enter the dentinal tubules where they function by transmitting pain stimuli from heat, cold or pressure (Standring, 2016)."}, {"name": "Anatomical Relations", "text": "Dental pulp is located in the root (radicular part) and crown (coronal part) of the tooth and is entirely surrounded and enclosed by dentin (Standring, 2016)."}, {"name": "Function", "text": "Dental pulp plays an important role in the defense process of the tooth whereby it houses cellular components necessary for the recognition and processing of antigens. Its sensory fibers additionally allow for the recognition of different stimuli including thermal change, mechanical deformation or trauma. The blood vessels and nerves housed by the pulp cavity provide nutritive support to the odontoblast layer, which facilitates the odontoblasts in their production of dentin (Yu and Abbott, 2007)."}, {"name": "List of Clinical Correlates", "text": "—Pulpitis"}, {"name": "References", "text": "Chiego, D. J. (2014) Essentials of Oral Histology and Embryology - E-Book: A Clinical Approach. Elsevier Health Sciences.

Dorland, W. (2011) Dorland's Illustrated Medical Dictionary. 32nd edn. Philadelphia, USA: Elsevier Saunders.

Standring, S. (2016) Gray's Anatomy: The Anatomical Basis of Clinical Practice. Gray's Anatomy Series 41 edn.: Elsevier Limited.

Yu, C. and Abbott, P. V. (2007) 'An overview of the dental pulp: its functions and responses to injury', Aust Dent J, 52(1 Suppl), pp. S4-16."}]

items.name: Blood Cells
items.info:
[{"name": "Quick Facts", "text": "Blood cells are the formed elements of blood and include the erythrocytes, leukocytes, and platelets (Dorland, 2011)."}, {"name": "Cell Morphology", "text": "Blood cells are the formed elements of blood and include the erythrocytes, leukocytes, and platelets. They constitute 45% of total blood’s volume. Erythrocytes make approximately 99% of the blood’s cellular component, while leukocytes and platelets account for only 1% of the blood cells. Erythrocytes are the densest component of blood, where their concentration is almost 1000 times greater than that of leukocytes (Pawlina, 2016). 

Erythrocytes are not true cells, in the sense that they possess unusual cellular features. Erythrocytes are small red biconcave cells that lack a nucleus and other cellular organelles. Erythrocytes have depressed thin centers, where the central thickness of the cell is approximately 0.8 μm and the edge is 2.6 μm (Pawlina, 2016). Their diameter is between 7 and 8 μm. The development of erythrocytes takes 5–9 days and they have a lifespan of around 100 to 120 days (Marieb, Wilhelm and Mallatt, 2012).

Leukocytes are white spherical cells and have organelles and prominent nuclei. Leukocytes protect the body from infectious agents. They can be subdivided in five types, the neutrophils, monocytes, lymphocytes, basophils, and eosinophils. Leukocytes take days to weeks to develop depending on their type, while their lifespan ranges from hours to years (Marieb, Wilhelm and Mallatt, 2012). 

Platelets are discoid cell fragments that lack a nucleus and are filled with granules. Their diameter is 2–4 μm and their lifespan is 5–10 days. Platelets take 4–5 days to develop (Marieb, Wilhelm and Mallatt, 2012).

Blood cells arise from pluripotent hematopoietic stem cells during hematopoiesis. Hematopoiesis takes place primarily in the red bone marrow. Production of blood cells is driven by growth factors. During hematopoiesis, only 25% of the developing cells will become erythrocytes. The remaining 75% will become leukocytes (Silverthorn et al., 2013)."}, {"name": "Function", "text": "Erythrocytes bind and deliver oxygen to tissues all around the body. Erythrocytes also bind carbon dioxide, thus removing it from the tissues.

Low numbers of erythrocytes may indicate a degenerative disease of the bone marrow (Marieb, Wilhelm and Mallatt, 2012).

Leukocytes function in the lymphatic system and interstitial fluid and are involved in the body’s immune defense. Different types of leukocytes are involved in phagocytosis, inflammation, and elicitation of immune responses. Elevated number of leukocytes, specifically immature neutrophils, indicates an infection.

Platelets are involved in blood clotting. Platelets clump to form a blood clot on small tears in an injured blood vessel, thus limiting bleeding (Marieb, Wilhelm and Mallatt, 2012)."}, {"name": "List of Clinical Correlates", "text": "—Anemia

—Polycythemia

—Sickle cell disease

—Leukemia

—Lymphoma

—Thrombocytopenia"}, {"name": "References", "text": "Dorland, W. (2011) Dorland's Illustrated Medical Dictionary. 32nd edn. Philadelphia, USA: Elsevier Saunders.

Marieb, E. N., Wilhelm, P. B. and Mallatt, J. (2012) Human Anatomy. 14th edn.: Benjamin Cummings.

Pawlina, W. 2016. Histology: A text and atlas with correlated cell and molecular biology. 7th ed. Philadelphia: Wolters Kluwer.

Silverthorn, D. U., Johnson, B. R., Ober, W. C., Garrison, C. W. and Silverthorn, A. C. (2013) Human Physiology: An Integrated Approach. Pearson Education."}]

items.name: Dorsal Artery of Penis
items.info:
[{"name": "Quick Facts", "text": "Origin: Internal pudendal artery.

Course: Penetrates the perineal membrane to reach the body of the penis. 

Branches: None.

Supplied Structures: Superficial tissues of the penis."}, {"name": "Origin", "text": "The dorsal artery of the penis arises as one of two terminal branches from the internal pudendal artery."}, {"name": "Course", "text": "The dorsal artery of the penis pierces the anterior margin of the perineal membrane to reach the dorsal surface of the body of the penis. This artery courses along its dorsal surface, medial to the dorsal nerve."}, {"name": "Branches", "text": "There are no named branches, however, the dorsal artery of penis anastomoses with branches of the deep artery of the penis and the urethral artery."}, {"name": "Supplied Structures", "text": "The dorsal artery of the penis supplies the superficial tissues of the penis."}]

items.name: Smooth Endoplasmic Reticulum (Anterosuperior Cut)
items.info:
[{"name": "Quick Facts", "text": "The smooth endoplasmic reticulum is a region of the endoplasmic reticulum composed of tubular elements lacking ribosomes and associated with many metabolic processes, including carbohydrate metabolism, the synthesis of lipids, cholesterol, and carbohydrates, and drug metabolism (Dorland, 2011)."}, {"name": "Structure and/or Key Feature(s)", "text": "Smooth endoplasmic reticulum is a network of interconnected membranous tubules and vesicles. It may be an extension of the rough endoplasmic reticulum or, be located separately. It’s also called agranular endoplasmic reticulum, because it has no ribosomes associated with it. In skeletal muscle cells and cardiomyocytes (cardiac muscle cells), the smooth endoplasmic reticulum is known as sarcoplasmic reticulum (Ross and Pawlina, 2006; Ovalle, Nahirney and Netter, 2013; McKinley, O'Loughlin and Pennefather-O'Brien, 2016)."}, {"name": "Anatomical Relations", "text": "The smooth endoplasmic reticulum is continuous with the rough endoplasmic reticulum."}, {"name": "Function", "text": "Smooth endoplasmic reticulum makes fatty acids, phospholipids, and steroids. It also contains a collection of enzymes that degrade toxic substances, drugs, and alcohol. It metabolizes glycogen and is involved with cell membrane production and recycling.

The sarcoplasmic reticulum (in skeletal muscle fibers and cardiomyocytes) stores and releases Ca2+ (Ross and Pawlina, 2006; Ovalle, Nahirney and Netter, 2013; McKinley, O'Loughlin and Pennefather-O'Brien, 2016)."}, {"name": "References", "text": "Dorland, W. (2011) Dorland's Illustrated Medical Dictionary. 32nd edn. Philadelphia, USA: Elsevier Saunders.

McKinley, M. P., O'Loughlin, V. D. and Pennefather-O'Brien, E. E. (2016) Human Anatomy. 5th edn.: McGraw-Hill Education.

Ovalle, W. K., Nahirney, P. C. and Netter, F. H. (2013) Netter's Essential Histology. ClinicalKey 2012: Elsevier Saunders.

Ross, M. H. and Pawlina, W. (2006) Histology: A text and atlas. Lippincott Williams & Wilkins."}]

items.name: Osteogenic Layer of Periosteum
items.info:
[{"name": "Quick Facts", "text": "Periosteum is a specialized connective tissue covering all bones of the body; in adults, it consists of two layers that are not sharply defined, the external fibrous layer being a network of dense connective tissue containing blood vessels, and the internal osteogenic layer composed of more loosely arranged collagenous bundles with spindle-shaped connective tissue cells, osteogenic precursor cells, and a network of thin elastic fibers (Dorland, 2011)."}, {"name": "Structure/Morphology", "text": "The inner, osteogenic layer of periosteum is populated with mesenchymal progenitor cells which can differentiate into osteoprogenitor cells. The osteoprogenitor cells, under the appropriate stimuli, may become osteoblasts. When there is no active bone formation, osteoblast cells are flat and have spindle-like nuclei but upon activation they appear cuboidal. All cells of the osteogenic layer sit in a loose connective tissue layer containing many fibroblasts. The osteogenic layer is well vascularized and has abundant innervation (Ross and Pawlina, 2006)."}, {"name": "Anatomical Relations", "text": "The osteogenic layer is in direct communication with the cortical bone whereby it provides osteoblasts for new bone formation. The osteoblasts form a layer adjacent to the cortical bone surface."}, {"name": "Function", "text": "The osteogenic periosteal layer provides the necessary cells for bone growth, modeling and remodeling. The periosteum works with its osteogenic counterpart, the endosteum, to define and maintain cortical thickness (Allen et al., 2004)."}, {"name": "References", "text": "Allen, M. R., Hock, J. M. and Burr, D. B. (2004) 'Periosteum: biology, regulation, and response to osteoporosis therapies', Bone, 35(5), pp. 1003-12.

Dorland, W. (2011) Dorland's Illustrated Medical Dictionary. 32nd edn. Philadelphia, USA: Elsevier Saunders.

Ross, M. H. and Pawlina, W. (2006) Histology: A text and atlas. Lippincott Williams & Wilkins."}]

items.name: Renal Corpuscle
Olfactory Epithelium
items.info:
[{"name": "Quick Facts", "text": "The olfactory epithelium is a type of pseudostratified epithelium that lines the olfactory region of the nasal cavity and contains olfactory receptors (Dorland, 2011)."}, {"name": "Structure and/or Key Features", "text": "The nose forms the initial part of the upper respiratory tract. It plays a role in warming, humidifying, and filtering air as it passes through the nasal cavity. The nasal cavity is lined by the olfactory epithelium.

The olfactory mucosa is composed of the olfactory epithelium and the lamina propria. The olfactory epithelium is a 60 μm thick pseudostratified columnar epithelial layer that lies external to the lamina propria. The lamina propria is a highly vascular connective tissue layer that sits between the cribriform plate of the ethmoid bone and the olfactory epithelium. It contains subepithelial olfactory glands. The glands are responsible for secreting the serous component of the mucus layer that covers the olfactory epithelium (Krstic, 2013; Conn, 2008).

The olfactory epithelium is highly disorganized and made up of various cell types such as basal cells, olfactory sensory neurons, and non-neuronal supporting cells. The olfactory sensory neurons lie among columnar supporting cells. Cilia, as well as microvilli of the supporting cells, are situated on the surface of the olfactory epithelium (Rao, Vemuri and Carpenter, 2007). 

The olfactory sensory neurons are bipolar and lie within the olfactory epithelium. Their cell bodies sit in the middle zone of the olfactory epithelium even though their cell bodies are distributed across several layers. They are responsible for detecting airborne odorant molecules (Standring, 2016).

The olfactory system is unique because, unlike other parts of the nervous system, it supports neurogenesis throughout life. New olfactory receptor neurons are produced during the process of neurogenesis in adult olfactory epithelium from horizontal basal stem cells in the olfactory epithelium. The enormity of neurogenesis is highest in the olfactory system compared to any other part of the nervous system. This is possibly as a result of the exposure and sensitivity of olfactory sensory neurons to noxious gases. The olfactory sensory neurons are programmed to identify chemical substances and so have to be regenerated often, since as they are likely vulnerable to the toxic effects of these substances (Standring, 2016; Kempermann, 2006)."}, {"name": "Anatomical Relations", "text": "The olfactory sensory neurons originate from the olfactory epithelium and travel through the cribriform foramina to terminate as olfactory nerves in the olfactory bulb."}, {"name": "Function", "text": "The olfactory epithelium is a part of the olfactory system, which is involved in facilitating the sense of smell. The olfactory sensory neurons within the epithelium are responsible for detecting airborne odorant molecules. Their axons aggregate to form the olfactory nerve fibers (CN I), which travels through the cribriform foramina to synapse within the olfactory bulb (Standring, 2016)."}, {"name": "Clinical Correlates", "text": "—Anosmia"}, {"name": "References", "text": "Conn, P. M. (2008) Neuroscience in Medicine. Humana Press.

Dorland, W. (2011) Dorland's Illustrated Medical Dictionary. 32nd edn. Philadelphia, USA: Elsevier Saunders.

Kempermann, G. (2006) Adult Neurogenesis: Stem Cells and Neuronal Development in the Adult Brain. Oxford University Press.

Krstic, R. V. (2013) Human Microscopic Anatomy: An Atlas for Students of Medicine and Biology. Springer Berlin Heidelberg.

Rao, M. S., Vemuri, M. C. and Carpenter, M. (2007) Neural Development and Stem Cells. Contemporary Neuroscience: Humana Press.

Standring, S. (2016) Gray's Anatomy: The Anatomical Basis of Clinical Practice. Gray's Anatomy Series 41st edition: Elsevier Limited."}]

items.name: Alveolar Epithelium
items.info:
[{"name": "Quick Facts", "text": "The alveolar epithelium is any cell of the walls of the pulmonary alveoli; the term is often limited to alveolar epithelial cells (type I and type II alveolar cells) and alveolar macrophages (Dorland, 2011)."}, {"name": "Structure", "text": "The alveolar epithelium consists of thin (squamous) type I pneumocytes (type I alveolar cells), cuboidal type II pneumocytes (type II alveolar cells) that bulge into the air luminal space and occasionally “Brush cells.” 

Whilst macrophages aren’t epithelial cells, they wander across the air surface of the type I pneumocytes removing unwanted particles e.g., dust."}, {"name": "Function", "text": "Gas exchange occurs across the type I pneumocytes. These cells cover about 95% of the alveolar surface. Whilst the type II pneumocytes are more numerous (60% of cells compared to 40% type I pneumocytes), they only occupy about 5% of the alveolar surface and secrete surfactant. Surfactant decreases the alveolar surface tension but is also involved with removing foreign materials (Ross and Pawlina, 2016).

Brush cells are scarce and probably provide information about the quality of the air entering the lungs."}, {"name": "References", "text": "Dorland, W. (2011) Dorland's Illustrated Medical Dictionary. 32nd edn. Philadelphia, USA: Elsevier Saunders.

Ross, M. H. and Pawlina, W. (2016) Histology: A Text and Atlas. Wolters Kluwer Health."}]

items.name: Submucosal Plexus (Duodenum)
items.info:
[{"name": "Quick Facts", "text": "The submucosal plexus is a nerve plexus that is part of the enteric plexus and is situated in the submucosa (Dorland, 2011)."}, {"name": "Structure/Morphology", "text": "The submucosal plexus is formed from branches of the myenteric plexus, which arise from the periarterial plexus that follows the superior and inferior mesenteric arteries and their terminal branches. Both the myenteric and the submucosal plexuses make up the enteric (or intrinsic) nervous system. The submucosal plexus itself may be subdivided into inner (or Meissner’s) and outer (or Schabadasch’s) submucosal plexuses (Brehmer, Rupprecht and Neuhuber, 2010). 

The enteric nervous system is unique to the digestive system and is autonomic in nature. It extends the entire length of the gastrointestinal tract and is composed of three types of neurons (Standring, 2016).

—Sensory neurons transmit information from receptors in the mucosa and muscle of the gut wall, which respond to mechanical, chemical, thermal, and osmotic stimuli. They project information to the interneurons.

—Motor neurons control the motility and secretions in the gut and may be inhibitory or excitatory.

—Interneurons go between the sensory and motor neurons, thus integrating the information between the two.

The enteric nervous system may function autonomously; however, it does communicate with the central nervous system via parasympathetic and sympathetic fibers. Cross connections between the two allow for information from the gut to be relayed to the CNS, and vice versa. Generally, sympathetic inputs cause inhibition of secretions and motor activity and contraction of sphincters and blood vessels (fight or flight response). Parasympathetic stimulation of the enteric nervous system promotes secretions and motor activity and dilation of the sphincters and blood vessels (rest and digest response) (Standring, 2016; Costa, Brookes and Hennig, 2000). 

In histological sections, the submucosal (Meissner’s) plexus is only visible as scattered ganglion cell bodies with satellite cells lying within the submucosal elements."}, {"name": "Key Features/Anatomical Relations", "text": "The submucosal plexus is superficial to the muscularis mucosae of the mucosa, and deep to the inner circular muscular layer."}, {"name": "Function", "text": "The submucosal plexus innervates the mucosal epithelium and the smooth muscle of the muscularis mucosa, which facilitate their respective functions of water and ion absorption and interstitial crypt emptying."}, {"name": "References", "text": "Brehmer, A., Rupprecht, H. and Neuhuber, W. (2010) 'Two submucosal nerve plexus in human intestines', Histochem Cell Biol, 133(2), pp. 149-61.

Costa, M., Brookes, S. J. and Hennig, G. W. (2000) 'Anatomy and physiology of the enteric nervous system', Gut, 47 Suppl 4(Suppl 4), pp. iv15-iv26.

Dorland, W. (2011) Dorland's Illustrated Medical Dictionary. 32nd edn. Philadelphia, USA: Elsevier Saunders.

Standring, S. (2016) Gray's Anatomy: The Anatomical Basis of Clinical Practice. Gray's Anatomy Series 41st edition edn.: Elsevier Limited."}]

items.name: Exocytosis (Posterior)
items.info: [{"name": "Quick Facts", "text": "Exocytosis is the discharge of material from a cell by fusion of a membrane-bound vesicle with the plasma membrane and subsequent release of the vesicle's contents into the extracellular environment (Dorland, 2011)."}, {"name": "Structure and/or Key Feature(s)", "text": "Many substances enter and leave the cell, and move between different cytoplasmic regions or organelles, by vesicular transport. Vesicles present in the cytoplasm (although appearing structurally similar) reflect different traffic pathways and functional states. In most cases, there is a continual renewal/replacement of the plasma membrane as new vesicles are formed from the cell membrane and enter the cell (endocytosis) or fuse with the plasma membrane to excrete substances (exocytosis).\n\nExocytosis is the release of bulk materials from the cell, a process whereby a membrane-bound structure within the cell approaches and fuses with the plasma membrane of the cell and release its content into the extracellular environment. An example of exocytosis is the release of digestive enzymes from salivary glands and the exocrine pancreas."}, {"name": "References", "text": "Dorland, W. (2011) Dorland's Illustrated Medical Dictionary. 32nd edn. Philadelphia, USA: Elsevier Saunders."}]

items.name: Smooth Muscle Cell (Contracted)
items.info:
[{"name": "Quick Facts", "text": "Smooth muscle is a type of muscle without transverse striations in its constituent fibers; it is found in the walls of the viscera and blood vessels and in the dermis and is not under voluntary control (Dorland, 2011)."}, {"name": "Structure and/or Key Features", "text": "Smooth muscle is composed of specialized cells that are elongated or fusiform, where they are larger at their midpoints and taper toward their ends. They can be a small as 20 μm (in the walls of small blood vessels); up to 200 μm (in the wall of the intestine), or up to about 500 μm in the uterus during pregnancy (Ross and Pawlina, 2016).

Smooth muscle cells are mononucleated, meaning they have a single nucleus which occupies the broadest region of the cell. In an uncontracted cell viewed in longitudinal section, the nucleus is an elongated structure with ends tapered. If the cell is sectioned transversely, the nucleus will appear as a circular/rounded profile. In a contracted smooth muscle cell, nuclei have a wrinkled, or corkscrew, appearance when viewed in a longitudinal section.

Each smooth muscle cell is encased by an external lamina (equivalent to the basal lamina in epithelial cells) and a network of fine reticular fibers. Reticular fibers are extremely thin (0.5-2 μm in diameter) and consist of mainly type III collagen. Adjacent cells are interconnected by gap junctions. 

The cytoplasm of smooth muscle cells is referred to as “sarcoplasm.” Most sarcoplasmic organelles, e.g., mitochondria, rough endoplasmic reticulum (rER), free ribosomes, glycogen granules and a Golgi apparatus, are located near the tapered ends of the nucleus (the perinuclear region). 

Unlike skeletal and cardiac muscle, smooth muscle does not contain any visible sarcomeres or striations, hence the name smooth muscle. The sarcoplasm of smooth muscle contains three filaments arranged obliquely and longitudinally. They include:

—thick myofilaments composed of myosin (14 nm diameter);

—thin myofilaments composed of actin and tropomyosin (6-8 nm diameter);

—intermediate filaments composed of desmin or vimentin (10 nm diameter) (Ovalle, Nahirney and Netter, 2013).

Dense bodies, which are unique to smooth muscle cells, contain attachment proteins (e.g., alpha actinin) for both the intermediate filaments and the thin myofilaments. These dense bodies (like Z lines of skeletal muscle fibers) are located at the sarcolemma (cell membrane) and distributed throughout the sarcoplasm. Thick myofilaments are scattered throughout the sarcoplasm and are arranged parallel to the thin myofilaments, with one myosin filament associated with 12 actin filaments (Ovalle, Nahirney and Netter, 2013).

Smooth muscle cells secrete components of its surrounding connective tissue matrix i.e., elastin, proteoglycans and adhesive glycoproteins, and type IV collagen (for the external lamina) and type III collagen (for the reticular fibers) that encases each smooth muscle cell. The reticular fibers create a flexible support for the sheet of smooth muscle cells as they change shape during contraction and relaxation."}, {"name": "Anatomical Relations", "text": "Smooth muscle cells form sheets or aggregated bundles of muscle found in most tissues of the body. It can be found in the walls of hollow tubes (such as blood vessels and the intestines), sacs (such as the stomach and bladder), sphincters, skin (arrector pili), and the intrinsic muscles of the eye."}, {"name": "Function", "text": "Since smooth muscle is found almost everywhere in the body, it ultimately controls functions of all organs and systems. Through its contraction and relaxation, smooth muscle regulates physiological functions such as digestion, respiration, reproduction, and blood flow."}, {"name": "Clinical Correlates", "text": "—Leiomyomas"}, {"name": "References", "text": "Dorland, W. (2011) Dorland's Illustrated Medical Dictionary. 32nd edn. Philadelphia, USA: Elsevier Saunders.

Ovalle, W. K., Nahirney, P. C. and Netter, F. H. (2013) Netter's Essential Histology. ClinicalKey 2012: Elsevier Saunders.

Ross, M. H. and Pawlina, W. (2016) Histology: A Text and Atlas. Wolters Kluwer Health."}]

items.name: Arteries of Skin
items.info: [{"name": "Quick Facts", "text": "The skin contains a rich network of blood and lymph vessels in the dermis and hypodermis (subcutaneous tissue). There are two major plexuses, one located at the region of the dermis and subcutaneous tissue, and one in the superficial part of the dermis that supplies a large network of capillaries to the dermal papillae."}, {"name": "Structure/Morphology", "text": "The skin contains a rich network of blood and lymph vessels in the dermis and subcutaneous tissue (hypodermis). There are two major plexuses, one located at the region of the dermis and subcutaneous tissue, and one in the superficial part of the dermis that supplies a large network of capillaries to the dermal papillae."}, {"name": "Function", "text": "These vessels supply nourishment to the three layers of the skin, the epidermis, dermis, and subcutaneous tissue. In addition, this vasculature acts as a thermoregulator. In cold conditions, blood flow is decreased in the papillary layer of the dermis to minimize heat lost from the body, while blood flow is increased in the papillary layer in hot conditions (Young, 2006)."}, {"name": "References", "text": "Young, B. (2006) Wheater's Functional Histology: A Text and Colour Atlas. Student consult: Churchill Livingstone/Elsevier."}]

items.name: Venule
Deep Epineurium
items.info:
[{"name": "Quick Facts", "text": "The epineurium is the outermost layer of connective tissue of a peripheral nerve, surrounding the entire nerve and containing its supplying blood vessels and lymphatics (Dorland, 2011)."}, {"name": "Structure/Morphology", "text": "The deep (or internal) epineurium is located between the fascicles of the nerve trunk and is an inward extension of the external epineurium. It is composed of loose connective tissue, which includes fibroblasts, collagen (types I and III), and variable amounts of adipose tissue, which separate nerve fascicles from each other, within the nerve trunk (Standring, 2016). The deep epineurium also contains lymphatics and vasa nervorum, a network of fine blood vessels passing across the perineurium communicating with the endoneurium."}, {"name": "Key Features/Anatomical Relations", "text": "Condensed loose connective tissue arising from the mesoderm forms the epineurium. The epineurium is then divided into the superficial and deep epineurium. The deep epineurium separates individual fascicles from one another while the superficial epineurium surrounds the entire nerve."}, {"name": "Function", "text": "The deep epineurium, like the superficial epineurium, protects the internal nerve fibers. Connective tissue in its structure acts as a cushion, preventing compression or damage of the nerve. The deep epineurium also facilitates gliding between the fascicles (Barral and Croibier, 2007)."}, {"name": "References", "text": "Barral, J. P. and Croibier, A. (2007) Manual Therapy for the Peripheral Nerves. Churchill Livingstone/Elsevier.

Dorland, W. (2011) Dorland's Illustrated Medical Dictionary. 32nd edn. Philadelphia, USA: Elsevier Saunders.

Standring, S. (2016) Gray's Anatomy: The Anatomical Basis of Clinical Practice. Gray's Anatomy Series: Elsevier Limited."}]

items.name: Cone Cell
items.info:
[{"name": "Quick Facts", "text": "A cone cell is one of the two types of visual cells, along with retinal rods, having synapses internally with bipolar retinal cells. Cones serve light and color vision and visual acuity. Their synaptic terminals are broad, flattened pedicles. Those outside the fovea centralis have dendritic inner segments that are relatively short and squat with blunt, rounded tips; those within the fovea centralis have inner segments that are more elongated and narrow, so that these cones resemble rods. There are 6 million to 7 million cones, of which about 10 percent are concentrated in the fovea centralis and the remainder are distributed fairly uniformly over the rest of the retina (Dorland, 2011)."}, {"name": "Structure and/or Key Features", "text": "Cone cells are one of the two classes of photoreceptor cell located in the retina of the eye. Long and radially oriented structures, photoreceptors are defined as highly differentiated neuroepithelial cells that are sensitive to light. Cone cells are approximately 40–50 µm long and it is estimated there are approximately 4.6 million cones in the human eye; but with significant inter-individual variation (Krstic, 2013; Molday and Moritz, 2015; Standring, 2016).

While cones are present along the entire extent of the retina, their maximum density is at the foveola, containing approximately 7000 cones. Cone cells here appear modified, narrower and more closely resemble rod cells. Further, cone density is up to 40–45% higher in the nasal retina compared to the temporal retina (Standring, 2016).

Cone cells have two distinct parts or segments, known as the outer and inner segments. They are connected to each other by a thin stalk. The outer segments are composed deep infoldings of cell membrane with the portion between folding forming a membranous disc. These discs are stacked on each other, having a larger diameter close to the connecting stalk, getting smaller as them move away. As a result, the entire outer segment takes on a conical shape. Rods outer segments share some similarities with cones but are shorter, o and the discs remain attached to the plasma membrane of cone cells. The great membranous surface area of the outer segments allows an accumulation of the visual pigments, or opsins, to be embedded in the cell membrane (Standring, 2016). The inner segments of cones are generally much wider than the inner segments of rods, measuring up to 5–6 µm and 1.5 µm, respectively. 

The nucleus of the cone is housed in the stoma (or cell body) and is larger and more oval than the nuclei in rod cells. Cone nuclei form a single layer that often fringes the outer limiting membrane (Standring, 2016).

At the junction between the outer nuclear layer and outer plexiform layer, the inner end of the photoreceptor widens to form a pedicle. Measuring 8–10 µm in diameter, cone pedicles are described as large, conical, flat end portions of the cone axon. The pedicle is where the presynaptic side of photoreceptor synapse is made. The processes of bipolar cells and horizontal cells invaginate into the pedicle and become the postsynaptic side of the connection. Electrical connections between neighboring photoreceptor cells also occur."}, {"name": "Anatomical Relations", "text": "Cone cells are located at high density in central retina and with decreasing frequency peripherally. They are the outermost cells of the neural retina and their outer segments cross the potential space of the embryonic optic ventricle to become engulfed by villous processes of the retinal pigment epithelial cells. From external to internal, cone cells span across four layers of the retina. Their cell bodies are located throughout the outer segments, the outer limiting membrane, and the outer nuclear layer, their synaptic terminals are found in the outer plexiform layer (Standring, 2016)."}, {"name": "Function", "text": "Photoreceptor cells are responsible for the absorption of electromagnetic radiation in the visible spectrum, transducing this to a voltage change in the cell, and conveying the signal to the cells at next level processing, bipolar and horizontal cells. More specifically, cone cells are photopic and function under bright light conditions. Light is absorbed by visual pigments, which are composed of a protein opsin, bounded by a light-absorbing chromophore, retinal (a form of vitamin A). Human photoreceptor cells can synthesize four different types of opsins, thus generating four spectrally distinct visual pigments. The rods contain one spectrally distinct visual pigment, while separate populations of cones contain one of three spectrally distinct visual pigments.

The three cone cell populations with spectrally distinct visual pigments are:

- maximally sensitive to short-wavelength light (blue cones);

- maximally sensitive to medium-wavelength light (green cones);

- maximally sensitive to long-wavelength light (red cones).

The visual pigments accumulate in the membranous discs in the outer segment of the photoreceptor cells. Further, the high density of cones at the foveola and the presence of more than one spectral cone type facilitates both high-resolution image processing and color vision. 

Note that activation of photoreceptor cells in humans results in hyperpolarization, or inhibition, of that cell. Moreover, when photoreceptors are not activated, for example in a dark room, they remain in a depolarized state, thus constantly releasing the neurotransmitter glutamate (called dark discharge). This release of glutamate at the synaptic terminal hyperpolarizes the connecting bipolar and horizontal cells; therefore, these cells are not activated, and the bipolar-ganglion synapse remains unexcited. When photoreceptors become activated by light, they hyperpolarize and the release of glutamate at the rod synaptic terminal ceases. The consequence of this is the depolarization of the connecting bipolar and horizontal cells and the transmission of the visual signal (Standring, 2016; Molday and Moritz, 2015)."}, {"name": "List of Clinical Correlates", "text": "- Cone-rod dystrophy

- Retinal degeneration

- Retinitis pigmentosa"}, {"name": "References", "text": "Dorland, W. (2011) Dorland's Illustrated Medical Dictionary. 32nd edn. Philadelphia, USA: Elsevier Saunders.

Krstic, R. V. (2013) Human Microscopic Anatomy: An Atlas for Students of Medicine and Biology. Springer Berlin Heidelberg.

Molday, R. S. and Moritz, O. L. (2015) 'Photoreceptors at a glance', J Cell Sci, 128(22), pp. 4039-45.

Standring, S. (2016) Gray's Anatomy: The Anatomical Basis of Clinical Practice. Gray's Anatomy Series 41 edn.: Elsevier Limited."}]

items.name: Lymphoid System
items.info:
[{"name": "Quick Facts", "text": "The lymphoid system includes the organs and tissues that produce lymphocytes (primary lymphoid organs [thymus and bone marrow]) or are largely composed of lymphoid tissue (secondary lymphoid organs [lymph nodes, tonsils, and spleen]) (Dorland, 2011)."}, {"name": "Description", "text": "The lymphoid system is composed of lymphatic vessels and lymphoid organs. The lymphatic vessels form a drainage system parallel to the cardiovascular system. It is responsible for draining interstitial (or extracellular) fluid that has escaped from the cardiovascular system, as well as the removal of cellular debris, and returning it to the venous system as lymph. 

Lymphatic vessels begin as small, endothelial-lined capillaries with an incomplete basement membrane, allowing interstitial fluid and debris to enter the capillaries (Földi et al., 2012). Capillary networks drain defined areas of the body into lymphatic vessels, which transports lymph through lymphoid organs and return it to the venous system.

Lymphoid organs are part of the immune system of the body. These organs are categorized into primary and secondary lymphoid organs, which are capable of detecting and combating pathogens, malignant or degenerative cells, and foreign material present in lymph.

Primary lymphoid organs include the bone marrow and the thymus. These organs are responsible for the generation of new, or de novo, lymphocytes. B and T lymphocytes differentiate and mature in the primary lymphoid organs (Standring, 2016).

Secondary lymphoid organs, such as the spleen and lymph nodes, are the sites in which B and T lymphocytes, along with antigen-presenting cells initiate an immune response."}, {"name": "References", "text": "Dorland, W. (2011) Dorland's Illustrated Medical Dictionary. 32nd edn. Philadelphia, USA: Elsevier Saunders.

Földi, M., Földi, E., Strößenreuther, R. and Kubik, S. (2012) Földi's Textbook of Lymphology: for Physicians and Lymphedema Therapists. Elsevier Health Sciences.

Standring, S. (2016) Gray's Anatomy: The Anatomical Basis of Clinical Practice. Gray's Anatomy Series: Elsevier Limited."}]

items.name: Inner Zone of Renal Cortex
items.info:
[{"name": "Quick Facts", "text": "The renal cortex is the outer part of the substance of the kidney, composed mainly of glomeruli and convoluted tubules; it is continuous with the renal columns, which are also composed of cortical tissue (Dorland, 2011)."}, {"name": "Structure and/or Key Features", "text": "The renal cortex is described as the highly vascularized, smooth, outer portion of the kidney. The renal corpuscles of the nephrons are located in the renal cortex. The cortex is subsequently divided into the outer and inner cortex depending on the distribution of the renal corpuscles (Zhang, 1999). Nephrons with their renal corpuscles located in the inner cortex are typically known as juxtamedullary nephrons."}, {"name": "Anatomical Relations", "text": "The inner cortex lies subjacent to the outer cortex and superjacent to the renal medulla."}, {"name": "Function", "text": "Both the outer and inner cortex contribute to ultrafiltration, fluid balance regulation, and the production of the red blood cell synthesizing hormone, erythropoietin (Pocock et al, 2013)."}, {"name": "References", "text": "Dorland, W. (2011) Dorland's Illustrated Medical Dictionary. 32nd edn. Philadelphia, USA: Elsevier Saunders.

Pocock, G., Richards, C. D. & Richards, D. A. (2013) Human Physiology, 4 edition. OUP Oxford.

Zhang, S. X. (1999) An Atlas of HistologySpringer."}]

items.name: Choroid
items.info:
[{"name": "Quick Facts", "text": "The choroid is the thin, pigmented, vascular coat of the eyeball extending from the ora serrata to the optic nerve; it furnishes blood supply to the retina and conducts arteries and nerves to the anterior structures (Dorland, 2011)."}, {"name": "Structure and/or Key Features", "text": "Along with the ciliary body and iris, the choroid forms part of the vascular layer of the eyeball. It is approximately 200 µm thick at birth, but this thickness decreases with age (Nickla and Wallman, 2010).

The choroid contains dense vascular beds supported by collagen and elastic connective tissue. The finest of these vessels are on the innermost aspect of the choroid and is called the capillary lamina of the choroid or choriocapillaris. This layer is so vascularized, it is responsible for the “red-eye” that can be observed when using flash photography. External to the choriocapillaris, the choroid contains much larger blood vessels that supply these vascular beds. These are called Haller’s and Sattler’s layers. 

The anterior choriocapillaris receives its blood supply from the long posterior ciliary arteries and recurrent branches of the anterior ciliary arteries, while the posterior choroid receives blood from the short posterior ciliary arteries.

The outermost layer of the choroid is the suprachoroid, which forms the transition between the choroid and the fibrous capsule surrounding it, the sclera. Here, the choroid contains numerous melanocytes that gives it a dark reddish pigmentation."}, {"name": "Anatomical Relations", "text": "The choroid sits between the outer sclera and the inner retina. It extends from the optic nerve posteriorly, where it’s continuous with the internal sheath of the optic nerve. Here, the choroid is firmly attached to the sclera, however, elsewhere it may only be loosely attached to the sclera."}, {"name": "Function", "text": "The vascular beds of the choriocapillaris are vital for supplying the adjacent avascular retina with oxygen and nutrients. These vascular beds are responsible for the “red-eye” that can be observed if reflected light is caught in flash photography. There is a strong oxygen/carbon dioxide diffusion gradient between the choroid and the outermost layers of the retina, where the outer segments and cell bodies of the rod and cone photoreceptors are located. These cells are highly metabolically active and therefore require a rich oxygen supply but must remain avascular to maintain clarity. Therefore, oxygen diffusion from the choroid is essential for retinal function. Additionally, the choroid is likely involved in thermoregulation and modulates intraocular pressure via vasomotor control of blood flow, and drainage of aqueous humor from the anterior chamber via the uveoscleral pathway (Nickla and Wallman, 2010)."}, {"name": "References", "text": "Dorland, W. (2011) Dorland's Illustrated Medical Dictionary. 32nd edn. Philadelphia, USA: Elsevier Saunders.

Nickla, D. L. and Wallman, J. (2010) 'The multifunctional choroid', Prog Retin Eye Res, 29(2), pp. 144-68."}]

items.name: Smooth Muscle Cell (Uncontracted)
items.info:
[{"name": "Quick Facts", "text": "Smooth muscle is a type of muscle without transverse striations in its constituent fibers; it is found in the walls of the viscera and blood vessels and in the dermis and is not under voluntary control (Dorland, 2011)."}, {"name": "Structure and/or Key Features", "text": "Smooth muscle is composed of specialized cells that are elongated or fusiform, where they are larger at their midpoints and taper toward their ends. They can be a small as 20 μm (in the walls of small blood vessels); up to 200 μm (in the wall of the intestine), or up to about 500 μm in the uterus during pregnancy (Ross and Pawlina, 2016).

Smooth muscle cells are mononucleated, meaning they have a single nucleus which occupies the broadest region of the cell. In an uncontracted cell viewed in longitudinal section, the nucleus is an elongated structure with ends tapered. If the cell is sectioned transversely, the nucleus will appear as a circular/rounded profile. In a contracted smooth muscle cell, nuclei have a wrinkled, or corkscrew, appearance when viewed in a longitudinal section.

Each smooth muscle cell is encased by an external lamina (equivalent to the basal lamina in epithelial cells) and a network of fine reticular fibers. Reticular fibers are extremely thin (0.5-2 μm in diameter) and consist of mainly type III collagen. Adjacent cells are interconnected by gap junctions. 

The cytoplasm of smooth muscle cells is referred to as “sarcoplasm.” Most sarcoplasmic organelles, e.g., mitochondria, rough endoplasmic reticulum (rER), free ribosomes, glycogen granules and a Golgi apparatus, are located near the tapered ends of the nucleus (the perinuclear region). 

Unlike skeletal and cardiac muscle, smooth muscle does not contain any visible sarcomeres or striations, hence the name smooth muscle. The sarcoplasm of smooth muscle contains three filaments arranged obliquely and longitudinally. They include:

—thick myofilaments composed of myosin (14 nm diameter);

—thin myofilaments composed of actin and tropomyosin (6-8 nm diameter);

—intermediate filaments composed of desmin or vimentin (10 nm diameter) (Ovalle, Nahirney and Netter, 2013).

Dense bodies, which are unique to smooth muscle cells, contain attachment proteins (e.g., alpha actinin) for both the intermediate filaments and the thin myofilaments. These dense bodies (like Z lines of skeletal muscle fibers) are located at the sarcolemma (cell membrane) and distributed throughout the sarcoplasm. Thick myofilaments are scattered throughout the sarcoplasm and are arranged parallel to the thin myofilaments, with one myosin filament associated with 12 actin filaments (Ovalle, Nahirney and Netter, 2013).

Smooth muscle cells secrete components of its surrounding connective tissue matrix i.e., elastin, proteoglycans and adhesive glycoproteins, and type IV collagen (for the external lamina) and type III collagen (for the reticular fibers) that encases each smooth muscle cell. The reticular fibers create a flexible support for the sheet of smooth muscle cells as they change shape during contraction and relaxation."}, {"name": "Anatomical Relations", "text": "Smooth muscle cells form sheets or aggregated bundles of muscle found in most tissues of the body. It can be found in the walls of hollow tubes (such as blood vessels and the intestines), sacs (such as the stomach and bladder), sphincters, skin (arrector pili), and the intrinsic muscles of the eye."}, {"name": "Function", "text": "Since smooth muscle is found almost everywhere in the body, it ultimately controls functions of all organs and systems. Through its contraction and relaxation, smooth muscle regulates physiological functions such as digestion, respiration, reproduction, and blood flow."}, {"name": "Clinical Correlates", "text": "—Leiomyomas"}, {"name": "References", "text": "Dorland, W. (2011) Dorland's Illustrated Medical Dictionary. 32nd edn. Philadelphia, USA: Elsevier Saunders.

Ovalle, W. K., Nahirney, P. C. and Netter, F. H. (2013) Netter's Essential Histology. ClinicalKey 2012: Elsevier Saunders.

Ross, M. H. and Pawlina, W. (2016) Histology: A Text and Atlas. Wolters Kluwer Health."}]

items.name: Bipolar Neurons
items.info:
[{"name": "Quick Facts", "text": "A bipolar cell is a nerve cell with two processes. Bipolar neurons located in the inner nuclear layer of the retina are the second neurons in the sensory pathway, making synaptic contacts with photoreceptors and retinal ganglion cells (Dorland, 2011)."}, {"name": "Structure and/or Key Features", "text": "Appropriately named, bipolar neurons are recognizable by two distinct projections, one axon and one dendrite, attached to a cell body. Known as the second-order neurons in the visual pathway, bipolar neurons are responsible for relaying information from photoreceptors cells to ganglion cells (Remington and Goodwin, 2011). 

In mammals, bipolar neurons are designated as cone bipolar cells or rod bipolar cells, depending on which photoreceptor cell they receive input from. There are approximately 10 distinct forms of cone bipolar cells but only one form of rod bipolar cell (Remington and Goodwin, 2011; Strettoi et al., 2010). 

According to size and connectivity, cone bipolar cells may be largely categorized as midget cone, blue cone, or diffuse cone bipolar cells. A subtype of midget bipolar cells, known as flat midget bipolar cells, synapses on the base of the cone pedicle. Most other midget bipolar cells make contact via direct invagination of the cone pedicle. In the peripheral retina, a midget bipolar cell may contact 2–3 cone cells. However, in the central retina, each midget bipolar cell synapses with just one cone photoreceptor cell, forming a direct channel from photoreceptor to ganglion cells, facilitating high spatial resolution (Standring, 2016). 

Another distinction between bipolar cells may be made from their response to light stimulation. There are ON bipolar cells and OFF bipolar cell differing in their response to the light-induced hyperpolarization of photoreceptor cells and the consequent cessation of glutamate release. Bipolar cells that depolarize following the activation and hyperpolarization of photoreceptor cells are classified as ON cells. On the other hand, bipolar cells that hyperpolarize following the light-induced hyperpolarization of photoreceptor cells are known as OFF cells (Standring, 2016).

Rod bipolar cells all share a single morphology. One rod bipolar cell will contact 40–45 rods in the peripheral retina and 30–35 rods in the central retina. Interestingly, bipolar rod cells do not directly contact ganglion cells, but instead make axodendritic or axoaxonic synapses with amacrine cells which proceed to excite ON retinal ganglion cells and inhibit OFF retinal ganglion cells by dendrodendritic connections. Thus on electron micrographs, one can see an arrangement called a serial synapse whereby a bipolar cell terminal is presynaptic to an amacrine terminal, which itself is presynaptic to a retinal ganglion cell terminal (Standring, 2016; Bloomfield and Dacheux, 2001)."}, {"name": "Anatomical Relations", "text": "Bipolar neurons are radially orientated. Their cell bodies are located in the inner nuclear layer. Within this layer they tend to be in the outer and middle portion, adjacent and vitreal to the horizontal cells. They are more sparse in the inner portion, which is mostly composed of Müller glia. The orientation of bipolar cells is perpendicular to the retinal layers. One process serves as a dendrite extending into the outer plexiform layer and is postsynaptic to photoreceptor cells, horizontal cells, and interplexiform cells. From the opposite side of the cell body, an axonal process extends into the inner plexiform layer where it is presynaptic to amacrine cells processes (Standring, 2016)."}, {"name": "Function", "text": "Bipolar cells are largely responsible for the direct and indirect transmission of visual signals from photoreceptor cells to ganglion cells. Specifically, the dendrites of bipolar cells receive input from photoreceptor cells, horizontal cells, and interplexiform cells and synapse directly onto ganglion cells or indirectly via amacrine cells (Remington and Goodwin, 2011).

Following the light-induced hyperpolarization of photoreceptor cells, the release of glutamate at the synaptic clefts is inhibited. ON bipolar cells will depolarize in response to the inhibition of glutamate, while OFF bipolar cells will hyperpolarize. As aforementioned, rod bipolar cells do not directly make contact with ganglion cells, but instead synapse with amacrine cells which excite surrounding ON bipolar cone cells and inhibit OFF bipolar cone cells. This results in an overriding of the cone pathway and facilitates the transmission of scotopic rod signals to ganglion cells in ambient light conditions (Standring, 2016; Bloomfield and Dacheux, 2001)."}, {"name": "List of Clinical Correlates", "text": "- Paraneoplastic retinopathy

- Congenital stationary night blindness"}, {"name": "References", "text": "Bloomfield, S. A. and Dacheux, R. F. (2001) 'Rod vision: pathways and processing in the mammalian retina', Prog Retin Eye Res, 20(3), pp. 351-84.

Dorland, W. (2011) Dorland's Illustrated Medical Dictionary. 32nd edn. Philadelphia, USA: Elsevier Saunders.

Remington, L. A. and Goodwin, D. (2011) Clinical Anatomy of the Visual System E-Book. Elsevier Health Sciences.

Standring, S. (2016) Gray's Anatomy: The Anatomical Basis of Clinical Practice. Gray's Anatomy Series 41 edn.: Elsevier Limited.

Strettoi, E., Novelli, E., Mazzoni, F., Barone, I. and Damiani, D. (2010) 'Complexity of retinal cone bipolar cells', Prog Retin Eye Res, 29(4), pp. 272-83."}]

items.name: Veins of the Perimysium
items.info:
[{"name": "Description", "text": "The contraction of muscle requires a vast amount of energy; therefore, an extensive vascular network is necessary in order to deliver this energy to the muscle tissue, in addition to removing the by-products (i.e., metabolic waste) of the muscle contraction.

Veins travel through the collagenous sheath, the perimysium, in between the fascicles, providing the muscle fibers within the fascicles with venous drainage. Nerves and blood vessels typically follow a similar branching course through the connective tissue of the perimysium."}, {"name": "List of Clinical Correlates", "text": "—Myopathy

—Necrotizing fasciitis

—Limb infarction"}]

items.name: Bulbous Corpuscle (Krause)
items.info:
[{"name": "Quick Facts", "text": "The Krause bulbous corpuscles are a type of small, spherical, encapsulated nerve ending found particularly in the dermis, lips, mouth, and conjunctiva; thought to function as a rapidly adapting mechanoreceptor (Dorland, 2011)."}, {"name": "Structure/Morphology", "text": "Bulbous corpuscles are mechanoreceptors located in the dermis of the skin. They are cylindrical/oval-shaped structures that contain encapsulated dendritic endings arranged into coils. The capsules are composed of a delicate layer of connective tissue, penetrated by a sensory neuron (Mescher, 2013). Krause bulbous corpuscles are found more superficial in the dermis than the Ruffini bulbous capsules."}, {"name": "Function", "text": "Bulbous corpuscles are responsible for detecting low frequency vibrations. They have also been described to be thermoreceptors, detecting cold temperatures (lower than 20 °C) (Thibodeau and Patton, 2013, Starr and Taggart, 2005)."}, {"name": "References", "text": "Dorland, W. Thibodeau, G. A. and Patton, K. T. (2013) Structure & Function of the Body - E-Book. Elsevier Health Sciences."}]

items.name: Myenteric Plexus (Jejunum)
items.info:
[{"name": "Quick Facts", "text": "The myenteric plexus is a nerve plexus that is part of the enteric plexus and is within the tunica muscularis (Dorland, 2011)."}, {"name": "Structure/Morphology", "text": "The myenteric (Auerbach’s) plexus is a network of thin bundles of axons and neurons, which may be grouped as small ganglionic clusters. It lies between the inner circular and outer longitudinal layers of the muscular layer (muscularis externa) of the small intestine. The myenteric plexus arises from the periarterial plexus that follows the superior and inferior mesenteric arteries and their terminal branches. All components of the myenteric plexus are continuous with the inner circular muscle nerve fiber bundles, which go on to synapse with the ganglionated and non-ganglionated plexuses of the submucosa. Both the myenteric and the submucosal plexuses make up the enteric (or intrinsic) nervous system.

The enteric nervous system is unique to the digestive system and is autonomic in nature. It extends the entire length of the gastrointestinal tract and is composed of three types of neurons (Standring, 2016).

—Sensory neurons transmit information from receptors in the mucosa and muscle of the gut wall, which respond to mechanical, chemical, thermal, and osmotic stimuli. They project information to the interneurons.

—Motor neurons control the motility and secretions in the gut and may be inhibitory or excitatory.

—Interneurons go between the sensory and motor neurons, thus integrating the information between the two.

The enteric nervous system may function autonomously; however, it does communicate with the central nervous system via parasympathetic and sympathetic fibers. Cross connections between the two allow information from the gut to be relayed to the CNS, and vice versa. Generally, sympathetic inputs cause inhibition of secretions and motor activity and contraction of sphincters and blood vessels (fight or flight response). Parasympathetic stimulation of the enteric nervous system promotes secretions and motor activity and dilation of the sphincters and blood vessels (rest and digest response) (Standring, 2016; Costa, Brookes and Hennig, 2000).

The interstitial cells of Cajal are flat, thin, branched cells are linked to the smooth muscle cells via gap junctions. They overlap with the myenteric plexus, and they are believed to act as pacemakers for myogenic contraction of the muscular layer, modulating the electrical slow wave activity to alter the rhythm of intestine contractions."}, {"name": "Key Features/Anatomical Relations", "text": "The myenteric plexus is situated between the two muscular layers; superjacent to the inner circular smooth muscle layer and subjacent to the outer longitudinal smooth muscle layer."}, {"name": "Function", "text": "The myenteric plexus houses most of the enteric neurons with motor function. These act on the different effector cells within the intestinal system. In conjunction with the interstitial cells of Cajal, this enables the coordinated muscular movements of the intestines, and contributes to immune and endocrine functions (Standring, 2016)."}, {"name": "References", "text": "Costa, M., Brookes, S. J. and Hennig, G. W. (2000) 'Anatomy and physiology of the enteric nervous system', Gut, 47 Suppl 4(Suppl 4), pp. iv15-iv26.

Dorland, W. (2011) Dorland's Illustrated Medical Dictionary. 32nd edn. Philadelphia, USA: Elsevier Saunders.

Standring, S. (2016) Gray's Anatomy: The Anatomical Basis of Clinical Practice. Gray's Anatomy Series 41st edition edn.: Elsevier Limited."}]

items.name: Capsule of Lymph Node
items.info: [{"name": "Quick Facts", "text": "The capsule is the outer layer of a lymph node, composed mainly of collagen fibers with a few fibroblasts and elastin fibers (Dorland, 2011)."}, {"name": "Structure/Morphology", "text": "Each lymph node is surrounded by a tough capsule of dense irregular connective tissue. The capsule is composed mainly of collagen and elastin fibers, with some fibroblasts interspersed. Smooth muscle is also present in the capsule of lymph nodes, especially those found in the axillary and inguinal regions (Ohtani and Ohtani, 2012). This smooth muscle is thought to be involved in the expulsion of lymph and lymphocytes into the efferent vessel of the lymph node."}, {"name": "Anatomical Relations", "text": "The capsule surrounds and supports the lobules of the lymph node and separated from it by the subcapsular sinus."}, {"name": "Function", "text": "Trabeculae extend from the capsule into the cortex of the lymph node to provide support within the node."}, {"name": "References", "text": "Dorland, W. (2011) Dorland's Illustrated Medical Dictionary. 32nd edn. Philadelphia, USA: Elsevier Saunders.\n\nOhtani, O. and Ohtani, Y. (2012) 'Recent Developments in Morphology of Lymphatic Vessels and Lymph Nodes', Annals of Vascular Diseases, 5(2), pp. 145-150."}]
