items.name: Enamel Striae
items.info:
[{"name": "Quick Facts", "text": "The enamel striae are lines showing the successive layers deposited in a tissue. In the enamel, they are brown striations visible under transmitted light and colorless in reflected light. They may be observed under the microscope in longitudinal sections as oblique lines running inward from the surface and toward the root and in cross-sections as rings similar to those in a tree trunk. Dry dentin often shows a series of somewhat parallel lines caused by imperfectly calcified dentin arranged in layers (Dorland, 2011)."}, {"name": "Structure and/or Key Feature(s)", "text": "Incremental growth lines known as enamel striae of Retzius are evident in tooth enamel. Histologically, they appear as a series of dark bands, with each line or band representing a period of between 6 and 12 days of enamel growth. This value is referred to as an individual’s periodicity, which remains constant in all teeth of one individual but varies considerably between individuals (Standring, 2016).

These bands travel in an oblique direction from the dentinoenamel junction near the surface of the crown. The striae subsequently end as a series of shallow furrows or curved grooves called perikymata. The proximate cause of the enamel striae of Retzius is changes in ameloblast activity; however, their ultimate cause is unknown (Reid and Ferrell, 2006).

While long-term striae of Retzius are more commonly reported in the literature, short-term daily growth lines are also evident in tooth enamel. These lines appear in intervals of between 2–3 µm at the dentinoenamel junction and 4–6 µm in outer enamel. When viewed microscopically, a small stria is evident across each prism, which likely reflects the diurnal swelling and shrinking of the prism diameter during growth. These short-term striae are called cross-striations (Birch and Dean, 2014)."}, {"name": "Function", "text": "While the etiology of the enamel striae of Retzius remains unclear, the striae occur with a constant periodicity in the teeth of an individual such that it can facilitate the determination of crown formation times. Knowledge of crown formation times is useful in forensic anthropology and for determining the age of juvenile remains. These incremental enamel lines are also useful for determining enamel growth trajectories and ages at death for humans (Birch and Dean, 2014; Reid and Ferrell, 2006)."}, {"name": "References", "text": "Birch, W. and Dean, M. C. (2014) 'A method of calculating human deciduous crown formation times and of estimating the chronological ages of stressful events occurring during deciduous enamel formation', J Forensic Leg Med, 22, pp. 127-44.

Dorland, W. (2011) Dorland's Illustrated Medical Dictionary. 32nd edn. Philadelphia, USA: Elsevier Saunders.

Reid, D. J. and Ferrell, R. J. (2006) 'The relationship between number of striae of Retzius and their periodicity in imbricational enamel formation', J Hum Evol, 50(2), pp. 195-202.

Standring, S. (2016) Gray's Anatomy: The Anatomical Basis of Clinical Practice. Gray's Anatomy Series 41 edn.: Elsevier Limited."}]

items.name: Tendon (of Biceps Femoris Muscle)
items.info:
[{"name": "Quick Facts", "text": "A tendon is a fibrous cord of connective tissue by which a muscle is attached. Tendons are usually named after the muscle to which they attach (Dorland, 2011)."}, {"name": "Structure and/or Key Feature(s)", "text": "Tendons are bands of fibrous connective tissue that appear white, as they are considerably avascular in nature. They are mainly made up of 30% collagen (mainly type 1 collagen) and 2% elastin, both of which are situated within an extracellular matrix of mucopolysaccharides and proteoglycan. The principal function of elastin in tendons is to provide flexibility. Tendons are able to extend up to 6–15% of their original length without issues (Maffulli, Renstrom and Leadbetter, 2005; Standring, 2016). 

Tendons attach muscles to bones, and their main function is to absorb mechanical forces from muscles and transit them to the bones to facilitate joint locomotion. Each muscle has two tendons, one located proximally, and the other distally.

The biceps femoris tendon has been described as a broad, flat tendon, shaped like a fan. Distally, it inserts into the fibular head, the lateral tibial condyle and the lateral ligament of the knee. It extends to the crucial fascia which covers a significant proportion of the anterior, posterior, and lateral aspects of the leg (Marshall, Girgis and Zelko, 1972). It is the most posterior structure on the proximal fibula. The biceps femoris tendon comprises an aggregation of tertiary fiber bundles. Tertiary fiber bundles are made up of several secondary fiber bundles, and secondary fiber bundles are made up of a collection of primary fiber bundles. The primary fiber bundles consist of aggregations of collagen fibers and fibrils."}, {"name": "Anatomical Relations", "text": "Tendons attach muscles to bones. Each muscle has two tendons, one located proximally, and the other distally."}, {"name": "Function", "text": "The principal function of tendons is to absorb mechanical forces produced by muscles and convey them to the corresponding bones to facilitate joint locomotion. 

The primary role of the biceps femoris tendon is to transmit force generated by the biceps femoris muscle to the bone to facilitate knee joint flexion and lateral rotation of the hip (when knee is flexed). The long head is part of the hamstring group of muscles, originates from the pelvis, and so is involved in hip extension. 

In addition, the tendon ensures the lateral collateral ligament is tight, and the iliotibial tract is unyielding in a number of different angles and degrees of knee flexion i.e., maintains lateral knee stability (Solomon and Stevenson, 2008)."}, {"name": "Clinical Correlates", "text": "—Tendon avulsion

—Tendon Rupture

—Enthesopathies

—Tendinitis

—Tenosynovitis"}, {"name": "References", "text": "Dorland, W. (2011) Dorland's Illustrated Medical Dictionary. 32nd edn. Philadelphia, USA: Elsevier Saunders.

Maffulli, N., Renstrom, P. and Leadbetter, W. B. (2005) Tendon Injuries: Basic Science and Clinical Medicine. Springer London.

Marshall, J. L., Girgis, F. G. and Zelko, R. R. (1972) 'The biceps femoris tendon and its functional significance', J Bone Joint Surg Am, 54(7), pp. 1444-50.

Solomon, L. B. and Stevenson, A. W. (2008) 'Tibial insertion of the biceps femoris tendon: anatomical and radiological description of an anatomical variant', Clin Anat, 21(8), pp. 802-4.

Standring, S. (2016) Gray's Anatomy: The Anatomical Basis of Clinical Practice. Gray's Anatomy Series 41 edn.: Elsevier Limited."}]

items.name: Cells of Nervous Tissue
items.info:
[{"name": "Quick Facts", "text": "Nervous tissue is the specialized tissue making up the central and peripheral nervous systems; it consists of neurons with their processes, other specialized or supporting cells such as the neuroglia, and extracellular material (Dorland, 2011)."}, {"name": "Structure and/or Key Features", "text": "The nervous system consists of two types of cells, neurons and the supporting cells, or neuroglia. The nervous system has more than ten billion neurons. Neurons are specialized cells that receive stimuli from other cells and conduct electrical impulses to other parts of the nervous system and other cells. The functional components of all neurons are the dendrites, cell body, axon, and synaptic junctions.

Neurons function at a high metabolic rate so they require a constant supply of oxygen and glucose. Neurons deprived of oxygen for more than a few minutes die (Marieb, Wilhelm and Mallatt, 2012).

Neuron cell bodies in the central nervous system (CNS) are either dispersed within the gray matter or are clustered into nuclei, columns, or layers. In contrast, neuron cell bodies in the peripheral nervous system (PNS) are confined within ganglia (Mancall and Brock, 2011). 

Neurons vary in size and shape and are classified into three major categories which are the sensory neurons, motor neurons, and interneurons. Sensory neurons receive information from the body’s sense organs and carry impulses from receptors to the central nervous system. They are also called afferent neurons. Motor neurons transmit impulses from the central nervous system or ganglia to their target cells and are also called efferent neurons. Interneurons, or intercalated neurons, form a communicating integrating network between sensory and motor neurons. 

Neurons are also classified, based on the number of processes extending from the cell body, into unipolar (pseudounipolar), bipolar, and multipolar neurons. In addition, neurons can also be classified, depending on the size of their axon, into Golgi type I and Golgi type II neurons. Golgi type I neurons have a very long axon (up to one meter or more in length). They are motor neurons in the CNS e.g., Purkinje cells in the cerebellar cortex and pyramidal cells in the cerebral cortex, or motor nerve fibers in the PNS. Golgi type II neurons have short axons, or may even be absent, and are numerous interneurons in the cerebral and cerebellar cortex (Ross and Pawlina, 2006; Splittgerber, 2018). Some neurons in the brain and elsewhere in the body act as neuroendocrine cells.

Neuroglia do not conduct electrical impulses and merely support neurons. Neuroglia in the CNS are the oligodendrocytes, astrocytes, microglia, and ependymal cells. Schwann cells and satellite cells are the supporting cells in the PNS as well as some specialized cells supporting sensory receptor cells in specific locations in the body (Ross and Pawlina, 2006)."}, {"name": "Anatomical Relations", "text": "Neurons are located within the CNS and PNS. They also form the enteric nervous system. Neuroendocrine cells are located in the brain and elsewhere in the body."}, {"name": "Function", "text": "Neurons are electrically excitable cells that process and transmit information. Neurons receive stimuli via their dendrites which conduct electrical nerve impulses towards the cell body. The axon of the neuron transmits electrical nerve impulses away from the cell body towards other neurons, cells, or glands. 

Sensory neurons receive information from the body’s sensory organs and carry impulses from receptors to the central nervous system. The processes of sensory neurons (i.e., the dendrites and axons) are found in somatic and visceral afferent fibers. Somatic afferent fibers are responsible for conveying sensations of pain, touch, temperature, and pressure from the surface of the body. Additionally, they carry sensations of proprioception and pain which is non-conscious sensation from body organs such as muscles, tendons, and joints towards the central nervous system. This provides the brain with information regarding the orientation of the body and the limbs. Visceral afferent fibers convey pain impulses and various sensations from internal organs, glands, mucous membranes, and blood vessels to the central nervous system. 

Motor neurons transmit impulses from the CNS or ganglia of the PNS to their target cells. Somatic efferent neurons are motor neurons that transmit voluntary impulses from the brain and spinal cord to skeletal muscles. Visceral efferent neurons are motor neurons that transmit involuntary impulses to glands, smooth muscle, and the Purkinje fibers which are cardiac conducting cells of the heart. 

Interneurons form a communicating, integrating network between sensory and motor neurons. Interneurons constitute more than 99.98% of all neurons (Marieb, Wilhelm and Mallatt, 2012).

Supporting cells of the nervous system have multiple functions such as:

—providing physical support and protection to neurons;

—insulating nerve cell bodies and axons for enabling rapid transmission of nerve impulses;

—repairing damaged neurons;

—regulating the internal fluid environment of the central nervous system;

—degradation or uptake of neurotransmitters from the synaptic cleft;

—metabolic exchange between neurons and the vasculature (Ross and Pawlina, 2006)."}, {"name": "References", "text": "Dorland, W. (2011) Dorland's Illustrated Medical Dictionary. 32nd edn. Philadelphia, USA: Elsevier Saunders.

Mancall, E. L. and Brock, D. G. (2011) Gray's Clinical Neuroanatomy: The Anatomic Basis for Clinical Neuroscience. Elsevier Health Sciences.

Marieb, E. N., Wilhelm, P. B. and Mallatt, J. (2012) Human Anatomy. fifth edn.: Benjamin Cummings.

Ross, M. H. and Pawlina, W. (2006) Histology: A text and atlas. Lippincott Williams & Wilkins.

Splittgerber, R. (2018) Snell's Clinical Neuroanatomy. Wolters Kluwer Health."}]

items.name: Cerebral Hemisphere
items.info:
[{"name": "Quick Facts", "text": "The cerebral hemisphere is either half of the cerebrum, lying on either side of the midline, partly separated by the longitudinal cerebral fissure, containing a central cavity (the lateral ventricle) and subcortical nuclei, and covered by the cerebral cortex; together they constitute the largest part of the human brain (Dorland, 2011)."}, {"name": "Structure", "text": "The cerebrum forms the largest part of the brain and is composed of right and left hemispheres. The cerebral hemispheres are connected by the corpus callosum, a mass of white matter. The cerebral hemispheres are separated from each other by a deep cleft known as the longitudinal fissure. An extension of the dura mater, the falx cerebri, extends into the longitudinal fissure. Posteriorly, the cerebral hemispheres are situated above the underlying cerebellum, separated from it be another dural extension, the tentorium cerebelli.

The outer layer of each cerebral hemisphere is composed of a thin (2–4 mm) gray matter, or cerebral cortex, which overlies a thick mass of white matter, or cerebral medulla. The cerebral cortex is made up of elevations which are twisted ridges of brain tissue that are known as gyri. The gyri are separated from each other by depressions, or shallow grooves, that are known as sulci. The sulci and gyri increase the surface area of the cerebral cortex by three times. Some of the deeper sulci are known as fissures and divide the cerebrum into five major lobes, which are the frontal, temporal, parietal, and occipital lobes and insula (Marieb, Wilhelm and Mallat, 2016). 

The cerebral cortex contains billions of neurons arranged in six layers, including the molecular, external granular, external pyramidal, internal granular, internal pyramidal, and multiform layers (Eroschenko, 2008). Additionally, the cerebral cortex is mapped into 47 structural areas that allowed the localization of functional regions. There are three main functional areas in the cerebral cortex which are the sensory, association, and motor areas."}, {"name": "Key Features/Anatomical Relations", "text": "The cerebral hemispheres are encased in the neurocranium and sit on the cranial base, which has three large depressions, the anterior, middle, and posterior cranial fossae. 

The frontal lobe occupies the anterior cranial fossa. It extends posteriorly to the central sulcus that separates it from the parietal lobe. The precentral gyrus is a prominent gyrus located on the posterior aspect of the frontal lobe and anterior to the central sulcus.

As mentioned above, the parietal lobe is separated anteriorly from the frontal lobe by the central sulcus. Posterior to the central sulcus is the postcentral gyrus. The parietal lobe extends posteriorly to the parietooccipital sulcus, which separates it from the occipital lobe. The inferior boundary of the parietal lobe is formed by the lateral sulcus which separates the temporal lobe from the frontal and parietal lobes. The temporal lobe occupies the lateral part of the middle cranial fossa. The insula is a small region of the cerebral cortex that lies deep within the lateral sulcus."}, {"name": "Function", "text": "The sensory areas of the cerebral cortex allow conscious awareness of sensation. The association areas of the cerebral cortex integrate diverse information, thus allowing purposeful action, while the motor areas are responsible for controlling voluntary motor function.

The frontal lobe consists of functional areas that are involved in planning, initiating, and enacting motor movement, along with movement of the eye and production of speech. The anterior region of the frontal lobe performs higher-order cognitive functions, e.g., decision-making, thinking, planning, and working memory.

The anterior parietal lobe contains the postcentral gyrus that contains the primary somatosensory cortex. The somatosensory cortex processes somatic sensations such as touch, pressure, cold, warmth, and pain. In addition, the parietal lobe processes sensory stimuli that allow spatial awareness of sounds, objects, body parts, and comprehension of speech.

The temporal lobe contains the auditory and olfactory cortices, which are responsible for sound and odor perception, respectively. The temporal lobe is also involved in the recognition of objects, faces, words, language comprehension, and emotional response and memory.

The occipital lobe contains the visual cortex, thus allowing reception, integration, and processing of visual information. The insula contains the visceral sensory cortex for taste and general visceral sensations."}, {"name": "References", "text": "Dorland, W. (2011) Dorland's Illustrated Medical Dictionary. 32nd edn. Philadelphia, USA: Elsevier Saunders.

Eroschenko, V. P. (2008) DiFiore's Atlas of Histology with Functional Correlations. Point (Lippincott Williams and Wilkins) Series: Wolters Kluwer Health/Lippincott Williams & Wilkins.

Marieb, E. N., Wilhelm, P. B. and Mallatt, J. (2012) Human Anatomy. fifth edn.: Benjamin Cummings."}]

items.name: Voltage-Gated Potassium Channel
items.info:
[{"name": "Quick Facts", "text": "A potassium channel is a voltage-gated channel selective for the passage of potassium ions, occurring in a wide variety of cells, including nerve, muscle, and secretory cells; its functions include regulation of cell membrane excitability, regulation of repetitive low-frequency firing in some neurons, and recovery of the nerve fiber membrane at the end of the action potential (Dorland, 2011)."}, {"name": "Structure", "text": "Voltage-gated potassium channels have four polypeptide subunits that form a pore between them. When the membrane is depolarized, the subunits change shape, allowing potassium ions to pass through the pore, thus allowing the efflux of potassium ions from the neuronal cell (Bear, Connors and Paradiso, 2007)."}, {"name": "Anatomical Relations", "text": "Generally, voltage-gated channels in the nervous system are mostly located on the cell body and dendrites of neurons, as well as on the nodes of Ranvier in myelinated axons, and on the axon hillock on unmyelinated axons."}, {"name": "Function", "text": "Most voltage-gated potassium channels open when the membrane is depolarized, and so, stop any further depolarization by allowing potassium ions to leave the cell.

The efflux of potassium ions causes the repolarization of the synaptic membrane potential, terminates the action potential, then hyperpolarizes the membrane potential (briefly) immediately afterwards and returns the depolarized synaptic membrane potential to its resting membrane potential (Bear, Connors and Paradiso, 2007)."}, {"name": "References", "text": "Bear, M. F., Connors, B. W. and Paradiso, M. A. (2007) Neuroscience. Lippincott Williams & Wilkins.

Dorland, W. (2011) Dorland's Illustrated Medical Dictionary. 32nd edn. Philadelphia, USA: Elsevier Saunders.

Ross, M. H. and Pawlina, W. (2006) Histology: A text and atlas. Lippincott Williams & Wilkins."}]

items.name: Hepatocyte
items.info:
[{"name": "Quick Facts", "text": "A hepatocyte is one of the polyhedral epithelial cells that constitute the substance of a liver acinus (Dorland, 2011)."}, {"name": "Structure/Morphology", "text": "Hepatocytes are the main epithelial cells of the liver parenchyma. They make up around 80% of the liver volume and 60% of the liver cell population (Standring, 2016). They are polygonal in shape and have six sides but may have as many as 12 sides per cell. The hepatocytes are arranged as hepatic plates, which distribute outwards as radial cords from the central vein. 

Hepatocytes have a large nucleus, spherical in shape, and located in the center of the cell. In the adult, many hepatocytes are binucleate and therefore are tetraploid (i.e., contain 4d amount of DNA). Two or more nucleoli are visible in each nucleus and heterochromatin is scattered almost evenly under the nuclear envelope (Mescher, 2013).

Hepatocytes are long-lived cells with an average lifespan of about five months. They are capable of considerable regeneration.

The cytoplasm of the hepatocytes has plentiful agranular (smooth) and granular (rough) endoplasmic reticulum, Golgi complexes, peroxisomes, and mitochondria, indicative of their high metabolic activity. Additionally, glycogen deposits and lipid droplets can be identified in the cytoplasm of hepatocytes."}, {"name": "Anatomical Relations", "text": "The basal surfaces of the hepatocytes face into the perisinusoidal space (of Disse) located adjacent to the sinusoids. These surfaces have numerous microvilli, which creates a large surface area that is exposed to the plasma that escapes from the sinusoids into this space.

The apical, or lateral, surfaces of adjacent hepatocytes are joined together via gap junctions and desmosomes. Localized intercellular spaces exist between the adjacent hepatocytes and are known as the bile canaliculi. Bile is secreted from the apical surfaces of the hepatocytes into the bile canaliculi. The tight junctions surrounding the canaliculi prevents bile from entering the sinusoids, thus creating a blood-bile barrier."}, {"name": "Function", "text": "Hepatocytes are the chief functional cells of the liver and are capable of completing metabolic, endocrine, and exocrine functions. The Golgi apparatus is involved in exocrine secretion of bile into the bile canaliculi, as well as synthesizing and secreting very low-density lipoproteins into the circulation (endocrine function). 

The agranular (smooth) endoplasmic reticulum contains enzymes that are involved in the degradation of toxins and drugs and the synthesis of cholesterol. Lysosomes store iron in the hepatocytes, while the peroxisomes are involved in the detoxification of alcohol, breaking down fatty acids, and gluconeogenesis (production of glucose) (Pawlina, 2016).

Glycogen is also stored in hepatocytes, where abundant amounts are seen after a meal, while minimal amounts are seen after prolonged fasting."}, {"name": "List of Clinical Correlates", "text": "- Hemochromatosis"}, {"name": "References", "text": "Dorland, W. (2011) Dorland's Illustrated Medical Dictionary. 32nd edn. Philadelphia, USA: Elsevier Saunders.

Mescher, A. (2013) Junqueira's Basic Histology: Text and Atlas. 13th edn.: McGraw-Hill Education.

Pawlina, W. 2016. Histology: A text and atlas with correlated cell and molecular biology. 7th ed. Philadelphia: Wolters Kluwer.

Standring, S. (2016) Gray's Anatomy: The Anatomical Basis of Clinical Practice. Gray's Anatomy Series 41st edn.: Elsevier Limited."}]

items.name: Thyroid Follicular Cell
items.info:
[{"name": "Quick Facts", "text": "A follicular cell, or T thyrocyte, is an epithelial cell of a thyroid follicle; these produce thyroid hormones and become enlarged in some forms of goiter (Dorland, 2011)."}, {"name": "Structure/Morphology", "text": "The thyroid follicle has two cell types, follicular cells, or T thyrocytes, and parafollicular cells, or C thyrocytes. 

Follicular cells, or T thyrocytes, are endocrine cells that form the wall of each thyroid follicle. Thyroid follicular cells are the only endocrine cells that synthesize its hormonal product and store it extracellularly. In inactive follicles, the follicular cells appear as low cuboidal or squamous. During their active secretory phase, they appear columnar.

The ultrastructure of the follicular cell reflects both secretory and absorptive functions. Thyroglobulin is synthesized on the rough endoplasmic reticulum inside the follicular cell. It is then glycosylated as it passes through the endoplasmic reticulum and Golgi apparatus. The Golgi apparatus has a supranuclear position and packages the thyroglobulin into vesicles, which move to the surface of the cell and are released into the lumen of the follicle as colloid by a process called exocytosis. The thyroglobulin is then reabsorbed by endocytosis from the colloid into the follicular cells, broken down, and transformed into the two thyroid hormones, T3 and T4. 

Iodide is absorbed into the follicular cell and highly concentrated. It is oxidized and passes into the colloid as iodine, which forms a complex with the thyroglobulin. This is a very important complex, since when its reabsorbed back into the cell, it contributes to the formation of the thyroid hormones. 

Thyroid follicular cells exhibit typical junctional complexes at their apical surfaces. They also possess microvilli. These projections wrap around segments of the colloid, then by endocytosis, the colloid is brought inside the cell as colloidal reabsorption droplets and fuse with lysosomes at the apex of the cell. Within the cell, the thyroglobulin reacts with lysosomal enzymes and other enzymes forming the thyroid hormones T3 and T4, which are released on the basal aspect of the cell into blood or lymphatic capillaries nearby (Ross and Pawlina, 2016). 

In tissue sections, the apical surface of the follicular cells appear as uneven boundaries close to the lumen, representing the endocytotic and exocytotic activity of the follicular cells.
"}, {"name": "Anatomical Relations", "text": "Follicular cells form the lining of each thyroid follicle."}, {"name": "Function", "text": "The thyroid follicular cell synthesizes and secretes the thyroid hormones, T3, and T4, which are released on the basal aspect of the cell into neighboring blood or lymphatic capillaries."}, {"name": "References", "text": "Dorland, W. (2011) Dorland's Illustrated Medical Dictionary. 32nd edn. Philadelphia, USA: Elsevier Saunders.
Ross, M. H. and Pawlina, W. (2016) Histology: A Text and Atlas. Wolters Kluwer Health.
"}]

items.name: Granulosa (of Secondary Ovarian Follicle)
items.info:
[{"name": "Quick Facts", "text": "Granulosa cells are cells surrounding the vesicular ovarian follicle and forming the stratum granulosum and cumulus oophorus; after ovulation they are transformed into lutein cells (Dorland, 2011)."}, {"name": "Structure and/or Key Feature(s)", "text": "When a primordial follicle develops into a primary follicle, the single layer of squamous follicular cells proliferates and becomes cuboidal. As the follicle develops, the oocyte secretes specific proteins to form an extracellular layer called the zona pellucida. It is located between the oocyte and the follicle cells. The single layer of cuboidal follicle cells undergoes rapid mitotic divisions to form a stratified epithelium called the granulosa that surrounds the oocyte. These follicular cells are now called granulosa cells. A basement membrane remains in position between the outermost layer of the granulosa cells (which are columnar) and the connective tissue stroma which is destined to become the thecal layers around the developing follicle. 

Extensive gap junctions form between adjacent granulosa cells but in the basal layer there are no tight junctions (zonulae occludens) most likely because nutrients, chemical messengers, etc. from the blood need to nourish the developing oocyte and granulosa cells (Ross and Pawlina, 2006)."}, {"name": "Anatomical Relations", "text": "The granulosa is situated between the primary oocyte and the follicular basement membrane."}, {"name": "Function", "text": "Under the influence of follicle-stimulating hormone (FSH), the granulosa cells transform androstenedione into estrogen. Estrogen then returns to the vascular theca interna and enters the blood stream to be transported throughout the body.

Estrogen stimulates granulosa cells to proliferate increasing the size of the follicle. A surge in the release of FSH and luteinizing hormone (LH) from the anterior pituitary gland occurs about 24 hours before ovulation, which desensitizes the LH receptors on the granulosa cells and the granulosa cells no longer produce estrogen (Ross and Pawlina, 2006; Mescher, 2013)."}, {"name": "References", "text": "Dorland, W. (2011) Dorland's Illustrated Medical Dictionary. 32nd edn. Philadelphia, USA: Elsevier Saunders.

Mescher, A. (2013) Junqueira's Basic Histology: Text and Atlas. 13th edn.: McGraw-Hill Education.

Ross, M. H. and Pawlina, W. (2006) Histology: A text and atlas. Lippincott Williams & Wilkins."}]

items.name: Cytoskeleton
items.info:
[{"name": "Quick Facts", "text": "The cytoskeleton is a three-dimensional cytoplasmic network of protein polymers (microfilaments, intermediate filaments, and microtubules), occurring in eukaryotes, that supports and maintains the shape of the cell and provides motility (both of the whole cell and of organelles and vesicles within the cell) (Dorland, 2011)."}, {"name": "Structure and/or Key Feature(s)", "text": "The cell cytoskeleton includes networks of protein microfilaments, intermediate filaments and microtubules. Microtubules radiate to the cell periphery from a microtubule organizing center (MTOC) which is usually located close to the cell nucleus (Ross and Pawlina, 2016)."}, {"name": "Anatomical Relations", "text": "The cytoplasm is located throughout the cell cytoplasm (Ross and Pawlina, 2016)."}, {"name": "Function", "text": "Microfilaments help to maintain cell shape and in some specialized cells (e.g., muscle cells) facilitate muscle contraction and intracellular movement.

Intermediate filaments stabilize cell junctions and provide structural support within the cell. 

Microtubules also maintain cell shape and are involved with moving organelles around the cell and supporting all those organelles within the cell. They affect motility of cilia and the tail piece of the mature sperm (flagellum) (McKinley, O'Loughlin and Pennefather-O'Brien, 2016; Ovalle, Nahirney and Netter, 2013; Ross and Pawlina, 2016)."}, {"name": "References", "text": "Dorland, W. (2011) Dorland's Illustrated Medical Dictionary. 32nd edn. Philadelphia, USA: Elsevier Saunders.

McKinley, M. P., O'Loughlin, V. D. and Pennefather-O'Brien, E. E. (2016) Human Anatomy. 5th edn.: McGraw-Hill Education.

Ovalle, W. K., Nahirney, P. C. and Netter, F. H. (2013) Netter's Essential Histology. ClinicalKey 2012: Elsevier Saunders.

Ross, M. H. and Pawlina, W. (2016) Histology: A Text and Atlas. Wolters Kluwer Health."}]

items.name: Fascia of Penis
items.info: [{"name": "Quick Facts", "text": "The fascia of penis is the firm inner fascial layer that surrounds the corpora cavernosa and the corpus spongiosum of the shaft of the penis collectively. It\u2019s continuous with the fascia of the ischiocavernosus and bulbospongiosus muscles (Dorland, 2011)."}, {"name": "Structure and/or Key Feature(s)", "text": "The fascia of the penis consists of a deep layer of fibrous tissue, which surrounds the corpora cavernosa, and splits to surround the corpus spongiosum. Distally, it blends with the tunica albuginea of all corporal bodies. Proximally, the fascia of the penis is continuous with the perineal fascia that invests the muscles of the superficial perineal space (i.e., bulbospongiosus, ischiocavernosus, and superficial transverse perineal muscles). It is also anchored to the suspensory ligament of the penis."}, {"name": "Anatomical Relations", "text": "The fascia of the penis surrounds the three corpora erectile bodies, as well as the deep dorsal vein, the dorsal arteries of the penis, and the dorsal nerves of the penis."}, {"name": "Function", "text": "The fascia of the penis is responsible for the structural integrity of the three erectile bodies of the penis."}, {"name": "References", "text": "Dorland, W. (2011) Dorland's Illustrated Medical Dictionary. 32nd edn. Philadelphia, USA: Elsevier Saunders."}]

items.name: Microtubule Organizing Center
items.info: [{"name": "Structure and/or Key Feature(s)", "text": "The centriole is associated with a zone of dense centrosomal matrix or pericentriolar material and collectively referred to as the microtubule organizing center (MTOC) or centrosome. The MTOC depends on the centrioles to exist (Ross and Pawlina, 2006)."}, {"name": "Function", "text": "The MTOC is where most microtubules radiate out to specific locations within the cell cytoplasm (Ross and Pawlina, 2006)."}, {"name": "References", "text": "Ross, M. H. and Pawlina, W. (2006) Histology: A text and atlas. Lippincott Williams & Wilkins."}]

items.name: Protoplasm
items.info: [{"name": "Quick Facts", "text": "Protoplasm is a general term for the substance of the cell (Dorland, 2011)."}, {"name": "Structure and/or Key Feature(s)", "text": "The protoplasm is the living components of the cell surrounded by the plasmalemma or cell membrane."}, {"name": "Function", "text": "The living components of the cell include the nucleus and the cell cytoplasm, which contains various specialized membranous and non-membranous components that perform all the cell\u2019s activities (Ross and Pawlina, 2006)."}, {"name": "References", "text": "Dorland, W. (2011) Dorland's Illustrated Medical Dictionary. 32nd edn. Philadelphia, USA: Elsevier Saunders.\n\nRoss, M. H. and Pawlina, W. (2006) Histology: A text and atlas. Lippincott Williams & Wilkins."}]

items.name: Lymphocyte
items.info:
[{"name": "Quick Facts", "text": "A lymphocyte is any of the mononuclear, nonphagocytic leukocytes, found in the blood, lymph, and lymphoid tissues, that are the body's immunologically competent cells and their precursors. They are divided on the basis of ontogeny and function into two classes, B and T lymphocytes, responsible for humoral and cellular immunity, respectively (Dorland, 2011)."}, {"name": "Cell Morphology", "text": "Lymphocytes are a type of white blood cell, or leukocyte, and are the chief cells of the immune system. There are three main classes of lymphocytes, B lymphocytes, T lymphocytes, and Natural Killer cells. Lymphocytes make 20–40% of the total leukocytes and 99% of cells in the lymphatic system (Owen et al., 2018). B lymphocytes make up 5–15% of human blood lymphocytes and T lymphocytes make up 70% of human blood lymphocytes (Todd, 2010). Natural killer cells make 10% of the lymphocyte population (Pawlina, 2016).

The majority of B and T lymphocytes are small. They have a round-shaped nucleus that occupies most of the cytoplasm. They also have little cytoplasm and condensed nuclear chromatin when inactive. Natural killer cells have a kidney-shaped nucleus and large cytoplasmic granules. The diameter of lymphocytes ranges from 5 to 17 μm. Activated lymphocytes are larger. Natural killer cells are larger than B and T lymphocytes (Pawlina, 2016).

B lymphocytes possess protein receptors for antigens and other proteins on their plasma membrane. T lymphocytes generally possess the CD4+ and CD8+ surface glycoproteins. Natural killer cells express the surface marker NK1 and cytotoxic granules (Owen et al., 2018).

T lymphocytes have a long lifespan while the lifespan of B lymphocytes varies. Natural killer cells live for around 2 weeks (Vivier et al., 2008)."}, {"name": "Production", "text": "Lymphocytes originate in the red bone marrow from hematopoietic stem cells that give rise to lymphoid stem cells, which give rise to lymphocytes. However, lymphocytes mature in different sites. Development of lymphocytes takes days to weeks (Marieb, Wilhelm and Mallatt, 2012).

B lymphocytes complete their maturation in the bone marrow and T lymphocytes leave the bone marrow as immature cells and complete their maturation and development in the thymus. After their maturation, they enter the bloodstream and migrate to the lymphoid tissues. 

Natural killer cells don't solely develop and mature in the bone marrow but in other lymphoid tissues, including the tonsils, spleen, and lymph nodes (Pawlina, 2016)."}, {"name": "Function", "text": "Lymphocytes are responsible for fighting infectious agents by recognizing antigens, proteins, or glycoproteins located in the plasma membrane of a foreign cell and eliciting an immune response. B lymphocytes are one type of the antigen-presenting cells, meaning that they present the antigens to T lymphocytes for destruction. B lymphocytes differentiate into:

—plasma cells, which secrete antibodies (IgA, IgG, IgE, IgM, IgD) that bind to the antigens and mark them for phagocytosis;

—Memory B cells, that remain in the lymphoid tissues until the same antigen is encountered again and elicit an immune response more vigorously. 

T lymphocytes differentiate into Helper T cells that assist with B lymphocyte differentiation via the secretion of cytokines, and Cytotoxic T cells, which kill the virus-infected host cells by causing them to lyse. 

Natural killer cells recognize surface proteins of infected, cancerous, or stressed cells. When activated, natural killer cells kill such cells via apoptosis. Natural killer cells are important cells of the innate immunity as they aid to control an infection until an adaptive immunity is developed (Owen et al., 2018)."}, {"name": "List of Clinical Correlates", "text": "—DiGeorge syndrome

—AIDS 

—Mononucleosis (“kissing disease”)

—Hodgkin’s lymphoma

—Non-Hodgkin’s lymphoma

—Lymphocytosis"}, {"name": "References", "text": "Dorland, W. (2011) Dorland's Illustrated Medical Dictionary. 32nd edn. Philadelphia, USA: Elsevier Saunders.

Marieb, E. N., Wilhelm, P. B. and Mallatt, J. (2012) Human Anatomy. 14th edn.: Benjamin Cummings.

Owen, J., Punt, J., Stranford, S. and Jones, P. (2018) Kuby Immunology. Macmillan Learning.

Pawlina, W. 2016. Histology: A text and atlas with correlated cell and molecular biology. 7th ed. Philadelphia: Wolters Kluwer.

Todd, I. (2010) 'Cells of the Immune System', eLS.

Vivier, E., Tomasello, E., Baratin, M., Walzer, T. and Ugolini, S. (2008) 'Functions of natural killer cells', Nat Immunol, 9(5), pp. 503-10."}]

items.name: Follicular Phase
items.info: [{"name": "Quick Facts", "text": "The follicular phase is the first part of the ovarian cycle, lasting from the end of the menstrual phase until ovulation and corresponding to the proliferative phase of the uterine cycle; it is characterized by the development of a dominant ovarian follicle, which reaches maturity by midcycle. At the end of this phase the luteinizing hormone surge and follicle-stimulating hormone surge begin, followed by ovulation (Dorland, 2011)."}, {"name": "Description", "text": "The follicular phase commences with the development of 10\u201320 primary follicles and then dominant follicles by days 5\u20137. It is influenced by follicle-stimulating hormone (FSH). During the first 8\u201310 days, FSH stimulates the granulosa and thecal cells to secrete estrogen into the lumen of the follicle. As the production of estrogens increases, FSH is inhibited by the pituitary gland in response to a negative feedback loop. The accumulation of estrogens in the lumen of the dominant follicles makes the follicle grow and develop independently of FSH and the amount of FSH in the circulation inhibits further production of FSH by the anterior pituitary. Late in the follicular phase, just before ovulation, progesterone levels rise in response to luteinizing hormone (LH), then a surge in LH induces ovulation about 10\u201312 hours later."}, {"name": "References", "text": "Dorland, W. (2011) Dorland's Illustrated Medical Dictionary. 32nd edn. Philadelphia, USA: Elsevier Saunders."}]
