Transit Amplifying Cell (Jejunum)
items.info: [{"name": "Quick Facts", "text": "Transit amplifying cells are the daughter cells of the intestinal stem cells found in the lower half of the intestinal glands (Ross and Pawlina, 2006)."}, {"name": "Structure/Morphology", "text": "Intermediate cells occupy much of the basal regions of the intestinal glands. This population of cells is known as the amplifying compartment as these cells are actively undergoing mitosis and will differentiate into absorptive cells or goblet cells as they migrate up the epithelium to the surfaces of the villi."}, {"name": "Key Features/Anatomical Relations", "text": "Intermediate cells occupy much of the basal regions of the intestinal glands."}, {"name": "Function", "text": "This population of cells will differentiate into absorptive cells or goblet cells as they migrate up the epithelium to surfaces of the villi."}, {"name": "References", "text": "Ross, M. H. and Pawlina, W. (2016) Histology: A Text and Atlas. Wolters Kluwer Health."}]

items.name: Adluminal Compartment
items.info: [{"name": "Quick Facts", "text": "The adluminal compartment of the convoluted seminiferous tubules contains the more mature spermatocytes and spermatids."}, {"name": "Structure", "text": "The position of supporting sustentocytes (Sertoli cells) on the basement membrane of the seminiferous epithelium, and the interconnecting tight junctions between cytoplasmic processes from adjacent Sertoli cells, subdivides the epithelium of the convoluted seminiferous tubules into basal and adluminal compartments, thereby dividing immature and mature progenitors into distinct anatomical and functional compartments.\n\nEarly formed spermatocytes in the basal compartment must past through the junctional complexes between adjacent Sertoli cells to access the adluminal compartment."}, {"name": "Anatomical Relations", "text": "The seminiferous epithelium has an adluminal compartment containing more mature germ cells adjacent to the lumen of the seminiferous tubule."}, {"name": "Function", "text": "The differentiation of the spermatogenic cells, meiosis and spermiogenesis occurs in the adluminal compartment with the differentiating spermatogenic cells still enveloped (and nurtured) by Sertoli cells."}]

items.name: Afferent Lymphatic Vessel
items.info:
[{"name": "Quick Facts", "text": "The afferent lymphatic vessels transport lymph to the lymph node."}, {"name": "Structure/Morphology", "text": "The lymphatic vessels form a secondary circulation system in the human body, the lymphatic circulation. The vessels form a drainage system, usually running parallel with veins.

Afferent lymphatic vessels are formed by the coalescence of blind ended lymphatic capillaries that permeate the vast majority of tissues within the body. Lymphatic capillaries are small with a diameter of about 10–60 µm and comprise a monolayer of endothelial cells that lack a continuous basal lamina (Margaris and Black, 2012). The unique arrangement of the endothelial cells allows them to act as one-way valves. This allows the entry of fluid and substances (such as antigens and cells) from the interstitium (or extracellular space) of tissues, thus producing lymph, which is relayed back to the afferent lymphatic vessels (Benias et al., 2018). 

As mentioned above, afferent lymphatic vessels are formed by the coalescence of lymphatic capillaries and transmits lymph to the lymph node. Each lobule of the lymph node has its own associated afferent vessel. The afferent vessels open through the capsule of the lymph node and delivers lymph to the subcapsular sinus. Since each afferent vessel brings lymph from a different region of tissue and delivers it to its own lobule in the node, it is possible for each lobule to be exposed to different sets of immunological agents, such as antigens, inflammatory mediators, etc. For this reason, cortical and medullary compartments of each lobule may not be uniform in appearance.

Afferent lymphatic vessels are composed of an internal endothelial layer, surrounded by an outer smooth muscle layer and connective tissue layer (Margaris and Black, 2012). The endothelial layer is organized in a monolayer. In some areas of the vessel the basal lamina is not continuous, thus allowing the entry of extracellular fluid and material, collectively known as lymph.

Afferent lymphatic vessels contain one or more layers of smooth muscle cells. The smooth muscle layer of the vessel aids the spontaneous contraction of the lymph vessels, thus, driving the propulsion of lymph through the vessels. 

Each afferent vessel contains valves, which prevent the backward flow of lymph. These are bi-leaflet valves composed of a thin layer of collagen between two layers of endothelial cells."}, {"name": "Function", "text": "Afferent lymphatic vessels convey lymph, lymphocytes and antigen-presenting accessory or dendritic cells into the subcapsular and medullary sinuses of lymph nodes. Lymphatic vessels also play an important role in homeostasis of extracellular fluid as they drain tissue, or interstitial, fluid. On average, 8–12 liters of afferent lymph is produced daily, of which 4–8 L is reabsorbed into the blood vessels in the lymph node. The remaining 4 L is transported in efferent lymphatic vessels back to the venous system directly. Accumulation of fluid results in edema of the affected area (Rovenska and Rovensky, 2011)."}, {"name": "References", "text": "Benias, P. C., Wells, R. G., Sackey-Aboagye, B., Klavan, H., Reidy, J., Buonocore, D., Miranda, M., Kornacki, S., Wayne, M., Carr-Locke, D. L. and Theise, N. D. (2018) 'Structure and Distribution of an Unrecognized Interstitium in Human Tissues', Scientific Reports, 8(1), pp. 4947.

Margaris, K. N. and Black, R. A. (2012) 'Modelling the lymphatic system: challenges and opportunities', J R Soc Interface, 9(69), pp. 601-12.

Rovenska, E. and Rovensky, J. (2011) 'Lymphatic vessels: structure and function', The Israel Medical Association Journal, 11, pp. 762-768."}]

items.name: Jejunum
items.info:
[{"name": "Quick Facts", "text": "Location: Abdominal cavity.

Arterial Supply: Jejunal arteries, which are branches of the superior mesenteric artery.

Venous Drainage: Jejunal veins, draining to the superior mesenteric vein.

Innervation: Parasympathetic: vagus nerve (CN X); Sympathetic: celiac ganglia; Visceral afferents: spinal ganglia of T5-T9; Enteric innervation. 

Lymphatic Drainage: Juxtaintestinal nodes to the central superior mesenteric nodes."}, {"name": "Structure", "text": "The jejunum is the second part of the small intestine, and entirely midgut. It begins at the duodenojejunal junction and ends at the ileum.

The cross-sectional microarchitecture of the jejunum demonstrates mucosa, submucosa, and muscular (inner circular and outer longitudinal) layers with a thin outer serosal covering (Standring, 2016). The jejunum has larger circular folds (plicae circulares) and villi, and a thicker mucosa than the ileum. It also has no Brunner’s glands (duodenum) nor Peyer’s patches (ileum)."}, {"name": "Key Features/Anatomical Relations", "text": "The jejunum is the second part of the small intestine. It is intraperitoneal and sits in the abdominal cavity, deep to the umbilical region and separated from the anterior abdominal wall by the greater omentum which overlays it. The jejunum is attached to the posterior abdominal wall by the mesentery that carries the superior mesenteric vasculature.

The jejunum begins at the duodenojejunal junction just distal to the suspensory ligament of the duodenum (or ligament of Treitz), roughly ventral and left of the L2 vertebra. The jejunum is roughly 2.5-3 m long and coils within the abdominal cavity to the start of the ileum. The transition from jejunum to ileum is not well defined."}, {"name": "Function", "text": "The jejunum is primarily a site of absorption but final enzymatic digestion of nutrients on the brush or striated border (microvilli) of enterocytes also occurs. 

Microvilli on the enterocytes that line the lumen of the jejunum are the site of absorption of nutrients. Lipids, which are primarily absorbed in the jejunum, are shuttled into the lymph system. All other nutrients are sent into the portal venous system (Standring, 2016)."}, {"name": "List of Clinical Correlates", "text": "—Crohn’s disease

—Jejunal diverticulosis

—Celiac Disease

—Jejunal atresia"}, {"name": "References", "text": "Standring, S. (2016) Gray's Anatomy: The Anatomical Basis of Clinical Practice. Gray's Anatomy Series 41 edn.: Elsevier Limited."}]

items.name: Artery
items.info: [{"name": "Quick Facts", "text": "An artery is a vessel through which the blood passes away from the heart to the various parts of the body. The wall of an artery consists typically of an outer coat (tunica externa), a middle coat (tunica media), and an inner coat (tunica intima) (Dorland, 2011)."}, {"name": "Structure/Morphology", "text": "Arteries supplying blood to the lymph node enter at the hilum, accompanied by a vein and an efferent lymphatic vessel which are exiting the lymph node.\n\nAs the artery enters the medullary region of the node, it divides to supply medullary arterioles and are conveyed in the medullary cords. Each lobule of the lymph node receives an arteriole, however, for descriptive purposes this is not shown in the 3D model. The arterioles continue to branch in the paracortex, or deep cortex, giving rise to capillary beds in the cortex."}, {"name": "References", "text": "Dorland, W. (2011) Dorland's Illustrated Medical Dictionary. 32nd edn. Philadelphia, USA: Elsevier Saunders."}]

items.name: Nucleus
Cochlea
items.info:
[{"name": "Quick Facts", "text": "The cochlea is a spirally wound tube, resembling a snail shell, which forms part of the internal ear. Its base lies against the lateral end of the internal acoustic meatus and its apex is directed anterolaterally. It consists of the modiolus, a bony canal, and the osseous spiral lamina, which partially divides the cochlea into the essential organs of hearing, the scala vestibuli and scala tympani; the scalae communicate through the helicotrema (Dorland, 2011)."}, {"name": "Structure and/or Key Feature(s)", "text": "The internal ear is composed of bony cavities, termed the bony labyrinth, and a serious of membranous sacs and ducts, termed the membranous labyrinth. The bony labyrinth is composed of the cochlea, vestibule, and semicircular canals and is lined with periosteum and contains perilymph. The membranous labyrinth is composed of the cochlear duct (found in the cochlea), the semicircular ducts (found in the semicircular canals), and the utricle and saccule (found in the vestibule). These ducts and sacs are filled with endolymph.

The cochlea is the most anterior portion of the bony labyrinth and communicates posteriorly with the vestibule. It is arranged as a spiral resembling a snail’s shell, as the cochlea twists about a central column of bone (the modiolus) two and three-quarter times. This arrangement produces a cone-shaped structure, with an apex protruding anterolaterally and a base facing posteromedially. This positions the modiolus toward the internal acoustic meatus where the cochlear nerve (from the vestibulocochlear nerve or CN VIII) can enter.

Internally, the cochlea consists of a continuous bony canal and spiral lamina. The cochlear duct, part of the membranous labyrinth, extends the length of the bony canal and is held in a central position by its attachment to the spiral lamina. Together, the lamina and cochlear duct divide the bony canal into two separate canals, the scala tympani and scala vestibuli. The scala vestibuli and scala tympani communicate at a narrow opening in the apex of the cochlea known as the helicotrema. 

The cochlear duct is separated from the scala vestibuli by a vestibular (or Reissner’s) membrane, while the cochlear duct is separated from the scala tympani by the basilar membrane. The basilar membrane contains the spiral organ of Corti situated on its superior aspect. The organ of Corti is composed of sensory epithelia which contribute to hearing."}, {"name": "Anatomical Relations", "text": "The cochlea is the anterior component of the internal ear, and so, it is continuous with the vestibule posteriorly. The base of the cochlea is lateral to the floor of the internal acoustic meatus, while the apex is medial to the tympanic membrane."}, {"name": "Function", "text": "The function of the cochlea is hearing by its participation in the process of auditory transduction. Briefly, this occurs by the movement of endolymph via sound, which results in a downstream activation of the auditory hair cells (and its stereocilia), facilitating neurotransmission of the cochlear afferent nerve fibers. Endolymph is a potassium-rich fluid located within the membranous labyrinth of the cochlea and bathes the stereocilia.

Auditory vibration passes from the external acoustic meatus to the middle ear, where it is transmitted from the tympanic membrane by the ossicles in the oval window in the internal ear. Essentially, these vibrations cause movement of this endolymph (through the oval window) which causes movement of the basilar membrane, stimulating the spiral organ (of Corti). This is detected by the displacement of stereocilia bundles of the hair cells, which activates the mechanoelectrical transduction ion channels. This facilitates the conversion of sound (vibrating mechanical energy) into electrochemical impulses along the cochlear nerve to its processing center in the cerebrum. 

While sound causes vibration of the different parts of the basilar membrane, maximal response is restricted to the region of the membrane attuned to the particularly specific frequency detection. As mentioned, this is based on the region of the basilar membrane, with narrow areas detecting frequencies as low as 0.1 kHz, while the broadest aspect detects up to 20 kHz (Yoshioka and Sakakibara, 2013)."}, {"name": "List of Clinical Correlates", "text": "—Sensorineural hearing loss"}, {"name": "References", "text": "Dorland, W. (2011) Dorland's Illustrated Medical Dictionary. 32nd edn. Philadelphia, USA: Elsevier Saunders.

Standring, S. (2016) Gray's Anatomy: The Anatomical Basis of Clinical Practice., 41st edition. Elsevier Limited.

Yoshioka, T. & Sakakibara, M. (2013) Physical aspects of sensory transduction on seeing, hearing and smelling. Biophysics (Nagoya-shi), 9, 183-91."}]

items.name: Bulbous Corpuscle (Ruffini)
items.info: [{"name": "Quick Facts", "text": "Ruffini bulbous corpuscles are a type of lamellated corpuscle in the dermis that is a slowly adapting receptor for sensations of continuous pressure (Dorland, 2011)."}, {"name": "Structure/Morphology", "text": "Bulbous corpuscles are slow adapting mechanoreceptors found in the reticular layer of the dermis, and are especially common on the plantar skin, or soles of the feet. They are highly branched nerve endings that are unmyelinated and traverse between bundles of collagen fibers. Ruffini bulbous corpuscles are located deeper in the dermis than the Krause bulbous corpuscles."}, {"name": "Function", "text": "Bulbous corpuscles act as stretch receptors in the dermis. They are also believed to be sensitive to heat."}, {"name": "References", "text": "Dorland, W. (2011) Dorland's Illustrated Medical Dictionary. 32nd edn. Philadelphia, USA: Elsevier Saunders."}]

items.name: Nerves of Transverse Colon
items.info:
[{"name": "Quick Facts", "text": "The transverse colon receives a vast innervation from the superior mesenteric plexus (proximal two thirds of transverse colon) and the inferior mesenteric plexus (distal one third of transverse colon)."}, {"name": "Description", "text": "Developmentally, the proximal two thirds of the transverse colon are components of the midgut, while the remaining distal third is hindgut. This developmental distinction is important in understanding the patterns of vascularization, innervation, and lymphatic drainage of the large intestine. 

The transverse colon receives a vast innervation from the superior mesenteric plexus (proximal two thirds) and the inferior mesenteric plexus (distal one third). It includes:

—autonomic nervous system (sympathetic and parasympathetic), which controls blood flow and motility of the gut;

—extrinsic sensory innervation (visceral afferents), which conveys sensation of colonic distension.

Sympathetic innervation is derived from the sympathetic chain and the aortic plexus. The proximal two thirds of the transverse colon is supplied by postganglionic neurons from the superior mesenteric plexus. The distal third of the transverse colon is supplied by the inferior mesenteric plexus. The vagus nerve (CN X) provides parasympathetic innervation to the proximal two thirds of the transverse colon, while the distal third receives parasympathetic innervation from pelvic splanchnic nerves (S2-S4). 

Visceral afferent nerves from the midgut ascend in tandem with the vagus nerve. In the hindgut, the cell bodies of the visceral afferents reside in the dorsal root ganglia of L2-L3 or S1-S2 (Standring, 2016).

The innervation of the large intestine also includes the enteric nervous system. It consists of two ganglionic plexuses of densely packed small neurons. Meissner’s plexus lies in the submucosal layer and Auerbach’s myenteric plexus sits between the inner circular and outer longitudinal muscular layers. The enteric nervous system controls mucosal and peristaltic function and its activity is regulated by the autonomic nervous system."}, {"name": "References", "text": "Standring, S. (2016) Gray's Anatomy: The Anatomical Basis of Clinical Practice. Gray's Anatomy Series 41st edition edn.: Elsevier Limited."}]

items.name: Eosinophil
items.info:
[{"name": "Quick Facts", "text": "An eosinophil is a granular leukocyte with a nucleus that usually has two lobes connected by a slender thread of chromatin, and cytoplasm containing coarse, round granules that are uniform in size (Dorland, 2011)."}, {"name": "Cell Morphology", "text": "Eosinophils are one type of leukocyte and account for only 1–4% of all leukocytes. There are around 100–400 eosinophils per microliter of blood. They are relatively the same size as neutrophils with a diameter of 12–15 μm and lifespan of around 5 days (Pawlina, 2016; Marieb, Wilhelm and Mallatt, 2012).

Eosinophils have bilobed nuclei and contain multiple large cytoplasmic granules. These granules contain digestive enzymes that are released during an allergic reaction or parasitic infection.

Eosinophils are predominately aggregated in the digestive tube, where parasites are more likely to be encountered. Eosinophils are also commonly found at sites of chronic inflammation."}, {"name": "Production", "text": "Eosinophils develop in the red bone marrow from myeloid stem cells that arise from hematopoietic stem cells and development usually takes 7–11 days (Marieb, Wilhelm and Mallatt, 2012). When eosinophils are fully developed, they are released into the blood and circulate there for around 10 hours, before migrating to connective tissue (Eroschenko, 2008). 

The number of eosinophils increases when the body is invaded by parasites or when an individual has an allergy. Production of eosinophils is driven by growth factors such as granulocyte-stimulating factor."}, {"name": "Function", "text": "Eosinophils provide defense against helminthic parasites by phagocytosis and releasing digestive enzymes. These digestive enzymes digest and destroy the parasites. 

Eosinophils end an allergic reaction by secreting an enzyme called histaminase which degrades histamine, and by releasing chemicals that neutralize inflammatory mediators (Marieb, Wilhelm and Mallatt, 2012; Pawlina, 2016)."}, {"name": "List of Clinical Correlates", "text": "—Eosinophilia

—Eosinopenia"}, {"name": "References", "text": "Dorland, W. (2011) Dorland's Illustrated Medical Dictionary. 32nd edn. Philadelphia, USA: Elsevier Saunders.

Eroschenko, V. P. (2008) DiFiore's Atlas of Histology with Functional Correlations. Wolters Kluwer Health/Lippincott Williams & Wilkins.

Marieb, E. N., Wilhelm, P. B. and Mallatt, J. (2012) Human Anatomy. 14th edn.: Benjamin Cummings.

Pawlina, W. 2016. Histology: A text and atlas with correlated cell and molecular biology. 7th ed. Philadelphia: Wolters Kluwer."}]

items.name: Sarcoplasmic Reticulum (Contracted Smooth Muscle)
items.info:
[{"name": "Quick Facts", "text": "The sarcoplasmic reticulum is a special form of smooth endoplasmic reticulum found in association with the T tubules in the sarcoplasm of striated muscle and comprising a system of cisternae and tubules forming a plexus around each myofibril. It contains large numbers of calcium pumps and ryanodine receptors and is a storage compartment for calcium ions, which it releases in response to an action potential in the adjacent T tubule to cause muscular contraction (Dorland, 2011)."}, {"name": "Structure and/or Key Features", "text": "The sarcoplasmic reticulum (SR) is an organelle that consists of a network of loose flattened tubules with various compartments, many of which contain Ca2+. The two ends of the SR are wider, thus form terminal sacs called cisternae. Two cisternae of adjacent sarcoplasmic reticula and one transverse tubule form a functional unit called a triad, which operates to elicit the release of Ca2+ from SR stores (Maclennan and Zvaritch, 2011)."}, {"name": "Anatomical Relations", "text": "Sarcoplasmic reticulum is a specialized type of smooth endoplasmic reticulum found in skeletal muscle. It forms a network of tubules that extend through a muscle fiber. The flattened tubules surround, but do not make direct contact with the myofibrils in a muscle fiber."}, {"name": "Function", "text": "The sarcoplasmic reticulum functions as an intracellular calcium store. Depolarization of the sarcoplasmic reticulum membrane results in the release of calcium ions (Ca2+). This release of calcium ions triggers the cascade required for contraction."}, {"name": "Clinical Correlates", "text": "—Fatigue

—Central core disease"}, {"name": "References", "text": "Dorland, W. (2011) Dorland's Illustrated Medical Dictionary. 32nd edn. Philadelphia, USA: Elsevier Saunders.

Maclennan, D. H. and Zvaritch, E. (2011) 'Mechanistic models for muscle diseases and disorders originating in the sarcoplasmic reticulum', Biochim Biophys Acta, 1813(5), pp. 948-64."}]

items.name: Vascular Endothelium (Artery)
Deep Dorsal Vein of Clitoris
items.info:
[{"name": "Quick Facts", "text": "Origin: Substance of the clitoris. 

Course: Crosses along the dorsal aspect of the clitoris and pierces the perineal membrane to drain into the vesical venous plexus. 

Tributaries: Deep veins of clitoris.

Drainage: Clitoris."}, {"name": "Origin", "text": "The deep dorsal vein of clitoris originates in the substance of the clitoris, between the fascia of the clitoris and the tunica albuginea."}, {"name": "Course", "text": "Along its course, the deep dorsal vein traverses the suspensory ligament of the clitoris and pierces the perineal membrane, close to the pubic symphysis, to drain into the vesical venous plexus."}, {"name": "Tributaries", "text": "Deep dorsal vein of the clitoris receives several tributaries from the deep veins of the clitoris."}, {"name": "Structures drained", "text": "The deep dorsal vein of the clitoris drains venous blood from the clitoris."}]

items.name: Glomerular Capsule
items.info:
[{"name": "Quick Facts", "text": "The glomerular capsule is the double-walled globular dilatation that forms the beginning of a renal tubule and surrounds the glomerulus; the inner wall is called the visceral layer and the outer wall is called the parietal layer (Dorland, 2011)."}, {"name": "Structure and/or Key Feature(s)", "text": "The glomerular capsule is described as a membranous, double walled capsule that forms an invaginated sphere around the glomerulus. It is the dilated proximal portion of the renal tubule. 

The glomerular capsule contains a thin, specialized layer of epithelial cells, an outer parietal layer, and an inner visceral layer. At the vascular pole, the inner visceral layer turns back, thus forming the outer parietal layer. The outer parietal layer, composed of simple squamous epithelium, is continuous with the cuboidal epithelium of the proximal convoluted tubule. 

The inner visceral layer is composed of specialized epithelial cells, called podocytes. Podocytes are distinct cells characterized by cytoplasmic extensions enveloping capillaries and their numerous secondary processes called foot processes, known as pedicels. Pedicels of adjacent podocytes interdigitate to form filtration slits covered by an ultra-thin filtration slit diaphragm. 

Between the inner visceral layer and the outer parietal layer, there is a space known as Bowman’s space. This space is continuous with the proximal convoluted tubule."}, {"name": "Anatomical Relations", "text": "The glomerular capsule is a dilated continuation of the proximal renal tubule that surrounds and forms an invaginated sphere around the glomerulus."}, {"name": "Function", "text": "The glomerular capsule is the first portion of the renal tubule that receives filtrate from the glomerulus. Further, the basal lamina of the podocytes and the filtration slits formed by the interdigitated processes of the podocytes are vital components of the renal corpuscle filtration apparatus."}, {"name": "Clinical Correlates", "text": "—Glomerular Disease"}, {"name": "References", "text": "Dorland, W. (2011) Dorland's Illustrated Medical Dictionary. 32nd edn. Philadelphia, USA: Elsevier Saunders."}]

items.name: Cortical Region
items.info:
[{"name": "Quick Facts", "text": "The cortex is the outer portion of the node, consisting mainly of dense lymphoid tissue and follicles (Dorland, 2011)."}, {"name": "Structure/Morphology", "text": "The cortex, primary lymphoid nodules, and secondary lymphoid nodules are collectively referred to as the cortical region. The cortical region is distinguishable by the presence of spherical lymphoid follicles, which are surrounded and separated by interfollicular (or diffuse) cortex. 

Primary lymphoid nodules are small spherical clusters of B lymphocytes, or B cells, tightly packed together within the reticular meshwork of the cortex. The secondary nodule has distinctive characteristics separating it from the primary nodule, in that it has a germinal center with a surrounding mantle zone.

Germinal centers are the major site for B lymphocyte (or B cell) proliferation, but also contains large and small lymphocytes, dendritic cells, and lymphoblasts. The mantle zone surrounds the germinal centers and contains small, dormant B lymphocytes (Standring, 2016)."}, {"name": "Anatomical Relations", "text": "The cortical tissue is located in the apical portion of the lymph node, between the subcapsular sinus and the paracortex. The lymphoid follicles present in the cortex are mainly populated with B cells and follicular dendritic cells (Standring, 2016). The number and the staining characteristics (during histological processing) of lymphoid follicles in the cortex greatly rely on the state of the antigen stimulation of the cells in the follicles."}, {"name": "Function", "text": "The cortex functions mainly to house quiescent lymphocytes, antigen-stimulated B-cells, and follicular dendritic cells."}, {"name": "References", "text": "Dorland, W. (2011) Dorland's Illustrated Medical Dictionary. 32nd edn. Philadelphia, USA: Elsevier Saunders.

Standring, S. (2016) Gray's Anatomy: The Anatomical Basis of Clinical Practice. Gray's Anatomy Series: Elsevier Limited."}]

items.name: Basement Membrane (of Primordial Ovarian Follicle)
items.info:
[{"name": "Quick Facts", "text": "The basement membrane is a thin sheet of amorphous extracellular material upon which the basal surfaces of epithelial cells rest; other cells associated with basement membranes are muscle cells, Schwann cells, and fat cells. The membrane is interposed between the cellular elements and the underlying connective tissue. It usually comprises two layers, the basal lamina and the reticular lamina, and is composed of Type IV collagen (which is unique to basement membranes), laminin, fibronectin, and heparan sulfate proteoglycans (Dorland, 2011)."}, {"name": "Structure and/or Key Feature(s)", "text": "Almost all epithelia are attached to some form of underlying connective tissues by a basal lamina. They are sheets of extracellular proteins and fibrils and are so thin that they can be seen only with an electron microscope. Under many epithelia, additional carbohydrate-rich material is appended to the lower face of the basal lamina. If the accumulation is sufficient to be seen under the light microscope, it is called a basement membrane. 

The basal lamina is synthesized by the epithelial cells and the additional material by the underlying connective tissue cells. Some epithelia do not have a basement membrane but almost all have a basal lamina (Mescher, 2013; Ross & Pawlina, 2016; McKinley et al, 2017)."}, {"name": "Anatomical Relations", "text": "Almost all epithelia are attached to some form of underlying connective tissues by a basal lamina."}, {"name": "Function", "text": "The basement membrane in the primordial ovarian follicle separates the follicular cells from the stroma of the ovary."}, {"name": "References", "text": "Dorland, W. (2011) Dorland's Illustrated Medical Dictionary. 32nd edn. Philadelphia, USA: Elsevier Saunders.

McKinley, M. P., O'Loughlin, V. D. and Pennefather-O'Brien, E. E. (2016) Human Anatomy. 5th edn.: McGraw-Hill Education.

Mescher, A. (2013) Junqueira's Basic Histology: Text and Atlas. 13th edn.: McGraw-Hill Education.

Ross, M. H. and Pawlina, W. (2006) Histology: A text and atlas. Lippincott Williams & Wilkins."}]

items.name: Vestibular Membrane
items.info:
[{"name": "Quick Facts", "text": "The vestibular wall of cochlear duct is the thin anterior wall of the cochlear duct, which separates it from the scala vestibuli (Dorland, 2011)."}, {"name": "Structure and/or Key Feature(s)", "text": "The vestibular (or Reissner’s) membrane is an elastic membrane that serves as a barrier, separating the scala vestibuli and the cochlear duct in the cochlea. It is notably thinner than the basilar membrane, which is the other elastic membrane associated with the cochlear duct. The vestibular membrane extends obliquely in the cochlea. It is attached from the stria vascularis overlying the osseous spiral ligament to the spiral limbus overlying the osseous spiral lamina.

The vestibular membrane is comprised of two distinct layers, both comprised of squamous epithelia, separated by a basal lamina. Given its anatomical position, the vestibular membrane has surfaces facing the scala vestibuli and the cochlear duct. The surface associated with the perilymph of the scala vestibuli is lined by flat perilymphatic cells. These cells form tight junctions between themselves, and results in the formation of the diffusion barrier between the scala vestibuli and the cochlear duct. The surface associated with the endolymph of the cochlear duct is lined by a squamous epithelium. These epithelial cells also form tight junctions and have a role in ion transport (Standring, 2016)."}, {"name": "Anatomical Relations", "text": "The vestibular membrane is interjacent between the scala vestibuli and the cochlear duct."}, {"name": "Function", "text": "The vestibular membrane serves as a barrier to separate the perilymph and endolymph located in the scala vestibuli and cochlear duct, respectively. While the perilymph and endolymph have a similar consistency, they differ in their ion concentrations. Perilymph has a high sodium content and a lower potassium content, while the opposite is true for the endolymph. The vestibular membrane serves as a diffusion barrier for ion exchange between these two fluids."}, {"name": "References", "text": "Dorland, W. (2011) Dorland's Illustrated Medical Dictionary. 32nd edn. Philadelphia, USA: Elsevier Saunders.

Standring, S. (2016) Gray's Anatomy: The Anatomical Basis of Clinical Practice., 41st edition. Elsevier Limited."}]

items.name: Eukaryotic Cell
Eukaryotic Cell
items.info:
[{"name": "Quick Facts", "text": "The cell is the smallest living unit capable of independent function, consisting of cytoplasm containing various subcellular compartments (organelles and cytosol) and separated from the external environment by the plasma membrane. Eukaryotic cells also include a nucleus containing the genome and nucleolus; prokaryotic cells lack a nucleus and DNA is present as a naked chromosome. Cells may exist as independent organisms or, with specialization for specific functions, be subunits of more complex organisms (Dorland, 2011)."}, {"name": "Structure and/or Key Feature(s)", "text": "The cell is the basic structural, functional, and reproductive unit of all multicellular organisms. All mature human cells have a surrounding barrier called the plasmalemma (cell or plasma membrane); a nucleus, which regulates the functions of the cell; and cytoplasm, which contains many components called organelles that perform specific cell functions embedded in an aqueous gel-like matrix called the cytosol. “Cytology” is the study of cells (Ross and Pawlina, 2006; Ovalle, Nahirney and Netter, 2013)."}, {"name": "Function", "text": "As it is the basic unit of life, the typical eukaryotic cell becomes specialized in various tissues and organs to perform body functions that sustain life."}, {"name": "List of Clinical Correlates", "text": "Most cells of the body divide to replace damaged, aged, or dead cells. Some cells, such as blood cells and cells in epithelia, are replaced often. Other cells, such as nerve cells (neurons) or cardiac muscle cells (cardiomyocytes), do not divide at all in the adult (McKinley, O'Loughlin and Pennefather-O'Brien, 2016).

The cell cycle has two phases:

- interphase, in which most cells spend most of their functional life:

- mitotic phase, when the cell divides into two cells. 

When some cell populations cannot properly control their cell cycle, they divide faster than they are dying and the resultant abnormal growth is called a neoplasm or tumor. A “benign” tumor is confined within a connective tissue boundary or capsule and is usually slow growing. A malignant tumor is not restricted by a capsule and so can easily spread to other tissues and organs. This is called metastasis. Cancer is the collective term used to describe malignant neoplasms (or tumors)."}, {"name": "References", "text": "Dorland, W. (2011) Dorland's Illustrated Medical Dictionary. 32nd edn. Philadelphia, USA: Elsevier Saunders.

McKinley, M. P., O'Loughlin, V. D. and Pennefather-O'Brien, E. E. (2016) Human Anatomy. 5th edn.: McGraw-Hill Education.

Ovalle, W. K., Nahirney, P. C. and Netter, F. H. (2013) Netter's Essential Histology. ClinicalKey 2012: Elsevier Saunders.

Ross, M. H. and Pawlina, W. (2006) Histology: A text and atlas. Lippincott Williams & Wilkins."}]

items.name: Heterochromatin
items.info:
[{"name": "Quick Facts", "text": "Heterochromatin is the form of chromatin that is darkly staining and tightly coiled in interphase; it is composed of repetitive DNA, is late to replicate, and is transcriptionally inactive (Dorland, 2011)."}, {"name": "Structure and/or Key Feature(s)", "text": "Compact or very condensed chromatin visible with the light microscope is called heterochromatin. It's more tightly packed DNA. 

A clump of chromatin (heterochromatin) frequently seen in female cells is called sex chromatin and is one of the two X chromosomes and is generally inactive.

Heterochromatin stains with basic dyes and hematoxylin (Ross and Pawlina, 2006; Ovalle, Nahirney and Netter, 2013; McKinley, O'Loughlin and Pennefather-O'Brien, 2016)."}, {"name": "Function", "text": "Heterochromatin is prominent in cells that are metabolically quiescent."}, {"name": "References", "text": "Dorland, W. (2011) Dorland's Illustrated Medical Dictionary. 32nd edn. Philadelphia, USA: Elsevier Saunders.

McKinley, M. P., O'Loughlin, V. D. and Pennefather-O'Brien, E. E. (2016) Human Anatomy. 5th edn.: McGraw-Hill Education.

Ovalle, W. K., Nahirney, P. C. and Netter, F. H. (2013) Netter's Essential Histology. ClinicalKey 2012: Elsevier Saunders.

Ross, M. H. and Pawlina, W. (2006) Histology: A text and atlas. Lippincott Williams & Wilkins."}]

items.name: Lateral Lacunae
items.info: [{"name": "Quick Facts", "text": "The lateral lacunae are venous meshworks within the dura mater on either side of, and continuous with, the superior sagittal sinus; arachnoidal granulations project into them (Dorland, 2011)."}, {"name": "Description", "text": "There are usually three irregularly shaped venous spaces, or lacunae, present inside the dura mater, on either side of the superior sagittal sinus. They can be considered as the lateral extensions of the sinus. These include a small frontal, large parietal, and intermediate occipital lacunae. The venous lacunae could potentially become confluent with age and form large single spaces on either side of the superior sagittal sinus. \n\nMost of the cerebral veins open into the venous lacunae and numerous arachnoid granulations project into them from below. The venous lacunae also drain diploid, emissary, and meningeal veins."}, {"name": "References", "text": "Dorland, W. (2011) Dorland's Illustrated Medical Dictionary. 32nd edn. Philadelphia, USA: Elsevier Saunders."}]

items.name: Skeletal Striated Muscle Tissue
items.info:
[{"name": "Quick Facts", "text": "Skeletal muscle is any of the striated muscles that are attached to bones and typically cross at least one joint; they are under voluntary control and facilitate movement of the skeleton (Dorland, 2011)."}, {"name": "Structure", "text": "Skeletal striated muscle (voluntary muscle) is formed by long parallel multinucleated cells packed together into fibers by collagenous sheaths. It is the most common type of muscle, the others being cardiac striated and smooth muscle. Cardiac and skeletal muscle are considered striated muscle, taken from their appearance when visualized under the microscope. 

Each individual fiber is enveloped in a delicate connective tissue sheath called the endomysium. Bundles of these fibers are surrounded by a thicker layer of connective tissue called the perimysium, these bundles are collectively known as the fascicles of the skeletal muscle. The entire external surface of the muscle is encased in a thick tough connective tissue sheath called the epimysium. Blood vessels and nerves run through all of these layers of connective tissue in order to nourish and innervate the muscle tissue. The three collagenous sheaths unite and fuse where the muscles connect to adjoining structures, such as tendons.

Skeletal muscle is well organized, allowing it to generate powerful contractions. The skeletal muscle fibers are long, cylindrical structures that can range from 10 to 100 µm in diameter, while they can vary from a few millimeters to many centimeters in length (Standring, 2016)."}, {"name": "Key Features/Anatomical Relations", "text": "Skeletal muscle is innervated by somatic motor nerves. For this reason, skeletal muscle is often termed “voluntary” muscle, since contractions are initiated under conscious control, such as walking. However, some skeletal muscle is involved at an unconscious level, such as breathing, blinking, which makes the term “voluntary” misleading."}, {"name": "Function", "text": "Skeletal muscle is responsible for producing strong contractions. These contractions shorten the muscle belly, which pulls on tendons attached to bone, thus producing movement."}, {"name": "List of Clinical Correlates", "text": "—Muscular dystrophy"}, {"name": "References", "text": "Dorland, W. (2011) Dorland's Illustrated Medical Dictionary. 32nd edn. Philadelphia, USA: Elsevier Saunders.

Standring, S. (2016) Gray's Anatomy: The Anatomical Basis of Clinical Practice. Gray's Anatomy Series 41 edn.: Elsevier Limited."}]

items.name: Axoneme (Middle Piece)
items.info:
[{"name": "Quick Facts", "text": "The axoneme is the central core of a cilium or flagellum, consisting of a central pair of microtubules surrounded by nine other microtubule pairs (Dorland, 2011)."}, {"name": "Structure and/or Key Feature(s)", "text": "The axoneme forms the core structure of the sperm tail. It is a cylindrical cytoskeletal structure that extends from the neck to the point where the tail terminates. 

The axoneme is composed of two centrally located microtubule singlets, which are encased by nine microtubule doublets. This is commonly referred to as the “9 + 2” complex. 

The major component proteins of the axoneme are cytoskeletal tubulin and the motor protein dynein. The microtubules are composed of dimers of α-tubulin and β-tubulin. Each of the microtubule doublets is made up of a complete α-microtubule, onto which a β-microtubule attaches. Two dynein arms extend from the α-microtubule to the β-microtubule of the neighboring doublet (Plant & Zeleznik, 2014)."}, {"name": "Anatomical Relations", "text": "The axoneme stretches across the entire length of the tail, from the neck region (just beneath the centriole) to the point where the tail terminates. The axoneme is the only structure present in the final 5–7 μm of the sperm tail (Standring, 2016).

The central pair of microtubules extend beyond the middle piece into the neck of the sperm, as far as the articular plate (capitulum). The outer doublets end just distal to the neck, where there is the remnants of the distal centriole (Plant & Zeleznik, 2014)."}, {"name": "Function", "text": "The axoneme acts as scaffold for the sperm tail, providing it with support and an ability to bend and unbend in various directions.

The motor dyneins associated with the microtubules of the axoneme have ATPase activity. Dyneins hydrolyze ATP and undergo a conformational change. They reach towards the minus end of the β-microtubule, resulting in the α- and β-microtubules in a doublet to slide past one another. The coordinated sliding in the doublets results in the propagation of a bending wave down the tail of the sperm, resulting in motility (Plant & Zeleznik, 2014).

The central pair of microtubules in the axoneme of the spermatozoon is involved in specific aspects of motility. The pair coordinates the sliding movements of the doublet microtubules, as well as taxis and reversal of the tail’s beating motion. These roles are essential for fertilization as evidence has shown that the absence of central pair form the spermatozoon tail results in the paralysis of the axoneme, and thus infertility (Linck et al, 2016)."}, {"name": "List of Clinical Correlates", "text": "- 9+0 syndrome"}, {"name": "References", "text": "Dorland, W. (2011) Dorland's Illustrated Medical Dictionary. 32nd edn. Philadelphia, USA: Elsevier Saunders.

Linck, R. W., Chemes, H. & Albertini, D. F. (2016) The axoneme: the propulsive engine of spermatozoa and cilia and associated ciliopathies leading to infertility. J Assist Reprod Genet, 33(2), 141-56.

Plant, T. M. & Zeleznik, A. J. (2014) Knobil and Neill's Physiology of Reproduction. Elsevier Science.

Standring, S. (2016) Gray's Anatomy: The Anatomical Basis of Clinical Practice. Gray's Anatomy Series 41st edition edn.: Elsevier Limited."}]

items.name: Cochlear Ganglion
items.info:
[{"name": "Quick Facts", "text": "The cochlear ganglion is the sensory ganglion located within the spiral canal of the modiolus. It consists of bipolar cells that send fibers peripherally through the foramina nervosa to the spiral organ and centrally through the internal acoustic meatus to the cochlear nuclei of the brainstem (Dorland, 2011)."}, {"name": "Structure and/or Key Feature(s)", "text": "The cochlear ganglion is a collection of neural cell bodies located within the bony labyrinth of the cochlea. Cochlear ganglia are situated throughout the body of the modiolus, within bony canals called Rosenthal’s canal. These canals share the same spiraling course as the osseous spiral lamina.

There are two distinguishable types of cells in the cochlear ganglion, type 1 and type 2 cells, making up roughly 95% and 5% of the population, respectively. Each cell body emits a central process that protrudes toward the organ of Corti and a central axon that projects back toward the cochlear nerve. Type 1 cells are larger, with a round nucleus and plentiful cytoplasmic organelles, and their central and peripheral branches are myelinated. Type 2 cells are smaller, with an irregularly shaped nucleus and a large number of neurofilaments in their cytoplasm. Their central and peripheral nerve branches are unmyelinated with a smaller diameter (Nayagam, Muniak and Ryugo, 2011). While the neurofilament proteins are in a greater abundance in the type 2 cell cytoplasm, they are also expressed in type1 cells albeit to a much lesser extent. These neurofilament proteins are involved in the development and maintenance of structural integrity of these neurons from childhood to adulthood. 

The processes of these cell bodies form afferent synapses at the bases of the hair cells. They are grouped into three different groups depending on the route to the hair cells. These groups are the inner radial group, the basilar group, and the outer spiral bundle."}, {"name": "Anatomical Relations", "text": "The cochlear ganglion occupies the open space of Rosenthal’s canal and so is in contact with the inner surface of this canal. Its path in this canal spirals up from the base to midway of the modiolus. On this course it provides slips of nerve fibers which travel interjacent to the two bony plates of the osseous spiral lamina."}, {"name": "Function", "text": "The cochlear ganglion relays efferent and afferent signals to and from the outer and inner hair cells of the cochlea. The spiral ganglion neurons allow for the feedback of auditory information via their central axons, which carry the signal to the auditory nerve, and from there to the auditory processing centers in the central nervous system. The primary neurotransmitter involved in cochlear neurotransmission is glutamate."}, {"name": "List of Clinical Correlates", "text": "—Degeneration of cochlear ganglion"}, {"name": "References", "text": "Dorland, W. (2011) Dorland's Illustrated Medical Dictionary. 32nd edn. Philadelphia, USA: Elsevier Saunders.

Nayagam, B. A., Muniak, M. A. & Ryugo, D. K. (2011) The spiral ganglion: connecting the peripheral and central auditory systems. Hear Res, 278(1-2), 2-20."}]

items.name: Superior Oblique Muscle
items.info:
[{"name": "Quick Facts", "text": "Origin: Body of sphenoid bone.

Insertion: Sclera on the superolateral part of posterior quadrant of the eyeball.

Action: Depresses, abducts, and medially rotates eyeball.

Innervation: Trochlear nerve (CN IV).

Arterial Supply: Ophthalmic and supraorbital artery."}, {"name": "Origin", "text": "The superior oblique muscle arises from the body of the sphenoid bone, superomedial to the optic canal and the superior rectus muscle."}, {"name": "Insertion", "text": "From its origin, the superior oblique muscle traverses anteriorly in the superomedial corner of the orbit to reach a fibrous cartilaginous loop, the trochlea, in the anterior, superomedial corner of the orbit. Here, the muscle becomes tendinous. The tendon passes through the trochlea and passes posterolaterally to attach to the superolateral part of the sclera at the posterior quadrant of the eyeball."}, {"name": "Action", "text": "The superior oblique muscle directs the pupil inferiorly (depression) around the horizontal (transverse) axis, a movement that is strongest when the eye is adducted. Additionally, it rotates the eye laterally (abduction) around the vertical axis (strongest when the eye is already partly abducted by lateral rectus) and intorts the eye (medial rotation) around the anteroposterior axis."}, {"name": "List of Clinical Correlates", "text": "—Lesions of trochlear nerve

—Diplopia, especially when looking downwards as in walking downstairs, leading to falls."}]

items.name: Endosteum
items.info: [{"name": "Quick Facts", "text": "The endosteum is the tissue lining all inner aspects of the bones, including the medullary cavity (Dorland, 2011)."}, {"name": "Structure/Morphology", "text": "The endosteum is a thin osteogenic layer that is lined with osteoblasts and precursors to osteoblasts. In times of inactivity, these cells are flat and are not easy to distinguish from each other. Upon activation, osteoblasts become cuboidal and are capable of producing osteoid which forms new lamellar bone."}, {"name": "Anatomical Relations", "text": "The endosteal layer is a thin but expansive layer. It covers all the trabeculae of the spongy bone along with the inner cortical surface from which the trabeculae are attached to. It also invaginates the perforations that allow the passage of blood vessels and continues into the cortical bone where it lines the perforating canals (Haversian and Volkmann\u2019s canals) (Standring, 2016)."}, {"name": "Function", "text": "The two osteogenic layers, the endosteum and periosteum, are responsible for the balance of bone deposition and resorption. Bone resorption is often greater than bone deposition and thus the marrow cavity expands as we age."}, {"name": "References", "text": "Dorland, W. (2011) Dorland's Illustrated Medical Dictionary. 32nd edn. Philadelphia, USA: Elsevier Saunders.\n\nStandring, S. (2016) Gray's Anatomy: The Anatomical Basis of Clinical Practice. Gray's Anatomy Series: Elsevier Limited."}]

items.name: Hypophyseal Cleft
Cribriform Plate of Ethmoid Bone
items.info:
[{"name": "Quick Facts", "text": "The cribriform plate is the horizontal plate of the ethmoid bone that forms the roof of the nasal cavity; it is perforated by many foramina for the passage of the olfactory nerves. On its superior surface is a projection called the crista galli (Dorland, 2011)."}, {"name": "Structure and/or Key Features", "text": "The cribriform plate is the horizontal, sieve-like plate of bone found along the superior aspect of the ethmoid bone. It is situated between the anterior cranial fossa and the nasal cavity and occupies the ethmoidal notch of the frontal bone, forming a significant portion of the roof of the nasal cavity. 

The cribriform plate is one of the three parts of the ethmoid bone that provides support to the olfactory bulb in the olfactory fossa. The ethmoid bone is made up of three components, the horizontal cribriform plate, the vertical perpendicular plate, and the two ethmoid labyrinths.

The cribriform plate possesses a number of perforations or foramina, through which the branches of the olfactory nerve (cranial nerve I) and their corresponding meninges (dura and arachnoid mater) pass through. 

The perpendicular plate is a thin, quadrilateral, midline bony projection that descends from the undersurface of the cribriform plate and constitutes a majority of the superior aspect of the nasal septum. The perpendicular plate continues superiorly as the crista galli. The pair of ethmoid labyrinths, which harbor the ethmoidal air cells, is situated on either side of the perpendicular plate. 

The crista galli is a thick, triangular part of the ethmoid bone, essentially a median ridge situated posterior to the foramen cecum, which projects superiorly from the cribriform plate. It aids the attachment of the falx cerebri to the ethmoid bone via its posterior edge. The cribriform plate is narrowed and indented on either side of the crista galli and is situated inferior to the gyrus rectus and the olfactory bulb. A small aperture, which is occupied by dura mater, is located on either side of the crista galli anteriorly. Anterolateral to this aperture is a foramen through which the anterior ethmoidal nerve and blood vessels pass on their way to the nasal cavity."}, {"name": "Anatomical Relations", "text": "The cribriform plate is one of the three parts of the ethmoid bone. The ethmoid bone is among one of the eight bones that make up the cranium, along with the frontal, sphenoidal, occipital, and symmetric pairs of the temporal and parietal bones. It forms a part of the viscerocranium and is situated in the midfacial aspect of the cranium, centered among the sinonasal structures."}, {"name": "Function", "text": "The main function of the cribriform plate is to provide support for the olfactory bulb, which sits superior to it. The cribriform plate possesses a number of perforations or foramina, through which the branches of the olfactory nerve, which is concerned with the sense of smell, and their corresponding meninges pass through."}, {"name": "Clinical Correlates", "text": "—Head trauma (blunt force trauma to the head) 

—Neurodegenerative diseases such as Alzheimer’s disease and Parkinson’s disease 

—Congenital anosmia

—Chronic sinus infection or inflammation"}, {"name": "References", "text": "Dorland, W. (2011) Dorland's Illustrated Medical Dictionary. 32nd edn. Philadelphia, USA: Elsevier Saunders."}]

items.name: Epineurial Arteries
items.info: [{"name": "Quick Facts", "text": "The epineurial arteries are part of the vasa nervorum and help supply the nerve."}, {"name": "Structure/Morphology", "text": "The epineurial arteries are located in the external epineurium and form part of the vasa nervorum, small blood vessels that supply nourishment to the peripheral nerves. This network of vessels supplies blood to the interior parts of the nerves and their coverings. The vasa nervorum are located within the connective tissue of the nerve scattered between the fascicles (Boissaud-Cooke, Pidgeon and Tunstall, 2015)."}, {"name": "Anatomical Relations", "text": "The vasa nervorum are the smallest vessels in the epineurial, perineurial, and endoneurial layers."}, {"name": "Function", "text": "The vasa nervorum supply the peripheral nerves with the molecular nutrients needed to carry out their cellular functions and for survival (Carp, 2015)."}, {"name": "References", "text": "Boissaud-Cooke, M., Pidgeon, T. E. and Tunstall, R. (2015) 'Chapter 37 - The Microcirculation of Peripheral Nerves: The Vasa Nervorum A2 - Tubbs, R. Shane', in Rizk, E., Shoja, M.M., Loukas, M., Barbaro, N. & Spinner, R.J. (eds.) Nerves and Nerve Injuries. San Diego: Academic Press, pp. 507-523.\n\nCarp, S. (2015) Peripheral Nerve Injury An Anatomical and Physiological Approach for Physical Therapy Intervention. EBL-Schweitzer: F. A. Davis Company."}]

items.name: Predentin
items.info:
[{"name": "Quick Facts", "text": "Predentin is the soft fibrillar substance composing the primitive dentin and forming the inner layer of the circumpulpar dentin (Dorland, 2011)."}, {"name": "Structure and/or Key Feature(s)", "text": "Predentin is progressively produced by odontoblasts at the surface of the pulp cavity, which reduces the size of the cavity throughout life (Standring, 2016). 

Predentin consists of randomly scattered type 1 collagen fibers embedded in an extracellular matrix of phosphoprotein and glycosaminoglycans (Lowe, Anderson and Anderson, 2018)."}, {"name": "Anatomical Relations", "text": "Adjacent to the odontoblast layer at the periphery of the pulp, there is a thin zone of immature uncalcified dentin, called predentin. The predentin layer is surrounded by the outer dentin layer, which typically stains darker than its unmineralized predentin counterpart (Lowe, Anderson and Anderson, 2018)."}, {"name": "Function", "text": "Predentin is a precursor to the mature, calcified dentin, which makes up the bulk of the tooth and ensures its structural integrity. Following its synthesis and formation by odontoblasts, predentin becomes mineralized at the border with previously mineralized dentin. As the predentin layer nears the predentin-dentin border, its collagen fibers become more numerous and tightly packed which facilitates dentin rigidity (Standring, 2016)."}, {"name": "References", "text": "Dorland, W. (2011) Dorland's Illustrated Medical Dictionary. 32nd edn. Philadelphia, USA: Elsevier Saunders.

Lowe, J. S., Anderson, P. G. and Anderson, S. I. (2018) Stevens & Lowe's Human Histology- E-Book. 5 edn.: Elsevier Health Sciences.

Standring, S. (2016) Gray's Anatomy: The Anatomical Basis of Clinical Practice. Gray's Anatomy Series 41 edn.: Elsevier Limited."}]

items.name: Intermediate Filament (Anterior)
items.info:
[{"name": "Quick Facts", "text": "An intermediate filament is a class of cytoplasmic filaments, 8–11 nm in diameter, that predominantly act as structural components of the cytoskeleton and also allow various movements in cellular processes. Different types contain different, tissue-specific proteins (Dorland, 2011)."}, {"name": "Structure and/or Key Feature(s)", "text": "Intermediate filaments are filaments structured like ropes and have a size range of 8-12 nm. They may consist of several proteins (Ross and Pawlina, 2006)."}, {"name": "Function", "text": "Intermediate filaments have a structural role maintaining the stability of cell to cell junctions and adherence of the cell to the extracellular matrix. They also function as part of the cytoskeleton, thus supporting the cell (Ross and Pawlina, 2006)."}, {"name": "Clinical Correlates", "text": "Several diseases can be attributed to defects in the assembly of intermediate filaments. A characteristic of Alzheimer’s disease is disarray of intermediate filaments in some neurons (Ross & Pawlina, 2016).

“Mallory bodies” in hepatocytes in alcoholic liver cirrhosis is the accumulation of inclusions containing predominantly keratin intermediate filaments (Ross and Pawlina, 2006).

Some specific types of intermediate filaments occurring in tumors allow the origins of the cell causing the tumor to be identified (Ovalle, Nahirney and Netter, 2013)."}, {"name": "References", "text": "Dorland, W. (2011) Dorland's Illustrated Medical Dictionary. 32nd edn. Philadelphia, USA: Elsevier Saunders.

Ovalle, W. K., Nahirney, P. C. and Netter, F. H. (2013) Netter's Essential Histology. ClinicalKey 2012: Elsevier Saunders.

Ross, M. H. and Pawlina, W. (2006) Histology: A text and atlas. Lippincott Williams & Wilkins."}]

items.name: Subcutaneous Tissue of Penis
items.info: [{"name": "Quick Facts", "text": "The subcutaneous tissue of penis is the loose external layer of fascial tissue of the penis, continuous with the dartos fascia and the subcutaneous perineal fascia (Dorland, 2011)."}, {"name": "Structure and/or Key Feature(s)", "text": "The subcutaneous tissue of the penis is a motile sheath of loose areolar connective tissue that surrounds the penis. Penile skin is loosely attached to this underlying loose connective tissue but at the glans penis it is extremely thin and tightly attached. There is no adipose tissue (fat) in the subcutaneous tissue of the penis (Quartey, 2006)."}, {"name": "Anatomical Relations", "text": "The subcutaneous tissue of the penis is located superficial to the fascia of the penis and deep to the skin of the penis. It is continuous with Dartos fascia of the scrotum, the membranous layer of abdominal subcutaneous tissue (Scarpa\u2019s fascia) and the membranous layer of subcutaneous tissue of the perineum (Colles\u2019 fascia) (Quartey, 2006)."}, {"name": "Function", "text": "The subcutaneous tissue of the penis permits a significant amount of movement of the skin of the penis over the underlying structures. This tissue region also transmits the passage of the superficial dorsal vein of the penis and its anastomoses."}, {"name": "References", "text": "Dorland, W. (2011) Dorland's Illustrated Medical Dictionary. 32nd edn. Philadelphia, USA: Elsevier Saunders.\n\nQuartey, J. K. M. (2006) 'Anatomy and Blood Supply of the Urethra and Penis', in Schreiter, F. and Jordan, G.H. (eds.) Urethral Reconstructive Surgery. Berlin, Heidelberg: Springer Berlin Heidelberg, pp. 11-17."}]

items.name: Cytoplasmic Inclusions
items.info:
[{"name": "Description", "text": "The cell cytoplasm contains a number of elements such as pigment granules, lipid droplets, and glycogen granules all resulting from the metabolic activity of the cell. They are not common in all cells (Ross and Pawlina, 2006; Ovalle, Nahirney and Netter, 2013; McKinley, O'Loughlin and Pennefather-O'Brien, 2016)."}, {"name": "References", "text": "McKinley, M. P., O'Loughlin, V. D. and Pennefather-O'Brien, E. E. (2016) Human Anatomy. 5th edn.: McGraw-Hill Education.

Ovalle, W. K., Nahirney, P. C. and Netter, F. H. (2013) Netter's Essential Histology. ClinicalKey 2012: Elsevier Saunders.

Ross, M. H. and Pawlina, W. (2006) Histology: A text and atlas. Lippincott Williams & Wilkins."}]

items.name: Renal Corpuscle
items.info:
[{"name": "Quick Facts", "text": "The renal corpuscle is a body that forms the beginning of a nephron, consisting of a glomerulus surrounded by the glomerular capsule (an expanded portion of the renal tubule) (Dorland, 2011)."}, {"name": "Structure and/or Key Feature(s)", "text": "The renal corpuscle is a small, spherical structure (about 200 μm in diameter) comprised of a central tuft of convoluted capillaries, known as the glomerulus, enveloped by an invaginated sphere, known as the glomerular capsule. The glomerular capsule is described as the dilated proximal part of the renal tubule (Kerr, 2007).

The glomerulus is described as a small tuft of convoluted capillaries structurally supported by mesangial cells and an extracellular mesangial matrix. The glomerular capsule contains an outer parietal layer and inner visceral layer. The inner visceral layer is composed of specialized epithelial cells, called podocytes. Podocytes are distinct cells that extend cytoplasmic processes around capillaries then numerous secondary processes, or foot processes, known as pedicels. Pedicels of adjacent podocytes interdigitate to form filtration slits. A small cavity between the inner visceral wall and the outer parietal wall of the glomerular capsule exists. This cavity is known as Bowman’s space and is continuous with the proximal convoluted tubule.

Each renal corpuscle has a vascular pole and a urinary pole. The vascular pole describes the site where the afferent and efferent arterioles enter and exit the corpuscle, whereas the urinary pole describes the point at which the proximal convoluted tubule arises. 

A key feature of the renal corpuscle is the filtration barrier. This is composed of:

—the fenestrated capillary endothelium; 

—the fused basal lamina of capillaries and podocytes called the glomerular filtration membrane (GBM); 

—and the filtration slits (with an ultrathin filtration slit diaphragm) of the podocytes."}, {"name": "Anatomical Relations", "text": "Renal corpuscles are present throughout the outer and inner cortex of the kidney. Generally, cortical nephrons have their renal corpuscle located in the outer cortex, while juxtamedullary nephrons have their renal corpuscle located in the inner cortex (Zhang, 1999). The glomerular capsule is continuous with the proximal segment of the renal tubule."}, {"name": "Function", "text": "The renal corpuscle facilitates the blood-filtering function of the nephron. Water and low-molecular weight substances such as glucose, amino acids, ions and waste products are filtered from blood plasma into the tubular filtrate. Whole proteins are not filtered. The presence of proteins in urine indicates there is damage to the filtration barrier (Pocock, Richards and Richards, 2013)."}, {"name": "Clinical Correlates", "text": "—Diabetic nephropathy

—Nephrotic syndrome 

—Nephritic syndrome"}, {"name": "References", "text": "Dorland, W. (2011) Dorland's Illustrated Medical Dictionary. 32nd edn. Philadelphia, USA: Elsevier Saunders.

Kerr, J. B. (2007) Atlas of Functional Histology. 2nd edn.: Elsevier Science Health Science Division.

Pocock, G., Richards, C. D. and Richards, D. A. (2013) Human Physiology. Oxford Core Texts 4th edn.: OUP Oxford.

Zhang, S. X. (1999) An Atlas of Histology. Springer Science & Business Media."}]

items.name: Submucosa of Small Intestine (Ileum)
items.info:
[{"name": "Quick Facts", "text": "The submucosa is the layer of dense connective tissue between the mucosa and the muscularis externa in most parts of the digestive, respiratory, urinary, and genital tracts (Dorland, 2011)."}, {"name": "Structure/Morphology", "text": "The submucosa is essentially a dense, irregular connective tissue layer found deep than the mucosa. It contains blood and lymphatic vessels. Blood vessels form large plexuses in the submucosa. Lacteals originating in the lamina propria of villi form a plexus near the muscularis mucosa (the outermost layer of the mucosa). From there, they flow to lymph nodules in the submucosa and unite to accompany blood vessels out of the intestine.

The submucosal (Meissner’s) nerve plexus is only visible as scattered ganglion cell bodies with satellite cells lying within the submucosal elements.

Glandular tissue is prominent in the duodenum (as “Brunner’s” or submucosal glands) where they dominate the lamina propria and the submucosa. These compound tubular glands have both serous (zymogen) and mucous secreting components.

The submucosa (and the lamina propria) in the ileum contains aggregations of lymphoid nodules known as “Peyer’s patches.” They are an important component of the gut associated lymphatic tissue (GALT). In humans there are about 30 patches. Each patch may contain 10–200 lymph nodules. At the luminal surface, they appear as a dome-shaped region devoid of villi. The epithelial surface consists of low cuboidal “M” (microfold) cells rather than absorptive cells (enterocytes) (Ross and Pawlina, 2016)."}, {"name": "Key Features/Anatomical Relations", "text": "Plicae circulares are circular transverse folds that extend up to two thirds the circumference of the lumen. They contain a core of the submucosa. They begin about 5–6 cm beyond the pylorus and are most numerous towards the end or distal part of the duodenum."}, {"name": "Function", "text": "The blood vessels within the submucosa nourish the layers of the intestinal wall as well as removing absorbed products of digestion.

The submucosal (Meissner’s) plexus is mainly responsible for innervating the smooth muscle layers of the muscularis mucosae.

Brunner’s glands secretions are between a pH of 8.1 and 9.3 and contain alkaline glycoproteins and bicarbonate which neutralizes the acidic containing chyme entering the duodenum from the stomach. Another function of these secretions is to create a pH ideal for the actions of pancreatic enzymes delivered to the duodenum.

M cells are antigen-transporting cells and carry antigens from the intestinal lumen to reach immune cells within the lamina propria of the digestive tract or gut associated lymphatic tissue (GALT).

Lacteals and the lymphatic vessels are important for the absorption of lipids."}, {"name": "References", "text": "Dorland, W. (2011) Dorland's Illustrated Medical Dictionary. 32nd edn. Philadelphia, USA: Elsevier Saunders.

Ross, M. H. and Pawlina, W. (2016) Histology: A Text and Atlas. Wolters Kluwer Health."}]

items.name: Perilymph of Scala Vestibuli
items.info:
[{"name": "Quick Facts", "text": "Perilymph is the fluid contained within the space separating the membranous labyrinth from the osseous labyrinth; it is entirely separate from the endolymph (Dorland, 2011)."}, {"name": "Structure and/or Key Feature(s)", "text": "The scala vestibuli is filled with perilymph, an extracellular fluid that is similar in consistency to that of cerebrospinal fluid and is dominant in sodium ions. In addition, its composition differs from the perilymph of the scala tympani in that it possesses higher concentrations of potassium, glucose, amino acids, and proteins. Given this, it is proposed that the perilymph of the scala vestibuli is derived from the endothelium of cochlear blood vessels (Standring, 2016)."}, {"name": "Function", "text": "The perilymph serves as a medium to transmit vibrations from the tympanic membrane (via the ossicles) to the endolymph in the cochlear duct, thus stimulating the spiral organ (of Corti). It also receives effluxing potassium released by the depolarization of the stereocilia.

The perilymph plays an important role in the sensory cell depolarization, as it receives the efflux of potassium from calcium-dependent channels in the stereocilia hair cells. It also contributes to the influx of calcium through specific channels located on the side and basal aspects of the hair cells."}, {"name": "References", "text": "Dorland, W. (2011) Dorland's Illustrated Medical Dictionary. 32nd edn. Philadelphia, USA: Elsevier Saunders.

Standring, S. (2016) Gray's Anatomy: The Anatomical Basis of Clinical Practice., 41st edition. Elsevier Limited."}]

items.name: Belly of Muscle
items.info: [{"name": "Quick Facts", "text": "The belly of a muscle is the fleshy contractile part of a muscle (Dorland, 2011)."}, {"name": "Structure", "text": "The \u201cbelly\u201d of the muscle is typically the largest or thickest portion of the muscle. The muscle belly is composed of the fascicles, which are groups of muscle fibers bundled together. The muscle belly is encased in a connective tissue sheath called the epimysium."}, {"name": "Key Features/Anatomical Relations", "text": "The muscle belly lies between the origin and insertion points of the muscle. In muscles which have multiple origins, for example the two-headed biceps femoris or biceps brachii muscles, the fibers from the multiple heads converge to form one muscle belly prior to the insertion point (MacIntosh et al., 2006)."}, {"name": "Function", "text": "The muscle belly is the collection of the muscle fibers contained within their connective tissue sheaths. The muscle fibers, or myocytes, contain myofibrils that contain the contractile units of the muscle called sarcomeres. The sarcomeres are responsible for the ability of the muscle to contract and relax."}, {"name": "References", "text": "Dorland, W. (2011) Dorland's Illustrated Medical Dictionary. 32nd edn. Philadelphia, USA: Elsevier Saunders.\n\nMacIntosh, B. R., Gardiner, P. F. and McComas, A. J. (2006) Skeletal Muscle: Form and Function. Human Kinetics."}]

items.name: Integument
items.info:
[{"name": "Quick Facts", "text": "The integument is the covering of the body; the skin and subcutaneous tissues, with its various layers and accessory structures, including the epidermis, dermis, hypodermis, hair, nails, cutaneous glands, and mammary glands (Dorland, 2011)."}, {"name": "Structure/Morphology", "text": "The integument consists of the skin and its appendages such as hair follicles and hair, sweat glands, sebaceous glands, nails, subcutaneous fat, and mammary glands.

The skin is the largest organ in the human body accounting for almost 15% of its weight. It covers the entire external surface of the body and is continuous with the mucosae of the urogenital, respiratory, digestive tracts. The thickness of the skin varies greatly from 1.5-5mm, depending on its location (Standring, 2016). 

The skin consists of three layers including the superficial epidermis, the dermis in the middle and the deep subcutaneous tissue. 

—The epidermis is an epithelial tissue layer that undergoes constant renewal throughout life, mediated by a stem cell population within it. It mainly consists of keratinized stratified squamous epithelium. 

—The dermis lies beneath the epidermis. It is a dense connective tissue that provides strength to the skin through a diffuse interwoven orientation of collagen and elastic fibers throughout it. It is in the dermis where the skin receives its neurovascular supplies. The dermis comprises two sub-layers, namely a superficial papillary layer and a deeper reticular layer. 

—The subcutaneous tissue is the deepest layer that is composed of a loose connective tissue with variable amounts of adipose cells interspersed (Ross and Pawlina, 2006).

Skin varies in different regions of the body, such as:

—arrangement (size and number of hairs, frequency and types of glands, the thickness of the keratinized layer, pigmentation, degree of vascularization, and innervation); 

—physical properties (thickness, strength, softness, and flexibility)."}, {"name": "Function", "text": "The skin functions as a barrier against the external environment, such as harmful microbial organisms and damage from mechanical, chemical, thermal, and UV stimuli. The skin also performs an important endocrine function, such as Vitamin D formation and synthesis of cytokines and growth factors. The skin is also involved in excretion, through the secretion of sweat and sebum. In addition, the skin is important in maintaining homeostasis by controlling the body's temperature and water loss. The various sensory receptors located inside the skin make it an important organ for receiving sensory information from the external environment."}, {"name": "References", "text": "Dorland, W. (2011) Dorland's Illustrated Medical Dictionary. 32nd edn. Philadelphia, USA: Elsevier Saunders.

Ross, M. H. and Pawlina, W. (2006) Histology: A text and atlas. Lippincott Williams & Wilkins.

Standring, S. (2016) Gray's Anatomy: The Anatomical Basis of Clinical Practice. Gray's Anatomy Series: Elsevier Limited."}]

items.name: Central Lymphatic Vessel (Duodenum)
items.info:
[{"name": "Quick Facts", "text": "The central lymphatic vessel, or lacteal, are any of the intestinal lymphatic vessels that transport chyle; so called because during absorption they are white from absorbed fat (Dorland, 2011)."}, {"name": "Structure/Morphology", "text": "Lymph vessels of the intestine begin as blind-ended or closed tubes near the tip of each villus. These vessels are called lacteals and although they are larger in diameter than neighboring blood vessels, they tend to collapse which makes them difficult to observe in routine histological sections.

Lacteals extend deep to the muscularis mucosa where they form a plexus. From there, they flow to lymph nodules in the submucosa then unite to accompany blood vessels out of the intestine. Smooth muscle cells accompany these lacteals."}, {"name": "Function", "text": "Lacteals are important for the absorption of lipids. It is thought that the rhythmic movement of villi is due to the contractions of the smooth muscle cells that travel vertically from the muscularis mucosa to the tips of villi. These contractions occur several times per minute and serve to pump lymph from lacteals into mesenteric lymphatics (Eroschenko, 2008)."}, {"name": "References", "text": "Dorland, W. (2011) Dorland's Illustrated Medical Dictionary. 32nd edn. Philadelphia, USA: Elsevier Saunders.

Eroschenko, V. P. (2008) DiFiore's Atlas of Histology with Functional Correlations. 11th edn.: Wolters Kluwer Health/Lippincott Williams & Wilkins."}]

items.name: Myelin Sheath Gap
items.info:
[{"name": "Quick Facts", "text": "The myelin sheath gap, or node of Ranvier, are the constrictions occurring on myelinated nerve fibers at regular intervals of about 1 mm; at these sites the myelin sheath is absent and the axon is enclosed only by Schwann cell processes (Dorland, 2011)."}, {"name": "Structure and/or Key Features", "text": "The myelin sheath is produced by oligodendrocytes in the central nervous system and by Schwann cells in the peripheral nervous system.

Oligodendrocytes are small cells and extend long processes towards neighboring axons. Each process wraps around a portion of the same axon or several axons. The myelin sheath that wraps around the axon becomes segmented at regular intervals by the nodes of Ranvier, or myelin sheath gaps.

The area between adjacent nodes of Ranvier is known as the internode. The length of the internode is correlated with the diameter of the axon (Ross and Pawlina, 2006)."}, {"name": "Anatomical Relations", "text": "Nodes of Ranvier are located in the intervals between adjacent myelin sheaths. “Foot processes” extending from the astrocyte cell body can be found in large numbers at the nodes of Ranvier (Splittgerber, 2018)."}, {"name": "Function", "text": "The nodes of Ranvier facilitate the rapid conduction of nerve impulses. Sodium channels embedded in the axolemma are greatest in density at the nodes of Ranvier and lowest in density at the internodes (Standring, 2016). The high concentration of sodium channels at the nodes facilitates “saltatory conduction” which is the process by which the action potential is propagated from node to node very rapidly along myelinated nerve fibers."}, {"name": "Clinical Correlates", "text": "Deficiencies in any of the oligodendrocytes myelin-specific proteins seem related to demyelinating diseases of the central nervous system. Multiple sclerosis is characterized by demyelination in white matter of the CNS. The degenerated myelin sheaths are removed by microglial cells and then astrocytes proliferate to form a gliotic scar (Splittgerber, 2018)."}, {"name": "References", "text": "Dorland, W. (2011) Dorland's Illustrated Medical Dictionary. 32nd edn. Philadelphia, USA: Elsevier Saunders.

Ross, M. H. and Pawlina, W. (2006) Histology: A text and atlas. Lippincott Williams & Wilkins.

Splittgerber, R. (2018) Snell's Clinical Neuroanatomy. Wolters Kluwer Health.

Standring, S. (2016) Gray's Anatomy: The Anatomical Basis of Clinical Practice. Gray's Anatomy Series 41 edn.: Elsevier Limited."}]

items.name: Theca Externa (of Tertiary Ovarian Follicle)
items.info:
[{"name": "Quick Facts", "text": "The theca externa is the outer, fibrous layer of the follicular theca (Dorland, 2011)."}, {"name": "Structure and/or Key Feature(s)", "text": "The theca externa is the outmost layer of connective tissue surrounding the follicle, containing collagen fibers and fibroblasts but also some smooth muscle cells.

There is no clear boundary between the two thecal layers and the stroma of the ovary. However, because the cells of the theca interna and the granulosa are morphologically different, as well as the existence of a thick basement membrane between them, the boundary between these layers is clear (Ross and Pawlina, 2006; Mescher, 2013)."}, {"name": "Anatomical Relations", "text": "The theca externa is the outmost layer of connective tissue surrounding the follicle, containing collagen fibers and fibroblasts but also some smooth muscle cells."}, {"name": "References", "text": "Dorland, W. (2011) Dorland's Illustrated Medical Dictionary. 32nd edn. Philadelphia, USA: Elsevier Saunders.

items.name: B Cell
items.info:
[{"name": "Quick Facts", "text": "B cell is the type of endocrine cell in the pancreatic islets (of Langerhans) that secretes insulin (Dorland, 2011)."}, {"name": "Structure and/or Key Feature(s)", "text": "About 60–70% of all the cells in the pancreatic islet are B cells and tend to congregate in the center of the islet. One characteristic feature of a B cell is the presence of numerous secretory granules that are about 300 nm in diameter and exhibit a dense polyhedral core (presumably crystallized insulin) and a pale matrix (Ross and Pawlina, 2016)."}, {"name": "Function", "text": "B cells secrete insulin. One function of insulin is enhancing the entry of glucose into cells of several tissues and so there is a decrease in blood glucose levels (Mescher, 2013)."}, {"name": "References", "text": "Dorland, W. (2011) Dorland's Illustrated Medical Dictionary. 32nd edn. Philadelphia, USA: Elsevier Saunders.

Mescher, A. (2013) Junqueira's Basic Histology: Text and Atlas. 13th edn.: McGraw-Hill Education.
