items.name: Exocrine Component of Pancreas
items.info: [{"name": "Quick Facts", "text": "The exocrine component of the pancreas is the part of the pancreas that acts as an exocrine gland, consisting of the pancreatic acini, which produce pancreatic juice and secrete it into the duodenum to aid in protein digestion (Dorland, 2011)."}, {"name": "Structure and/or Key Feature(s)", "text": "The exocrine pancreas is an example of a compound serous acinar gland. The serous secretory cells are simple, pyramidal in shape and form clusters or secretory units which are acinar or tubuloacinar in shape.\n\nConnective tissue surrounds the pancreas and forms a thin capsule and septa penetrate the parenchyma dividing the pancreas into lobules."}, {"name": "Function", "text": "Exocrine secretions from the pancreas contains (inactive) precursors of digestive enzymes that can digest most food substances."}, {"name": "References", "text": "Dorland, W. (2011) Dorland's Illustrated Medical Dictionary. 32nd edn. Philadelphia, USA: Elsevier Saunders."}]

items.name: Thin Myofilament (Contracted Smooth Muscle)
items.info:
[{"name": "Quick Facts", "text": "The thin filament is one of the thin contractile myofilaments in a muscle cell, composed mainly of actin (Dorland, 2011)."}, {"name": "Structure and/or Key Features", "text": "Thin myofilaments are composed of actin, tropomyosin, and caldesmon. 

Actin is the main component of the thin myofilament. It is a long filamentous (F-actin) polymer consisting of two strands of globular (G-actin) monomers twisted around each other to form a double helical formation about 1 μm long and 8 nm wide. Each G-actin monomer has a binding site for myosin (Mescher, 2013).

Tropomyosin is a long (about 40 nm), thin molecule consisting of two polypeptide chains and bound head to tail to form filaments that coil over the two actin strands. Each tropomyosin molecule extends along a length of seven G-actin molecules (Mescher, 2013).

Unlike skeletal muscle, smooth muscle cells do not contain troponin (Ovalle, Nahirney and Netter, 2013). Instead, caldesmon interacts with tropomyosin forming a caldesmon-tropomyosin complex, which regulates the interaction of actin with myosin. 

In relaxed smooth muscle, the caldesmon-tropomyosin complex blocks the myosin binding sites on the actin filaments. This is controlled by regulatory molecules (such as calmodulin) that are dependent on Ca2+. Calmodulin binds to Ca2+ creating a Ca2+-calmodulin complex. This complex binds to caldesmon and releases it from actin, thus exposing the myosin binding sites (Ross and Pawlina, 2016; Vetterkind and Morgan, 2012)."}, {"name": "Anatomical Relations", "text": "The bulk of the smooth muscle sarcoplasm contains thin myofilaments of the contractile apparatus. They are attached to cytoplasmic densities or dense bodies (similar to Z lines of skeletal muscle fibers) located at the cell membrane and distributed throughout the sarcoplasm linked to intermediate filaments."}, {"name": "Function", "text": "Muscle contraction results from the binding of myosin to actin myofilaments, allowing myosin to function as a motor that drives myofilament sliding and creating movement."}, {"name": "References", "text": "Dorland, W. (2011) Dorland's Illustrated Medical Dictionary. 32nd edn. Philadelphia, USA: Elsevier Saunders.

Mescher, A. (2013) Junqueira's Basic Histology: Text and Atlas. 13th edn.: McGraw-Hill Education.

Ovalle, W. K., Nahirney, P. C. and Netter, F. H. (2013) Netter's Essential Histology. ClinicalKey 2012: Elsevier Saunders.

Ross, M. H. and Pawlina, W. (2016) Histology: A Text and Atlas. Wolters Kluwer Health.

Vetterkind, S. and Morgan, K. G. (2012) 'Chapter 87 - Regulation of Smooth Muscle Contraction', in Hill, J.A. and Olson, E.N. (eds.) Muscle. Boston/Waltham: Academic Press, pp. 1173-1180."}]

Their distribution in the marrow follows the course of the vessels towards the epiphyses where they branch off into smaller lymph vessels."}, {"name": "Anatomical Relations", "text": "The lymph vessels of the medullary cavity follow the same course as the nutrient vessels and travel towards the epiphyses."}]

The ovary is suspended within the layers of peritoneum that make up the mesovarium."}, {"name": "Function", "text": "The mesovarium suspends and supports the ovaries while allowing ovarian vessels to reach its hilum (Standring, 2016)."}, {"name": "List of Clinical Correlates", "text": "—Adhesions"}, {"name": "References", "text": "Dorland, W. items.name: Myofibril and Endomembrane System
items.info:
[{"name": "Quick Facts", "text": "A myofibril is one of the slender threads that can be made visible in a muscle fiber by maceration in certain acids. They run parallel with the long axis of the fiber, and are composed of numerous myofilaments (Dorland, 2011). The endomembrane system refers to the sarcoplasmic reticulum and the transverse tubules (Wirtz et al., 2012)."}, {"name": "Structure", "text": "Myofibrils are arranged in bundles enclosed by a plasma membrane called the sarcolemma. Each myofibril is surrounded by a sarcoplasmic reticulum and by transverse tubules, which are collectively known as the endomembrane system (Wirtz et al., 2012). 

The sarcoplasmic reticulum is a specialized type of smooth endoplasmic reticulum found in skeletal muscle. It forms a network of tubules that extend through the muscle fiber. The flattened tubules surround, but do not make direct contact with the myofibrils in a muscle fiber. 

Transverse tubules are extensions of the sarcolemma, made up of interconnecting rings, each of which surround individual myofibrils."}, {"name": "Key Features/Anatomical Relations", "text": "Myofibrils are arranged in bundles enclosed by a plasma membrane called the sarcolemma. This structure is collectively called a muscle fiber. A connective tissue layer, the endoneurium, surrounds the sarcolemma. 

Each myofibril is made up of numerous sarcomeres that are positioned end to end. The light regions of the sarcomere do not refract light and are considered isotropic. These regions are called I-bands. I-bands are composed of thin filaments of the protein actin and its associated proteins, such as tropomyosin and troponin. I-bands are dissected by a Z-line. The area between successive Z-lines are called sarcomeres. The sections of thick filament that are not superimposed by the thin filaments when the myofibril is relaxed is called the H-band (Laing and Nowak, 2005).

The sarcoplasmic reticulum (SR) is an organelle that consists of a network of loose flattened tubules with various compartments, many of which contain Ca2+. The two ends of the SR are wider, to from terminal sacs, called cisternae. Two cisternae of adjacent sarcoplasmic reticula and one transverse tubule form a functional unit called a triad, which operates to elicit the release of Ca2+ from SR stores."}, {"name": "Function", "text": "The protein bands of the myofibril facilitate contraction and relaxation of the muscle by gliding the thin actin and thick myosin filaments over each other. 

The primary function of transverse tubules is to facilitate the conduction of signals from outside the fiber to the myofibrils. Transverse tubules are the site for excitation-contraction coupling. When an electric signal excites the sarcolemma, the signal travels down along the T-tubules to the sarcoplasmic reticulum, which releases Ca2+ for contraction. 

The sarcoplasmic reticulum functions as an intracellular calcium store. Depolarization of the sarcoplasmic reticulum membrane results in the release of calcium ions (Ca2+). This release of calcium ions triggers the cascade required for contraction."}, {"name": "List of Clinical Correlates", "text": "—Myofibrillar myopathy

—Actin myopathy

—Hyaline body myopathy

—Muscular dystrophy"}, {"name": "References", "text": "Dorland, W. (2011) Dorland's Illustrated Medical Dictionary. 32nd edn. Philadelphia, USA: Elsevier Sauders.

Laing, N. G. and Nowak, K. J. (2005) 'When contractile proteins go bad: the sarcomere and skeletal muscle disease', Bioessays, 27(8), pp. 809-22.

Wirtz, K. W. A., Packer, L., Gustafsson, J. Å., Evangelopoulos, A. E. and Changeux, J. P. (2012) New Developments in Lipid-Protein Interactions and Receptor Function. Nato Science Series A:: Springer US."}]

items.name: Elongated Spermatid
items.info:
[{"name": "Quick Facts", "text": "A spermatid is a cell derived from a secondary spermatocyte by fission, and capable of undergoing spermiogenesis to develop into a spermatozoon (Dorland, 2011)."}, {"name": "Structure/Morphology", "text": "The younger generation of spermatids are small round cells (7–8 μm in diameter), with condensed chromatin in their round nuclei, and are located adjacent to the lumen of the seminiferous tubule. Quickly the round spermatids will enter the differentiation process called spermiogenesis with the end of the process characterized by more elongated spermatids.

Spermiogenesis involves the development of the acrosome, condensation and elongation of the nucleus, development of the flagellum, and loss of the majority of the cytoplasm. The spermatozoon is then released into the lumen of the seminiferous tubule. This morphological transformation enables the spermatozoon to be highly specialized to deliver the male DNA to the ovum.

There are three phases in spermiogenesis including the Golgi, acrosomal, and maturation phase.

—During the Golgi phase, spermatids contain free ribosomes, tubules of smooth endoplasmic reticulum, and very prominent Golgi complexes adjacent to the nucleus. Small pro-acrosomal granules (rich in glycoproteins) accumulate in the Golgi complex and rapidly coalesce into acrosomal granules housed within a membrane-bound acrosomal vesicle. The location of the vesicle defines the anterior pole of the developing sperm. A flagellar axoneme begins forming as the centrioles move to a location opposite the site of the future acrosomal cap.

—During the acrosomal phase, the acrosomal vesicle extends over the anterior portion of the condensed nucleus to become the acrosome. It is a specialized lysosome containing hydrolytic enzymes, in particular hyaluronidase, neuraminidase, acid phosphatase and a protease with trypsin-like activity. These enzymes will disperse the cells of the corona radiata and digest the zona pellucida. Also during this phase, the spermatid becomes oriented so that the condensed nucleus elongates and faces the seminiferous epithelium and the axoneme extends into the lumen of the seminiferous tubule. One centriole forms the flagellum and mitochondria begin to collect around its proximal portion, forming a region called the middle piece.

—The maturation phase is characterized by shedding of the cytoplasm and the cytoplasmic bridges as residual bodies which are phagocytosed by sustentocytes (Sertoli cells). Spermatozoa are then released into the seminiferous tubule lumen.

A proportion of spermatids degenerate during maturation, reducing the expected yield (Standring, 2020)."}, {"name": "Anatomical Relations", "text": "Spermatids occupy the adluminal compartment of the seminiferous epithelium."}, {"name": "Function", "text": "Spermatids undergo spermiogenesis and differentiate into spermatozoa."}, {"name": "List of Clinical Correlates", "text": "Some pharmacological treatments, toxic agents and any decrease in gonadotrophins can prevent spermiation and so the spermatids are phagocytized by Sertoli cells."}, {"name": "References", "text": "Dorland, W. (2011) Dorland's Illustrated Medical Dictionary. 32nd edn. Philadelphia, USA: Elsevier Saunders.

Standring, S. (2020) Gray's Anatomy: The Anatomical Basis of Clinical Practice. 42nd edn.: Elsevier Health Sciences."}]

items.name: Blood Testis Barrier
Epineurial Veins
items.info: [{"name": "Quick Facts", "text": "The epineurial veins are part of the vasa nervorum and help drain the nerve."}, {"name": "Structure/Morphology", "text": "The epineurial veins are located in the external epineurium and form part of the vasa nervorum, small vessels that supply blood to peripheral nerves. This network of vessels supplies blood to the interior parts of the nerves and their coverings. The vasa vasorum are located within the connective tissue of the nerve scattered between the fascicles (Boissaud-Cooke, Pidgeon and Tunstall, 2015)."}, {"name": "Anatomical Relations", "text": "The vasa nervorum are the smallest vessels in the epineurial, perineurial, and endoneurial layers."}, {"name": "Function", "text": "The vasa nervorum supply the peripheral nerves with the molecular nutrients needed to carry out their cellular functions and for survival (Carp, 2015)."}, {"name": "References", "text": "Boissaud-Cooke, M., Pidgeon, T. E. and Tunstall, R. (2015) 'Chapter 37 - The Microcirculation of Peripheral Nerves: The Vasa Nervorum A2 - Tubbs, R. Shane', in Rizk, E., Shoja, M.M., Loukas, M., Barbaro, N. & Spinner, R.J. (eds.) Nerves and Nerve Injuries. San Diego: Academic Press, pp. 507-523.\n\nCarp, S. (2015) Peripheral Nerve Injury An Anatomical and Physiological Approach for Physical Therapy Intervention. EBL-Schweitzer: F. A. Davis Company."}]

items.name: Sarcoplasm (Contracted Smooth Muscle; Posterior)
items.info: [{"name": "Quick Facts", "text": "The sarcoplasm is the interfibrillary matter of the striated muscles; the substance in which the fibrillae of the muscle fiber are embedded (Dorland, 2011)."}, {"name": "Structure and/or Key Features", "text": "The sarcoplasm is the cytoplasm equivalent within muscle cells. It contains many of the same organelles, cytoskeleton, and matrix which is important in many cell functions. The sarcoplasm is slightly adapted to respond to the high energy demands of muscle cells, such as having a higher concentration of glycosomes and myoglobin."}, {"name": "Anatomical Relations", "text": "The sarcoplasm is an aqueous substance found within the sarcolemma, which contains many cellular organelles such as the sarcoplasmic reticulum, mitochondria, ribosomes, and Golgi apparatus."}, {"name": "Function", "text": "Similar to the cytoplasm in other cells, the sarcoplasm acts as a medium for many important metabolic processes."}, {"name": "References", "text": "Dorland, W. (2011) Dorland's Illustrated Medical Dictionary. 32nd edn. Philadelphia, USA: Elsevier Saunders."}]

items.name: Periosteal Vein
items.info: [{"name": "Quick Facts", "text": "Periosteal veins follow the same course as the periosteal arteries."}, {"name": "Structure/Morphology", "text": "Periosteal veins arise from the microvascular network in cortical bone and form efferent venules which course towards the periosteum and drain into the periosteal venous network (Buck and Dumanian, 2012)."}, {"name": "Anatomical Relations", "text": "In cortical bone, periosteal veins follow the same course as the periosteal arteries within the perforating canals and form venous plexus between the two layers of the periosteum."}, {"name": "Function", "text": "Periosteal veins drain blood from the outer one third of cortical bone and periosteum."}, {"name": "References", "text": "Buck, D. W., 2nd and Dumanian, G. A. (2012) 'Bone biology and physiology: Part I. The fundamentals', Plast Reconstr Surg., 129(6), pp. 1529-4242."}]

items.name: Zona Pectinata
items.info: [{"name": "Quick Facts", "text": "The zona pectinata is the outer two-thirds of the basilar membrane, running between the floor of the inner tunnel and the spiral ligament (Dorland, 2011)."}, {"name": "Structure and/or Key Feature(s)", "text": "The zona pectinata is one of the two regions of the basilar membrane, the other being the zona arcuata. The zona pectinata forms the outer part of the basilar membrane. It is trilaminar and thicker than the zona arcuata. The zona pectinata attaches from the base of the outer pillar cells and inserts into the basal (or spiral) crest, a triangular projection from the spiral ligament. On its insertion in the basal crest, the top and bottom layers of this trilaminar basilar membrane blend together."}, {"name": "Anatomical Relations", "text": "The zona pectinata forms the outermost part of the basilar membrane, which is interjacent between the scala tympani and the cochlear duct. The inferior surface of the zona pectinata is lined by periosteum, which, in turn, is lined with perilymphatic cells."}, {"name": "Function", "text": "The zona pectinata provides a sturdy foundation to the zona arcuata. Together, the two layers comprise a barrier which separates the cochlear duct and the scala tympani, as well as the endolymph and perilymph that occupy those canals. These two fluids have different ion concentrations involved in the transmission of vibrations. However, the zona arcuata is permeable to the perilymph of the scala tympani to an extent, thus allowing the spiral organ (of Corti) to bathe in perilymph (also referred to cortilymph in this region due to some minor alterations of its composition) (Standring, 2016)."}, {"name": "References", "text": "Dorland, W. (2011) Dorland's Illustrated Medical Dictionary. 32nd edn. Philadelphia, USA: Elsevier Saunders.\n\nStandring, S. (2016) Gray's Anatomy: The Anatomical Basis of Clinical Practice., 41st edition. Elsevier Limited."}]

items.name: Perivascular Islet of Mesangial Cell
items.info: [{"name": "Quick Facts", "text": "The perivascular islet is the region of the juxtaglomerular apparatus between the glomerulus and the afferent and efferent arterioles, containing lacelike lacis cells and lying in close contact with the mesangium and the macula densa (Dorland, 2011)."}, {"name": "Structure and/or Key Feature(s)", "text": "Mesangial cells are located within the renal corpuscle and along the vascular pole as a component of the juxtaglomerular apparatus and are called extraglomerular mesangial (or lacis) cells."}, {"name": "Function", "text": "The primary function of mesangial cells is to remove trapped residue, etc. from the glomerular basement membrane and filtration slit diaphragm and so maintain these structures free of debris. Whilst they are phagocytic cells they are not derived from precursor cells of the mononuclear phagocytic system (monocytes). Mesangial cells also structurally support podocytes where the basement membrane is absent and synthesize and secrete molecules which have a role in responses to injury to the glomerulus. Mesangial cells also have contractile properties."}, {"name": "References", "text": "Dorland, W. (2011) Dorland's Illustrated Medical Dictionary. 32nd edn. Philadelphia, USA: Elsevier Saunders."}]

items.name: Cytoplasm
items.info:
[{"name": "Quick Facts", "text": "The cytoplasm is the protoplasm of a cell exclusive of that of the nucleus; it consists of a continuous aqueous solution (cytosol) and the organelles and inclusions suspended in it and is the site of most of the chemical activities of the cell (Dorland, 2011)."}, {"name": "Structure and/or Key Feature(s)", "text": "The cytoplasm consists of the ectoplasm and endoplasm. 

Ectoplasm is cytoplasm immediately underneath the plasmalemma (or cell membrane) and doesn't contain any organelles but does contain very fine actin filaments that help to support the very delicate plasmalemma. 

The endoplasm is cytoplasm that contains all the organelles, those structures that serve specific functions in the cell, and the cytoskeleton. In some individual cell populations, the endoplasm also includes cytoplasmic inclusions. 

The cytosol or cytoplasmic matrix is the aqueous cell sap or cell fluid (McKinley, O'Loughlin and Pennefather-O'Brien, 2016)."}, {"name": "Function", "text": "The cytoplasm with all its organelles and inclusions is the location of the many functions of the cell under the control of the nucleus (Ross and Pawlina, 2006; Ovalle, Nahirney and Netter, 2013; McKinley, O'Loughlin and Pennefather-O'Brien, 2016)."}, {"name": "References", "text": "Dorland, W. (2011) Dorland's Illustrated Medical Dictionary. 32nd edn. Philadelphia, USA: Elsevier Saunders.

McKinley, M. P., O'Loughlin, V. D. and Pennefather-O'Brien, E. E. (2016) Human Anatomy. 5th edn.: McGraw-Hill Education.

Ovalle, W. K., Nahirney, P. C. and Netter, F. H. (2013) Netter's Essential Histology. ClinicalKey 2012: Elsevier Saunders.

Ross, M. H. and Pawlina, W. (2006) Histology: A text and atlas. Lippincott Williams & Wilkins."}]

items.name: Ovary
items.info:
[{"name": "Quick Facts", "text": "The ovary is the female gonad, one of the two sexual glands in which the oocytes are formed. It is an oval body along the lateral wall of the pelvic cavity, attached to the mesovarium portion of the broad ligament. It consists of a cortex and medulla; the former is composed of stroma and ovarian follicles in various stages of maturation, and the latter, occupying a small area in the hilar region, receives the vessels and nerves. The ovary is covered by a tunica albuginea and peritoneum (Dorland, 2011)."}, {"name": "Structure/Morphology", "text": "The ovaries are approximately 4x2x3cm in size, whitish in color, and consist of an inner medulla and an outer cortex (Standring, 2020). The cortex surrounds the medulla except at the hilum, where the ovarian vessels and nerves enter the ovary. The cortex itself is covered by a collagenous tunica albuginea and an epithelial layer and contains the ovarian follicles."}, {"name": "Anatomical Relations", "text": "The ovaries sit on the lateral pelvic wall and are retained in place within the pelvic cavity by a portion of the broad ligament called the mesovarium, which encloses the ovary and helps form the ovarian bursa. In addition, the ovary is supported by the suspensory ligament of the ovary and the proper ovarian ligament (round ligament of the ovary).

The fimbriae of the uterine tube, fingerlike mucosal folds of the uterine tube, lie in close proximity to the superior pole of the ovary. On the right-hand side, the ileocecal junction, cecum, and appendix are located superolaterally to the ovary, while on the left, the sigmoid colon and upper rectum are located superolaterally to the ovary.

During pregnancy, the ovaries ascend within the pelvic cavity and during the third trimester are situated in the abdominal cavity."}, {"name": "Function", "text": "At birth, females have their full complement of primordial follicles. After puberty, each month, up to 20 primordial follicles begin to develop. However, only one follicle becomes the dominant follicle and undergoes ovulation. The remnant of this follicle becomes the corpus luteum and secretes progesterone and estrogen."}, {"name": "Arterial Supply", "text": "The ovarian arteries arise within the abdominal cavity as branches of the abdominal aorta. They descend into the pelvic cavity where they run within the suspensory ligament and divide into ovarian and tubal branches."}, {"name": "Venous Drainage", "text": "The venous drainage of the ovary forms via a pampiniform plexus, which form two ovarian veins that travel with the ovarian artery. These veins usually unite to form a single right and left ovarian vein that drains into the inferior vena cava on the right side and the left renal vein on the left side."}, {"name": "Innervation", "text": "Innervation of the ovary is supplied primarily through fibers that pass through the ovarian plexus. The upper region of the ovary is innervated by nerves derived from renal and aortic plexuses, while the lower portion is innervated by branches of the superior and inferior hypogastric plexuses. Sympathetic innervation of the ovary travels from the thoracic and sacral splanchnic nerves, whereas parasympathetic innervation is supplied through pelvic splanchnic nerves."}, {"name": "Lymphatic Drainage", "text": "Lymph from the ovaries is received by the right and left lumbar lymph nodes (Földi et al., 2012)."}, {"name": "List of Clinical Correlates", "text": "—Polycystic ovarian disease characterized by enlarged ovaries with numerous follicular cysts (Ross and Pawlina, 2006).

—Ovarian cancer is a primary malignancy in the ovaries. It may originate from any structure but about 90% are epithelial tumors. Not all tumors are malignant (Ovalle, Nahirney and Netter, 2013)."}, {"name": "References", "text": "Földi, M., Földi, E., Strößenreuther, R. and Kubik, S. (2012) Földi's Textbook of Lymphology: for Physicians and Lymphedema Therapists. Elsevier Health Sciences.

Ovalle, W. K., Nahirney, P. C. and Netter, F. H. (2013) Netter's Essential Histology. ClinicalKey 2012: Elsevier Saunders.

Ross, M. H. and Pawlina, W. (2006) Histology: A text and atlas. Lippincott Williams & Wilkins.

Standring, S. (2020) Gray's Anatomy: The Anatomical Basis of Clinical Practice. Elsevier Health Sciences."}]

items.name: Enteric Plexus
items.info:
[{"name": "Quick Facts", "text": "The enteric plexus is a plexus of autonomic nerve fibers within the wall of the intestine, and made up of the submucosal, myenteric, and subserosal plexuses; it contains autonomic ganglia, and visceral afferent, sympathetic postganglionic, parasympathetic preganglionic and postganglionic fibers. It is sometimes considered separately from the autonomic nervous system because the viscera display independent local reflex activity (Dorland, 2011)."}, {"name": "Description", "text": "The central nervous system influences the activities of the digestive system via autonomic (sympathetic and parasympathetic) inputs. However, the digestive canal can perform functions such as secretion, absorption, movement, independent of these inputs. This is thanks to the presence of an intrinsic network of nerves called the enteric nervous system or enteric plexus. It consists of two ganglionic plexuses of densely packed small neurons. Meissner’s plexus lies in the submucosal layer and Auerbach’s myenteric plexus sits between the inner circular and outer longitudinal muscular layers.

The enteric nervous system extends the entire length of the gastrointestinal tract and is composed of three types of neurons (Standring, 2016).

—Sensory neurons transmit information from receptors in the mucosa and muscle of the gut wall, which respond to mechanical, chemical, thermal, and osmotic stimuli. They project information to the interneurons.

—Motor neurons control the motility and secretions in the gut and are inhibitory or excitatory.

—Interneurons go between the sensory and motor neurons, thus integrating the information between the two.

The enteric nervous system may function autonomously; however, it does communicate with the central nervous system via parasympathetic and sympathetic fibers. Cross connections between the two allow for information from the gut to be relayed to the CNS, and vice versa. In general, sympathetic inputs cause inhibition of secretions and motor activity and contraction of sphincters and blood vessels (fight or flight response). Parasympathetic stimulation of the enteric nervous system promotes secretions and motor activity and dilation of the sphincters and blood vessels (rest and digest response) (Standring, 2016; Costa, Brookes and Hennig, 2000)."}, {"name": "List of Clinical Correlates", "text": "—Hirschsprung disease

—Neuropathic chromic intestinal pseudoobstruction 

—Irritable bowel syndrome

—Gastroesophageal reflux"}, {"name": "References", "text": "Costa, M., Brookes, S. J. and Hennig, G. W. (2000) 'Anatomy and physiology of the enteric nervous system', Gut, 47 Suppl 4(Suppl 4), pp. iv15-iv26.

Dorland, W. (2011) Dorland's Illustrated Medical Dictionary. 32nd edn. Philadelphia, USA: Elsevier Saunders.

Standring, S. (2016) Gray's Anatomy: The Anatomical Basis of Clinical Practice. Gray's Anatomy Series 41st edition edn.: Elsevier Limited."}]

items.name: Enteroendocrine Cell (Duodenum)
items.info: [{"name": "Quick Facts", "text": "Enteroendocrine cells are a group of APUD cells (amine precursor uptake and decarboxylation cells), which may be divided into several populations based on polypeptide hormone and biogenic amine production, found scattered throughout the gastrointestinal epithelium, mainly at the base of the epithelium; their numerous small secretory granules are concentrated chiefly between the nucleus and the cell base. Their secretions affect gastrointestinal motility, pancreatic and biliary secretions, and gastrointestinal epithelial growth, as well as being regulators of other enteroendocrine products (Dorland, 2011)."}, {"name": "Structure/Morphology", "text": "The enteroendocrine cells in the small intestine are like those in the stomach mucosa and form part of the diffuse neuroendocrine system (DNS). They tend to occupy the lower part of the intestinal glands."}, {"name": "Function", "text": "The activity of the small intestine includes some modulation by a complex system of locally produced peptide hormones from enteroendocrine cells."}, {"name": "References", "text": "Dorland, W. (2011) Dorland's Illustrated Medical Dictionary. 32nd edn. Philadelphia, USA: Elsevier Saunders."}]

items.name: Germinal Epithelium
items.info:
[{"name": "Quick Facts", "text": "The germinal epithelium is the former term for the thickened coelomic epithelium covering the gonad from earliest development; misnamed because it was thought to give rise to the primordial germ cells (Dorland, 2011)."}, {"name": "Structure and/or Key Feature(s)", "text": "A mesothelial layer of columnar or cuboidal cells covers the surface of the ovary. This is incorrectly referred to as the “germinal epithelium.” This germinal epithelium is continuous with the squamous mesothelium that covers the mesovarium. The tunica albuginea, a dense connective tissue capsule, is deep to the germinal epithelium (Ross and Pawlina, 2006; Mescher, 2013)."}, {"name": "Anatomical Relations", "text": "The germinal epithelium covers the surface of the ovary."}, {"name": "List of Clinical Correlates", "text": "About 70% of ovarian cancers are tumors that arise from the epithelial surface of the ovary (Ross and Pawlina, 2006)."}, {"name": "References", "text": "Dorland, W. (2011) Dorland's Illustrated Medical Dictionary. 32nd edn. Philadelphia, USA: Elsevier Saunders.

Mescher, A. (2013) Junqueira's Basic Histology: Text and Atlas. 13th edn.: McGraw-Hill Education.

Ross, M. H. and Pawlina, W. (2006) Histology: A text and atlas. Lippincott Williams & Wilkins."}]

items.name: Renal Medulla
items.info:
[{"name": "Quick Facts", "text": "The renal medulla is the inner part of the substance of the kidney, composed chiefly of collecting tubule elements, loops of Henle, and vasa recta, organized grossly into renal pyramids (Dorland, 2011)"}, {"name": "Structure and/or Key Features", "text": "The renal medulla is the pale, innermost portion of the kidney which houses a series of approximately 5–11 large conical masses known as renal pyramids. Renal pyramids are individually separated by thin medullary extensions of the renal cortex, known as renal columns. The columns also contribute to dividing the kidney into lobes, which contains a renal pyramid and the adjacent renal columns and their corresponding cortex.

Renal pyramids primarily consist of renal tubules. At the site of renal papillae, the urinary tubules of the renal pyramids drain urine into minor calyces. 

The renal medulla can be divided into the outer and inner zones, each of which houses different segments of the renal tubule (Dudek, 2006)."}, {"name": "Anatomical Relations", "text": "The renal medulla is surrounded and enclosed by the renal cortex. The point where the cortex and the medulla meet is known as the corticomedullary junction. This junction is often demarcated by arcuate blood vessels."}, {"name": "Function", "text": "The renal tubule of nephrons are generally located in the medulla. The hypertonic environment in the medulla is the basis of the countercurrent multiplier system, allowing water to be reabsorbed and ultimately facilitating the kidney’s role in salt and water balance (Pocock et al, 2013)."}, {"name": "References", "text": "Dorland, W. (2011) Dorland's Illustrated Medical Dictionary. 32nd edn. Philadelphia, USA: Elsevier Saunders.

Dudek, R. W. (2006) High-yield KidneyLippincott Williams & Wilkins.

Pocock, G., Richards, C. D. & Richards, D. A. (2013) Human Physiology, 4 edition. OUP Oxford."}]

items.name: Follicular Fluid (of Secondary Ovarian Follicle)
items.info:
[{"name": "Quick Facts", "text": "Follicular fluid is an albuminous fluid in the follicular antrum of a vesicular ovarian follicle (Dorland, 2011)."}, {"name": "Structure and/or Key Feature(s)", "text": "As granulosa cells increase in size and number, the follicles grow and become embedded deeper in the ovarian cortex. When the granulosa has reached a thickness of between 6 and 12 cell layers, fluid-filled spaces appear amongst the granulosa cells. This hyaluronan-rich fluid is called liquor folliculi and as it continues to accumulate, and the spaces coalesce, and a follicular antrum is formed. The follicle is then called a secondary follicle or antral follicle (Ross and Pawlina, 2006; Mescher, 2013)."}, {"name": "Function", "text": "Follicular fluid provides an important microenvironment for the developing oocyte."}, {"name": "References", "text": "Dorland, W. (2011) Dorland's Illustrated Medical Dictionary. 32nd edn. Philadelphia, USA: Elsevier Saunders.

Mescher, A. (2013) Junqueira's Basic Histology: Text and Atlas. 13th edn.: McGraw-Hill Education.

Ross, M. H. and Pawlina, W. (2006) Histology: A text and atlas. Lippincott Williams & Wilkins."}]

items.name: Blood Vessels of Tongue
items.info:
[{"name": "Quick Facts", "text": "The lingual artery provides the majority of blood supply to the tongue via its dorsal and deep lingual branches."}, {"name": "Description", "text": "The lingual artery provides the majority of blood supply to the tongue via its dorsal and deep lingual branches. 

The lingual artery is derived from the external carotid artery. It moves towards the bottom of the oral cavity, sharply meandering upwards and proceeding to the tip of the tongue, where it joins with its fellow lingual artery of the opposite side. Here they form a dense anastomosis to richly supply the surround musculature with blood. 

The dorsal lingual branch of the lingual artery supplies the posterior third of the tongue. They provide blood to the mucous membrane and surrounding structures of the oropharynx. These include the palatine tonsils, soft palate, epiglottis, and palatoglossal arches. This supply is consolidated by the formation of anastomosis among the dorsal lingual arteries. There is partial contribution to this by branches from the superior laryngeal anastomoses.

The deep lingual artery is the terminal branch of the lingual artery. At the anterior border of the hyoglossus muscle, it ascends between the inferior longitudinal muscle of the tongue laterally and the genioglossus muscle medially. It passes forwards in a tortuous manner near the lingual surface adjacent to the frenulum. Here it is accompanied by the lingual nerve.

Venous drainage occurs via the lingual vein and its tributaries. The lingual vein is formed by the joining of the dorsal and deep lingual veins. The dorsum and sides of the tongue are drained by dorsal lingual veins, while the tip of the tongue and deeper mass are drained by the deep lingual vein. The lingual vein travels between the hyoglossus and genioglossus muscles to link up to the internal jugular vein."}]

items.name: Lymphatic Capillary
items.info:
[{"name": "Quick Facts", "text": "A lymphatic capillary is one of the minute vessels of the lymphatic system, having a caliber greater than a blood capillary; they form closed networks (rete lymphocapillare) by which they communicate freely with one another (Dorland, 2011)."}, {"name": "Structure/Morphology", "text": "Almost half of the body's lymph is formed in the liver. Some of the plasma that passes from the highly fenestrated hepatic sinusoids towards the hepatocytes remains in the perisinusoidal space (of Disse).

Fluid in the perisinusoidal space drains into a small space, the periportal space (of Mall) located between the outermost hepatocytes and the perivascular fibrous capsule of the portal canal. The fluid is collected by lymphatic capillaries that travels with the components of the portal triad.

The lymphatic capillaries are highly permeable, blind-ended thin vessels, lined by a layer of lymphatic endothelial cells. They allow for passage of interstitial fluid and immune cells through it. They eventually consolidate into lymph collecting vessels, which are covered in smooth muscle cells and possess a basement membrane (Maby-El Hajjami and Petrova, 2008).

The lymph drains towards the porta hepatis of the liver where lymph enters hepatic lymph nodes. Lymph passes through the celiac nodes and eventually drains into the thoracic duct or cisterna chyli."}, {"name": "Anatomical Relations", "text": "The lymphatic capillaries accompany the components of the portal triad."}, {"name": "Function", "text": "The lymph capillaries drain lymph from the parenchyma of the liver. They have smooth muscle cells which contract to propel the lymph in the direction of the lymph nodes."}, {"name": "References", "text": "Dorland, W. (2011) Dorland's Illustrated Medical Dictionary. 32nd edn. Philadelphia, USA: Elsevier Saunders.

Maby-El Hajjami, H. and Petrova, T. V. (2008) 'Developmental and pathological lymphangiogenesis: from models to human disease', Histochemistry and Cell Biology, 130(6), pp. 1063-1078."}]

items.name: Interlobar Veins of Kidney
items.info: [{"name": "Structure and/or Key Features", "text": "Interlobar veins receive filtered blood from arcuate veins. They descend past the renal pyramids towards the hilum of the kidney, where they anastomose to form the renal vein."}, {"name": "Function", "text": "Interlobar veins are responsible for draining the renal lobes."}]

items.name: Axoneme (Principal Piece)
items.info:
[{"name": "Quick Facts", "text": "The axoneme is the central core of a cilium or flagellum, consisting of a central pair of microtubules surrounded by nine other microtubule pairs (Dorland, 2011)."}, {"name": "Structure and/or Key Feature(s)", "text": "The axoneme forms the core structure of the sperm tail. It is a cylindrical cytoskeletal structure that extends from the neck to the point where the tail terminates. 

The axoneme is composed of two centrally located microtubule singlets, which are encased by nine microtubule doublets. This is commonly referred to as the “9 + 2” complex. 

The major component proteins of the axoneme are cytoskeletal tubulin and the motor protein dynein. The microtubules are composed of dimers of α-tubulin and β-tubulin. Each of the microtubule doublets is made up of a complete α-microtubule, onto which a β-microtubule attaches. Two dynein arms extend from the α-microtubule to the β-microtubule of the neighboring doublet (Plant & Zeleznik, 2014)."}, {"name": "Anatomical Relations", "text": "The axoneme stretches across the entire length of the tail, from the neck region (just beneath the centriole) to the point where the tail terminates. The axoneme is the only structure present in the final 5–7 μm of the sperm tail (Standring, 2016).

The central pair of microtubules extend beyond the middle piece into the neck of the sperm, as far as the articular plate (capitulum). The outer doublets end just distal to the neck, where there is the remnants of the distal centriole (Plant & Zeleznik, 2014)."}, {"name": "Function", "text": "The axoneme acts as scaffold for the sperm tail, providing it with support and an ability to bend and unbend in various directions.

The motor dyneins associated with the microtubules of the axoneme have ATPase activity. Dyneins hydrolyze ATP and undergo a conformational change. They reach towards the minus end of the β-microtubule, resulting in the α- and β-microtubules in a doublet to slide past one another. The coordinated sliding in the doublets results in the propagation of a bending wave down the tail of the sperm, resulting in motility (Plant & Zeleznik, 2014).

The central pair of microtubules in the axoneme of the spermatozoon is involved in specific aspects of motility. The pair coordinates the sliding movements of the doublet microtubules, as well as taxis and reversal of the tail’s beating motion. These roles are essential for fertilization as evidence has shown that the absence of central pair form the spermatozoon tail results in the paralysis of the axoneme, and thus infertility (Linck et al, 2016)."}, {"name": "List of Clinical Correlates", "text": "- 9+0 syndrome"}, {"name": "References", "text": "Dorland, W. (2011) Dorland's Illustrated Medical Dictionary. 32nd edn. Philadelphia, USA: Elsevier Saunders.

Linck, R. W., Chemes, H. & Albertini, D. F. (2016) The axoneme: the propulsive engine of spermatozoa and cilia and associated ciliopathies leading to infertility. J Assist Reprod Genet, 33(2), 141-56.

Plant, T. M. & Zeleznik, A. J. (2014) Knobil and Neill's Physiology of Reproduction. Elsevier Science.

Standring, S. (2016) Gray's Anatomy: The Anatomical Basis of Clinical Practice. Gray's Anatomy Series 41st edition edn.: Elsevier Limited."}]

items.name: Omental Tenia
items.info:
[{"name": "Quick Facts", "text": "The omental tenia is the band of longitudinal muscle fibers of the large intestine along the site of attachment of the gastrocolic ligament of the greater omentum to the transverse colon (Dorland, 2011)."}, {"name": "Structure/Morphology", "text": "The omental tenia is one of three distinct bands of longitudinal smooth muscle that are collectively termed the teniae coli. These strips of longitudinal smooth muscle cells run along the large intestine and reside beneath its outer serosal surface."}, {"name": "Anatomical Relations", "text": "The three teniae coli are termed the mesocolic tenia, the free tenia, and the omental tenia. The free tenia is located opposite to the mesentery, the omental tenia is located on the posterolateral aspect of the colon, and the mesocolic tenia is located on the posteromedial aspect of the colon.

Due to the hepatic flexure at the junction of the transverse colon the teniae coli have a rotated position. Thus, the anterior free tenia becomes inferior, the posteromedial mesocolic tenia becomes posterior, and the posterolateral omental tenia becomes superior. 

Once they reach the sigmoid colon, the teniae expand to take up a greater portion of the circumference of the colon where they form distinct bands located anteriorly and posteriorly. Both of these bands eventually converge and unite to form a complete longitudinal muscle layer, a feature characteristic of the rectum."}, {"name": "Function", "text": "The longitudinal and circular layers of the muscular layer of the colon are responsible for producing peristaltic contractions of the gut, thus propelling the ingested substance through the lumen of the gut. Additionally, contraction of the teniae coli results in bulging of the colonic haustra, giving rise to the sacculation, which give the colon its segmented appearance."}, {"name": "References:", "text": "Dorland, W. (2011) Dorland's Illustrated Medical Dictionary. 32nd edn. Philadelphia, USA: Elsevier Saunders."}]

items.name: Lactiferous Sinuses (Superior Medial Quadrant; Left)
items.info: [{"name": "Structure/Morphology", "text": "The lactiferous sinus is an expansion of the terminal end of each lactiferous duct."}, {"name": "Function", "text": "The lactiferous sinus allows for milk secreted by the lobules of the mammary glands to be stored in the breast."}]

items.name: Nucleus
items.info:
[{"name": "Quick Facts", "text": "The nucleus is a spheroid body within a eukaryotic cell, separated from the cytoplasm by the nuclear envelope, and containing chromatin, a nucleolus, and nucleoplasm. In the nucleus, the cell's genetic information is stored on the chromosomes and RNA transcription and processing occur (Dorland, 2011)."}, {"name": "Structure and/or Key Feature(s)", "text": "The nucleus is usually a rounded or elongated centrally located structure. It generally measures 3–12 μm in diameter but can be much larger in some special cells. During the interphase part of the cell cycle, when the cell is not undergoing mitosis, the nucleus is bound by a nuclear envelope or a nuclear membrane. 

The normal cytoplasmic-nuclear ratio, i.e., the ratio between the volume of the cytoplasm and the nucleus, is usually about 3:1 or 2:1 in most eukaryotic cells. 

Most cells are mononucleated i.e., they only have one nucleus. However, the erythrocyte (or red blood cell) and the thrombocyte (or platelet), don't have a nucleus at all. Some cells may have two nuclei or they're binucleate. A skeletal muscle cell or fiber is multinucleated. 

In normal histological sections, a very dark-stained nucleolus sits in the nucleus. The dark-stained material within the nucleus is chromatin (Ross and Pawlina, 2006; Ovalle, Nahirney and Netter, 2013; McKinley, O'Loughlin and Pennefather-O'Brien, 2016)."}, {"name": "Anatomical Relations", "text": "In most cells, the nucleus is located in the central part of the cell. In some epithelial and secretory cells, due to the accumulation of secretory granules near the apical border of the cell, it becomes located toward the basal portion of the cell."}, {"name": "Function", "text": "The nucleus is the control center of the cell and houses the genome (genetic information) in eukaryotic cells. It enables DNA replication and synthesizes ribosomal (rRNA), messenger (mRNA), and transfer (tRNA). The nucleus does not synthesize proteins needed for some of its activities. These proteins are sequestered from the cytoplasm."}, {"name": "List of Clinical Correlates", "text": "Inherited genetic diseases would be initiated by the cell nucleus."}, {"name": "References", "text": "Dorland, W. (2011) Dorland's Illustrated Medical Dictionary. 32nd edn. Philadelphia, USA: Elsevier Saunders.

McKinley, M. P., O'Loughlin, V. D. and Pennefather-O'Brien, E. E. (2016) Human Anatomy. 5th edn.: McGraw-Hill Education.

Ovalle, W. K., Nahirney, P. C. and Netter, F. H. (2013) Netter's Essential Histology. ClinicalKey 2012: Elsevier Saunders.

Ross, M. H. and Pawlina, W. (2006) Histology: A text and atlas. Lippincott Williams & Wilkins."}]

items.name: Photoreceptor Cells
items.info:
[{"name": "Quick Facts", "text": "Photoreceptor cells are the neuroepithelial cells of the retina, the first neurons of the vertical linkage of the retina, consisting of two kinds of cells: the retinal cones and retinal rods. Each rod or cone has an inner axonal process synapsing with one or more horizontal or bipolar retinal cells, has a soma in the outer nuclear layer, and has a photosensitive outer dendritic process that extends toward the pigment epithelium (Dorland, 2011)."}, {"name": "Structure and/or Key Features", "text": "Photoreceptor cells are the cells that transduce physical energy, in this case electromagnetic radiation in the visible spectrum, to a voltage change that can be used as a signal by nerve cells. Photoreceptors are found in an array at the outer portion of the retina. There are two types of photoreceptor cells, the rod cells and cone cells. While both cell types are long and radially orientated they differ in external morphology, connections and function. 

The photoreceptor cells are composed of different regions that extend from the pigmented layer to the outer plexiform layer of the retina. These regions include the:

- outer segment;

- inner segment;

- soma (or cell body);

- axonal process;

- synaptic terminal.

The outer and inner segments are connected by a structure known as the connecting stalk or cilium, which acts as a conduit between the two segments. The inner segment of the photoreceptors is continuous with the soma, or the cell body of the cell. The soma houses the nucleus of the cell. 

From the soma, an axonal process extends toward the outer plexiform layer, where they terminate. Synaptic terminals of rod cells are in the form of lobular expansions called spherules. Spherules contain the presynaptic apparatus for chemical and/or electrical connections with bipolar cells, horizontal cells, and/or other rod cells (Standring, 2016; Kolb, 1995). The similar terminals of cone cells are called pedicles, which are larger and more “pyramidal” in shape but are also responsible for making synaptic connections with bipolar cells, horizontal cells, or other photoreceptor (rod and cone) cells. Both cone and rod synaptic terminals release glutamate (Standring, 2016; Kolb, 1995; Remington and Goodwin, 2011).

There are, on average, 92 million rods and 4.6 million cones in the human retina (Standring, 2016). Neither cell types are evenly distributed across the retinal surface. The foveola is completely free of rod cells but packed at high density with cones. Traveling outward, the density of rod cells increases reaching peak density at the optic disc, before declining again toward the periphery. Cone density remains high, though gradually decreases, in the foveal, perifoveal and macular regions but are relatively sparse in the periphery. Further, cone density is up to 40–45% higher in the nasal compared to the temporal retina (Standring, 2016)."}, {"name": "Anatomical Relations", "text": "Photoreceptor cell processes extend across four layers of the retina. Specifically, its inner and outer segments are located in the layer of inner and outer segments of the retina (also known as the layer of rods and cones). The cell then traverses the outer limiting membrane into the outer nuclear layer, where its cell body is located. Finally, the synaptic terminals of the cell are in the outer plexiform layer (Standring, 2016). There are no other cells except for photoreceptors in these layers, although the external processes of Müller glia pass between the synaptic terminals and cell bodies on their way to form the outer limiting membrane. The photoreceptor outer segment tips are surrounded by the microvilli of retinal pigment epithelium that can engulf and incorporate the used distal tips of photoreceptors for phagocytosis and disposal."}, {"name": "Function", "text": "Photoreceptor cells are responsible for the absorption and processing of electromagnetic radiation in the visible wavelength of the spectrum and converting it into an electrical signal. All rod cells are maximally sensitive to light of the same wavelength, so monochromatic. They are also sensitive to low light conditions, so-called scotopic. Cones in humans are maximally sensitive to one of three wavelengths (red, green, or blue) of the visible spectrum, so taken as a whole, the population of cones is trichromatic. They function best in bright light, which is called photopic. The high density of cones at the foveola and surrounding regions, plus the presence of more than one spectral cone type, makes cones well adapted for both high-resolution image processing and color vision.

Light is absorbed by visual pigments that are composed of a protein called opsin, bounded by a light-absorbing chromophore, called retinal (a form of vitamin A). Human photoreceptor cells can synthesize four types of opsins, thus generating four spectrally distinct visual pigments. The rods contain one spectrally distinct visual pigment, while the cones contain three spectrally distinct visual pigments.

Specifically, rod cells contain a visual pigment called rhodopsin (visual purple) that they synthesize. There are three cone cell populations that contain three spectrally distinct visual pigments:

- blue cones or short-wave cones;

- green cones or middle-wave cones;

- red cones or long-wave cones.

The visual pigments are embedded at high density in the membranous discs in the outer segment of the photoreceptor cells. 

Note that activation of photoreceptor cells in humans results in hyperpolarization, or inhibition, of that cell. Moreover, when photoreceptors are not activated, for example in a dark room, they remain in a depolarized state, thus constantly releasing the neurotransmitter glutamate, a phenomenon called dark discharge. This release of glutamate at the synaptic terminal hyperpolarizes the connecting bipolar and horizontal cells; therefore, these cells are not activated, and the bipolar-ganglion synapse remains unexcited. When photoreceptors become activated by light, they hyperpolarize and the release of glutamate at the rod synaptic terminal ceases. The consequence of this is the depolarization of the connecting bipolar and horizontal cells and the transmission of the visual signal (Standring, 2016; Molday and Moritz, 2015)."}, {"name": "List of Clinical Correlates", "text": "- Cone-rod dystrophy

- Retinal degeneration

- Retinitis pigmentosa"}, {"name": "References", "text": "Dorland, W. (2011) Dorland's Illustrated Medical Dictionary. 32nd edn. Philadelphia, USA: Elsevier Saunders.

Kolb, H. (1995) 'Photoreceptors', in Kolb, H., Fernandez, E. and Nelson, R. (eds.) Webvision: The Organization of the Retina and Visual System. Salt Lake City (UT): University of Utah Health Sciences Center. Copyright: (c) 2019 Webvision.

Molday, R. S. and Moritz, O. L. (2015) 'Photoreceptors at a glance', J Cell Sci, 128(22), pp. 4039-45.

Standring, S. (2016) Gray's Anatomy: The Anatomical Basis of Clinical Practice. Gray's Anatomy Series 41 edn.: Elsevier Limited."}]

items.name: Cytoplasm (Head; Right)
items.info:
[{"name": "Quick Facts", "text": "The cytoplasm is the protoplasm of a cell exclusive of that of the nucleus; it consists of a continuous aqueous solution (cytosol) and the organelles and inclusions suspended in it and is the site of most of the chemical activities of the cell (Dorland, 2011)."}, {"name": "Structure and/or Key Feature(s)", "text": "The cytoplasm of a cell includes an aqueous solution, the cytosol, and the organelles of the cell suspended in it. It is tightly enclosed by the plasma membrane. The sperm contains a limited amount of cytoplasm. During normal spermatogenesis (or maturation), spermatids lose most of their cytoplasm. Remnants may remain as a cytoplasmic droplet at the neck region of the sperm and is shed during ejaculation. However, retention of the droplets may indicate failure of normal maturation and cause infertility (Rengan et al, 2012).

The mature sperm retains a thin layer of cytoplasm underneath the plasma membrane. In the head, the space occupied by cytoplasm between the acrosome and the nucleus is known as the subacrosomal (or perinuclear) space. The cytoplasm between the outer membrane of the acrosome and the plasma membrane is the periacrosomal space."}, {"name": "Function", "text": "The cytoplasm is the site where most chemical activities of the cell occur."}, {"name": "References", "text": "Dorland, W. (2011) Dorland's Illustrated Medical Dictionary. 32nd edn. Philadelphia, USA: Elsevier Saunders.

Rengan, A. K., Agarwal, A., van der Linde, M. & du Plessis, S. S. (2012) An investigation of excess residual cytoplasm in human spermatozoa and its distinction from the cytoplasmic droplet. Reproductive biology and endocrinology : RB&E, 10, 92-92."}]

items.name: Nerves of the Eyelid
items.info: [{"name": "Structure and/or Key Feature(s)", "text": "The eyelids receive cutaneous innervation from the ophthalmic (upper eyelid) and maxillary (lower eyelid) divisions of the trigeminal nerve. Primary innervation of the upper eyelid is from the supraorbital branch of the frontal nerve. Further innervation is from the lacrimal nerve, the supratrochlear branch of the frontal nerve, and the infratrochlear branch of the nasociliary nerve. Nerve supply to the lower eyelid is primarily from the infraorbital branch of the maxillary nerve. Additional contributions are from the infratrochlear and the lacrimal nerves."}, {"name": "Function", "text": "To provide nerve supply to the eyelids and associated structures of the eyelids."}]

items.name: Cumulus Oophorus
items.info: [{"name": "Quick Facts", "text": "The cumulus oophorus is a solid mass of follicular cells surrounding the oocyte in the side of a developing tertiary ovarian follicle (Dorland, 2011)."}, {"name": "Structure and/or Key Feature(s)", "text": "The oocyte becomes embedded in a thickened region of granulosa epithelium called the cumulus oophorus, which projects into the fluid-filled antrum cavity. Cells of the cumulus oophorus that immediately surround the oocyte are released with it at ovulation. At this point it is called the corona radiata (Ross and Pawlina, 2006)."}, {"name": "References", "text": "Dorland, W. (2011) Dorland's Illustrated Medical Dictionary. 32nd edn. Philadelphia, USA: Elsevier Saunders.\n\nRoss, M. H. and Pawlina, W. (2006) Histology: A text and atlas. Lippincott Williams & Wilkins."}]

items.name: Zona Pellucida (Superior)
items.info:
[{"name": "Quick Facts", "text": "The zona pellucida is a thick, transparent, noncellular layer or envelope of uniform thickness surrounding an oocyte (Dorland, 2011)."}, {"name": "Structure", "text": "The zona pellucida is a 6-8 μm dense, acellular transparent membrane that encircles the oocyte (Harrison, Bonnar and Thompson, 2012). 

The zona pellucida is produced during folliculogenesis. The primary oocyte is located within the primordial follicle in the ovary. During the ovarian cycle, granulosa epithelial cells make intimate contact with the oocyte and deposit an acellular glycoprotein layer around the surface of the oocyte. As it increases in thickness, it forms the zona pellucida and remains present up until the end of the pre-implantation phase of pregnancy. The zona pellucida can only be penetrated by sperm, which must undergo an acrosomal reaction."}, {"name": "Key Features/Anatomical Relations", "text": "The zona pellucida is situated immediately internal to the corona radiata, to which it is adherent to, and external to the perivitelline space. The perivitelline space is an area that lies between the zona pellucida and the plasma membrane of the oocyte. The perivitelline space is the site where the contents of cortical granules were discharged following the fusion of the oocyte and the sperm (Plant and Zeleznik, 2014)."}, {"name": "Function", "text": "The zona pellucida plays a vital role in ensuring that the processes of fertilization and implantation occur efficiently. Glycoproteins present in the zona pellucida allow for sperm binding, acrosomal activation, and species-specific fertilization. The zona pellucida plays a vital role in preventing polyspermy during the sperm-oocyte fusion (Gupta et al., 2009)."}, {"name": "List of Clinical Correlates", "text": "- Infertility 

- Contraception

- Assisted reproductive technology"}, {"name": "References", "text": "Chiras, D. D. (2005) Human Biology. Jones and Bartlett Publishers.

DePamphilis, M. L. (2002) Gene Expression at the Beginning of Animal Development. Elsevier Science.

Dorland, W. (2011) Dorland's Illustrated Medical Dictionary. 32nd edn. Philadelphia, USA: Elsevier Saunders.

Gupta, S. K., Bansal, P., Ganguly, A., Bhandari, B. and Chakrabarti, K. (2009) 'Human zona pellucida glycoproteins: functional relevance during fertilization', J Reprod Immunol, 83(1-2), pp. 50-5.

Harrison, R. F., Bonnar, J. and Thompson, W. (2012) Fertility and Sterility: The Proceedings of the XIth World Congress on Fertility and Sterility, Dublin, June 1983, held under the Auspices of the International Federation of Fertility Societies. Springer Netherlands.

Plant, T. M. and Zeleznik, A. J. (2014) Knobil and Neill's Physiology of Reproduction. Elsevier Science.

Standring, S. (2016) Gray's Anatomy: The Anatomical Basis of Clinical Practice. Gray's Anatomy Series 41st edition: Elsevier Limited."}]

items.name: Intercalated Duct (Inferior)
items.info: [{"name": "Quick Facts", "text": "An intercalated duct is a slender initial portion of the duct systems of salivary glands and the pancreas, interposed between an acinus of a gland and a secretory duct (Dorland, 2011)."}, {"name": "Structure/Morphology", "text": "Centroacinar cells form the initial segment of the intercalated duct system. Intercalated ducts are short and drain to intralobular ducts."}, {"name": "Function", "text": "The intercalated duct adds water and bicarbonate to the pancreatic secretions which neutralizes the acidity of the chyme as it enters the duodenum from the stomach and ensures an optimal pH for the activities of the pancreatic enzymes that are secreted."}, {"name": "References", "text": "Dorland, W. (2011) Dorland's Illustrated Medical Dictionary. 32nd edn. Philadelphia, USA: Elsevier Saunders."}]

items.name: Outer Hair Cell
items.info:
[{"name": "Quick Facts", "text": "The outer hair cells are cylindrical auditory hair cells, arranged in three rows on the lateral side of the Corti tunnel, supported by outer phalangeal cells; they receive sound waves and transmit them to the inner hair cells for transformation into electrical impulses that the cochlear nerve can receive and transmit toward the auditory cortex of the brain (Dorland, 2011)."}, {"name": "Structure and/or Key Feature(s)", "text": "The hair cells of the cochlea are mechanosensory cells which are found on the superior aspect of the basilar membrane. There are two types, inner and outer hair cells, which possess common features. They are typically elongated cells that contain stereocilia on their apical pole and are associated with a synaptic complex at their basal pole. The inner and outer hair cells are also arranged in rows and the apices of the hair cells inclining in toward each other, at the same angle as the neighboring inner and outer pillar cells. The structural inclination of the hair cells is supported by the closely related supporting cells. These include the border cells and the phalangeal cells. The apices of the hair cells and the supporting cells are linked by tight junctions, adherens junctions, and desmosomes. This forms an impermeable barrier, called the reticular lamina, for the passage of ions. Endolymph (high potassium and low sodium concentrations) engulfs the apical surfaces of the hair cells and the supporting cells, while perilymph (high sodium and low potassium) bathes their lateral and basal aspects. This separation generates an electrochemical gradient along the lamina, forming an endocochlear potential which is necessary for the depolarization of hair cells (Standring, 2016). 

Some differences in the outer and inner hair cells structure separate the distinctive roles both cell types have is sound transduction. There are roughly 12,000 outer hair cells in the human cochlea, arranged in anywhere from three to five rows. The rows are positioned between the outer pillar cells and the columnar external supporting cells. Each outer hair cell has a lengthy, uniform cylindrical appearance throughout. However, the outer hair cells are much longer than the inner hair cells, reaching almost twice their length. One important feature is the variance in size of these outer hair cells which is correlated with their respective position within the cochlea. The outer row of the outer hair cells is the longest of the rows, as well as that hair cells in the apex of the cochlea are taller than hair cells in the base.

The outer hair cells also have a different arrangement than the single line of inner hair cells. Regarding the three rows of outer hair cells, the innermost and outermost rows run parallel to each other, while the middle row cells are positioned in a slightly oblique position. This is due to the alignment of the underlying phalangeal epithelial cells. Phalangeal processes from the phalangeal epithelial cells extend toward the apices of the outer hair cells, giving a chessboard type appearance when viewed from above. 

At the apical surface of each outer hair cell, fine wispy projections known as the stereocilia emerge. There are usually 100 stereocilia per outer hair cell. They are organized into three rows of graded height and the rows form a “V” or “W” pattern, depending on the region in the cochlea, with the longest stereocilia situated at the outer aspect of each apical surface. 

The bases of the outer hair cells do not rest on the basilar membrane, but rather sit in the cup-shaped apical surface of the external phalangeal epithelial cells, and so, are anchored to the basilar membrane via the bases of these supporting cells. 

At the base of each hair cell, there is a cluster of nerve fibers that form a synaptic complex. Unlike the inner hair cell, efferent nerve fibers directly synapse at the base of each outer hair cell. These terminations at the base of each outer hair cell are from efferent axons that originate from cells within the brain. In contrast to the inner hair cell nerve fibers, only a single efferent nerve fiber innervates multiple outer hair cells."}, {"name": "Anatomical Relations", "text": "The outer hair cells are located on the superior aspect of the basilar membrane and are the closer of the two hair cell types to the outer spiral sulcus. The apical aspects of the outer hair cells and the apical processes of the supporting cells form a mosaic-like structure known as the reticular lamina. The hair cells are inferior and closely related to the tectorial membrane; their projected stereocilia are embedded in a thickened ridge on the underside of the tectorial membrane.

The hair cells are arranged in three rows and have a variety of anatomical neighbors. The inner row of outer hair cells is positioned external to the outer pillar cells and the middle row is interjacent to the innermost and outermost row of the outer hair cells. The outer row is interjacent to the middle row of hair cells and the columnar external supporting cells, the latter of which have numerous rows leading to the outer spiral sulcus."}, {"name": "Function", "text": "The hair cells function to transduce the vibrations of the sound energy coming from the middle ear into the cochlea into nerve impulses. The hair cells are extremely sensitive and can detect the frequency and amplification of these sounds. 

Sound waves result in disruption of the surrounding cochlear fluid, which creates deflections of the stereocilia at their base from their original position, thus resulting in mechanotransduction. This is facilitated by the opening of the mechanotransduction cation channels, resulting in a graded depolarization due to ionic transfer between the surrounding endolymph. This information is carried through the afferent synapses and all the way to the auditory processing centers. 

Given the efferent supply to each outer hair cell, the nerve synapses provide an amplification ability. The outer hair cells can increase auditory sensitivity at specific frequencies by mechanically amplification of low-level sound that enters the cochlea by quickly oscillating in length. This results in a greater amplification of quiet sounds over louder sounds. This differs from the inner hair cell function, as they mainly provide information about the acoustic environment itself and relay it back to the auditory cortex (Goutman, Elgoyhen and Gómez-Casati, 2015)."}, {"name": "List of Clinical Correlates", "text": "—Sensorineural hearing loss"}, {"name": "References", "text": "Dorland, W. (2011) Dorland's Illustrated Medical Dictionary. 32nd edn. Philadelphia, USA: Elsevier Saunders.

Goutman, J. D., Elgoyhen, A. B. & Gómez-Casati, M. E. (2015) Cochlear hair cells: The sound-sensing machines. FEBS letters, 589(22), 3354-3361.

Standring, S. (2016) Gray's Anatomy: The Anatomical Basis of Clinical Practice., 41st edition. Elsevier Limited."}]

items.name: Superficial Epineurium
items.info:
[{"name": "Quick Facts", "text": "The epineurium is the outermost layer of connective tissue of a peripheral nerve, surrounding the entire nerve and containing its supplying blood vessels and lymphatics (Dorland, 2011)."}, {"name": "Structure/Morphology", "text": "The superficial (or external) epineurium is found encasing all fascicles of the nerve. It is about 60–100 nm thick. However thickness is related to the number of fasciculi present; the more fasciculi present the thicker the epineurium (Barral and Croibier, 2007). This structure contains fibroblasts, collagen fibers (types I and III), lymphocytes, and mast cells. The superficial epineurium also contains lymphatic vessels, vasa nervorum, and the nervi nervorum, which innervate the sheaths of nerve trunks (Standring, 2016)."}, {"name": "Anatomical Relations", "text": "The epineurium is formed of loose connective tissue. It is divided into the superficial and deep epineurium. The superficial epineurium can be observed surrounding the nerve trunk, which contains multiple fascicles. It can be traced backwards to spinal meninges where spinal dura mater merges with the external epineurium just when the spinal nerve exits the intervertebral foramen. The deep epineurium refers to the layer of epineurium which penetrates within the nerve and separates the fascicles from one another (Snell, 2011)."}, {"name": "Function", "text": "The superficial epineurium plays a role in protecting the internal nerve fiber it surrounds, cushioning it from damage e.g., during compression."}, {"name": "List of Clinical Correlates", "text": "—Pressure palsies in bedridden patients"}, {"name": "References", "text": "Barral, J. P. and Croibier, A. (2007) Manual Therapy for the Peripheral Nerves. Churchill Livingstone/Elsevier.

Dorland, W. (2011) Dorland's Illustrated Medical Dictionary. 32nd edn. Philadelphia, USA: Elsevier Saunders.

Snell, R. S. (2011) Clinical Anatomy by Regions. Lippincott Williams & Wilkins.

Standring, S. (2016) Gray's Anatomy: The Anatomical Basis of Clinical Practice. Gray's Anatomy Series: Elsevier Limited."}]

items.name: Epidermal Ridges
items.info:
[{"name": "Quick Facts", "text": "The epidermal ridges are the inward projections of the epidermis into the dermis at the dermal-epidermal junction, as seen histologically in vertical sections (Dorland, 2011)."}, {"name": "Structure/Morphology", "text": "The epidermis has many downward projections into the dermis, known as epidermal ridges. Likewise, the dermis has alternated upward projections between the epidermal ridges, the dermal papillae. 

Below the epidermal ridges lies the dermoepidermal junction. This is an acellular zone between the dermis and the epidermis. The adhesion of the epidermis to the dermis is maintained at this junction by the interaction of hemidesmosome junctions and keratin filaments of the epidermis, and collagen and anchoring fibrils of the dermis (Baroni et al., 2012)."}, {"name": "Function", "text": "This organization of epidermal ridges and dermal papillae at the dermoepidermal border increases the surface area of contact between the dermis and epidermis, thus strengthening the connection."}, {"name": "References", "text": "Baroni, A., Buommino, E., De Gregorio, V., Ruocco, E., Ruocco, V. and Wolf, R. (2012) 'Structure and function of the epidermis related to barrier properties', Clin Dermatol, 30(3), pp. 257-62.

Dorland, W. (2011) Dorland's Illustrated Medical Dictionary. 32nd edn. Philadelphia, USA: Elsevier Saunders."}]

items.name: Peripheral Membrane Protein
items.info:
[{"name": "Quick Facts", "text": "A membrane protein is a protein found in association with the cell membrane, either attached to (peripheral or extrinsic) or inserted in (integral or intrinsic) the membrane; possible roles include an enzyme, a receptor for a hormone or other molecule, and a mediator of active or passive transport of lipid-insoluble substances across the membrane (Dorland, 2011)."}, {"name": "Structure and/or Key Feature(s)", "text": "Protein molecules make up about 50% of total membrane mass (Ross and Pawlina, 2016). They are either integral membrane proteins or peripheral membrane proteins. Peripheral membrane proteins are not embedded in the lipid bilayer and have a looser association with the membrane surfaces (Lowe, Anderson and Anderson, 2018).

Peripheral membrane proteins do not interact with the hydrophobic core of the phospholipid bilayer but bind indirectly with integral membrane proteins or by direct interactions with the polar heads of the lipids (Lowe, Anderson and Anderson, 2018)."}, {"name": "Anatomical Relations", "text": "Peripheral membrane proteins are not embedded in the lipid bilayer and have a looser association with the membrane surfaces (Lowe, Anderson and Anderson, 2018)."}, {"name": "Function", "text": "Peripheral proteins on the extracellular surface of the membrane include some proteins of the extracellular matrix. Peripheral proteins on the cytosolic face of the cell membrane include the cytoskeletal proteins (Lowe, Anderson and Anderson, 2018)."}, {"name": "References", "text": "Dorland, W. (2011) Dorland's Illustrated Medical Dictionary. 32nd edn. Philadelphia, USA: Elsevier Saunders.

Lowe, J. S., Anderson, P. G. and Anderson, S. I. (2018) Stevens & Lowe's Human Histology- E-Book. 5 edn.: Elsevier Health Sciences.

Ross, M. H. and Pawlina, W. (2016) Histology: A Text and Atlas. Wolters Kluwer Health."}]

items.name: Capillaries (of Convoluted Seminiferous Tubules)
items.info:
[{"name": "Quick Facts", "text": "A capillary is any of the minute vessels that connect the arterioles and venules, forming a network in nearly all parts of the body. Their walls act as semipermeable membranes for the interchange of various substances, including fluids, between the blood and tissue fluid. The three principal types are continuous, discontinuous or sinusoidal, and fenestrated capillaries (Dorland, 2011)."}, {"name": "Structure/Morphology", "text": "Capillaries are blood vessels with the smallest diameter and are classified into three types. 

—Continuous capillaries have a continuous endothelial lining. 

—Discontinuous, or sinusoidal, capillaries have the largest diameter and have large openings and intercellular spaces with a discontinuous supporting basal lamina. 

—Fenestrated capillaries have a continuous supporting basal lamina but have numerous small openings or windows (i.e., fenestrae) in the capillary wall.

Many capillaries have undifferentiated mesenchymal cells close by called pericytes."}, {"name": "Anatomical Relations", "text": "Blood capillaries are located in the interstitial tissue compartment between seminiferous tubules."}, {"name": "Function", "text": "Capillaries act as semipermeable vessels, which allow for the exchange of various substances between the blood and tissue."}, {"name": "References", "text": "Dorland, W. (2011) Dorland's Illustrated Medical Dictionary. 32nd edn. Philadelphia, USA: Elsevier Saunders."}]

items.name: Tunica Albuginea of Corpora Cavernosa of Clitoris
items.audio: Tunica Albuginea of Corpora Cavernosa of Clitoris.mp3
items.info: [{"name": "Quick Facts", "text": "The tunica albuginea of corpora cavernosa of clitoris is the dense, white, fibroelastic sheath that encloses the corpora cavernosa clitoris. Its superficial, longitudinal fibers form a tunic surrounding both corpora, and the deep circularly coursing fibers surround them separately, uniting medially to form the septum of the clitoris (Dorland, 2011)."}, {"name": "Structure and/or Key Feature(s)", "text": "The tunica albuginea of the corpora cavernosa of the clitoris is a relatively thin fibroelastic connective tissue layer that surrounds the erectile tissue of the clitoris."}, {"name": "Anatomical Relations", "text": "A thin incomplete septum of fibrous connective tissue extends from the tunica albuginea, dividing this erectile tissue in the clitoris into two thin columns. Nerve fiber bundles are present superficial to the tunica albuginea, while blood vessels are present deep and superficial to the sheath. Unlike the penis, the rich venous plexus of the subalbugineal space is not present in the clitoris (Toesca, Stolfi and Cocchia, 1996)."}, {"name": "References", "text": "Dorland, W. (2011) Dorland's Illustrated Medical Dictionary. 32nd edn. Philadelphia, USA: Elsevier Saunders.\n\nToesca, A., Stolfi, V. M. and Cocchia, D. (1996) 'Immunohistochemical study of the corpora cavernosa of the human clitoris', Journal of anatomy, 188 (Pt 3), pp. 513-520."}]

items.name: Visceral Layer of Glomerular Capsule
items.info:
[{"name": "Quick Facts", "text": "The visceral layer is the layer of the glomerular capsule that faces inward toward the capillaries and is composed of podocytes; it is separated from the parietal layer by the urinary space (Dorland, 2011)."}, {"name": "Structure and/or Key Feature(s)", "text": "The visceral layer of the glomerular (Bowman’s) capsule contains specialized visceral epithelial cells called podocytes. Each podocyte extends primary cytoplasmic processes around glomerular capillaries. Each primary process extends numerous secondary processes, called foot processes, which interdigitate with those of a neighboring podocyte. 

Elongated spaces (around 40 nm wide), call filtration slits, extend between the interdigitating foot processes . They are covered by an ultra-thin filtration slit diaphragm (Ovalle, Nahirney and Netter, 2013; Ross and Pawlina, 2006).

The filtration slit diaphragm is a complex protein structure. A transmembrane protein, “nephrin,” is the key structural and functional component. Nephrin molecules emerge from foot processes and attach to the filtration slit forming a central density with pores on both sides. The filtration slit diaphragm contains other adhesion molecules, such as Neph-1 and -2, P-cadherin, and FAT1 and FAT2, and is anchored to numerous actin filaments in the foot processes of podocytes (Ross and Pawlina, 2006)."}, {"name": "Anatomical Relations", "text": "The visceral layer of the glomerular capsule contains specialized epithelial cells called podocytes. Each podocyte extends cytoplasmic processes and numerous secondary processes called pedicels or foot processes around glomerular capillaries."}, {"name": "Function", "text": "Podocytes or visceral epithelial cells are a major component of the filtration apparatus."}, {"name": "Clinical Correlates", "text": "Regulation and maintenance of the actin cytoskeleton of podocytes are critical for the functional integrity of the filtration slit diaphragm. Mutations in the nephrin gene (NPHS1) are associated with congenital nephrotic syndrome, a disease characterized by massive proteinuria and edema."}, {"name": "References", "text": "Dorland, W. (2011) Dorland's Illustrated Medical Dictionary. 32nd edn. Philadelphia, USA: Elsevier Saunders.

Ovalle, W. K., Nahirney, P. C. and Netter, F. H. (2013) Netter's Essential Histology. ClinicalKey 2012: Elsevier Saunders.

Ross, M. H. and Pawlina, W. (2006) Histology: A text and atlas. Lippincott Williams & Wilkins."}]

items.name: Origin of Long Head of Triceps Brachii Muscle
Taste Buds of Vallate Papillae
items.info:
[{"name": "Quick Facts", "text": "A taste bud is one of the minute, bud-shaped sensory organs of the tongue, situated around the bases of the vallate, fungiform, and foliate papillae. It contains several types of specialized epithelial cells, including taste receptor, supporting, and basal cells, and is innervated by gustatory nerve fibers (Dorland, 2011)."}, {"name": "Structure and/or Key Feature(s)", "text": "Taste buds are located all over the tongue, but predominantly within the gustatory lingual papillae. The taste buds are not distributed equally and have different populations among the gustatory lingual papillae. 

The taste buds are most abundant towards the posterior parts of the tongue and the vallate papillae, on average, contain 250 buds each (Standring, 2016). The taste buds of the vallate papillae are located in the lateral walls of the papillae."}, {"name": "Function", "text": "The sensation of taste is mediated by the taste buds.
